  Content: No specific agreed ultrasound diagnostic criteria exist (D). With an empty uterus, suggestive transvaginal findings include a broad echogenic ring enclosing an anechoic area on the ovary; a yolk sac or embryo is less often seen. Unlike a separate adnexal lesion, the structure or sac cannot be moved off the ovary by gentle palpation, yielding a negative sliding-organ sign. Identify the corpus luteum separately. Colour Doppler can help reveal a fetal heartbeat within the ovary. A complex echogenic adnexal lesion with pouch-of-Douglas fluid can indicate rupture (Evidence level 3). Organic amenorrhea (WHO IV) includes genital malformations such as Meier–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome and hymenal atresia, often first identified because of primary amenorrhea or dysmenorrhea. Reported incidences of the various causes differ so greatly by study and population that no general statement can be made. Absent follicular maturation can prevent adequate estrogenization and endometrial thickening, so bleeding does not occur. In the short term, estrogen deficiency can prevent pubertal onset and secondary sexual development; in the long term, it can impair bone, cognitive, and cardiovascular health. Girls with hypo- or hypergonadotropic hypogonadism consequently need treatment to induce puberty and sustain adequate estrogenization.

  Content: Interpret proteinuria alongside a complete clinical assessment of symptoms, signs and other findings relevant to pre-eclampsia. In secondary care, use an automated reagent-strip reader for initial dipstick screening; a result of 1+ or more should be quantified with an albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio.   Name: Gestational hypertension
  Description: Hypertension first appearing after 20 weeks of pregnancy without significant proteinuria.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Full assessment in secondary care
      Purpose: Evaluate gestational hypertension and factors requiring closer assessment and follow-up.
      When indicated: At presentation, by a healthcare professional trained in managing hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
      Interpretation: Factors requiring additional assessment and follow-up include nulliparity, age 40 years or older, pregnancy interval of more than 10 years, family history of pre-eclampsia, multi-fetal pregnancy, BMI of 35 kg/m2 or more, gestational age at presentation, previous pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension, and pre-existing vascular or kidney disease.
    - Test: Blood pressure measurement
      Purpose: Assess severity and response to treatment.
      When indicated: For hypertension, once or twice a week depending on blood pressure until it is 135/85 mmHg or less; for severe hypertension, every 15 to 30 minutes until it is less than 160/110 mmHg.
      Interpretation: Once antihypertensive treatment is given, the target is 135/85 mmHg or less.
    - Test: Dipstick proteinuria testing
      Purpose: Monitor for proteinuria.
      When indicated: Once or twice a week alongside blood pressure measurement for hypertension; daily during admission for severe hypertension.
      Interpretation: A result of 1+ or more prompts quantification with albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio.
    - Test: Full blood count, liver function and renal function
      Purpose: Monitor maternal haematological, liver and kidney status.
      When indicated: At presentation and then weekly.
    - Test: Placental growth factor (PLGF)-based testing
      Purpose: Help rule out pre-eclampsia.
      When indicated: On 1 occasion if pre-eclampsia is suspected, between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days of pregnancy.
    - Test: Fetal heart auscultation
      Purpose: Assess fetal heart activity.
      When indicated: At every antenatal appointment.
    - Test: Ultrasound for fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume assessment
      Purpose: Assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume.
      When indicated: At diagnosis; if findings are normal, repeat every 2 to 4 weeks if clinically indicated. If severe hypertension persists, repeat every 2 weeks.
    - Test: Umbilical artery doppler velocimetry
      Purpose: Assess the fetal circulation.
      When indicated: At diagnosis; if findings are normal, repeat every 2 to 4 weeks if clinically indicated. In severe gestational hypertension, subsequent monitoring is determined by scan findings.
    - Test: Cardiotocography (CTG)
      Purpose: Assess fetal status.
      When indicated: For gestational hypertension, only if clinically indicated; for severe gestational hypertension, at diagnosis and subsequently if clinically indicated.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: After birth, offer women still receiving antihypertensive treatment a medical review 2 weeks after transfer to community care. Offer all women a medical review 6 to 8 weeks after birth.
    Recommended tests:
      - Measure blood pressure daily for the first 2 days after birth and at least once between day 3 and day 5.
      - Measure blood pressure as clinically indicated if antihypertensive treatment changes after birth.
    Long term effects:
      - After gestational hypertension in a previous or current pregnancy, hypertension of any type in a future pregnancy occurs in approximately 22% (1 in 5 women), pre-eclampsia in approximately 7% (1 in 14 women), gestational hypertension in between approximately 11% and 15% (up to 1 in 7 women), and chronic hypertension in approximately 3% (up to 1 in 34 women).

Document sections:
  Heading: Examination of the Stillborn Fetus
  Content: Examine the fetus promptly for dysmorphic findings and measure weight, length, and head circumference (1C Strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). Before 23 weeks, foot length may be especially helpful for estimating gestational age. Whole-body photographs without clothing, frontal and profile facial images, extremity and palm images, and close-ups of anomalies support later specialist review, particularly where a geneticist is unavailable. Offer fetal autopsy because it is among the most informative tests for cause of death (1A Strong recommendation, high-quality evidence); its yield is greater with dysmorphism, discordant growth measurements, anomalies, hydrops, or growth restriction. When families decline complete autopsy, options include partial autopsy, trained-pathologist gross examination, ultrasonography, and especially magnetic resonance imaging. Parents should have an opportunity to hold their baby and observe cultural or religious practices before autopsy. Wholebody X-ray in anterior–posterior and lateral views can reveal or clarify skeletal abnormalities. A full autopsy should follow published perinatal protocols, including measurements such as foot length and body weight to estimate gestational age, an estimate of time from death to delivery, investigation of developmental and intrinsic abnormalities, and evaluation for infection. Preferably, an experienced perinatal pathologist performs it and a clinician experienced in genetics and dysmorphology examines the fetus. The obstetric and relevant medical history and requests for additional tissue collection should be conveyed to pathology.

Main conclusion: The authors regard hormonal treatment as the initial approach to adenomyosis and reserve radiological or conservative surgical options for cases in which medical treatment fails. Because uterus-preserving surgery is technically demanding, particularly with concomitant endometriosis, they conclude that experienced surgeons in dedicated centers should perform it.

Narrative summary: This narrative review examines medical, radiological and uterus-preserving surgical approaches to adenomyosis, emphasizing symptom control, uterine volume and treatment choice. The authors place hormonal therapy first during reproductive life; radiological procedures and conservative surgery are considered when medication fails. UAE is associated with a reported 50% reduction in uterine volume at 12 months after treatment. For HIFU, cited follow-up data report complete symptom relief in 68% of treated women at 2 years, although treatment response varies with the form of adenomyosis.

Among surgical options, adenomyomectomy addresses focal disease, while cytoreductive techniques can address focal or diffuse disease. The review reports improvement in pelvic pain and AUB of >70% at 12 months after conservative surgery and an estimated 3.1-fold reduction in uterine volume; it does not establish that one conservative procedure is superior. Osada et al. reported uterine rupture during pregnancy in 5% of patients after adenomyomectomy. RFA has produced uterine volume reductions ranging from 41% to 57% across cited studies, but evidence concerning fertility and pregnancy remains inconclusive. Hysteroscopic treatment is discussed for lesions close to the endometrium. The authors stress individualized planning, careful uterine reconstruction and specialist surgical experience, especially when endometriosis requires concurrent treatment.

Main conclusion: Menstrual irregularity during the first 2 years after menarche is often physiological, but associated anemia or dysmenorrhea warrants treatment or investigation. Identifying pathological causes without prematurely labeling adolescents, and coordinating care across specialties, may improve quality of life and help prevent serious health problems.

Narrative summary: This review examined the causes, diagnosis, and treatment of menstrual disorders in adolescence. The authors searched PubMed in April 2024, screened 1724 abstracts, assessed 115 full texts, and included 71 articles in a narrative analysis; they also consulted relevant ESHRE and awmf guidance. In the first 2 years after menarche, irregular cycles commonly reflect anovulation and immaturity of the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis rather than disease. Disabling heavy bleeding, anemia, or pain are exceptions that require attention. The review distinguishes this physiological pattern from conditions including bleeding disorders, amenorrhea, hypogonadism, premature ovarian insufficiency, hyperandrogenemia, endometriosis, and genital malformations. Assessment is guided by symptoms and developmental stage and may include history, examination, abdominal sonography, and selected laboratory or other investigations. Treatment depends on the cause: options discussed include hormonal management of heavy bleeding, correction of anemia, restoration of adequate estrogenization in hypogonadism, and appropriate management of suspected endometriosis or obstructive malformations. The authors caution against diagnosing PCOS prematurely in adolescence and favor individualized monitoring when features indicate increased risk. They emphasize collaboration among primary care, pediatric, gynecological, and hematological clinicians, particularly when adolescents fall between pediatric and adult services. Remaining knowledge gaps include blood-test reference ranges, drug doses, and alternative treatments.

Vaginal pH, normally 4.5, often rises to >5 during infection, although infection can occur with a normal pH. Colpitis macularis, also called “strawberry cervix,” is observed in about 5% of women during pelvic examination and nearly 50% during colposcopy. Reported complications in women include Skene and Bartholin gland infection and, among women with HIV, increased pelvic inflammatory disease risk. In men, infection can cause urethritis, epididymitis, prostatitis, and reduced sperm motility.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 6.5.2.1. Lesiones del plexo braquial
  Content: Afectan al 8-23% de los casos de distocia de hombros; el daño permanente después de una distocia se estima en tan solo 1,6%. Según la clasificación de Seldon, en gravedad creciente, la neuroapraxia corresponde a estiramiento o contusión leve con desmielinización focal, sin interrupción axonal y con epineuro, perineuro y endoneuro intactos; su pronóstico es muy favorable y se espera recuperación completa en los dos primeros meses. En la axonotmesis se interrumpen los axones, pero el epineuro permanece íntegro; es una lesión incompleta más grave, con recuperación impredecible y pronóstico peor que la neuroapraxia. La neurotmesis supone arrancamiento o sección completa, incluida la interrupción del epineuro, con formación de un neuroma proximal y un glioma distal; tiene el pronóstico más desfavorable y la recuperación siempre es incompleta y limitada aun con el mejor tratamiento. La avulsión separa la raíz de la médula espinal; es una lesión preganglionar devastadora con escaso potencial de recuperación sin cirugía. Anatómicamente, la parálisis del plexo ALTA o de Erb-Duchenne es la más frecuente (60%), afecta C5, C6 y a veces C7, y produce aducción del brazo, rotación interna del hombro, extensión y rotación del codo, flexión de muñeca y extensión de dedos, con postura «Waiter´s tip». La parálisis del plexo BAJA o de Klumpke afecta C8 y T1; representa menos del 2% de las parálisis braquiales obstétricas y se caracteriza por ausencia de agarre manual con musculatura proximal conservada. La parálisis braquial total de Kerer afecta de C5 a C8 y a veces T1; es la segunda más frecuente, la de mayor gravedad y peor pronóstico, produce mano en garra y brazo flácido e insensible, y suele asociarse a partos instrumentales. La lesión derecha es más frecuente, en relación con la posición fetal habitualmente occipitoiliaca izquierda anterior. El documento cifra la recuperación espontánea completa de la mayoría en «7095%» durante los primeros «34 meses» de vida; estas cifras aparecen sin separación clara entre sus extremos. La localización y gravedad condicionan el pronóstico: las lesiones altas suelen ser menos graves; las lesiones totales o bajas, las avulsiones radiculares importantes y la asociación con síndrome de Horner o fracturas indican peor pronóstico.

Document sections:
  Heading: 6.8.3 Investigations
  Content: History and assessment should seek the cause; despite an extensive differential diagnosis, most cases reflect infection or inflammation. Initial history should address the symptom and systemic health and establish whether blood truly originates in semen. Apparent haemospermia can instead reflect haematuria or a partner's blood entering the urethra during intercourse. Sexual history should assess STI risk; travel to areas affected by schistosomiasis or tuberculosis and possible hypertension, liver disease, coagulopathy, weight loss, appetite loss or bone pain should also be considered. Examination should include blood pressure because case reports suggest an association with uncontrolled hypertension. Authors broadly agree on initial investigations but have not reached consensus. Urinalysis, urine microscopy, culture and sensitivity testing are advised. If tuberculosis or schistosomiasis is suspected, semen or prostatic secretions should be analysed. A full STI screen using first-void urine, serum and genitourinary samples should test for Chlamydia, Ureaplasma and Herpes Simplex virus; this may identify infection in cases otherwise called idiopathic. Appropriately counselled men aged > 40 years should have serum PSA measured. Full blood count, liver function and clotting tests can help identify systemic disease. Decisions about further tests depend on clinical judgement, age and risk factors. Digital rectal examination is advised, with re-examination of the meatus afterwards for bloody discharge. A palpable prostatic nodule matters because an association of haemospermia with PCa has been proposed but not fully established. MRI is increasingly used to investigate haemospermia and can show structural changes in the prostate, seminal vesicles, vas-deferens ampulla and ejaculatory ducts, particularly the origin of midline or paramedian prostatic cysts and information needed for surgical planning. An endorectal coil can improve accuracy in locating and explaining bleeding. Cystoscopy is included in many proposed protocols for higher-risk patients with persistent haemospermia unresponsive to conservative treatment; direct inspection can reveal polyps, urethritis, prostatic cysts, foreign bodies, calcifications or vascular abnormalities. Small-diameter ureteroscopes permit examination of ejaculatory ducts and seminal vesicles. In a prospective study of 106 patients with prolonged haemospermia, transrectal US plus seminal vesiculoscopy established a diagnosis in 87.7%; diagnostic yields were 45.3% for TRUS and 74.5% for seminal vesiculoscopy (P < 0.001). Melanospermia due to genitourinary malignant melanoma is rare and has been reported in two case reports; semen chromatography can detect melanin when distinction is needed.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_04
  Name: Pre-eclampsia
  Description: New hypertension, over 140 mmHg systolic or over 90 mmHg diastolic, after 20 weeks of pregnancy together with 1 or more newly occurring findings: proteinuria, maternal organ dysfunction or uteroplacental dysfunction.
  Epidemiology: The guideline states that less than 1 woman in every million who gives birth now dies from pre-eclampsia.
  Clinical presentation: Possible symptoms include severe headache, blurred vision or flashing before the eyes, severe pain below the ribs, vomiting, and sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet. Maternal organ dysfunction may affect the kidneys, liver, nervous system or blood. Uteroplacental findings may include fetal growth restriction, abnormal umbilical artery doppler waveform analysis or stillbirth.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Severe pre-eclampsia
      Distinguishing features: Pre-eclampsia with severe hypertension unresponsive to treatment or accompanied by specified persistent symptoms, worsening blood results, impaired fetal growth or abnormal doppler findings.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Full clinical assessment
      Purpose: Evaluate maternal and fetal wellbeing and determine whether hospital surveillance is needed.
      When indicated: At every antenatal appointment, by a healthcare professional trained in managing hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
      Interpretation: Concerning findings include sustained systolic blood pressure of 160 mmHg or higher; a new, persistent rise in creatinine to 90 micromol/litre or more, 1 mg/100 ml or more; a rise in alanine transaminase to over 70 IU/litre, or twice upper limit of normal range; a fall in platelet count to under 150,000/microlitre; impending eclampsia or pulmonary oedema; other severe features; or suspected fetal compromise.
    - Test: Automated reagent-strip reading device for dipstick proteinuria screening
      Purpose: Screen for urinary protein in secondary care.
      When indicated: During assessment of a pregnant woman for proteinuria.
      Interpretation: A screening result of 1+ or more calls for quantification with albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio. For the definition of pre-eclampsia, dipstick proteinuria is at least 1 g/litre [2+].
    - Test: Urine protein:creatinine ratio
      Purpose: Quantify proteinuria.
      When indicated: After a positive dipstick result of 1+ or more; a first morning urine void should not be used for quantification.
      Interpretation: 30 mg/mmol or more indicates significant proteinuria. If the result is 30 mg/mmol or above and diagnosis remains uncertain, consider testing a new sample alongside clinical review.
    - Test: Urine albumin:creatinine ratio
      Purpose: Provide an alternative measure of proteinuria when diagnosing pre-eclampsia in a pregnant woman with hypertension.
      When indicated: After a positive dipstick result of 1+ or more; a first morning urine void should not be used for quantification.
      Interpretation: The diagnostic threshold is 8 mg/mmol. If the result is 8 mg/mmol or above and diagnosis remains uncertain, consider testing a new sample alongside clinical review.
    - Test: 24-hour urine collection
      Purpose: Quantify proteinuria.
      When indicated: Not for routine use; the guideline notes that it may be more appropriate on rare occasions, such as in women with renal complications.
    - Test: Placental growth factor (PLGF)-based testing
      Purpose: Help rule out pre-eclampsia.
      When indicated: For suspected pre-eclampsia between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days of pregnancy.
    - Test: Serum creatinine
      Purpose: Assess renal involvement and monitor maternal condition.
      When indicated: During assessment and subsequent blood-test monitoring.
      Interpretation: Creatinine of 90 micromol/litre or more, 1.02 mg/100 ml or more, is a renal-insufficiency criterion in the definition of pre-eclampsia.
    - Test: Liver transaminases
      Purpose: Assess liver involvement and monitor maternal condition.
      When indicated: During assessment and subsequent blood-test monitoring.
      Interpretation: Alanine aminotransferase or aspartate aminotransferase over 40 IU/litre is a liver-involvement criterion in the definition of pre-eclampsia.
    - Test: Platelet count
      Purpose: Assess haematological involvement and monitor maternal condition.
      When indicated: During assessment and subsequent blood-test monitoring.
      Interpretation: A count below 150,000/microlitre is a thrombocytopenia criterion in the definition of pre-eclampsia.
    - Test: Full blood count, liver function and renal function
      Purpose: Monitor maternal haematological, liver and kidney status.
      When indicated: Twice a week with hypertension or 3 times a week with severe hypertension.
    - Test: Fetal heart auscultation
      Purpose: Assess fetal heart activity.
      When indicated: At every antenatal appointment.
    - Test: Ultrasound for fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume assessment
      Purpose: Assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume.
      When indicated: At diagnosis and, if normal, every 2 weeks.
    - Test: Umbilical artery doppler velocimetry
      Purpose: Assess the fetal circulation and uteroplacental dysfunction.
      When indicated: At diagnosis if conservative management is planned; repeat fetal growth, amniotic fluid or umbilical artery doppler assessment every 2 weeks according to findings.
      Interpretation: An abnormal umbilical artery doppler waveform may indicate uteroplacental dysfunction.
    - Test: Cardiotocography (CTG)
      Purpose: Assess fetal status.
      When indicated: At diagnosis; subsequently if clinically indicated, including a change in fetal movement, vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain or deterioration in maternal condition.
  Prognostic tools:
    - Name: fullPIERS
      Interpretation: May help guide place-of-care and intervention decisions at any time during pregnancy by predicting adverse maternal outcomes; it does not predict outcomes for babies.
    - Name: PREP-S
      Interpretation: May help guide place-of-care and intervention decisions only up to 34 weeks of pregnancy by predicting adverse maternal outcomes; it does not predict outcomes for babies.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: After transfer to community care, offer a review at 2 weeks to women who remain on antihypertensive treatment. Offer all women a medical review 6 to 8 weeks after birth. Persistent proteinuria of 1+ or more at that review calls for a further kidney-function review at 3 months.
    Recommended tests:
      - For women who received no antihypertensive treatment, measure blood pressure at least 4 times a day while admitted, at least once between day 3 and day 5 after birth, and on alternate days until normal if it was abnormal on days 3 to 5.
      - For women who received antihypertensive treatment, measure blood pressure at least 4 times a day while admitted and every 1 to 2 days for up to 2 weeks after transfer to community care, until treatment has stopped and hypertension has resolved.
      - Ask about severe headache and epigastric pain whenever blood pressure is measured after birth.
      - For mild or moderate hypertension, or after step-down from critical care, measure platelet count, transaminases and serum creatinine 48 to 72 hours after birth or step-down; do not repeat normal measurements at that time. Repeat abnormal results as clinically indicated until normal.
      - Perform a urinary reagent-strip test 6 to 8 weeks after birth; assess kidney function at 3 months if proteinuria remains 1+ or more.
    Long term effects:
      - After pre-eclampsia in a previous or current pregnancy, hypertension of any type in a future pregnancy occurs in approximately 20% (1 in 5 women), and pre-eclampsia in up to approximately 16% (1 in 6 women). If birth was at 28 to 34 weeks, the reported recurrence of pre-eclampsia is approximately 33% (1 in 3 women); if birth was at 34 to 37 weeks, it is approximately 23% (1 in 4 women).
      - No evidence was identified for recurrence after birth at less than 28 weeks; the committee considered the risk likely to be at least as high as, if not higher than, after birth between 28 and 34 weeks.
      - After pre-eclampsia in a previous or current pregnancy, the table reports future gestational hypertension in between approximately 6 and 12% (up to 1 in 8 women) and chronic hypertension in approximately 2% (up to 1 in 50 women).
      - For women with pre-eclampsia in a current or previous pregnancy, the table reports an approximately 1.5 to 3 times increased risk of a major adverse cardiovascular event, an approximately 2 times increased risk of cardiovascular mortality, an approximately 2 to 3 times increased risk of stroke, and an approximately 2 to 5 times increased risk of later hypertension.
    Survivorship notes: If neither proteinuria nor hypertension is present at the postnatal review at 6 to 8 weeks, the guideline states that the relative risk of end-stage kidney disease remains increased but its absolute risk is low, and no further follow-up is necessary. Consider specialist kidney assessment if kidney function is abnormal at 3 months. Women are advised to reach and maintain a BMI of 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m2 before a subsequent pregnancy; recurrence becomes more likely when the inter-pregnancy interval exceeds 10 years.

Main conclusion: Los autores concluyen que la suplementación durante el embarazo debe ajustarse al riesgo, al estado nutricional y a las circunstancias que afectan la adherencia de cada mujer. Consideran posible que futuras recomendaciones amplíen el uso sistemático de suplementos múltiples, especialmente en países de ingresos bajos y medios, pero señalan que aún hacen falta datos sobre dosis, factibilidad y seguridad.

Narrative summary: Esta revisión reúne evidencia y recomendaciones sobre hierro, ácido fólico, calcio, vitamina D y suplementación múltiple durante el embarazo. Los autores presentan la suplementación con hierro y ácido fólico como la estrategia aceptada para todas las embarazadas. Para prevenir defectos del tubo neural, la OMS recomienda 400 mcg/d de ácido fólico desde antes del embarazo y durante la gestación; una revisión Cochrane citada comunicó RR: 0.31; IC 95%:0.170.58. La OMS recomienda 30-60 mg/d de hierro elemental, con preferencia por 60 mg/d donde la anemia gestacional supera > 40%. Si el hierro diario no puede utilizarse por efectos secundarios y la prevalencia de anemia es < 20%, contempla 120 mg de hierro elemental más 2.8 mg de ácido fólico una vez a la semana.

Para prevenir preeclampsia, la OMS recomienda 1.5 a 2.0 g/d de calcio en contextos de bajo consumo, particularmente ante alto riesgo hipertensivo. En cambio, no recomienda vitamina D de forma habitual para mejorar resultados maternos o perinatales, aunque el artículo recoge evidencia posterior y recomendaciones específicas para mujeres con deficiencia. La suplementación múltiple exige individualización: una revisión Cochrane citada halló menos bajo peso al nacer frente a hierro con o sin ácido fólico (RR: 0.88; IC 95%: 0.85-0.91), sin diferencias en mortalidad perinatal (RR: 1.00; IC 95%: 0.90-1.11). Los autores subrayan que las decisiones deben considerar deficiencias, riesgo perinatal y adherencia, mientras se aclaran dosis y seguridad.

Document sections:
  Heading: Diagnóstico de la vulvovaginitis candidiásica recurrente
  Content: La mayoría de las pacientes con síntomas de vaginitis pueden diagnosticarse en consulta mediante pH vaginal y examen microscópico en fresco. El pH se mide aplicando una tira en la pared lateral vaginal. Habitualmente es de 4,0 a 4,5, aunque con niveles bajos de estrógenos puede considerarse normal un valor más próximo a 7. Un pH superior a 4,7 indica vaginosis bacteriana, tricomoniasis o infección mixta y descarta VVC; un valor inferior a 4,5 es compatible con candidiasis. La microscopía del exudado permite diagnosticar aproximadamente el 50% de los casos. Se recomiendan 2 muestras: una para examen en fresco y otra para el test de aminas. Observar micelios o hifas permite diagnosticar infección por cándidas; las «clue cells» indican infección bacteriana y la presencia de tricomonas descarta infección por cándidas. Para el test de aminas se añade KOH al 10% a la segunda muestra. Al facilitar la observación microscópica de hifas de C. albicans o de esporas agrupadas de Candida glabrata, el KOH aumenta la sensibilidad (6585%). El olor a pescado tras añadirlo indica vaginosis bacteriana y descarta VVC. Numerosos polimorfonucleares sugieren infección mixta. En VVC simple puede omitirse el cultivo si síntomas, exploración, pH y microscopía concuerdan con candidiasis. En cambio, ante clínica recurrente siempre debe cultivarse, con independencia de las demás pruebas. El cultivo de exudado vaginal tiene sensibilidad elevada y permite valorar cantidad de colonias, cepa y sensibilidad terapéutica. Es especialmente importante ante especies no-albicans, como C. glabrata, C. tropicalis y C. krusei, o levaduras de otros géneros, como Saccharomyces, por su posible resistencia a azoles. El diagnóstico diferencial incluye vaginosis bacteriana recurrente, tricomoniasis no detectada, herpes genital recurrente, dermatitis y dermatosis, vaginitis atrófica, citolítica o descamativa inflamatoria, liquen, manifestaciones vulvares de enfermedades del colágeno y leucorrea fisiológica. La tabla diagnóstica compara exudado, pH, microscopía, test de aminas, cultivo y otros signos de distintas entidades; una figura presenta el algoritmo diagnóstico.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: abnormal uterine bleeding
  Synonyms:
    - AUB
  Description: Nongestational bleeding arising from the uterine corpus is characterized using FIGO AUB System 1 before potential causes are assessed with FIGO AUB System 2. More than one condition may contribute to a patient's bleeding, and a structural finding may be incidental.
  Epidemiology: Reported prevalence among women of reproductive age is approximately 3%–30%, with higher estimates in adolescents and women in the fifth decade of life and some variation by country. Approximately one third of women are affected at some point. Estimates reach 35% or higher when irregular and intermenstrual bleeding are included alongside heavy menstrual bleeding. Available evidence suggests that as many as half of affected women do not seek care.
  Clinical presentation: Bleeding may differ in duration, volume, frequency or regularity. Its effects range from modest to severe impairment of work productivity and quality of life; pre-existing AUB-related anemia is associated with increased maternal morbidity and mortality during pregnancy.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: chronic nongestational AUB
      Distinguishing features: Bleeding from the uterine corpus that differs from normal in duration, volume, frequency and/or regularity for the majority of the preceding 6 months.
    - Name: acute AUB
      Distinguishing features: An episode of heavy bleeding judged by the clinician to require immediate intervention to limit further blood loss; it may occur with or without preceding chronic AUB.
    - Name: heavy menstrual bleeding
      Distinguishing features: HMB is a symptom rather than a diagnosis. In clinical use, it denotes menstrual blood loss that interferes with physical, social, emotional and/or material quality of life.
    - Name: intermenstrual bleeding
      Distinguishing features: Bleeding arising spontaneously between menstrual periods, either cyclically or at random.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: History and physical examination
      Purpose: Characterize bleeding with FIGO AUB System 1, assess possible contributors and distinguish uterine bleeding from bleeding elsewhere in the genital, urinary or gastrointestinal tract.
      When indicated: Initial assessment of suspected AUB.
      Interpretation: A detected abnormality should be assessed for whether it actually contributes to the symptoms.
    - Test: Urine or serum assay for the β-subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
      Purpose: Determine whether bleeding is pregnancy-related.
      When indicated: Assessment of reproductive-age women with suspected acute or chronic AUB.
      Interpretation: Determining pregnancy location or viability lies outside the FIGO AUB systems.
    - Test: Examination of the bleeding source
      Purpose: Establish whether bleeding comes through the cervical canal rather than from the vagina, vulva, perineum or perianal region.
      When indicated: Initial assessment of suspected AUB.
    - Test: Serum ferritin
      Purpose: Assess iron deficiency.
      When indicated: Acute or chronic AUB, if testing is possible.
    - Test: Hemoglobin and/or hematocrit, preferably a full blood count including platelets
      Purpose: Assess associated anemia.

  Heading: 6.10. Endometriosis
  Content: Dysmenorrhea means painful menstruation. Primary dysmenorrhea occurs without a specific pathological condition; secondary dysmenorrhea occurs with a reproductive-system disorder causing menstrual cramps, such as endometriosis or fibroids. Endometriosis affects approximately 2% of adolescent women. It is an estrogen-dependent inflammatory condition involving functional endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity. Refractory pain, noncyclic lower abdominal pain, dysmenorrhea, dysuria, dyschezia, or dyspareunia makes it a likely diagnosis; increased absence from school or sport can also be a clue. Pain often accompanies nausea, vomiting, dyschezia, constipation, or vasovagal reactions. Definitive confirmation requires histology, but medication is first-line treatment. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for pain and hormonal treatment with progestogens or an extended-use contraceptive pill (off-label use) can be used to limit disease progression until childbearing is desired. GnRH analogs warrant great caution in adolescents because of adverse skeletal effects and long-term osteoporosis risk. Persistent symptoms may justify surgery, which should be performed at a highly experienced center to preserve ovarian reserve. Diagnosis appears delayed and treatment often inadequate in both adolescents and adults. Possible reasons include low ultrasonographic detection and reluctance to operate on adolescents. Clinical findings can nevertheless justify treatment without histological confirmation, and girls benefit from such treatment.

Document sections:
  Heading: 2. Ovarian Cysts 2.1. Fetuses
  Content: Fetal ovarian cysts are the most frequent abdominal cysts in female fetuses, occurring at 1:2500 and generally identified in the third trimester. They are usually functional or benign; increased fetal gonadotropins, maternal estrogens, and placental human chorionic gonadotropins are implicated. Cysts < 20 mm in diameter are considered physiological maturing follicles, whereas those > 20 mm are abnormal. Simple cysts are round, anechoic, unilocular, and thin-walled; complex cysts have thick walls, mixed echogenicity, fluid-debris levels, or internal septations. Identifying the organ of origin and surrounding anatomy helps distinguish these lesions from simple renal cysts, multicystic dysplastic kidneys, hydronephrosis, urachal cysts, hydrocolpos, enteric duplication cysts, meconium pseudocysts, choledochal cysts, lymphatic malformations, and cystic sacrococcygeal teratoma. MRI may be useful with maternal obesity, fetal malposition, or oligohydramnios. A daughter cyst is a small anechoic round structure within the main cyst and is a characteristic ultrasound finding. Usual ultrasound diagnostic criteria are female sex, a regular cystic structure away from the midline, and urinary and gastrointestinal tracts of normal appearance. Perinatal care prioritizes monitoring growth and changes to avoid torsion, ovarian necrosis, and compression of abdominal organs. Optimal treatment remains disputed: percutaneous aspiration has been suggested particularly for diameter ≥40 mm or growth ≥10 mm per week, while expectant care has also been advocated because spontaneous resolution is possible, especially for simple cysts. A fetal cyst should not change delivery timing or method because torsion risk, onset, and duration cannot be predicted.

  Content: Adenomyosis is a benign uterine condition involving endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium. TVS is currently the first-line imaging approach. A cited meta-analysis using hysterectomy histopathology as the reference standard reported sensitivity and specificity of 78% each. The same source reported that 3D TVS may improve diagnostic accuracy by showing junctional-zone alterations in more detail than 2D ultrasound. No imaging-based system for diagnosis or severity classification has yet gained uniform acceptance or validation. The international MUSA group published sonographic terminology in 2015 and proposed a consistent approach to classification and reporting of disease morphology and extent in 2019. A cited pilot study found poor agreement between raters using MUSA features, whether their experience was high or moderate. Another study found good agreement between an expert and a trained non-expert for 2D-TVS images but poor agreement for 3D-TVS images. Unclear feature definitions may contribute to this variability. Main conclusion: Early recognition and treatment of ectopic pregnancy are essential to reduce the risk of rupture and severe hemorrhage. Management should reflect hemodynamic stability, implantation site, diagnostic findings, and the patient’s fertility goals, with urgent surgery when rupture is suspected.

Narrative summary: This educational review examines the presentation, diagnosis, and management of ectopic pregnancy rather than reporting a new clinical study. Ectopic pregnancy affects approximately 1% to 2% of pregnancies in the United States and accounts for 2.7% of pregnancy-related deaths. Approximately 97% occur in the fallopian tube. Lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding are common, while dizziness, fainting, shoulder pain, or severe pelvic pain may indicate rupture.

Evaluation combines serum β-hCG measurements with ultrasound, particularly TVUS. A β-hCG level >2000 mIU/mL without a visible intrauterine pregnancy is highly suggestive of ectopic pregnancy; the review also notes a suggested discriminatory cutoff of up to 3500 mIU/mL to avoid misdiagnosing a viable pregnancy. When pregnancy location remains uncertain, serial β-hCG measurements and repeat imaging may be needed.

Hemodynamic instability or suspected rupture requires urgent surgical intervention. For selected asymptomatic patients with low, declining β-hCG, expectant management may be considered; 88% of ectopic pregnancies with an initial β-hCG level of <200 mIU/mL resolved spontaneously. In appropriate candidates, methotrexate is a medical option, with reported success of approximately 70% to 95%; β-hCG monitoring continues until the level is undetectable. Surgical options include salpingostomy and salpingectomy. For cesarean scar ectopic pregnancy, expectant management is not recommended except in select cases of confirmed fetal demise, and systemic methotrexate alone is not recommended.

Document sections:
  Heading: 6.2. Amenorrhea
  Content: Amenorrhea can have hormonal or organic causes and may be primary or secondary. Primary amenorrhea denotes no menarche by age 16; secondary amenorrhea means no menstruation for more than 90 days after previous periods. Pregnancy should be excluded before further investigation, and a previously regular cycle that becomes irregular warrants assessment. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (WHO I) occurs with pubertas tarda and is largely constitutional without pathological significance, although gonadal, hypothalamic, pituitary, or genetic disorders—including Sheehan syndrome and Kallmann syndrome—can cause it. Common adolescent causes of hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction (WHO II) are a high-risk constellation for polycystic ovary syndrome and central dysregulation associated with stress, anorexia, or competitive sport. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (WHO III), or premature ovarian insufficiency, involves loss of ovarian activity before age 40 years and affects approximately 1:10,000 patients under age 20. Potential causes are Turner syndrome, a Fragile X premutation, autoimmune predisposition, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or ovarian surgery. Organic amenorrhea (WHO IV) includes genital malformations such as Meier–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome and hymenal atresia, often first identified because of primary amenorrhea or dysmenorrhea. Reported incidences of the various causes differ so greatly by study and population that no general statement can be made. Absent follicular maturation can prevent adequate estrogenization and endometrial thickening, so bleeding does not occur. In the short term, estrogen deficiency can prevent pubertal onset and secondary sexual development; in the long term, it can impair bone, cognitive, and cardiovascular health. Girls with hypo- or hypergonadotropic hypogonadism consequently need treatment to induce puberty and sustain adequate estrogenization.

Document sections:
  Heading: Letrozole
  Content: The aromatase p450 enzyme is abnormally expressed in uterine endometrium and ectopic implants, and high endometrial expression is associated with poorer IVF outcomes. Combining an aromatase inhibitor with gonadotropins during stimulation might improve endometrial receptivity and FSH-related follicular response while reducing gonadotropin requirements. A retrospective study of 47 women with endometriosis who were negative for endometrial integrins reported higher clinical pregnancy and delivery with added letrozole than without it: 11/18 (61%) vs 4/29 (14%), and 9/18 (50%) vs 2/29 (7%), respectively. A cohort of 64 women found similar oocyte and embryo yields with or without added letrozole but did not examine pregnancy. Evidence is insufficient to recommend letrozole cotreatment with gonadotropins.

Document sections:
  Heading: 5.2 What are the surgical, pharmacological or conservative treatment options for cervical pregnancy?
  Content: Consider methotrexate (D); reserve surgical approaches, which have high failure rates, for life-threatening bleeding (D). Early accurate diagnosis is central to conservative care. Gestation less than 12+0 weeks, absent fetal cardiac activity and lower serum b-hCG are associated with greater conservative-treatment success (Evidence level 2–). Described treatments include dilatation and curettage, systemic methotrexate and local potassium chloride or methotrexate injection. A retrospective review of 62 cases estimated approximately 91% efficacy for systemic methotrexate, but protocols varied and successful cases also needed surgical debulking or local methotrexate. Gestation more than 9+0 weeks, b-hCG greater than 10 000 iu/l, crown–rump length greater than 10 mm and fetal cardiac activity increased primary systemic-treatment failure risk; intra-amniotic combination treatment seemed to improve success in that review (Evidence level 2–). Haemorrhage-control adjuncts include uterine artery ligation and uterine artery embolisation (UAE). Small case series describe success when combined with intracervical or systemic methotrexate, but report infection, uterine infarction, sciatic-nerve injury, and bladder or rectal necrosis. Traditionally, dilatation and curettage required bleeding-control measures; because excessive bleeding requiring hysterectomy was frequent, restrict it to women for whom alternatives are unsuitable (Evidence level 3). A small series of five women treated by hysteroscopic resection and UAE reported no need for transfusion or additional techniques, but UAE has complications and long-term follow-up was unavailable.

Document sections:
  Heading: ABSTRACT
  Content: Cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT) accounts for 0.5% to 3% of strokes. Young people, women of reproductive age, and people with prothrombotic states are particularly vulnerable. Symptoms vary and include headache and seizures, so diagnosis requires substantial clinical suspicion. Diagnosis relies chiefly on magnetic resonance imaging with magnetic resonance venography or computed tomography with computed tomographic venography. The course can be unpredictable; despite intensive medical care, 10% to 15% of patients die or become dependent. This statement updates the 2011 American Heart Association statement, concentrating on diagnostic advances and decisions about anticoagulation, endovascular treatment, and craniectomy. It also presents an approach to management when neurological status worsens or a thrombus extends despite maximal medical treatment.

Document sections:
  Heading: B A C K G R O U N D Description of the condition
  Content: HMB, also termed menorrhagia, is a common gynaecological problem that harms health and quality of life and uses substantial healthcare resources. In the UK, one in 20 women aged 30 to 49 years consult a doctor for HMB each year (NICE 2018); a European study found symptoms during the preceding 12 months in 27% of women of reproductive age (Fraser 2014). Research has often defined HMB as MBL of 80 mL or more per period without pregnancy or a known pelvic or systemic disease, but this volume is difficult to quantify clinically. Women usually judge bleeding to be unacceptable when its quantity or frequency disrupts physical or psychosocial well-being; that judgment commonly drives treatment and assessment of its effect. The International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) defined HMB from the woman's perspective of increased menstrual volume, irrespective of cycle regularity, frequency, or duration (Munro 2011). Studies have commonly measured blood loss with alkaline haematin; the pictorial blood loss assessment chart (PBAC) provides a simpler method based on scores assigned to used sanitary products. Total menstrual fluid loss (TMFL), determined from the change in pad or tampon weight, has also been proposed: it correlates with changes in objectively measured MBL and may matter particularly to women concerned about flooding. Although surgery has traditionally been prominent, 80% of surgically treated women have no anatomical pathology, and over a third of hysterectomies for excessive bleeding remove a normal uterus (Clarke 1995; Gath 1982). Medical therapy can therefore avoid potentially unnecessary surgery and preserve fertility.

  Heading: Clinical Presentation of T. vaginalis
  Content: Most infected women (85%) and men (77%) have no symptoms. Half of initially asymptomatic women may develop symptoms within 6 months. Symptomatic women may have vaginal erythema, dyspareunia, dysuria, genital pruritus, and discharge that is often widespread, malodorous, and yellow-green. Vaginal pH, normally 4.5, often rises to >5 during infection, although infection can occur with a normal pH. Colpitis macularis, also called “strawberry cervix,” is observed in about 5% of women during pelvic examination and nearly 50% during colposcopy. Document sections:
  Heading: Fetal Laboratory Studies
  Content: After appropriate parental permission, genetic analysis should be performed for every stillbirth because of its diagnostic yield (1A Strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). Karyotype and microarray yield more information with dysmorphism, inconsistent growth measures, anomalies, hydrops, or growth restriction. Comparative genomic hybridization or single nucleotide probe and copy number probe microarrays provide almost the same information as karyotype while detecting smaller chromosomal abnormalities; single nucleotide probe arrays also identify uniparental disomy and consanguinity. Fetal karyotyping matters if a parent carries a balanced rearrangement, such as translocation or inversion, or has mosaicism. Suitable samples include amniotic fluid, a placental block beneath cord insertion incorporating the chorionic plate, cord tissue, and internal fetal tissue able to grow at low oxygen tension, such as costochondral or patellar tissue. Fetal skin is suboptimal. Amniocentesis for karyotyping has the greatest yield, particularly if delivery is not imminent. Laboratory requests should provide relevant history and examination findings for cytogenetic interpretation (Best practice). Because costs can affect parental decisions, anticipated genetic-testing costs should be communicated when possible.

Document sections:
  Heading: Anemia in Pregnancy
  Content: Normal physiologic changes of pregnancy can complicate recognition of hematologic disease. During a singleton gestation, plasma volume increases by 40–50% and erythrocyte mass by 15–25%, increasing iron requirements. Because plasma generally expands more than erythrocyte mass, hemoglobin and hematocrit usually decline. Total body iron reflects intake, losses, and storage; women have approximately 2.3 g. Pregnancy requires additional iron stores of approximately 1 g to support expanded erythrocyte mass, the fetus and placenta, and blood loss expected with vaginal delivery. With adequate iron availability, more than 70% of body iron is functional and the rest is stored. More than 80% of functional iron is in erythrocyte hemoglobin; myoglobin and respiratory enzymes contain the remainder.

A PCOS task force described 7 phenotypes (A to G) using hyperandrogenism, hirsutism, oligo-anovulation, and polycystic ovaries. The most common, phenotype A or the classic phenotype, has all 4 features: hyperandrogenism, hirsutism, oligo/anovulation, and polycystic ovaries. Phenotypes tend to improve with age, alongside reduced hyperandrogenism and increased FSH.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: STATEMENT TWENTY-FIVE
  Content: Obtain UA and urine culture when signs or symptoms suggest UTI in NLUTD (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Five observational studies informed the recommendation; risk of bias was very serious, and evidence about symptom-based prediction was further downgraded for inconsistency. Altered sensation, neurological diagnosis and severity, and bladder-management method can change the presentation. Possible findings include fever, new incontinence or catheter leakage, increased spasticity, malaise, lethargy, cloudy or malodorous urine, back or bladder pain, dysuria, and AD; MS patients may also show apparent relapse. No symptom set alone has adequate sensitivity and specificity across NLUTD. Culture supports organism-directed treatment. In Linsenmayer and Oakley's series of 147 consecutive SCI patients (101 male; 106 at T6 or higher), UTI required new clinical findings, >104 CFU/mL and >10 WBC/hpf. Symptoms predicted UTI in 61% (n=90), but not in 39% (n=57); bladder-management method did not affect this ability. In Massa et al.'s study of 51 SCI patients (34 male, 26 at T6 or higher), negative self-assessment had a predictive value of 82.8%, compared with 32.6% for positive or uncertain self-assessment. Urinary leukocytes had sensitivity of 82.8% and negative predictive value of 93.8%; cloudy urine had positive predictive value of 61.3% and sensitivity of 65.5%. Fever and AD had specificity of 99% but sensitivity of 6.9% and 0%, respectively. Alavinia et al. found the greatest sensitivity with malodorous urine and the greatest specificity with new incontinence; cloudy urine had positive predictive value of 71%, rising to 78% when accompanied by malodor. Applicability of that study of 55 subacute inpatients with SCI to all NLUTD patients is uncertain. Ronco et al. examined 381 symptomatic episodes in 209 men with SCI and 277 asymptomatic episodes in 205 men. No individual finding established UTI. Among symptomatic episodes, cloudy and/or malodorous urine occurred in 51.4%, new UI in 51.2%, fatigue in 41.7%, and fever in 30.7%. Those findings did not correlate with higher colony counts or urinary WBC when symptomatic and asymptomatic episodes were compared; the authors speculated that fever could have other infectious causes. AD and other nonspecific symptoms also have non-UTI causes. An earlier consensus used >102 CFU/mL for CIC and >104 CFU/mL for condom catheters. IDSA 2010 CAUTI criteria require compatible symptoms, no other identified infectious source, and >103 CFU/mL; IDSA does not use pyuria alone to decide antibiotic treatment, while absent pyuria should prompt consideration of another cause. In one rehabilitation-center review of 93 SCI patients, multidrug resistance affected 48% of strains from asymptomatic bacteriuria and 66.6% from symptomatic UTI. Weekly cultures in 52 SCI patients changed in an average of 60% of those with indwelling catheters and 36% using CIC. Clark and Welk found 55.8% organism concordance among 81 patients with at least two positive cultures; concordance fell significantly with each 30-day interval (p=0.02). Susceptibility concordance was ciprofloxacin: 77.3%; nitrofurantoin: 78.5%; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: 75% and did not decline with time. Previous cultures can inform empirical selection while a new UA and culture are pending.

Document sections:
  Heading: 7. Conclusions
  Content: Conservative medical, radiological and surgical treatments can relieve AUB and pelvic pain and reduce uterine volume. Hormonal medication is considered the primary approach during reproductive life; radiological or conservative surgical treatment is considered when medication fails. Conservative operations are technically complex, and open surgery may sometimes be preferable because finger palpation helps identify the boundary between adenomyosis and healthy myometrium. Published findings suggest that surgical, early postoperative and pregnancy complications, including hematomas, suture anastomotic leakage and adhesions, do not appear particularly frequent after either laparoscopy or laparotomy. Temporary uterine-artery occlusion or ligation and intramyometrial vasopressin or oxytocin injection have been proposed to reduce intraoperative blood loss and may be options in some cases. Reported complication rates may be underestimated because the procedures come mainly from highly experienced centers with limited bleeding, reliable suturing and reduced bowel and urinary injury. Coexisting pelvic endometriosis, especially DE, and uterine myomas often require concurrent multidisciplinary care. Some authors question whether outcomes from expert centers apply to general gynecological practice and caution surgeons with limited experience against reproducing these complex procedures. The authors conclude that experienced surgeons in dedicated centers should perform conservative adenomyosis surgery, particularly for laparoscopy or concomitant endometriosis. For selected premenopausal women with symptomatic focal disease resistant to hormonal treatment, RFA or hysteroscopy may offer alternatives.

Document sections:
  Heading: Treatment
  Content: Timely recognition and a short interval between initial manifestations and definitive surgery are essential. Once rupture is diagnosed, immediate maternal stabilization and fetal delivery are imperative. After frank rupture, the interval before major fetal morbidity is generally only 10-37 minutes; when rupture is suspected, available resources should be mobilized rapidly for definitive surgical care. After delivery, maternal surgery is guided by rupture type and extent, bleeding severity, maternal condition, and wishes about future childbearing. Longitudinal tears generally bleed more heavily than transverse tears. Uterine repair as conservative surgical treatment should be reserved for women desiring future childbearing who have a low transverse rupture without extension into the broad ligament, cervix, or paracolpos; readily controlled bleeding; good general condition; and no clinical or laboratory evidence of developing coagulopathy. Hysterectomy should be considered the preferred treatment for uncontrollable uterine hemorrhage or multiple, longitudinal, or low-lying rupture sites. Clinicians should maintain strong suspicion, especially in high-risk patients, and act rapidly and decisively when uncertain.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 6.10. Endometriosis
  Content: Dysmenorrhea means painful menstruation. Primary dysmenorrhea occurs without a specific pathological condition; secondary dysmenorrhea occurs with a reproductive-system disorder causing menstrual cramps, such as endometriosis or fibroids. Endometriosis affects approximately 2% of adolescent women. It is an estrogen-dependent inflammatory condition involving functional endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity. Refractory pain, noncyclic lower abdominal pain, dysmenorrhea, dysuria, dyschezia, or dyspareunia makes it a likely diagnosis; increased absence from school or sport can also be a clue. Pain often accompanies nausea, vomiting, dyschezia, constipation, or vasovagal reactions. Definitive confirmation requires histology, but medication is first-line treatment. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for pain and hormonal treatment with progestogens or an extended-use contraceptive pill (off-label use) can be used to limit disease progression until childbearing is desired. GnRH analogs warrant great caution in adolescents because of adverse skeletal effects and long-term osteoporosis risk. Persistent symptoms may justify surgery, which should be performed at a highly experienced center to preserve ovarian reserve. Diagnosis appears delayed and treatment often inadequate in both adolescents and adults. Possible reasons include low ultrasonographic detection and reluctance to operate on adolescents. Clinical findings can nevertheless justify treatment without histological confirmation, and girls benefit from such treatment.

Irregularity is defined as < 21 or > 45 days at 1 to < 3 years post menarche; < 21 or > 35 days, or < 8 cycles per year, from 3 years post menarche to perimenopause; or any cycle > 90 days from 1 year post menarche. Primary amenorrhea by age 15 or > 3 years post thelarche also meets the stated definition.
    - Test: History and physical examination for clinical hyperandrogenism
      Purpose: Identify clinical signs and assess their onset and progression.
      When indicated: When assessing possible PCOS or marked or worsening hyperandrogenism.
      Interpretation: Severe acne and hirsutism are pertinent adolescent signs. New severe or worsening symptoms warrant investigation for androgen-secreting tumors and ovarian hyperthecosis. A rapid course is particularly relevant when assessing for an androgen-secreting tumor.
    - Test: Total and free testosterone
      Purpose: Assess biochemical hyperandrogenism.
      When indicated: When biochemical assessment is needed for PCOS diagnosis.
      Interpretation: Free testosterone may be estimated with the calculated free androgen index. Validated tandem mass spectrometry is preferred for total testosterone; free testosterone should be assessed by calculation, equilibrium dialysis, or ammonium sulfate precipitation. Direct immunoassays have limited diagnostic accuracy. A cited meta-analysis found sensitivity of 80.3% for calculated free testosterone and 80.2% for the free androgen index, with specificity of 93.3% and 86.4%, respectively.
    - Test: Androstenedione and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate
      Purpose: Provide additional assessment of biochemical hyperandrogenism.
      When indicated: May be considered if testosterone or free testosterone is not elevated.
      Interpretation: These measures have poorer specificity; the greater age-related decrease in dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate applies only to adult women. Validated tandem mass spectrometry should be used if measurement is needed.
    - Test: Biochemical androgen assessment during COCP use
      Purpose: Assess androgen levels when measurement is essential despite current COCP use.
      When indicated: Only if biochemical androgen assessment is imperative in someone taking COCP.
      Interpretation: COCP makes reliable assessment difficult. The document advises withdrawing it for a minimum of three months and arranging other contraception during that period.
    - Test: modified Ferriman Gallwey (mFG) score
      Purpose: Assess hirsutism using a standardized visual measure.
      When indicated: When evaluating clinical hyperandrogenism.
      Interpretation: A score of ≥ 4–6 indicates hirsutism. Cosmetic self-treatment can obscure examination findings; only terminal hairs count toward hirsutism assessment.
    - Test: Ludwig or Olsen visual scales
      Purpose: Assess female pattern hair loss.
      When indicated: When this finding is suspected; it is rare in adolescents.
    - Test: Serum progesterone
      Purpose: Confirm anovulation.
      When indicated: If confirmation is needed despite apparently regular cycles.
      Interpretation: Ovarian dysfunction remains possible with regular cycles.
    - Test: Evaluation for other causes of hyperandrogenemia
      Purpose: Exclude disorders that can resemble PCOS.
      When indicated: Particularly when androgen levels markedly exceed laboratory reference ranges or symptoms develop rapidly.
      Interpretation: The differential includes ovarian and adrenal neoplastic growths, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing’s syndrome, iatrogenic causes, and syndromes of severe insulin resistance; ovarian hyperthecosis is specified after menopause. Some androgen-secreting neoplasms produce only mild to moderate androgen elevations.
    - Test: Pelvic ultrasonography for polycystic ovarian morphology
      Purpose: Assess whether ovarian morphology can contribute to diagnosis.
      When indicated: Not recommended for diagnosing PCOS during adolescence.
      Interpretation: Definitive adolescent ultrasound criteria are unavailable. Assessment for diagnostic purposes may become appropriate at approximately 8 years postmenarche.
    - Test: AMH
      Purpose: Assess whether this marker can contribute to diagnosis.
      When indicated: Should not yet be used to diagnose adolescents.
      Interpretation: Its potential diagnostic use is discussed for approximately 8 years postmenarche, rather than during adolescence.
    - Test: Glycemic assessment
      Purpose: Identify glucose abnormalities.
      When indicated: At diagnosis in all adolescents with PCOS, with regular assessment thereafter.
      Interpretation: The guideline does not specify a preferred dysglycemia test for adolescents because evidence is lacking.
    - Test: Regionally validated depression screening tools
      Purpose: Detect depressive symptoms or depression.
      When indicated: In all adolescents with PCOS; repeat screening according to clinical judgment, life changes, and risk factors.
      Interpretation: A cited meta-analysis reported up to a four-fold higher prevalence of depression in adolescents with PCOS than in those without PCOS.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Longitudinal care should continue through a planned transition to adult services; the document does not set a fixed visit interval.
    Recommended tests:
      - Regular glycemic assessment
      - Repeat depression screening according to clinical judgment, life changes, and risk factors
      - Monitoring of hirsutism, acne, and female pattern hair loss during treatment
    Long term effects:
      - Increased risk of impaired fasting glucose, impaired glucose tolerance, and type 2 diabetes
      - Depressive symptoms and depression
      - Obesity, dysglycemia, dyslipidemia, depression, and subfertility may progress during prolonged gaps in care
    Survivorship notes: The recommended lifelong health plan includes age-appropriate reproductive education, healthy lifestyles, prevention of excess weight gain, assessment of long-term metabolic risks, and preparation for adult care.

  Content: Assessment should account for a family history of PCOS or metabolic syndrome and possible fetal androgen exposure. Document sections:
  Heading: History and Physical
  Content: Patients may have no symptoms; when symptoms occur, abnormal uterine bleeding is the most common. Abdominal pain, pelvic pain, and infertility may also occur. One in four reproductive-aged women with abnormal bleeding has an endometrial polyp in the cavity. Evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding should establish its cause and severity, associated symptoms, and comorbidities. A thorough medical and surgical history helps exclude other causes. No bleeding pattern is diagnostic of a polyp, but the bleeding history should be characterized; menorrhagia and intermenstrual spotting are reported most often. Tamoxifen, commonly used for breast cancer, can act as an agonist or antagonist in tissues bearing estrogen receptors. It has anticancer effects in breast tissue but carcinogenic effects in endometrial tissue. Chronic tamoxifen use is associated with endometrial polyps at an incidence of 20% to 35%. Hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms may also be associated with polyp formation, irregular bleeding, and ultrasound evidence of endometrial thickening. Clinical examination should include a general assessment, bimanual examination, and sterile speculum examination. The cervix and vaginal vault should be examined completely to exclude other structural explanations for symptoms. A pedunculated polyp may be visible at the external os.

Document sections:
  Heading: 4.2. Fallopian Tube Torsion
  Content: Fallopian tube torsion is isolated rotation of the tube without ovarian torsion, either along its middle segment or around its supporting ligaments. Pain can be acute or chronic, generalized or nonspecific, and may accompany nausea and vomiting. Missed torsion can destroy tubal function and lead to hydrosalpinx, necrosis, or resorption. Potential contributors include hydrosalpinx, segmental tubal agenesis with proximal hydrosalpinx, broad ligament or paratubal cysts, neoplasms, ectopic pregnancy, congenital anomalies, ovarian masses, infection, abnormal peristalsis or spasm, and external lesions such as adhesions. Imaging may show a dilated tube, an adjacent normal ovary, or a cystic mass separate from the ovary. Diagnosis is generally made during surgical exploration. Detorsion can prevent irreversible ischemic damage and loss of the tube.

Document sections:
  Heading: 6. Conclusions and future directions
  Content: Mental, physical, and social factors have been associated with DED symptoms and signs and with other ocular surface diseases. Most associations come from cross-sectional studies; longitudinal work should address confounding and DED’s multifactorial nature. Mechanistic and animal studies may help examine these relationships. Across populations, depression, anxiety, and stress relate more consistently to DED symptoms than signs, but mechanisms and optimal treatment of coexisting psychological disorders remain unclear. Sleep quality and duration are strongly associated with DED symptoms; whether this persists after accounting for psychosocial disorders requires study. Obesity has been linked to meibomian gland and eyelid abnormalities, potentially influenced by sleep apnea. Face-mask wear has emerged as a DED risk factor, particularly for evaporative DED and meibomian gland dysfunction. Sexual and reproductive issues have been linked to DED, but mechanisms and preventive or therapeutic approaches need investigation. Chronic pain conditions, particularly migraine, chronic pain syndrome, and fibromyalgia, commonly coexist with DED; the literature chiefly concerns symptoms, and heterogeneity calls for research into signs, aqueous deficient versus evaporative subtypes, and standardized pain measurement. Recreational-drug ocular effects depend on the substance and delivery route; evidence is often limited to case reports and series rather than case-control studies.

  Content: Evidence guiding surveillance after unexplained stillbirth is limited. Relative to women whose first infant was live born, those with a first stillborn infant were 2.5 times (95% CI, 1.4–4.7) more likely to experience another stillbirth. Depending on race and features of the earlier death—including cause, gestational age, and growth restriction—risk may reach a 10-fold increase. Linked maternal cohort data reported 22.7 per 1,000 with prior stillbirth versus 4.7 per 1,000 without. Prior cause also affects whether testing can prevent recurrence, but frequently is unknown. With a cause such as hypertension or diabetes, surveillance should follow management guidance for that condition. After a stillbirth at or after 32 0/7 weeks, once- or twice-weekly surveillance is recommended from 32 0/7 weeks or 1–2 weeks before the gestational age of the earlier death; after loss before 32 0/7 weeks, individualized initiation may be considered (2C Weak recommendation, low-quality evidence). Surveillance can impose costs and harm: delivery following abnormal or equivocal findings occurred in 16.3% at or before 39 weeks and 1% before 36 weeks. One study estimated that testing before 37 weeks produces a 1.5% rate of iatrogenic prematurity from false-positive results. Document sections:
  Heading: Signs and Symptoms of Uterine Rupture During Pregnancy
  Content: Clinical findings depend on when rupture occurs and on defect location and extent. Rupture through a previous scar is generally less dramatic than spontaneous or traumatic rupture because the scar is relatively less vascular. Classically described findings include fetal distress, usually reflected in fetal heart-rate abnormalities; reduced baseline uterine pressure; loss of contractility; abdominal pain; recession of the presenting fetal part; hemorrhage; and shock. Modern studies show that some are rare or difficult to distinguish from findings in less serious obstetric situations. Table 2 summarizes associated findings and their frequency. Prolonged, late, or recurrent variable fetal-heart-rate decelerations and bradycardia are often the earliest and sole clues. Bujold and Gauthier found an abnormal fetal-heart-rate pattern as the first manifestation in 87%; Leung et al observed prolonged decelerations in 79%, their most common associated finding; and Rodriguez et al reported fetal distress in 78%, also the most common finding. Across 4 studies from 1983-2000, prolonged deceleration or bradycardia occurred in 114 (80%) of 143 ruptures. Prolonged decelerations invariably accompanied fetal and placental extrusion into the abdomen. Abrupt or atypical maternal abdominal pain is less frequent than fetal deceleration or bradycardia: across 9 studies from 19802002 it occurred in 13-60% of ruptures. Among 10,967 TOLAC patients, only 22% of complete ruptures presented with pain, versus 76% with fetal distress on continuous electronic monitoring. Bujold and Gauthier found pain as the first manifestation in only 5%, occurring without epidural analgesia but not with an epidural block. Pain is therefore an uncommon, unreliable indicator. Concerns that epidural anesthesia conceals rupture pain have not been verified, and no diagnostic delay attributable to epidural anesthesia has been reported. ACOG's 2010 guideline suggests no absolute contraindication to epidural anesthesia during TOLAC, since it rarely masks rupture findings. Phelan et al found that uterine tetany and hyperstimulation often did not signal rupture; their externally monitored study defined tetany as a contraction longer than 90 seconds and hyperstimulation as more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes. Rodriguez et al found no support for IUPCs as a rupture diagnostic aid: none of 76 rupture patients showed the classically described decline in uterine tone or activity, including the 39 with IUPCs. Fetal and maternal morbidity and mortality after rupture were similar with IUPC and external monitoring. Across 8 reports from 1980-2002, vaginal bleeding occurred in 11-67% of rupture cases. Across 3 studies, hypovolemic maternal shock occurred in 29-46%.

Offer transvaginal ultrasound during investigation and consider transabdominal ultrasound when the transvaginal approach is unsuitable (Grade 1A). MRI is not a first-line diagnostic investigation, but is recommended when deeply infiltrative disease of the bowel, bladder or ureter is suspected (Grade 1B).   Content: Oral progestogens have been proposed instead of GnRH analogues to prevent a premature LH surge during controlled ovarian stimulation, with oral dosing and lower cost as possible advantages. They make the endometrium unreceptive, requiring all embryos to be frozen for later transfer. No RCT directly compares oral progestogens with GnRH analogues for pituitary suppression during ART stimulation in endometriosis. A retrospective case-controlled study of 244 women with advanced disease undergoing IVF/ICSI and FET found no differences in oocyte, embryo, implantation, clinical pregnancy or ongoing pregnancy outcomes between medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA), dosed at 4 or 10 mg/day from menstrual cycle day 3, and GnRH agonist protocols.       Summary: Recommend postponing pushing in nulliparous women with epidural analgesia; this may lessen the need for rotational or midpelvic intervention.

Document sections:
  Heading: 11.1 Definition and classification
  Content: Infertility means that a sexually active couple using no contraception has not conceived spontaneously within 12 months. Primary infertility applies when a couple has never had a child and has not conceived after at least 12 consecutive months of intercourse without contraception; secondary infertility applies when a couple has conceived previously, whether with the same or another partner. In 30-40% of cases, impaired sperm parameters have no identified male-associated explanation; this has historically been called idiopathic male infertility. Such men lack a history, examination findings or endocrine, genetic or biochemical test abnormalities explaining infertility, although semen findings may be abnormal. Possible previously unrecognised contributors include pollution-related endocrine disruption, reactive oxygen species (ROS)/sperm DNA damage, and genetic or epigenetic abnormalities. Unexplained male infertility denotes infertility of unknown origin despite normal sperm parameters and partner assessment; it affects between 20 and 30% of couples.

Pharmacokinetics: El acetato de medroxiprogesterona para administración parenteral es un esteroide progestágeno de acción prolongada.
Absorción:
La prolongada duración de su acción deriva de su lenta absorción que se va produciendo desde el lugar de la inyección. Tras su administración por vía intramuscular, el acetato de medroxiprogesterona se libera lentamente, obteniéndose niveles bajos pero persistentes en la circulación. Inmediatamente tras la administración intramuscular de una dosis de 150 mg/ml de acetato de medroxiprogesterona se alcanzaron niveles plasmáticos de 1,7 + 0,3 nmol/l. Dos semanas después los niveles fueron 6,8 + 0,8 nmol/l. El tiempo medio hasta alcanzar el máximo es aproximadamente de 4 a 20 días, después de una dosis intramuscular. Los niveles de acetato de medroxiprogesterona en suero disminuyen gradualmente y permanecen relativamente constantes a 1 ng/ml durante 2-3 meses. Los niveles circulantes pueden detectarse durante un tiempo de hasta 7 a 9 meses tras una inyección intramuscular.
Distribución:
El acetato de medroxiprogesterona se une a las proteínas entre un 90 y 95% aproximadamente. Se ha comunicado que el volumen de distribución es 20 ± 3 litros. El acetato de medroxiprogesterona atraviesa la barrera hematoencefálica y la barrera placentaria (ver sección 4.6.). Se han detectado niveles bajos de acetato de medroxiprogesterona en leche de mujeres en período de lactancia que recibieron 150 mg de acetato de medroxiprogesterona por vía intramuscular (ver sección 4.6.).
Biotransformación:
El acetato de medroxiprogesterona se metaboliza en el hígado.
Eliminación:
La vida media de eliminación después de una inyección única intramuscular es aproximadamente 6 semanas. El acetato de medroxiprogesterona se excreta principalmente en las heces, vía secreción biliar. Aproximadamente un 30% de la dosis intramuscular se excreta en la orina al cabo de 4 días.

When diagnosis is early, the patient is stable, and the affected tube remains intact, options include intramuscular methotrexate, salpingostomy to remove the pregnancy while retaining the tube, or salpingectomy to remove part or all of that tube. Clinical findings, ultrasound, serum βhCG, and patient preference inform selection between medication and surgery. With initial β-hCG <200 mIU/mL, 88% of ectopic pregnancies resolved spontaneously under expectant management. Although rarely used, observation may be considered for selected asymptomatic patients with low and declining β-hCG who accept the risks of tubal rupture and hemorrhage. Pain, persistent or rising β-hCG, or signs of tubal rupture instead warrant medical or surgical treatment.

Main conclusion: Surgical practice for idiopathic abnormal uterine bleeding did not align with the guidelines discussed by the authors: recommended 2G procedures were used in only ten percent of cases. Curettage had the highest failure rate, whereas hysterectomy had the lowest failure rate but the highest severe-complication rate and cost. The authors call for observational research comparing the clinical and economic consequences of current practice.

Narrative summary: This retrospective study used the exhaustive French hospital discharge database to compare surgical treatment of idiopathic abnormal uterine bleeding from 2009 to 2015. It included 109,884 women aged 35–55 years; 88,165 could be followed for 18 months. The procedures were 2G surgery in 7,863 women (7.2%), 1G surgery in 39,935 (36.3%), curettage in 38,923 (35.4%), and hysterectomy in 23,163 (21.1%). At 18 months, failure occurred in 9.9% after 2G surgery, 12.7% after 1G surgery, 20.6% after curettage and 2.8% after hysterectomy. Severe-complication rates at the same time were 1.9%, 1.5%, 1.4% and 5.3%, respectively. Median 18-month costs were € 1 173, € 1 059, € 782 and € 3 090, respectively. Compared with 2G surgery, 1G surgery and curettage had significantly greater risks of failure at 18 months (HR: 1.30 and HR: 2.21, respectively; p<0.0001); hysterectomy had a significantly greater risk of severe complications (HR 2.89; p<0.0001). The authors conclude that curettage and hysterectomy remained common despite the clinical and cost outcomes observed, while guideline-preferred 2G procedures were infrequently used.
