  Heading: History and Physical
  Content: Patients may have no symptoms; when symptoms occur, abnormal uterine bleeding is the most common. Abdominal pain, pelvic pain, and infertility may also occur. One in four reproductive-aged women with abnormal bleeding has an endometrial polyp in the cavity. Evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding should establish its cause and severity, associated symptoms, and comorbidities. A thorough medical and surgical history helps exclude other causes. No bleeding pattern is diagnostic of a polyp, but the bleeding history should be characterized; menorrhagia and intermenstrual spotting are reported most often. Tamoxifen, commonly used for breast cancer, can act as an agonist or antagonist in tissues bearing estrogen receptors. It has anticancer effects in breast tissue but carcinogenic effects in endometrial tissue. Chronic tamoxifen use is associated with endometrial polyps at an incidence of 20% to 35%. Hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms may also be associated with polyp formation, irregular bleeding, and ultrasound evidence of endometrial thickening. Clinical examination should include a general assessment, bimanual examination, and sterile speculum examination. The cervix and vaginal vault should be examined completely to exclude other structural explanations for symptoms. A pedunculated polyp may be visible at the external os.

Document sections:
  Heading: 6.4. Delayed Puberty/Pubertas Tarda
  Content: Delayed puberty, formerly “pubertas tarda”, means absent breast development after around 13.5 years or interruption of pubertal progression for more than 18 months. It occurs in 0.3% of adolescents and is frequently a nonpathological normal variant. Constitutional delay in growth and development often clusters in families. Nevertheless, causes should be evaluated and puberty induction considered when breast development has not begun by age 13 and menarche has not occurred by age 16. Family pubertal history may support constitutional familial delay. A pathological cause becomes more likely with older age at initial assessment. Evaluation should consider competitive sport, malnutrition, drugs such as cannabis, chronic diseases including anorexia, chronic inflammatory bowel disease, and cystic fibrosis, and malformations; gonadal, hypothalamic, pituitary, and genetic disorders should be excluded. Recommended assessment includes clinical examination, bone age, exclusion of chronic disease, and blood testing of thyroid function, LH, FSH, estradiol, and prolactin. Low LH and FSH in constitutional delay or hypogonadotropic hypogonadism resemble a prepubertal hormone profile, whereas LH and FSH are significantly elevated in hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. Depending on the suspected cause, olfactory testing, a GnRH test, brain MRI, abdominal ultrasound, or genetic testing may help. Prader Willi and Leopard syndrome are other possible contexts. Despite differing causes, puberty induction is usually needed to establish a normal phenotype and sufficient estrogen. It is also recommended when delayed development remains possible because of chronic or mental illness, to reduce long-term consequences or improve well-being. Induction generally starts at 11–13 years. Estradiol is increased at 6-month intervals under close monitoring; after approximately 2 years, progestogens may initiate bleeding, for example Utrogestan 200 mg cyclically for 14 days. Table 1 outlines age-specific puberty induction and estrogen replacement, including dose escalation and later cyclic progesterone.

  Content: The updated search on when postmenarcheal irregular cycles indicate persistent dysfunction found no studies meeting its selection criteria. Definitions by years since menarche therefore remained unchanged and draw on the natural history of cycles and ovulation in healthy adolescents. Physiological maturation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis can cause irregular cycles during the early postmenarcheal years, making the precise point at which irregularity signals PCOS uncertain. Document sections:
  Heading: 6.10. Endometriosis
  Content: Dysmenorrhea means painful menstruation. Primary dysmenorrhea occurs without a specific pathological condition; secondary dysmenorrhea occurs with a reproductive-system disorder causing menstrual cramps, such as endometriosis or fibroids. Endometriosis affects approximately 2% of adolescent women. It is an estrogen-dependent inflammatory condition involving functional endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity. Refractory pain, noncyclic lower abdominal pain, dysmenorrhea, dysuria, dyschezia, or dyspareunia makes it a likely diagnosis; increased absence from school or sport can also be a clue. Pain often accompanies nausea, vomiting, dyschezia, constipation, or vasovagal reactions. Definitive confirmation requires histology, but medication is first-line treatment. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for pain and hormonal treatment with progestogens or an extended-use contraceptive pill (off-label use) can be used to limit disease progression until childbearing is desired. GnRH analogs warrant great caution in adolescents because of adverse skeletal effects and long-term osteoporosis risk. Persistent symptoms may justify surgery, which should be performed at a highly experienced center to preserve ovarian reserve. Diagnosis appears delayed and treatment often inadequate in both adolescents and adults. Possible reasons include low ultrasonographic detection and reluctance to operate on adolescents. Clinical findings can nevertheless justify treatment without histological confirmation, and girls benefit from such treatment.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Lee et al. 2025 Comparison of Urinary Red Blood Cell Distribution ( URDspan__JC__000113
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Lee et al. 2025 Comparison of Urinary Red Blood Cell Distribution ( URDspan
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 1 | Introduction
  Content: Hematuria means RBCs are present in urine and may be visible or detectable only microscopically. It is a fundamental manifestation of glomerulonephritis (GN); microscopic assessment of urinary sediment is presented as its most effective detection method. Birch et al. proposed in 1979 that urinary RBC morphology could distinguish glomerular from non-glomerular origins. Passage through glomeruli can damage RBC membranes and produce dysmorphic RBCs (dRBCs). Shichiri et al. reported in 1988 that erythrocytes were smaller in glomerular than in non-glomerular disease, and Hyodo et al. later proposed an RBC size range of 4–6 μm for discriminating the origins. Compared with blood, urine has much less albumin and more urea; this environment increases membrane vulnerability and changes RBC shape. High urea concentrations particularly favor burr-cell formation. Passage across the glomerular basement membrane may produce acanthocytes through membrane injury. RBCs in renal disease are also more susceptible to factors including iron deficiency, osmotic lysis, shape distortion, and vesicle formation. Reliable recognition of urinary dRBCs requires an experienced observer, and observer-dependent interpretation may explain differences between laboratories. The authors consider continuing education in RBC morphology essential and mention deep learning for microscopy as another possible approach. Instrument-measured small-RBC fractions are easier to obtain and less dependent on interpretation, making them potentially more objective and standardized. The fully automated UF-5000 uses fluorescence flow cytometry to classify urine particles and reports morphological RBC information, including non-lysed RBCs, lysed RBCs, large RBCs, small RBCs, and RBC-Info. Its classification uses forward scatter light (FSC), side scatter light (SSC), side fluorescence light (SFL), and depolarized side scattered light (DSS). A small RBC has FSC intensity < 70; a non-lysed RBC has a strong FSC signal and morphological stability indicated by SSC. URD is the small-RBC count divided by the non-lysed-RBC count. Earlier studies investigated possible clinical uses, but most were single-center studies. Reported cutoffs for distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular hematuria varied from 30.1% to 40.5% for small RBCs and from 0% to 30.0% for dRBCs. The authors therefore considered a multicenter assessment using the same equipment necessary for clinical application. Across four hospitals, they collected urine microscopy findings, urine measures, serum markers, and kidney-function information to compare institutional dRBC and URD measurements and cutoffs and assess their clinical significance.

question: Which of the following factors is not an impoant risk factor for tubal ectopic?

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Ectopic Pregnancy StatPearls NCBI Bookshelf__JC__000151
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Ectopic Pregnancy StatPearls NCBI Bookshelf
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Etiology
  Content: An ectopic pregnancy is an embryo implanted outside the uterine cavity. The fallopian tube is the most frequent site, although implantation can occur in a cesarean scar, endocervical canal, ovary, or peritoneal cavity. Within the tube, the ampulla accounts for 70%; other possible sites include the cornua, fimbriae, and proximal isthmic segment. A heterotopic pregnancy combines an ectopic pregnancy with a normally developing pregnancy in the endometrial cavity. Tubal injury can impair transport and retain an oocyte or embryo; tubal ligation and other surgical changes can likewise alter tubal function. Extranubal implantation need not involve tubal dysfunction or customary risk factors. Recurrence risk is 10% after 1 previous ectopic pregnancy and >25% after 2 or more. Additional associated factors are tubal damage from gonorrhea, chlamydia, pelvic or tubal surgery, or endometriosis; pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) or complications of ascending infection; and infertility or assisted reproductive technology. With assisted reproduction, risk is higher with more embryo transfers, fresh rather than frozen transfers, and cleavage-stage (Day 3) transfers. IUD users have a lower overall risk of pregnancy, but 53% of pregnancies arising with an IUD are ectopic. Smoking is associated with increased risk through effects on tubal function. Women older than 35, those with congenital reproductive tract anomalies, and those with previous cesarean delivery—particularly after breech presentation—may have increased risk. Progesterone-only contraception carries a slightly higher risk than other contraceptive methods. Conversely, oral contraceptives, previous pregnancy termination, failure of emergency contraception, and cesarean delivery are described as not associated with increased risk.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__GINECOLOGÍA Y OBSTETRICIA__JC__000580

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Función endocrina
  Content: La gonadotropina coriónica (HCG) es una glucoproteína de doble cadena: una subunidad se asemeja a LH, FSH y TSH, mientras que la subunidad ß específica, producida por el sincitiotrofoblasto, se cuantifica en las pruebas de embarazo. Es detectable en sangre desde la implantación, al final de la tercera semana desde la última regla o al 8.º-9.º día postovulación. Sus concentraciones se duplican cada 1,4-2 días hasta un máximo alrededor de la 10.ª semana (50.000 mUI/ml), y luego disminuyen hasta estabilizarse entre la semana 17-18 durante el resto del embarazo. Mantiene el cuerpo lúteo y la secreción de progesterona durante las 6-8 primeras semanas, estimula la síntesis de gestágenos y andrógenos y tiene actividad tirotrófica. Puede elevarse en enfermedad trofoblástica gestacional, gestaciones múltiples y algunas cromosomopatías. La prueba inmunológica de embarazo (PIE) detecta HCG urinaria en la 5.ª semana de amenorrea para diagnosticar gestación. El Lactógeno placentario (HPL) es una glucoproteína relacionada con prolactina y con un 96 % de semejanza con GH; se sintetiza en sincitiotrofoblasto, se detecta 5-10 días postimplantación, aumenta durante la gestación, alcanza su máximo en las semanas 24-28 y llega a una meseta en la semana 34-36. Responde a la hipoglucemia, asegura glucosa fetal, estimula lipólisis materna y producción de cuerpos cetónicos, e interfiere con la insulina en la segunda mitad del embarazo. Su papel en la preparación mamaria es muy inferior al de prolactina y ejerce una pequeña acción sobre el crecimiento fetal. Su utilidad clínica es escasa, salvo como indicador de función placentaria al final de la gestación. La progesterona procede inicialmente del cuerpo lúteo y desde la 7.ª-8.ª semana de la placenta; deriva de colesterol y acetatos maternos, favorece implantación y mantenimiento gestacional, participa en la supresión inmunitaria materna y reduce la contracción del músculo liso. No indica adecuadamente el bienestar fetal. Los estrógenos aumentan hasta la semana 40 y se usan como indicador de función placentaria. La dehidroepiandrosterona-sulfato (DHEAS) fetal se hidroxila en el hígado mediante 16-alfa-hidroxilasa y se transforma en estriol en la placenta. El estriol, principal estrógeno gestacional, refleja la función fetoplacentaria y sirve como indicador de bienestar fetal; disminuye en cromosomopatías y está ausente en la mola completa. La tabla 1 sintetiza concentraciones gestacionales, acciones e interés clínico de las hormonas fundamentales del embarazo.

Document sections:
  Heading: Cervical and Cesarean Scar Ectopic Pregnancy
  Content: Cervical and cesarean-scar pregnancies need specialized management. Expectant management of cesarean-scar pregnancy is not recommended because of uterine rupture and hemorrhage risk, apart from selected cases with confirmed fetal demise. Transvaginal or laparoscopic resection has shown low complication rates. Curettage alone is not recommended because bleeding and incomplete trophoblastic removal are risks. Hysterectomy may be considered if fertility preservation is not a priority. Medical treatment of cesarean-scar pregnancy usually uses local or intragestational methotrexate, frequently combined with systemic methotrexate. Systemic methotrexate alone is not recommended because failure and complications are more frequent. Ultrasound-guided aspiration can supplement medication. Follow-up is essential because β-hCG and mass size may require weeks to resolve.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Cararach Tur et al. 2013 La vulvovaginitis candidiásica recurrente__JC__000125
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Cararach Tur et al. 2013 La vulvovaginitis candidiásica recurrente
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Manifestaciones clínicas de la vulvovaginitis candidiásica recurrente
  Content: Las manifestaciones son las de una VVC aislada no complicada. Aunque suelen ser menos intensas, producen molestias crónicas que afectan seriamente la calidad de vida y las relaciones de pareja. El prurito vulvar es el síntoma más habitual y aparece prácticamente en todos los casos (90%). La leucorrea puede faltar o ser escasa; algunas pacientes refieren sequedad. Son casi constantes otras molestias, como dolor, irritación, ardor vulvar, escozor o dolor al orinar y dispareunia. El ardor es especialmente frecuente durante la micción. La dispareunia superficial puede ser intensa, sobre todo en nulíparas, y progresar hasta impedir las relaciones sexuales, situación que debe suscitar sospecha de síndrome de vestibulitis vulvar. La VVCR también puede causar o desencadenar vulvodinia localizada. Los síntomas suelen empeorar durante la semana anterior a la menstruación y justo después de las relaciones sexuales, y mejorar al comenzar el sangrado. En la exploración son habituales eritema vaginal y vulvar, edema de la vulva —especialmente de labios menores y clítoris— y exudado blanco-amarillento espeso, grumoso, adherente y sin olor característico. Puede haber placas blancas grumosas sobre vagina y vulva. La inflamación puede extenderse a periné e ingles con placas eritematoescamosas, descamación de bordes geográficos o lesiones pápulo-pustulosas periféricas, en ocasiones satélites. El rascado puede producir erosiones y fisuras; también puede aparecer liquenificación, especialmente en labios mayores. Ningún signo o síntoma es específico ni patognomónico. Por ello, no debe diagnosticarse solo mediante anamnesis y exploración, y deben considerarse otras causas infecciosas y no infecciosas. Hasta el 70% de las presuntas candidiasis vaginales no corresponden realmente a esta infección.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: A) Definición de Hemorragia Postparto
  Content: La hemorragia postparto (HPP) permanece entre las tres principales causas de mortalidad materna mundial, especialmente en países en desarrollo. La definición actualmente más aceptada comprende cualquier pérdida sanguínea que produzca signos de hipovolemia y/o inestabilidad hemodinámica. Otras guías emplean umbrales de >500ml tras parto vaginal y más de 1000ml tras cesárea, una reducción de un 10% del hematocrito basal o una pérdida de 500ml o más durante las 24 horas posteriores al parto. La HPP grave corresponde a una pérdida de 1.000 ml o más en ese período. También se considera HPP cualquier sangrado posparto con compromiso hemodinámico. La HPP primaria aparece en las primeras 24 hs. posteriores al nacimiento; la secundaria ocurre después de 24 horas y hasta 12 semanas después del parto, y entre sus causas figuran los restos placentarios retenidos y/o la infección. La valoración visual del sangrado suele ser inexacta y subestimarlo retrasa el tratamiento. Para medirlo objetivamente puede emplearse, inmediatamente después del parto, una bolsa calibrada provista de una lámina plástica que se sitúa bajo las nalgas.

  Title: Fetal heart rate monitoring and invasive monitoring decisions
  Source heading: 1.12 Fetal monitoring
  Description: Step 1: In suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour, discuss the purpose and consequences of fetal monitoring and, when appropriate, the option not to monitor fetal heart rate. For women between 23+0 and 25+6 weeks, involve a senior obstetrician in deciding whether and how to monitor. Step 2: In established preterm labour without other risk factors, offer a choice between cardiotocography using external ultrasound and intermittent auscultation. Explain that evidence does not establish improved outcomes from cardiotocography compared with intermittent auscultation. Step 3: Below 34+0 weeks, do not use a fetal scalp electrode unless external cardiotocography and intermittent auscultation are both impossible, a senior obstetrician has been consulted, likely benefits outweigh potential risks, and the woman has discussed and does not accept immediate birth, intermittent ultrasound or no monitoring. Between 34+0 and 36+6 weeks, discuss possible use of a fetal scalp electrode if neither external method can monitor fetal heart rate. Step 4: Below 34+0 weeks, do not perform fetal blood sampling. Between 34+0 and 36+6 weeks, discuss its possible use if likely benefits outweigh potential risks. When offering sampling, advise that inability to obtain a sample is likely to lead to caesarean section.
  Summary: This pathway covers choice of fetal monitoring and the gestational-age restrictions on a fetal scalp electrode and fetal blood sampling. It includes circumstances requiring senior obstetric input and discussion with the woman.

Document sections:
  Heading: Management options
  Content: For tubal pregnancy, laparoscopy is preferred to open surgery (A). With a healthy opposite tube, salpingectomy is preferred to salpingotomy (B); consider salpingotomy when prior ectopic pregnancy, contralateral tubal damage, earlier abdominal surgery or previous pelvic inflammatory disease may impair fertility (C). After salpingotomy, explain persistent-trophoblast risk, the need for serum b-hCG surveillance and the small possibility of further systemic methotrexate or salpingectomy (good practice point). Suitable women may be offered systemic methotrexate; do not give it at the initial visit unless ectopic pregnancy is unequivocally diagnosed and viable intrauterine pregnancy excluded (B). Expectant care is possible in clinically stable women with ultrasound-confirmed ectopic pregnancy and declining b-hCG initially less than 1500 iu/l (B). For cervical pregnancy, methotrexate can be considered (D); because surgical approaches have high failure rates, reserve them for life-threatening haemorrhage (D). Counsel women with caesarean scar pregnancy about serious maternal morbidity and mortality (D). In the first trimester, consider medical or surgical treatment, with or without supplementary haemostatic measures (D). Evidence cannot establish a preferred individual intervention, although existing literature favours surgery over medicine for effectiveness (D). Stable interstitial pregnancy can be managed without surgery (D); expectant care is appropriate only with low or substantially falling b-hCG when adding methotrexate may not improve outcome (D). Methotrexate is effective, but evidence does not favour local over systemic administration (D). Laparoscopic cornual resection or salpingotomy is effective (D), and hysteroscopic resection under laparoscopic or ultrasound guidance may be considered (D). Evidence on future-pregnancy safety and complications does not support recommending other nonsurgical techniques (D). Excise the rudimentary horn in cornual pregnancy by laparoscopy or laparotomy (D). If ovarian pregnancy requires diagnostic laparoscopy, definitive surgery is preferred (D); systemic methotrexate can be used when surgical risk is high or after surgery for residual persistent trophoblast or persistently elevated b-hCG (D). Laparoscopic removal is an option for early abdominal pregnancy (D); systemic methotrexate combined with ultrasound-guided fetocide is a possible alternative (D). Manage advanced abdominal pregnancy by laparotomy (D). In heterotopic pregnancy, the intrauterine gestation must shape management (B). Consider methotrexate only if that gestation is nonviable or the woman does not wish to continue it (D). For clinically stable women, local potassium chloride or hyperosmolar glucose injection with sac aspiration is an option (D). Remove the ectopic pregnancy surgically when haemodynamically unstable; surgery is also an option when stable (D). Expectant care may be considered when ultrasound indicates a nonviable ectopic gestation (D).

Interpretation: PCOS is presented as a lifelong, heterogeneous condition with reproductive and metabolic consequences. Insulin resistance and androgen excess interact in its pathophysiology, while clinical presentation and diagnostic prevalence vary with the criteria applied. Delayed diagnosis may allow associated conditions to progress. Lifestyle changes and modest weight loss can improve symptoms and fertility, but management needs to reflect each patient's reproductive, metabolic, and personal goals. Although risks of several conditions are elevated, the article notes that a prospective study did not find evidence of increased all-cause or cardiovascular mortality.

Comparison with prior evidence: The article contrasts diagnostic frameworks: Rotterdam Criteria include a broader population than National Institute of Health 1990 Criteria, while RCAES is described as more sensitive than RC for a phenotype involving PCOM and infertility. It reports that RC-defined patients had less prevalent IR than patients identified through NIH or RCAES criteria. Evidence on long-term outcomes is mixed: a retrospective Western Australian cohort reported more hospital admissions and several diagnoses among women with PCOS than in the general population, whereas a 32-year prospective study found no evidence of increased all-cause or cardiovascular mortality. The treatment discussion cites studies favoring COC with low-dose spironolactone over metformin alone for hyperandrogenic manifestations, and metformin with low-dose spironolactone over either drug alone for symptom relief and adherence. It also describes evidence of greater weight loss and insulin sensitivity with GLP-1 agonists than with metformin.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_06
  Name: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (P-PROM)
  Synonyms:
    - P-PROM
  Description: Membranes rupture before 37+0 weeks of pregnancy while established labour has not begun.
  Clinical presentation: A woman may report symptoms suggestive of membrane rupture; examination may show a pool of amniotic fluid.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Speculum examination
      Purpose: Look for pooling of amniotic fluid.
      When indicated: When symptoms suggest P-PROM and labour has not become established.
      Interpretation: Visible pooling supports care for P-PROM without further diagnostic testing. If no pooling is seen, test vaginal fluid with insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 or placental alpha-microglobulin-1.
    - Test: insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 test
      Purpose: Help assess possible P-PROM when amniotic fluid is not seen on speculum examination.
      When indicated: When symptoms suggest P-PROM but pooling of amniotic fluid is absent.
      Interpretation: A positive result must be considered alongside clinical condition, medical and pregnancy history, and gestational age; it is not sufficient on its own to determine care. A negative result with no visible amniotic fluid makes P-PROM unlikely.
    - Test: placental alpha-microglobulin-1 test
      Purpose: Help assess possible P-PROM when amniotic fluid is not seen on speculum examination.
      When indicated: When symptoms suggest P-PROM but pooling of amniotic fluid is absent.
      Interpretation: A positive result must be considered alongside clinical condition, medical and pregnancy history, and gestational age; it is not sufficient on its own to determine care. A negative result with no visible amniotic fluid makes P-PROM unlikely.
    - Test: Clinical assessment
      Purpose: Contribute to diagnosis of intrauterine infection alongside laboratory tests and fetal heart rate assessment.
      When indicated: When assessing a woman with P-PROM for intrauterine infection.
      Interpretation: Discordant clinical and test findings warrant continued observation and consideration of repeat testing.
    - Test: C-reactive protein
      Purpose: Contribute to diagnosis of intrauterine infection.
      When indicated: When assessing a woman with P-PROM for intrauterine infection.
      Interpretation: A single result must not be used alone to confirm or exclude intrauterine infection.
    - Test: White blood cell count
      Purpose: Contribute to diagnosis of intrauterine infection.
      When indicated: When assessing a woman with P-PROM for intrauterine infection.
      Interpretation: It must not be used alone to confirm or exclude intrauterine infection.
    - Test: Measurement of fetal heart rate using cardiotocography
      Purpose: Contribute to diagnosis of intrauterine infection.
      When indicated: When assessing a woman with P-PROM for intrauterine infection.
      Interpretation: It must not be used alone to confirm or exclude intrauterine infection.
    - Test: nitrazine
      Purpose: The guideline advises against using this test to diagnose P-PROM.
  Follow up:
    Recommended tests:
      - After a positive vaginal-fluid test, re-evaluate diagnostic status at a later time as an alternative to offering care consistent with P-PROM.
      - If clinical assessment and tests for intrauterine infection disagree, continue observation and consider repeating the tests.
    Survivorship notes: After a negative vaginal-fluid test with no amniotic fluid observed, advise return for reassessment if further symptoms suggest P-PROM or preterm labour.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Prevención de la vulvovaginitis candidiásica recurrente
  Content: Las opciones preventivas son limitadas. Tras un episodio aislado de VVC conviene valorar medidas para disminuir episodios posteriores, centradas en la flora vaginal y los factores de riesgo. Sin embargo, salvo eliminar el agente causal mediante tratamiento profiláctico para evitar reinfección o recidiva, no existe evidencia científica de eficacia para otras medidas preventivas. Se han propuesto probióticos, incluido lactobacillus, para favorecer el equilibrio microbiano, pero los resultados de los estudios son discrepantes. También se ha señalado la conveniencia de ropa holgada, preferentemente de algodón, para evitar condiciones perineales de temperatura y humedad favorables al crecimiento de cándida. El yogur se ha propuesto como profilaxis, aunque los datos publicados son contradictorios. Reducir hidratos de carbono podría limitar el crecimiento de cándida en reservorios intestinales y urinarios; aunque alguna publicación describe beneficio con una dieta baja en hidratos de carbono, la evidencia todavía es insuficiente para recomendar una dieta estricta. No está justificado tratar con antifúngicos a las parejas sexuales de mujeres con VVCR; solo debe indicarse tratamiento antifúngico tópico si el compañero presenta signos o síntomas de balanitis. Tanto la higiene íntima excesiva como la insuficiente pueden alterar la flora, por lo que se recomiendan productos formulados para la zona vaginal que mantengan un pH adecuado. Continúan en estudio la inmunoterapia con alérgenos de C. albicans, los antagonistas de receptores de leucotrieno y los inhibidores de la recaptación de serotonina (sertralina) como posibles opciones para mujeres que no toleran el mantenimiento con azoles.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Main results
  Content: Overall, NSAIDs reduced HMB more effectively than placebo but less effectively than tranexamic acid, danazol, or the levonorgestrelreleasing intrauterine system (LNG IUS). Compared with NSAIDs, danazol shortened menstruation but caused more adverse events; the trials informing this comparison dated from 1980 to 1990, and treatment acceptability did not appear to differ. Danazol is currently neither usual nor recommended for HMB. No clear difference was established against oral luteal progestogen, ethamsylate, an older progesterone-releasing intrauterine system, or the oral contraceptive pill (OCP); most studies lacked adequate power. Evidence did not show a difference between naproxen and mefenamic acid for reducing HMB. Evidence quality ranged from low to moderate, chiefly because of bias risk and imprecision.

Document sections:
  Heading: Complicaciones
  Content: Son embarazos de alto riesgo por el aumento de morbilidad materna y fetal. Se incrementan el aborto, especialmente en monocigotos; la preeclampsia, que puede comenzar antes de la 20 semana; la hiperemesis gravídica y la hipertensión inducida por el embarazo. La amenaza de parto pretérmino aumenta por sobredistensión uterina y por polihidramnios, presente en el 15 % de los embarazos gemelares; la prematuridad es la principal causa de morbimortalidad neonatal. Son más frecuentes la rotura prematura de membranas, las malformaciones congénitas —cuya frecuencia se multiplica por 3, sobre todo defectos del tubo neural y cardiopatías—, el prolapso de cordón en monoamnióticos o con polihidramnios y el abruptio placentae tras la descompresión que sigue al nacimiento del primer gemelo. En gestaciones monocoriales, las anastomosis placentarias arteriovenosas pueden causar síndrome de transfusión feto-fetal: el receptor recibe sangre del donante, pesa más y presenta un hematocrito superior al nacimiento (>15 % ó 5 g de Hb); puede desarrollar hipervolemia, HTA, policitemia, polihidramnios e insuficiencia cardiaca de alto gasto. El donante puede presentar hipovolemia, hipotensión, anemia y CIR. Su expresión máxima se denomina secuencia TRAP (twinreversed arterial perfusion sequence): el gemelo bomba mantiene su circulación y la del feto acardio.

question: Endosalpingitis is best diagnosed by

Document sections:
  Heading: Diagnosis of endometriosis
  Content: Key recommendations: Consider endometriosis when a woman has at least one of chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea that disrupts daily activities, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel symptoms—especially dyschezia—cyclical urinary symptoms—especially dysuria or haematuria—or infertility (Best practice). Offer abdominal and pelvic examination when symptoms suggest endometriosis; look for restricted organ mobility, tender posterior vaginal nodules and pelvic or abdominal masses (Grade 1C). Do not delay discussion or initiation of empirical treatment for suspected disease, since treatment may improve quality of life (Best practice). Refer suspected or confirmed cases to a Gynaecologist for severe, persistent or recurrent symptoms; examination findings; associated infertility; ineffective, intolerable or contraindicated initial management; or imaging suggestive of a higher stage or deeply infiltrating disease, including endometrioma or invasion of other organs (Best practice). Refer suspected or confirmed deeply infiltrative disease affecting the bowel, bladder or ureter to a specialist endometriosis service (Best practice). Offer transvaginal ultrasound during investigation and consider transabdominal ultrasound when the transvaginal approach is unsuitable (Grade 1A). MRI is not a first-line diagnostic investigation, but is recommended when deeply infiltrative disease of the bowel, bladder or ureter is suspected (Grade 1B). Do not use computed tomography (CT) or positron emission tomography-CT (PET-CT) to diagnose endometriosis (Best practice). Negative imaging must not be used to exclude endometriosis (Grade 1B). Do not use biomarkers, including serum CA-125, for diagnosis (Grade 1A). Consider laparoscopy for suggestive symptoms when empirical treatment fails or is unsuitable, including when imaging is negative (Best practice). Biopsy suspected lesions during laparoscopy for histological confirmation; negative histology does not completely exclude disease (Grade 1B). Refer for laparoscopy to a Gynaecologist with suitable laparoscopic training and skills to optimise assessment of the abdomen and pelvis (Best practice).

question: Earliest sign of intrauterine death is

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Ectopic Pregnancy StatPearls NCBI Bookshelf__JC__000157
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Ectopic Pregnancy StatPearls NCBI Bookshelf
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Diagnostic Evaluation of Ectopic Pregnancy
  Content: Evaluation principally combines serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) measurement with transvaginal ultrasonography (TVUS) and transabdominal ultrasonography (TAUS). TVUS is described as the most sensitive and accurate method for early detection, particularly with 3-dimensional imaging and color Doppler ultrasound. A β-hCG level >2000 mIU/mL without a visible intrauterine pregnancy (IUP) strongly suggests ectopic pregnancy. In a viable IUP starting at β-hCG <1500 mIU/mL, there is a 99% likelihood of a minimum 49% increase over 48 hours. A slower increase or a decline of at least 21% over 48 hours points more toward miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy; falling serum β-hCG more strongly suggests spontaneous early pregnancy loss. The discriminatory β-hCG threshold above which TVUS should show an IUP depends on equipment, operator expertise, and gestational number. Although historically between 1000 and 2000 mIU/mL, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has suggested a cutoff of up to 3500 mIU/mL to reduce misdiagnosis and avoid unnecessary termination of a viable pregnancy. Stable patients whose β-hCG is falling but whose possible ectopic pregnancy remains unexcluded should have serial measurements until β-hCG becomes undetectable. TVUS is the diagnostic gold standard; visualization of a yolk sac or embryo outside the uterus confirms ectopic pregnancy. Because many cases do not develop far enough for this finding, serial β-hCG tests, repeat ultrasound, or uterine aspiration may be needed. When neither IUP nor ectopic pregnancy is identified, the designation is pregnancy of unknown location (PUL); serial β-hCG and sometimes manual vacuum aspiration can distinguish a failing IUP from ectopic pregnancy. Serial transvaginal imaging, serum hCG measurements, or both are required for confirmation. The earliest ultrasonographic IUP finding is a small sac eccentrically placed in the decidua; surrounding tissue rings produce the “double decidual” sign. This sign is typically apparent in the fifth week of pregnancy on abdominal ultrasound. The yolk sac appears around the same time but is accurately identified with transvaginal imaging. A transvaginal scan can show an embryonic pole at approximately 6 weeks of pregnancy. Fibroids or a high body mass index can reduce ultrasound accuracy for an early IUP. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may help in extreme circumstances, such as large obstructing fibroids, but its sensitivity and specificity need further study, and risks of gadolinium contrast exposure require careful consideration.

Pregnancy and lactation: Embarazo
No existen estudios adecuados o bien controlados relativos al uso de este medicamento en mujeres embarazadas. El uso prolongado o repetido de corticoides durante el embarazo se ha asociado con un mayor riesgo de retraso en el crecimiento intrauterino. Se debe hacer un especial seguimiento de los recién nacidos de madres que han recibido dosis sustanciales de corticosteroides durante el embarazo debido a posibles signos de insuficiencia suprarrenal (ver sección 4.4). Los estudios realizados en animales han mostrado toxicidad para la reproducción tras la administración sistémica. La administración oftálmica de dexametasona al 0,1% también causó anomalías fetales en conejos (ver sección 5.3).
No se recomienda utilizar Maxidex durante el embarazo.
Lactancia
Se desconoce si la dexametasona oftálmica se excreta en la lecha materna. No hay datos disponibles sobre el paso de la dexametasona a la leche materna. No es probable que después de la administración oftálmica de este medicamento, se pueda detectar una cantidad suficiente de dexametasona en la leche materna o que pueda causar efectos clínicos en el lactante. No se puede excluir el riesgo en recién nacidos/niños. Se debe decidir si es necesario interrumpir la lactancia o interrumpir el tratamiento tras considerar el beneficio de la lactancia para el niño y el beneficio del tratamiento para la madre.
Fertilidad
No se han realizado estudios para evaluar el efecto de la administración oftálmica de este medicamento sobre la fertilidad. Existen pocos datos clínicos para evaluar el efecto de la dexametasona sobre la fertilidad masculina o femenina. La dexametasona no produjo efectos adversos sobre la fertilidad en un modelo de rata cebado con gonadotropina coriónica.

question: Mean half life of oxytocin?

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Syntocinon 10 UI ml solución inyectable y para perfusión__JC__000010

retrieved_chunks.text:
Pharmacokinetics: Absorción
La oxitocina se absorbe rápidamente en el lugar de administración intramuscular. Los niveles plasmáticos de oxitocina en mujeres embarazadas a término que recibieron perfusión intravenosa de 4 miliunidades por minuto fueron de 2 a 5 microunidades/ml.
Distribución
El volumen de distribución en estado estacionario determinado en 6 varones sanos después de inyección intravenosa es de 12,2 l o 0,17 l/kg. La unión de oxitocina a proteínas plasmáticas es insignificante. La oxitocina atraviesa la placenta en ambas direcciones. La oxitocina puede encontrarse en pequeñas cantidades en la leche materna.
Biotransformación
Durante el embarazo se produce oxitocinasa, una glicoproteína aminopeptidasa, que aparece en el plasma. Es capaz de degradar la oxitocina. Es producida tanto por la madre como por el feto. El hígado y los riñones desempeñan un papel importante en el metabolismo y en el aclaramiento de la oxitocina. Por lo tanto, el hígado, el riñón y la circulación sistémica contribuyen a la biotransformación de la oxitocina.
Eliminación
La vida media plasmática de la oxitocina oscila entre 3 y 20 minutos. Los metabolitos se eliminan en la orina, mientras que menos del 1% de la oxitocina se elimina de forma intacta en la orina. La tasa de aclaramiento metabólico asciende a 20 ml/kg/min en la mujer embarazada.
Relación farmacocinética/farmacodinámicas
Cuando se administra mediante inyección intravenosa o intramuscular para la prevención o tratamiento de la hemorragia postparto oxitocina actúa rápidamente con un periodo de latencia inferior a 1 minuto tras la inyección intravenosa, y de 2 a 4 minutos tras la inyección intramuscular. La respuesta oxitócica dura de 30 a 60 minutos después de la administración intramuscular, pudiendo ser más corta con la inyección intravenosa.
Cuando oxitocina se administra mediante infusión intravenosa continua a dosis adecuadas para la inducción del parto, se inicia la respuesta uterina de forma gradual y alcanza el estado estacionario normalmente entre los 20 y 40 minutos. Los niveles plasmáticos correspondientes de oxitocina son comparables a los determinados durante la primera fase de un parto espontáneo. Tras la interrupción de la infusión o después de una reducción sustancial de la velocidad de infusión, p.ej. en el caso de sobreestimulación, la actividad uterina declina rápidamente pero puede continuar en un nivel inferior adecuado.
Insuficiencia renal
No se han realizado estudios en pacientes con insuficiencia renal. Sin embargo, teniendo en cuenta la excreción urinaria de la oxitocina y su reducida eliminación en la orina debido a sus propiedades anti-diuréticas, se puede producir una acumulación de oxitocina.
Insuficiencia hepática
No se han realizado estudios en pacientes con insuficiencia hepática. Es poco probable que haya alteración farmacocinética en pacientes con insuficiencia hepática, ya que la metabolización de la enzima oxitocinasa, no se limita solo al hígado y los niveles de oxitocinasa en la placenta durante la última fase del embarazo aumentan significativamente. Por lo tanto, la biotransformación de la oxitocina en presencia de insuficiencia hepática no debería dar lugar a cambios sustanciales en el aclaramiento metabólico de la oxitocina (ver sección 4.4.).

Document sections:
  Heading: 6.2. Amenorrhea
  Content: Amenorrhea can have hormonal or organic causes and may be primary or secondary. Primary amenorrhea denotes no menarche by age 16; secondary amenorrhea means no menstruation for more than 90 days after previous periods. Pregnancy should be excluded before further investigation, and a previously regular cycle that becomes irregular warrants assessment. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (WHO I) occurs with pubertas tarda and is largely constitutional without pathological significance, although gonadal, hypothalamic, pituitary, or genetic disorders—including Sheehan syndrome and Kallmann syndrome—can cause it. Common adolescent causes of hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction (WHO II) are a high-risk constellation for polycystic ovary syndrome and central dysregulation associated with stress, anorexia, or competitive sport. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (WHO III), or premature ovarian insufficiency, involves loss of ovarian activity before age 40 years and affects approximately 1:10,000 patients under age 20. Potential causes are Turner syndrome, a Fragile X premutation, autoimmune predisposition, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or ovarian surgery. Organic amenorrhea (WHO IV) includes genital malformations such as Meier–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome and hymenal atresia, often first identified because of primary amenorrhea or dysmenorrhea. Reported incidences of the various causes differ so greatly by study and population that no general statement can be made. Absent follicular maturation can prevent adequate estrogenization and endometrial thickening, so bleeding does not occur. In the short term, estrogen deficiency can prevent pubertal onset and secondary sexual development; in the long term, it can impair bone, cognitive, and cardiovascular health. Girls with hypo- or hypergonadotropic hypogonadism consequently need treatment to induce puberty and sustain adequate estrogenization.

  Content: UAB is a clinical diagnosis; DU requires urodynamic diagnosis. Invasive urodynamics is the only broadly accepted diagnostic method, although diagnostic criteria lack consensus. Proposed measures include Griffiths’ Watt factor, combining voiding pressure, contraction speed, and bladder volume and expressed in W/m2; the appropriate measurement and threshold remain disputed, although expert opinion suggests Wmax 7.0 W/m2. Schafer’s detrusor-adjusted mean PURR factor (DAMPF) uses linPURR in the Schafer nomogram to classify contractility as very weak, weak, normal, or strong. Document sections:
  Heading: Etiology
  Content: An ectopic pregnancy is an embryo implanted outside the uterine cavity. The fallopian tube is the most frequent site, although implantation can occur in a cesarean scar, endocervical canal, ovary, or peritoneal cavity. Within the tube, the ampulla accounts for 70%; other possible sites include the cornua, fimbriae, and proximal isthmic segment. A heterotopic pregnancy combines an ectopic pregnancy with a normally developing pregnancy in the endometrial cavity. Tubal injury can impair transport and retain an oocyte or embryo; tubal ligation and other surgical changes can likewise alter tubal function. Extranubal implantation need not involve tubal dysfunction or customary risk factors. Recurrence risk is 10% after 1 previous ectopic pregnancy and >25% after 2 or more. Additional associated factors are tubal damage from gonorrhea, chlamydia, pelvic or tubal surgery, or endometriosis; pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) or complications of ascending infection; and infertility or assisted reproductive technology. With assisted reproduction, risk is higher with more embryo transfers, fresh rather than frozen transfers, and cleavage-stage (Day 3) transfers. IUD users have a lower overall risk of pregnancy, but 53% of pregnancies arising with an IUD are ectopic. Smoking is associated with increased risk through effects on tubal function. Women older than 35, those with congenital reproductive tract anomalies, and those with previous cesarean delivery—particularly after breech presentation—may have increased risk. Progesterone-only contraception carries a slightly higher risk than other contraceptive methods. Conversely, oral contraceptives, previous pregnancy termination, failure of emergency contraception, and cesarean delivery are described as not associated with increased risk.

    - Refer women and girls planning pregnancy or already pregnant to an epilepsy specialist team to review antiseizure medication options, and coordinate their care with specialist obstetrics and primary care.

Other manifestations related to intracranial pressure include nausea, transient visual obscurations or vision loss (13%–27%), papilledema, diplopia (6%–14%), and other cranial neuropathies (6%–11%). Approximately 20% to 40% of patients present with seizures, 20% to 50% with focal neurological deficits, and up to 20% with encephalopathy or coma. Onset is generally less abrupt than with other stroke types; most patients present >48 hours after symptoms begin. A minority have thunderclap headache or subarachnoid hemorrhage (<5%), or sudden focal deficits (5%–40%). Additional presentation details are summarized in Supplemental Table 1.

Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_07
  Type: algorithm
  Title: Box 3. SIBICC I Tiers for ICP Treatment of Intracranial Hypertension for Patients with ICP Monitoring
  Source heading: Tiered Treatments
  Description: Step 1, Tier One: Target CPP 60–70 mm Hg; increase analgesia or sedation to reduce ICP; keep PaCO2 at 35–38 mm Hg/4.7–5.1 kPa; give intermittent boluses of mannitol (0.25–1.0 g/kg) or hypertonic saline; drain CSF through an existing EVD or consider EVD placement if monitoring began with a parenchymal probe; consider antiseizure prophylaxis for 1 week only unless continuation is indicated, and consider EEG monitoring. Step 2, Tier Two: If further treatment is needed, maintain PaCO2 at 32–35 mm Hg/4.3–4.6 kPa; try neuromuscular paralysis in an adequately sedated patient and continue infusion only if the trial lowers ICP; perform a MAP Challenge to guide individualized MAP and CPP targets, returning MAP to baseline with impaired autoregulation or raising its target to lower ICP when autoregulation is intact. Step 3, Tier Three: If further escalation is appropriate, give pentobarbital or sodium thiopentone only if a test shows ICP benefit, titrating to ICP control without exceeding the dose producing burst suppression and avoiding hypotension; alternatively, perform secondary decompressive craniectomy or use active cooling for mild hypothermia at 35–36°C. Document sections:
  Heading: TIERED MANAGEMENT OF INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE
  Content: Treat raised ICP after severe TBI to limit secondary injury; untreated elevation can cause herniation, brainstem compression, reduced CPP, ischemia, or, in extreme cases, cessation of brain perfusion. Invasive monitors are currently preferred for accuracy and can detect expanding lesions, guide targeted treatment, calculate CPP and autoregulatory status, and provide waveform information about compliance. SIBICC developed three treatment tiers through a rigorous Delphi-based expert-consensus process to address gaps in evidence-based guidance. Treatments with more favorable risk–benefit profiles generally precede those with less favorable profiles, while clinicians retain discretion within tiers and can target suspected physiological disturbances. These algorithms are suggestions that can standardize care, not standards of practice; relevant disciplines should review and approve or adapt them locally. Document sections:
  Heading: ASSOCIATED CONDITIONS
  Content: Diuretics, antihistamines, anticholinergics, antidepressants, and systemic retinoids such as isotretinoin may aggravate symptoms. Frequently instilled eye medicines, for example more than four drops a day, can disturb tear-film maintenance, with preservatives contributing to epithelial breakdown. Low humidity, wind, drafts, air conditioning, heating, and reduced blinking during prolonged screen use, reading, or driving may worsen discomfort. External irritants and allergens may aggravate symptoms without being considered causes. Rosacea can worsen dry eye and ocular-surface disease. Although more frequently observed in fair skin, it occurs in all skin types; findings include facial erythema, telangiectasia, papules, pustules, enlarged sebaceous glands, and rhinophyma. Darker skin may obscure flushing and telangiectasia. Children may develop ocular manifestations before obvious skin disease, allowing misdiagnosis. Rosacea is more prevalent in women but can be more severe in men. Subtle signs can be overlooked, particularly in children presenting with recurrent blepharokeratoconjunctivitis, punctate erosions, peripheral keratitis, meibomian gland disease, or recurrent chalazia. Pediatric ocular disease often includes asymmetric corneal involvement with potentially sight-threatening impairment; skin manifestations are less frequent and atopy is common. Childhood styes are associated with increased adult rosacea risk. In Sjögren's syndrome, inflammatory infiltration of exocrine glands impairs salivary and tear production. About 10% of patients with clinically significant aqueous deficient dry eye have underlying primary Sjӧgren’s syndrome. Primary disease is multisystemic and increases lymphoma risk; about 5% of patients with Sjögren syndrome develop a lymphoid malignancy. A cited meta-analysis found the strongest rheumatic-disease association with lymphoid malignancy for primary Sjӧgren’s syndrome, reporting an incidence rate of 18.9% (95% CI, 9.4–37.9) and an increased incidence of 320 cases per 100,000 patient years. Ophthalmologists should therefore maintain strong suspicion and a low threshold for diagnostic serology in clinically significant dry eye. Infiltration or replacement of lacrimal secretory tissue in lymphoma, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, or amyloidosis can cause aqueous deficiency. Dry eye has also been reported with Epstein-Barr virus, human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1, HIV, hepatitis C, and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, with or without GVHD. One AIDS group had dry eye in 21%; diffuse infiltrative lymphadenopathy syndrome has been described in HIV, predominantly among children. Hepatitis C has been associated with decreased secretion and tear lactoferrin. Primary or persistent Epstein-Barr virus infection has been linked to gland enlargement, dry eye, and Sjögren’s syndrome. Chronic GVHD can cause lacrimal and conjunctival infiltration and fibrosis through T-cell interaction with fibroblasts. Ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid and Stevens-Johnson syndrome may destroy conjunctival goblet cells through inflammation and scarring. Atopy may contribute through blepharitis, conjunctival scarring, or antihistamines. Dry eye in younger patients or males warrants suspicion of an associated local or systemic disorder. Relevant eyelid or neurologic conditions include malposition, lagophthalmos, exophthalmos, thyroid-associated ocular disease, blepharitis, Parkinson disease, and Bell’s palsy; orbital or eyelid surgery, radiation, and injury may also contribute. Incomplete blinking was associated with a two-fold increase in evaporative dry eye, greater meibomian gland loss, poorer meibum, and thinner tear-film lipid layer. Greater screen exposure can reduce blinking and worsen ocular-surface disease in adults and children.

After sodium valproate, lamotrigine and levetiracetam performed next best on time to treatment failure, so the January 2025 update made all 3 first-line monotherapy options subject to MHRA restrictions. Document sections:
  Heading: 4.3.1. Sturge-Weber-syndrome
  Content: Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS) is an uncommon sporadic neurocutaneous disorder, formerly categorized as a phakomatosis. Among its three variants, types 1 and 2 are suggested by a characteristic facial port-wine angioma, whereas type 3 has leptomeningeal angiomatosis without that readily visible feature. Seizures occur in 75 %–90 % of cases. Extensive pial angiomatosis causes seizures and can affect one lobe or much of a hemisphere; the epileptogenic cortex is presumed to extend beyond visible angiomatous plaques. Native bone-setting computed tomography (CT), contrast-enhanced T1W MRI and especially contrast-enhanced fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) help define the extent of calcified pial angiomatosis. Approximately 60 % of patients develop drug resistance. Patients whose plaques remain strictly unilateral are suitable candidates for disconnection, with reported long-term seizure freedom of 80 %.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Introduction
  Content: IIH involves raised cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure without an identified cause. Headache, visual disturbance and papilloedema are typical, while the rest of the neurological examination is generally normal. Headache is the most frequently reported symptom, occurring in 7599% of cases as printed in the document. Pseudotumour Cerebri Syndrome (PTCS) is another term that also covers secondary causes. Heinrich Quincke described the condition in the late nineteenth century and attributed it to excessive CSF production. Later names included ‘pseudotumor cerebri’ in 1904 and ‘benign intracranial hypertension’ in 1955; reports of visual loss made the description ‘benign’ inappropriate. Subsequent terminology included PTCS and IIH. The classical modified Dandy criteria suggest that IIH diagnosis requires symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (ICP), no focal neurological signs other than unilateral or bilateral sixth nerve palsies, increased CSF opening pressure with otherwise normal CSF, normal brain imaging without hydrocephalus, and no alternative explanation for raised ICP. Some authors consider these criteria sufficient. Friedman’s criteria provide an alternative. For definite IIH, they require A) papilloedema; B) a normal neurological examination apart from cranial nerve abnormalities; C) normal brain parenchyma without hydrocephalus, a mass, a structural lesion or abnormal meningeal enhancement on MRI with and without gadolinium in typical patients (female and obese), with MRI with and without gadolinium plus MRV for others; if MRI cannot be obtained or is contraindicated, contrast-enhanced CT may be used; D) normal CSF composition; and E) opening pressure of ≥280mm CSF in children, or 250mm CSF if the child is not sedated and not obese, measured during a properly performed lumbar puncture. Without papilloedema, IIH can still be diagnosed under these criteria when abducens nerve palsy and all of B-E are present. The document also describes diagnosis with B-E plus at least three of four imaging features: empty sella, flattening of the posterior globe, enlargement of the perioptic subarachnoid space with or without optic nerve tortuosity, and transverse venous sinus stenosis. A ‘probable’ diagnosis is possible with A-D and bilateral papilloedema when CSF pressure does not meet the diagnostic threshold in E. Diagnosis requires exclusion of underlying structural causes, including malignancy or autoimmune conditions. Potential imaging findings include secondary empty sella syndrome, flattened globes, abnormal optic nerve sheaths, optic nerve protrusion, posterior globe flattening and transverse sinus stenosis. A UK cohort reported IIH incidence of 0.71 per 100,000 among children aged 1-16 years, rising with age and weight to 4.18 per 100,000 in obese boys aged 12-15 years and 10.7 per 100,000 in obese girls of the same age. Other estimates for children range from 0.17 to 1.32 per 100,000. Treatment aims to protect vision and relieve headache. Weight control has been effective in adults. Drug treatment commonly involves acetazolamide or topiramate; a possible weight-loss benefit from topiramate has not yet been established in larger studies. Procedural options include CSF diversion, such as ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VPS) or lumboperitonral shunt, optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF), and venous sinus stenting (VSS). Choices depend on symptoms, the extent of visual loss and local availability. Lumbar puncture (LP) has been examined for both diagnosis and treatment, but doubts about its therapeutic efficacy have increased interest in surgery. How best to measure pressure and respond clinically to elevated measurements remains uncertain. With no randomised control trials of paediatric IIH management, this three-round Delphi study examined diagnosis, investigation and management to provide clinicians with recommendations from experienced professionals, following international adult consensus recommendations.

Document sections:
  Heading: Abstract
  Content: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the most frequent chronic complication of herpes zoster. It is a form of neuropathic pain that can substantially impair quality of life, particularly in older or immunocompromised people, despite the availability of vaccination. This review examines the effectiveness and safety of oral and topical medicines for PHN-related neuropathic pain. It draws on 49 scientific publications identified through PubMed, PubMedCentral, NCBI and Via Medica Journals and published between 2008–2024. Pharmacological treatment includes several oral and topical drug groups. Gabapentinoids and tricyclic anti-depressants are regarded as first-line options; lidocaine 5% patches have that position in some circumstances. Capsaicin 8% and opioids are considered second-line options. Because monotherapy relatively often fails to control pain, multimodal treatment is increasingly used. PHN remains difficult to manage, and the review emphasizes combining medicines with different mechanisms of action and selecting treatment according to the individual clinical situation.

Conditions:

  Name: intracranial hypertension
  Synonyms:
    - elevated ICP
  Description: Sustained ICP elevation is a measurable secondary insult after severe TBI and may compromise cerebral perfusion or lead to herniation.
  Clinical presentation: Possible warning findings include neurological decline, new pupillary asymmetry, or an unreactive dilated pupil, although physiological changes can precede an observable examination change.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: ICP monitoring with EVD
      Purpose: Measure pressure and permit CSF drainage.
      When indicated: When invasive monitoring is indicated, especially in comatose patients with structural damage on initial CT.
      Interpretation: An EVD connected to an external strain-gauge transducer is the stated measurement standard. An initial treatment threshold of 22 mm Hg is useful; interpretation should also account for duration and trend.
    - Test: Intraparenchymal ICP transducer
      Purpose: Monitor pressure when selected instead of an EVD.
      When indicated: When ICP monitoring is clinically indicated.
      Interpretation: Provides reliable pressure measurements but cannot drain CSF.
    - Test: Serial neurological examinations and head CT
      Purpose: Assess deterioration and identify evolving structural lesions.
      When indicated: Alongside ICP monitoring or when more advanced monitoring is unavailable.
      Interpretation: Monitoring pressure alone does not replace clinical and radiographic reassessment.
    - Test: MAP challenge
      Purpose: Assess cerebral autoregulation and help individualize CPP goals.
      When indicated: Consider when raised ICP does not respond to initial therapy.
      Interpretation: In a patient with a closed cranium, rising ICP as MAP increases indicates impaired autoregulation; falling or substantially unchanged ICP indicates intact autoregulation.
    - Test: PRx
      Purpose: Continuously assess pressure autoregulation to inform CPP targets.
      When indicated: When the required technical expertise and equipment are available.
      Interpretation: The guideline describes PRx slope > 0.13 as impaired autoregulation and PRx slope < 0.13 as intact autoregulation.

      - Persistently elevated ICP predicts a poor outcome.

Conditions:

  Name: Gestational hypertension
  Description: Hypertension first appearing after 20 weeks of pregnancy without significant proteinuria.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Full assessment in secondary care
      Purpose: Evaluate gestational hypertension and factors requiring closer assessment and follow-up.
      When indicated: At presentation, by a healthcare professional trained in managing hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
      Interpretation: Factors requiring additional assessment and follow-up include nulliparity, age 40 years or older, pregnancy interval of more than 10 years, family history of pre-eclampsia, multi-fetal pregnancy, BMI of 35 kg/m2 or more, gestational age at presentation, previous pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension, and pre-existing vascular or kidney disease.
    - Test: Blood pressure measurement
      Purpose: Assess severity and response to treatment.
      When indicated: For hypertension, once or twice a week depending on blood pressure until it is 135/85 mmHg or less; for severe hypertension, every 15 to 30 minutes until it is less than 160/110 mmHg.
      Interpretation: Once antihypertensive treatment is given, the target is 135/85 mmHg or less.
    - Test: Dipstick proteinuria testing
      Purpose: Monitor for proteinuria.
      When indicated: Once or twice a week alongside blood pressure measurement for hypertension; daily during admission for severe hypertension.
      Interpretation: A result of 1+ or more prompts quantification with albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio.
    - Test: Full blood count, liver function and renal function
      Purpose: Monitor maternal haematological, liver and kidney status.
      When indicated: At presentation and then weekly.
    - Test: Placental growth factor (PLGF)-based testing
      Purpose: Help rule out pre-eclampsia.
      When indicated: On 1 occasion if pre-eclampsia is suspected, between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days of pregnancy.
    - Test: Fetal heart auscultation
      Purpose: Assess fetal heart activity.
      When indicated: At every antenatal appointment.
    - Test: Ultrasound for fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume assessment
      Purpose: Assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume.
      When indicated: At diagnosis; if findings are normal, repeat every 2 to 4 weeks if clinically indicated. If severe hypertension persists, repeat every 2 weeks.
    - Test: Umbilical artery doppler velocimetry
      Purpose: Assess the fetal circulation.
      When indicated: At diagnosis; if findings are normal, repeat every 2 to 4 weeks if clinically indicated. In severe gestational hypertension, subsequent monitoring is determined by scan findings.
    - Test: Cardiotocography (CTG)
      Purpose: Assess fetal status.
      When indicated: For gestational hypertension, only if clinically indicated; for severe gestational hypertension, at diagnosis and subsequently if clinically indicated.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: After birth, offer women still receiving antihypertensive treatment a medical review 2 weeks after transfer to community care. Offer all women a medical review 6 to 8 weeks after birth.
    Recommended tests:
      - Measure blood pressure daily for the first 2 days after birth and at least once between day 3 and day 5.
      - Measure blood pressure as clinically indicated if antihypertensive treatment changes after birth.
    Long term effects:
      - After gestational hypertension in a previous or current pregnancy, hypertension of any type in a future pregnancy occurs in approximately 22% (1 in 5 women), pre-eclampsia in approximately 7% (1 in 14 women), gestational hypertension in between approximately 11% and 15% (up to 1 in 7 women), and chronic hypertension in approximately 3% (up to 1 in 34 women).

Document sections:
  Heading: Treatment of chronic hypertension
  Content: Offer pregnant women with chronic hypertension advice on weight management, exercise, healthy eating and reducing dietary salt, consistent with NICE guidance for hypertension in adults. Continue an existing pregnancy-safe antihypertensive or change to a suitable alternative unless sustained systolic pressure is less than 110 mmHg, sustained diastolic pressure is less than 70 mmHg, or symptomatic hypotension occurs. Offer treatment to an untreated woman when sustained systolic pressure is 140 mmHg or higher or sustained diastolic pressure is 90 mmHg or higher; aim for 135/85 mmHg with medicines. Consider labetalol, then nifedipine if labetalol is unsuitable, then methyldopa if both are unsuitable; consider existing treatment, adverse effects, fetal and other risks, and preference. Offer aspirin 75 mg to 150 mg once daily from 12 weeks. If pre-eclampsia is suspected, offer PLGF-based testing between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days to help rule it out. [2019; 2019, amended 2023] At publication in June 2019, some nifedipine brands were manufacturer-contraindicated in pregnancy, so check the preparation's product information. Aspirin lacked UK authorisation for this indication despite common use and, in England, requires a prescription rather than pharmacy sale for prevention of pre-eclampsia.

question: Most common intracranial tumor in adults is -

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Goldbrunner et al. 2021 EANO guideline on the diagnosis and management of meningiomas__JC__000135
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Goldbrunner et al. 2021 EANO guideline on the diagnosis and management of meningiomas
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Abstract
  Content: Meningiomas are the most frequent intracranial tumors, but the small number of controlled trials has contributed to differences in care between countries and centers. Advances in molecular genetics and trial evidence prompted the European Association of Neuro-Oncology (EANO) to revise its guidance. Neuroimaging, principally MRI, usually provides an initial diagnosis, sometimes incidentally. Observation with serial imaging is suitable for a substantial proportion of patients, particularly those who are asymptomatic or elderly. Definitive WHO classification requires tissue, generally obtained through surgery. Gene-panel sequencing and genomic methylation profiling have an emerging diagnostic role. Complete removal, including affected dura, is often curative. Tumors that require treatment but are inoperable or recurrent may receive radiosurgery when size and nearby critical structures permit, or fractionated RT. Combined surgery and irradiation are used increasingly, although the timing, technique, and dose of RT remain disputed. Somatostatin receptor-targeted radionuclide treatment and all systemic drug approaches remain experimental. Bevacizumab and multikinase inhibitors directed at vascular endothelial growth factor receptor have produced the most encouraging, though modest, drug results; no standard systemic treatment has been established.

Document sections:
  Heading: 4.1.2. Neurology [63]
  Content: Ventricular-outflow obstruction, especially from cerebellar or tectal lesions, can cause raised intracranial pressure and obstructive hydrocephalus. Headache and nausea or vomiting are common; increased head circumference may be the sole presenting sign in infants. Focal manifestations include weakness, sensory loss, language or cognitive difficulty, personality change and declining school or athletic performance. Cortical lesions often cause focal deficits or seizures. Brainstem lesions can produce fatigue, ataxia and multiple cranial neuropathies. Cerebellar lesions can cause impaired coordination or balance, raised-pressure signs and/or 6th cranial nerve palsy. Some posterior-fossa tumors extend through cerebellar peduncles into both brainstem and cerebellum; involvement of the area postrema can cause vomiting without other signs of raised pressure. Frontal, temporal and parietal tumors are more often associated with seizures than occipital tumors, and cortical lesions more often than deeper noncortical lesions. Gangliogliomas and dysplastic neuroepithelial tumours can be associated with chronic drug-resistant epilepsy. Infratentorial tumors seldom cause seizures.

Descripción de las reacciones adversas seleccionadas
1Las anomalías hematológicas y la linfadenopatía pueden o no estar asociadas a la reacción farmacológica con eosinofilia y síntomas sistémicos (DRESS)/síndrome de hipersensibilidad (ver sección 4.4 y Trastornos del sistema inmunológico).
2La erupción cutánea también se ha notificado como parte de este síndrome, también conocido como DRESS. Este síndrome se asocia con un patrón variable de síntomas sistémicos entre los que se incluyen fiebre, linfadenopatía, edema facial y anomalías de la sangre, hígado y riñón. El síndrome de hipersensibilidad muestra un amplio espectro de gravedad clínica y en raras ocasiones puede producir coagulación intravascular diseminada y fallo multiorgánico. Es importante resaltar que incluso cuando la erupción cutánea no es evidente, pueden aparecer manifestaciones tempranas de hipersensibilidad (ej. fiebre, linfadenopatía). Si tales signos y síntomas aparecen, el paciente debe ser evaluado inmediatamente y se debe suspender el tratamiento con lamotrigina si no se puede establecer una etiología alternativa (ver sección 4.4).
3Estas reacciones adversas se han notificado durante otros usos clínicos. Se ha notificado que la administración de lamotrigina puede empeorar los síntomas en pacientes con enfermedad de Parkinson preexistente, así como producir en casos aislados efectos extrapiramidales y coreoatetosis en pacientes sin enfermedad previa.
4La insuficiencia hepática normalmente aparece en asociación con reacciones de hipersensibilidad, pero también se han comunicado casos aislados sin la aparición de signos de hipersensibilidad.
5En ensayos clínicos en adultos, aparecieron erupciones cutáneas hasta en un 8-12% de los pacientes tratados con lamotrigina y en un 5-6% de los pacientes a los que se les administró placebo. Las erupciones cutáneas dieron lugar a la retirada del tratamiento con lamotrigina en un 2% de los pacientes. La erupción cutánea, normalmente de aspecto maculopapular, aparece generalmente en las primeras 8 semanas tras el inicio del tratamiento y desaparece al retirar la lamotrigina (ver sección 4.4).
Se han dado casos de erupciones cutáneas graves potencialmente mortales, que incluyen el síndrome de Stevens-Johnson, necrólisis epidérmica tóxica (síndrome de Lyell) y reacción farmacológica con eosinofilia y síntomas sistémicos (DRESS). Aunque la mayoría de los pacientes se recupera con la retirada del tratamiento con lamotrigina, algunos pacientes experimentan lesiones cutáneas irreversibles, que raramente pueden provocar la muerte (ver sección 4.4).
El riesgo global de aparición de erupción cutánea está altamente asociado con:
- dosis iniciales elevadas de lamotrigina que exceden la pauta de escalada de dosis recomendada (ver sección 4.2).
- uso concomitante de valproato (ver sección 4.2).
En tratamientos de larga duración con lamotrigina se ha notificado una disminución de la densidad mineral del hueso, osteopenia, osteoporosis y fracturas. Se desconoce el mecanismo por el cual la lamotrigina afecta al metabolismo del hueso.
Notificación de sospechas de reacciones adversas
Es importante notificar las sospechas de reacciones adversas al medicamento tras su autorización. Ello permite una supervisión continuada de la relación beneficio/riesgo del medicamento. Se invita a los profesionales sanitarios a notificar las sospechas de reacciones adversas a través del Sistema Español de Farmacovigilancia de Medicamentos de Uso Humano: www.notificaRAM.es.

  Heading: 1.1 Referral after a first seizure or remission and assessing risk of a second seizure
  Content: After a first suspected seizure, urgently refer children, young people and adults for assessment within 2 weeks. Adults should see a clinician experienced in first-seizure assessment and epilepsy diagnosis; children and young people should see a paediatrician with that expertise. Refer urgently for assessment within 2 weeks when seizures return after remission. After a first seizure, assess the individual's likelihood of another seizure. In adults, check potentially modifiable contributors: mental health problems, including depression, anxiety, psychosis or alcohol or substance misuse; vascular risks, including diabetes, hypertension and atrial fibrillation; and sepsis. Compared with children whose first seizure is febrile, those with a first afebrile seizure have greater risk of another afebrile seizure, particularly within 6 to 12 months. Complicated febrile seizures lasting longer than 10 minutes or accompanied by features such as one-sided weakness may carry greater epilepsy risk, especially alongside other predispositions. Discuss each person's mental, physical and social risks and possible modifications with them and, where appropriate, their family and carers. After a first seizure, explain how to recognise recurrence, give first-aid and initial safety advice, discuss ways to reduce recurrence risk, and identify whom to contact if another seizure occurs before assessment. After a child's first afebrile seizure, tell parents or carers how to obtain urgent assessment through self-referral if it recurs.

Document sections:
  Heading: ● Location of the tumour
  Content: Reported anatomical distributions are 39–40 % in supratentorial midline structures, including the hypothalamus, optic chiasm and nerves, ventricles and other midline sites; 32–36 % in the cerebellum; 13.1–18.0 % in the cerebral cortex; 8.3–10 % in the brainstem; and 3.5–4.5 % in the spinal cord. Resectability depends on site, tumor grade and the risk of lasting neurological injury. Hemispheric and cerebellar tumors are often operable, but perirolandic, mesial temporal or dominant-language locations can make surgery harmful. After cerebellar LGG surgery, patients can have fine-motor, coordination, sensory, oculomotor, cognitive or learning deficits. Posterior-fossa resection can also cause cerebellar mutism syndrome, though less often than medulloblastoma surgery, particularly with involvement of the middle cerebellar peduncle, dentate nucleus or fourth-ventricle floor. Chiasmatic hypothalamic gliomas (CHG) and other optic pathway gliomas may be NF1-related or sporadic, with differing natural history and imaging. NF1-related tumors generally have better PFS, and many need no treatment. Either type can cause visual loss, endocrine disease, hypothalamic symptoms including diencephalic syndrome in young children, or hydrocephalus from third-ventricle obstruction. Complete resection is generally not feasible, although accessible exophytic portions may be removed to improve control. Thalamic pLGGs account for 1–2 % and often present with hemiplegia and/or hemianopsia. Tectal plate gliomas occur predominantly in children, constitute 5 % of pediatric brainstem tumors and typically present with raised intracranial pressure; CSF diversion is usually needed at diagnosis and can often be accomplished by endoscopic third ventriculostomy. Cervico-medullary pLGGs grow slowly and present with lower-brainstem symptoms. Long-term survival is high, but progression or recurrence, including late recurrence, is common; treatment should control local disease while preserving or restoring neurological function. Spinal pLGGs are uncommon and insidious. Young children may have either definite deficits or vague symptoms, delaying diagnosis until symptoms become severe. Infiltration and poorly defined tissue boundaries can obstruct complete removal; indicated resection requires intraoperative neuromonitoring. Feasible gross total resection appears most important for PFS. Repeated chemotherapy may help control disease and lessen morbidity and appears to provide tumor control comparable with radiotherapy.
