Gabapentina atraviesa la placenta humana.
Los datos de un estudio observacional nórdico de más de 1700 embarazos expuestos a gabapentina en el primer trimestre, no mostraron un mayor riesgo de malformaciones congénitas importantes entre los niños expuestos a gabapentina en comparación con los niños no expuestos y en comparación con los niños expuestos a pregabalina, lamotrigina y pregabalina o lamotrigina. Asimismo, no se observó un aumento del riesgo de trastornos del neurodesarrollo en niños expuestos a la gabapentina durante el embarazo.
Hubo limitadas evidencias de un mayor riesgo de bajo peso al nacer y parto prematuro, pero no de muerte fetal, pequeño para la edad gestacional, puntuación de Apgar baja a los 5 minutos y microcefalia en recién nacidos de mujeres expuestas a gabapentina.
Los estudios en animales han mostrado toxicidad reproductiva (ver sección 5.3).
Se puede usar gabapentina durante el primer trimestre de embarazo si fuese necesario clínicamente.
Se ha notificado síndrome de abstinencia neonatal en recién nacidos expuestos a gabapentina en el útero. La exposición concomitante a gabapentina y a opioides durante el embarazo puede incrementar el riesgo de síndrome de abstinencia neonatal. Debe supervisarse atentamente a los recién nacidos.

Lactancia
Gabapentina se excreta en la leche materna. Al desconocer el posible efecto sobre los lactantes, debe prestarse atención cuando se administre gabapentina a madres lactantes. Gabapentina solo se utilizará en madres lactantes, si los beneficios superan claramente los riesgos.

Fertilidad
No hay efectos sobre la fertilidad en los estudios en animales (ver sección 5.3).

Distinguishing vascular from other lesions guides subsequent workup and care. Because the orbital space is restricted, either a soft-tissue or vascular mass may cause proptosis. Document sections:
  Heading: Clinical presentation
  Content: The relative prominence of low back and leg pain matters for DS treatment and prognosis. The authors describe these symptoms as potentially arising from different processes that require different management. Missing the principal source of pain can lead either to insufficient treatment and relief or to unnecessary treatment and complications. Leg pain and radiculopathy generally indicate focal neural compression and are typically treated most directly by decompressing stenotic sites. Without symptomatic deformity or instability, fusion may offer these patients less additional benefit; decompression alone would be less invasive and more cost-effective. Predominantly mechanical low back pain, by contrast, is often taken as a sign of instability, making stabilization of the painful segment particularly important for relief. Several cited studies reported suboptimal results when patients with low back pain received decompression without fusion. CARDS incorporates leg pain, while DSIC and Kulkarni incorporate back pain, but none assesses their relative severity; that comparison has been shown to predict postoperative functional improvement. In the Spine Patient Outcomes Research Trial (SPORT), predominantly leg-related symptoms were associated with less severe pain at baseline and greater improvement after surgery than predominantly low back pain; patients with equally severe symptoms had intermediate outcomes.

  Name: Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma
  Description: These visual field abnormalities can result from compression of, or pathology within, the optic chiasm or the junction between the optic nerve and chiasm. The variant addresses suspected sellar or parasellar disease.
  Clinical presentation: Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma may accompany a sellar or suprasellar mass. Most neoplastic causes develop with gradually progressive visual symptoms; pituitary apoplexy may instead produce headache and rapid visual change.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Pituitary macroadenomas
      Distinguishing features: May extend above the sella and compress the optic chiasm or neighboring optic nerves or tracts.
    - Name: Sellar/suprasellar region meningiomas
      Distinguishing features: May involve sellar, suprasellar or parasellar structures and exert mass effect on the optic nerves or chiasm.
    - Name: Craniopharyngiomas
      Distinguishing features: Suprasellar masses that commonly compress the optic chiasm; the papillary type described in adults is usually solid and enhancing and rarely calcifies.
    - Name: Pituitary apoplexy
      Distinguishing features: Often follows hemorrhagic infarction of an existing adenoma and may cause rapid enlargement, headache and visual changes.
    - Name: Aneurysms
      Distinguishing features: Large lesions of the internal carotid artery or Circle of Willis vessels can compress the optic nerves or chiasm.

      Purpose: Characterize suspected sellar or parasellar pathology, its extent and its relationship to the optic chiasm and neighboring structures.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: Best practices guidelines traumatic brain injury
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Prognostic Assessment
  Content: Severe TBI carries high risks of death and long-term disability, but current markers cannot predict a poor individual outcome with high certainty, particularly in the first weeks. Outcomes acceptable to a patient or family can occur in up to 20% of those still unconscious during the first 4 weeks. Population-validated IMPACT and CRASH TBI models combine initial factors such as age, GCS, pupil responses, and imaging to provide estimates with CI. They are not recommended for exact individual prognostication; describe their probabilities as uncertain estimates and discuss best-case, worst-case, and most-likely possibilities. Studies across neurocritical conditions associate reflexively early do-not-resuscitate orders or life-support withdrawal with worse outcomes independently of other characteristics. Very early long-term predictions after severe TBI are often unreliable, particularly in the first days; clinician expectations and institutional practices may contribute to variable care limits and self-fulfilling poor outcomes. When consistent with patient or family goals, best practice is a trial of aggressive surgery, ICU care, and appropriate intracranial monitoring. A previously advocated minimum of 72 hours is arbitrary and lacks evidence; recovery remains possible after 4 or more weeks unconscious, so longer observation is generally needed. Exceptions include declared brain death, a contrary preinjury advance directive, and surrogate preference for comfort measures alone. Do not use age alone to limit care. Consider frailty, comorbidities, persistent bilateral pupillary nonreactivity, absent neurologic improvement, and injury severity; exclude medication or orbital-injury confounding of pupil findings and sedation, analgesia, or seizures confounding the neurologic examination. The Coma Recovery Scale–Revised reportedly detects consciousness better than qualitative bedside examination and may be considered.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_12
  Name: Hypopituitarism
  Description: Reduced pituitary activity that can follow a head injury of any severity. It may become apparent immediately or hours, weeks or months later.
  Epidemiology: The committee noted that risk is higher after more severe head injuries, although mild injury can also cause the condition.
  Clinical presentation: Manifestations vary by hormone deficiency. Adrenocorticotropic hormone deficiency may cause weakness, fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia or anaemia. Growth hormone deficiency may cause low energy or mood, cognitive or neuropsychiatric symptoms, altered body composition or metabolism, and reduced exercise capacity. Sex hormone deficiency may cause delayed puberty, hot flushes, loss of body hair, reduced libido, menstrual irregularity, erectile dysfunction or reduced fertility. Thyroid-stimulating hormone deficiency may cause slow growth, fatigue, lethargy, cold intolerance or weight gain. Vasopressin deficiency may cause polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia or incontinence.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: sodium levels
      Purpose: Identify a biochemical finding that may prompt investigation for hypopituitarism.
      When indicated: Consider investigations in a person admitted after head injury if sodium remains abnormally low.
      Interpretation: Persistently low levels are a reason to consider further investigation; they do not establish the diagnosis by themselves.
    - Test: blood pressure
      Purpose: Identify a clinical finding that may prompt investigation for hypopituitarism.
      When indicated: Consider investigations in a person admitted after head injury if blood pressure remains low.
      Interpretation: Persistent hypotension can prompt further investigation.
    - Test: investigations for hypopituitarism
      Purpose: Assess suspected pituitary dysfunction after head injury.
      When indicated: Consider for persistent compatible symptoms presenting in primary or community care in the weeks or months after injury, or for persistently low sodium levels or blood pressure during admission.
    - Test: endocrinology investigations
      Purpose: Further assess possible hypopituitarism after discharge.
      When indicated: Consider if compatible symptoms persist or recovery is not as expected.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Symptoms may first appear immediately, hours, weeks or months after the head injury.
    Recommended tests:
      - Consider investigations for hypopituitarism for persistent compatible symptoms or persistently low sodium levels or blood pressure.
      - Consider further endocrinology investigations after discharge if symptoms persist or recovery is not as expected.
    Long term effects:
      - Hormonal, growth, cognitive, metabolic and reproductive difficulties associated with pituitary hormone deficiencies
    Survivorship notes: In people under 16, the committee emphasised urgent referral to a paediatric endocrinologist when hypopituitarism is suspected.

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_07
  Condition: head injury
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: People 16 and over with any specified high-risk feature after head injury.
  Decision rules:
    - Perform CT head imaging if initial emergency department GCS is 12 or less, GCS remains below 15 at 2 hours after injury, an open or depressed skull fracture is suspected, a basal skull fracture sign is present, a post-traumatic seizure or focal neurological deficit occurs, or vomiting occurs more than 1 time.

      Duration cycles: Within 1 hour of identifying the risk factor

    - Name: MRI scanning
      Reason: The guideline advises against using it as the primary investigation for clinically important traumatic brain injury for safety, logistical and resource reasons; it can sometimes provide additional prognostic information.
    - Name: Plain X-rays of the skull
      Reason: Do not use them to diagnose important traumatic brain injury before discussion with a neuroscience unit.
    - Name: Neuroimaging by direct access from the community

  Special considerations: Arrange transfer to an appropriate hospital if CT is indicated but unavailable locally.

  Heading: MRI Head Without and With IV Contrast
  Content: Head MRI may accompany or follow orbital MRI, which is the best initial examination for a suspected optic nerve abnormality. For suspected inflammatory or demyelinating ON, head MRI can assess intracranial disease. Brain MRI lesion features and number can predict subsequent MS risk after a first acute ON episode. Postcontrast 3-D Cube T1-weighted whole-brain MRI has shown high sensitivity and accuracy for enhancement in acute ON. Document sections:
  Heading: History
  Content: Ask about blurred or fluctuating vision, including morning worsening and later improvement; photophobia, redness, tearing, foreign-body sensation, pain, recent ocular procedures and complications, age and speed of onset, persistence, laterality, and modifying conditions. Edema usually develops over weeks, months, or longer, but elevated IOP, substantial inflammation, hydrops, and trauma can produce more abrupt symptoms. Most noninfectious opacities develop gradually, apart from acute medication-related band keratopathy; infectious opacities often appear acutely. Edema caused by inflammation or pressure can resolve when its cause resolves. Edema after neonatal forceps injury may resolve after Descemet’s membrane heals but recur years later if endothelial injury was substantial. Endothelial dysfunction may produce transient blur after waking, humidity, or showering that improves later through evaporation. Most noninflammatory opacities persist; inflammatory infiltrates often resolve with their cause, and some metabolic deposits may respond to treatment. Laterality may distinguish usually unilateral herpes simplex virus keratitis from typically bilateral dystrophies. Low humidity and modest airflow may improve vision in endothelial dysfunction. Visual acuity can understate disability: a patient with mild Fuchs dystrophy edema or granular corneal dystrophy opacity may measure 20/40 or better yet be unable to drive because of glare; lighting, reflections, screens, and higher order aberrations can impair function. Contact lenses, particularly RGP lenses, may improve vision by regularizing the refracting surface. Review ocular disease, surgery, infection, inflammation, trauma, glaucoma, and keratoconus; systemic inflammatory, developmental, metabolic, hereditary, and immune-mediated disease; malabsorption-associated vitamin A deficiency; topical and systemic exposures; contact lens practices; family history; sun exposure, travel, animal exposure, diet, and chemical exposure. Short exposure to Amantadine may cause reversible endothelial dysfunction, whereas long exposure may cause permanent dysfunction. Accidental corneal exposure to chlorhexidine during facial surgical preparation may predispose to endothelial failure. Other exposures noted include carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, Bupropion, Amiodarone, calcium supplements, periocular radiation, chemotherapeutic agents, and Rho kinase inhibitor-related verticillate changes.

  Content: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) provides an early, standardised assessment of brain dysfunction and injury seriousness in relation to outcome. Eye opening, verbal response and motor response receive independent numerical assessments, which are added to produce a total from 3 for no response in any domain to 15 for no responsiveness deficit.   Content: Patients may have no symptoms; when symptoms occur, abnormal uterine bleeding is the most common. Abdominal pain, pelvic pain, and infertility may also occur. One in four reproductive-aged women with abnormal bleeding has an endometrial polyp in the cavity. Evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding should establish its cause and severity, associated symptoms, and comorbidities. A thorough medical and surgical history helps exclude other causes. No bleeding pattern is diagnostic of a polyp, but the bleeding history should be characterized; menorrhagia and intermenstrual spotting are reported most often. Tamoxifen, commonly used for breast cancer, can act as an agonist or antagonist in tissues bearing estrogen receptors. Clinical examination should include a general assessment, bimanual examination, and sterile speculum examination.   Content: Ventricular-outflow obstruction, especially from cerebellar or tectal lesions, can cause raised intracranial pressure and obstructive hydrocephalus. Cortical lesions often cause focal deficits or seizures. Brainstem lesions can produce fatigue, ataxia and multiple cranial neuropathies. question: Which of the following antiepileptic drugs acts by affecting the levels of GABA?

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Bęben et al. 2024 Post herpetic neuralgia currently available oral and topical medications in the management of pain__JC__000099
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Bęben et al. 2024 Post herpetic neuralgia currently available oral and topical medications in the management of pain
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Gabapentinoids.
  Content: Gabapentin and pregabalin were initially used for epilepsy and are now recommended first-line for PHN and other neuropathic pain. Although structurally related to gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), they do not bind its receptors; they attach to the α2δ-1 subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels. Proposed analgesic mechanisms include limiting excessive, α2δ-1-dependent release of neurotransmitters involved in pain transmission, reducing α2δ-1 accumulation in synaptic vesicles of spinal dorsal root ganglia, and activating descending noradrenergic inhibition. Neither drug binds plasma proteins or undergoes metabolism by liver enzymes, and they do not alter concentrations of drugs metabolized by cytochrome CYP450. Both are eliminated chiefly in urine. Depending on dose, gabapentin has a half-life of five to seven hours; pregabalin has a half-life of about 6.3 hours. Oral gabapentin is supplied in immediate-release and extended-release forms. Studies found immediate-release gabapentin more effective than placebo for PHN symptoms at 1,800mg to 3,600mg per day. Its non-linear gastrointestinal absorption lowers bioavailability as doses rise, complicating titration to an effective dose without adverse reactions. A Cochrane Review found the extended-release formulations gastroretentive gabapentin and gabapentin enacarbil more effective than placebo for PHN; these formulations are easier to dose and have greater bioavailability. Gastroretentive gabapentin is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract for up to 15h and is taken once daily. Its recommended starting dose is 900mg per day, followed by gradual titration to a therapeutic dose over two weeks. An 11-week, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled phase three study demonstrated PHN pain control with 1,800mg per day. Gabapentin enacarbil is a prodrug that needs less frequent administration than immediate-release gabapentin and produces less variation in plasma concentration. Its minimum therapeutic dose is 1,200mg per day, reached through gradual dosing over four days. Compared with gabapentin, pregabalin has high bioavailability and linear gastrointestinal absorption, making its pharmacokinetics more predictable; maximum plasma concentration follows oral dosing after one hour. An assessment based on 14 randomized clinical trials found pregabalin more effective than gabapentin for PHN pain but associated with more frequent side-effects. Its recommended starting dose is 150mg/day in two or three divided doses, with gradual titration over about one week; the maximum recommended, relatively well-tolerated therapeutic dose is 600mg/day. Common central nervous system effects include dizziness, reported in 19% when taking gabapentin, and balance disorders and drowsiness, with drowsiness reported at 14% for gabapetin. With pregabalin, dizziness occurred in 24% and drowsiness in 17%. Moderate weight gain can occur with gabapentinoids and may affect up to 25% of pregabalin users, although for most patients receiving pregabalin the gain within a year does not exceed 7% of baseline weight. Bloating, constipation, altered appetite and nausea are relatively common. Gabapentinoids may also produce withdrawal symptoms. In available case reports, symptoms after stopping gabapentin began between 12 hours and seven days after the last dose; agitation, confusion, tremor, insomnia, gastric symptoms and excessive sweating were most frequent, while akathisia, catatonia and convulsions were reported in isolated cases. Renal failure raises the risk of gabapentinoid toxicity, particularly in dialysis patients, because these drugs are excreted in urine. Toxicity may present with sedation, confusion, impaired balance, tremors, myoclonus or ataxia. Respiratory depression has been described with combined gabapentinoid and opioid administration. Particular care is therefore required in older people, among whom respiratory disease and opioid use are common.

  Content: Early FG manifestations may include localized pain, swelling, erythema, and warmth. Progression can produce fever, chills, generalized weakness, and eventually septic shock. Diagnosis primarily depends on clinical assessment because treatment is urgent, and suspicion warrants prompt surgical consultation. Among FG severity and outcome scores, Fournier Gangrene Severity Index (FGSI) and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) are described as the most reliable predictors of in-hospital mortality. Interpretation: Pain control in post-herpetic neuralgia remains difficult despite the availability of oral and topical medicines. The authors consider gabapentinoids and tricyclic antidepressants the principal oral first-line options, while emphasizing that treatment should be tailored to the patient and may require medicines with different mechanisms of action. The place of lidocaine 5% patches remains uncertain because efficacy findings and guideline positions conflict. Capsaicin 8% and opioids are generally positioned as second-line options, although opioids are sometimes placed in the third line because of their risks and limited efficacy for neuropathic pain.

Comparison with prior evidence: The review reports that an analysis of 14 randomized clinical trials found pregabalin more effective than gabapentin for pain relief in post-herpetic neuralgia, but associated with more frequent adverse effects. A meta-analysis of four randomized trials involving 1,272 patients found a single application of an 8% capsaicin patch significantly more effective than 0.014% topical capsaicin. Evidence for lidocaine 5% patches is inconsistent: some studies reported significant pain reduction versus placebo, whereas a double-blind trial found no significant difference. In one study, gabapentin combined with morphine controlled pain more effectively than either drug alone, but adverse events were frequent. These findings are evidence discussed by the authors, not results of new trials conducted in this review.

Document sections:
  Heading: Why this is important
  Content: Available strategies include permanent urethral or suprapubic catheterisation, intermittent self-catheterisation, penile sheath collection systems and pads. Evidence on acceptability to patients, families and carers is very sparse; existing research mainly concerns spinal injury and may apply to other neurological diseases. These long-term methods affect health and quality of life, so informed choice requires evidence about benefits and risks. Little evidence establishes which methods are most likely to cause renal impairment, urinary stones, infections, hydronephrosis or bladder malignancy, and comparative quality-of-life effects for patients, families and carers are unknown. Research is complicated by heterogeneous neurological conditions, long treatment courses and cognitive impairment in some groups. Proposed prospective disease-specific cohorts could compare methods using generic and disease-specific quality-of-life measures and prospective screening for renal impairment, stones and infection. Family and carer quality of life deserves particular attention, especially when they care for someone with cognitive impairment.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_03
  Name: Ischaemic priapism
  Synonyms:
    - Low-Flow or Veno-Occlusive Priapism
  Description: A persistent erection with rigid corpora cavernosa and minimal or absent cavernosal arterial inflow. Progressive hypoxia, hypercapnia, glucopenia and acidosis develop within the corpora. Beyond 4 hours, the condition resembles a compartment syndrome and requires emergency intervention.
  Epidemiology: It accounts for > 95% of priapism episodes. No specific cause is identified in most cases. It may follow intracavernosal injection of erectogenic agents in 0.4-35% of cases; the reported risk after prostaglandin E1 injection is < 1%. SCD accounts for 63% of childhood cases and is the primary cause in 23% of adult cases.
  Clinical presentation: The corpora are generally fully rigid and tender, the glans remains soft, and penile pain is usually severe and progressive. Erection duration is the most significant predictor of irreversible consequences, including erectile dysfunction. After 48-72 hours from onset, intervention may relieve pain and the erection but offers little clinical benefit in preventing long-term erectile dysfunction.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: malignant priapism
      Distinguishing features: A rare infiltrative form associated with regional tumour invasion, metastasis or haematological malignancy.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Comprehensive medical and sexual history
      Purpose: Identify the priapism subtype and possible cause.
      When indicated: At presentation.
      Interpretation: Assess SCD and other haematological abnormalities; pelvic, genital or perineal trauma; erection duration and pain; prescribed and recreational drugs; previous episodes and their treatment; and erectile function before the current episode.
    - Test: Examination of the genitalia, perineum and abdomen
      Purpose: Assess rigidity, tenderness and possible underlying disease.
      When indicated: During diagnostic evaluation.
      Interpretation: Fully rigid, tender corpora with a soft glans support ischaemic priapism. Pelvic examination may reveal pelvic or genitourinary malignancy.
    - Test: Full blood count, white blood cell count with blood cell differential, platelet count and coagulation profile
      Purpose: Assess anaemia and detect haematological abnormalities.
      When indicated: During initial laboratory evaluation.
    - Test: Corporal blood aspiration and blood gas analysis
      Purpose: Distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism.
      When indicated: As an initial investigation.
      Interpretation: The first corporal aspirate is usually dark; typical ischaemic values are pO2 < 30 mmHg, pCO2 > 60 mmHg and pH < 7.25.
    - Test: Haemoglobinopathy screen, including haemoglobin electrophoresis when indicated
      Purpose: Investigate SCD or another haemoglobinopathy.
      When indicated: For patients with low-flow priapism at high risk of sickle cell disease or thalassemia; further testing is guided by the history, examination and laboratory findings.
    - Test: Colour duplex ultrasound of the penis and perineum
      Purpose: Distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism and assess cavernosal flow.
      When indicated: After clinical diagnosis and before corporal aspiration.
      Interpretation: Sluggish or absent cavernosal blood flow supports ischaemic priapism. Flow assessed after intervention can be misleading because of reperfusion.
    - Test: Penile MRI
      Purpose: Assess cavernosal smooth-muscle viability and penile fibrosis.
      When indicated: Selected cases of prolonged or refractory ischaemic priapism, including delayed presentation (> 48 hours).
      Interpretation: A prospective study of 38 patients reported 100% sensitivity for predicting non-viable smooth muscle when MRI findings were compared with corpus cavernosum biopsies.
    - Test: Corpus cavernosum biopsy
      Purpose: Assess smooth-muscle necrosis to inform decisions about immediate penile prosthesis insertion.
      When indicated: Selected refractory or delayed cases (> 48 hours).
      Interpretation: Evidence of necrosis suggests that shunting is likely to fail.
  Follow up:
    Recommended tests:
      - Assessment of erectile function
      - Assessment for penile fibrosis and deformity
    Long term effects:
      - Corporal smooth-muscle necrosis and fibrosis
      - Permanent erectile dysfunction
      - Penile scarring, shortening or deformity
      - Occasional penile tissue loss
    Survivorship notes: These consequences may occur despite treatment that successfully resolves the erection. Erectile recovery after shunt surgery is related to episode duration, pre-operative erectile status and age.

Document sections:
  Heading: Observation
  Content: Wider use of neuroimaging has increased incidental diagnoses. Incidental meningiomas occur on brain MRI in 0.9% to 1.0% of the general population. In a prospective 5-year study, none of 64 patients developed tumor-related symptoms during 5 years, despite volume increases of 15% or more in 48 tumors (75%). More than 60% showed growth that eventually limited itself, supporting serial imaging for asymptomatic tumors until sustained radiological or symptomatic growth. In a separate prospectively followed series of 232 untreated patients observed from 1997 to 2013, Lee et al reported rapid growth in 59 tumors (25.4%). Predictors were size (odds ratio per cm3 1.07, P = .000), absent calcification (odds ratio 3.87, P = .004), peritumoral edema (odds ratio 2.74, P = .025), and T2-weighted hyperintensity or isointensity (odds ratio 3.76, P = .049); those authors proposed a weighted rapid-growth score. Whether every incidental tumor requires prolonged follow-up is debated. Islim et al proposed individualized low-, medium-, and high-risk monitoring based on age, performance status, comorbidities, and MRI features comprising signal intensity, edema, proximity to neurovascular structures, and size. Moreau et al developed diagnostic and prognostic methods and an app. By consensus, suspected meningiomas and WHO grade 1 tumors should receive annual MRI for 5 years, after which the interval may be doubled (good practice point).

  Content: Only personnel competent in head-injury assessment should undertake inpatient observation. If such a person deteriorates at any point after the initial 2-hour period, return to half-hourly observation and repeat the original schedule. [2003] A supervising doctor should urgently reassess agitation or unusual behaviour; a GCS reduction of 1 point sustained for at least 30 minutes, especially in motor response; a fall of 3 or more points in eye opening or verbal response, or 2 or more in motor response; severe or worsening headache or persistent vomiting; or emerging or changing neurological findings, including unequal pupils or asymmetric facial or limb movements. If possible, have another observation-competent staff member promptly verify deterioration before contacting the doctor, reducing observer variation and unnecessary referral; if immediate verification is unavailable, contact the doctor without waiting. Once such a change is confirmed, consider immediate CT, reassess clinically and manage accordingly.   Content: The guideline uses GRADE to support decisions about stroke-related visual impairment. Table 14 and Figure 14 bring together its recommendations and expert-consensus statements. Visual problems affect about 75% of stroke survivors by reported prevalence and about 60% by reported incidence. Rowe and colleagues identified impaired central acuity in 56%, eye-movement abnormalities in 40%, field loss in 28%, visual inattention in 27% and perceptual disorders in 5%. Assessment and care are unequal; females, people of black ethnicity, those with lower socioeconomic status or educational attainment, and older people are described as particularly disadvantaged. Stroke may disrupt interpretation and integration of sensory input; an estimated 70% of perceived sensory information is visual. Visual impairment is negatively associated with rehabilitation and quality of life and can affect mobility, navigation, interaction, self-care, independence, mood and driving. Screening should therefore cover acuity, fields, neglect and eye movements so that a survivor whose impairment breaches applicable driving rules is not discharged without driving-related information; requirements vary between countries, and follow-up should reassess visual requirements. Treating diplopia with prisms or a patch may restore visual function needed for driving. No standardised stroke-vision detection protocol currently exists. Variation in screening, specialist referral, treatment, information and communication adapted to visual impairment contributes to unmet need, inequity and poorer patient experience. Norup et al. identified visual problems in 24% at initial neurological examination; some who declined further assessment said they had not noticed a problem. Among survivors with neglect, unawareness of visuospatial deficits predicted poorer daily functioning more strongly than deficit severity or time since stroke. An estimated 40–60% with new visual impairment do not or cannot report symptoms; some remain unaware despite caregivers observing collisions or accidents. Missed deficits may mean missed rehabilitation, and unrecognised field loss may create road-safety risks.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: Saposnik et al. 2024 Diagnosis and Management of Cerebral Venous Thrombosis A Scientific Statement From the American Hea
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: BRAIN AND VASCULAR IMAGING FOR THE DIAGNOSIS OF CVT
  Content: Conventional computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is often obtained first for nonspecific acute symptoms. Suspicion can arise from direct thrombus visualization, absent venous filling, tissue consequences of venous obstruction—venous infarction, edema, hemorrhagic transformation, intracranial hypertension, or hydrocephalus—or vascular consequences such as enlarged veins. Supplemental Table 2 summarizes imaging difficulties. Thin-slice CT can improve direct visualization. On noncontrast CT, increased hemoglobin and red blood cells within a thrombus produce hyperattenuation, termed the dense vessel sign. A serpiginous or linear venous hyperdensity, described as the cord or string sign, or a dense triangle sign can remain visible up to 14 days after symptom onset. Indirect CT and MRI clues include low-density areas that do not follow a usual wedge-shaped infarct pattern or arterial territory, or that spare the overlying cortex. Sagittal sinus or deep cerebral vein involvement can produce bilateral hypodensities. Hemorrhage occurs in up to 40% of patients and may represent hemorrhagic transformation within a hypodense area or intracerebral hemorrhage accompanied by subarachnoid or subdural bleeding; isolated subarachnoid and basal ganglia hemorrhages are uncommon. A juxtacortical C-shaped hyperdensity, the cashew nut sign, has reportedly high specificity but low sensitivity. Bilateral or multifocal hemorrhage is also frequent. A meta-analysis covering 27 publications and 2812 cases estimated CT sensitivity at 0.79 (95% CI, 0.76–0.82) and specificity at 0.90 (95% CI, 0.89– 0.91), below the figures previously described in the 2011 American Heart Association statement. Conventional MRI can show the thrombus directly, but its signal changes with thrombus age as oxyhemoglobin becomes deoxyhemoglobin and methemoglobin. Early thrombus can be isointense or hypointense on T2 and resemble a normal sinus flow void, complicating diagnosis. Time-of-flight magnetic resonance venography (MRV) can likewise mislead when absent flow is not confirmed on T1//T2. Corroboration using gradient-recalled echo, susceptibility-weighted imaging, or contrast-enhanced MRV is often useful. Thrombosed blood produces a blooming artifact on gradient-recalled echo and susceptibility-weighted sequences; for subtle cortical vein thrombosis, their sensitivity and specificity approach 100%. T1-based black-blood imaging is described as promising. MRI detects parenchymal injury secondary to venous occlusion more sensitively than CT; resulting lesions can be bilateral and cross arterial territories. A meta-analysis of 21 studies involving 1773 patients with CVT estimated sensitivity of conventional MRI sequences at 0.82 (95% CI, 0.78–0.85) and specificity at 0.92 (95% CI, 0.91–0.94). The figures illustrate venous-system anatomy and sinus involvement, examples of thrombosis and hemorrhage on noncontrast CT, and venous thrombosis, infarction, edema, and filling defects on MRI. Sinus-involvement percentages in the anatomy figure may exceed 100% because >1 sinus can be affected; internal jugular vein thrombosis there refers to its coexistence with CVT, not isolated jugular thrombosis.

Document sections:
  Heading: 6.7. Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH)/Late-Onset Adrenogential Syndrome (AGS)
  Content: This autosomal recessive condition is attributed to mutation of the 21-hydroxylase gene on chromosome 6 in approximately 90% of congenital adrenal hyperplasia cases, reducing enzyme activity by 30–50%. Most affected people have compound heterozygous or homozygous mutations; a single affected gene does not produce the disease. Approximately 4% of women with hyperandrogenemia have 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Early-cycle 17-OH progesterone above 2 ng/mL calls for exclusion of CAH as a major differential diagnosis of PCOS. Insufficient or absent 21-hydroxylase raises its substrate 17-OH-progesterone, reduces cortisol, increases ACTH, and thereby stimulates adrenal steroid synthesis, including androgen production. A 17-OH progesterone result >2 ng/mL warrants additional assessment. A dexamethasone inhibition test can help exclude Cushing’s syndrome: cortisol suppression is checked the morning after 1 mg of dexamethasone at 11 pm. In an ACTH test, ACTH is given intravenously; a rise in 17-OH progesterone of more than 2.5 ng/mL should prompt genetic testing for 21hydroxylase deficiency. Less common causes of CAH include 11-β-hydroxylase deficiency and a 3-β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase defect. Girls may have no symptoms for a long period. Manifestations range from early pubarche, tall stature, and accelerated bone maturation to clitoral hypertrophy, hirsutism, acne, alopecia, oligo-amenorrhea, and infertility. Future childbearing requires attention because a partner who also carries a mutation creates a risk of a child homozygous for a severe mutation, with very low enzyme activity, severe salt-wasting CAH, and possible genital virilization in girls. The authors advise diagnosing both partners, discussing the risk, and, if necessary, giving cortisol during pregnancy, since later full correction may be difficult or impossible depending on severity. Outside that context, glucocorticoids are recommended only for puberty praecox or accelerated bone age. An anti-androgen pill can regulate cycles and reduce androgens, addressing both hyperandrogenic symptoms and menstrual disturbance. Follicular stimulation can help when pregnancy is desired because ovulation is often insufficient.

  Content: Recurrent infections cause substantial morbidity: they may worsen incontinence, cause malaise or involve the upper urinary tract with possible renal-function loss. In multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease and dementia, infection-related temperature rises can worsen neurological function and can even trigger a multiple sclerosis relapse. retrieved_chunks.document_id: Amin et al. 2024 Consensus recommendations for the assessment and management of idiopathic intracranial hypertension
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Introduction
  Content: IIH involves raised cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure without an identified cause. Headache, visual disturbance and papilloedema are typical, while the rest of the neurological examination is generally normal. Headache is the most frequently reported symptom, occurring in 7599% of cases as printed in the document. Pseudotumour Cerebri Syndrome (PTCS) is another term that also covers secondary causes. Heinrich Quincke described the condition in the late nineteenth century and attributed it to excessive CSF production. Later names included ‘pseudotumor cerebri’ in 1904 and ‘benign intracranial hypertension’ in 1955; reports of visual loss made the description ‘benign’ inappropriate. Subsequent terminology included PTCS and IIH. The classical modified Dandy criteria suggest that IIH diagnosis requires symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (ICP), no focal neurological signs other than unilateral or bilateral sixth nerve palsies, increased CSF opening pressure with otherwise normal CSF, normal brain imaging without hydrocephalus, and no alternative explanation for raised ICP. Some authors consider these criteria sufficient. Friedman’s criteria provide an alternative. For definite IIH, they require A) papilloedema; B) a normal neurological examination apart from cranial nerve abnormalities; C) normal brain parenchyma without hydrocephalus, a mass, a structural lesion or abnormal meningeal enhancement on MRI with and without gadolinium in typical patients (female and obese), with MRI with and without gadolinium plus MRV for others; if MRI cannot be obtained or is contraindicated, contrast-enhanced CT may be used; D) normal CSF composition; and E) opening pressure of ≥280mm CSF in children, or 250mm CSF if the child is not sedated and not obese, measured during a properly performed lumbar puncture. Without papilloedema, IIH can still be diagnosed under these criteria when abducens nerve palsy and all of B-E are present. The document also describes diagnosis with B-E plus at least three of four imaging features: empty sella, flattening of the posterior globe, enlargement of the perioptic subarachnoid space with or without optic nerve tortuosity, and transverse venous sinus stenosis. A ‘probable’ diagnosis is possible with A-D and bilateral papilloedema when CSF pressure does not meet the diagnostic threshold in E. Diagnosis requires exclusion of underlying structural causes, including malignancy or autoimmune conditions. Potential imaging findings include secondary empty sella syndrome, flattened globes, abnormal optic nerve sheaths, optic nerve protrusion, posterior globe flattening and transverse sinus stenosis. A UK cohort reported IIH incidence of 0.71 per 100,000 among children aged 1-16 years, rising with age and weight to 4.18 per 100,000 in obese boys aged 12-15 years and 10.7 per 100,000 in obese girls of the same age. Other estimates for children range from 0.17 to 1.32 per 100,000. Treatment aims to protect vision and relieve headache. Weight control has been effective in adults. Drug treatment commonly involves acetazolamide or topiramate; a possible weight-loss benefit from topiramate has not yet been established in larger studies. Procedural options include CSF diversion, such as ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VPS) or lumboperitonral shunt, optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF), and venous sinus stenting (VSS). Choices depend on symptoms, the extent of visual loss and local availability. Lumbar puncture (LP) has been examined for both diagnosis and treatment, but doubts about its therapeutic efficacy have increased interest in surgery. How best to measure pressure and respond clinically to elevated measurements remains uncertain. With no randomised control trials of paediatric IIH management, this three-round Delphi study examined diagnosis, investigation and management to provide clinicians with recommendations from experienced professionals, following international adult consensus recommendations.

question: All are predisposing causes of cerebral venous thrombosis except:

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Saposnik et al. 2024 Diagnosis and Management of Cerebral Venous Thrombosis A Scientific Statement From the American Hea__JC__000005
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Saposnik et al. 2024 Diagnosis and Management of Cerebral Venous Thrombosis A Scientific Statement From the American Hea
retrieved_chunks.text:
Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: CVT
  Synonyms:
    - cerebral venous thrombosis
  Description: A thrombus affects the dural venous sinuses, cerebral veins, or both. Predisposing conditions may be transient or chronic. Reported factors include oral contraception, pregnancy or the puerperium, hormonal therapy, obesity, infections, dehydration, anemia, autoimmune disease, malignancy, thrombophilia, head trauma, neurosurgical procedures, and lesions compressing a venous sinus.
  Epidemiology: CVT accounts for 0.5% to 3% of strokes. Registry and cohort data suggest that affected people are predominantly <55 years of age and that two-thirds are women. Rates are highest among younger women. Estrogen-based oral contraception and hormonal therapies may increase the odds of CVT nearly 8-fold, with a possible additional interaction with obesity.
  Clinical presentation: Symptoms may arise from raised intracranial pressure or focal parenchymal injury, with or without mass effect. Headache occurs in nearly 90% of cases. Other manifestations include nausea, transient visual obscurations or vision loss (13%–27%), papilledema, diplopia (6%–14%), and other cranial neuropathies (6%–11%). Seizures occur at presentation in approximately 20% to 40%, focal neurological deficits in 20% to 50%, and encephalopathy or coma in up to 20%. Onset is generally more gradual than in other stroke types; the majority present >48 hours after symptom onset. A minority present acutely with thunderclap headache or subarachnoid hemorrhage (<5%) or an abrupt focal neurological deficit (5%–40%).
  Subtypes:
    - Name: cortical vein thrombosis
      Distinguishing features: Small cortical venous thrombi can be inconspicuous and require particular attention to contrast-enhanced or susceptibility-sensitive imaging.
    - Name: deep cerebral vein thrombosis
      Distinguishing features: Deep venous involvement may produce bilateral parenchymal abnormalities; the illustrated findings include bilateral thalamic signal changes.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: computed tomography (CT)
      Purpose: Assess an acute presentation for a visible thrombus and the tissue consequences of venous obstruction.
      When indicated: Often obtained initially when symptoms are nonspecific.
      Interpretation: A hyperattenuating thrombus may produce a dense vessel sign. A cord or string sign or dense triangle sign can persist up to 14 days after symptom onset. Suspicious indirect findings include hypodensities that do not follow an arterial territory, bilateral abnormalities, and hemorrhage. Hemorrhages occur in up to 40% of CVT cases. In a meta-analysis of 27 publications with 2812 cases, CT sensitivity was 0.79 (95% CI, 0.76–0.82) and specificity was 0.90 (95% CI, 0.89– 0.91).
    - Test: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
      Purpose: Identify venous thrombus and associated parenchymal injury.
      When indicated: Used in the initial assessment and alongside venous imaging to establish the diagnosis.
      Interpretation: Thrombus signal changes with age on T1 and T2 sequences; early thrombosis may resemble a normal venous flow void. MRI is more sensitive than CT for parenchymal lesions caused by venous occlusion, which may cross arterial territories or be bilateral. A meta-analysis of 21 studies with 1773 patients with CVT reported sensitivity of 0.82 (95% CI, 0.78–0.85) and specificity of 0.92 (95% CI, 0.91–0.94) for conventional MRI sequences.
    - Test: computed tomographic venography (CTV)
      Purpose: Confirm CVT by depicting the superficial and deep cerebral venous systems.
      When indicated: An optimal confirmatory test and a reasonable alternative to MRI/MRV where resources are limited or pretest probability is low.
      Interpretation: Thrombi appear as venous filling defects. CTV is less sensitive than MRI for cortical vein thrombosis.
    - Test: magnetic resonance venography (MRV)
      Purpose: Confirm thrombosis in the cerebral venous system.
      When indicated: MRI/MRV is the recommended noninvasive confirmatory study.
      Interpretation: Venous filling abnormalities must be assessed with awareness that flow-dependent techniques can produce artifacts or flow gaps.
    - Test: contrast-enhanced MRV
      Purpose: Assess luminal filling directly and improve detection of thrombus in smaller veins.
      When indicated: Useful when findings from noncontrast sequences require corroboration and recommended for diagnosing cortical vein thrombosis.
      Interpretation: Its sensitivity and specificity are comparable to those of CTV; it better distinguishes a low-flow state from a hypoplastic sinus.
    - Test: time-of-flight (TOF) MRV
      Purpose: Image cerebral venous flow without contrast.
      When indicated: Particularly useful when gadolinium administration may be precluded, including pregnancy, breastfeeding, or severe renal failure.
      Interpretation: Complex flow can cause artifacts, and absent flow may not be corroborated by T1 or T2 findings. Compared with 3-dimensional TOF, 2-dimensional TOF is more sensitive when flow is slow.
    - Test: phase-contrast MRV
      Purpose: Provide noncontrast venous imaging.
      Interpretation: Complex flow can cause artifacts. Its use is less frequent because selection of the velocity-encoding parameter is difficult and operator dependent, and acquisition takes longer.
    - Test: gradient-recalled echo
      Purpose: Corroborate suspected venous thrombus through susceptibility-related findings.
      When indicated: Helpful when conventional MRI or flow-dependent MRV is uncertain; recommended for diagnosing cortical vein thrombosis.
      Interpretation: Thrombosed blood produces a blooming artifact, particularly useful for identifying cortical venous thrombi.
    - Test: susceptibility-weighted imaging
      Purpose: Corroborate venous thrombosis, including subtle cortical venous thrombi.
      When indicated: Helpful when conventional findings are uncertain; recommended for diagnosing cortical vein thrombosis.
      Interpretation: Thrombus produces susceptibility-related signal changes. For thrombosed cortical veins, the reported sensitivity and specificity approach 100%.
    - Test: T1-based black-blood imaging
      Purpose: Depict thrombus while suppressing signal from flowing blood.
      Interpretation: Described as a promising advanced MRI technique.
    - Test: digital subtraction angiography
      Purpose: Evaluate cerebral venous anatomy when an invasive intervention is being considered.
      When indicated: Typically reserved for consideration of invasive treatment.
  Genetic molecular:
    - Marker: JAK2 mutations
      Clinical significance: Cited among established predisposing factors for CVT.
    - Marker: protein C and protein S deficiency
      Clinical significance: Cited as genetic thrombophilias associated with CVT; the table notes that either deficiency can also be acquired.
    - Marker: Factor V Leiden mutation
      Clinical significance: Listed among genetic thrombophilias associated with CVT.
    - Marker: Prothrombin 20210A mutation
      Clinical significance: Listed among genetic thrombophilias associated with CVT.
    - Marker: MTHFR (C677T) polymorphism
      Clinical significance: Listed in the table of genetic thrombophilias associated with CVT.
    - Marker: Antithrombin deficiency
      Clinical significance: Listed in the table of genetic thrombophilias associated with CVT.
  Follow up:
    Long term effects:
      - Residual headache, fatigue, low mood, and cognitive difficulties may persist despite functional independence and may hinder a return to previous activities.
      - Epilepsy may affect >10% of individuals with CVT; reported risk factors include seizures at onset, reduced consciousness or focal deficits, initial hemorrhagic lesions, superior sagittal sinus involvement, and craniectomy.
      - Dural arteriovenous fistula can develop after CVT, although CVT can also follow a dural arteriovenous fistula.
      - Recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) after CVT has a reported incidence of 1% to 4% per year; recurrence of CVT is generally reported as <1% to 2% per year.
    Survivorship notes: Overall, 80% to 90% of patients achieve functional independence, defined as a modified Rankin Scale score of 0–2, but persistent symptoms can affect quality of life. Death or dependence occurs in 10% to 15% despite intensive medical treatment. A study of 303 previously employed patients or students found that 42% had not returned to work or school at 6 months, although 87% were functionally independent when assessed. Using subsequent CTV or MRV recanalization to determine anticoagulation duration remains uncertain.

Document sections:
  Heading: Craniopharyngiomas
  Content: Craniopharyngiomas constitute 1% of intracranial tumours and 5–10% of sellar tumours in children. Adamantinomatous lesions are described as invariably cystic, often calcified and limited to the sella; papillary lesions more often look solid or mixed cystic–solid. Wall enhancement and T1-weighted hyperintensity can occur. Calcification, a normal-sized sella and a suprasellar cyst favour adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma over other cystic lesions. Post-contrast 3D T2-FLAIR can help distinguish these lesions from RCCs, whose walls enhance less often. Craniopharyngiomas may behave more aggressively than other cysts. Treatment at diagnosis or upon growth may improve outcomes, particularly below age <65 years and for papillary tumours potentially responsive to medication. Decompression can relieve mass effects; gross total resection can achieve remission, while subtotal resection plus radiation may provide comparable long-term control. Because both surgery and radiation can cause morbidity, observation until documented growth may also be reasonable.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: DISEASE DEFINITION
  Content: DR is an ocular manifestation of diabetic end-organ injury in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Although traditionally considered a retinal microvascular disorder, evidence suggests early neurodegeneration may contribute to vascular abnormalities. OCT and psychophysical testing have identified neural changes before vascular lesions. Early visible findings include microaneurysms in mild NPDR and intraretinal hemorrhages in moderate NPDR. Capillary nonperfusion, cotton wool spots, hemorrhages, venous changes, and IRMA characterize more severe disease. Increased permeability can produce edema or exudates and impair central vision. PDR involves new vessels on the disc, retina, iris, or filtration angle and can cause vitreous hemorrhage, fibrosis, tractional detachment, or neovascular glaucoma. Macular edema or nonperfusion can markedly impair sight at either nonproliferative or proliferative stages. Experimental and clinical findings also implicate inflammation and leukocytes: chronic hyperglycemia increases adhesion molecules, including ICAM-1 and VCAM-1, promoting leukostasis; early blood-ocular barrier disruption and leukocyte accumulation contribute to endothelial-cell and pericyte injury. Inflammatory cytokines are elevated in aqueous and vitreous samples from advanced DR and DME.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 5: Adult. Acute or chronic vision loss, optic nerve abnormality suspected. Initial imaging.
  Content: Neoplastic, inflammatory, ischemic, demyelinating, and traumatic processes can affect the optic nerve or its sheath and produce acute, subacute, or chronic visual loss. Neoplasms tend to develop more slowly than other optic neuropathies. Optic nerve gliomas are the most common primary optic nerve neoplasm; they can be incidental, including in younger patients with neurofibromatosis type 1, or present with visual symptoms or proptosis, and are more likely to be malignant when presenting in adults. Orbital meningiomas can arise from the optic nerve sheath or extend from an intracranial mass; symptomatic sheath lesions classically cause gradual, painless visual decline. Inflammatory and demyelinating ON can resemble one another clinically and radiologically; enhancement reflects edema, inflammation, or demyelination. Possible causes of demyelinating ON include MS, NMO, and MOGAD. ON can also reflect chronic relapsing-remitting inflammatory disease, steroid-dependent recurrence, systemic inflammation, or infection. Enhancement patterns overlap but may help: bilateral simultaneous and longer optic nerve involvement occur more often with MOGAD or NMO than MS, which characteristically affects a shorter unilateral segment. Sheath or perioptic enhancement is more distinctive of MOGAD. Anterior involvement is more typical of MS or MOGAD; NMO tends toward posterior nerves, chiasm, or tracts. Brain and spine MRI may identify associated abnormalities; asymptomatic optic nerve lesions may help distinguish relapsing-remitting MS or clinically isolated syndrome from NMO or MOGAD. Optic perineuritis can arise from idiopathic orbital inflammation, autoimmunity, infection, or other inflammation and may mimic acute demyelinating ON, including visual loss and pain worsened by eye movement. Patients with perineuritis tend to be older and more likely to retain central vision. Ischemic optic neuropathy is anterior, AION, when involving the nerve head, or posterior, PION, when involving the retrobulbar nerve. AION classically causes disc edema and altitudinal field loss. Either form may be nonarteritic, in patients with vascular risk factors such as hypertension or diabetes, or arteritic, most commonly from giant cell arteritis. Imaging aims to identify optic nerve disease, narrow overlapping diagnoses, and inform management.

Document sections:
  Heading: 5.5. Caffeine
  Content: Caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine) is a psychostimulant in tea, coffee, and cacao; more than 70% of adults in modern Western societies consume it daily. At physiological concentrations, it antagonizes adenosine receptors. Two population-based cross-sectional studies associated regular intake with lower DED odds (OR 0.75 and 0.82, respectively, both p < 0.05), but other adjusted studies showed non-significant trends. One study that included caffeine from coffee, tea, cola, and energy drinks found no significant association with Women’s Health Study-defined DED; no dedicated study examined synthetic caffeine from energy drinks. Variation in DED definitions and self-reported intake limits these findings. Two prospective placebo-controlled crossover studies reported a rise in tear meniscus height (+0.08 mm; 95% CI +0.05 to +0.10 mm; p < 0.001) and Schirmer values (+2.96 mm; 95% CI +1.21 to +4.71 mm; p < 0.001) within the first 2 h after one dose of 5–7 mg/kg caffeine. During the ovulatory phase, an observational study associated intake with longer tear breakup time (r = 0.5, p = 0.02) and higher phenol red thread values (r = 0.5, p = 0.01). Mechanisms remain uncertain; stimulation of aqueous secretion through inhibition of 3′,5′-cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase has been hypothesized. Caffeine may protect the ocular surface, but larger, higher-quality prospective or randomized studies are needed before a preventive or therapeutic role in DED can be established.

Document sections:
  Heading: 1.2 Specialist assessment and diagnosis
  Content: After a first suspected seizure, obtain a detailed history and examine the person; involve family or carers when appropriate and use witness descriptions or recordings when available. Obtain a 12-lead ECG to identify cardiac conditions that can resemble epileptic seizures. Consider metabolic disturbances, including hypoglycaemia, as potential causes. Offer brain imaging when a structural cause is suspected. If the history and examination suggest an epileptic seizure and epilepsy is suspected, consider an awake routine EEG to support diagnosis and characterise the seizure or syndrome; do not use EEG to rule epilepsy out. If requested after a first seizure, perform EEG promptly, ideally within 72 hours. Discuss the benefits and risks of hyperventilation and photic stimulation, and use agreed provoking procedures during routine EEG. If routine EEG is normal, consider sleep-deprived EEG after discussing benefits and risks and obtaining agreement. If both studies are normal but uncertainty remains, consider ambulatory EEG for up to 48 hours.

  Name: Lichen simplex chronicus
  Description: Anogenital condition involving persistent itching and lichenification. It can arise on previously normal vulval skin or over another pruritic vulval disorder.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Discussion
  Content: The guideline uses GRADE to support decisions about stroke-related visual impairment. Table 14 and Figure 14 bring together its recommendations and expert-consensus statements. Visual problems affect about 75% of stroke survivors by reported prevalence and about 60% by reported incidence. Rowe and colleagues identified impaired central acuity in 56%, eye-movement abnormalities in 40%, field loss in 28%, visual inattention in 27% and perceptual disorders in 5%. Assessment and care are unequal; females, people of black ethnicity, those with lower socioeconomic status or educational attainment, and older people are described as particularly disadvantaged. Stroke may disrupt interpretation and integration of sensory input; an estimated 70% of perceived sensory information is visual. Visual impairment is negatively associated with rehabilitation and quality of life and can affect mobility, navigation, interaction, self-care, independence, mood and driving. Screening should therefore cover acuity, fields, neglect and eye movements so that a survivor whose impairment breaches applicable driving rules is not discharged without driving-related information; requirements vary between countries, and follow-up should reassess visual requirements. Treating diplopia with prisms or a patch may restore visual function needed for driving. No standardised stroke-vision detection protocol currently exists. Variation in screening, specialist referral, treatment, information and communication adapted to visual impairment contributes to unmet need, inequity and poorer patient experience. Norup et al. identified visual problems in 24% at initial neurological examination; some who declined further assessment said they had not noticed a problem. Among survivors with neglect, unawareness of visuospatial deficits predicted poorer daily functioning more strongly than deficit severity or time since stroke. An estimated 40–60% with new visual impairment do not or cannot report symptoms; some remain unaware despite caregivers observing collisions or accidents. Missed deficits may mean missed rehabilitation, and unrecognised field loss may create road-safety risks.

Document sections:
  Heading: Conclusions
  Content: Ocular coloboma has widely varying presentations. Inherited and chromosomally associated forms are described, but sporadic cases are more common; environmental and maternal factors probably contribute to these. The lesion itself can impair vision by involving the disc or fovea, and complications including RD or choroidal neovascularisation can also reduce vision. Detecting ICM detachment is essential to assess whether coloboma contributes to RD. Pars plana vitrectomy with silicone oil and endolaser along the lesion edge is associated with good surgical success. Cataract surgery carries a higher-than-usual complication risk. Proposed research priorities are better identification of causes of non-syndromic coloboma; wider-field anatomical assessment through longer swept source OCT scans; randomized controlled trials of preventive laser photocoagulation for RD; and randomized controlled trials comparing internal tamponades for coloboma-related RD.

  Name: Vulvodynia
  Description: Vulvar pain lasting at least 3 months without a clearly identifiable cause, although associated factors may be present. The document describes altered peripheral and central sensory processing and classifies symptoms by distribution and provocation.

Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 5: Adult. Acute or chronic vision loss, optic nerve abnormality suspected. Initial imaging.
  Content: Neoplastic, inflammatory, ischemic, demyelinating, and traumatic processes can affect the optic nerve or its sheath and produce acute, subacute, or chronic visual loss. Neoplasms tend to develop more slowly than other optic neuropathies. Optic nerve gliomas are the most common primary optic nerve neoplasm; they can be incidental, including in younger patients with neurofibromatosis type 1, or present with visual symptoms or proptosis, and are more likely to be malignant when presenting in adults. Orbital meningiomas can arise from the optic nerve sheath or extend from an intracranial mass; symptomatic sheath lesions classically cause gradual, painless visual decline. Inflammatory and demyelinating ON can resemble one another clinically and radiologically; enhancement reflects edema, inflammation, or demyelination. Possible causes of demyelinating ON include MS, NMO, and MOGAD. ON can also reflect chronic relapsing-remitting inflammatory disease, steroid-dependent recurrence, systemic inflammation, or infection. Enhancement patterns overlap but may help: bilateral simultaneous and longer optic nerve involvement occur more often with MOGAD or NMO than MS, which characteristically affects a shorter unilateral segment. Sheath or perioptic enhancement is more distinctive of MOGAD. Anterior involvement is more typical of MS or MOGAD; NMO tends toward posterior nerves, chiasm, or tracts. Brain and spine MRI may identify associated abnormalities; asymptomatic optic nerve lesions may help distinguish relapsing-remitting MS or clinically isolated syndrome from NMO or MOGAD. Optic perineuritis can arise from idiopathic orbital inflammation, autoimmunity, infection, or other inflammation and may mimic acute demyelinating ON, including visual loss and pain worsened by eye movement. Patients with perineuritis tend to be older and more likely to retain central vision. Ischemic optic neuropathy is anterior, AION, when involving the nerve head, or posterior, PION, when involving the retrobulbar nerve. AION classically causes disc edema and altitudinal field loss. Either form may be nonarteritic, in patients with vascular risk factors such as hypertension or diabetes, or arteritic, most commonly from giant cell arteritis. Imaging aims to identify optic nerve disease, narrow overlapping diagnoses, and inform management.

Document sections:
  Heading: Hyperandrogenism Diagnostic Evaluation
  Content: In adult women, hirsutism, alopecia, and acne indicate clinical hyperandrogenism and can signal biochemical hyperandrogenism. Assessment should measure total and free testosterone; the calculated free androgen index can estimate free testosterone. If neither measure is elevated, androstenedione and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) may be considered, recognizing their lower specificity and the tendency of DHEA to decline with age. Laboratories should favor LC-MS/MS assays rather than direct immunoassays, including radiometric or enzyme-linked methods, for total or free testosterone because direct assays have limited accuracy, sensitivity, and precision in this setting. Androgen concentrations substantially above laboratory reference ranges should prompt consideration of ovarian or adrenal neoplasms, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing's syndrome, ovarian hyperthecosis—particularly after menopause—iatrogenic effects, and severe-insulin-resistance syndromes. Some androgen-secreting neoplasms cause only mild or moderate elevations, so the timing of onset and speed of progression are important clinical-history details.

Document sections:
  Heading: Infantile spasms syndrome
  Content: Infantile spasms are a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy requiring urgent care and immediate tertiary paediatric neurology guidance. Untreated spasms risk poor long-term neurodevelopment, whereas prompt diagnosis and treatment are associated with better prognosis. Monitor during and after therapy for recurrent spasms, new seizure types and treatment harms. Evidence suggested that steroids combined with vigabatrin stop spasms more effectively than either treatment alone. Evidence did not clearly favour oral over injected steroids, but the committee considered oral treatment easier. Steroids may be unsuitable for some children under 2 years, including those with neurological impairments or other comorbidities; consider vigabatrin alone when steroid adverse-effect risk is high. Evidence supported vigabatrin alone initially for spasms associated with tuberous sclerosis, adding high-dose oral prednisolone if it is ineffective after 1 week. Discuss steroid effects with parents and carers, including infection, high blood pressure and high blood glucose, and explain reducing exposure to infections such as chickenpox and responding to possible exposure. Higher doses of vigabatrin and oral steroids improved freedom from spasms in the reviewed evidence; increase doses in accordance with BNF for children. Vigabatrin above specified doses may be needed if spasms persist, but only with specialist supervision. Robust second-line evidence is absent, so subsequent options rely on specialist experience. The lack of controlled trial data after first-line failure prompted a research recommendation. The recommendations reinforce best practice.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Pharmacotherapy.
  Content: Most drug treatments require physiological-range haematological, liver and kidney results and exclusion of major pulmonary or cardiac disease or infection before and during treatment. Most patients receive an alkylating agent during their disease course. Temozolomide is the most commonly used glioma drug; it is an oral DNA alkylator that crosses the blood–brain barrier. Its main dose-limiting toxicity is myelosuppression, particularly thrombocytopenia, and liver function needs regular monitoring. Nitrosoureas such as lomustine, carmustine, nimustine and fotemustine cause later leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, at 4–6 weeks rather than 2–3 weeks, often with cumulative effects that may require interruption, dose reduction, discontinuation or another treatment. Pulmonary fibrosis is reported mainly with carmustine and rarely with lomustine. PCV combines lomustine, procarbazine and vincristine. Implanted carmustine wafers produced a modest OS benefit in newly diagnosed WHO grade 3 or 4 glioma or recurrent glioblastoma, but the pivotal trial found no statistically significant outcome difference after excluding WHO grade 3 cases from survival analysis. Benefits demonstrated for alkylating therapy in RCTs need weighing against late toxicity and a treatment-induced hypermutator phenotype linked to greater malignancy, particularly in longer-surviving patients with IDH-mutant disease. Bevacizumab, an anti-VEGF antibody, is approved for recurrent glioblastoma in the USA, Canada, Switzerland and other countries outside the European Union, without demonstrated OS benefit. Patients on systemic therapy should carry treatment records with laboratory results, complications and contraindications. Treating centres should maintain standardized procedures for chemotherapy delivery and complication management.
