Pembrolizumab en combinación con enfortumab vedotina (ver sección 4.2)
Cuando pembrolizumab se administre en combinación con enfortumab vedotina, consulte el SmPC de enfortumab vedotina antes de iniciar el tratamiento.
Se ha evaluado la seguridad de pembrolizumab en combinación con enfortumab vedotina entre los 564 pacientes con carcinoma urotelial irresecable o metastásico que recibieron 200 mg de pembrolizumab el Día 1 y 1,25 mg/kg de enfortumab vedotina los Días 1 y 8 de cada ciclo de 21 días.
En general, se observó que la incidencia de reacciones adversas para pembrolizumab en combinación con enfortumab vedotina era mayor que para pembrolizumab en monoterapia, lo que refleja la contribución de enfortumab vedotina y la mayor duración del tratamiento con la combinación.
Las reacciones adversas fueron generalmente similares a las observadas en pacientes que recibieron pembrolizumab o enfortumab vedotina como monoterapia. La incidencia de erupción maculopapular fue de 36% en todos los Grados (10% Grados 3‑4), que es mayor que la observada con pembrolizumab en monoterapia.
En general, las frecuencias de acontecimientos adversos fueron mayores en pacientes de ≥ 65 años de edad en comparación con los de < 65 años de edad, en especial para acontecimientos adversos graves (56,3% y 35,3%, respectivamente) y acontecimientos ≥ de Grado 3 (80,3% y 64,2%, respectivamente), de manera similar a las observaciones con el comparador de quimioterapia.
Se ha evaluado la seguridad de pembrolizumab en combinación con enfortumab vedotina en 167 pacientes con CVMI que recibieron 200 mg de pembrolizumab el Día 1 y enfortumab vedotina 1,25 mg/kg los Días 1 y 8 de cada ciclo de 21 días como tratamiento neoadyuvante y continuado después de la cistectomía radical como tratamiento adyuvante. En general, se observó que la incidencia de reacciones adversas de pembrolizumab en combinación con enfortumab vedotina fue mayor que con pembrolizumab en monoterapia, lo que refleja la contribución de enfortumab vedotina. Las reacciones adversas fueron generalmente similares a las que ocurren en pacientes con carcinoma urotelial irresecable o metastásico tratados con pembrolizumab en combinación con enfortumab vedotina.
Descripción de reacciones adversas seleccionadas
Los datos de las siguientes reacciones adversas inmunomediadas se basan en pacientes que recibieron pembrolizumab en cuatro dosis (2 mg/kg de peso corporal cada 3 semanas, 10 mg/kg de peso corporal cada 2 o 3 semanas o 200 mg cada 3 semanas) en ensayos clínicos (ver sección 5.1). Las directrices para el manejo de estas reacciones adversas se describen en la sección 4.4.
Reacciones adversas inmunomediadas (ver sección 4.4)
Neumonitis inmunomediada
Se produjo neumonitis en 324 (4,2%) pacientes, incluidos casos de Grados 2, 3, 4 o 5 en 143 (1,9%), 81 (1,1%), 19 (0,2%) y 9 (0,1%) pacientes, respectivamente, que recibieron pembrolizumab. La mediana de tiempo hasta la aparición de neumonitis fue de 3,9 meses (rango: 2 días a 27,2 meses). La mediana de duración fue de 2,0 meses (rango: 1 día a 51,0+ meses). La neumonitis se produjo más frecuentemente en pacientes con antecedentes de radiación torácica previa (8,1%) que en pacientes que no recibieron radiación torácica previa (3,9%). La neumonitis condujo a la suspensión definitiva de pembrolizumab en 131 (1,7%) pacientes y se resolvió en 196 pacientes, 6 con secuelas.
En pacientes con CPNM, se produjo neumonitis en 230 (6,1%), incluidos casos de Grados 2, 3, 4 o 5 en 103 (2,7%), 63 (1,7%), 17 (0,4%) y 10 (0,3%) pacientes, respectivamente. En pacientes con CPNM localmente avanzado o metastásico, se produjo neumonitis en el 8,9% con antecedentes de radiación torácica previa. En pacientes con LHc, la incidencia de neumonitis (todos los Grados) osciló entre 5,2% y 10,8% para pacientes con LHc en el ensayo KEYNOTE-087 (n=210) y en el ensayo KEYNOTE-204 (n=148), respectivamente.
Colitis inmunomediada
Se produjo colitis en 158 (2,1%) pacientes, incluidos casos de Grados 2, 3 o 4 en 49 (0,6%), 82 (1,1%) y 6 (0,1%) pacientes, respectivamente, que recibieron pembrolizumab. La mediana de tiempo hasta la aparición de colitis fue de 4,3 meses (rango: 2 días a 24,3 meses). La mediana de duración fue de 1,1 mes (rango: 1 día a 45,2 meses). La colitis condujo a la suspensión definitiva de pembrolizumab en 48 (0,6%) pacientes y se resolvió en 132 pacientes, 2 con secuelas. En pacientes con cáncer colorrectal tratados con pembrolizumab en monoterapia (n=153), la incidencia de colitis fue de 6,5% (todos los Grados) con 2,0% de Grado 3 y 1,3% de Grado 4.
Hepatitis inmunomediada
Se produjo hepatitis en 80 (1,0%) pacientes, incluidos casos de Grados 2, 3 o 4 en 12 (0,2%), 55 (0,7%) y 8 (0,1%) pacientes, respectivamente, que recibieron pembrolizumab. La mediana de tiempo hasta la aparición de hepatitis fue de 3,5 meses (rango: 8 días a 26,3 meses). La mediana de duración fue de 1,3 meses (rango: 1 día a 29,0+ meses). La hepatitis condujo a la suspensión definitiva de pembrolizumab en 37 (0,5%) pacientes y se resolvió en 60 pacientes.
Nefritis inmunomediada
Se produjo nefritis en 37 (0,5%) pacientes, incluidos casos de Grados 2, 3 o 4 en 11 (0,1%), 19 (0,2%) y 2 (< 0,1%) pacientes, respectivamente, que recibieron pembrolizumab en monoterapia. La mediana de tiempo hasta la aparición de nefritis fue de 4,2 meses (rango: 12 días a 21,4 meses). La mediana de duración fue de 3,3 meses (rango: 6 días a 28,2+ meses). La nefritis condujo a la suspensión definitiva de pembrolizumab en 17 (0,2%) pacientes y se resolvió en 25 pacientes, 5 con secuelas. En pacientes con CPNM no escamoso tratados con pembrolizumab en combinación con pemetrexed y quimioterapia basada en platino (n=488), la incidencia de nefritis fue de 1,4% (todos los Grados) con 0,8% de Grado 3 y 0,4% de Grado 4.
Endocrinopatías inmunomediadas
Se produjo insuficiencia suprarrenal en 74 (1,0%) pacientes, incluidos casos de Grados 2, 3 o 4 en 34 (0,4%), 31 (0,4%) y 4 (0,1%) pacientes, respectivamente, que recibieron pembrolizumab. La mediana de tiempo hasta la aparición de insuficiencia suprarrenal fue de 5,4 meses (rango: 1 día a 23,7 meses). La mediana de duración no se alcanzó (rango: 3 días a 40,1+ meses). La insuficiencia suprarrenal condujo a la suspensión definitiva de pembrolizumab en 13 (0,2%) pacientes y se resolvió en 28 pacientes, 11 con secuelas.
Se produjo hipofisitis en 52 (0,7%) pacientes, incluidos casos de Grados 2, 3 o 4 en 23 (0,3%), 24 (0,3%) y 1 (< 0,1%) pacientes, respectivamente, que recibieron pembrolizumab. La mediana de tiempo hasta la aparición de hipofisitis fue de 5,9 meses (rango: 1 día a 17,7 meses). La mediana de duración fue de 3,6 meses (rango: 3 días a 48,1+ meses). La hipofisitis condujo a la suspensión definitiva de pembrolizumab en 14 (0,2%) pacientes y se resolvió en 23 pacientes, 8 con secuelas.
Se produjo hipertiroidismo en 394 (5,2%) pacientes, incluidos casos de Grados 2 o 3 en 108 (1,4%) y 9 (0,1%) pacientes, respectivamente, que recibieron pembrolizumab. La mediana de tiempo hasta la aparición de hipertiroidismo fue de 1,4 meses (rango: 1 día a 23,2 meses). La mediana de duración fue de 1,6 meses (rango: 4 días a 43,1+ meses). El hipertiroidismo condujo a la suspensión definitiva de pembrolizumab en 4 (0,1%) pacientes y se resolvió en 326 (82,7%) pacientes, 11 con secuelas. En pacientes con melanoma, CPNM y CCR tratados con pembrolizumab en monoterapia en el contexto adyuvante (n=2 060), la incidencia de hipertiroidismo fue del 11,0%, la mayoría de los cuales fueron de Grado 1 o 2.
Se produjo hipotiroidismo en 939 (12,3%) pacientes, incluidos casos de Grados 2 o 3 en 687 (9,0%) y 8 (0,1%) pacientes, respectivamente, que recibieron pembrolizumab. La mediana de tiempo hasta la aparición de hipotiroidismo fue de 3,4 meses (rango: 1 día a 25,9 meses). La mediana de duración no se alcanzó (rango: 2 días a 63,0+ meses). El hipotiroidismo condujo a la suspensión definitiva de pembrolizumab en 6 (0,1%) pacientes. El hipotiroidismo se resolvió en 216 (23,0%) pacientes, 16 con secuelas. En pacientes con LHc (n=389) la incidencia de hipotiroidismo fue de 17%, de la que todos los casos fueron de Grados 1 o 2. En pacientes con CCECC recurrente o metastásico tratados con pembrolizumab en monoterapia (n=909), la incidencia de hipotiroidismo fue de 16,1% (todos los Grados), con 0,3% de Grado 3. En pacientes con CCECC recurrente o metastásico tratados con pembrolizumab en combinación con quimioterapia basada en platino y 5-FU (n=276), la incidencia de hipotiroidismo fue de 15,2%, de los cuales todos fueron de Grados 1 o 2. En pacientes con CCECC localmente avanzado resecable tratado con pembrolizumab como tratamiento neoadyuvante y en combinación con radioterapia con o sin cisplatino concomitante para el tratamiento adyuvante (n=361), la incidencia de hipotiroidismo fue 24,7%, de los cuales todos fueron de Grado 1 o 2. En pacientes tratados con pembrolizumab en combinación con axitinib o lenvatinib (n=1 456), la incidencia de hipotiroidismo fue de 46,2% (todos los Grados) con 0,8% de Grado 3 o 4. En pacientes con melanoma, CPNM y CCR tratados con pembrolizumab en monoterapia en el contexto adyuvante (n=2 060), la incidencia de hipotiroidismo fue del 18,5%, la mayoría de los cuales fueron de Grado 1 o 2.
Reacciones adversas cutáneas inmunomediadas
Se produjeron reacciones adversas cutáneas graves inmunomediadas en 130 (1,7%) pacientes, incluidos casos de Grados 2, 3, 4 o 5 en 11 (0,1%), 103 (1,3%), 1 (< 0,1%) y 1 (? 0,1%) pacientes, respectivamente, que recibieron pembrolizumab. La mediana de tiempo hasta la aparición de reacciones cutáneas graves fue de 2,8 meses (rango: 2 días a 25,5 meses). La mediana de duración fue de 1,9 meses (rango: 1 día a 47,1+ meses). Las reacciones cutáneas graves condujeron a la suspensión definitiva de pembrolizumab en 18 (0,2%) pacientes. Las reacciones cutáneas graves se resolvieron en 95 pacientes, 2 con secuelas.
Se han observado casos raros de SSJ y NET, algunos de ellos con desenlace mortal (ver las secciones 4.2 y 4.4).
Complicaciones del TPH alogénico en LHc
En el ensayo KEYNOTE-013, de 14 pacientes que se sometieron a un TPH alogénico después del tratamiento con pembrolizumab, 6 pacientes notificaron EICH aguda y 1 paciente notificó EICH crónica, sin ser ninguno de los casos mortal. Dos pacientes sufrieron enfermedad veno-oclusiva hepática, siendo uno de los casos mortal. Un paciente sufrió síndrome del injerto postrasplante.
En el ensayo KEYNOTE-087, de 32 pacientes que se sometieron a un TPH alogénico después del tratamiento con pembrolizumab, 16 pacientes notificaron EICH aguda y 7 pacientes notificaron EICH crónica, siendo dos de los casos mortales. Ningún paciente sufrió enfermedad veno-oclusiva hepática. Ningún paciente sufrió síndrome del injerto postrasplante.
En el ensayo KEYNOTE-204, de 14 pacientes que se sometieron a un TPH alogénico después del tratamiento con pembrolizumab, 8 pacientes notificaron EICH aguda y 3 pacientes notificaron EICH crónica, sin ser ninguno de los casos mortal. Ningún paciente sufrió enfermedad veno-oclusiva hepática. Un paciente sufrió síndrome del injerto postrasplante.
Enzimas hepáticas elevadas cuando pembrolizumab se combina con axitinib en CCR
En un ensayo clínico con pacientes con CCR, no tratados previamente, que recibieron pembrolizumab en combinación con axitinib, se observó una incidencia más alta de lo esperado en ALT elevada (20%) y AST elevada (13%) de Grados 3 y 4. La mediana de tiempo hasta la aparición de ALT elevada fue de 2,3 meses (rango: 7 días a 19,8 meses). En pacientes con ALT ≥ 3 veces el LSN (Grados 2-4, n=116), ALT se resolvió a Grados 0-1 en el 94%. El cincuenta y nueve por ciento de los pacientes con ALT elevada recibieron corticosteroides sistémicos. De los pacientes que se recuperaron, a 92 (84%) se les volvió a administrar pembrolizumab (3%) o axitinib (31%) en monoterapia, o con ambos (50%). De estos pacientes, el 55% no tuvieron recidiva de ALT > 3 veces el LSN, y de estos pacientes con recurrencia de ALT > 3 veces el LSN, todos se recuperaron. No hubo acontecimientos hepáticos de Grado 5.
Anomalías de laboratorio
En pacientes tratados con pembrolizumab en monoterapia, el porcentaje de pacientes que experimentaron un cambio desde el estado basal hasta una anomalía de laboratorio de Grados 3 o 4 fue el siguiente: 9,9% para linfocitos disminuidos, 7,3% para sodio disminuido, 5,7% para hemoglobina disminuida, 4,6% para glucosa elevada, 4,5% para fosfato disminuido, 3,1% para ALT elevada, 2,9% para AST elevada, 2,6% para fosfatasa alcalina elevada, 2,2% para potasio disminuido, 2,1% para neutrófilos disminuidos, 1,7% para bilirrubina elevada, 1,7% para plaquetas disminuidas, 1,7% para potasio elevado, 1,6% para calcio elevado, 1,4% para albúmina disminuida, 1,3% para calcio disminuido, 1,2% para creatinina elevada, 0,8% para leucocitos disminuidos, 0,8% para magnesio elevado, 0,6% para glucosa disminuida, 0,2% para magnesio disminuido y 0,2% para sodio elevado.
En pacientes tratados con pembrolizumab en combinación con quimioterapia, RT o CRT, el porcentaje de pacientes que experimentaron un cambio desde el estado basal hasta una anomalía de laboratorio de Grados 3 o 4 fue el siguiente: 36,4% para neutrófilos disminuidos, 31,7% para linfocitos disminuidos, 23,7% para leucocitos disminuidos, 20,2% para hemoglobina disminuida, 11,4% para plaquetas disminuidas, 9,5% para sodio disminuido, 7,8% para potasio disminuido, 7,2% para fosfato disminuido, 5,5% para glucosa elevada, 5,3% para ALT elevada, 4,7% para AST elevada, 3,4% para calcio disminuido, 3,1% para creatinina elevada, 3,0% para bilirrubina elevada, 3,0% para potasio elevado, 2,4% para albúmina disminuida, 2,3% para fosfatasa alcalina elevada, 1,6% para calcio elevado, 0,9% para glucosa disminuida, 0,4% para sodio elevado y 0,2% para hemoglobina elevada.
En los pacientes tratados con pembrolizumab en combinación con axitinib o lenvatinib, la proporción de pacientes que experimentaron un cambio desde el estado basal hasta una anomalía de laboratorio de Grado 3 o 4 fue la siguiente: 23,0% para lipasa elevada (no medida en los pacientes tratados con pembrolizumab y axitinib), 12,3% para linfocitos disminuidos, 11,4% para sodio disminuido, 11.2% para amilasa elevada, 11,2% para triglicéridos elevados, 10,4% para ALT elevada, 8,9% para AST elevada, 7,8% para glucosa elevada, 6,8% para fosfato disminuido, 6,1% para potasio disminuido, 5,1% para potasio elevado, 4,5% para colesterol elevado, 4,4% para creatinina elevada, 4,2% para hemoglobina disminuida, 4,0% para neutrófilos disminuidos, 3,1% para fosfatasa alcalina elevada, 3,0% para plaquetas disminuidas, 2,8% para bilirrubina elevada, 2,2% para calcio disminuido, 2,2% para magnesio elevado, 1,7% para leucocitos disminuidos, 1,5% para magnesio disminuido, 1,5% para protrombina INR elevada, 1,4% para glucosa disminuida, 1,2% para albúmina disminuida, 1,0% para calcio elevado, 0,4% para sodio aumentado y 0,1% para hemoglobina elevada.
Inmunogenicidad
En ensayos clínicos en pacientes tratados con pembrolizumab 2 mg/kg de peso corporal cada tres semanas, 200 mg cada tres semanas o 10 mg/kg de peso corporal cada dos o tres semanas en monoterapia, 36 (1,8%) de 2 034 pacientes evaluables dió positivo a anticuerpos generados por el organismo frente a pembrolizumab, de los cuales 9 (0,4%) pacientes tuvieron anticuerpos neutralizantes contra pembrolizumab. No hubo evidencia de alteración de la farmacocinética o del perfil de seguridad con el desarrollo de anticuerpos de unión anti-pembrolizumab o anticuerpos neutralizantes.
Población pediátrica
Se ha evaluado la seguridad de pembrolizumab como monoterapia en 161 pacientes pediátricos de 9 meses a 17 años con melanoma avanzado, linfoma o tumores sólidos PD-L1 positivos avanzados, en recaída o refractarios en dosis de 2 mg/kg de peso corporal cada 3 semanas en el ensayo de Fase I/II KEYNOTE-051. La población con LHc (n=22) incluyó a pacientes de 11 a 17 años. De manera general, el perfil de seguridad en pacientes pediátricos fue similar al observado en adultos tratados con pembrolizumab. Las reacciones adversas más frecuentes (notificadas en al menos el 20% de los pacientes pediátricos) fueron pirexia (33%), vómitos (30%), cefalea (26%), dolor abdominal (22%), anemia (21%), tos (21%) y estreñimiento (20%). La mayoría de las reacciones adversas notificadas en monoterapia fueron de gravedad Grados 1 o 2. Setenta y seis (47,2%) pacientes tuvieron 1 o más reacciones adversas de Grados 3 a 5, de los cuales 5 (3,1%) pacientes tuvieron 1 o más reacciones adversas que derivaron en muerte. Las frecuencias se basan en todas las reacciones adversas medicamentosas notificadas, con independencia de la evaluación de causalidad por el investigador. Actualmente no se dispone de datos de seguridad a largo plazo de pembrolizumab en adolescentes con melanoma en estadio IIB, IIC y III tratados en el contexto adyuvante.
Notificación de sospechas de reacciones adversas
Es importante notificar sospechas de reacciones adversas al medicamento tras su autorización. Ello permite una supervisión continuada de la relación beneficio/riesgo del medicamento. Se invita a los profesionales sanitarios a notificar las sospechas de reacciones adversas a través del sistema nacional de notificación incluido en el Apéndice V.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_12
  Name: Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma
  Description: These visual field abnormalities can result from compression of, or pathology within, the optic chiasm or the junction between the optic nerve and chiasm. The variant addresses suspected sellar or parasellar disease.
  Clinical presentation: Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma may accompany a sellar or suprasellar mass. Most neoplastic causes develop with gradually progressive visual symptoms; pituitary apoplexy may instead produce headache and rapid visual change.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Pituitary macroadenomas
      Distinguishing features: May extend above the sella and compress the optic chiasm or neighboring optic nerves or tracts.
    - Name: Sellar/suprasellar region meningiomas
      Distinguishing features: May involve sellar, suprasellar or parasellar structures and exert mass effect on the optic nerves or chiasm.
    - Name: Craniopharyngiomas
      Distinguishing features: Suprasellar masses that commonly compress the optic chiasm; the papillary type described in adults is usually solid and enhancing and rarely calcifies.
    - Name: Pituitary apoplexy
      Distinguishing features: Often follows hemorrhagic infarction of an existing adenoma and may cause rapid enlargement, headache and visual changes.
    - Name: Aneurysms
      Distinguishing features: Large lesions of the internal carotid artery or Circle of Willis vessels can compress the optic nerves or chiasm.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: MRI sella without and with IV contrast
      Purpose: Characterize suspected sellar or parasellar pathology, its extent and its relationship to the optic chiasm and neighboring structures.
      When indicated: Usually Appropriate and the preferred initial imaging examination.
      Interpretation: The small-field-of-view, thin-section protocol provides greater anatomical detail than routine head MRI.
    - Test: MRI head without and with IV contrast
      Purpose: Assess disease extending beyond the sella, including granulomatous, metastatic or lymphomatous processes.
      When indicated: May Be Appropriate.
      Interpretation: Routine head MRI can identify a large pituitary macroadenoma but generally provides less sellar detail than a dedicated protocol.
    - Test: CTA head with IV contrast; MRA head with IV contrast; MRA head without IV contrast
      Purpose: Establish whether a lesion suggested by initial MRI is an aneurysm.
      When indicated: These vascular studies are not recommended by the variant table as routine initial imaging; CTA or MRA may follow MRI if aneurysm is suspected.
    - Test: CT sella without IV contrast; CT sella with IV contrast
      Purpose: Provide complementary information on calcification, bone invasion or a mass of osseous origin; noncontrast CT may reveal acute hemorrhage in pituitary apoplexy.
      When indicated: Usually Not Appropriate as routine initial imaging for this variant.
      Interpretation: MRI is more sensitive for diagnosing pituitary apoplexy and can assess an underlying pituitary mass.

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_02
  Condition: CRPS
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients beginning affected-limb reactivation, including those with sensory disturbance, edema, or movement avoidance.
  Decision rules:
    - Start with gentle, tolerable activities and increase sensory input and loading progressively.
    - Keep exercise within the patient's tolerance; both excessive activity and prolonged inactivity can worsen symptoms.
    - Do not perform physical therapy while the limb is insensate, including immediately after a block.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Desensitization
      Evidence level: level 4
      Summary: Gradually expose the affected area to sensory stimulation alongside increasing functional use.
    - Name: Edema management
      Evidence level: level 4
      Summary: Use appropriate garments and manual edema mobilization while progressing movement and limb use.
    - Name: Stress loading
      Evidence level: level 4
      Summary: Introduce scrubbing and carrying to load affected joints; progressively increase load and activity time while encouraging use of the limb during daily tasks.
      Key outcomes: The guideline describes clinical utility but states that comparative efficacy against other functional loading approaches requires study.
    - Name: Gentle progressive exercise
      Evidence level: level 2
      Summary: Progress active movement, flexibility, posture, gait, coordination, and strengthening as tolerated, incorporating pacing, breaks, and relaxation.
      Key outcomes: Trials by Oerlemans et al. found better pain ratings and active mobility with physical therapy than with counseling alone in upper-extremity CRPS.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: Aquatic therapy
      Summary: Use buoyancy and water resistance to introduce movement and, particularly for the lower limb, weight bearing; avoid water temperatures that exacerbate symptoms.
      Conditions for use: May be especially useful when early land-based loading is difficult.
    - Name: Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF)
      Summary: Use movement patterns to develop strength, balance, and performance of daily activities.
      Conditions for use: May be incorporated as functional movement becomes more tolerable.
    - Name: Feldenkrais
      Evidence level: level 4
      Summary: Use gentle active mat-based movement to develop body awareness and appropriate movement patterns.
      Conditions for use: An option for non-weight-bearing movement practice.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: Inappropriately aggressive physical therapy
      Reason: It can provoke severe pain, edema, distress, and fatigue and may worsen inflammatory and sympathetic features.
    - Name: Physical therapy while the affected limb is insensate
      Reason: The guideline says therapy should never be undertaken under this condition.
    - Name: Prolonged ice application and inactivity
      Reason: Both may aggravate CRPS.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: Throughout rehabilitation
      Method: Monitor tolerance, edema, pain, range of motion, movement quality, and everyday limb use.
      Interpretation: Increase or reduce activity according to therapeutic response while continuing gradual functional progression.
  Supportive care:
    - Teach pacing and incorporate rest breaks.
    - Maintain normal posture and movement where possible to limit secondary compensatory problems.
  Special considerations: Patients with CRPS-Type II and pronounced hypoesthesia require particular avoidance of exercise when the affected limb is insensate.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_08
  Name: Non-ischaemic priapism
  Synonyms:
    - high-flow or arterial priapism
  Description: A persistent erection caused by unregulated arterial inflow into the corpora. Blunt trauma can produce a fistula between a cavernosal artery or its branches and the sinusoidal spaces.
  Epidemiology: It comprises 5% of priapism cases. Epidemiological information comes almost entirely from small case series, and blunt perineal or penile trauma is the most frequent cause.
  Clinical presentation: The corpora are tumescent but usually not fully rigid. Penile pain is generally absent, although discomfort is possible, and rigidity may fluctuate. After trauma, onset may be delayed by several hours to weeks; the guide also describes delays of up to two to three weeks. Sexual stimulation can produce full rigidity, so intercourse is usually possible. Erectile dysfunction or distal penile flaccidity may develop over time.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: traumatic
      Distinguishing features: Associated with injury, especially blunt perineal or penile trauma.
    - Name: neurogenic
      Distinguishing features: May follow acute spinal cord injury.
    - Name: iatrogenic
      Distinguishing features: Reported after certain procedures, including shunting for ischaemic priapism.
    - Name: idiopathic
      Distinguishing features: No cause is identified.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Comprehensive medical and sexual history
      Purpose: Establish the diagnosis and distinguish the priapism subtype.
      When indicated: At presentation.
      Interpretation: A history of pelvic, perineal or genital trauma, little or no penile pain, and a persistent erection without full rigidity support arterial priapism.
    - Test: Abdominal, penile and perineal examination
      Purpose: Assess tumescence and identify evidence of trauma.
      When indicated: During diagnostic evaluation.
      Interpretation: The corpora are generally tumescent without being fully rigid.
    - Test: Neurological examination
      Purpose: Investigate a possible neurogenic cause.
      When indicated: If neurogenic non-ischaemic priapism is suspected.
    - Test: Complete blood count with white blood cell differential and coagulation profile
      Purpose: Assess anaemia and other haematological abnormalities.
      When indicated: During laboratory evaluation.
    - Test: Corporal blood aspiration and blood gas analysis
      Purpose: Differentiate non-ischaemic from ischaemic priapism.
      When indicated: During diagnostic evaluation.
      Interpretation: The aspirate is bright red and has normal arterial blood gas values; the listed arterial values are pO2 > 90 mmHg, pCO2 < 40 mmHg and pH 7.40.
    - Test: Colour duplex ultrasound of the penis and perineum
      Purpose: Distinguish priapism subtypes and locate an arterial fistula.
      When indicated: During diagnostic evaluation, without intracavernosal vasoactive drug injection.
      Interpretation: A fistula may appear as a focal colour blush with turbulent, high-velocity flow. Cavernosal arterial velocities are normal to high.
    - Test: Selective pudendal arteriography
      Purpose: Identify the site of arterial injury for planned embolisation.
      When indicated: When embolisation is being considered.
      Interpretation: A characteristic blush may appear at the injury site.
    - Test: MRI
      Purpose: Evaluate selected cases or assess distal penile fibrosis during follow-up.
      When indicated: Its diagnostic role in non-ischaemic priapism is limited; it may be used during close follow-up.
      Interpretation: Small penile vessels and fistulae are difficult to demonstrate with MRI.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Close follow-up is described during conservative management and after selective arterial embolisation; no fixed interval is specified.
    Recommended tests:
      - Physical examination during conservative management
      - Colour duplex ultrasound during conservative management
      - Colour duplex ultrasound and MRI to detect distal penile fibrosis
      - Clinical examination, colour duplex ultrasound and erectile function assessment after embolisation
      - Repeat arteriography if findings remain uncertain
    Long term effects:
      - Erectile dysfunction
      - Distal penile flaccidity
      - Distal penile fibrosis
      - Recurrence after treatment
    Survivorship notes: Follow-up assesses treatment success, recurrence, and anatomical and functional consequences.

Document sections:
  Heading: Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes
  Content: Children generally outgrow this syndrome by their early teens. Some have infrequent seizures with little effect on wellbeing, so treatment is not always chosen. Discuss treatment versus no treatment, seizure hazards, adverse effects and the very rare risk of SUDEP. The committee considered current antiseizure treatment effective in practice. Direct medicine evidence was limited; because seizures are usually focal, first- and second-line options were informed by focal-epilepsy studies. Those studies found longer continuation of lamotrigine and levetiracetam, suggesting possible effectiveness and tolerability benefits, but no greater remission at 6 and 12 months and a less favourable time to first seizure than carbamazepine. Lamotrigine, levetiracetam and gabapentin may have more tolerable adverse events, although inconsistent reporting limits comparisons. The committee supported lamotrigine and levetiracetam first, followed by carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine or zonisamide as second-line monotherapy. Carbamazepine and potentially similar oxcarbazepine and eslicarbazepine acetate carry particular serious-complication risks for people of Han Chinese, Thai, European or Japanese family background. Long-term carbamazepine may reduce bone mineral density and increase osteomalacia risk; consider supplementation for those at risk. Evidence showed seizure reduction with sulthiame, but its limited evidence and licensing position led the committee to place it third-line after licensed choices, following tertiary paediatric neurology discussion. A November 2025 note states that sulthiame is now licensed in the UK and recommendations 6.4.2 to 6.4.4 are under review. In a small number of children, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine or lamotrigine may increase seizures or coincide with another syndrome. Concerning changes should prompt sleep EEG to exclude developmental epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep; poor school performance should prompt neuropsychology assessment. Tailor reviews to seizure frequency, treatment and other needs, and discuss withdrawal after 2 seizure-free years or at age 14 years. Recommendations mainly reinforce existing practice.

Document sections:
  Heading: 1. Background
  Content: Childhood CNS tumours can disrupt visual anatomy and development, producing reduced visual acuity (VA), visual field (VF) defects, diplopia and abnormal eye movements. Manifestations depend substantially on tumour location and involvement of afferent visual pathways or the cranial nerves of the efferent system. Obstructive hydrocephalus, brain oedema, leptomeningeal spread or cerebral venous thrombosis can raise intracranial pressure, produce papilledema and further threaten sight. During early visual development, additional deprivation from refractive errors, keratopathy, cataracts or strabismus may cause amblyopia and further loss. Adult survivors have increased long-term risks of unilateral or bilateral blindness (RR 14.8), cataracts (RR = 11.9) and diplopia (RR 8.8), with potential effects on cognition, independence, driving and education. Large tertiary-centre series reported that less than 50% of newly diagnosed children received baseline ophthalmological referral, at a median of 9 months (range 0-94 months) after diagnosis. Acute illness and prioritization of lifesaving care can delay assessment; visual symptoms may also be underreported, especially in infants, young children and those with VF defects. Standardized assessment and follow-up recommendations aim to improve detection and enable earlier intervention that might prevent or lessen irreversible visual loss.

  Content: Tumour location affects the symptom pattern. Frontal lobe tumours may impair planning, organisation, social skills, behaviour, personality, mood, walking, smell, sight or speech and may cause facial or one-sided weakness. Temporal lobe tumours may impair recall, learning, comprehension or sound recognition and cause seizures with unusual sensations, smells or deja vu. Pituitary gland tumours may cause headache, peripheral or other visual loss, nausea, vomiting, erection difficulties, reduced sexual interest and thyroid or other hormonal changes. Brain stem tumours may cause poor coordination, swallowing or speech difficulties, double vision, facial weakness or numbness, limb weakness, fatigue and altered sleep–wake patterns. Cerebellar tumours may cause impaired balance or coordination, uncontrolled eye movement, neck stiffness, dizziness or staccato speech. Spinal cord tumours may cause back or neck pain, limb tingling or numbness, altered muscle tone, clumsiness, gait problems, bowel or bladder incontinence, altered genital or anal sensation, or erection problems.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: Gnech et al. 2024 Update and Summary of the European Association of UrologyEuropean Society of Paediatric Urology Pae
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 3.3.1.1. CAP
  Content: Many prospective studies have examined whether CAP prevents recurrent febrile UTI and focal radionuclide uptake defects. CAP is not required for every child with VUR; trials found no or minimal benefit for low-grade reflux. In PREDICT, a randomised controlled trial across 39 European centres, Morello et al. studied infants with grade III, IV, or V VUR and no prior UTI. Treating seven children for 2 yr was necessary to prevent one UTI, without differences in renal scarring, kidney function, or UTI hospitalisation. CAP gave a small but significant reduction in first UTI, alongside increases in non-Escherichia coli organisms and antibiotic resistance. Among children with VUR receiving CAP, younger age at initial febrile UTI diagnosis ( 12 mo), bilateral reflux, and BBD independently predict febrile breakthrough UTI. Toilet-trained children and those with LUTD gain more benefit from CAP. RIVUR reported a 50% reduction in recurrent febrile UTI risk with prophylaxis, but no effect on focal radionuclide uptake defects or their consequences of hypertension and renal failure; antimicrobial resistance increased. Further risk-stratified analyses of RIVUR identified uncircumcised boys, children with BBD, and those with high-grade reflux as a high-risk group deriving significant CAP benefit. Rather than using CAP uniformly, medical care should shift from prophylaxis for dilating reflux toward selective use based on risk. Relevant febrile UTI risk factors include young age, high-grade VUR, toilet-training status, LUTD, female sex, and circumcision status. Reliable evidence for CAP duration is lacking; using it until BBD resolves is a practical approach. Recommendations in the literature generally use antibiotics every day at a quarter to half of the regular therapeutic dose. Common CAP drugs are Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMZ), amoxicillin, and nitrofurantoin. TMP-SMZ must be avoided at age <6 wk because of hepatic injury risk and in severe renal insufficiency because of possible kidney toxicity. Nitrofurantoin is best avoided before 4 mo because of haemolytic anaemia risk. After a febrile breakthrough UTI, changing to another prophylactic antibiotic may be considered; an available antibiogram can guide the choice. Initial medical care remains an option for a child with febrile UTI and high-grade VUR. Surgery is reserved for failure to adhere to CAP, febrile breakthrough UTIs despite CAP, or symptomatic VUR persisting over long-term follow-up, including recurrent flank pain with or without febrile UTIs. The best point to stop CAP is disputed. Recurrences are more likely after CAP for <1 yr following the last febrile UTI and in bilateral VUR. Surveillance, antireflux intervention, and CAP discontinuation should be decided individually with patients and caregivers. Detailed discussion of risks, benefits, and alternatives is strongly advised, taking access to care during febrile UTI into account. Long-term CAP effects concern patients, caregivers, and clinicians. In a secondary RIVUR analysis, TMP-SMZ prophylaxis for 2 yr was not associated with adverse changes in complete blood count, serum electrolytes, or creatinine; routine laboratory testing is not mandatory in otherwise healthy children. Effects of prolonged CAP on gut microbiota remain disputed and need further study. CAP can prevent new febrile UTIs in children with a febrile UTI history and antenatal hydronephrosis with presumed or confirmed VUR. Whether it also helps infants whose asymptomatic VUR is discovered while investigating antenatal hydronephrosis remains unclear.

Document sections:
  Heading: 1. Background
  Content: Childhood CNS tumours can disrupt visual anatomy and development, producing reduced visual acuity (VA), visual field (VF) defects, diplopia and abnormal eye movements. Manifestations depend substantially on tumour location and involvement of afferent visual pathways or the cranial nerves of the efferent system. Obstructive hydrocephalus, brain oedema, leptomeningeal spread or cerebral venous thrombosis can raise intracranial pressure, produce papilledema and further threaten sight. During early visual development, additional deprivation from refractive errors, keratopathy, cataracts or strabismus may cause amblyopia and further loss. Adult survivors have increased long-term risks of unilateral or bilateral blindness (RR 14.8), cataracts (RR = 11.9) and diplopia (RR 8.8), with potential effects on cognition, independence, driving and education. Large tertiary-centre series reported that less than 50% of newly diagnosed children received baseline ophthalmological referral, at a median of 9 months (range 0-94 months) after diagnosis. Acute illness and prioritization of lifesaving care can delay assessment; visual symptoms may also be underreported, especially in infants, young children and those with VF defects. Standardized assessment and follow-up recommendations aim to improve detection and enable earlier intervention that might prevent or lessen irreversible visual loss.

Document sections:
  Heading: Gabapentinoids.
  Content: Gabapentin and pregabalin were initially used for epilepsy and are now recommended first-line for PHN and other neuropathic pain. Although structurally related to gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), they do not bind its receptors; they attach to the α2δ-1 subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels. Proposed analgesic mechanisms include limiting excessive, α2δ-1-dependent release of neurotransmitters involved in pain transmission, reducing α2δ-1 accumulation in synaptic vesicles of spinal dorsal root ganglia, and activating descending noradrenergic inhibition. Neither drug binds plasma proteins or undergoes metabolism by liver enzymes, and they do not alter concentrations of drugs metabolized by cytochrome CYP450. Both are eliminated chiefly in urine. Depending on dose, gabapentin has a half-life of five to seven hours; pregabalin has a half-life of about 6.3 hours. Oral gabapentin is supplied in immediate-release and extended-release forms. Studies found immediate-release gabapentin more effective than placebo for PHN symptoms at 1,800mg to 3,600mg per day. Its non-linear gastrointestinal absorption lowers bioavailability as doses rise, complicating titration to an effective dose without adverse reactions. A Cochrane Review found the extended-release formulations gastroretentive gabapentin and gabapentin enacarbil more effective than placebo for PHN; these formulations are easier to dose and have greater bioavailability. Gastroretentive gabapentin is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract for up to 15h and is taken once daily. Its recommended starting dose is 900mg per day, followed by gradual titration to a therapeutic dose over two weeks. An 11-week, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled phase three study demonstrated PHN pain control with 1,800mg per day. Gabapentin enacarbil is a prodrug that needs less frequent administration than immediate-release gabapentin and produces less variation in plasma concentration. Its minimum therapeutic dose is 1,200mg per day, reached through gradual dosing over four days. Compared with gabapentin, pregabalin has high bioavailability and linear gastrointestinal absorption, making its pharmacokinetics more predictable; maximum plasma concentration follows oral dosing after one hour. An assessment based on 14 randomized clinical trials found pregabalin more effective than gabapentin for PHN pain but associated with more frequent side-effects. Its recommended starting dose is 150mg/day in two or three divided doses, with gradual titration over about one week; the maximum recommended, relatively well-tolerated therapeutic dose is 600mg/day. Common central nervous system effects include dizziness, reported in 19% when taking gabapentin, and balance disorders and drowsiness, with drowsiness reported at 14% for gabapetin. With pregabalin, dizziness occurred in 24% and drowsiness in 17%. Moderate weight gain can occur with gabapentinoids and may affect up to 25% of pregabalin users, although for most patients receiving pregabalin the gain within a year does not exceed 7% of baseline weight. Bloating, constipation, altered appetite and nausea are relatively common. Gabapentinoids may also produce withdrawal symptoms. In available case reports, symptoms after stopping gabapentin began between 12 hours and seven days after the last dose; agitation, confusion, tremor, insomnia, gastric symptoms and excessive sweating were most frequent, while akathisia, catatonia and convulsions were reported in isolated cases. Renal failure raises the risk of gabapentinoid toxicity, particularly in dialysis patients, because these drugs are excreted in urine. Toxicity may present with sedation, confusion, impaired balance, tremors, myoclonus or ataxia. Respiratory depression has been described with combined gabapentinoid and opioid administration. Particular care is therefore required in older people, among whom respiratory disease and opioid use are common.

Document sections:
  Heading: Nerve Targets and Patient Considerations
  Content: Relatively focal PDN pain may make a patient suitable for PNS. Predominantly plantar-foot pain, for example, may be addressed through the tibial nerve. That nerve passes from the popliteal fossa through the deep posterior leg compartment and tarsal tunnel, then divides into the lateral plantar nerve (LPN), medial plantar nerve (MPN), and medial calcaneal nerve (MCN). Leads are generally placed behind the tibia and proximal to the tarsal tunnel. Other possible lower-extremity targets are the common peroneal, superficial peroneal, and sciatic nerves; median and ulnar nerves are possible upper-extremity targets. SCS and DRG-S studies have mainly addressed lower-extremity PDN. The tibial and common peroneal nerves may be entrapped at the tarsal tunnel and fibular head, respectively. Increased compression in diabetes has been proposed to contribute to injury and irreversible sensory change. Decompression neurolysis of upper- and lower-extremity nerves in people with diabetes has yielded promising results. PNS may be an option when focal pain persists after decompression; placing leads proximal to a suspected lesion, entrapment, or injury is advisable.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: Stillbirth
  Synonyms:
    - fetal death
  Description: The document uses stillbirth for delivery of a fetus without signs of life. Reporting criteria vary among U.S. states; the suggested threshold is 20 weeks or greater of gestation when gestational age is known, or a weight greater than or equal to 350 grams when it is unknown. U.S. vital statistics include fetal deaths at a stated or presumed gestation of 20 weeks or more. Terminations for life-limiting fetal anomalies and inductions for previable premature rupture of membranes are classified as pregnancy terminations rather than stillbirths.
  Epidemiology: In the United States, stillbirth occurs in 1 in 160 deliveries, with approximately 23,600 reported annually at 20 weeks or greater of gestation. The U.S. rate in 2013 was 5.96 per 1,000 live births, compared with 6.61 in 2006 and 6.05 per 1,000 births in 2012. From 2012 to 2013, the early stillbirth rate fell from 3.11 to 3.01 per 1,000 births; the late stillbirth rates of 2.96 and 2.97 per 1,000 births, respectively, did not differ significantly. Associated factors include non-Hispanic black race, nulliparity, advanced maternal age, obesity, preexisting diabetes, chronic hypertension, smoking, alcohol use, assisted reproductive technology, multiple gestation, male fetal sex, unmarried status, and adverse obstetric history. Some factors, such as smoking, are modifiable, whereas many are not. Infection is associated with approximately 10–20% of stillbirths in developed countries, placental abruption is identified as the cause in 5–10% of cases, and umbilical cord abnormalities account for approximately 10%, although a cord-related cause requires cautious assessment. A substantial proportion remains unexplained after thorough evaluation.
  Clinical presentation: At delivery, breathing, heartbeats, umbilical cord pulsation, and definite voluntary muscle movements are absent. Examination may identify dysmorphic features, inconsistent growth measurements, anomalies, hydrops, or growth restriction; these findings can increase the diagnostic yield of fetal autopsy and genetic analysis.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: early stillbirth
      Distinguishing features: Occurs at 20–27 weeks of gestation.
    - Name: late stillbirth
      Distinguishing features: Occurs at 28 weeks or greater of gestation.
    - Name: unexplained stillbirth
      Distinguishing features: A definite cause cannot be assigned despite evaluation.
    - Name: antepartum stillbirth
      Distinguishing features: Identified separately in the document's analysis of genetic diagnostic yield.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: fetal autopsy
      Purpose: Investigate the cause of death, developmental abnormalities, growth, and evidence of infection.
      When indicated: Offer during stillbirth evaluation; obtain appropriate parental permission. Diagnostic yield is greater when dysmorphic features, inconsistent growth measurements, anomalies, hydrops, or growth restriction are present.
      Interpretation: In a study of 512 fully evaluated stillbirths, autopsy was considered useful for establishing a cause in 42.4% (95% CI, 36.9–48.4).
    - Test: gross and histologic examination of the placenta, umbilical cord, and membranes
      Purpose: Assess placental disease, infection, genetic abnormalities, anemia, abruption, cord thrombosis, velamentous insertion, and vasa previa.
      When indicated: Essential to stillbirth evaluation; a trained pathologist should perform the examination. In multifetal gestations, establish chorionicity and identify vascular anastomoses.
      Interpretation: In a study of 512 fully evaluated stillbirths, placental pathology was considered useful for establishing a cause in 64.6% (95% CI, 57.9–72.0). Knots or entanglement alone do not establish a cord-related cause of death.
    - Test: prompt general examination of the stillborn fetus
      Purpose: Document dysmorphic findings and measure weight, length, and head circumference.
      When indicated: As soon as possible after delivery.
      Interpretation: Foot length can be especially useful for estimating gestational age before 23 weeks of gestation.
    - Test: photographs of the stillborn fetus
      Purpose: Preserve whole-body, facial, extremity, palm, and abnormality-specific findings for later specialist review.
      When indicated: During fetal examination, particularly when a geneticist is unavailable locally.
    - Test: partial autopsy or external examination by a trained pathologist
      Purpose: Provide an alternative assessment when a complete autopsy is unacceptable to the family.
      When indicated: If the family declines complete autopsy.
    - Test: ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging
      Purpose: Provide alternatives or adjuncts to examination when complete autopsy is declined.
      When indicated: If the family is uncomfortable with complete autopsy.
    - Test: wholebody X-ray with anterior–posterior and lateral views
      Purpose: Look for an unrecognized skeletal abnormality or further characterize an apparent deformity.
      When indicated: During assessment of the stillborn fetus when skeletal findings warrant imaging.
    - Test: genetic analyses
      Purpose: Identify genetic contributors to stillbirth.
      When indicated: Perform in all cases after appropriate parental permission; select evaluations for specific abnormalities according to clinical history and detected fetal abnormalities.
      Interpretation: In a study of 512 fully evaluated stillbirths, karyotype or microarray testing was considered useful for establishing a cause in 11.9% (95% CI, 9.1–15.3).
    - Test: microarray analysis
      Purpose: Detect aneuploidy and copy number variants, including smaller deletions and duplications not detected by karyotype.
      When indicated: Preferred genetic evaluation in the stillbirth workup, subject to cost and availability.
      Interpretation: Compared with karyotype analysis, microarray analysis increased diagnosis of a genetic cause to 41.9% in all stillbirths, 34.5% in antepartum stillbirths, and 53.8% in stillbirths with anomalies. Its ability to analyze nonviable tissue contributes to its higher diagnostic yield.
    - Test: karyotype
      Purpose: Identify chromosomal abnormalities and assess the fetus when a parent has a balanced chromosomal rearrangement or mosaic karyotype.
      When indicated: An option when microarray is not readily available; particularly important with a parental translocation, inversion, or mosaic karyotype.
      Interpretation: An abnormal karyotype is found in approximately 6–13% of stillbirths. Cell culture fails in up to 50% of karyotype attempts.
    - Test: amniocentesis for fetal karyotyping
      Purpose: Obtain a cytogenetic specimen before delivery.
      When indicated: Particularly valuable when delivery is not imminent.
      Interpretation: It has the highest yield among the specimen approaches described. In a Netherlands study, invasive testing achieved a tissue culture rate of 85%, compared with 28% for fetal tissue sampled after birth.
    - Test: placental block, umbilical cord segment, or internal fetal tissue specimen for cytogenetic analysis
      Purpose: Provide tissue for genetic analysis when needed, including when invasive testing is declined.
      When indicated: A placental block should come from below the cord insertion and include the chorionic plate; internal specimens that tolerate low-oxygen conditions include costochondral or patellar tissue.
      Interpretation: Fetal skin is a suboptimal specimen.
    - Test: comparative genomic hybridization or single nucleotide probe and copy number probe microarrays

Document sections:
  Heading: 3.3.1.1. CAP
  Content: Many prospective studies have examined whether CAP prevents recurrent febrile UTI and focal radionuclide uptake defects. CAP is not required for every child with VUR; trials found no or minimal benefit for low-grade reflux. In PREDICT, a randomised controlled trial across 39 European centres, Morello et al. studied infants with grade III, IV, or V VUR and no prior UTI. Treating seven children for 2 yr was necessary to prevent one UTI, without differences in renal scarring, kidney function, or UTI hospitalisation. CAP gave a small but significant reduction in first UTI, alongside increases in non-Escherichia coli organisms and antibiotic resistance. Among children with VUR receiving CAP, younger age at initial febrile UTI diagnosis ( 12 mo), bilateral reflux, and BBD independently predict febrile breakthrough UTI. Toilet-trained children and those with LUTD gain more benefit from CAP. RIVUR reported a 50% reduction in recurrent febrile UTI risk with prophylaxis, but no effect on focal radionuclide uptake defects or their consequences of hypertension and renal failure; antimicrobial resistance increased. Further risk-stratified analyses of RIVUR identified uncircumcised boys, children with BBD, and those with high-grade reflux as a high-risk group deriving significant CAP benefit. Rather than using CAP uniformly, medical care should shift from prophylaxis for dilating reflux toward selective use based on risk. Relevant febrile UTI risk factors include young age, high-grade VUR, toilet-training status, LUTD, female sex, and circumcision status. Reliable evidence for CAP duration is lacking; using it until BBD resolves is a practical approach. Recommendations in the literature generally use antibiotics every day at a quarter to half of the regular therapeutic dose. Common CAP drugs are Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMZ), amoxicillin, and nitrofurantoin. TMP-SMZ must be avoided at age <6 wk because of hepatic injury risk and in severe renal insufficiency because of possible kidney toxicity. Nitrofurantoin is best avoided before 4 mo because of haemolytic anaemia risk. After a febrile breakthrough UTI, changing to another prophylactic antibiotic may be considered; an available antibiogram can guide the choice. Initial medical care remains an option for a child with febrile UTI and high-grade VUR. Surgery is reserved for failure to adhere to CAP, febrile breakthrough UTIs despite CAP, or symptomatic VUR persisting over long-term follow-up, including recurrent flank pain with or without febrile UTIs. The best point to stop CAP is disputed. Recurrences are more likely after CAP for <1 yr following the last febrile UTI and in bilateral VUR. Surveillance, antireflux intervention, and CAP discontinuation should be decided individually with patients and caregivers. Detailed discussion of risks, benefits, and alternatives is strongly advised, taking access to care during febrile UTI into account. Long-term CAP effects concern patients, caregivers, and clinicians. In a secondary RIVUR analysis, TMP-SMZ prophylaxis for 2 yr was not associated with adverse changes in complete blood count, serum electrolytes, or creatinine; routine laboratory testing is not mandatory in otherwise healthy children. Effects of prolonged CAP on gut microbiota remain disputed and need further study. CAP can prevent new febrile UTIs in children with a febrile UTI history and antenatal hydronephrosis with presumed or confirmed VUR. Whether it also helps infants whose asymptomatic VUR is discovered while investigating antenatal hydronephrosis remains unclear.

Amnesia is unassessable in preverbal children and unlikely to be assessable under 5. [2023] If only 1 of these latter factors applies, observe for a minimum of 4 hours from injury; obtain head CT within 1 hour if GCS falls below 15, vomiting recurs or another episode of abnormal drowsiness occurs. retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: BRAIN AND VASCULAR IMAGING FOR THE DIAGNOSIS OF CVT
  Content: Conventional computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is often obtained first for nonspecific acute symptoms. Suspicion can arise from direct thrombus visualization, absent venous filling, tissue consequences of venous obstruction—venous infarction, edema, hemorrhagic transformation, intracranial hypertension, or hydrocephalus—or vascular consequences such as enlarged veins. Supplemental Table 2 summarizes imaging difficulties. Thin-slice CT can improve direct visualization. On noncontrast CT, increased hemoglobin and red blood cells within a thrombus produce hyperattenuation, termed the dense vessel sign. A serpiginous or linear venous hyperdensity, described as the cord or string sign, or a dense triangle sign can remain visible up to 14 days after symptom onset. Indirect CT and MRI clues include low-density areas that do not follow a usual wedge-shaped infarct pattern or arterial territory, or that spare the overlying cortex. Sagittal sinus or deep cerebral vein involvement can produce bilateral hypodensities. Hemorrhage occurs in up to 40% of patients and may represent hemorrhagic transformation within a hypodense area or intracerebral hemorrhage accompanied by subarachnoid or subdural bleeding; isolated subarachnoid and basal ganglia hemorrhages are uncommon. A juxtacortical C-shaped hyperdensity, the cashew nut sign, has reportedly high specificity but low sensitivity. Bilateral or multifocal hemorrhage is also frequent. A meta-analysis covering 27 publications and 2812 cases estimated CT sensitivity at 0.79 (95% CI, 0.76–0.82) and specificity at 0.90 (95% CI, 0.89– 0.91), below the figures previously described in the 2011 American Heart Association statement. Conventional MRI can show the thrombus directly, but its signal changes with thrombus age as oxyhemoglobin becomes deoxyhemoglobin and methemoglobin. Early thrombus can be isointense or hypointense on T2 and resemble a normal sinus flow void, complicating diagnosis. Time-of-flight magnetic resonance venography (MRV) can likewise mislead when absent flow is not confirmed on T1//T2. Corroboration using gradient-recalled echo, susceptibility-weighted imaging, or contrast-enhanced MRV is often useful. Thrombosed blood produces a blooming artifact on gradient-recalled echo and susceptibility-weighted sequences; for subtle cortical vein thrombosis, their sensitivity and specificity approach 100%. T1-based black-blood imaging is described as promising. MRI detects parenchymal injury secondary to venous occlusion more sensitively than CT; resulting lesions can be bilateral and cross arterial territories. A meta-analysis of 21 studies involving 1773 patients with CVT estimated sensitivity of conventional MRI sequences at 0.82 (95% CI, 0.78–0.85) and specificity at 0.92 (95% CI, 0.91–0.94). The figures illustrate venous-system anatomy and sinus involvement, examples of thrombosis and hemorrhage on noncontrast CT, and venous thrombosis, infarction, edema, and filling defects on MRI. Sinus-involvement percentages in the anatomy figure may exceed 100% because >1 sinus can be affected; internal jugular vein thrombosis there refers to its coexistence with CVT, not isolated jugular thrombosis.

Document sections:
  Heading: Plain language summary
  Content: Up to three quarters of stroke survivors experience visual problems; most, about 60%, are caused by stroke, while others usually reflect pre-existing eye conditions. Patients and clinical teams may not recognise that stroke has affected vision. Possible impairments involve eye movements, central or peripheral vision, attention to part of the visual environment, and processing of visual information such as colour or recognition. The optimal screening method, timing and management remain uncertain. The reviewed studies identify screening approaches usable within days of onset and treatment options that depend on the impairment; they also expose areas needing better research. The guideline recommends vision screening to improve detection, using a validated tool or specialist vision team, with early screening within 3–4days of onset. For treatment, it recommends visual scanning or visual search to support adaptation to field loss; thrombolysis within 4.5h of onset for ocular stroke; early measures such as glasses to improve acuity; referral for specialist management of eye movement disorders; and interventions tailored to visual neglect or perceptual deficits. It recommends collaboration among stroke teams, particularly occupational therapy, neuropsychology and eye care, alongside suitable information, resources and vision aids for survivors and caregivers.

  Heading: Pediatric Considerations
  Content: Consensus guidance based on pooled retrospective evidence supports considering ICP monitoring in severe pediatric TBI. Studies finding no functional-survival improvement or increased morbidity and mortality could not adequately account for differences between monitored and unmonitored groups. Recent retrospective evidence suggests similar long-term outcomes with EVD and intraparenchymal transducers, although EVD drainage may produce slightly lower acute ICP. Select a technique according to clinical risks and advantages. Cerebral blood flow, autoregulation, blood pressure, ICP, and CPP vary with development; children's appropriate MAP and CPP are below adult values. Document sections:
  Heading: 1. Introduction
  Content: CNS tumours are the most common solid neoplasms in children and adolescents. Their histological diversity, age at diagnosis, location, stage and genetic features contribute to markedly different courses and long-term outcomes. Management ranges from observation or surgery alone to combined surgery, chemotherapy, sometimes at high dose, and radiotherapy. More detailed MRI has improved tumour characterization and surgical planning. Neurosurgical advances include neuro-navigation, stereotactic techniques, intra-operative ultrasound and MRI, alongside better peri-operative support. Diagnosis of sampled tissue now integrates morphology with immunohistochemical, genetic and epigenetic findings; this has refined tumour subdivisions in the WHO classification of tumours of the central nervous system. Radiotherapy developments seek to lower doses, restrict fields or avoid irradiation when possible; adopted techniques include IMRT, Tomotherapy and Proton Beam Therapy. Care requires early and continuing coordination among paediatric (neuro)oncology, neurosurgery, neuroradiology, radiotherapy, neuropathology, neuropaediatrics, neuro-ophthalmology, endocrinology, rehabilitation and other disciplines. Increasing survival has made late effects important both when choosing initial therapy and during long-term follow-up. Separate chapters address disciplines and specific CNS tumour entities.

Document sections:
  Heading: Tonic or atonic seizures
  Content: Atonic loss of tone or sustained tonic stiffening can cause a sudden fall. These seizures occur in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome and other conditions, often cause injury and can substantially affect quality of life. Assessment by a neurologist with epilepsy expertise helps establish the syndrome and guide investigations and treatment. Direct first-line evidence was absent, so the committee extrapolated from generalised tonic-clonic seizures. It judged sodium valproate the most effective option relative to other antiseizure medicines. Following January 2025 MHRA changes, sodium valproate and lamotrigine are first-line monotherapy or add-on options, with reproductive precautions for sodium valproate. Long-term sodium valproate may reduce bone mineral density and raise osteomalacia risk; consider supplementation for those at risk. Evidence supports add-on lamotrigine for seizure or drop-attack control, making it an option for women and girls able to have children. Sodium valproate may still be an option for some of them only after thorough risk–benefit discussion, unsuccessful alternatives, MHRA safeguards and shared decision making. Evidence indicates that clobazam, rufinamide and topiramate may also help as second-line monotherapy or add-ons; no clear cost-effectiveness evidence established one as superior. Topiramate requires Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions for women and girls of childbearing potential. Low-quality evidence without direct comparisons prevented clear prioritisation of further options. A ketogenic diet may be considered as an add-on under a ketogenic diet team; felbamate may be considered subsequently under an epilepsy-expert neurologist. Some other antiseizure medicines may worsen seizures. Prescribing order may change, and sodium valproate or topiramate may require additional counselling, clinical assessment and administration.

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_01
  Condition: traumatic brain injury
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients requiring acute care after TBI
  Decision rules:
    - Aim to keep physiologic measurements within the recommended ranges while weighing the risks of interventions needed to achieve them.
    - When ICP is not monitored, treatment targeting SBP ≥ 110 mm Hg/MAP > 80 mm Hg generally supports cerebral perfusion.
    - Use CPP ≥ 60 mm Hg as an initial practical target, adjusting it according to cerebral autoregulation.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Goal-directed physiologic management
      Summary: Initial targets include SpO2 ≥ 94%, PaO2 80–100 mm Hg, PaCO2 35–45 mm Hg, pH 7.35–7.45, ICP < 22 mm Hg, PbtO2 ≥ 15 mm Hg when monitored, CPP 60–70 mm Hg, serum sodium 135–145 mEq/L, serum osmolality ≤ 320 mOsm, INR ≤ 1.4, temperature 36.0–37.9°C, platelets ≥ 75 × 103/mm3, glucose 100–180 mg/dL, and hemoglobin ≥ 7 g/dL. These are ideal ranges rather than goals to pursue regardless of treatment risk.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: Individualized pulmonary targets
      Summary: Patients with significant pulmonary disease may need lung-directed targets, including permissive hypercapnia, while other interventions control elevated ICP.
      Conditions for use: Significant pulmonary problems such as acute respiratory distress syndrome
  Not recommended:
    - Name: PaO2 > 100 mm Hg
      Reason: Avoid hyperoxia unless brain oximetry guides the higher target.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: Throughout acute treatment
      Method: Repeated assessment of blood pressure, gas exchange, temperature, sodium, glucose, coagulation, and monitored cerebral parameters
      Interpretation: Adjust treatment to the patient's condition and the risks of further intervention.
  Supportive care:
    - Treat fever aggressively and maintain normothermia.
    - Prevent hyponatremia; monitor serum sodium frequently when indicated.
    - Measure osmolality when mannitol is used.
    - Monitor glucose more often when nutritional support begins, particularly with confirmed or suspected diabetes mellitus.
    - Assess coagulopathy early; TEG, ROTEM, and platelet function assays may inform targeted reversal.

  Content: Older-adult-specific evidence for multimodal monitoring is limited, and aging physiology can alter the usefulness and interpretation of findings.   Heading: 4.1. Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis
  Content: Early FG manifestations may include localized pain, swelling, erythema, and warmth. Progression can produce fever, chills, generalized weakness, and eventually septic shock. Isolated penile swelling despite normal-appearing skin has also been documented. Clinicians should consider FG with swelling, fever, leukocytosis, or pain disproportionate to examination findings, particularly in older people; genital bruising, crepitus, and bullae are additional reported signs. Diagnosis primarily depends on clinical assessment because treatment is urgent, and suspicion warrants prompt surgical consultation. Laboratory abnormalities include leukocytosis, raised serum creatinine, and metabolic acidosis. Blood cultures help establish the polymicrobial cause and guide antibiotics. CT can delineate perineal anatomy and assess possible retroperitoneal extension. Among FG severity and outcome scores, Fournier Gangrene Severity Index (FGSI) and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) are described as the most reliable predictors of in-hospital mortality. The authors cite a decline in mortality to 7.3% in the last 20 years alongside improvements in care.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 3.3.1.1. CAP
  Content: Many prospective studies have examined whether CAP prevents recurrent febrile UTI and focal radionuclide uptake defects. CAP is not required for every child with VUR; trials found no or minimal benefit for low-grade reflux. In PREDICT, a randomised controlled trial across 39 European centres, Morello et al. studied infants with grade III, IV, or V VUR and no prior UTI. Treating seven children for 2 yr was necessary to prevent one UTI, without differences in renal scarring, kidney function, or UTI hospitalisation. CAP gave a small but significant reduction in first UTI, alongside increases in non-Escherichia coli organisms and antibiotic resistance. Among children with VUR receiving CAP, younger age at initial febrile UTI diagnosis ( 12 mo), bilateral reflux, and BBD independently predict febrile breakthrough UTI. Toilet-trained children and those with LUTD gain more benefit from CAP. RIVUR reported a 50% reduction in recurrent febrile UTI risk with prophylaxis, but no effect on focal radionuclide uptake defects or their consequences of hypertension and renal failure; antimicrobial resistance increased. Further risk-stratified analyses of RIVUR identified uncircumcised boys, children with BBD, and those with high-grade reflux as a high-risk group deriving significant CAP benefit. Rather than using CAP uniformly, medical care should shift from prophylaxis for dilating reflux toward selective use based on risk. Relevant febrile UTI risk factors include young age, high-grade VUR, toilet-training status, LUTD, female sex, and circumcision status. Reliable evidence for CAP duration is lacking; using it until BBD resolves is a practical approach. Recommendations in the literature generally use antibiotics every day at a quarter to half of the regular therapeutic dose. Common CAP drugs are Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMZ), amoxicillin, and nitrofurantoin. TMP-SMZ must be avoided at age <6 wk because of hepatic injury risk and in severe renal insufficiency because of possible kidney toxicity. Nitrofurantoin is best avoided before 4 mo because of haemolytic anaemia risk. After a febrile breakthrough UTI, changing to another prophylactic antibiotic may be considered; an available antibiogram can guide the choice. Initial medical care remains an option for a child with febrile UTI and high-grade VUR. Surgery is reserved for failure to adhere to CAP, febrile breakthrough UTIs despite CAP, or symptomatic VUR persisting over long-term follow-up, including recurrent flank pain with or without febrile UTIs. The best point to stop CAP is disputed. Recurrences are more likely after CAP for <1 yr following the last febrile UTI and in bilateral VUR. Surveillance, antireflux intervention, and CAP discontinuation should be decided individually with patients and caregivers. Detailed discussion of risks, benefits, and alternatives is strongly advised, taking access to care during febrile UTI into account. Long-term CAP effects concern patients, caregivers, and clinicians. In a secondary RIVUR analysis, TMP-SMZ prophylaxis for 2 yr was not associated with adverse changes in complete blood count, serum electrolytes, or creatinine; routine laboratory testing is not mandatory in otherwise healthy children. Effects of prolonged CAP on gut microbiota remain disputed and need further study. CAP can prevent new febrile UTIs in children with a febrile UTI history and antenatal hydronephrosis with presumed or confirmed VUR. Whether it also helps infants whose asymptomatic VUR is discovered while investigating antenatal hydronephrosis remains unclear.

Document sections:
  Heading: Gaucher disease management during pregnancy
  Content: 2.1 Standard high-risk pregnancy care alone is insufficient; each pregnant patient with GD requires an individualized program led by an expert multidisciplinary team (Strong Agreement). 2.2 In the first trimester, measure lysoGb1 and/or chitotriosidase and/or, calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12 levels (Strong Agreement). 2.3 Patients who conceive through IVF may receive Aspirin if platelet function is normal and thrombocytopenia does not preclude its use (Weak Agreement). 2.4 Provide calcium and vitamin D during pregnancy and preventive vitamin B12 sufficient to meet daily requirements before and during pregnancy because of particular anemia and neuropathy risks. If low B12 is found at pregnancy diagnosis, up to week 9, provide therapeutic doses (Strong Agreement). 2.5 During the second and third trimesters, measure lysoGb1 and/or chitotriosidase and/or lysoGb1, calcium and vitamin D levels (Strong Agreement). 2.6 In the third trimester, assess platelet function and, if not previously assessed during pregnancy, examine liver and spleen size by ultrasound (Strong Agreement). Available in vitro approaches to primary-hemostasis assessment include platelet function analyzer (PFA)100/200, platelet aggregometry, flow cytometry, and cone and platelet analyzer. PFA-100/200 is widely used for platelet-function assessment and has been proposed in place of ‘skin bleeding time’ to assess presurgical bleeding risk, but has not been tested in GD. In the sole cited GD study using the cone platelet (let) analyzer, reduced platelet adhesion was associated with mucosal bleeding whereas an aggregation defect was not. Neither method has specific evidence in pregnant women with GD. A last-trimester ultrasound is also recommended to establish whether hepatosplenomegaly is present, particularly when cesarean delivery is contemplated (Weak Agreement); a low transversal incision is recommended if cesarean delivery occurs. 2.7 Perform magnetic resonance imaging for bone crises or worsening bone disease during pregnancy (Strong Agreement). 2.8 Adjust the ERT dose when GD worsens during pregnancy (Strong Agreement). 2.9 Offer prenatal genetic diagnosis when the partner carries GD or, for IVF, the donor’s status is unknown (Weak Agreement). Preconception assessment of carrier status in couples is recommended to distinguish embryos carrying one GD mutation from those carrying two and affected by GD, and to inform decisions according to mutation type and risk.

Document sections:
  Heading: Status epilepticus
  Content: Convulsive status epilepticus requires immediate emergency antiseizure treatment. Follow an available individual emergency plan specifying the prescribed rescue medicine, trained administrator and timing. Evidence favoured benzodiazepines overall without clearly identifying a superior one; rapid delivery matters more than which benzodiazepine is selected. Buccal or rectal administration is usual in the community when intravenous access is unavailable. Intravenous lorazepam is the hospital first choice because of rapid action and less respiratory depression and sedation than alternatives. Buccal midazolam remains the community first choice; rectal diazepam can substitute according to previous use or availability. After 2 benzodiazepine doses, evidence supports intravenous levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate without showing an efficacy advantage for 1. Levetiracetam may be prepared and administered more quickly and may cause fewer adverse effects; another second-line medicine can be considered if the initial one fails. January 2025 MHRA sodium valproate safeguards also apply to intravenous use. Limited evidence supported phenobarbital or general anaesthesia as third-line options under expert guidance. Some causes require additional treatment, and non-epileptic attacks need to be distinguished from convulsive status epilepticus. Recommendations reflect current practice and are not expected to have a substantial resource effect.

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_08
  Condition: Suspected preterm labour
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Women with intact membranes who report symptoms of preterm labour.
  Decision rules:
    - Offer assessment comprising clinical history, the observations specified for initial labour assessment, and a speculum examination.
    - If cervical dilatation cannot be assessed with the speculum, follow with a digital vaginal examination; when fetal fibronectin sampling is anticipated, obtain the swab before digital examination.
    - At 29+6 weeks of pregnancy or less, advise treatment for preterm labour when clinical assessment suggests suspected preterm labour.
    - At 30+0 weeks of pregnancy or more, consider transvaginal cervical-length measurement to assess the likelihood of birth within 48 hours. A length of 15 mm or less indicates diagnosed preterm labour and calls for treatment; with a length of more than 15 mm, explain that preterm labour is unlikely and consider other diagnoses.
    - If cervical-length measurement is indicated but unavailable or unacceptable at 30+0 weeks or more, consider fetal fibronectin testing. A concentration more than 50 ng/ml indicates diagnosed preterm labour and calls for treatment; a concentration 50 ng/ml or less makes preterm labour unlikely.
    - If neither test is performed to exclude preterm labour at 30+0 weeks or more, offer treatment as for diagnosed preterm labour.
    - Do not combine cervical-length measurement with fetal fibronectin testing to diagnose preterm labour.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: Within 48 hours of assessment
      Method: Transvaginal ultrasound measurement of cervical length when indicated and available.
      Interpretation: 15 mm or less supports diagnosed preterm labour; more than 15 mm makes preterm labour unlikely.
    - Timepoint: Within 48 hours of assessment when indicated cervical-length measurement is unavailable or unacceptable
      Method: Fetal fibronectin testing.
      Interpretation: More than 50 ng/ml supports diagnosed preterm labour; 50 ng/ml or less makes it unlikely.
  Supportive care:
    - Explain the available assessment and tests, how they are performed, and their benefits, risks and possible consequences, including false-positive and false-negative findings in the context of gestational age.
    - When testing makes preterm labour unlikely, discuss discharge versus hospital monitoring and treatment; advise return if symptoms persist or recur.

Document sections:
  Heading: INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE MONITORING
  Content: ICP monitoring supplements rather than replaces serial neurological and CT assessment. It is recommended in comatose patients with GCS ≤ 8 and structural brain injury on initial CT. Consider it carefully in patients with GCS > 8 and progressive-risk lesions such as large or multiple contusions; when ICP information would facilitate extracranial surgery or potentially ICP-raising treatments; after radiographic progression or clinical deterioration; or when urgent extracranial surgery, airway compromise, or respiratory failure necessitates sedation. It is generally not indicated for coma without structural damage or evidence of elevated ICP on initial CT; neurological examinations and serial CT can be used instead. Persistent ICP elevation predicts poor outcome. Monitoring allows calculation of CPP from MAP – ICP = CPP, supports decisions about cerebral perfusion, and may warn of lesion progression, swelling, or postoperative complications.

question: What is the best preventive measure for neural tube defects?
