retrieved_chunks.document_id: Perichart Perera et al. 2023 Importancia de la suplementación en el embarazo papel de la suplementación con hierro, ácido fólico
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Ácido fólico
  Content: Los defectos del tubo neural afectan tempranamente al cerebro, la columna vertebral o la médula espinal por cierre inadecuado del tubo neural embrionario, y pueden causar discapacidad o muerte. El ácido fólico, vitamina hidrosoluble B9, favorece ese cierre mediante proliferación celular; participa como cofactor en el metabolismo del carbono y en la regulación epigenética de genes relacionados con el cierre neural. La ingestión diaria recomendada durante el embarazo es de 600-750 mcg/d. La anemia megaloblástica por deficiencia de folato es la segunda más frecuente entre las embarazadas. Una dieta insuficiente, la absorción alterada y la mayor demanda por eritropoyesis y crecimiento fetal pueden ocasionar deficiencia, particularmente sin suplementación. Para prevenir defectos del tubo neural, la OMS recomienda 400 mcg/d de ácido fólico a todas las mujeres en edad reproductiva, desde antes del embarazo y durante la gestación, en cualquier contexto (intervención recomendada). La Sociedad de Obstetras y Ginecólogos de Canadá (SOGC) recomienda a mujeres y parejas de bajo riesgo, sin antecedentes personales ni familiares de defectos congénitos sensibles a ácido fólico, 400 mcg/d desde 3 meses antes de concebir, durante el embarazo y hasta 4 a 6 semanas posparto o durante la lactancia materna (grado II-2A); también indica aconsejar un mayor consumo de alimentos fuente de folato (grado III-A). Una revisión Cochrane con 6,708 nacimientos halló que el ácido fólico diario, solo o combinado con otros micronutrimentos, previno defectos del tubo neural frente a placebo o suplementos sin ácido fólico (riesgo relativo [RR]: 0.31; intervalo de confianza del 95% [IC 95%]: 0.17-0.58; 5 estudios; evidencia de alta calidad), y redujo su recurrencia (RR: 0.34; IC 95%: 0.18-0.64; 4 estudios; 1,846 nacimientos). El efecto no varió según las dosis estudiadas, de 400 mcg o más, ni según su administración aislada o combinada. Una revisión sistemática del Grupo de Trabajo de Servicios Preventivos de EE.UU. (USPSTF) recomienda 400 a 800 mcg diarios a quienes planean embarazarse o pueden hacerlo para prevenir estos defectos (recomendación grado A), por considerar sustancial el beneficio. Para riesgo moderado propio o de la pareja, la SOGC indica un multivitamínico con 1 mg de ácido fólico desde 3 meses antes de la concepción hasta las primeras 12 semanas de gestación (sdg) (grado II-2A), seguido de 400 mcg/d a 1 mg/d desde la semana 12 hasta la semana 4-6 posparto o durante la lactancia. Incluye en este grupo antecedentes familiares de primer o segundo grado de defectos del tubo neural, antecedentes personales de otros defectos congénitos sensibles a ácido fólico, diabetes mellitus, uso de medicamentos teratogénicos —entre ellos anticonvulsivos, metformina, metotrexato y colestiramina— y malabsorción gastrointestinal importante por enfermedad de Crohn, enfermedad celiaca activa, cirugía bariátrica, diálisis, enfermedad hepática avanzada o consumo crónico de alcohol. Para riesgo alto, definido por antecedentes personales de defectos del tubo neural en la mujer o su pareja, o por un embarazo previo afectado, la SOGC recomienda 4 mg/d desde 3 meses antes de la concepción hasta las primeras 12 sdg, y después 400 mcg/d a 1 mg/d durante embarazo y posparto (grado I-A). Si cualquiera de los integrantes de la pareja tuvo previamente un embarazo afectado, ambos deben seguir el mismo esquema (grado II-2A). Como la mayoría de los multivitamínicos contiene 400 mcg a 1 mg/d, las mujeres que precisan dosis altas deben añadir ácido fólico (grado II-2A). El Colegio de Obstetricia y Ginecología de Reino Unido (RCOG, Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists) indica 5 mg/d para obesidad, con índice de masa corporal [IMC] mayor o igual a 30, desde al menos 1 mes antes hasta el final del primer trimestre; también para talasemia o enfermedad de células falciformes, desde 3 meses antes del embarazo (talasemia: recomendación A; enfermedad de células falciformes/ obesidad: recomendación D). Una revisión Cochrane del 2015 no encontró evidencia de prevención de paladar hendido (RR: 0.73; IC 95%: 0.05-10.89; 3 estudios; evidencia de baja calidad), labio leporino (RR: 0.79; IC 95%: 0.14-4.36; 3 estudios; evidencia de baja calidad), defectos cardiovasculares congénitos (RR: 0.57; IC 95%: 0.24-1.33; 3 estudios; evidencia de baja calidad), abortos (RR: 1.10; IC 95%: 0.94-1.28; 5 estudios; evidencia de moderada calidad) u otros defectos del nacimiento (RR: 0.94; IC 95%: 0.53-1.66; 3 estudios; evidencia de baja calidad). Un metaanálisis de países de ingresos bajos y medios incluyó 17 estudios, 13 cohortes y 4 ensayos clínicos aleatorizados [ECA], con n = 275,421 mujeres. Encontró un peso al nacer mayor por 0.37 kg (IC 95%: 0.24-0.50; 9 estudios; heterogeneidad entre estudios τ2: 0.03; χ2: 28.13; df: 8; p = 0.00004; I2: 72%); el efecto fue mayor en los ECA (0.56 kg; IC 95%: 0.15-0.97; 3 estudios), con bajo riesgo de sesgo. También encontró menor riesgo de bajo peso al nacer (BPN) (razón de momios [RM]: 0.59; IC 95%: 0.47-0.74; 10 estudios; heterogeneidad entre estudios τ2: 0.07; χ2: 44.34; df: 9; p < 0.00001; I2: 80%), aunque con cierto riesgo de sesgo. Un metaanálisis observacional asoció las concentraciones altas de folato con una reducción del 28% del riesgo de parto pretérmino (RM: 0.72; IC 95%: 0.56-0.93; 6 cohortes y 4 casos y controles). Una mayor exposición a suplementos con ácido fólico, solos o combinados, se asoció con una reducción del 10% (RM: 0.90; IC 95%: 0.85-0.95; 19 estudios). El inicio preconcepcional se asoció significativamente con menor riesgo (RM: 0.87; IC 95%: 0.84-0.91; p < 0.001; 9 estudios). Hubo efecto con dosis < 1 mg/d (RM: 0.90; IC 95%: 0.85-0.95; p < 0.001), pero no con dosis mayores; la ausencia de ensayos clínicos limita la evidencia a un nivel bajo. Un metaanálisis de 14 estudios, 13 cohortes y 1 ECA, encontró menor riesgo de preeclampsia con suplementación de ácido fólico (RM: 0.69; IC 95%: 0.58-0.83; p < 0.01; 12 estudios; alta heterogeneidad, I2: 86%; p < 0.01). El multivitamínico con ácido fólico sí redujo ese riesgo (RM: 0.70; IC 95%: 0.53-0.93; p = 0.01; 7 estudios), mientras que el ácido fólico solo no lo redujo (RM: 0.97; IC 95%: 0.80-1.17; p = 0.73; 5 estudios). Estos posibles beneficios perinatales adicionales aún no forman parte de las recomendaciones. El ácido fólico suele ser seguro durante el embarazo. Se ha planteado, sin evidencia contundente, que podría ocultar una deficiencia de vitamina B12. Para mujeres que necesitan dosis altas de ácido fólico se recomienda añadir 2.6 mcg/d de vitamina B12, posiblemente en el mismo multivitamínico (grado II-2A). Entre los efectos asociados se mencionan interacciones con fármacos que inhiben el metabolismo del folato, menor absorción de zinc y reacciones de hipersensibilidad.

Document sections:
  Heading: 3.2. Regional Vulnerability to Ischemia
  Content: Anatomy and injury mechanisms affect regional ischemic susceptibility and support tailoring hemodynamic care. Principal vessels described are the anterior spinal artery (0.2–0.8 mm), posterolateral spinal artery (0.1–0.4 mm), and arteria radicularis magna or artery of Adamkiewicz (0.5–1.2 mm). The cervical cord may be more ischemia-prone than thoracic or lumbar regions because of its greater metabolic demand and dependence on the anterior spinal artery. Its cervical enlargement contains many motor neurons serving upper-limb innervation, while numerous ascending sensory and descending motor pathways add to metabolic demand. Vascular differences produce distinct syndromes: anterior spinal artery syndrome causes motor impairment and loss of pain and temperature sensation; posterior spinal artery syndrome affects proprioception and vibration. Other presentations include sulcal artery syndrome, conus medullaris infarction, which can be mistaken for cauda equina syndrome, and central spinal infarction, often following cardiac arrest or severe prolonged hypotension. Table 1 describes arterial and venous supply, anatomy, and clinical vulnerability across cervical (C1–C8), upper thoracic (T1–T6), and lower thoracic (T7–T12) regions. Traumatic SCI frequently combines vascular disruption, compression, and immediate ischemia; vascular insufficiency or degenerative causes of non-traumatic SCI may produce more gradual ischemia. MAP goals and vasopressor choice should therefore account for mechanism and neurological level. Available evidence chiefly concerns traumatic cervical SCI, which often causes neurogenic shock with marked bradycardia, hypotension, and autonomic disturbance. Thoracic and lumbar injuries are less likely to cause neurogenic shock but may call for attention to venous stasis and systemic perfusion. Cervical and high thoracic lesions interrupt sympathetic outflow while preserving parasympathetic activity, causing bradycardia, lower cardiac output, and hypotension, particularly with exertion or upright posture. Reduced vascular tone promotes peripheral pooling and decreased venous return. These patients face a high risk of life-threatening autonomic dysreflexia triggered by noxious stimuli, with abrupt hypertension below the lesion and compensatory vasodilation above it. Management calls for close monitoring, vasopressors to sustain MAP, and prevention of triggers. Primary and secondary processes, including ischemia, inflammation, and glial scarring, vary by injury type and level.

Document sections:
  Heading: BRAIN AND VASCULAR IMAGING FOR THE DIAGNOSIS OF CVT
  Content: Conventional computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is often obtained first for nonspecific acute symptoms. Suspicion can arise from direct thrombus visualization, absent venous filling, tissue consequences of venous obstruction—venous infarction, edema, hemorrhagic transformation, intracranial hypertension, or hydrocephalus—or vascular consequences such as enlarged veins. Supplemental Table 2 summarizes imaging difficulties. Thin-slice CT can improve direct visualization. On noncontrast CT, increased hemoglobin and red blood cells within a thrombus produce hyperattenuation, termed the dense vessel sign. A serpiginous or linear venous hyperdensity, described as the cord or string sign, or a dense triangle sign can remain visible up to 14 days after symptom onset. Indirect CT and MRI clues include low-density areas that do not follow a usual wedge-shaped infarct pattern or arterial territory, or that spare the overlying cortex. Sagittal sinus or deep cerebral vein involvement can produce bilateral hypodensities. Hemorrhage occurs in up to 40% of patients and may represent hemorrhagic transformation within a hypodense area or intracerebral hemorrhage accompanied by subarachnoid or subdural bleeding; isolated subarachnoid and basal ganglia hemorrhages are uncommon. A juxtacortical C-shaped hyperdensity, the cashew nut sign, has reportedly high specificity but low sensitivity. Bilateral or multifocal hemorrhage is also frequent. A meta-analysis covering 27 publications and 2812 cases estimated CT sensitivity at 0.79 (95% CI, 0.76–0.82) and specificity at 0.90 (95% CI, 0.89– 0.91), below the figures previously described in the 2011 American Heart Association statement. Conventional MRI can show the thrombus directly, but its signal changes with thrombus age as oxyhemoglobin becomes deoxyhemoglobin and methemoglobin. Early thrombus can be isointense or hypointense on T2 and resemble a normal sinus flow void, complicating diagnosis. Time-of-flight magnetic resonance venography (MRV) can likewise mislead when absent flow is not confirmed on T1//T2. Corroboration using gradient-recalled echo, susceptibility-weighted imaging, or contrast-enhanced MRV is often useful. Thrombosed blood produces a blooming artifact on gradient-recalled echo and susceptibility-weighted sequences; for subtle cortical vein thrombosis, their sensitivity and specificity approach 100%. T1-based black-blood imaging is described as promising. MRI detects parenchymal injury secondary to venous occlusion more sensitively than CT; resulting lesions can be bilateral and cross arterial territories. A meta-analysis of 21 studies involving 1773 patients with CVT estimated sensitivity of conventional MRI sequences at 0.82 (95% CI, 0.78–0.85) and specificity at 0.92 (95% CI, 0.91–0.94). The figures illustrate venous-system anatomy and sinus involvement, examples of thrombosis and hemorrhage on noncontrast CT, and venous thrombosis, infarction, edema, and filling defects on MRI. Sinus-involvement percentages in the anatomy figure may exceed 100% because >1 sinus can be affected; internal jugular vein thrombosis there refers to its coexistence with CVT, not isolated jugular thrombosis.

Neoplasms tend to develop more slowly than other optic neuropathies. Optic nerve gliomas are the most common primary optic nerve neoplasm; they can be incidental, including in younger patients with neurofibromatosis type 1, or present with visual symptoms or proptosis, and are more likely to be malignant when presenting in adults. Orbital meningiomas can arise from the optic nerve sheath or extend from an intracranial mass; symptomatic sheath lesions classically cause gradual, painless visual decline. Inflammatory and demyelinating ON can resemble one another clinically and radiologically; enhancement reflects edema, inflammation, or demyelination. Possible causes of demyelinating ON include MS, NMO, and MOGAD. ON can also reflect chronic relapsing-remitting inflammatory disease, steroid-dependent recurrence, systemic inflammation, or infection. Enhancement patterns overlap but may help: bilateral simultaneous and longer optic nerve involvement occur more often with MOGAD or NMO than MS, which characteristically affects a shorter unilateral segment. Sheath or perioptic enhancement is more distinctive of MOGAD. Anterior involvement is more typical of MS or MOGAD; NMO tends toward posterior nerves, chiasm, or tracts. Brain and spine MRI may identify associated abnormalities; asymptomatic optic nerve lesions may help distinguish relapsing-remitting MS or clinically isolated syndrome from NMO or MOGAD. Optic perineuritis can arise from idiopathic orbital inflammation, autoimmunity, infection, or other inflammation and may mimic acute demyelinating ON, including visual loss and pain worsened by eye movement. Patients with perineuritis tend to be older and more likely to retain central vision. Ischemic optic neuropathy is anterior, AION, when involving the nerve head, or posterior, PION, when involving the retrobulbar nerve. AION classically causes disc edema and altitudinal field loss. Either form may be nonarteritic, in patients with vascular risk factors such as hypertension or diabetes, or arteritic, most commonly from giant cell arteritis. Imaging aims to identify optic nerve disease, narrow overlapping diagnoses, and inform management.

  Heading: Imaging
  Content: Combined MRI and CT permit a highly probable diagnosis of intracranial meningioma in most cases. Typical findings are isointensity on T1-weighted MRI, hyperintensity on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, marked enhancement, and a peripheral dural tail. Extensive FLAIR edema and heterogeneous enhancement can raise suspicion of WHO grade 2 or 3 histology. Bone-window CT helps assess neighboring hyperostosis and intraosseous spread. Somatostatin receptor 2 expression allows PET delineation after administration of agents such as 68Ga-DOTATATE or 90Y-DOTATOC. Although this is not standardly available, it can help separate tumor from normal tissue and postoperative changes. Figure 1 illustrates 68Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT alongside CT and contrast-enhanced MRI views. Conventional angiography has a diminishing diagnostic role but may help if invasion of a lateral sinus or superior sagittal sinus is suspected and MRI angiography is inconclusive; 3D venous angiography can clarify sinus openness and collateral drainage. Routine preoperative embolization is not recommended because it has been associated with more postoperative cardiovascular complications. A randomized trial identified reduced operating time as its sole potential advantage. The surgical team should decide individually; embolization may help when feeding vessels cannot be reached surgically, including petroclival tumors, with the aim of closing the meningeal branch of the ascending pharyngeal artery or tentorial branch of the internal carotid artery. For observational follow-up, MRI is the reference imaging method. Size is generally assessed on gadolinium-enhanced T1 images; axial T2 images yield comparable measurement information. Surveillance based on gadolinium-enhanced T1 imaging remains a good practice point, although T2-only follow-up can be considered for small lesions. MRI-based machine-learning models may improve diagnosis in selected future settings.

Document sections:
  Heading: BRAIN AND VASCULAR IMAGING FOR THE DIAGNOSIS OF CVT
  Content: Conventional computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is often obtained first for nonspecific acute symptoms. Suspicion can arise from direct thrombus visualization, absent venous filling, tissue consequences of venous obstruction—venous infarction, edema, hemorrhagic transformation, intracranial hypertension, or hydrocephalus—or vascular consequences such as enlarged veins. Supplemental Table 2 summarizes imaging difficulties. Thin-slice CT can improve direct visualization. On noncontrast CT, increased hemoglobin and red blood cells within a thrombus produce hyperattenuation, termed the dense vessel sign. A serpiginous or linear venous hyperdensity, described as the cord or string sign, or a dense triangle sign can remain visible up to 14 days after symptom onset. Indirect CT and MRI clues include low-density areas that do not follow a usual wedge-shaped infarct pattern or arterial territory, or that spare the overlying cortex. Sagittal sinus or deep cerebral vein involvement can produce bilateral hypodensities. Hemorrhage occurs in up to 40% of patients and may represent hemorrhagic transformation within a hypodense area or intracerebral hemorrhage accompanied by subarachnoid or subdural bleeding; isolated subarachnoid and basal ganglia hemorrhages are uncommon. A juxtacortical C-shaped hyperdensity, the cashew nut sign, has reportedly high specificity but low sensitivity. Bilateral or multifocal hemorrhage is also frequent. A meta-analysis covering 27 publications and 2812 cases estimated CT sensitivity at 0.79 (95% CI, 0.76–0.82) and specificity at 0.90 (95% CI, 0.89– 0.91), below the figures previously described in the 2011 American Heart Association statement. Conventional MRI can show the thrombus directly, but its signal changes with thrombus age as oxyhemoglobin becomes deoxyhemoglobin and methemoglobin. Early thrombus can be isointense or hypointense on T2 and resemble a normal sinus flow void, complicating diagnosis. Time-of-flight magnetic resonance venography (MRV) can likewise mislead when absent flow is not confirmed on T1//T2. Corroboration using gradient-recalled echo, susceptibility-weighted imaging, or contrast-enhanced MRV is often useful. Thrombosed blood produces a blooming artifact on gradient-recalled echo and susceptibility-weighted sequences; for subtle cortical vein thrombosis, their sensitivity and specificity approach 100%. T1-based black-blood imaging is described as promising. MRI detects parenchymal injury secondary to venous occlusion more sensitively than CT; resulting lesions can be bilateral and cross arterial territories. A meta-analysis of 21 studies involving 1773 patients with CVT estimated sensitivity of conventional MRI sequences at 0.82 (95% CI, 0.78–0.85) and specificity at 0.92 (95% CI, 0.91–0.94). The figures illustrate venous-system anatomy and sinus involvement, examples of thrombosis and hemorrhage on noncontrast CT, and venous thrombosis, infarction, edema, and filling defects on MRI. Sinus-involvement percentages in the anatomy figure may exceed 100% because >1 sinus can be affected; internal jugular vein thrombosis there refers to its coexistence with CVT, not isolated jugular thrombosis.

  Content: More than 2 nightly episodes occur in 4–18% of women aged 20–40 years and 28–62% of women aged > 70 years. In a study of 1,000 community-dwelling older adults, nocturia in women correlated with greater age, African American race, UI history, leg oedema and hypertension. A report involving > 5,000 adults aged 30–79 years found nocturia in around 28% and additional associations with cardiac disease, type 2 diabetes and diuretic use. A GRADE-assessed review found that the higher nocturia incidence associated with hypertension was more pronounced, at 1.2 to 1.3-fold, among Black and Asian women, independently of age or BMI; certainty was moderate. Another review, also with moderate certainty, associated nocturia with a 1.2-fold higher fall risk and possibly an approximately 1.3-fold higher fracture risk. A further review concluded that an ~1.3-fold higher mortality risk was probable. Causes may be urological—OAB, BOO, DU or dysfunctional voiding—or non-urological, including 24-hour polyuria, congestive heart failure, sleep apnoea, restless leg syndrome, peripheral vascular disease, sleep disorders, night-time eating, dependent oedema and excessive fluid intake. Document sections:
  Heading: Topical Capsaicin
  Content: Capsaicin acts on sensory neurons through selective agonism of transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1), expressed by nociceptive C and A-delta fibers. At 8% prescription concentration, it activates TRPV1 within the epidermis. Initial depolarization may cause warmth, itching, or pain before nociceptor desensitization. Sustained high-dose exposure increases intracellular calcium and can temporarily impair nociceptor function through membrane-potential loss, receptor desensitization, substance P depletion, and reduced fiber density. Activation of TRPV1 in immune cells may also lessen inflammation. Trials by the Capsaicin Study Group and Tandan et al found 0.075% cream significantly better than placebo over 8 and 12 weeks, respectively; Biesbroeck et al found similar results over 8 weeks. Skin irritation contributed to high dropout in these lower-dose studies. Mou et al reviewed evidence suggesting one application of an 8% patch might relieve focal neuropathic pain for up to 12 weeks. In a randomized trial of 369 patients by Simpson et al, average daily pain changed significantly more from baseline through weeks 2–8 with capsaicin (−27.4%) than placebo (−20.9%) (p<0.001), while adverse-event incidence was similar. In a randomized trial of 50 participants by Anand et al, 8% capsaicin plus standard of care (SOC) significantly improved NRS pain at 3-month follow-up compared with SOC alone. The 8% patch is FDA-approved for PDN and should be considered for moderate relief, especially after initial oral agents fail or help only partly. Table 6 summarizes the trials.

  Heading: 3.2 Epidemiology
  Content: Among males, incidence rises sharply after 55 years of age; mean age is 45.1, and estimated overall incidence is 229-627 per 100,000 males. The anterior urethra accounts for 92.2% of affected sites, particularly the bulbar urethra (46.9%). Among females with refractory lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), 2-29% have bladder outflow obstruction (BOO), of whom 4-20% have a urethral stricture; true FUS therefore affects 0.08-5.4% of women with refractory LUTS. Incidence increases markedly after 64 years of age. Following hypospadias repair, meatal stenosis or stricture is reported in 1.3-20% of cases, varying with severity and technique; incidence is significantly higher in well-resourced countries, where repair is more frequent. Up to 18% of all strictures involve the meatus or fossa navicularis, commonly following failed hypospadias repair (FHR), lichen sclerosus (LS), trauma or instrumentation, or without identified cause. Meatal stenosis after neonatal circumcision is reported in less than 0.2% of children. Strictures affect 2-56% of female-to-male (FtM) transgender patients (‘transmen’) and 4-40% of male-to-female (MtF) transgender patients (‘transwomen’); in transwomen, they arise almost exclusively at the neomeatus.

Document sections:
  Heading: Macrocytic Anemia
  Content: Macrocytic anemia may be megaloblastic or nonmegaloblastic. Megaloblastic causes include deficiencies of folate and vitamin B12 and pernicious anemia. Nonmegaloblastic causes include alcoholism, liver disease, myelodysplasia, aplastic anemia, hypothyroidism, and increased reticulocytes. MCV is greater than 100 fL in macrocytic anemia; values greater than 115 fL occur almost exclusively with folic acid or vitamin B12 deficiency. Serum folic acid or vitamin B12 measurement may confirm the diagnosis, and red cell folate measurement has also been proposed. In the United States, folic acid deficiency accounts for an overwhelming majority of macrocytic anemia that begins during pregnancy and is associated with diets lacking fresh leafy vegetables, legumes, or animal proteins. Daily folic acid needs rise during pregnancy from 50 micrograms to 400 micrograms. Treatment of folic acid deficiency arising in pregnancy should combine a nutritious diet with folic acid and iron supplementation; oral folic acid at 1 mg each day usually produces an appropriate response. Pregnancy-associated macrocytic anemia due to vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) deficiency may occur after partial or total gastric resection or with Crohn disease. After total gastrectomy, women require intramuscular vitamin B12 at 1,000 micrograms at monthly intervals.

  Content: The relative prominence of low back and leg pain matters for DS treatment and prognosis. The authors describe these symptoms as potentially arising from different processes that require different management. Missing the principal source of pain can lead either to insufficient treatment and relief or to unnecessary treatment and complications. Leg pain and radiculopathy generally indicate focal neural compression and are typically treated most directly by decompressing stenotic sites. Document sections:
  Heading: 3.5.6 Erythrocytosis
  Content: Raised haematocrit is testosterone therapy's most common adverse effect and reflects stimulation of erythropoiesis. An increase above normal usually appears between three and twelve months after starting treatment; it can also follow dose escalation, a switch from topical to parenteral therapy, or development of a relevant respiratory or haematological comorbidity. There is no evidence of harm from a haematocrit increase up to and including 54%. Above 54%, studies associate haematocrit weakly with greater cardiovascular events and mortality independently of testosterone; those studies include varied causes of secondary polycythaemia, and none isolates testosterone-induced erythrocytosis. In TRAVERSE, pulmonary embolism occurred in 0.9% of the testosterone group versus 0.5% of the placebo group among symptomatic hypogonadal men aged 45-80 years with established or high CVD risk. Three earlier large studies found no evidence of increased venous-thromboembolism risk overall, although one observed a risk peak at six months after treatment initiation that subsequently declined. In another study, venous thromboembolism occurred in 42 cases, 40 of whom had underlying thrombophilia. A meta-analysis linked many events to previously unrecognised thrombophilia-hypofibrinolysis; another meta-analysis and systematic review found no increased venous-thromboembolism risk. An RCT in stable angina found no adverse change in measured coagulation markers. Higher baseline haematocrit, smoking, and respiratory disease increase the likelihood of elevated haematocrit during therapy. Parenteral products raise haematocrit more often than topical ones; a retrospective registry found more haematocrit results > 50% with long-acting testosterone undecanoate than with gels. Existing CVD calls for particular diagnostic certainty and haematocrit and testosterone monitoring. Without comorbidity or acute cardiovascular or thromboembolic disease, elevated haematocrit may be managed by reducing dose, changing formulation, or, if very high, venesection (500 mL), repeated if necessary, usually without stopping testosterone.

Document sections:
  Heading: Cation-Channel Blockers
  Content: Neuronal sodium- or calcium-entry blockers have substantial evidence in other neuropathic pain conditions (level 1 evidence), but CRPS-specific findings are limited. Gabapentin acts at the alpha(2)-delta auxiliary subunit of voltage-dependent calcium channels and has demonstrated efficacy in postherpetic neuralgia and diabetic neuropathy (level 2 evidence). CRPS case reports and series suggest possible benefit (level 4 evidence), whereas its sole CRPS RCT was negative at a sub-maximal 1800mg/day (level 2). Pregabalin has essentially the same described mode of action and may permit twice-daily administration for some patients, but costs differ and no CRPS trial data exist. A preliminary study suggested some analgesic effect of carbamazepine 600 mg/day over 8 days in selected CRPS patients. Oxcarbazepine may cause fewer serious adverse effects than carbamazepine but can cause headache, dizziness and nausea; it has not been studied specifically in CRPS. Phenytoin has many adverse effects and no reported CRPS outcomes. Lamotrigine has not been trialed for CRPS. Evidence for levetiracetam and topiramate in CRPS is anecdotal (level 4), without compelling clinical trials.

  Heading: 4.1.2. Neurology [63]
  Content: Ventricular-outflow obstruction, especially from cerebellar or tectal lesions, can cause raised intracranial pressure and obstructive hydrocephalus. Headache and nausea or vomiting are common; increased head circumference may be the sole presenting sign in infants. Focal manifestations include weakness, sensory loss, language or cognitive difficulty, personality change and declining school or athletic performance. Cortical lesions often cause focal deficits or seizures. Brainstem lesions can produce fatigue, ataxia and multiple cranial neuropathies. Cerebellar lesions can cause impaired coordination or balance, raised-pressure signs and/or 6th cranial nerve palsy. Some posterior-fossa tumors extend through cerebellar peduncles into both brainstem and cerebellum; involvement of the area postrema can cause vomiting without other signs of raised pressure. Frontal, temporal and parietal tumors are more often associated with seizures than occipital tumors, and cortical lesions more often than deeper noncortical lesions. Gangliogliomas and dysplastic neuroepithelial tumours can be associated with chronic drug-resistant epilepsy. Infratentorial tumors seldom cause seizures.

Document sections:
  Heading: 4.6.1. What is chronic pain?
  Content: The International Association for the Study of Pain defines pain as a sensory and emotional experience related to actual or potential tissue injury. Pain persisting or recurring for longer than three months despite treatment of its original cause, or because that cause cannot be successfully treated, is considered chronic and can itself become the main clinical problem [288–290]. Estimates suggest 20% of adults have chronic pain [291–295]. Chronic pain disorders are associated with aspects of DED, and chronic pain shares pathophysiological features with DED symptoms [296]. Observational findings are reviewed here; section 4.6.6 addresses a systematic review and meta-analysis [16]. In n = 3,265,894 US veterans, ICD-coded DED co-occurred with headache, migraine, temporomandibular joint dysfunction, central pain syndrome, fibromyalgia, osteoarthritis, and post-herpetic neuralgia [297]. Traumatic brain injury was associated with more DED under both tear-insufficiency and pain coding categories [59]. In a Dutch cross-sectional study of 425 DED patients, 17% reported at least one chronic pain syndrome. These syndromes accompanied worse Ocular Surface Disease Index symptoms, with 10 items significantly higher, but not worse DED signs; patients with chronic pain had significantly less corneal staining and higher Schirmer scores [298].

Document sections:
  Heading: 10.2.1 Stuttering (recurrent or intermittent) priapism
  Content: Stuttering, intermittent, or recurrent priapism consists of repeated painful prolonged erections that resolve spontaneously between episodes. Episodes resemble recurrent ischaemic priapism but are generally shorter; their frequency and duration vary, and one can develop into prolonged ischaemic priapism. Robust epidemiological evidence is lacking. Recurrent episodes occur in 42-64% of men with SCD. Among adolescents and young men, reported priapism incidence is 35%, of whom 72% have a stuttering-priapism history. Causes resemble those of ischaemic priapism: SCD is most common, but idiopathic and neurologically associated cases occur. Acute ischaemic priapism, particularly lasting more than 4 hours, increases subsequent risk. Proposed mechanisms include inflammation, cellular adhesion, NO metabolism, vascular reactivity, and coagulation. An androgen association is disputed; lowering serum testosterone to hypogonadal levels is one proposed means of suppressing androgen-related triggers of recurrence.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: EAUN Guideline Urethral intermittent catheterisation in adults 2024
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 6.1.1 Nosocomial infection
  Content: Nosocomial or healthcare-associated infections develop during healthcare and were absent on admission. Because intermittent catheters remain in the body briefly, they do not pose a biofilm-formation risk; the guideline describes a lower risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI), while also calling CAUTI the most common IC complication, particularly with neurogenic disease. True infection frequency and comparative risk are hard to establish because studies differ in definitions, assessment periods, reporting and cohorts. Estimated CAUTI incidence following IC is 2.6 and 2.7 per person per year. The 1-year UTI incidence ranges from 62% to 77% in users with neurogenic disorders and from 38% to 42% in users with non-neurogenic disorders. Lamin and colleagues reported asymptomatic bacteriuria in 50% and symptomatic CAUTI in 10–15% of IC users. During the first year of IC, Welk and colleagues found higher values for neurogenic than non-neurogenic users for CAUTI (54.9% vs. 38.9%), CAUTI-related admission (11.3% vs. 4.0%) and ≥ 3 CAUTIs (17% vs. 9.6%); this suggests neurogenic disease independently increases risk. Symptomatic infections are most prevalent when residual urine at catheterisation is greater. Bladder volume should preferably stay at or below 400–500 ml; incomplete emptying increases UTI risk. Only symptomatic UTI should be treated in IC users because antibiotics carry resistance and adverse-effect risks (LE 1b; GR A). Bladder volumes above 400–500 ml should be explored in all users (LE 3; GR C). Hydrophilic or pre-lubricated catheters are associated with reduced CAUTI risk. Ye et al. reported a significant reduction in symptomatic CAUTI with non-touch technique combined with ready-to-use, preactivated hydrophilic or gel-lubricated catheters. It remains uncertain why hydrophilic catheters show lower infection incidence; proposed explanations include less pain and microtrauma, greater satisfaction and adherence, and avoidance of touching the catheter for additional lubrication. Håkansson and colleagues reported pyelonephritis incidence < 1% per patient per year in people with neurogenic or non-neurogenic bladders. A table identifies infection risk factors and their evidence levels.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_10
  Name: extracranial BCVI
  Synonyms:
    - blunt cerebrovascular injury
  Description: Traumatic injury of the extracranial carotid or vertebral arteries can lead to thromboembolism and ischemic stroke if it goes undetected.
  Epidemiology: Reported BCVI incidence is 2.7% to 7.6% among patients who underwent CT angiography after blunt trauma. The guideline cites mortality as high as 38% for untreated carotid injuries and 18% for untreated vertebral injuries.
  Clinical presentation: Injury may be asymptomatic or accompanied by transient ischemic symptoms, focal deficits, or infarction. Cervical spine fractures are the strongest single predictor identified in the guideline, particularly for vertebral artery injury.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: carotid artery injury
      Distinguishing features: May produce cerebral ischemia; the document discusses stenting in selected injuries.
    - Name: vertebral artery injury
      Distinguishing features: Especially associated with spine fractures; selected injuries may be considered for stenting or embolic occlusion.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: CT angiography
      Purpose: Screen for and exclude extracranial BCVI.
      When indicated: When BCVI risk factors are present; the guideline calls for liberal screening in at-risk older adults.
      Interpretation: The recommended radiographic screening modality. Strict application of Denver and Memphis screening criteria nevertheless misses 20% to 30% of BCVIs.
    - Test: Formal angiography
      Purpose: Further assess uncertain lesions or injuries potentially suitable for endovascular treatment.
      When indicated: When CT angiography leaves an injury in question or endovascular treatment is being considered.
    - Test: Head CT or MRI
      Purpose: Identify cerebral ischemia or edema in a vascular territory.
      When indicated: When neurological findings or injury assessment raise concern for BCVI.

Indica que actualmente se realizan pocas biopsias con arpón o excisionales en quirófano. Considera sospechosos los nódulos irregulares, de bordes imprecisos, consistencia leñosa o movilidad reducida, los signos inflamatorios y las adenopatías homolaterales duras y fijas. Puede haber telorrea; el 20 % presenta retracción o eccema areolomamilar. En fases avanzadas describe ulceraciones, retracción marcada, edema cutáneo o piel de naranja y adenopatías axilares palpables; también puede presentarse como carcinoma inflamatorio.   Heading: 3.1. Hemodynamic Autoregulation
  Content: Acute SCI often markedly disrupts the mechanisms that normally stabilize spinal cord blood flow despite systemic pressure changes. Neural, humoral, and local influences ordinarily adjust vascular tone as flow and pressure vary. Direct cord injury can impair these responses and cause systemic hypotension, bradycardia, and vasodilation below the lesion. Loss of sympathetic tone leaves parasympathetic activity unopposed, producing pronounced vasodilation below the injury and contributing to hypotension. Loss of autoregulatory responses also increases ischemic vulnerability. Blood–brain barrier impairment and local edema aggravate secondary ischemia. Failure to sustain adequate MAP and SCPP can cause irreversible neural injury and poor neurological outcomes.

  Content: For every emergency department arrival, stabilise airway, breathing and circulation (ABC) before addressing other injuries. Treat pain to help avert raised intracranial pressure, with reassurance, fracture splinting and bladder catheterisation when required. Document sections:
  Heading: Study Summary
  Content: Blumenthal and colleagues described a prospective, single-center series of 40 patients aged 50-80 years with Grade I spondylolisthesis, neurogenic claudication and stability defined by less than 3 mm flexion-extension motion and no severe mechanical back pain. All received D. Baseline imaging assessed slip, disc height, facet angle, flexion-extension segmental motion and sagittal rotation. During mean follow-up of 3.6 years, 15 (37%) underwent reoperation for mechanical back pain presumed to reflect instability at the index level. Reoperation occurred in 45% with disc height >6.5 mm, 39% with facet angle >50°, and 54% with motion at the slipped segment of more than 1.25 mm. The rate was 75% when all three factors were present and 0% when none was present. Although data were collected prospectively at one center, the 40 patients were not enrolled consecutively; the review consequently describes the study as appearing to be a retrospective single-center study with prospectively collected data. It had one treatment arm and no comparator. Disc height and facet angle were measured on preoperative CT; other variables came from lateral lumbar radiographs. CT disc-height measurements may be less dependable than X-ray measurements for evaluating mechanical loading. The authors did not justify stepwise multivariate forward-selection logistic regression with threshold P-value of 0.35. Mean time to reoperation follow-up, described as 3.6 years, did not appear prespecified. Reoperation was the principal efficacy endpoint, but criteria for undertaking it were absent. Minimally invasive surgery was not evaluated. These methodological issues restrict generalizability, and the evidence level was described as very low. The findings suggest segmental motion >1.25 mm, disc height >6.5 mm and facet angle >50° as important reoperation-risk markers after D in DLS: the rate was 75% with all three, while at least one marker was associated with rates of 39%–54%. Small size and nonstandardized outcomes further limit application. Surgeons should nevertheless examine preoperative images for instability indicators when deciding whether fusion might benefit a patient. The present review calls this a level 4 retrospective study, assigns evidence quality Low and gives a Conditional recommendation that radiographic evaluation may help determine when fusion should accompany planned D for DLS.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_18
  Name: Testicular microcalcification (TM)
  Description: An ultrasound finding within the testicular parenchyma that can occur with benign conditions as well as GCNIS or TGCT. The calcification itself is not malignant, and its association with future cancer remains clinically complex.
  Epidemiology: Reported in 0.6-9% of men referred for testicular US and in 6-46% of men with TGCT. A cited meta-analysis of infertile men reported an association with testicular cancer of pooled OR: 18.11, 95% CI: 8.09, 40.55; p < 0.0001. In a cited 5-year follow-up, testicular cancer did not develop in 98.4% of men with TM.
  Clinical presentation: Often detected on imaging. Additional factors relevant to malignancy assessment include infertility, bilateral TM, testicular atrophy, undescended testes and a history of TGCT.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Isolated TM
      Distinguishing features: Microcalcification without associated risk factors or suspicious lesions.
    - Name: Bilateral TM
      Distinguishing features: A finding included among factors that may raise concern for GCNIS, especially with other risks.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Scrotal US
      Purpose: Identify TM and assess for associated lesions.
      When indicated: Testicular imaging or evaluation of associated risk factors.
      Interpretation: TM alone does not establish malignancy.
    - Test: Testicular biopsy
      Purpose: Investigate GCNIS in selected higher-risk men.
      When indicated: May be offered to infertile men with TM and higher-risk features; suspicious associated findings require discussion of invasive assessment.
    - Test: Physical examination and multidisciplinary assessment
      Purpose: Assess suspicious findings and choose among surveillance, biopsy or orchidectomy.
      When indicated: TM with an associated lesion or other concerning findings.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Regular self-examination is advised, including for men without additional risk factors; a specific imaging schedule is not established for higher-risk men.
    Recommended tests:
      - Testicular self-examination.
    Long term effects:
      - Higher testicular cancer risk in infertile men with TM.
    Survivorship notes: For isolated TM without associated risk factors, the guideline advises against testicular biopsy, follow-up scrotal US, biochemical tumour markers and abdominal or pelvic computed tomography.

  Content: For every emergency department arrival, stabilise airway, breathing and circulation (ABC) before addressing other injuries. Do not attribute reduced consciousness to intoxication until important traumatic brain injury has been excluded. Clinicians assessing head injury should be able to identify the listed risk factors for head and cervical spine CT, with training provided as necessary. A trained staff member should assess impaired consciousness, defined here as GCS less than 15, immediately. Consult the tranexamic acid recommendations for GCS 12 or less. Those initially classified as low risk need reassessment by an emergency department clinician. Base final imaging decisions on the relevant age-specific criteria after discussion with radiology. Reassess anyone returning with persistent symptoms from the original injury, discuss the case with a senior clinician experienced in head injury and consider CT. Treat pain to help avert raised intracranial pressure, with reassurance, fracture splinting and bladder catheterisation when required. Consider or suspect abuse, neglect or other safeguarding concerns as a possible cause or contributor. Document sections:
  Heading: Pediatrics
  Content: A GCS of 12–15 reflects higher integrative function, which can be difficult to assess before neurological maturation. Expected verbal and motor behavior should therefore reflect developmental stage; standard GCS does not suit infants or preverbal children. The 1998 pediatric course supports full verbal score(5) for spontaneous cooing in preverbal children. In children aged 5–18years, Nesiama et al. found scene and arrival scores agreed strongly (Cohen’s kappa 0.69); mean scene scores were 0.43 points lower than ED means, without a median difference. Both predicted discharge function measured by GOS and Disability Rating Scale. In a German severe-TBI cohort that included 8.9% aged 15years, Emami et al. found lower pediatric than adult mortality overall and among patients with GCS 3 and bilateral fixed pupils (80.9% vs. 85% in that subgroup). Greater use of pediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation might have contributed. In the combined cohort, absent motor response, bilateral fixed pupils, and dilation independently accompanied higher mortality; pediatric functional outcomes were better, and the authors suggested early aggressive care may benefit patients 15years of age. The update incorporated 18 new studies, strengthened recommendations, set a 30minutes reassessment interval, and added documentation of confounders and routine hospital communication. It weakly permits simplified scoring within suitable trauma systems. Research priorities include causes and prognostic effects of scene-to-ED score changes, effects of transmitting scores, effects of central-nervous-system depressants, reliability of simplified scoring, training interventions, examination findings relevant to triage, and improved documentation.

Document sections:
  Heading: Location of lumbar stenosis
  Content: LSS is pathological narrowing of the central canal, lateral recess or neural foramen and commonly contributes to DS symptoms. Facet arthrosis, reactive ligamentous hypertrophy or disc herniation can cause soft-tissue or bony compression. Direct removal of compressive tissue, traditionally from posteriorly, can often treat uncomplicated central or lateral-recess stenosis through laminectomy, laminotomy or foraminotomy. Foraminal stenosis may instead require wider lateral exposure and partial or complete facet removal. Because facetectomy can destabilize the segment, fusion is often added to prevent iatrogenic instability. In the Spinal Laminectomy vs. Instrumented Pedicle Screw (SLIP) Trial, patients with Meyerding Grade 1 DS without overt preoperative clinical or radiographic instability underwent revision significantly more often after decompression alone involving wide laminectomy and partial facetectomy than after instrumented posterolateral fusion: 34% vs 14%, p = 0.05. Revision indications were same-segment instability in the decompression group and junctional complications in the fusion group, raising concern about surgically induced instability. Foraminal narrowing may be transverse, craniocaudal or circumferential. Hasegawa identified foraminal height less than or equal to 15 mm and posterior disc height less than or equal to 4 mm as significant indicators of lumbar foraminal stenosis. Transverse narrowing can result from dorsal facet disease, ventral foraminal disc protrusion or anterior subluxation of the superior facet; ligamentum flavum hypertrophy and osteophytes can worsen it. Foraminal stenosis without up/down narrowing may be correctable by decompression alone. With more advanced degeneration, disc collapse, olisthesis or malalignment can narrow the foramen vertically. Loss of disc height may bring pedicles into contact, and posterolateral endplate osteophytes may compress the nerve along its foraminal course. Posterior-element resection alone often does not adequately address this up/down stenosis. Distraction with an interbody device can restore disc height, limit ligamentous buckling and indirectly decompress neural structures. Although some foraminal stenosis is amenable to decompression alone, fusion that restores foraminal height can effectively increase foraminal space. Despite its frequency and relevance to symptoms and surgery, stenosis location has not previously been a formal classification component.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_02
  Name: suspected COAG
  Description: A suspected glaucoma status monitored for optic nerve head damage, visual field defects and conversion to COAG.
  Clinical presentation: Suspected COAG is asymptomatic.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Goldmann-type applanation tonometry
      Purpose: Measure IOP before referral.
      When indicated: During case-finding for COAG and related conditions.
      Interpretation: An IOP of 24 mmHg or more is a referral criterion. Consider repeating the measurement on another occasion unless urgent or emergency referral is needed.
    - Test: Goldmann applanation tonometry (slit lamp mounted)
      Purpose: Measure IOP at diagnosis and during follow-up.
      When indicated: At diagnostic assessment and every reassessment.
    - Test: standard automated perimetry
      Purpose: Investigate visual field defects and assess possible conversion to COAG.
      When indicated: Use full-threshold or supra-threshold central assessment during case-finding and a central thresholding test at diagnosis, repeating if necessary to establish severity. Repeat when clinically indicated, using a central thresholding test for suspected defects or either a central thresholding or supra-threshold test if a central thresholding test previously documented normal fields.
      Interpretation: A defect consistent with glaucoma is a referral criterion. Consider confirming a defect on another occasion before referral unless urgent or emergency referral is needed. Once a defect is detected, use the same measurement strategy at later assessments.
    - Test: stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy
      Purpose: Assess the optic nerve and examine the fundus.
      When indicated: Use during case-finding, with dilatation if needed, and at diagnosis with pupil dilatation. Reassess the optic nerve head when clinically indicated; dilate pupils if an adequate view is unavailable.
      Interpretation: Optic nerve head damage is a referral criterion. If a change is detected, obtain a new optic nerve head image for subsequent comparison.
    - Test: optic nerve head image or OCT
      Purpose: Record optic nerve head status for comparison.
      When indicated: Use during case-finding if available, obtain a baseline optic nerve head image at diagnosis and repeat imaging when clinically indicated.
    - Test: gonioscopy
      Purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber configuration and depth.
      When indicated: Use during case-finding if available and at diagnosis. Repeat when clinically indicated, including after an inconclusive examination or suspected angle-status change.
    - Test: van Herick test
      Purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber depth.
      When indicated: An alternative during case-finding if gonioscopy is unavailable or not preferred; use at diagnosis if gonioscopy is precluded by clinical circumstances and during reassessment when clinically indicated.
    - Test: OCT
      Purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber configuration and depth.
      When indicated: An alternative during case-finding if gonioscopy is unavailable or the person prefers it.
    - Test: central corneal thickness (CCT) measurement
      Purpose: Contribute to diagnostic assessment.
      When indicated: At diagnosis.
    - Test: anterior segment slit lamp examination
      Purpose: Examine the anterior segment during follow-up.
      When indicated: At each assessment, with van Herick peripheral anterior chamber depth assessment when clinically indicated.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: At every assessment, reconsider conversion and sight-loss risk. If conversion is not detected or is uncertain and IOP is uncontrolled, review management and reassess between 1 month and 4 months; if conversion is uncertain and IOP is controlled, reassess between 6 months and 12 months; if conversion is not detected and IOP is controlled, reassess between 12 months and 18 months. After conversion, follow the COAG diagnosis and reassessment recommendations. Select the appointment within the applicable interval using clinical judgement, including the need to evaluate a newly started treatment. If low lifetime visual impairment risk and acceptable IOP lead to stopping treatment, offer an IOP assessment in 1 month to 4 months, followed by reassessment if clinically indicated.
    Recommended tests:
      - Goldmann applanation tonometry (slit lamp mounted) and anterior segment slit lamp examination at every assessment.
      - van Herick peripheral anterior chamber depth assessment and repeat gonioscopy when clinically indicated.
      - Repeat standard automated perimetry when clinically indicated, with the strategy determined by whether a defect or normal fields were previously documented.
      - Repeat optic nerve head assessment when clinically indicated and obtain a new image if examination detects a change.
      - At every assessment, review general health and, when appropriate, adherence-related factors, cognitive impairment and treatment side effects.
    Survivorship notes: Uncertain conversion includes assessments lacking sufficiently accurate information. If COAG is no longer suspected after referral, discharge to primary eye care and advise regular visits at clinically appropriate intervals.

  Heading: Infantile spasms syndrome
  Content: Infantile spasms are a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy requiring urgent care and immediate tertiary paediatric neurology guidance. Untreated spasms risk poor long-term neurodevelopment, whereas prompt diagnosis and treatment are associated with better prognosis. Monitor during and after therapy for recurrent spasms, new seizure types and treatment harms. Evidence suggested that steroids combined with vigabatrin stop spasms more effectively than either treatment alone. Evidence did not clearly favour oral over injected steroids, but the committee considered oral treatment easier. Steroids may be unsuitable for some children under 2 years, including those with neurological impairments or other comorbidities; consider vigabatrin alone when steroid adverse-effect risk is high. Evidence supported vigabatrin alone initially for spasms associated with tuberous sclerosis, adding high-dose oral prednisolone if it is ineffective after 1 week. Discuss steroid effects with parents and carers, including infection, high blood pressure and high blood glucose, and explain reducing exposure to infections such as chickenpox and responding to possible exposure. Higher doses of vigabatrin and oral steroids improved freedom from spasms in the reviewed evidence; increase doses in accordance with BNF for children. Vigabatrin above specified doses may be needed if spasms persist, but only with specialist supervision. Robust second-line evidence is absent, so subsequent options rely on specialist experience. The lack of controlled trial data after first-line failure prompted a research recommendation. The recommendations reinforce best practice.

Document sections:
  Heading: Opioids.
  Content: Morphine was the first opioid used to treat pain and was isolated from opium in the early 19th century. Other opioids subsequently developed include tramadol, buprenorphine and oxycodone. Their antinociceptive action involves opioid receptors in the brain, spinal cord and peripheral tissues, chiefly MOP, for which most exogenous opioids have the greatest affinity; the other main receptor types are KOP and DOP. Receptor stimulation inhibits transmission of painful stimuli. Opioid effectiveness is reduced in neuropathic pain. Possible mechanisms include reduced MOP receptor-protein expression in the spinal dorsal horn and increased activity of pain-transmitting neuropeptides such as substance P after nerve injury. Because of limited efficacy for neuropathic pain and associated risks, opioids are currently regarded as second-line and sometimes only third-line therapy. They may be combined with other medicines or used for PHN pain while TCAs or gabapentinoids are titrated to their intended therapeutic effect. Administration for PHN is mainly oral, although studies and case reports suggest that transdermal delivery can control pain in selected patients. In one study involving people with severe paresthesia, transdermal oxycodone was effective and caused fewer gastrointestinal side-effects than oral oxycodone. Transdermal opioids may sometimes work better for patients who have difficulty following dosing instructions or taking oral medication. Prolonged opioid treatment carries potentially serious consequences, including substantial risks of physical and psychological dependence. Common adverse effects include constipation and nausea; constipation can occur after a single dose and may prompt dose reduction or discontinuation, leaving pain inadequately treated. Other very common effects are dizziness, which increases falls and serious fracture risk particularly in older people, vomiting, myoclonus and muscle rigidity. Opioids also suppress the brainstem respiratory centre and should not be used in patients with respiratory failure. These adverse effects and dependence risks support their use as second- or third-line PHN treatment or within multimodal therapy.

Document sections:
  Heading: Plain language summary
  Content: Up to three quarters of stroke survivors experience visual problems; most, about 60%, are caused by stroke, while others usually reflect pre-existing eye conditions. Patients and clinical teams may not recognise that stroke has affected vision. Possible impairments involve eye movements, central or peripheral vision, attention to part of the visual environment, and processing of visual information such as colour or recognition. The optimal screening method, timing and management remain uncertain. The reviewed studies identify screening approaches usable within days of onset and treatment options that depend on the impairment; they also expose areas needing better research. The guideline recommends vision screening to improve detection, using a validated tool or specialist vision team, with early screening within 3–4days of onset. For treatment, it recommends visual scanning or visual search to support adaptation to field loss; thrombolysis within 4.5h of onset for ocular stroke; early measures such as glasses to improve acuity; referral for specialist management of eye movement disorders; and interventions tailored to visual neglect or perceptual deficits. It recommends collaboration among stroke teams, particularly occupational therapy, neuropsychology and eye care, alongside suitable information, resources and vision aids for survivors and caregivers.

Saccular or berry-shaped aneurysms are the most common intracranial type and usually arise at bifurcations with a distinct neck. For spindle-shaped aneurysms, a cited study attributed origin to dissection in 73%, atherosclerosis in 18%, and collagen disease in 9% of cases; the label ‘fusiform’ therefore conveys little about cause by itself. Nonetheless, the authors recommend using ‘fusiform’ for a spindle-shaped aneurysm as a pragmatic morphological description. ‘Dissecting aneurysm’ should describe a false, irregularly shaped aneurysm, often accompanied by stenosis or evidence of intimal injury or underlying vasculopathy. ‘Blister’ should be reserved for particular half-dome-shaped carotid lesions.

Leg pain and radiculopathy generally indicate focal neural compression and are typically treated most directly by decompressing stenotic sites. Without symptomatic deformity or instability, fusion may offer these patients less additional benefit; decompression alone would be less invasive and more cost-effective.   Content: Because FG can progress rapidly and become fatal, early recognition and vigorous resuscitation are essential. An A–E assessment and indicated resuscitation may need to precede a full history, depending on haemodynamic stability. Symptoms are often nonspecific and can resemble scrotal cellulitis, scrotal abscess, or severe epididymo-orchitis. Local manifestations include scrotal swelling, scrotal or perineal pain, erythema, and skin necrosis; advanced infection may cause fever, vomiting, and altered consciousness. Progression varies but can occur over 3–5days, beginning with increasing discomfort or pain and pruritus. Swelling and skin changes indicate more advanced soft-tissue gangrene. Diabetes mellitus, HIV infection, or immunosuppressive medication should lower the threshold for suspecting FG. Genital and perineal examination is performed with a chaperone. Swelling, erythema, warmth, and tenderness indicate inflammation; the edge of erythema should be marked for comparison at later examinations. Palpable crepitus indicates subcutaneous gas from gas-producing anaerobic infection. Any wound discharge should be sampled for culture. Extension from the genital or perineal area to the thighs or abdominal wall is concerning. Foul-smelling, purple-black skin necrosis is characteristic. PR examination should assess perianal involvement and may reveal a perianal or perirectal abscess as the infectious source.

Document sections:
  Heading: Discussion
  Content: The guideline uses GRADE to support decisions about stroke-related visual impairment. Table 14 and Figure 14 bring together its recommendations and expert-consensus statements. Visual problems affect about 75% of stroke survivors by reported prevalence and about 60% by reported incidence. Rowe and colleagues identified impaired central acuity in 56%, eye-movement abnormalities in 40%, field loss in 28%, visual inattention in 27% and perceptual disorders in 5%. Assessment and care are unequal; females, people of black ethnicity, those with lower socioeconomic status or educational attainment, and older people are described as particularly disadvantaged. Stroke may disrupt interpretation and integration of sensory input; an estimated 70% of perceived sensory information is visual. Visual impairment is negatively associated with rehabilitation and quality of life and can affect mobility, navigation, interaction, self-care, independence, mood and driving. Screening should therefore cover acuity, fields, neglect and eye movements so that a survivor whose impairment breaches applicable driving rules is not discharged without driving-related information; requirements vary between countries, and follow-up should reassess visual requirements. Treating diplopia with prisms or a patch may restore visual function needed for driving. No standardised stroke-vision detection protocol currently exists. Variation in screening, specialist referral, treatment, information and communication adapted to visual impairment contributes to unmet need, inequity and poorer patient experience. Norup et al. identified visual problems in 24% at initial neurological examination; some who declined further assessment said they had not noticed a problem. Among survivors with neglect, unawareness of visuospatial deficits predicted poorer daily functioning more strongly than deficit severity or time since stroke. An estimated 40–60% with new visual impairment do not or cannot report symptoms; some remain unaware despite caregivers observing collisions or accidents. Missed deficits may mean missed rehabilitation, and unrecognised field loss may create road-safety risks.
