Pharmacokinetics: Absorción
Lamotrigina se absorbe completa y rápidamente en el intestino sin efecto significativo de metabolismo de primer paso. El pico de concentraciones plasmáticas se produce aproximadamente 2,5 horas tras la administración oral del fármaco. El tiempo hasta conseguir la concentración máxima se retrasa ligeramente después de ingerir alimentos, aunque la extensión de la absorción no se ve afectada. Existe una considerable variación interindividual en las concentraciones máximas en estado de equilibrio estacionario, pero dentro del mismo individuo las concentraciones raramente varían.
Distribución
La unión de lamotrigina a proteínas plasmáticas es de alrededor del 55%; es muy poco probable que el desplazamiento de las proteínas plasmáticas diera lugar a toxicidad.
El volumen de distribución es 0,92 a 1,22 l/kg.
Biotransformación
Las UDP-glucuronil transferasas han sido identificadas como las enzimas responsables del metabolismo de lamotrigina.
Lamotrigina induce su propio metabolismo de forma modesta y dosis dependiente. Sin embargo, no existe evidencia de que lamotrigina afecte a la farmacocinética de otros fármacos antiepilépticos y los datos sugieren que las interacciones entre lamotrigina y fármacos metabolizados por enzimas del citocromo P450 son poco probables.
Eliminación
El aclaramiento plasmático aparente en sujetos sanos es de 30 ml/min. El aclaramiento de lamotrigina es primariamente metabólico con eliminación posterior del glucurónido conjugado en orina. Menos del 10% se excreta inalterado en orina. Sólo el 2% del material relacionado con el fármaco se excreta en heces. El aclaramiento y la semivida son independientes de la dosis. La semivida plasmática aparente en sujetos sanos es de aproximadamente 33 horas (intervalo de 14 a 103 horas). En un estudio de sujetos con el Síndrome de Gilbert, el aclaramiento medio aparente se redujo en un 32% comparado con los controles normales, aunque los valores estaban dentro del rango para la población general.
La semivida de eliminación de la lamotrigina se ve ampliamente afectada por la medicación concomitante. La semivida media se redujo aproximadamente a 14 horas cuando se administró con fármacos inductores de la glucuronidación tales como carbamazepina y fenitoína y se incrementa a una media de 70 horas aproximadamente cuando se administra conjuntamente con valproato solo (ver sección 4.2).
Linealidad
La farmacocinética de lamotrigina es lineal hasta 450 mg, la dosis única más alta probada.
Poblaciones especiales
Niños
El aclaramiento ajustado al peso corporal es mayor en niños que en adultos, con los valores más altos en niños menores de cinco años. La semivida de lamotrigina es generalmente más corta en niños que en adultos con un valor medio de aproximadamente 7 horas cuando se administra con fármacos inductores enzimáticos tales como carbamazepina y fenitoína y se incrementa a valores medios de 45 a 50 horas cuando se administra conjuntamente con valproato solo (ver sección 4.2).
Niños entre 2 y 26 meses
En 143 pacientes pediátricos de edades comprendidas entre 2 y 26 meses, con un peso entre 3 y 16 kg, que recibieron dosis orales por kg de peso corporal similares a las de niños mayores de 2 años, hubo una reducción del aclaramiento en comparación con niños de mayor edad con el mismo peso corporal. La semivida estimada fue de 23 horas en niños menores de 26 meses con terapia de inducción enzimática, de 136 horas cuando se les coadministró valproato y de 38 horas en pacientes tratados sin inhibidores/inductores de enzimas. La variabilidad interindividual del aclaramiento oral fue mayor en el grupo de pacientes pediátricos de 2 a 26 meses (47%). La predicción de los niveles de concentración sérica en niños de 2 a 26 meses fue en general en el mismo rango que los niños mayores, aunque es probable el observar niveles más altos de la concentración máxima (Cmax) en algunos niños con un peso corporal por debajo de 10 kg.
Personas de edad avanzada
Los resultados obtenidos a partir de un análisis farmacocinético poblacional, que incluyó adultos, jóvenes y ancianos con epilepsia, procedentes de los mismos ensayos, indicaron que el aclaramiento de lamotrigina no varió de forma clínicamente relevante. Después de administrar dosis únicas, el aclaramiento aparente disminuyó en un 12% desde 35 ml/min a la edad de 20 años a 31 ml/min a los 70 años. La disminución tras 48 semanas de tratamiento fue del 10%, desde 41 a 37 ml/min, entre grupos de jóvenes y ancianos. Además, se estudió la farmacocinética de lamotrigina en 12 ancianos voluntarios sanos tras administración de una dosis única de 150 mg. El aclaramiento medio en los ancianos (0,39 ml/min/kg) está dentro del intervalo de los valores de aclaramiento medio (0,31 a 0,65 ml/min/kg) obtenidos en 9 estudios con adultos no ancianos tras la administración de dosis únicas de 30 a 450 mg.
Pacientes con insuficiencia renal
Se administró una dosis única de 100 mg de lamotrigina a doce voluntarios con insuficiencia renal crónica y a otros 6 individuos sometidos a hemodiálisis. El aclaramiento medio fue de 0,42 ml/min/kg (insuficiencia renal crónica), 0,33 ml/min/kg (entre hemodiálisis) y 1,57 ml/min/kg (durante la hemodiálisis) comparado con 0,58 ml/min/kg en voluntarios sanos. Las semividas plasmáticas medias fueron de 42,9 horas (insuficiencia renal crónica), 57,4 horas (entre hemodiálisis) y 13,0 horas (durante la hemodiálisis), comparadas con 26,2 horas en voluntarios sanos. Como media, aproximadamente un 20% (rango = 5,6 a 35,1) de la cantidad de lamotrigina presente en el cuerpo, se eliminó durante una sesión de cuatro horas de hemodiálisis. Para esta población de pacientes, la dosis inicial de lamotrigina se debe ajustar según la medicación concomitante que reciba; una reducción en la dosis de mantenimiento puede ser eficaz en pacientes con insuficiencia renal funcional significativa (ver secciones 4.2 y 4.4).
Pacientes con insuficiencia hepática
Se realizó un estudio farmacocinético de dosis única en el que participaron 24 sujetos con grados variables de insuficiencia hepática y 12 sujetos sanos como controles. La media del aclaramiento aparente de lamotrigina fue de 0,31, 0,24 ó 0,10 ml/min/kg en pacientes con insuficiencia hepática de grado A, B o C (clasificación Child-Pugh), respectivamente, en comparación con 0,34 ml/min/kg en los controles sanos. Las dosis iniciales, las dosis posteriores de escalada y las dosis de mantenimiento, deberán reducirse en pacientes con insuficiencia hepática moderada o grave (ver sección 4.2).

Document sections:
  Heading: 1.9 Antihypertensive treatment during the postnatal period, including during breastfeeding
  Content: Explain that antihypertensive treatment can be adapted for breastfeeding and does not itself prevent it. Medicines can enter milk, but most antihypertensives result in very low milk concentrations and infant exposure unlikely to have clinical effects. Manufacturer disclaimers often reflect a lack of testing in pregnant or breastfeeding women rather than specific evidence of harm; agree treatment with the woman according to her preferences. Consider checking blood pressure in symptomatic infants, particularly preterm infants, during the first few weeks, and advise mothers after discharge to watch for drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, cold extremities or poor feeding. [2019] Offer enalapril after birth with appropriate maternal kidney-function and serum-potassium monitoring. For women of black African or Caribbean family origin, consider nifedipine or amlodipine if amlodipine previously controlled their pressure successfully. If a single drug is insufficient, consider nifedipine or amlodipine with enalapril; if that combination fails or is not tolerated, consider adding atenolol or labetalol or replacing 1 medicine with either. Prefer once-daily medicines where possible. Where possible, avoid diuretics and angiotensin receptor blockers during breastfeeding or milk expression. For women neither breastfeeding nor planning to do so, use NICE guidance on hypertension in adults. [2010, amended 2019; 2019] An MHRA clarification in 2014 states that ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists are generally not recommended in breastfeeding but are not absolutely contraindicated if essential for the mother. For mothers feeding older infants, captopril, enalapril or quinapril may be considered if an ACE inhibitor is necessary, with careful infant follow-up for hypotension. As noted at publication in June 2019, some nifedipine brands had a manufacturer pregnancy contraindication.

Document sections:
  Heading: ● Location of the tumour
  Content: Reported anatomical distributions are 39–40 % in supratentorial midline structures, including the hypothalamus, optic chiasm and nerves, ventricles and other midline sites; 32–36 % in the cerebellum; 13.1–18.0 % in the cerebral cortex; 8.3–10 % in the brainstem; and 3.5–4.5 % in the spinal cord. Resectability depends on site, tumor grade and the risk of lasting neurological injury. Hemispheric and cerebellar tumors are often operable, but perirolandic, mesial temporal or dominant-language locations can make surgery harmful. After cerebellar LGG surgery, patients can have fine-motor, coordination, sensory, oculomotor, cognitive or learning deficits. Posterior-fossa resection can also cause cerebellar mutism syndrome, though less often than medulloblastoma surgery, particularly with involvement of the middle cerebellar peduncle, dentate nucleus or fourth-ventricle floor. Chiasmatic hypothalamic gliomas (CHG) and other optic pathway gliomas may be NF1-related or sporadic, with differing natural history and imaging. NF1-related tumors generally have better PFS, and many need no treatment. Either type can cause visual loss, endocrine disease, hypothalamic symptoms including diencephalic syndrome in young children, or hydrocephalus from third-ventricle obstruction. Complete resection is generally not feasible, although accessible exophytic portions may be removed to improve control. Thalamic pLGGs account for 1–2 % and often present with hemiplegia and/or hemianopsia. Tectal plate gliomas occur predominantly in children, constitute 5 % of pediatric brainstem tumors and typically present with raised intracranial pressure; CSF diversion is usually needed at diagnosis and can often be accomplished by endoscopic third ventriculostomy. Cervico-medullary pLGGs grow slowly and present with lower-brainstem symptoms. Long-term survival is high, but progression or recurrence, including late recurrence, is common; treatment should control local disease while preserving or restoring neurological function. Spinal pLGGs are uncommon and insidious. Young children may have either definite deficits or vague symptoms, delaying diagnosis until symptoms become severe. Infiltration and poorly defined tissue boundaries can obstruct complete removal; indicated resection requires intraoperative neuromonitoring. Feasible gross total resection appears most important for PFS. Repeated chemotherapy may help control disease and lessen morbidity and appears to provide tumor control comparable with radiotherapy.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: Saposnik et al. 2024 Diagnosis and Management of Cerebral Venous Thrombosis A Scientific Statement From the American Hea
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: BRAIN AND VASCULAR IMAGING FOR THE DIAGNOSIS OF CVT
  Content: Conventional computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is often obtained first for nonspecific acute symptoms. Suspicion can arise from direct thrombus visualization, absent venous filling, tissue consequences of venous obstruction—venous infarction, edema, hemorrhagic transformation, intracranial hypertension, or hydrocephalus—or vascular consequences such as enlarged veins. Supplemental Table 2 summarizes imaging difficulties. Thin-slice CT can improve direct visualization. On noncontrast CT, increased hemoglobin and red blood cells within a thrombus produce hyperattenuation, termed the dense vessel sign. A serpiginous or linear venous hyperdensity, described as the cord or string sign, or a dense triangle sign can remain visible up to 14 days after symptom onset. Indirect CT and MRI clues include low-density areas that do not follow a usual wedge-shaped infarct pattern or arterial territory, or that spare the overlying cortex. Sagittal sinus or deep cerebral vein involvement can produce bilateral hypodensities. Hemorrhage occurs in up to 40% of patients and may represent hemorrhagic transformation within a hypodense area or intracerebral hemorrhage accompanied by subarachnoid or subdural bleeding; isolated subarachnoid and basal ganglia hemorrhages are uncommon. A juxtacortical C-shaped hyperdensity, the cashew nut sign, has reportedly high specificity but low sensitivity. Bilateral or multifocal hemorrhage is also frequent. A meta-analysis covering 27 publications and 2812 cases estimated CT sensitivity at 0.79 (95% CI, 0.76–0.82) and specificity at 0.90 (95% CI, 0.89– 0.91), below the figures previously described in the 2011 American Heart Association statement. Conventional MRI can show the thrombus directly, but its signal changes with thrombus age as oxyhemoglobin becomes deoxyhemoglobin and methemoglobin. Early thrombus can be isointense or hypointense on T2 and resemble a normal sinus flow void, complicating diagnosis. Time-of-flight magnetic resonance venography (MRV) can likewise mislead when absent flow is not confirmed on T1//T2. Corroboration using gradient-recalled echo, susceptibility-weighted imaging, or contrast-enhanced MRV is often useful. Thrombosed blood produces a blooming artifact on gradient-recalled echo and susceptibility-weighted sequences; for subtle cortical vein thrombosis, their sensitivity and specificity approach 100%. T1-based black-blood imaging is described as promising. MRI detects parenchymal injury secondary to venous occlusion more sensitively than CT; resulting lesions can be bilateral and cross arterial territories. A meta-analysis of 21 studies involving 1773 patients with CVT estimated sensitivity of conventional MRI sequences at 0.82 (95% CI, 0.78–0.85) and specificity at 0.92 (95% CI, 0.91–0.94). The figures illustrate venous-system anatomy and sinus involvement, examples of thrombosis and hemorrhage on noncontrast CT, and venous thrombosis, infarction, edema, and filling defects on MRI. Sinus-involvement percentages in the anatomy figure may exceed 100% because >1 sinus can be affected; internal jugular vein thrombosis there refers to its coexistence with CVT, not isolated jugular thrombosis.

  Content: Most BM enhance on MRI or CT, indicating absence of a functional blood–brain barrier in those lesions. The distribution of intravenous drugs might therefore resemble that of intravenous imaging contrast, potentially allowing systemic therapy to work as effectively in enhancing BM as in extracranial disease. Whether gadolinium uptake predicts adequate entry of larger molecules, including monoclonal antibodies and antibody–drug conjugates, is uncertain. Drug selection depends primarily on tumour histology and molecular features rather than intracranial location. When feasible, consider molecular genetic analysis of BM instead of the primary to select tumour-specific targeted therapy or immunotherapy [EANO: IV, C; ESMO: IV, B]. Better blood–brain barrier penetration is predicted to improve control, especially where that barrier remains partially intact. Decisions should account for prior treatment and, where several systemic options exist, CNS and extracranial activity and each option’s toxicity [EANO: IV, A; ESMO: IV, B]. Document sections:
  Heading: 6.3. Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism
  Content: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is described as the most common cause of both primary and secondary amenorrhea and involves impaired hypothalamic function and gonadotropin release. In adolescents it is usually associated with competitive sport, stress, or an eating disorder. Sports activity and body-fat mass correlate with amenorrhea likelihood and adverse bone-density effects. The “female athlete triad”, also termed “relative energy deficiency in sport” by the International Olympic Committee, combines low energy availability, menstrual disturbance, and low bone density. Calorie restriction can disrupt menstruation even when BMI is within the normal range; eating disorders should therefore be treated early to prevent lasting harm. Less frequent causes include brain tumors, craniocerebral trauma, perinatal asphyxia, brain radiotherapy, systemic disease such as histiocytosis, Wilson’s disease, or thalassemia, and genetic defects such as Kallmann syndrome, septo-optic dysplasia, or a GnRH receptor defect. Testing shows low-to-normal gonadotropins and usually low estradiol; sonography may show a thin endometrium and ovaries without follicular maturation. Even brief dietary restriction can produce a prepubertal gonadotropin-secretion pattern, particularly for LH. LH pulses then become too infrequent for follicular maturation, resulting in estrogen deficiency and menstrual disorders, including amenorrhea. Adequate estrogenization supports peak bone mass and long-term skeletal health. Menstruation usually resumes approximately 6–12 months after normal weight is restored, but amenorrhea persists despite weight gain in around 10–30% of cases. Bone density can require years to recover or may never reach an appropriate peak, leaving lifelong excess fracture risk associated with osteoporosis. Care should involve psychologists and psychiatrists, with bone-density measurements during treatment. The preferred approach is weight gain, restoration of normal cycles, and adequate estrogenization, potentially requiring less exercise and increased calories and BMI into the normal range. Estrogenization also influences neurological and psychological development and health. Gynecological treatment emphasizes estrogenization to limit long-term effects, particularly on bone. Estradiol appears most beneficial for this purpose, although achieving estrogenization is especially important; contraceptive pills and a contraceptive patch, particularly for patients with bulimia, are alternatives with positive effects. Progesterone is also needed for endometrial transformation and protection. Vitamin D and calcium should be supplemented; calcium supplementation is unnecessary with a normal diet, but 1000–1500 mg daily should be supplied in an eating disorder such as anorexia nervosa.

Document sections:
  Heading: ● Location of the tumour
  Content: Reported anatomical distributions are 39–40 % in supratentorial midline structures, including the hypothalamus, optic chiasm and nerves, ventricles and other midline sites; 32–36 % in the cerebellum; 13.1–18.0 % in the cerebral cortex; 8.3–10 % in the brainstem; and 3.5–4.5 % in the spinal cord. Resectability depends on site, tumor grade and the risk of lasting neurological injury. Hemispheric and cerebellar tumors are often operable, but perirolandic, mesial temporal or dominant-language locations can make surgery harmful. After cerebellar LGG surgery, patients can have fine-motor, coordination, sensory, oculomotor, cognitive or learning deficits. Posterior-fossa resection can also cause cerebellar mutism syndrome, though less often than medulloblastoma surgery, particularly with involvement of the middle cerebellar peduncle, dentate nucleus or fourth-ventricle floor. Chiasmatic hypothalamic gliomas (CHG) and other optic pathway gliomas may be NF1-related or sporadic, with differing natural history and imaging. NF1-related tumors generally have better PFS, and many need no treatment. Either type can cause visual loss, endocrine disease, hypothalamic symptoms including diencephalic syndrome in young children, or hydrocephalus from third-ventricle obstruction. Complete resection is generally not feasible, although accessible exophytic portions may be removed to improve control. Thalamic pLGGs account for 1–2 % and often present with hemiplegia and/or hemianopsia. Tectal plate gliomas occur predominantly in children, constitute 5 % of pediatric brainstem tumors and typically present with raised intracranial pressure; CSF diversion is usually needed at diagnosis and can often be accomplished by endoscopic third ventriculostomy. Cervico-medullary pLGGs grow slowly and present with lower-brainstem symptoms. Long-term survival is high, but progression or recurrence, including late recurrence, is common; treatment should control local disease while preserving or restoring neurological function. Spinal pLGGs are uncommon and insidious. Young children may have either definite deficits or vague symptoms, delaying diagnosis until symptoms become severe. Infiltration and poorly defined tissue boundaries can obstruct complete removal; indicated resection requires intraoperative neuromonitoring. Feasible gross total resection appears most important for PFS. Repeated chemotherapy may help control disease and lessen morbidity and appears to provide tumor control comparable with radiotherapy.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: Salih et al. 2024 The effectiveness of various CSF diversion surgeries in idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus a
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Discussion
  Content: The authors describe this as the largest review and meta-analysis to date of CSF diversion outcomes in iNPH, covering 54 studies and 4811 patients. Improvement was frequent but had not risen over the last 19 years. Although procedures had similar pooled efficacy, between-study heterogeneity and few direct comparisons prevent firm comparative conclusions. Overall improvement of 74% at follow-up may inform discussions of treatment success and serve as a research benchmark. Earlier reviews reported lower improvement. The authors attribute some historical variation to early descriptions emphasising striking reversals and to patient selection complicated by overlap with neurodegenerative conditions that do not respond to shunting. Their consensus-aligned eligibility criteria sought to strengthen the pooled estimates.

Gait ataxia improved more consistently than cognition or urinary symptoms. Earlier reports described early, sustained gait improvement in 64–77% of cases. Cognitive improvement in this analysis was around 50%, resembling findings of the Study of Idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus on Neurological Improvement 2 (SINPHONI-2) trial. The authors suggest gait may respond to mechanical CSF decompression because its relevant frontal subcortical and periventricular pathways are affected by ventricular enlargement. Cognition involves wider networks, including the hippocampus, and may overlap with shunt-unresponsive dementias. Urinary symptoms improved in about half of patients; the authors propose that pressure normalisation in periventricular bladder-control pathways may contribute, while extensive control networks and concomitant neurodegeneration may limit recovery.

Sustained improvement at longer follow-up contrasted with previous reports of waning long-term benefit. The authors suggest that large tertiary centres and stringent follow-up may partly explain this pattern. Nevertheless, up to 20% deteriorate several years after initial benefit and are termed ‘late shunt non-responders’; shunt dysfunction and advancing neurodegeneration are proposed contributors, although this phenomenon remains poorly characterised. Adjustable valves can permit CSF-flow titration and address deterioration in some patients.

Across operations, improvement was generally around 69–75%, with overlapping confidence intervals, but direct comparative studies were insufficient. Guidelines since the first description of normal-pressure hydrocephalus in 1965 have supported CSF shunting without specifying an operation. VP remains the most common procedure worldwide. LP shunts, historically less favoured because of failure and overdrainage, are more common in Japan and elsewhere to reduce intracranial risks. Earlier studies reported LP safety and non-inferior efficacy relative to VP; the authors' results do not support definitively preferring either. Comparisons may be influenced by geography, diagnostic thresholds, younger average ages in European studies, and differing obesity and cardiovascular comorbidity burdens. VA shunts place the distal catheter in the right cardiac atrium and may shorten surgery, but are generally considered when VP is not feasible, including with abdominal adhesions. Concern about serious haematological and cardiopulmonary events largely derives from paediatric evidence, with limited adult data. Hung et al. reported in 2017 that VA significantly reduced obstruction and revision relative to VP among iNPH patients and observed no cardiopulmonary events; confirmation in more definitive, updated studies is needed. Pending such evidence, the authors favour choosing a shunt according to local expertise and patient characteristics.

ETV creates an opening in the third-ventricle floor for CSF flow toward basal cisterns. Its iNPH evidence requires caution because samples were generally small, apart from Gangemi et al., and heterogeneous. Recent guidelines do not recommend ETV because findings are inconsistent. This analysis found modest improvement with a wide confidence interval and a high revision rate. Anatomical eligibility can also be limited by magnetic resonance imaging findings.

Adverse events can be severe. Subdural haematomas and hygromas range from incidental imaging findings to emergencies. Earlier evidence indicates most subdural haematomas resolve spontaneously after valve-pressure increases, with only 10% requiring evacuation. The authors found mechanical problems, including obstruction and migration, to be frequent contributors to reoperation. Prompt treatment of obstruction matters because approximately 75% of affected patients can subsequently improve symptomatically. Early iNPH studies reported complications up to 40%; this review found a significantly lower rate around 20%, consistent with the European multicentre iNPH study. The authors relate the reduction to better operations, gravitational control devices and antibiotic protocols. Previous evidence indicates adjustable valves halve subdural collections relative to fixed-pressure valves, supporting their greater cost.

Despite initial consensus guidelines in 2005, this review found no significant rise in surgical success through 2024; a 2013 meta-analysis reported a similar efficacy of 71%. The authors suggest diagnostic difficulty in identifying shunt-responsive patients may contribute. Extended lumbar drainage and intracranial pressure monitoring have been reported to identify responders reliably, though operator and centre effects may occur; their replication suggests potential diagnostic value. In this study, greater baseline neurological morbidity measured by mRS predicted greater improvement, possibly because more severe symptoms make response easier to classify. Fixed valves were associated with worse LP outcomes; the authors suggest gravity and position may make valve settings more consequential for LP than VP. Disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus (DESH) has been reported to predict shunt response, but too few included studies reported DESH for this analysis.

Declared limitations are substantial between-study heterogeneity with high I2 values, lack of a standard iNPH outcome measure requiring multiple scales, differences in surgical eligibility, prognostic testing, valves and antisiphon devices, few randomised interprocedural trials, a predominantly retrospective evidence base, and study-level rather than patient-level data. Sensitivity analyses were used to address heterogeneity, and retrospective design did not affect the overall estimate. The authors conclude that improvement is consistently high across procedures, while heterogeneity complicates evaluation. They support selecting among VP, LP and VA according to surgeon preference and medical history, and identify better patient selection and potentially advanced diagnostic methods as research and clinical priorities after two decades of unchanged success.

Document sections:
  Heading: 4.6.5.2. Central sensitization.
  Content: Prolonged peripheral nerve injury and persistent inflammation may reorganize central neural pathways, allowing pain without an ongoing peripheral stimulus or after injury resolves. This could help explain coexistence of ocular and systemic chronic pain [311,316–321]. Selective corneal-nerve injury has been linked to inflammatory cytokine expression in the trigeminal ganglion; direct central nervous system injury, as in traumatic brain injury, can also initiate chronic pain [318,322,323]. Trigeminal central sensitization has been demonstrated in animal DED models [324]. Preclinical findings implicate substance P in ocular-surface pain and inflammation [314,325], while clinical findings associate C-reactive protein with greater cold-evoked pain sensitivity [326]. Vitamin D deficiency has been associated with altered corneal-nerve morphology, dendritic-cell recruitment, and pain in chronic DED [327]. The literature more strongly connects chronic pain with DED symptoms than signs. Heterogeneity in design, methods, and populations requires further work. Future studies are advised to measure multiple DED symptoms and signs, distinguish aqueous-deficient from evaporative DED, and standardize pain assessment in line with International Association for the Study of Pain suggestions.

Document sections:
  Heading: Clinical presentation
  Content: The relative prominence of low back and leg pain matters for DS treatment and prognosis. The authors describe these symptoms as potentially arising from different processes that require different management. Missing the principal source of pain can lead either to insufficient treatment and relief or to unnecessary treatment and complications. Leg pain and radiculopathy generally indicate focal neural compression and are typically treated most directly by decompressing stenotic sites. Without symptomatic deformity or instability, fusion may offer these patients less additional benefit; decompression alone would be less invasive and more cost-effective. Predominantly mechanical low back pain, by contrast, is often taken as a sign of instability, making stabilization of the painful segment particularly important for relief. Several cited studies reported suboptimal results when patients with low back pain received decompression without fusion. CARDS incorporates leg pain, while DSIC and Kulkarni incorporate back pain, but none assesses their relative severity; that comparison has been shown to predict postoperative functional improvement. In the Spine Patient Outcomes Research Trial (SPORT), predominantly leg-related symptoms were associated with less severe pain at baseline and greater improvement after surgery than predominantly low back pain; patients with equally severe symptoms had intermediate outcomes.

  Heading: 6.2.3.4 Drug-coated balloon dilatation
  Content: Drug (paclitaxel)-coated balloon dilatation (DCBD) following ordinary dilatation or DVIU aims to reduce scar formation through paclitaxel's antimitotic action. ROBUST-3 randomised patients with predominantly bulbar strictures < 3cm and at least two failed endoscopic treatments to DCBD (n=79) or standard dilatation/DVIU (n=48). Cystoscopic anatomic patency at six months was 75% versus 27% (p<0.001); estimated survival without retreatment at one year was 83% versus 22% (p<0.001). No serious DCBD-related adverse events occurred, although haematuria and dysuria were more frequent with DCBD than in controls (11.4% versus 2.1%). Paclitaxel remained detectable in semen up to six months, prompting contraception when a partner could bear children. If DCBD is used, careful review and prospective data collection, ideally through a post-marketing registry or trial, are advised. The comparative finding is graded LE 1b. Offer DCBD for a recurrent short (< 3 cm) bulbar stricture after at least two endoscopic treatments only when urethroplasty is not an option (Weak).

  Content: La respuesta a la pregunta 52 presenta mastitis y/o abscesos de la lactancia como causa más frecuente del cuadro descrito; cita S. aureus, S. epidermidis y estreptococos como gérmenes habituales. Describe dolor localizado en un cuadrante mamario con fiebre y linfangitis. Para mastitis aguda indica tratamiento sintomático más cloxacilina o eritromicina si existe alergia; para absceso, drenaje. La respuesta a la pregunta 53 considera la mamografía la principal técnica de imagen mamaria, usada para tamizaje de mujeres asintomáticas y diagnóstico de las sintomáticas; habitualmente se obtienen dos proyecciones por mama, craneocaudal y oblicua externa a 60º. La respuesta a la pregunta 54 señala la histología como diagnóstico definitivo para toda mujer con sospecha por imagen. Si la lesión es palpable, propone BAG directamente sobre ella; si no lo es, BAG guiada por estereotaxia, con sensibilidad del 91 % y especificidad del 96 %. Indica que actualmente se realizan pocas biopsias con arpón o excisionales en quirófano. La respuesta a la pregunta 55 señala que el cáncer de mama suele comenzar sin síntomas y que un tumor o induración es la primera manifestación en el 80 % de los casos. Considera sospechosos los nódulos irregulares, de bordes imprecisos, consistencia leñosa o movilidad reducida, los signos inflamatorios y las adenopatías homolaterales duras y fijas. Puede haber telorrea; el 20 % presenta retracción o eccema areolomamilar. En fases avanzadas describe ulceraciones, retracción marcada, edema cutáneo o piel de naranja y adenopatías axilares palpables; también puede presentarse como carcinoma inflamatorio. La respuesta a la pregunta 56 considera signos mamográficos de malignidad un nódulo denso, espiculado e irregular con retracción o edema cutáneo por bloqueo linfático subdérmico; microcalcificaciones agrupadas, finas e irregulares en número >6, descritas como el signo mamográfico más precoz; y pérdida de arquitectura mamaria. Atribuye estos hallazgos a BI-RADS 5, de alta sospecha. La respuesta a la pregunta 57 enumera antecedentes familiares de cáncer mamario, especialmente premenopáusico o bilateral, y mutaciones BRCA-1, BRCA-2 y p53. Señala transmisión autosómica dominante para BRCA-1 y BRCA-2, riesgo vital de cáncer de mama del 60-85 % en portadoras y riesgo de cáncer ovárico mayor con BRCA-1 (40-60 %) que con BRCA-2 (10-20 %). Añade primer embarazo después de los 30 años, menarquia precoz, menopausia tardía, nuliparidad, terapia hormonal sustitutiva, irradiación, antecedentes personales de cáncer de ovario, endometrio o colon, síndrome de Lynch II, nivel socioeconómico alto, dieta rica en grasas, obesidad y síndrome de Klinefelter.

Document sections:
  Heading: Imaging
  Content: Combined MRI and CT permit a highly probable diagnosis of intracranial meningioma in most cases. Typical findings are isointensity on T1-weighted MRI, hyperintensity on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, marked enhancement, and a peripheral dural tail. Extensive FLAIR edema and heterogeneous enhancement can raise suspicion of WHO grade 2 or 3 histology. Bone-window CT helps assess neighboring hyperostosis and intraosseous spread. Somatostatin receptor 2 expression allows PET delineation after administration of agents such as 68Ga-DOTATATE or 90Y-DOTATOC. Although this is not standardly available, it can help separate tumor from normal tissue and postoperative changes. Figure 1 illustrates 68Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT alongside CT and contrast-enhanced MRI views. Conventional angiography has a diminishing diagnostic role but may help if invasion of a lateral sinus or superior sagittal sinus is suspected and MRI angiography is inconclusive; 3D venous angiography can clarify sinus openness and collateral drainage. Routine preoperative embolization is not recommended because it has been associated with more postoperative cardiovascular complications. A randomized trial identified reduced operating time as its sole potential advantage. The surgical team should decide individually; embolization may help when feeding vessels cannot be reached surgically, including petroclival tumors, with the aim of closing the meningeal branch of the ascending pharyngeal artery or tentorial branch of the internal carotid artery. For observational follow-up, MRI is the reference imaging method. Size is generally assessed on gadolinium-enhanced T1 images; axial T2 images yield comparable measurement information. Surveillance based on gadolinium-enhanced T1 imaging remains a good practice point, although T2-only follow-up can be considered for small lesions. MRI-based machine-learning models may improve diagnosis in selected future settings.

Document sections:
  Heading: INTRODUCTION
  Content: GCA and TAK are systemic vasculitides affecting predominantly large- and medium-sized arteries. GCA may involve cranial or extracranial vessels. Cranial symptoms include headache, scalp tenderness, visual loss and jaw claudication. Extracranial disease can cause arterial stenoses and aneurysms, with absent pulses or limb claudication. GCA occurs more often in people of Northern European ancestry older than 50 years of age. Diagnosis rests on clinical findings, temporal artery biopsy abnormalities and/or vascular imaging evidence of large vessel disease. Glucocorticoids are central to treatment, and tocilizumab has US Food and Drug Administration approval for GCA. TAK produces granulomatous inflammation in the aorta and its branches and is more common in younger women. Its manifestations include constitutional symptoms, raised inflammation markers, and stenoses and/or aneurysms that can cause limb claudication and absent pulses. Treatment options include glucocorticoids, nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive agents and surgery for vascular abnormalities. Because the diseases share manifestations, they raise similar management questions. Recent studies have expanded options for GCA, while vascular imaging has become more common in diagnosis and management; these developments motivated the guideline.

  Content: Following an acute neurological event causing NLUTD, defer risk stratification until neurological stabilization (Clinical Principle). Early brain or spinal findings may change over days, weeks, months, or up to 1-2 years, so evaluation timing should be discussed with the patient. Spinal shock can follow partial or complete SCI, producing absent reflex activity, flaccid paralysis, detrusor areflexia, and preserved sphincter tone. It commonly resolves in approximately 3-6 months but can persist for 1-2 years. Early UDS does not reliably predict later function and may be postponed. Premature classification can therefore misrepresent long-term risk.

Document sections:
  Heading: Evaluating longitudinal changes: neointimal lining and stenosis
  Content: Some intimal growth is needed for treatment success. Characterizing it may become more important as FD surfaces and healing processes change. Because ‘intimal hyperplasia’ implies excessive, undesirable growth and has been reported in more than 50% of cases after FD placement, the authors suggest using ‘neointimal lining’ instead. Resulting stenosis should be recorded independently; the findings can later be analyzed together. They suggest rating neointimal lining as yes, no, or indeterminate on unsubtracted angiograms, separately for each FD at proximal, middle, and distal positions. DSA, FP-CTA, and CTA can support this assessment. MRA cannot show neointimal lining in most cases and should generally be avoided for that purpose. Stenosis means apparent narrowing of the contrast-filled vessel lumen relative to its expected diameter at that position; it does not necessarily correspond to the diameter of the visible FD braid. Measurement compares the narrowest lumen, Dstenosis, with a nearby normal reference segment, Dnormal. At pre-procedure, post-procedure, and follow-up assessments, parent artery percent diameter stenosis should use the narrowest relevant arterial segment and an adjacent normal segment, generally within 5mm proximal to, within, or within 5mm distal to the FD. Reference selection should follow the criteria used in the Warfarin-Aspirin Symptomatic Intracranial Disease (WASID) study. The first reference choice is the widest normal, non-tortuous proximal parent-artery segment. If that segment is diseased, the second choice is the widest normal, non-tortuous distal parent-artery segment. If that too is diseased, the third choice is the most distal normal, non-tortuous feeding-artery segment. Figure 2 illustrates a proximal Dnormal of 4.1 mm and a Dstenosis of 2.4 mm, yielding 42% stenosis by ((Dnormal–Dstenosis)/Dnormal)). In-stent stenosis (ISS) may reflect lumen loss, termed ‘true ISS’, or negative remodeling around a stenotic lumen despite full mesh expansion. Reversible ISS might involve thrombus beneath endothelialization, which routine imaging cannot reliably distinguish. Based on the authors’ core laboratory experience, MRA permits stenosis measurement in approximately half of cases; feasibility depends on FD type, acquisition method, anatomy, and orientation relative to the magnetic field. They define stenosis greater than 25% as ‘relevant’ and greater than 50% as ‘significant’. To make use of available MRA images, they advise considering a qualitative significant-stenosis rating of yes, no, or indeterminate. Only thrombus inside the FD lumen counts as thrombus on the device; aneurysm-sac clot does not, because its formation is a treatment goal. Reporting should rely on the final angiographic series or run.

  Heading: Pathogenesis
  Content: In Eke’s review of over 1700 cases, sepsis arose chiefly from the anorectum (30–50%), urogenitalia (20–40%), and genital skin (20%); colorectal origins carried a worse prognosis. Frequent sources include perianal, perirectal, and ischiorectal abscesses. Scrotal abscesses and urinary tract infections are also implicated; less common reported causes include trauma, vasectomy, and foreign-body insertion into the penile urethra. FG infection is polymicrobial, often yielding several organisms from one wound. Reported pathogens include Staphylococcus species, Streptococcus species, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas species, and Bacteroides species; Candida species are the most frequent nonbacterial pathogens. Prevalence differs between studies, making local microbiological guidance and resistance patterns important. Infection produces obliterative endarteritis, inflammation, and oedema. Reduced cutaneous and subcutaneous blood supply causes necrosis and purple-black skin discoloration. Hypoxic tissue supports anaerobes that generate hydrogen and nitrogen; subcutaneous accumulation can produce palpable crepitus. Spread along fascial planes can destroy tissue in the perineum, scrotum, lower abdominal wall, and upper thighs. Spread beneath muscle layers into muscle is uncommon. The testis and epididymis are usually spared because their blood supply has a separate origin.

  Heading: Degenerative spondylolisthesis instability classification (DSIC)
  Content: Proposed in 2015, DSIC is a qualitative aid to selecting an operation according to baseline spinal stability. It arose from a systematic review of biomechanical and clinical stability research and combines back pain, signs of restabilization such as disc-height loss, osteophytes and endplate sclerosis, facet-joint effusion, disc angle and dynamic translation. Its categories link Type I (stable) with decompression alone, Type II (potentially unstable) with decompression and posterior fusion, and Type III (unstable) with decompression, posterior fusion and interbody placement. DSIC centers the surgical decision on stability without incorporating other structural and clinical determinants.

Document sections:
  Heading: Occupational Therapy
  Content: OT evaluates affected-limb use, active movement, edema, dexterity, vasomotor and sensory findings, pain and activities of daily living. Treatment may begin with graded motor imagery (GMI) or mirror visual feedback (MVF). A study (level 3) found MVF beneficial in early and intermediate CRPS but no significant effect in chronic CRPS. GMI progresses through laterality recognition, imagined movement and mirror viewing. The mechanisms of GMI and MVF remain uncertain, and treatment should follow symptoms and individual response. The MVF home approach emphasizes sessions lasting no more than 5 minutes, repeated 5–6 times throughout the day. The described GMI program lasts 6-week, with 2weeks in each phase. Inability to experience ownership of the mirrored limb, greater pain or worsening movement disorders are identified contraindications. A small randomized GMI trial (n= 13; intervention n =7; level 2) found significantly greater pain improvement than standard treatment, but larger subsequent studies did not confirm pain benefit and one suggested increased pain and edema. A controlled pilot of virtual body swapping improved body-perception disturbance briefly without significantly changing pain (level 3). Definitive clinical value remains uncertain. Subsequent OT goals are edema reduction, normalized sensation and positioning, less guarding, and greater independence in work, leisure and daily activities. Functional splinting may help severe cases, but sustained splinting can aggravate symptoms. Edema garments, manual mobilization and superficial desensitization are described at level 4. Stress loading combines scrubbing with progressively heavier carrying. Symptoms can initially rise before pain and swelling usually begin to fall after several days. Loading amount and duration increase gradually; the DystrophileV has no demonstrated advantage over a simple brush. The clinical usefulness of stress loading remains supported mainly at level 4, and comparative efficacy requires study. With improved edema and loading tolerance, treatment advances to active movement, coordination and strengthening; PNF patterns may aid strength, balance and everyday activities. Programs should be adjusted to response. OT and vocational counseling should jointly assess work demands and possible accommodations. Job-site analysis, conditioning, capacity assessment, transferable skills review and trial work periods should be considered. Work releases should specify relevant physical limitations, especially for sedentary or light duties; these vocational recommendations are level 4.

Document sections:
  Heading: Introduction
  Content: IIH involves raised cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure without an identified cause. Headache, visual disturbance and papilloedema are typical, while the rest of the neurological examination is generally normal. Headache is the most frequently reported symptom, occurring in 7599% of cases as printed in the document. Pseudotumour Cerebri Syndrome (PTCS) is another term that also covers secondary causes. Heinrich Quincke described the condition in the late nineteenth century and attributed it to excessive CSF production. Later names included ‘pseudotumor cerebri’ in 1904 and ‘benign intracranial hypertension’ in 1955; reports of visual loss made the description ‘benign’ inappropriate. Subsequent terminology included PTCS and IIH. The classical modified Dandy criteria suggest that IIH diagnosis requires symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (ICP), no focal neurological signs other than unilateral or bilateral sixth nerve palsies, increased CSF opening pressure with otherwise normal CSF, normal brain imaging without hydrocephalus, and no alternative explanation for raised ICP. Some authors consider these criteria sufficient. Friedman’s criteria provide an alternative. For definite IIH, they require A) papilloedema; B) a normal neurological examination apart from cranial nerve abnormalities; C) normal brain parenchyma without hydrocephalus, a mass, a structural lesion or abnormal meningeal enhancement on MRI with and without gadolinium in typical patients (female and obese), with MRI with and without gadolinium plus MRV for others; if MRI cannot be obtained or is contraindicated, contrast-enhanced CT may be used; D) normal CSF composition; and E) opening pressure of ≥280mm CSF in children, or 250mm CSF if the child is not sedated and not obese, measured during a properly performed lumbar puncture. Without papilloedema, IIH can still be diagnosed under these criteria when abducens nerve palsy and all of B-E are present. The document also describes diagnosis with B-E plus at least three of four imaging features: empty sella, flattening of the posterior globe, enlargement of the perioptic subarachnoid space with or without optic nerve tortuosity, and transverse venous sinus stenosis. A ‘probable’ diagnosis is possible with A-D and bilateral papilloedema when CSF pressure does not meet the diagnostic threshold in E. Diagnosis requires exclusion of underlying structural causes, including malignancy or autoimmune conditions. Potential imaging findings include secondary empty sella syndrome, flattened globes, abnormal optic nerve sheaths, optic nerve protrusion, posterior globe flattening and transverse sinus stenosis. A UK cohort reported IIH incidence of 0.71 per 100,000 among children aged 1-16 years, rising with age and weight to 4.18 per 100,000 in obese boys aged 12-15 years and 10.7 per 100,000 in obese girls of the same age. Other estimates for children range from 0.17 to 1.32 per 100,000. Treatment aims to protect vision and relieve headache. Weight control has been effective in adults. Drug treatment commonly involves acetazolamide or topiramate; a possible weight-loss benefit from topiramate has not yet been established in larger studies. Procedural options include CSF diversion, such as ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VPS) or lumboperitonral shunt, optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF), and venous sinus stenting (VSS). Choices depend on symptoms, the extent of visual loss and local availability. Lumbar puncture (LP) has been examined for both diagnosis and treatment, but doubts about its therapeutic efficacy have increased interest in surgery. How best to measure pressure and respond clinically to elevated measurements remains uncertain. With no randomised control trials of paediatric IIH management, this three-round Delphi study examined diagnosis, investigation and management to provide clinicians with recommendations from experienced professionals, following international adult consensus recommendations.

  Content: Fluorescein, rose bengal, and lissamine green help assess ocular-surface abnormalities. Mild staining can occur in normal eyes, particularly in the morning; dry eye often produces exposure-zone punctate or blotchy staining, more readily seen on cornea than conjunctiva. Rose bengal may be applied with a moistened strip or 1% solution; advise patients that it can irritate, so topical anesthetic is typically used first. Lissamine green has a staining pattern resembling rose bengal with less irritation, but waiting 1 to 2 minutes reduces visibility; unlike fluorescein, it is not recommended to assess corneal epithelial disease. Diffuse corneal and conjunctival staining commonly accompanies viral keratoconjunctivitis or medicamentosa. Inferior corneal and bulbar conjunctival staining is typical of staphylococcal blepharitis, meibomian gland disease, lagophthalmos, or exposure; superior bulbar conjunctival staining is typical of superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis. Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 1: Adult. Acute posttraumatic visual defect. Suspect orbital injury. Initial imaging.
  Content: Orbital fractures most often follow assault or a direct blow, motor-vehicle collisions, falls, or sports injuries. They can occur alone or alongside zygomaticomaxillary complex, Le Fort II and III, or nasoethmoidal complex fractures. Diplopia can accompany depressed orbital-floor fractures, especially anterior- or middle-third injuries and small- to medium-sized defects with soft-tissue herniation. Fractures >2 cm are more likely to produce enophthalmos. Blowout injury can involve the lamina papyracea, but extraocular-muscle herniation and serious immediate complications are less common than with orbital-floor blowout fractures. Most orbital fractures can undergo delayed repair after swelling improves; CT can reveal injuries needing more urgent action, including trapdoor fractures and orbital compartment syndrome. Lateral- and superior-wall fractures carry increased traumatic optic neuropathy risk because blunt force can reach the optic canal and shear the nerve. With associated brain injury or obtundation, an afferent pupillary defect may be its sole clinical sign. Urgent diagnosis permits timely intervention when needed. Although optic-canal fractures increase nerve-injury risk, emergency surgery for traumatic optic neuropathy is generally reserved for a bone fragment impinging on the nerve, hematoma in the canal, or enlarging retrobulbar hematoma with proptosis. Severe proptosis with posterior globe tenting requires emergency orbital decompression to preserve vision. An orbital-apex fracture involving the superior orbital fissure can affect multiple traversing cranial nerves. Retrobulbar hematoma, emphysema, or a blow-in fracture can increase orbital mass effect and cause compartment syndrome and vision loss. Imaging evidence of retrobulbar bleeding does not sensitively predict subsequent compartment syndrome: diagnose it from clinical evidence of optic nerve compression. Extraocular-muscle entrapment after an orbital-floor fracture is likewise a clinical diagnosis; muscle herniation and altered contour have low positive predictive values for entrapment. Imaging aims to identify orbital injuries and complications early enough to guide timely care and prevent permanent visual loss.

Document sections:
  Heading: Introduction
  Content: Concern about movement in patients with possible spinal cord injury arose during the Second World War. Howlett proposed that excessive movement with vertebral fractures could produce neck or back hyperflexion or hyperextension and irreversible cord damage; transport in an anatomically aligned, padded position was recommended. In the 1950s and 1960s, two case series proposing that movement after injury could cause paralysis and three instructional papers on transferring patients from cars onto hard boards helped establish immobilization. In 1957, Rogers reviewed 87 patients treated for cervical spine injury, of whom eight reported delayed neurological deficits. Rogers attributed paralysis to cervical movement before definitive treatment and proposed that a collar of his own design could have prevented it. Despite evidence limited to uncontrolled case reports and retrospective causal claims, the American Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons (AAOS) presented immobilization as standard care in a 1971 emergency medical services (EMS) textbook. Its guidance called for splinting and long-backboard transport without excessive spinal movement and warned that movement with a broken neck might contribute to paralysis or death. This approach paralleled splinting of other bone injuries; magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) did not become available to characterize cord injury until the late 1980s. Evidence of pain, respiratory suppression, and pressure ulcers from hard boards prompted NAEMSP and the American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma (ACS-COT) to advise judicious backboard use in 2013, accompanied by a 2014 resource document, because harms might outweigh the presumed, unproven benefit. Updated 2018 guidance from ACS-COT, the American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP), and NAEMSP treated immobilization and SMR as the same underlying concept. It distinguished backboards for immobilization from devices such as scoop stretchers, vacuum splints, and ambulance cots for SMR, while continuing to advocate cervical collars to limit neck movement. A 2013 guideline from the American Association of Neurological Surgeons and the Congress of Neurological Surgeons likewise presented rigid collars as limiting cervical movement and thereby preventing delayed injury, relying on a case series. From proposals in the 1940s to adoption as standard care in the 1970s, movement of an unstable spine was repeatedly treated as the cause of delayed deficits. The authors identify scant literature establishing either that causal claim or a clinical benefit from immobilization or SMR. Their aim was to assess the pathophysiology of delayed neurological injury after trauma, the effectiveness of movement-restricting practices, and their documented harms relative to possible benefit.

Document sections:
  Heading: 4.3.2. Rasmussen encephalitis
  Content: Rasmussen encephalitis (RE) is a rare unilateral inflammatory neurological disease, with an estimated incidence of 2.4 cases in 1,000,000. It involves progressive neurological and cognitive decline alongside drug-resistant epilepsy. Recent findings suggest T-cell-driven inflammation. Its typical course comprises a prodromal stage, an acute stage lasting 8–12 months and a residual stage. Neurological deterioration and epilepsy generally signal the acute stage; MRI can identify progressively worsening unilateral atrophy, usually beginning in the insula. Despite the disease's immunological background, it usually affects only one hemisphere. Hemiplegia and, with dominant-hemisphere disease, aphasia may develop. Drug resistance occurs in almost all cases, and about 50 % develop epilepsia partialis continua (EPC). HDP is the only curative seizure treatment. Surgery can be difficult to time because early hemiparesis is often mild. Immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory treatment can slow progression and may be suitable before surgery, especially with slow progression and mild or absent neurological symptoms; whether it improves long-term outcome remains debated, and it does not cure RE. Its effect on epilepsy is little or absent, so it should not delay surgery, particularly during rapid progression. The prospect of seizure cure must be balanced against hemiplegia and hemianopia. Most patients regain independent walking with rehabilitation, although fine finger movements remain impaired. For operations on the language-dominant side, age-dependent preoperative fMRI or Wada assessment is advisable to estimate language risk. Publications on pre- and young adolescent patients report acute language deterioration after left dominant-side functional HDP, followed by possible longer-term recovery with intensive rehabilitation. Fig. 2 shows a 13yrs old male with left-arm EPC and progressive hemiparesis; FDG-PET/CT and T2 weighted MRI demonstrate right-hemisphere hypometabolism and slight hemiatrophy.

  Heading: Nerve Targets and Patient Considerations
  Content: Relatively focal PDN pain may make a patient suitable for PNS. Predominantly plantar-foot pain, for example, may be addressed through the tibial nerve. That nerve passes from the popliteal fossa through the deep posterior leg compartment and tarsal tunnel, then divides into the lateral plantar nerve (LPN), medial plantar nerve (MPN), and medial calcaneal nerve (MCN). Leads are generally placed behind the tibia and proximal to the tarsal tunnel. Other possible lower-extremity targets are the common peroneal, superficial peroneal, and sciatic nerves; median and ulnar nerves are possible upper-extremity targets. SCS and DRG-S studies have mainly addressed lower-extremity PDN. The tibial and common peroneal nerves may be entrapped at the tarsal tunnel and fibular head, respectively. Increased compression in diabetes has been proposed to contribute to injury and irreversible sensory change. Decompression neurolysis of upper- and lower-extremity nerves in people with diabetes has yielded promising results. PNS may be an option when focal pain persists after decompression; placing leads proximal to a suspected lesion, entrapment, or injury is advisable.

Document sections:
  Heading: Posterior Fossa (PF)
  Content: PF tumours are the most common CNS neoplasms of childhood and affect sight through several mechanisms. Raised intracranial pressure commonly causes acute papilledema in the vast majority of children with PF masses. Papilledema usually resolves when the pressure is adequately treated, but severe or prolonged pressure can lead to optic atrophy, axonal death and visual loss. In very young children, papilledema can be absent because unfused sutures allow head enlargement. Early papilledema may cause few symptoms apart from an enlarged blind spot; nasal, arcuate or central VF defects can follow. CN-VI palsy from dorsal pontine compression or brainstem displacement may cause esotropia, horizontal diplopia and compensatory head turning. Reported findings in children with PF tumours include gaze palsy and strabismus (42%), upbeat nystagmus (23%) and abnormal acuity (15%), defined as VA below 20/40 (or > 0.3 logMAR) in one or both eyes. Frequent tumour types are WHO grade IV Medulloblastoma (MBL), cerebellar WHO grade I pilocytic astrocytoma (PA), and ependymoma (EP); MBL and EP carry greater abnormal-vision risk than cerebellar PA. Survivors of MB or cerebellar PA frequently have persistent strabismus (25-29%) or nystagmus (12.5- 18%). ATRT and rare embryonal tumours can occur here with similar features.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: ocular hypertension (OHT)
  Synonyms:
    - OHT
  Description: A condition assessed for the likelihood of future visual impairment and conversion to COAG. The guideline uses an IOP threshold of 24 mmHg for referral and for treatment decisions in people at risk of visual impairment within their lifetime.
  Clinical presentation: OHT is asymptomatic.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Goldmann-type applanation tonometry
      Purpose: Measure IOP before referral.
      When indicated: During case-finding for COAG and related conditions.
      Interpretation: An IOP of 24 mmHg or more is a referral criterion; consider confirming this measurement on another occasion unless urgent or emergency referral is indicated. An IOP below 24 mmHg calls for continued regular visits to a primary eye care professional.
    - Test: Goldmann applanation tonometry (slit lamp mounted)
      Purpose: Measure IOP for diagnosis and at each subsequent assessment.
      When indicated: At diagnostic assessment and every reassessment.
      Interpretation: IOP level contributes to assessment of future visual impairment risk.
    - Test: standard automated perimetry
      Purpose: Assess the central visual field before referral, establish its status at diagnosis and monitor for change.
      When indicated: Use a full-threshold or supra-threshold assessment during case-finding and a central thresholding test at diagnosis. Repeat testing when clinically indicated; a central thresholding or supra-threshold test may be used during reassessment when a central thresholding test previously documented a normal field.
      Interpretation: A visual field defect consistent with glaucoma is a referral criterion. If a defect was previously found, retain the same measurement strategy at subsequent assessments.
    - Test: stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy
      Purpose: Examine the optic nerve and fundus before referral and at diagnosis.
      When indicated: Use pupil dilatation during diagnostic examination and during case-finding if needed. Repeat optic nerve head assessment when clinically indicated; dilate pupils at reassessment if the optic nerve head and surrounding area cannot be seen adequately.
      Interpretation: Optic nerve head damage is a referral criterion. A change detected on examination calls for a new optic nerve head image as a reference for later assessments.
    - Test: optic nerve head image or OCT
      Purpose: Document the optic nerve head and provide a baseline for comparison.
      When indicated: Obtain imaging during case-finding if available and an optic nerve head image at diagnosis. Repeat imaging when clinically indicated or when examination identifies a change in optic nerve head status.
    - Test: gonioscopy
      Purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber configuration and depth.
      When indicated: Use during case-finding if available and at diagnosis. Repeat when clinically indicated, including after an inconclusive examination or suspected change in anterior chamber angle status.
    - Test: van Herick test
      Purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber depth.
      When indicated: May replace gonioscopy during case-finding if gonioscopy is unavailable or the person prefers it. Use at diagnosis if clinical circumstances preclude gonioscopy, and during reassessment when clinically indicated.
    - Test: OCT
      Purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber configuration and depth.
      When indicated: An option during case-finding if gonioscopy is unavailable or the person prefers an alternative.
    - Test: central corneal thickness (CCT) measurement
      Purpose: Contribute to diagnosis and assessment of future visual impairment risk.
      When indicated: At diagnostic assessment.
      Interpretation: CCT is a risk factor to consider, but knowledge of corneal thickness is not required to decide whether to treat OHT.
    - Test: anterior segment slit lamp examination
      Purpose: Examine the anterior segment during follow-up.
      When indicated: At each assessment, with van Herick peripheral anterior chamber depth assessment when clinically indicated.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Re-evaluate conversion and sight-loss risk at every assessment. For treated OHT with baseline IOP of 24 mmHg or more and a normal optic nerve head and visual field at the most recent assessment: if conversion is not detected or is uncertain and IOP is uncontrolled, review management and reassess between 1 month and 4 months; if conversion is uncertain and IOP is controlled, reassess between 6 months and 12 months; if conversion is not detected and IOP is controlled, reassess between 18 months and 24 months. If conversion occurs, follow the diagnosis and reassessment recommendations for COAG. Use clinical judgement within each interval, including when assessing a newly started treatment. If low lifetime visual impairment risk and acceptable IOP lead to a decision to stop treatment, offer an IOP assessment in 1 month to 4 months and further reassessment if clinically indicated.
    Recommended tests:
      - Goldmann applanation tonometry (slit lamp mounted) at every assessment.
      - Anterior segment slit lamp examination at every assessment, adding van Herick peripheral anterior chamber depth assessment when clinically indicated.
      - Repeat gonioscopy when clinically indicated.
      - Repeat visual field testing when clinically indicated, using a central thresholding or supra-threshold test if a central thresholding test previously documented a normal field.
      - Repeat optic nerve head assessment when clinically indicated; obtain a new image if stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy detects a change.
      - At every assessment, review general health and, when appropriate, adherence-related factors, cognitive impairment and treatment side effects.

Document sections:
  Heading: Culture
  Content: Corneal scrapings are inoculated onto blood agar, chocolate agar, and Sabouraud dextrose agar in C-shaped streaks; given the small inoculum, growth is considered significant only within the streaked area. An Indian study comparing growth and cost reported fungal growth on 56% of blood agar, 46% of chocolate blood, and 43% of Sabouraud dextrose agar plates. Its authors concluded that blood and chocolate agar support some, but not every, causative fungus and are more cost-effective than Sabouraud dextrose agar. In settings with limited resources and prevalent disease, however, animal blood can be difficult to obtain. Sabouraud dextrose agar or potato dextrose agar is still advised for optimal growth and dependable identification of filamentous fungi. Liquid media such as brain–heart infusion and thioglycolate broths are commonly used to improve organism recovery and dilute the effects of prior antimicrobial treatment. Although smears and culture together constitute the current diagnostic gold standard, culture lacks sensitivity. The involvement of >100 species also demands substantial mycological expertise to identify pathogens promptly and exclude contaminants. Fungal growth usually takes 48–72 h, so reliance on culture alone delays diagnosis and microscopy is always advised. Less common species can require 2 weeks before absence of growth is confirmed; some specimens have taken up to 35 days to grow. Delayed diagnosis and treatment contribute to poor prognosis. Cultures still positive at 6 days of therapy indicated poor outcome. Corneal biopsy may be needed for microbiological diagnosis when other methods fail.

Clinical implications:
  - A prior cesarean scar carries a rupture risk even without a subsequent trial of labor; risks observed during TOLAC should be interpreted against that baseline.
  - Uterine scar dehiscence and complete rupture have different clinical consequences and management options and must not be treated as equivalent findings.
  - Fetal compromise can develop rapidly after rupture, especially when the fetus or placenta enters the abdominal cavity. The general 20-30-minute target for starting cesarean delivery after a diagnosis of fetal distress offers limited protection against permanent fetal injury in that circumstance.
  - Fetal heart-rate abnormalities are more useful for recognizing rupture than maternal abdominal pain or changes in measured uterine activity. Epidural anesthesia has not been reported to delay diagnosis of rupture.
  - The article identifies subgroups whose rupture risk exceeds its illustrative threshold of 1 in 200 women (0.5%), including women with multiple cesarean scars, certain prior uterine incisions or closures, a short interdelivery interval, prior myomectomy, and selected circumstances involving induction, augmentation, or fetal macrosomia.
