retrieved_chunks.document_id: NCCN Prostate Cancer Early Detection Version 2.2024 — March 6, 2024
retrieved_chunks.text:
Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: Prostate cancer
  Description: Prostate cancer ranges from slow-growing disease that may not require immediate treatment to aggressive disease that can threaten life. This guideline addresses early detection and decisions about prostate biopsy, not prostate cancer treatment.
  Epidemiology: In the United States, prostate cancer accounts for 29% of new cancer diagnoses in males and is the second leading cause of cancer death in American men. For 2024, the cited estimates are 299,010 diagnoses and 35,250 deaths. The lifetime estimates for men in the United States are about 1 chance in 8 (12.9%) of diagnosis and about 1 chance in 41 (2.4%) of death from prostate cancer. U.S. prostate cancer death rates fell by 53% from 1993 to 2018, although they stabilized toward the end of that period. Risk is higher in Black/African American individuals, people with certain germline mutations, and people with a concerning family or personal cancer history.
  Clinical presentation: Early prostate cancer has no identifiable symptoms. Advanced disease may cause urinary obstruction, prostatic bleeding, hematospermia, or bone pain. Lower urinary tract symptoms in people considering screening may instead arise from benign prostatic enlargement.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Grade Group 1
      Distinguishing features: Described as lower-risk disease in the biopsy comparisons; a diagnosis may not require immediate treatment.
    - Name: Grade Group ≥2
      Distinguishing features: Used as a threshold for clinically significant or higher-grade disease in several diagnostic studies.
    - Name: Grade Group ≥3
      Distinguishing features: Used to identify higher-risk disease in comparisons of biopsy methods.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: History and physical (H&P)
      Purpose: Assess health, life expectancy, preferences, cancer history, inherited risk, prostate disease, prior testing, medications, environmental exposure, and symptoms.
      When indicated: Before decisions about participation in early detection.
      Interpretation: A concerning family history, relevant germline mutation, or Black/African American identity informs the assessment of elevated risk.
    - Test: PSA
      Purpose: Provide the principal serum test for early detection and guide the need for further evaluation.
      When indicated: As baseline testing in informed, healthy individuals choosing early detection, with timing determined by risk and age; repeat an abnormally high result, particularly near an evaluation threshold.
      Interpretation: Risk rises with PSA, but no PSA concentration eliminates cancer risk. PSA >3 ng/mL prompts further evaluation in the principal algorithm; PSA ≥4 ng/mL is the further-evaluation threshold for selected individuals >75 years. Infection, instrumentation, ejaculation, trauma, and medications can affect results. Values from differently calibrated commercial assays are not directly interchangeable.
    - Test: DRE
      Purpose: Complement PSA and help determine whether further assessment or biopsy is warranted.
      When indicated: May be considered at baseline; perform when PSA is elevated if it was not part of the initial assessment.
      Interpretation: DRE should not be used alone for early detection. A finding very suspicious for cancer warrants further evaluation regardless of PSA; an abnormal finding with elevated PSA has greater predictive value.
    - Test: Workup for benign disease
      Purpose: Assess noncancer explanations for an elevated PSA.
      When indicated: During evaluation before a biopsy decision, particularly with PSA >3 ng/mL.
    - Test: mpMRI
      Purpose: Inform whether to biopsy and identify areas for targeted sampling.
      When indicated: Strongly recommended before image-guided biopsy if available; also considered after a negative biopsy when suspicion persists and high-quality mpMRI was not previously performed.
      Interpretation: A negative result does not rule out clinically significant cancer. PSA density and other biomarkers can inform a biopsy decision despite a negative scan. High-quality imaging and radiologic expertise are important.
    - Test: PSA density
      Purpose: Help distinguish PSA elevation associated with prostate enlargement from cancer risk.
      When indicated: Consider with elevated PSA in a biopsy-naïve individual or when deciding about biopsy after a negative mpMRI.
      Interpretation: It is calculated as PSA in ng/mL divided by prostate volume in cc; higher values are associated with greater risk of high-grade cancer. Earlier studies used 0.15 ng/mL/g, but later studies questioned that cutoff's sensitivity.
    - Test: %fPSA
      Purpose: Improve the specificity of PSA-based assessment.
      When indicated: An option before initial biopsy and after a prior negative biopsy.
      Interpretation: A lower result is associated with greater prostate cancer risk. The document describes FDA approval for individuals aged ≥50 years with a non-suspicious DRE and PSA between 4 and 10 ng/mL.
    - Test: PHI
      Purpose: Refine the likelihood of cancer, including higher-grade disease, before a biopsy decision.
      When indicated: An option before initial biopsy or following a negative biopsy.
      Interpretation: Combines tPSA, fPSA, and proPSA; studies cited in the guideline report an association with cancer grade.
    - Test: 4Kscore
      Purpose: Estimate the probability of Grade Group ≥2 cancer on biopsy.
      When indicated: May be considered before biopsy or after a negative biopsy when clinically significant cancer remains a concern.
      Interpretation: Uses fPSA, tPSA, human kallikrein 2 (hK2), intact PSA, age, DRE, and prior biopsy status. No optimal cutoff is established.
    - Test: SelectMDx
      Purpose: Help identify clinically significant cancer before biopsy.
      When indicated: May be considered in individuals without a prior biopsy.
      Interpretation: Measures urinary DLX1 and HOXC6 expression after DRE, using KLK3 as an internal reference.
    - Test: ExoDx Prostate (IntelliScore)
      Purpose: Refine the likelihood of Grade Group ≥2 disease.
      When indicated: May be considered before an initial or repeat biopsy.
      Interpretation: Also called EPI; evaluates urinary exosomal PCA3 and ERG RNA normalized to SPDEF.
    - Test: MyProstateScore (MPS)
      Purpose: Refine biopsy decisions concerning clinically significant cancer.
      When indicated: May be considered before biopsy or after a negative biopsy when higher-risk disease remains a concern.
      Interpretation: Combines total serum PSA with urinary PCA3 and TMPRSS2:ERG expression after DRE.
    - Test: IsoPSA
      Purpose: Assess the risk of higher-grade cancer before a biopsy decision.
      When indicated: May be considered before biopsy or after a negative biopsy in individuals thought to have increased risk of clinically significant disease.
      Interpretation: A blood assay that separates and detects PSA isoforms.
    - Test: PCA3
      Purpose: Help decide whether a repeat biopsy is appropriate.
      When indicated: An option after a prior negative biopsy; the panel considers it inappropriate for the initial-biopsy setting.
      Interpretation: Measures PCA3 in urine obtained after DRE.
    - Test: ConfirmMDx
      Purpose: Further stratify cancer risk after a negative biopsy.
      When indicated: May be considered when deciding on repeat biopsy.
      Interpretation: Assesses promoter hypermethylation of GSTP1, APC, and RASSF1 in previously obtained biopsy tissue.
    - Test: Image-guided biopsy
      Purpose: Establish a tissue diagnosis and assess cancer grade.
      When indicated: Encouraged when suspicion of clinically significant cancer is high; a transrectal or transperineal approach may be used.
      Interpretation: MRI targeting is preferred when available. The panel favors combining targeted and systematic sampling because some high-grade cancers are detected only systematically.
    - Test: Systematic biopsy
      Purpose: Sample the prostate and contribute to risk stratification if cancer is found.
      When indicated: When systematic sampling is performed, the panel recommends an extended pattern with at least 12 cores.
      Interpretation: A negative biopsy does not exclude cancer on a later biopsy.
    - Test: MRI-targeted biopsy
      Purpose: Sample suspicious regions and improve detection of clinically significant disease.
      When indicated: When MRI targeting is available, including in selected individuals with a prior negative biopsy and persistent suspicion.
      Interpretation: Targeting may be cognitive, performed with TRUS-MRI fusion, or undertaken directly under MR guidance.
    - Test: Genetic testing
      Purpose: Investigate inherited susceptibility when the family history is suspicious.
      When indicated: For patients with a suspicious family history; referral to a cancer genetics professional is recommended when a susceptibility gene is known or suspected.
      Interpretation: A negative result does not remove the need to discuss PSA-testing timing and frequency when family history remains concerning.
    - Test: Sunnybrook-, ERSPC-, and PCPT-based risk calculators
      Purpose: Estimate the likelihood of biopsy-detectable cancer and high-grade cancer using clinical factors.
      When indicated: May inform discussion about biopsy, but should not alone determine whether biopsy is indicated.
      Interpretation: Their risk cutoffs have not been linked to reduced prostate cancer mortality in randomized trials.
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: Grade Group
      Clinical significance: Distinguishes lower-grade findings from clinically significant or higher-risk cancer in biopsy studies; Grade Group ≥2 and Grade Group ≥3 are thresholds used for different study outcomes.
    - Marker: Gleason score
      Clinical significance: The guideline identifies Gleason score ≥3+4 alongside Grade Group 2 or higher when describing high-grade cancer risk assessment.
  Genetic molecular:
    - Marker: BRCA2
      Technique: Germline genetic testing
      Clinical significance: Carriers have increased prostate cancer risk, with concern for earlier-onset or potentially lethal disease; early detection is recommended at age 40.
    - Marker: BRCA1
      Technique: Germline genetic testing
      Clinical significance: Listed among prostate cancer susceptibility genes, although evidence for increased risk is less consistent than for BRCA2.
    - Marker: ATM
      Technique: Germline genetic testing
      Clinical significance: Listed among germline genes relevant to inherited prostate cancer risk.
    - Marker: CHEK2
      Technique: Germline genetic testing
      Clinical significance: Listed among germline genes relevant to inherited prostate cancer risk.
    - Marker: PALB2
      Technique: Germline genetic testing
      Clinical significance: Listed among germline genes assessed for inherited prostate cancer susceptibility.
    - Marker: HOXB13
      Technique: Germline genetic testing
      Clinical significance: The rare G84E mutation is associated with substantially increased risk and earlier-onset familial disease; X285K is another rare variant described in the guideline.
    - Marker: MLH1
      Technique: Germline genetic testing
      Clinical significance: A gene associated with Lynch syndrome and included in hereditary-risk assessment.
    - Marker: MSH2
      Technique: Germline genetic testing
      Clinical significance: A gene associated with Lynch syndrome and included in hereditary-risk assessment.
    - Marker: MSH6
      Technique: Germline genetic testing
      Clinical significance: A gene associated with Lynch syndrome and included in hereditary-risk assessment.
    - Marker: PMS2
      Technique: Germline genetic testing
      Clinical significance: A gene associated with Lynch syndrome and included in hereditary-risk assessment.
    - Marker: EPCAM
      Technique: Germline genetic testing
      Clinical significance: Included among genes associated with Lynch syndrome and hereditary prostate cancer risk assessment.
    - Marker: TP53
      Technique: Germline genetic testing
      Clinical significance: Pathogenic germline variants cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome; the guideline associates these variants with increased risk of aggressive prostate cancer.
    - Marker: PCA3
      Technique: Post-DRE urine testing
      Clinical significance: Overexpressed in prostate cancer and used in assays that help assess whether biopsy, particularly repeat biopsy, is warranted.
    - Marker: TMPRSS2:ERG
      Technique: Post-DRE urine testing
      Clinical significance: A fusion gene measured by MyProstateScore (MPS); the guideline describes the fusion as a frequent, apparently early event in prostate cancer development.
  Prognostic tools:
    - Name: Sunnybrook-based risk calculator
      Components:
      - Clinical variables that can include age, family history, ancestry, DRE, and PSA
      Interpretation: Estimates biopsy-detectable prostate cancer and high-grade cancer risk. The panel does not recommend using a risk calculator alone to decide on biopsy.
    - Name: ERSPC-based risk calculator
      Components:
      - Clinical variables that can include age, family history, ancestry, DRE, and PSA
      Interpretation: May support biopsy discussions, but risk thresholds associated with reduced prostate cancer mortality remain unknown.
    - Name: PCPT-based risk calculator
      Components:
      - Clinical variables that can include age, family history, ancestry, DRE, and PSA
      Interpretation: Estimates biopsy-detectable cancer risk; clinical judgment and patient preferences remain necessary.
    - Name: 4Kscore
      Components:
      - fPSA
      - tPSA
      - human kallikrein 2 (hK2)
      - intact PSA
      - age
      - DRE
      - prior biopsy status
      Interpretation: Reports a percentage likelihood of Grade Group ≥2 cancer on biopsy; the guideline states that no optimal cutoff is established.
    - Name: Prostate Health Index (PHI)
      Components:
      - tPSA
      - fPSA
      - proPSA
      Interpretation: Helps assess cancer risk and correlates with cancer grade.
    - Name: Stockholm3
      Components:
      - age
      - first-degree family history of prostate cancer
      - previous biopsy
      - PSA
      - fPSA
      - %fPSA
      - hK2
      - MIC1
      - MSMB
      - genetic score based on 254 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)
      - HOXB13 SNP
      - prostate volume
      - DRE
      Interpretation: Described as a multivariate model investigated for more specific detection; the panel does not recommend routine use of the additional models discussed in that section pending further validation.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: For average-risk individuals aged 45–75 years with PSA <1 ng/mL and a normal DRE if performed, repeat testing at 2- to 4-year intervals; with PSA 1–3 ng/mL, repeat at 1 to 2-year intervals. For higher-risk individuals aged 40–75 years with PSA ≤3 ng/mL and a normal DRE if performed, repeat at 1 to 2-year intervals. In carefully selected individuals >75 years with PSA <4 ng/mL, a normal DRE if performed, and no other biopsy indication, repeat at 1 to 3-year intervals or consider stopping screening when clinically appropriate. When suspicion for clinically significant cancer is low after further evaluation, follow up in 6–12 mo.
    Recommended tests:
      - PSA
      - DRE
    Survivorship notes: These intervals concern early detection before a cancer diagnosis. The guideline directs care after a cancer diagnosis to the NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer.

Ensayo de fase 3 aleatorizado de nivolumab en combinación con cabozantinib frente a sunitinib (CA2099ER)
La seguridad y eficacia de nivolumab 240 mg en combinación con cabozantinib 40 mg para el tratamiento de primera línea del CCR avanzado/metastásico, se evaluó en un ensayo de fase 3, aleatorizado, abierto (CA2099ER). El ensayo incluyó pacientes (18 años o mayores) con CCR con un componente de células claras avanzado o metastásico, estado funcional de Karnofsky (KPS) ≥ 70% y enfermedad medible según RECIST, versión 1.1 con independencia de su estado PD‑L1 o grupo de riesgo IMDC. El ensayo excluyó pacientes con enfermedad autoinmune u otra condición médica que requiriera inmunosupresión sistémica, pacientes con tratamiento previo con un anticuerpo anti‑PD‑1, anti‑PD‑L1, anti‑PD‑L2, anti‑CD137 o anti‑CTLA‑4, hipertensión mal controlada a pesar del tratamiento antihipertensivo, metástasis cerebrales activas e insuficiencia suprarrenal no controlada. Los pacientes se estratificaron por la puntuación pronóstica IMDC, la expresión tumoral PD‑L1 y la región.
Se aleatorizaron un total de 651 pacientes para recibir nivolumab 240 mg (n = 323) administrados por vía intravenosa cada 2 semanas en combinación con cabozantinib 40 mg diarios por vía oral o sunitinib (n = 328) 50 mg al día, administrado por vía oral durante 4 semanas seguidas de 2 semanas de descanso. El tratamiento continuó hasta progresión de la enfermedad o toxicidad inaceptable con la administración de nivolumab durante un máximo de 24 meses. Se permitió el tratamiento más allá de la progresión definida por RECIST, versión 1.1 evaluada por el investigador si el paciente tenía un beneficio clínico y toleraba el medicamento del ensayo, según lo determinado por el investigador. La primera evaluación tumoral después del inicio se realizó a las 12 semanas (± 7 días) después de la aleatorización. Las evaluaciones tumorales posteriores se realizaron cada 6 semanas (± 7 días) hasta la semana 60, y luego cada 12 semanas (± 14 días) hasta la progresión radiográfica, confirmada por el BICR. La variable primaria de eficacia fue la SLP determinada por un BICR. Las variables de eficacia adicionales incluyeron la SG y la TRO como variables secundarias clave.
En general, las características basales estaban equilibradas entre los dos grupos. La mediana de edad fue de 61 años (rango: 28‑90) con 38,4% ≥ 65 años de edad y 9,5% ≥ 75 años de edad. La mayoría de los pacientes eran hombres (73,9%) y de raza blanca (81,9%). El 8% de los pacientes eran de raza asiática, el 23,2% y el 76,5% de los pacientes tenían un KPS basal de 70 a 80% y de 90 a 100%, respectivamente. La distribución de pacientes por categorías de riesgo IMDC fue 22,6% bajo, 57,6% intermedio y 19,7% alto. Para la expresión tumoral PD‑L1, el 72,5% de los pacientes tenían expresión de PD‑L1 < 1% o indeterminada y el 24,9% de los pacientes tenían expresión de PD‑L1 ≥ 1%. El 11,5% de los pacientes tenían tumores con características sarcomatoides. La mediana de la duración del tratamiento fue de 14,26 meses (rango: 0,2‑27,3 meses) en los pacientes tratados con nivolumab en combinación con cabozantinib y de 9,23 meses (rango: 0,8‑27,6 meses) en pacientes tratados con sunitinib.
El ensayo demostró un beneficio estadísticamente significativo en SLP, SG y TRO para los pacientes aleatorizados a nivolumab en combinación con cabozantinib en comparación con sunitinib. Los resultados de eficacia del análisis primario (seguimiento mínimo de 10,6 meses; mediana de seguimiento de 18,1 meses) se muestran en la Tabla 40.

Ensayo de fase 3 aleatorizado de nivolumab en monoterapia frente a everolimus (CA209025)
La seguridad y eficacia de nivolumab 3 mg/kg para el tratamiento del CCR avanzado con componente de células claras se evaluaron en un ensayo de Fase 3, aleatorizado y abierto (CA209025). El ensayo incluyó pacientes (con 18 años o mayores) que habían experimentado progresión de la enfermedad durante o después de 1 o 2 regímenes de tratamiento antiangiogénico y no más de 3 tratamientos sistémicos previos. Los pacientes tenían que tener una puntuación de ≥ 70% del Karnofsky Performance Score (KPS). Este ensayo incluyó pacientes independientemente de la expresion de PD‑L1 en el tumor. Pacientes con antecedentes o presencia de metástasis cerebrales, tratados previamente con un inhibidor de la diana de rapamicina en células de mamífero (mTOR, por sus siglas en inglés, mammalian Target of Rapamycin), cualquier enfermedad autoinmune activa, o condición médica que requiriera tratamiento sistémico de inmunosupresión fueron excluidos del ensayo.
Un total de 821 pacientes fueron aleatorizados para recibir nivolumab (n = 410) administrado por vía intravenosa durante 60 minutos con una concentración de 3 mg/kg cada 2 semanas o everolimus (n = 411) 10 mg al día, administrado por vía oral. El tratamiento continuó mientras se observó beneficio clínico o hasta que el tratamiento no fuera tolerado. Las primeras evaluaciones del tumor se realizaron 8 semanas después de la aleatorización y se siguieron efectuando cada 8 semanas durante el primer año y después cada 12 semanas hasta alcanzar progresión o suspensión del tratamiento, lo que ocurra más tarde. Las evaluaciones del tumor se continuaron después de la suspensión de tratamiento en pacientes que lo habían suspendido por razones que no fueran progresión. El tratamiento más allá de la progresión, establecida por el investigador según criterios RECIST, versión 1.1, se permitió si el paciente presentaba beneficio clínico y toleraba el medicamento del ensayo según lo determinado por el investigador. La variable primaria de eficacia fue la SG y las variables secundarias de eficacia evaluadas por el investigador fueron TRO y SLP.
Las características basales fueron generalmente similares para ambos grupos. La mediana de edad fue 62 años (rango: 18‑88) con 40% ≥65 años de edad y 9% ≥75 años de edad. La mayoría de los pacientes eran varones (75%) y de raza blanca (88%), estaban representados todos los grupos de riesgo del Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC), y el 34% y 66% de los pacientes tenían puntuación de KPS basal del 70 al 80% y del 90 al 100%, respectivamente. La mayoría de los pacientes (72%) fueron tratados después de un régimen de tratamiento antiangiogénico. La mediana de duración de tiempo desde el diagnóstico inicial hasta la aleatorización fue de 2,6 años en ambos grupos, el de nivolumab y el de everolimus. La mediana de duración de tratamiento fue de 5,5 meses (rango: 0‑29,6+ meses) en pacientes tratados con nivolumab y fue de 3,7 meses (rango: 6 días‑25,7+ meses) en pacientes tratados con everolimus.
El tratamiento con nivolumab se continuó después de la progresión en un 44% de los pacientes.

Ensayo de fase 3 aleatorizado de nivolumab en combinación con AVD frente a brentuximab vedotina en combinación con AVD (CA2098UT)
La seguridad y eficacia de nivolumab en combinación con doxorubicina, vinblastina y dacarbacina (AVD) para el tratamiento de adultos y adolescentes a partir de 12 años de edad con LHc en estadio III o IV no tratado previamente se evaluaron en un ensayo clínico de fase 3, abierto, multicéntrico y aleatorizado.
Un total de 994 pacientes fueron aleatorizados 1:1 para recibir nivolumab con quimioterapia con AVD (n = 496) o brentuximab vedotina con quimioterapia con AVD (BV + AVD) (n = 498). Los factores de estratificación para la aleatorización fueron la edad (12‑17 años frente a 18‑60 años frente a > 60 años), la puntuación pronóstica internacional (IPS) (0‑3 frente a 4‑7) y radioterapia guiada por PET de enfermedad residual preespecificada (sí frente a no). Las evaluaciones del tumor se realizaron 4‑8 semanas después del ciclo 6 de administración o en el momento de interrumpir el tratamiento del estudio. La variable primaria de eficacia fue la SLP evaluada por el investigador. Las variables de eficacia adicionales fueron la SG, la SLE y la tasa de respuesta metabólica completa al final del tratamiento.
La población del estudio estaba formada por sujetos recién diagnosticados de LHc en estadio III o IV no tratado previamente y confirmado histológicamente (nodular esclerosante, celularidad mixta, rico en linfocitos o con depleción linfocítica, o no especificado de otra manera) y enfermedad medible bidireccionalmente (al menos una lesión con un diámetro mayor > 1,5 cm). No se consideraron aptos los sujetos con linfoma de Hodgkin con predominio linfocitario nodular. Los sujetos se sometieron a una exploración PET‑TAC de cuerpo entero o de cuerpo entero limitada en los 42 días previos a la aleatorización. Se excluyeron del ensayo clínico a los pacientes con enfermedad autoinmune activa, condiciones médicas que requerían inmunosupresión sistémica, neuropatía periférica de Grado > 2, neumonitis intersticial activa o enfermedad pulmonar intersticial o linfoma del SNC.

  Content: Relevant literature does not support noncontrast orbital MRI alone as the initial test. Although its sequences provide information, postcontrast imaging is necessary for the most complete initial optic nerve assessment. Orbital MRI has thinner, higher-resolution, fat-saturated T2-weighted imaging than routine head MRI. An expansile nerve-associated mass with chronic progressive loss may strongly suggest glioma, but adult gliomas may be malignant and enhancement can suggest higher grade. Nerve or sheath enhancement helps distinguish optic neuropathy and demyelinating ON from optic perineuritis. Noncontrast MRI can detect ON lesions but cannot reliably distinguish acute from chronic disease; enhancement suggests acute inflammation. In AION, particularly the arteritic type, nerve-head enhancement has been reported more consistently than diffusion restriction.

Condition or topic: Chemotherapy for retinoblastoma

Clinical background: Retinoblastoma is the most common childhood ocular malignancy and affects approximately 1 in 15,000–20,000 live births. Without prompt treatment, it can be fatal. In high-income countries, detection usually precedes invasion of surrounding structures and disease-free survival approaches 100%; in low-and-middle-income countries, presentation with invasive disease is more common and survival is substantially lower. Treatment has evolved from a primary emphasis on survival toward preserving eyes and vision while limiting complications. Chemotherapy delivered through several routes is central to this approach, but the choice of treatment depends on the clinical circumstances.

Objectives:
  - Summarize current knowledge and emerging trends in chemotherapy for retinoblastoma across different administration routes.
  - Review treatment considerations, doses, administration methods, outcomes, and potential complications.
  - Examine emerging treatments and future directions intended to improve treatment outcomes.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_05
  Name: Retinal detachment
  Description: Separation involving the retina can cause acute visual loss. Prompt treatment may be needed to avoid permanent impairment. Diagnosis usually relies on clinical and ophthalmologic examination rather than initial cross-sectional imaging.
  Epidemiology: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is the most common form.
  Clinical presentation: Acute vision loss may occur. Vitreous hemorrhage can prevent visualization of the posterior eye during funduscopic examination.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
      Distinguishing features: A defect in the neurosensory retina allows vitreous fluid to collect between the sensory and pigmented retinal layers.
    - Name: Exudative (serous) retinal detachment
      Distinguishing features: Subretinal fluid accumulates without a break in the neurosensory epithelium. An underlying inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic, vascular or degenerative process may be responsible.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Dilated funduscopic examination
      Purpose: Establish the diagnosis of retinal detachment.
      When indicated: Used in the initial clinical assessment.
    - Test: Ocular US
      Purpose: Establish the diagnosis when funduscopic visualization of the posterior eye is obscured.
      When indicated: May be used, for example, in the presence of vitreous hemorrhage; avoid if globe rupture is known or suspected.
    - Test: MRI orbits without and with IV contrast
      Purpose: Characterize a suspected mass or another cause of exudative retinal detachment.
      When indicated: Usually Not Appropriate for the initial evaluation of suspected retinal structural abnormality; it may be used selectively after the initial diagnosis.
    - Test: Optical coherence tomography
      Purpose: Provide high-resolution cross-sectional retinal imaging.
      When indicated: Used by ophthalmologists to assess retinal pathology; the guideline does not assign it an appropriateness category for this variant.
  Follow up:
    Long term effects:
      - Permanent vision loss can result if an acute retinal detachment is not treated promptly.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Specular microscopy
  Content: Specular microscopy describes endothelial density in cells per mm2, percent hexagonality, cell-size variation, and shape variation. Unless specified otherwise, measurements represent the central pupillary region; because this region spans 28 to 50 mm2, reporting sampled fields or the proportion examined is useful. One study found that accurate representation of the full endothelial surface required sampling greater than 20%. The test is most useful alongside pachymetry and slit-lamp findings. It does not directly assess function, whereas serial pachymetry can assess endothelial function over time. Progressive cell loss may favor surgery and a stable count may favor conservative care. Diffuse confluent guttae often make endothelial imaging difficult and limit the test's value.

  Description: Separation involving the retina can cause acute visual loss. Prompt treatment may be needed to avoid permanent impairment. Diagnosis usually relies on clinical and ophthalmologic examination rather than initial cross-sectional imaging.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Mian et al. 2024 Corneal Edema and Opacification Preferred Practice Pattern®__JC__000274
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Mian et al. 2024 Corneal Edema and Opacification Preferred Practice Pattern®
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Specular microscopy
  Content: Specular microscopy describes endothelial density in cells per mm2, percent hexagonality, cell-size variation, and shape variation. Unless specified otherwise, measurements represent the central pupillary region; because this region spans 28 to 50 mm2, reporting sampled fields or the proportion examined is useful. One study found that accurate representation of the full endothelial surface required sampling greater than 20%. The test is most useful alongside pachymetry and slit-lamp findings. It does not directly assess function, whereas serial pachymetry can assess endothelial function over time. Progressive cell loss may favor surgery and a stable count may favor conservative care. Diffuse confluent guttae often make endothelial imaging difficult and limit the test's value.

Document sections:
  Heading: HIGHLIGHTED FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CARE
  Content: Only 60% of people with diabetes receive the recommended annual DR screening. Dilated fundus examination is the screening reference standard, although validated digital imaging can also detect disease. People with type 1 diabetes should begin annual screening 5 years after onset; those with type 2 diabetes should be screened promptly at diagnosis and at least annually afterward. Patients should be advised that control of glucose and blood pressure reduces DR onset or progression, while rapid intensive glucose lowering can accelerate or precipitate DR, as observed with semaglutides and other newer agents. Pregnant women with pre-existing diabetes should be examined early and monitored closely; an examination during pregnancy is not required for gestational diabetes. Closer monitoring is needed during puberty because DR can progress faster. Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents, including agents that also address other targets, effectively treat CI-DME with vision loss and PDR and can reduce DR severity. PRP remains important for PDR. With CI-DME and good acuity, deferral until acuity is affected (20/30 or worse) is reasonable. The ophthalmologist and patient should choose the biological product together. Infectious endophthalmitis is the gravest ocular complication of intravitreal injections; topical povidone iodine is recommended because omission has been associated with an unacceptably high risk.

  Heading: Variant 1: Adult. Acute posttraumatic visual defect. Suspect orbital injury. Initial imaging.
  Content: Orbital fractures most often follow assault or a direct blow, motor-vehicle collisions, falls, or sports injuries. They can occur alone or alongside zygomaticomaxillary complex, Le Fort II and III, or nasoethmoidal complex fractures. Diplopia can accompany depressed orbital-floor fractures, especially anterior- or middle-third injuries and small- to medium-sized defects with soft-tissue herniation. Fractures >2 cm are more likely to produce enophthalmos. Blowout injury can involve the lamina papyracea, but extraocular-muscle herniation and serious immediate complications are less common than with orbital-floor blowout fractures. Most orbital fractures can undergo delayed repair after swelling improves; CT can reveal injuries needing more urgent action, including trapdoor fractures and orbital compartment syndrome. Lateral- and superior-wall fractures carry increased traumatic optic neuropathy risk because blunt force can reach the optic canal and shear the nerve. With associated brain injury or obtundation, an afferent pupillary defect may be its sole clinical sign. Urgent diagnosis permits timely intervention when needed. Although optic-canal fractures increase nerve-injury risk, emergency surgery for traumatic optic neuropathy is generally reserved for a bone fragment impinging on the nerve, hematoma in the canal, or enlarging retrobulbar hematoma with proptosis. Severe proptosis with posterior globe tenting requires emergency orbital decompression to preserve vision. An orbital-apex fracture involving the superior orbital fissure can affect multiple traversing cranial nerves. Retrobulbar hematoma, emphysema, or a blow-in fracture can increase orbital mass effect and cause compartment syndrome and vision loss. Imaging evidence of retrobulbar bleeding does not sensitively predict subsequent compartment syndrome: diagnose it from clinical evidence of optic nerve compression. Extraocular-muscle entrapment after an orbital-floor fracture is likewise a clinical diagnosis; muscle herniation and altered contour have low positive predictive values for entrapment. Imaging aims to identify orbital injuries and complications early enough to guide timely care and prevent permanent visual loss.

Document sections:

  Content: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) is a persistent, progressive ocular inflammatory disease that can threaten vision and mainly affects children and young adults. Its prevalence ranges from <2 per 10,000 in the United States to as high as 1,100 per 10,000 in parts of Africa. Dilated fundus examination is the screening reference standard, although validated digital imaging can also detect disease. People with type 1 diabetes should begin annual screening 5 years after onset; those with type 2 diabetes should be screened promptly at diagnosis and at least annually afterward. Patients should be advised that control of glucose and blood pressure reduces DR onset or progression, while rapid intensive glucose lowering can accelerate or precipitate DR, as observed with semaglutides and other newer agents. Pregnant women with pre-existing diabetes should be examined early and monitored closely; an examination during pregnancy is not required for gestational diabetes. Closer monitoring is needed during puberty because DR can progress faster. Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents, including agents that also address other targets, effectively treat CI-DME with vision loss and PDR and can reduce DR severity. PRP remains important for PDR. With CI-DME and good acuity, deferral until acuity is affected (20/30 or worse) is reasonable. The ophthalmologist and patient should choose the biological product together. Infectious endophthalmitis is the gravest ocular complication of intravitreal injections; topical povidone iodine is recommended because omission has been associated with an unacceptably high risk.

Document sections:
  Heading: Clinical Features
  Content: Assessment of suspected disease should establish onset and course, which are usually insidious and gradual, and inquire about trauma, contact lenses, systemic illness, and medication use. Symptoms include blurred vision, irritation, redness, photophobia, tearing, and discharge. Pain is usually less pronounced than in bacterial or Acanthamoeba keratitis and does not track the clinical findings. Findings include circumcorneal ciliary hyperemia, corneal infiltration and edema, diminished corneal luster, and typically feathery ulcer margins. Grey or yellow stromal infiltration commonly extends past the ulcer edge. A grey infiltrative ring can appear as raised, fluffy lesions with dirty yellow or brown pigmentation; dense endothelial-level infiltration may form plaques. Multifocal satellite microabscesses occur in more than 10% of cases, and thick hypopyon occurs in more than half. Appearance varies with the causative species. Serrated or feathery margins, raised borders, satellites, and infiltrate color can assist clinical distinction from bacterial keratitis. Candida and other yeast-associated ulcers may have a collar-button configuration: typically a small ulcer with expanding stromal infiltration. Although they resemble bacterial ulcers, they progress more slowly, have more discrete stromal infiltration, and do not respond to topical antibiotics.   Content: Most cases are detected because parents or a paediatrician notice an abnormal-looking eye, such as a visibly small globe, marked nystagmus, strabismus, or an evident iris defect. Persistent poor vision can arise without RD through uncorrected refractive error, amblyopia, or foveal involvement and may become apparent when schooling begins. Document sections:
  Heading: I Clinical features
  Content: The meibomian glands are sebaceous glands of the upper and lower tarsal plates. Their secretion reaches the tear surface through approximately 30–40 upper-lid and 20–30 lower-lid orifices. Meibum includes non-polar and polar lipids and is believed to support tear-film stability; the extent to which it prevents evaporation remains under investigation. MGD mechanisms are incompletely understood and differ between low- and high-delivery disease. Conventionally, ductal hyperkeratinization was thought to make meibum cloudy and viscous, obstruct its exit and reduce delivery. Aging, inflammation, hormonal imbalance, bacterial growth, eye drops and oral drugs may contribute; altered meibocytes have also been proposed as a core mechanism. High-delivery disease has been associated with inflammation and an increased amount of qualitatively abnormal expressed meibum, but its detailed mechanism remains unresolved.

Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 5: Adult. Acute or chronic vision loss, optic nerve abnormality suspected. Initial imaging.
  Content: Neoplastic, inflammatory, ischemic, demyelinating, and traumatic processes can affect the optic nerve or its sheath and produce acute, subacute, or chronic visual loss. Neoplasms tend to develop more slowly than other optic neuropathies. Optic nerve gliomas are the most common primary optic nerve neoplasm; they can be incidental, including in younger patients with neurofibromatosis type 1, or present with visual symptoms or proptosis, and are more likely to be malignant when presenting in adults. Orbital meningiomas can arise from the optic nerve sheath or extend from an intracranial mass; symptomatic sheath lesions classically cause gradual, painless visual decline. Inflammatory and demyelinating ON can resemble one another clinically and radiologically; enhancement reflects edema, inflammation, or demyelination. Possible causes of demyelinating ON include MS, NMO, and MOGAD. ON can also reflect chronic relapsing-remitting inflammatory disease, steroid-dependent recurrence, systemic inflammation, or infection. Enhancement patterns overlap but may help: bilateral simultaneous and longer optic nerve involvement occur more often with MOGAD or NMO than MS, which characteristically affects a shorter unilateral segment. Sheath or perioptic enhancement is more distinctive of MOGAD. Anterior involvement is more typical of MS or MOGAD; NMO tends toward posterior nerves, chiasm, or tracts. Brain and spine MRI may identify associated abnormalities; asymptomatic optic nerve lesions may help distinguish relapsing-remitting MS or clinically isolated syndrome from NMO or MOGAD. Optic perineuritis can arise from idiopathic orbital inflammation, autoimmunity, infection, or other inflammation and may mimic acute demyelinating ON, including visual loss and pain worsened by eye movement. Patients with perineuritis tend to be older and more likely to retain central vision. Ischemic optic neuropathy is anterior, AION, when involving the nerve head, or posterior, PION, when involving the retrobulbar nerve. AION classically causes disc edema and altitudinal field loss. Either form may be nonarteritic, in patients with vascular risk factors such as hypertension or diabetes, or arteritic, most commonly from giant cell arteritis. Imaging aims to identify optic nerve disease, narrow overlapping diagnoses, and inform management.

question: Which grade of ROP (Retinopathy of Prematurity) shows a ridge with retinal fibrovascular proliferation and neovasularisation?

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Chiang et al. 2021 International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity, Third Edition__JC__000006
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Chiang et al. 2021 International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity, Third Edition
retrieved_chunks.text:
Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)
  Description: A disorder of the developing retinal vasculature in premature infants. ICROP3 classifies each eye by the location of vascularization or disease, vascular changes, the appearance of the lesion at the vascular–avascular junction, and its circumferential extent. It also describes regression, reactivation, and late sequelae.
  Clinical presentation: Findings range from a demarcation line, ridge, or extraretinal neovascularization to partial or total retinal detachment. Posterior vessel dilation and tortuosity range continuously from normal through preplus disease to plus disease. After spontaneous regression or treatment, abnormalities may resolve incompletely, persist, or reactivate.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: preplus disease
      Distinguishing features: Retinal vascular dilation, tortuosity, or both are abnormal but do not reach the severity of plus disease.
    - Name: plus disease
      Distinguishing features: Posterior retinal vessels show dilation and tortuosity. Iris vascular engorgement, poor pupillary dilation, and peripheral vascular engorgement with vitreous haze can indicate advanced disease but are not required for this designation.
    - Name: persistent avascular retina (PAR)
      Distinguishing features: Vascularization remains incomplete after spontaneous or treatment-associated regression; the avascular area may be peripheral or posterior and is described by location and extent.
    - Name: reactivation
      Distinguishing features: Acute-phase vascular changes or lesions recur after regression. Findings can range from a new, self-limiting demarcation line to stage 3 disease with plus disease and need not follow the usual acute-stage sequence.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: ophthalmoscopy
      Purpose: Assess vascularization, vascular abnormalities, lesions, retinal detachment, and visibility of the optic disc.
      When indicated: During examination and classification of an eye at risk for or affected by ROP.
      Interpretation: Record zone, plus disease, stage, and extent for each eye; also note A-ROP if present. A visible optic disc distinguishes stage 5A from stage 5B and stage 5C.
    - Test: 28-diopter (D) lens
      Purpose: Estimate the temporal limit of zone I during ophthalmoscopy.
      When indicated: When assessing the retinal zone.
      Interpretation: With the nasal edge of the optic disc at one edge of the view, the temporal edge approximately marks the zone I limit.
    - Test: retinal photography
      Purpose: Document vascular and retinal findings.
      When indicated: When retinal imaging is used for assessment.
      Interpretation: Before 39 weeks’ postmenstrual age, the fovea may be difficult to identify; its position may instead be estimated from the macular center. Plus-disease assessment should not rely solely on vessels visible in narrow-angle photographs.
    - Test: OCT
      Purpose: Show features at the vascular–avascular junction and determine whether a partial detachment involves the fovea.
      When indicated: Particularly when foveal involvement is subtle or difficult to judge clinically.
      Interpretation: An attached fovea corresponds to stage 4A; foveal detachment corresponds to stage 4B.
    - Test: B-scan ultrasonography
      Purpose: Determine the extent of retinal detachment.
      When indicated: When fibrosis prevents visualization of the posterior pole.
      Interpretation: Can reveal total detachment and its funnel configuration despite an obstructed fundus view.
    - Test: fluorescein angiography
      Purpose: Characterize vascular abnormalities, avascular retina, leakage, or subtle neovascularization.
      When indicated: When additional vascular assessment is useful, including assessment of late abnormalities or possible reactivation.
      Interpretation: The illustrated findings include persistent avascular retina, leakage in incompletely regressed disease, and leakage at sites of reactivation.
    - Test: OCT angiography
      Purpose: Illustrate macular vascular abnormalities.
      Interpretation: The document illustrates an incompletely developed foveal contour and a poorly defined foveal avascular zone after ROP.
  Staging:
    System: ICROP3
    Definitions:
      - Stage: stage 1
        Description: A relatively flat, thin, white demarcation line lies within the retina at the vascular–avascular junction. Peripheral vessel dilation or tortuosity alone does not establish this stage.
      - Stage: stage 2
        Description: A ridge develops from the demarcation line, acquiring width and height. Isolated neovascular tufts called popcorn may lie behind it without constituting stage 3.
      - Stage: stage 3
        Description: Extraretinal neovascular tissue extends toward the vitreous from the ridge. Apparent flat neovascularization in zone I or posterior zone II also qualifies, even without an obvious ridge or demarcation line.
      - Stage: stage 4
        Description: Partial retinal detachment, which may be tractional or exudative.
      - Stage: stage 4A
        Description: Partial retinal detachment with the fovea remaining attached.
      - Stage: stage 4B
        Description: Partial retinal detachment involving the fovea. A posterior volcano-shaped tractional detachment remains stage 4B if the peripheral retina is attached.
      - Stage: stage 5
        Description: Total retinal detachment.
      - Stage: stage 5A
        Description: Total retinal detachment with an optic disc visible on ophthalmoscopy, suggesting an open funnel.
      - Stage: stage 5B
        Description: Total retinal detachment in which retrolental fibrovascular tissue or a closed funnel obscures the optic disc.
      - Stage: stage 5C
        Description: Findings of stage 5B accompanied by anterior segment abnormalities, such as marked anterior chamber shallowing, adhesions, or corneal opacification, suggesting a closed funnel.
    Additional rules: The most posterior vascularization or lesion determines the eye’s zone. Zone I extends from the optic disc center to a radius twice the estimated disc-center–to–foveal-center distance. Zone II extends from zone I to the nasal ora serrata, with comparable reach in other directions; posterior zone II extends 2 disc diameters beyond the zone I border. Zone III is the remaining peripheral crescent; its designation requires nasal vessels to reach the ora serrata and no ROP in the 2 nasal-most clock hours. A lesion entering a more posterior zone for 1 to 2 clock hours is classified by that zone with the qualifier “secondary to notch.” When stages coexist, use the most severe stage. Assess the preplus-to-plus spectrum using vessels within zone I rather than a quadrant count or only the narrow-angle photographic field. The document describes extent as 12 clock-hour sectors in Table 1 but as 30 sectors in the Extent section; these statements conflict. Document reactivated lesions with their zone and stage and the modifier “reactivated.”
  Follow up:
    Long term effects:
      - Late tractional, rhegmatogenous, or, rarely, exudative retinal detachment.
      - Retinoschisis that can extend into the macula and threaten visual field or acuity.
      - Persistent avascular retina, which is prone to thinning, holes, latticelike changes, and later retinal detachment.
      - Macular abnormalities, including a smaller foveal avascular zone and a blunted or absent foveal depression.
      - Persistent vessel tortuosity, straightened vascular arcades with macular dragging, a falciform retinal fold, abnormal branching, circumferential vascular connections, and telangiectatic vessels.
      - Vitreous hemorrhage.
      - Secondary angle-closure glaucoma later in life.
    Survivorship notes: Describe persistent avascular retina by location and extent. A late detachment without signs of active ROP is a sequela rather than reactivation. Reactivation is reported more often after anti-VEGF treatment than after spontaneous regression and rarely, if ever, after complete laser photocoagulation; current evidence places its most common occurrence after anti-VEGF injection between 37 and 60 weeks’ postmenstrual age, although later reactivation may occur.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: People with diabetes
  Content: The number of people with diabetes has increased across countries during the past 30 years alongside lifestyle changes. Diabetic retinopathy is the most common diabetic microvascular complication and a leading preventable cause of vision impairment and blindness. If existing trends persist, a cited estimate projects a 1.2-fold rise in affected people, from 146 million in 2014 to 180.6 million in 2030. Most associated vision impairment can be avoided through risk-factor control, early identification and timely treatment. Many national and international professional societies have long endorsed systematic retinal screening of people with diabetes to detect vision-threatening disease, annually or biennially according to setting, followed by treatment when needed. Approaches include ophthalmoscopy by trained eye-care staff and retinal imaging interpreted locally or centrally through telemedicine. Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 4: Adult. Acute vision loss, retinal structural abnormality suspected. Initial imaging.
  Content: Acute vision loss from retinal detachment is an emergency because delayed treatment can result in permanent impairment. Rhegmatogenous detachment is the most common type: a neurosensory retinal break lets vitreous fluid enter the potential space between sensory and pigmented retina. Clinical assessment and dilated funduscopy establish the diagnosis, ordinarily without imaging. If vitreous hemorrhage or another obstacle obscures the posterior eye, ocular US may establish detachment. Exudative or serous detachment instead involves subretinal fluid without a neurosensory epithelial break. Inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic, vascular, or degenerative conditions can disrupt the blood-retinal barrier and cause it. Central retinal artery occlusion presents with abrupt, painless monocular vision loss and an afferent pupillary defect; clinical findings and funduscopy, rather than initial radiologic imaging, establish the diagnosis. IV fibrinolytic therapy may be given within the designated treatment window. For exudative detachment, imaging may identify an underlying choroidal mass or uveomeningeal syndrome after clinical diagnosis. Acute detachment often needs prompt treatment to prevent permanent vision loss.

  Content: Primary angle closure suspect denotes ITC with normal IOP and no glaucomatous optic neuropathy.   Heading: Clinical Features
  Content: Assessment of suspected disease should establish onset and course, which are usually insidious and gradual, and inquire about trauma, contact lenses, systemic illness, and medication use. Symptoms include blurred vision, irritation, redness, photophobia, tearing, and discharge. Pain is usually less pronounced than in bacterial or Acanthamoeba keratitis and does not track the clinical findings. Findings include circumcorneal ciliary hyperemia, corneal infiltration and edema, diminished corneal luster, and typically feathery ulcer margins. Grey or yellow stromal infiltration commonly extends past the ulcer edge. A grey infiltrative ring can appear as raised, fluffy lesions with dirty yellow or brown pigmentation; dense endothelial-level infiltration may form plaques. Multifocal satellite microabscesses occur in more than 10% of cases, and thick hypopyon occurs in more than half. Appearance varies with the causative species. Serrated or feathery margins, raised borders, satellites, and infiltrate color can assist clinical distinction from bacterial keratitis. Candida and other yeast-associated ulcers may have a collar-button configuration: typically a small ulcer with expanding stromal infiltration. Although they resemble bacterial ulcers, they progress more slowly, have more discrete stromal infiltration, and do not respond to topical antibiotics. retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Mian et al. 2024 Corneal Edema and Opacification Preferred Practice Pattern®__JC__000292

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Management of Band Keratopathy
  Content: Band keratopathy involves hydroxyapatite deposits on the anterior Bowman’s layer and epithelial basement membrane associated with inflammation, local injury, or systemic hypercalcemia. It usually causes no symptoms, so debridement is reserved for glare, impaired vision, or pain caused by epithelial disruption. Deposits may be removed mechanically, chemically, or by combining both approaches: forceps can lift thick plaques, while finer material may require epithelial debridement followed by ethylene-diamine-tetra-acetic acid (EDTA) chelation. Studies support the safety and efficacy of alternative compounded EDTA sources where access is difficult. EDTA concentration and exposure time vary with calcium density and technique. A comparison reported mean healing times of 5–7 days after EDTA chelation versus 2–3 days for a similarly sized abrasion in normal eyes. Limiting EDTA exposure, including at the limbus, might hasten re-epithelialization. Slow healing increases the risk of stromal scarring and infection. When limbal stem cell deficiency, neurotrophic keratopathy, or severe dry eye coexists, amniotic membrane grafting or temporary tarsorrhaphy may support healing. With severe ocular surface disease, keratectomy risks may exceed its benefits. PTK is another option, but calcium ablates faster than adjacent tissue and may leave surface depressions and irregularities.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Vision Loss__JC__000110
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Vision Loss
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 1: Adult. Acute posttraumatic visual defect. Suspect orbital injury. Initial imaging.
  Content: Orbital fractures most often follow assault or a direct blow, motor-vehicle collisions, falls, or sports injuries. They can occur alone or alongside zygomaticomaxillary complex, Le Fort II and III, or nasoethmoidal complex fractures. Diplopia can accompany depressed orbital-floor fractures, especially anterior- or middle-third injuries and small- to medium-sized defects with soft-tissue herniation. Fractures >2 cm are more likely to produce enophthalmos. Blowout injury can involve the lamina papyracea, but extraocular-muscle herniation and serious immediate complications are less common than with orbital-floor blowout fractures. Most orbital fractures can undergo delayed repair after swelling improves; CT can reveal injuries needing more urgent action, including trapdoor fractures and orbital compartment syndrome. Lateral- and superior-wall fractures carry increased traumatic optic neuropathy risk because blunt force can reach the optic canal and shear the nerve. With associated brain injury or obtundation, an afferent pupillary defect may be its sole clinical sign. Urgent diagnosis permits timely intervention when needed. Although optic-canal fractures increase nerve-injury risk, emergency surgery for traumatic optic neuropathy is generally reserved for a bone fragment impinging on the nerve, hematoma in the canal, or enlarging retrobulbar hematoma with proptosis. Severe proptosis with posterior globe tenting requires emergency orbital decompression to preserve vision. An orbital-apex fracture involving the superior orbital fissure can affect multiple traversing cranial nerves. Retrobulbar hematoma, emphysema, or a blow-in fracture can increase orbital mass effect and cause compartment syndrome and vision loss. Imaging evidence of retrobulbar bleeding does not sensitively predict subsequent compartment syndrome: diagnose it from clinical evidence of optic nerve compression. Extraocular-muscle entrapment after an orbital-floor fracture is likewise a clinical diagnosis; muscle herniation and altered contour have low positive predictive values for entrapment. Imaging aims to identify orbital injuries and complications early enough to guide timely care and prevent permanent visual loss.

question: The most common cause of glaucoma with elevated IOP and optic nerve damage present in only ONE eye is

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__The Management of Angle Closure Glaucoma Clinical Guidelines__JC__000171
retrieved_chunks.document_id: The Management of Angle Closure Glaucoma Clinical Guidelines
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 1.1 Background
  Content: Glaucoma affects an estimated 80 million people worldwide and is a major cause of blindness. It is an intermittently progressive optic neuropathy that produces visual field defects attributable to injury at the pre-laminar optic nerve head. Lowering intraocular pressure slows or stops progression in the vast majority of cases. Secondary glaucoma arises from another ocular or systemic disorder, commonly neovascularization, uveitis or ocular trauma, and typically causes a marked pressure rise. Primary glaucoma has no such precipitating disease. Primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG) and primary open angle glaucoma (POAG) are distinguished by whether the iris obstructs the iridocorneal drainage angle. They differ in presentation and treatment; PACG depends more strongly on pressure, and its treatment aims to remove barriers to aqueous circulation. In primary angle-closure suspects (PACS), the iris contacts the trabecular meshwork, but intraocular pressure (IOP), optic nerve structure and visual function remain normal, without peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS). Primary angle-closure (PAC) involves current or previous IOP elevation and/or PAS, without glaucomatous optic nerve injury or visual field abnormality. PACG can arise without previously detected high IOP or PAS. Acute angle-closure (AAC) occurs when sudden complete trabecular obstruction produces extreme ocular hypertension; pain, abrupt visual reduction or loss, nausea and/or vomiting may be severe. Prompt presentation and suitable treatment have improved its outlook. PACG causes severe visual loss more often than POAG: approximately 60 million people worldwide have POAG versus 20 million with PACG, yet the numbers blinded by the two conditions are roughly equal. This greater threat has encouraged consideration of prevention.

Document sections:
  Heading: A B S T R A C T
  Content: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) is a persistent, progressive ocular inflammatory disease that can threaten vision and mainly affects children and young adults. Its prevalence ranges from <2 per 10,000 in the United States to as high as 1,100 per 10,000 in parts of Africa. Where VKC is uncommon, distinguishing it from other conditions can be difficult; treatment may begin only after disease progression and substantial impairment of quality of life. Although VKC was formerly regarded chiefly as an immunoglobulin E-mediated disorder, approximately 50% of affected patients lack allergic sensitization. Multiple inflammatory pathways contribute to its manifestations and characteristic conjunctival eosinophilic and fibroproliferative lesions. This review examines changes in understanding of VKC immunopathology, available and emerging treatments, their clinical implications, and priorities for research and practice.

  Heading: Examination
  Content: Every patient should receive comprehensive medical eye assessment and follow-up at recommended intervals, including tear-film and ocular-surface evaluation, particularly before cataract or refractive surgery. Symptoms suggestive of dry eye warrant additional relevant tests. External and slit-lamp examinations document signs, tear quality, quantity, and stability, and alternative causes. External assessment may inspect skin for scleroderma, rosacea, or seborrhea; lids for closure, position, blinking, inflammation, secretions, or spasm; everted lids for tarsal conjunctival inflammation, allergy, or fibrosis; lacrimal-gland enlargement, proptosis, cranial nerves, and hand findings associated with systemic disease. Conditions:

  Name: Diabetic retinopathy
  Description: A diabetes-related eye condition that can be prevented or delayed by controlling hyperglycemia, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. Early disease may be asymptomatic.

  Clinical presentation: Early stages can have no symptoms; vision-threatening disease can result in vision impairment or blindness.

    - Name: advanced proliferative diabetic retinopathy
      Distinguishing features: An advanced form listed among the indications for vitreoretinal surgery.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Systematic retinal screening
      Purpose: Detect diabetic retinopathy early, including its vision-threatening stages.
      When indicated: For people with diabetes, annually or biennially depending on the setting.
      Interpretation: Refer for assessment and treatment when indicated.
    - Test: Ophthalmoscopy
      Purpose: Examine the retina during diabetic retinopathy screening.

    - Test: Retinal imaging
      Purpose: Screen for diabetic retinopathy using local interpretation or centralized grading through telemedicine.

    - Test: Slit lamp examination
      Purpose: Assess retinal status when screening images are of poor quality.

question: Fluorescein stain is used in the eye to stain

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Amescua et al. 2024 Dry Eye Syndrome Preferred Practice Pattern®__JC__000206
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Amescua et al. 2024 Dry Eye Syndrome Preferred Practice Pattern®
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: OCULAR SURFACE DYE STAINING
  Content: Fluorescein, rose bengal, and lissamine green help assess ocular-surface abnormalities. Fluorescein penetrates epithelium where intercellular junctions are sufficiently disrupted; use a saline-moistened strip or 1% to 2% sodium fluorescein and examine with slit lamp and cobalt blue illumination. Staining may become clearer after about 2 minutes and with a yellow filter. Mild staining can occur in normal eyes, particularly in the morning; dry eye often produces exposure-zone punctate or blotchy staining, more readily seen on cornea than conjunctiva. Rose bengal may be applied with a moistened strip or 1% solution; advise patients that it can irritate, so topical anesthetic is typically used first. Leave saline against the strip for at least a minute before application. Rose bengal stains conjunctiva more intensely than cornea, highlighting cells lacking mucus coating and tear debris; a red-free filter can aid viewing. Lissamine green has a staining pattern resembling rose bengal with less irritation, but waiting 1 to 2 minutes reduces visibility; unlike fluorescein, it is not recommended to assess corneal epithelial disease. Diffuse corneal and conjunctival staining commonly accompanies viral keratoconjunctivitis or medicamentosa. Inferior corneal and bulbar conjunctival staining is typical of staphylococcal blepharitis, meibomian gland disease, lagophthalmos, or exposure; superior bulbar conjunctival staining is typical of superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis. Interpalpebral corneal and bulbar conjunctival staining commonly accompanies aqueous deficiency.

Document sections:
  Heading: Technology Femtosecond Lasers
  Content: Femtosecond lasers produce pulses lasting on the order of 10−15 s. Their near-infrared output at 1053 nm creates tissue photodisruption while avoiding effects such as the thermal injury associated with earlier lasers. Power, repetition rate, and spot size permit further adjustment of the laser–tissue interaction. Photodisruption proceeds through plasma formation, shock-wave generation, and cavitation. Tissue separation occurs through ablation and cleaving, with pulse energy chiefly determining their relative contributions. The threshold for photodisruption varies with tissue characteristics, numerical aperture (NA), and wavelength. Higher-energy pulses produce more tissue ablation through expanding gas bubbles; lower-energy pulses ablate less tissue and rely more on cleaving, requiring higher frequencies and closer spot spacing.

Document sections:
  Heading: Visual Acuity (VA)
  Content: VA measures visual resolution and remains the most important visual measure for children with CNS tumours. Assess best-corrected VA (BCVA) in each eye, at far and near distances if possible, and report the threshold optotype detail in logMAR, from 0.0 for normal vision to 2.0. A change of 0.2 LogMAR VA or more is clinically relevant. If quantitative measurement is infeasible, fixation observations can help establish whether vision is present; document Hand Motion (HM), counting fingers (CF), Light Perception (LP) or No Light Perception (NLP), as appropriate. Testing depends on age and cooperation: Teller Acuity preferential looking Cards (TAC) are commonly used for infants and preverbal children, whereas Lea symbols, Cardiff Acuity Test, Kays Picture Chart and later HOTV or Snellen charts suit older children.

Changing VA test methods can slightly overestimate or underestimate longitudinal results. Because vision develops rapidly over the first 2-3 years and reaches full potential only after 5 years of age, age-specific normal ranges should be used in young children.

Document sections:
  Heading: Management of Band Keratopathy
  Content: Band keratopathy involves hydroxyapatite deposits on the anterior Bowman’s layer and epithelial basement membrane associated with inflammation, local injury, or systemic hypercalcemia. It usually causes no symptoms, so debridement is reserved for glare, impaired vision, or pain caused by epithelial disruption. Deposits may be removed mechanically, chemically, or by combining both approaches: forceps can lift thick plaques, while finer material may require epithelial debridement followed by ethylene-diamine-tetra-acetic acid (EDTA) chelation. Studies support the safety and efficacy of alternative compounded EDTA sources where access is difficult. EDTA concentration and exposure time vary with calcium density and technique. A comparison reported mean healing times of 5–7 days after EDTA chelation versus 2–3 days for a similarly sized abrasion in normal eyes. Limiting EDTA exposure, including at the limbus, might hasten re-epithelialization. Slow healing increases the risk of stromal scarring and infection. When limbal stem cell deficiency, neurotrophic keratopathy, or severe dry eye coexists, amniotic membrane grafting or temporary tarsorrhaphy may support healing. With severe ocular surface disease, keratectomy risks may exceed its benefits. PTK is another option, but calcium ablates faster than adjacent tissue and may leave surface depressions and irregularities.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: RISK FACTORS
  Content: Diabetes duration is a major DR risk factor. In type 1 diabetes, retinopathy affects approximately 25% after 5 years, almost 60% after 10 years, and 80% after 15 years. WESDR found PDR in approximately 50% of people aged 30 and younger after 20 years of type 1 diabetes. LALES and Proyecto VER found PDR in 18% of participants with diabetes for more than 15 years, without a difference between diabetes types. The Singapore Eye Disease Study identified Indian ethnicity, diabetes duration, HbA1c, serum glucose, and systolic blood pressure as independent predictors of any DR; lower diastolic pressure, total cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol were associated with lower odds. In a Canadian First Nations study, elevated HbA1c predicted two-step DR progression (HR =1.42; P < 0.0001), as did systolic blood pressure (HR = 1.24 per 10 mmHg; P = 0.009). Among people older than 30 with type 2 diabetes of known duration less than 5 years, DR occurred in 40% using insulin and 24% not using it; with documented duration up to 19 years, corresponding rates were 84% and 53%. PDR developed in 2% with type 2 diabetes for less than 5 years and 25% with duration of 25 years or more. Differences between historical cohorts may reflect changing glucose and hypertension care. Glycemia and blood pressure are principal modifiable risks; once DR exists, glycemic control appears more predictive of progression than duration. An HbA1c target of 7% or lower is recommended for most patients, with possible benefit from 6.5% in selected patients. Higher HbA1c corresponds to greater DME risk. The VISS Study associated long-term weighted HbA1c from type 1 diagnosis to 30+ years with PDR and nephropathy and proposed HbA1c 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) or lower, as near normal as possible, to avoid PDR and macroalbuminuria. In a prospective cohort of 3322 people with type 2 diabetes followed for 10 to 25 years, diagnosis at ages 15 up to age 40 carried adjusted OR 2.8 for DR versus diagnosis at ages 60 to under 70. Hypertension treatment remains important. A meta-analysis found modest DR-prevention benefit from lowering blood pressure for up to 5 years, especially with hypertension and type 2 diabetes, but little evidence that lowering it slows DR progression without hypertension. Large studies suggest lipid management may reduce progression and treatment need; findings about age, diabetes type, clotting, renal disease, inactivity, inflammatory markers, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are less consistent. Ophthalmologists should encourage adherence to care for all medical aspects of diabetes. DR is more prevalent among patients receiving dialysis; an association was reported with systolic, but not diastolic, pressure, fasting glucose, HbA1c, and high HDL cholesterol. A 2018 meta-analysis found lipid-lowering agents protective against DR progression and possibly DME onset, without an effect on acuity or hard exudates. A 2023 Cochrane review found that fenofibrate probably did not change DR progression across type 2 diabetes patients with and without existing DR but probably reduced progression in those with DR (I+, Moderate Quality). A later trial associated fenofibrate with a 27% reduction in progression or treatment among patients with early DR, with equivalent effects by diabetes type. A study suggested omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, docosahexaenoic acid, and eicosapentaenoic acid might relate to less severe DR; a systematic review found that nutraceutical evidence needs further research (III, Insufficient quality). Evidence on genetic and epigenetic explanations of differing progression is conflicting: one study found associations of longer duration and higher HbA1c with PDR in haplogroup H (P = 0.0001 and P = 0.011, respectively), but not haplogroup UK; a larger study did not reproduce that association. One study associated HMGA1 rs139876191 carriage with significantly lower PDR risk and proposed reduced VEGF A expression as an explanation. A meta-analysis of 13 studies associated VEGF variants rs2010963, rs833061, and rs699947 with NPDR or PDR. In a type 2 diabetes study, patients with metabolic syndrome versus those without it had more albuminuria (40.8% vs. 21.8%; P < 0.001), retinopathy (37.9% vs. 28.6%; P < 0.001), coronary disease (19.4% vs. 11.6%; P < 0.001), cerebrovascular disease (5.8% vs. 3.2%; P = 0.014), and ankle-brachial index less than 0.9 or 1.3 or higher (6.1% vs. 3.0%; P = 0.015). These outcomes tended to rise with the number of syndrome components (all P for trend < 0.05); screening may help identify higher-risk patients. In 50,254 eyes, baseline NPDR features predicted 5-year PDR progression: IRMA versus venous beading carried HR = 1.77; P = 0.0013 for PDR, and dot-blot hemorrhages in 4-quadrants carried HR = 3.84; P = 0.0095 for vitreous hemorrhage. Protocol S associated worse baseline PDR with worsening despite anti-VEGF or PRP (64% [high-risk PDR or worse] vs. 23% [moderate PDR or better]; HR = 3.97; P < 0.001). Within its PRP group, worsening was more frequent after pattern scan than conventional single-spot PRP (60% vs. 39%; HR = 2.04; P = 0.008), regardless of spot count. OCT and OCTA have identified additional progression biomarkers.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_04
  Name: Diabetic retinopathy
  Description: A diabetes-related eye condition that can be prevented or delayed by controlling hyperglycemia, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. Early disease may be asymptomatic.
  Epidemiology: It is the most common microvascular complication of diabetes and a leading global cause of preventable vision impairment and blindness. If current trends persist, the estimated number of affected people rises 1.2-fold, from 146 million in 2014 to 180.6 million in 2030.
  Clinical presentation: Early stages can have no symptoms; vision-threatening disease can result in vision impairment or blindness.

    - Test: Systematic retinal screening
      Purpose: Detect diabetic retinopathy early, including its vision-threatening stages.

    - Test: Ophthalmoscopy
      Purpose: Examine the retina during diabetic retinopathy screening.

    - Test: Retinal imaging
      Purpose: Screen for diabetic retinopathy using local interpretation or centralized grading through telemedicine.

  Content: Many tumors, tumor-like conditions, systemic diseases, metastases, and high- or low-flow vascular malformations can involve the orbit. Document sections:
  Heading: 1. Introduction
  Content: Retinoblastoma is the most frequent childhood ocular malignancy and affects approximately 1 in 15,000–20,000 live births. Without timely treatment, it can be fatal. In high-income countries, diagnosis generally precedes invasion of the optic nerve, choroid, sclera, or orbit, and disease-free survival approaches 100%. In low-and-middle-income countries, particularly in Africa, invasive presentation is more common, increasing local and distant metastatic risk and substantially lowering survival. Treatment aims to preserve life, prevent metastasis, retain the eye, and maximize vision, although protocols differ between centers. Before the 1990 s, enucleation and external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) predominated but could cause vision loss and serious adverse effects. Subsequent approaches improved disease-free survival, globe salvage, and, in selected cases, vision preservation. Plaque radiotherapy, cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, and transpupillary thermotherapy contributed to this change, while chemotherapy delivered by different routes had a particularly important role. The authors searched PubMed for English-language articles dating back to January 1, 1960, targeting publications from January 1, 1990, to January 31, 2024. Search terms covered retinoblastoma, chemotherapy, intravenous chemotherapy, chemoreduction, intra-arterial chemotherapy, ophthalmic artery chemosurgery, intravitreal chemotherapy, intracameral chemotherapy, and periocular chemotherapy. Their aim was to summarize current knowledge and emerging chemotherapy trends in retinoblastoma.

Document sections:
  Heading: 4.3.2. Eye rubbing, DED, and keratoconus
  Content: Prolonged or vigorous rubbing may alter ocular tissues and contribute to DED or keratoconus [195]. Reported associations also include corneal ectasia, conjunctivitis, glaucoma, iris and posterior-capsule complications, intraocular-lens dislocation, retinal detachment, and extrusion of implanted silicone oil [197]. Ocular allergy may be connected through rubbing or keratoconus, but evidence conflicts; one systematic review and meta-analysis of keratoconus and allergic eye disease was retracted in 2022 [204]. Among 61 patients with vernal keratoconjunctivitis and corneal ectasia, n = 53 had keratoconus and pathological rubbing was frequent [205]. DED with allergic conjunctivitis and asthma in children have also been linked to ocular allergy [206,207]. Contact lenses and chemical irritants can provoke rubbing by stimulating ocular-surface nociceptors; removal-relief rubbing associated with contact lenses may partly contribute to DED among long-term wearers [208,209,210,211,285]. Psychiatric conditions accompanied by chronic fatigue or stress have also been linked to rubbing [209]. Among 212 institutionalized patients, including Trisomy 21 (n = 30), neonatal asphyxia (n = 15), and pregnancy-related infection (n = 9), 7.5% (n = 16) had keratoconus and were more likely to rub their eyes than those without keratoconus (p = 0.008) [212]. A 2021 systematic review pooling six case-control studies associated rubbing with keratoconus (OR 6.46, 95% CI 4.12–10.1), but found heterogeneous studies with limited methodological quality and called for standardized measurement of rubbing frequency, force, and technique [213].
