  Content: Orbital infection can cause cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess, or orbital abscess and is an ophthalmologic emergency because of potential visual loss and intracranial complications, including meningitis, cerebritis, intracranial abscess, and cavernous sinus thrombosis. Pain and swelling near the orbit, reduced acuity, and ophthalmoplegia may occur. Infection most commonly spreads from adjacent structures, often from bacterial paranasal sinus disease. Clinical and imaging differentiation of periorbital from postseptal disease helps determine whether inpatient IV antibiotics are needed. Subperiosteal abscess usually needs surgical drainage. Acute invasive fungal sinusitis can also cause orbital complications; it is aggressive, associated with high mortality, and typically affects immunocompromised patients. Orbital inflammation can be idiopathic or secondary to granulomatous, inflammatory, or autoimmune disease, including sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, or Graves’ disease. Its manifestations and risk of visual loss depend on the cause and affected orbital structures. Cellulitis, orbital inflammatory syndrome, and lymphoproliferative lesions may overlap clinically and radiologically. Imaging seeks to define disease extent and complications, particularly abscess, to guide intervention and avert lasting vision loss, intracranial extension, or cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Clinical background: Fungal keratitis is a major cause of microbial corneal infection that can lead to blindness, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions. Fungi rarely invade an intact cornea, but trauma, especially involving vegetable matter, immunosuppression, topical steroid use, and ocular surface disease can increase susceptibility. Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 1: Adult. Acute posttraumatic visual defect. Suspect orbital injury. Initial imaging.
  Content: Orbital fractures most often follow assault or a direct blow, motor-vehicle collisions, falls, or sports injuries. They can occur alone or alongside zygomaticomaxillary complex, Le Fort II and III, or nasoethmoidal complex fractures. Diplopia can accompany depressed orbital-floor fractures, especially anterior- or middle-third injuries and small- to medium-sized defects with soft-tissue herniation. Fractures >2 cm are more likely to produce enophthalmos. Blowout injury can involve the lamina papyracea, but extraocular-muscle herniation and serious immediate complications are less common than with orbital-floor blowout fractures. Most orbital fractures can undergo delayed repair after swelling improves; CT can reveal injuries needing more urgent action, including trapdoor fractures and orbital compartment syndrome. Lateral- and superior-wall fractures carry increased traumatic optic neuropathy risk because blunt force can reach the optic canal and shear the nerve. With associated brain injury or obtundation, an afferent pupillary defect may be its sole clinical sign. Urgent diagnosis permits timely intervention when needed. Although optic-canal fractures increase nerve-injury risk, emergency surgery for traumatic optic neuropathy is generally reserved for a bone fragment impinging on the nerve, hematoma in the canal, or enlarging retrobulbar hematoma with proptosis. Severe proptosis with posterior globe tenting requires emergency orbital decompression to preserve vision. An orbital-apex fracture involving the superior orbital fissure can affect multiple traversing cranial nerves. Retrobulbar hematoma, emphysema, or a blow-in fracture can increase orbital mass effect and cause compartment syndrome and vision loss. Imaging evidence of retrobulbar bleeding does not sensitively predict subsequent compartment syndrome: diagnose it from clinical evidence of optic nerve compression. Extraocular-muscle entrapment after an orbital-floor fracture is likewise a clinical diagnosis; muscle herniation and altered contour have low positive predictive values for entrapment. Imaging aims to identify orbital injuries and complications early enough to guide timely care and prevent permanent visual loss.

Document sections:
  Heading: 1. Introduction
  Content: Retinoblastoma is the most frequent childhood ocular malignancy and affects approximately 1 in 15,000–20,000 live births. Without timely treatment, it can be fatal. In high-income countries, diagnosis generally precedes invasion of the optic nerve, choroid, sclera, or orbit, and disease-free survival approaches 100%. In low-and-middle-income countries, particularly in Africa, invasive presentation is more common, increasing local and distant metastatic risk and substantially lowering survival. Treatment aims to preserve life, prevent metastasis, retain the eye, and maximize vision, although protocols differ between centers. Before the 1990 s, enucleation and external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) predominated but could cause vision loss and serious adverse effects. Subsequent approaches improved disease-free survival, globe salvage, and, in selected cases, vision preservation. Plaque radiotherapy, cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, and transpupillary thermotherapy contributed to this change, while chemotherapy delivered by different routes had a particularly important role. The authors searched PubMed for English-language articles dating back to January 1, 1960, targeting publications from January 1, 1990, to January 31, 2024. Search terms covered retinoblastoma, chemotherapy, intravenous chemotherapy, chemoreduction, intra-arterial chemotherapy, ophthalmic artery chemosurgery, intravitreal chemotherapy, intracameral chemotherapy, and periocular chemotherapy. Their aim was to summarize current knowledge and emerging chemotherapy trends in retinoblastoma.

  Heading: OCULAR SURFACE DYE STAINING
  Content: Fluorescein, rose bengal, and lissamine green help assess ocular-surface abnormalities. Fluorescein penetrates epithelium where intercellular junctions are sufficiently disrupted; use a saline-moistened strip or 1% to 2% sodium fluorescein and examine with slit lamp and cobalt blue illumination. Staining may become clearer after about 2 minutes and with a yellow filter. Mild staining can occur in normal eyes, particularly in the morning; dry eye often produces exposure-zone punctate or blotchy staining, more readily seen on cornea than conjunctiva. Rose bengal may be applied with a moistened strip or 1% solution; advise patients that it can irritate, so topical anesthetic is typically used first. Leave saline against the strip for at least a minute before application. Rose bengal stains conjunctiva more intensely than cornea, highlighting cells lacking mucus coating and tear debris; a red-free filter can aid viewing. Lissamine green has a staining pattern resembling rose bengal with less irritation, but waiting 1 to 2 minutes reduces visibility; unlike fluorescein, it is not recommended to assess corneal epithelial disease. Diffuse corneal and conjunctival staining commonly accompanies viral keratoconjunctivitis or medicamentosa. Inferior corneal and bulbar conjunctival staining is typical of staphylococcal blepharitis, meibomian gland disease, lagophthalmos, or exposure; superior bulbar conjunctival staining is typical of superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis. Interpalpebral corneal and bulbar conjunctival staining commonly accompanies aqueous deficiency.

Document sections:
  Heading: People with diabetes
  Content: The number of people with diabetes has increased across countries during the past 30 years alongside lifestyle changes. Diabetic retinopathy is the most common diabetic microvascular complication and a leading preventable cause of vision impairment and blindness. If existing trends persist, a cited estimate projects a 1.2-fold rise in affected people, from 146 million in 2014 to 180.6 million in 2030. Most associated vision impairment can be avoided through risk-factor control, early identification and timely treatment. Many national and international professional societies have long endorsed systematic retinal screening of people with diabetes to detect vision-threatening disease, annually or biennially according to setting, followed by treatment when needed.   Content: An estimated three out of five people with diabetes in the United States have at least one associated complication. Warnings and precautions: Administrar únicamente por vía oftálmica.
Este medicamento puede incrementar la presión intraocular, especialmente en pacientes con antecedentes familiares de glaucoma, por lo que únicamente debe emplearse bajo control facultativo.
El uso prolongado de corticosteroides oftálmicos puede ocasionar hipertensión ocular y/o glaucoma, con deterioro del nervio óptico, disminuyendo la agudeza visual y causando defectos en el campo visual. También puede producir catarata subcapsular posterior. Debe controlarse la presión intraocular de forma rutinaria y frecuente. Esto es especialmente importante en pacientes pediátricos ya que el riesgo de hipertensión ocular inducido por corticosteroides, puede ser mayor en niños y puede ocurrir antes que en adultos. El riesgo de presión intraocular elevada y/o formación de cataratas inducido por corticosteroides es mayor en pacientes propensos (p.ej. diabetes).
Se puede producir síndrome de Cushing y/o supresión adrenal asociado a la absorción sistémica de dexametasona administrada por vía oftálmica, después de un tratamiento intensivo o continuado a largo plazo en pacientes predispuestos, incluidos niños y pacientes tratados con inhibidores del CYP3A4 (incluyendo ritonavir y cobicistat). En estos casos, el tratamiento se debe interrumpir de forma progresiva.
Los corticosteroides pueden aumentar la sensibilidad a infecciones: reducen la resistencia a infecciones y dificultan la localización de las mismas pudiendo enmascarar los signos clínicos.
El uso prolongado de tratamientos con corticosteroides por vía oftálmica en afecciónes agudas purulentas del ojo podría enmascarar la infección o intensificar la misma.
Con el uso prolongado de tratamientos con corticosteroides por vía oftálmica podrían producirse infecciones fúngicas persistentes de la córnea, las cuales deberian sospecharse en pacientes con ulceración corneal persistente. Si aparece una infección fúngica debería suprimirse el tratamiento.
El uso oftálmico de corticosteroides puede retrasar la cicatrización de heridas corneales.
También se sabe que los AINES oftálmicos enlentecen o retrasan la cicatrización. El uso concomitante de AINES y esteroides oftálmicos puede aumentar el potencial de problemas de cicatrización (ver sección 4.5).
Se sabe que en pacientes con enfermedades que causan adelgazamiento de la córnea o la esclerótica, el uso oftálmico de corticosteroides provoca perforación corneal.
Alteraciones visuales
Se pueden producir alteraciones visuales con el uso sistémico y tópico de corticosteroides. Si un paciente presenta síntomas como visión borrosa u otras alteraciones visuales, se debe consultar con un oftalmólogo para que evalúe las posibles causas, que pueden ser cataratas, glaucoma o enfermedades raras como coriorretinopatía serosa central (CRSC), que se ha notificado tras el uso de corticosteroides sistémicos y tópicos.
Lentes de contacto
No se recomienda el uso de lentes de contacto durante el tratamiento de una inflamación ocular.
Advertencias sobre excipientes
Este medicamento contiene 0,5 mg de cloruro de benzalconio en cada frasco de 5 ml, equivalente a 0,1 mg/ml.
El cloruro de benzalconio puede producir irritación ocular y alterar el color de las lentes de contacto blandas. En caso de que sea necesario utilizar lentes de contacto durante el tratamiento, debe aconsejarse a los pacientes que se retiren las lentes de contacto antes de la aplicación y que esperen 15 minutos antes de volver a colocarlas.
Se han notificado casos de queratopatía puntiforme y/o queratopatía ulcerativa tóxica producidos por el cloruro de benzalconio. Puesto que este medicamento contiene cloruro de benzalconio, se aconseja un seguimiento cuidadoso de aquellos pacientes que padezcan ojo seco y que utilicen el producto con frecuencia o durante periodos prolongados; o en aquellas condiciones en las que la córnea esté comprometida.
Se debe vigilar a los pacientes en caso de uso prolongado.

Document sections:
  Heading: Visual Acuity (VA)
  Content: VA measures visual resolution and remains the most important visual measure for children with CNS tumours. Assess best-corrected VA (BCVA) in each eye, at far and near distances if possible, and report the threshold optotype detail in logMAR, from 0.0 for normal vision to 2.0. A change of 0.2 LogMAR VA or more is clinically relevant. If quantitative measurement is infeasible, fixation observations can help establish whether vision is present; document Hand Motion (HM), counting fingers (CF), Light Perception (LP) or No Light Perception (NLP), as appropriate. Testing depends on age and cooperation: Teller Acuity preferential looking Cards (TAC) are commonly used for infants and preverbal children, whereas Lea symbols, Cardiff Acuity Test, Kays Picture Chart and later HOTV or Snellen charts suit older children.

Changing VA test methods can slightly overestimate or underestimate longitudinal results. Because vision develops rapidly over the first 2-3 years and reaches full potential only after 5 years of age, age-specific normal ranges should be used in young children.

  Name: Corneal edema
  Description: Excess fluid accumulates in one or more corneal layers. Causes include endothelial dysfunction, elevated intraocular pressure, inflammation, trauma, dystrophies, infection, hypoxia, surgery, and toxicity.
  Clinical presentation: Vision may be blurred or fluctuate, often worsening on waking and improving later in the day. Photophobia, redness, tearing, foreign-body sensation, and pain may occur. Onset is usually gradual, although pressure elevation, substantial inflammation, and hydrops can produce a more acute presentation. Peripheral disease may cause few symptoms, while central involvement generally affects vision; functional disability can exceed that suggested by standard visual acuity.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Idiopathic corneal edema
    - Name: Secondary corneal edema
    - Name: Corneal edema due to wearing contact lenses
      Distinguishing features: Contact lens use is the identified cause.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: History and functional-vision assessment
      Purpose: Establish onset, fluctuation, laterality, symptoms, effects on daily activities, and potential causes.
      When indicated: Initial evaluation.
      Interpretation: Morning blur that clears later may accompany endothelial dysfunction; visual acuity alone may understate glare-related disability.
    - Test: Visual acuity, pinhole testing, manifest refraction, and glare testing
      Purpose: Measure visual loss, best-corrected potential, and functional impairment.
      When indicated: Initial evaluation; assessment of visual potential is particularly important before surgery.
      Interpretation: Functional status and measured acuity need not agree.
    - Test: External examination and slit-lamp biomicroscopy
      Purpose: Examine the lids and ocular surface; distinguish epithelial from stromal edema; identify guttae, epithelial breakdown, inflammation, scarring, Descemet’s membrane abnormalities, deposits, and other potential causes.
      When indicated: Initial evaluation and subsequent assessment as clinically indicated.
      Interpretation: Sectoral edema with keratic precipitates or an anterior chamber reaction can point toward endotheliitis. Inferior edema can accompany retained material or a foreign body in the inferior angle.
    - Test: Intraocular pressure measurement
      Purpose: Identify pressure elevation or hypotony contributing to edema.
      When indicated: Evaluation and monitoring, particularly when pressure-related disease or corticosteroid treatment is relevant.
      Interpretation: Goldmann applanation tonometry may be unreliable in an abnormal cornea. Alternative methods include a pneumotonometer, handheld electronic applanation tonometer, dynamic contour tonometer, ocular response analyzer, rebound tonometer, and digital palpation; consistent use of the same valid method supports serial comparison.
    - Test: Fundus examination and B-scan ultrasonography
      Purpose: Assess posterior-segment conditions associated with hypotony and secondary edema when examination warrants it.
      When indicated: When posterior-segment assessment is needed.
      Interpretation: Chronic serous choroidal detachment or retinal detachment may contribute through hypotony.
    - Test: Gonioscopy
      Purpose: Look for retained lens fragments, foreign bodies, or iridocorneal adhesions.
      When indicated: When angle pathology or retained material is suspected.
      Interpretation: Findings can help establish the cause of localized edema.
    - Test: Potential acuity meter or illuminated near-card pinhole testing
      Purpose: Estimate visual potential despite anterior-segment pathology.
      When indicated: Particularly before a surgical treatment decision.
      Interpretation: Better performance than on conventional acuity testing supports the possibility of improvement after treatment; a poor result does not necessarily establish poor visual potential.
    - Test: RGP contact lens over-refraction
      Purpose: Determine whether surface irregularity substantially contributes to visual loss.
      When indicated: When edema or scarring disturbs the central or paracentral surface.
      Interpretation: Improvement with the lens, but not with spectacles, favors surface irregularity as a major contributor.
    - Test: Pachymetry
      Purpose: Measure corneal thickness and assess serial change.
      When indicated: When endothelial function or progression requires assessment.
      Interpretation: Serial thickness measurements can help assess endothelial function. Measurements from different device types are not directly interchangeable.
    - Test: Corneal topography and tomography
      Purpose: Assess irregular astigmatism, corneal thickness, posterior-surface findings, and the depth of associated opacification.
      When indicated: When evaluating visual impairment, prognosis, or surgical planning.
      Interpretation: Peripheral pathology may create visually important central irregularity.
    - Test: Specular microscopy
      Purpose: Assess endothelial cell density, shape, and uniformity.
      When indicated: When endothelial assessment can contribute to evaluation or serial monitoring.
      Interpretation: Cell imaging does not directly measure endothelial function or reserve; diffuse confluent guttae can prevent useful imaging.
    - Test: Confocal microscopy
      Purpose: Image corneal layers and investigate endothelial, stromal, or infectious causes.
      When indicated: Particularly helpful in unilateral edema or when specular imaging is limited by moderate edema.
      Interpretation: Characteristic appearances may help identify iridocorneal endothelial syndrome, epithelial or fibrous ingrowth, PPCD, fungal hyphae, or Acanthamoeba cysts.
    - Test: Anterior segment optical coherence tomography
      Purpose: Image corneal and retrocorneal structures, measure thickness, and assess surgical anatomy.
      When indicated: When deeper structural pathology is suspected or after endothelial keratoplasty.
      Interpretation: Can reveal a detached Descemet’s membrane, retrocorneal membrane, stromal cleft, or an area where donor tissue has not adhered.
    - Test: Ultrasound biomicroscopy
      Purpose: Examine anterior-segment structures despite opacity and locate small foreign bodies.
      When indicated: Especially useful in congenital or traumatic cases and for surgical planning.
      Interpretation: Can show displaced or ruptured Descemet’s membrane, adhesions, and retrocorneal membranes.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Visit intervals depend on clinical judgment, improvement or stability, and the intervention performed. A bandage contact lens used for an extended period requires regular review and periodic replacement; in most cases, the same lens should not remain for longer than one month.
    Recommended tests:
      - Serial pachymetry when monitoring endothelial function
      - Intraocular pressure assessment when pressure elevation or corticosteroid response is a concern
      - Reassessment of the ocular surface, symptoms, and contact lens fit when a bandage contact lens is used
    Long term effects:
      - Persistent endothelial damage may cause edema to recur years after an initially resolving injury.
    Survivorship notes: New or worsening pain, redness, photophobia, or vision changes warrant prompt medical attention.

Document sections:
  Heading: Stage 4: Partial Retinal Detachment
  Content: Stage 4A is partial detachment with an attached fovea; stage 4B includes foveal detachment. Findings suggesting detachment include diminished fine detail in choroidal vessels or granular retinal pigment epithelium, a ground-glass appearance compared with adjacent attached retina, or both. Macular displacement and straightening of arcade vessels suggest peripheral traction. OCT can be particularly useful for detecting subtle foveal involvement; photographs may not clearly reveal the detachment's extent. Stage 4 can be exudative or tractional, can occur in treated or untreated eyes, and can differ according to traction direction and associated exudation. Exudative stage 4 detachment occurs most often within days after laser treatment and is usually convex, sometimes localized, and self-limited. Tractional detachment accompanies progressive fibrovascular organization and vitreous haze and may coexist with lipid, subretinal hemorrhage, or both. Clinical examination may not readily distinguish retinoschisis from detachment. A-ROP can produce a posterior volcano-shaped tractional detachment, generally involving the fovea while peripheral retina stays attached. Despite resemblance to a funnel-shaped stage 5 detachment, it is stage 4B because detachment is not total. Figures 8 and 9 illustrate stage 4A and stage 4B appearances, including the value of OCT for identifying foveal detachment. Figure 8 includes an example of stage 4A detachment with 360 traction along the peripheral ridge.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_05
  Name: Retinal detachment
  Description: Separation involving the retina can cause acute visual loss. Prompt treatment may be needed to avoid permanent impairment. Diagnosis usually relies on clinical and ophthalmologic examination rather than initial cross-sectional imaging.
  Epidemiology: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is the most common form.
  Clinical presentation: Acute vision loss may occur. Vitreous hemorrhage can prevent visualization of the posterior eye during funduscopic examination.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
      Distinguishing features: A defect in the neurosensory retina allows vitreous fluid to collect between the sensory and pigmented retinal layers.
    - Name: Exudative (serous) retinal detachment
      Distinguishing features: Subretinal fluid accumulates without a break in the neurosensory epithelium. An underlying inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic, vascular or degenerative process may be responsible.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Dilated funduscopic examination
      Purpose: Establish the diagnosis of retinal detachment.
      When indicated: Used in the initial clinical assessment.
    - Test: Ocular US
      Purpose: Establish the diagnosis when funduscopic visualization of the posterior eye is obscured.
      When indicated: May be used, for example, in the presence of vitreous hemorrhage; avoid if globe rupture is known or suspected.
    - Test: MRI orbits without and with IV contrast
      Purpose: Characterize a suspected mass or another cause of exudative retinal detachment.
      When indicated: Usually Not Appropriate for the initial evaluation of suspected retinal structural abnormality; it may be used selectively after the initial diagnosis.
    - Test: Optical coherence tomography
      Purpose: Provide high-resolution cross-sectional retinal imaging.
      When indicated: Used by ophthalmologists to assess retinal pathology; the guideline does not assign it an appropriateness category for this variant.
  Follow up:
    Long term effects:
      - Permanent vision loss can result if an acute retinal detachment is not treated promptly.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_04
  Name: Diabetic retinopathy
  Description: A diabetes-related eye condition that can be prevented or delayed by controlling hyperglycemia, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. Early disease may be asymptomatic.
  Epidemiology: It is the most common microvascular complication of diabetes and a leading global cause of preventable vision impairment and blindness. If current trends persist, the estimated number of affected people rises 1.2-fold, from 146 million in 2014 to 180.6 million in 2030.
  Clinical presentation: Early stages can have no symptoms; vision-threatening disease can result in vision impairment or blindness.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy
      Distinguishing features: Stages targeted for detection through systematic retinal screening and timely treatment.
    - Name: advanced proliferative diabetic retinopathy
      Distinguishing features: An advanced form listed among the indications for vitreoretinal surgery.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Systematic retinal screening
      Purpose: Detect diabetic retinopathy early, including its vision-threatening stages.
      When indicated: For people with diabetes, annually or biennially depending on the setting.
      Interpretation: Refer for assessment and treatment when indicated.
    - Test: Ophthalmoscopy
      Purpose: Examine the retina during diabetic retinopathy screening.
      When indicated: When screening is carried out by trained eye care personnel.
    - Test: Retinal imaging
      Purpose: Screen for diabetic retinopathy using local interpretation or centralized grading through telemedicine.
      When indicated: For people with diabetes undergoing retinal screening.
    - Test: Slit lamp examination
      Purpose: Assess retinal status when screening images are of poor quality.
      When indicated: For people referred from the English National Screening Programme because their retinal images are of poor quality.
    - Test: Optical coherence tomography (OCT)
      Purpose: Diagnose and monitor treatment for retinal disorders.
      When indicated: Where available; its cost limits availability in many low- and middle-income countries.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Retinal screening is described as annual or biennial, depending on the setting; longer-term care is needed for this chronic eye condition.
    Recommended tests:

      - Vision impairment or blindness may develop without early detection and timely management.

  Heading: 1. Introduction
  Content: VKC is a persistent and progressive inflammatory eye disorder with potential to impair vision. It mainly occurs in children and adolescents (<20 years), and onset precedes 10 years of age in most cases. Although it commonly subsides at puberty, prospective and retrospective analyses indicate that up to 12% of patients with VKC are adults and that up to 82% of adult cases begin after puberty. Document sections:
  Heading: Microbial keratitis:
  Content: A damaged cornea, including one affected by exposure keratopathy, is particularly susceptible to rapidly developing bacterial invasion. Infection may remain superficial, but deeper infection can cause severe permanent injury and loss of vision. Most cases are bacterial and present with a red, possibly watery or sticky eye and a corneal ulcer: a fluorescein-staining epithelial defect over a white, grey or yellowish opacity. Less often, debilitated patients develop herpes simplex keratitis, which may show epithelial dendrites or ulcers staining yellow with fluorescein, or non-staining grey corneal areas. Any of these findings requires urgent ophthalmic help.

question: Blow out fracture of orbit involved ?

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Vision Loss__JC__000110
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Vision Loss
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 1: Adult. Acute posttraumatic visual defect. Suspect orbital injury. Initial imaging.
  Content: Orbital fractures most often follow assault or a direct blow, motor-vehicle collisions, falls, or sports injuries. They can occur alone or alongside zygomaticomaxillary complex, Le Fort II and III, or nasoethmoidal complex fractures. Diplopia can accompany depressed orbital-floor fractures, especially anterior- or middle-third injuries and small- to medium-sized defects with soft-tissue herniation. Fractures >2 cm are more likely to produce enophthalmos. Blowout injury can involve the lamina papyracea, but extraocular-muscle herniation and serious immediate complications are less common than with orbital-floor blowout fractures. Most orbital fractures can undergo delayed repair after swelling improves; CT can reveal injuries needing more urgent action, including trapdoor fractures and orbital compartment syndrome. Lateral- and superior-wall fractures carry increased traumatic optic neuropathy risk because blunt force can reach the optic canal and shear the nerve. With associated brain injury or obtundation, an afferent pupillary defect may be its sole clinical sign. Urgent diagnosis permits timely intervention when needed. Although optic-canal fractures increase nerve-injury risk, emergency surgery for traumatic optic neuropathy is generally reserved for a bone fragment impinging on the nerve, hematoma in the canal, or enlarging retrobulbar hematoma with proptosis. Severe proptosis with posterior globe tenting requires emergency orbital decompression to preserve vision. An orbital-apex fracture involving the superior orbital fissure can affect multiple traversing cranial nerves. Retrobulbar hematoma, emphysema, or a blow-in fracture can increase orbital mass effect and cause compartment syndrome and vision loss. Imaging evidence of retrobulbar bleeding does not sensitively predict subsequent compartment syndrome: diagnose it from clinical evidence of optic nerve compression. Extraocular-muscle entrapment after an orbital-floor fracture is likewise a clinical diagnosis; muscle herniation and altered contour have low positive predictive values for entrapment. Imaging aims to identify orbital injuries and complications early enough to guide timely care and prevent permanent visual loss.

Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 1: Adult. Acute posttraumatic visual defect. Suspect orbital injury. Initial imaging.
  Content: Orbital fractures most often follow assault or a direct blow, motor-vehicle collisions, falls, or sports injuries. They can occur alone or alongside zygomaticomaxillary complex, Le Fort II and III, or nasoethmoidal complex fractures. Diplopia can accompany depressed orbital-floor fractures, especially anterior- or middle-third injuries and small- to medium-sized defects with soft-tissue herniation. Fractures >2 cm are more likely to produce enophthalmos. Blowout injury can involve the lamina papyracea, but extraocular-muscle herniation and serious immediate complications are less common than with orbital-floor blowout fractures. Most orbital fractures can undergo delayed repair after swelling improves; CT can reveal injuries needing more urgent action, including trapdoor fractures and orbital compartment syndrome. Lateral- and superior-wall fractures carry increased traumatic optic neuropathy risk because blunt force can reach the optic canal and shear the nerve. With associated brain injury or obtundation, an afferent pupillary defect may be its sole clinical sign. Urgent diagnosis permits timely intervention when needed. Although optic-canal fractures increase nerve-injury risk, emergency surgery for traumatic optic neuropathy is generally reserved for a bone fragment impinging on the nerve, hematoma in the canal, or enlarging retrobulbar hematoma with proptosis. Severe proptosis with posterior globe tenting requires emergency orbital decompression to preserve vision. An orbital-apex fracture involving the superior orbital fissure can affect multiple traversing cranial nerves. Retrobulbar hematoma, emphysema, or a blow-in fracture can increase orbital mass effect and cause compartment syndrome and vision loss. Imaging evidence of retrobulbar bleeding does not sensitively predict subsequent compartment syndrome: diagnose it from clinical evidence of optic nerve compression. Extraocular-muscle entrapment after an orbital-floor fracture is likewise a clinical diagnosis; muscle herniation and altered contour have low positive predictive values for entrapment. Imaging aims to identify orbital injuries and complications early enough to guide timely care and prevent permanent visual loss.

  Heading: Variant 6: Adult. Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma. Sellar or parasellar mass suspected. Initial imaging.
  Content: Bitemporal hemianopia and junctional scotoma can arise from external compression or intrinsic disease of the optic chiasm and the optic nerve–chiasm junction, respectively. A pituitary macroadenoma may extend above the sella and compress the chiasm, adjacent nerves, or tracts. Meningiomas account for a small fraction of sellar-region masses but can involve sellar, suprasellar, or parasellar structures and compress the nerves or chiasm. Sellar or suprasellar meningiomas most often enhance homogeneously; a dural tail is common but not universal. Imaging cannot always distinguish them from a pituitary adenoma when their origin relative to the gland is uncertain. Craniopharyngiomas commonly compress the chiasm. The adamantinomatous type, more frequent in children, is often mixed cystic and solid, calcified, and heterogeneously enhancing; the adult papillary type is generally solid and enhancing and rarely calcifies. Hypophysitis, large Rathke cleft cysts, and other suprasellar masses may compress the chiasm or posterior optic nerves. Neoplastic causes usually produce gradual symptoms, whereas pituitary apoplexy, most often hemorrhagic infarction of an existing adenoma, can rapidly enlarge a lesion and cause headache and visual change. Large internal carotid artery or Circle of Willis aneurysms may also compress the visual pathway. Optic pathway glioma, inflammatory or demyelinating disease, granulomatous disease, and lymphoma may affect the chiasm, optic nerves, or pituitary infundibulum. Imaging aims to identify a sellar or suprasellar mass causing the field defect, demonstrate chiasmal compression, and guide care.

  Content: Infectious corneal ulcers, also termed microbial keratitis, are a leading cause of visual loss, particularly in developing countries. Bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites can cause them. Microbial proliferation and inflammation destroy corneal tissue, reduce transparency, and impair vision. Fungi rarely invade an intact cornea but can become pathogenic with immunosuppression, trauma—especially trauma involving vegetable matter—topical steroid exposure, or ocular surface disease. Fungal keratitis, also called mycotic keratitis (MK), is an important cause of microbial keratitis and possible corneal blindness, particularly in tropical and subtropical countries. More than a million cases are estimated to be diagnosed annually; perforation risk is about 10%, and more than half of affected patients lose vision and live with monocular blindness. Laboratory identification is difficult, and antifungal availability and efficacy pose treatment problems. Intensive, prolonged topical therapy may be inadequate, warranting consideration of systemic, intrastromal, or intracameral delivery. New treatments are also needed to produce faster responses and address drug resistance.

Document sections:
  Heading: People with diabetes
  Content: The number of people with diabetes has increased across countries during the past 30 years alongside lifestyle changes. Diabetic retinopathy is the most common diabetic microvascular complication and a leading preventable cause of vision impairment and blindness. If existing trends persist, a cited estimate projects a 1.2-fold rise in affected people, from 146 million in 2014 to 180.6 million in 2030. Most associated vision impairment can be avoided through risk-factor control, early identification and timely treatment. Many national and international professional societies have long endorsed systematic retinal screening of people with diabetes to detect vision-threatening disease, annually or biennially according to setting, followed by treatment when needed. Approaches include ophthalmoscopy by trained eye-care staff and retinal imaging interpreted locally or centrally through telemedicine. Lower-cost retinal cameras and artificial-intelligence approaches may improve access and quality closer to home.

  Content: A damaged cornea, including one affected by exposure keratopathy, is particularly susceptible to rapidly developing bacterial invasion. Infection may remain superficial, but deeper infection can cause severe permanent injury and loss of vision. Most cases are bacterial and present with a red, possibly watery or sticky eye and a corneal ulcer: a fluorescein-staining epithelial defect over a white, grey or yellowish opacity. question: Blow out fracture affects which orbital wall ?

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Vision Loss__JC__000110
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Vision Loss
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 1: Adult. Acute posttraumatic visual defect. Suspect orbital injury. Initial imaging.
  Content: Orbital fractures most often follow assault or a direct blow, motor-vehicle collisions, falls, or sports injuries. They can occur alone or alongside zygomaticomaxillary complex, Le Fort II and III, or nasoethmoidal complex fractures. Diplopia can accompany depressed orbital-floor fractures, especially anterior- or middle-third injuries and small- to medium-sized defects with soft-tissue herniation. Fractures >2 cm are more likely to produce enophthalmos. Blowout injury can involve the lamina papyracea, but extraocular-muscle herniation and serious immediate complications are less common than with orbital-floor blowout fractures. Most orbital fractures can undergo delayed repair after swelling improves; CT can reveal injuries needing more urgent action, including trapdoor fractures and orbital compartment syndrome. Lateral- and superior-wall fractures carry increased traumatic optic neuropathy risk because blunt force can reach the optic canal and shear the nerve. With associated brain injury or obtundation, an afferent pupillary defect may be its sole clinical sign. Urgent diagnosis permits timely intervention when needed. Although optic-canal fractures increase nerve-injury risk, emergency surgery for traumatic optic neuropathy is generally reserved for a bone fragment impinging on the nerve, hematoma in the canal, or enlarging retrobulbar hematoma with proptosis. Severe proptosis with posterior globe tenting requires emergency orbital decompression to preserve vision. An orbital-apex fracture involving the superior orbital fissure can affect multiple traversing cranial nerves. Retrobulbar hematoma, emphysema, or a blow-in fracture can increase orbital mass effect and cause compartment syndrome and vision loss. Imaging evidence of retrobulbar bleeding does not sensitively predict subsequent compartment syndrome: diagnose it from clinical evidence of optic nerve compression. Extraocular-muscle entrapment after an orbital-floor fracture is likewise a clinical diagnosis; muscle herniation and altered contour have low positive predictive values for entrapment. Imaging aims to identify orbital injuries and complications early enough to guide timely care and prevent permanent visual loss.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_04
  Name: Diabetic retinopathy
  Description: A diabetes-related eye condition that can be prevented or delayed by controlling hyperglycemia, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. Early disease may be asymptomatic.
  Epidemiology: It is the most common microvascular complication of diabetes and a leading global cause of preventable vision impairment and blindness. If current trends persist, the estimated number of affected people rises 1.2-fold, from 146 million in 2014 to 180.6 million in 2030.
  Clinical presentation: Early stages can have no symptoms; vision-threatening disease can result in vision impairment or blindness.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy
      Distinguishing features: Stages targeted for detection through systematic retinal screening and timely treatment.
    - Name: advanced proliferative diabetic retinopathy
      Distinguishing features: An advanced form listed among the indications for vitreoretinal surgery.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Systematic retinal screening
      Purpose: Detect diabetic retinopathy early, including its vision-threatening stages.
      When indicated: For people with diabetes, annually or biennially depending on the setting.
      Interpretation: Refer for assessment and treatment when indicated.
    - Test: Ophthalmoscopy
      Purpose: Examine the retina during diabetic retinopathy screening.
      When indicated: When screening is carried out by trained eye care personnel.
    - Test: Retinal imaging
      Purpose: Screen for diabetic retinopathy using local interpretation or centralized grading through telemedicine.
      When indicated: For people with diabetes undergoing retinal screening.
    - Test: Slit lamp examination
      Purpose: Assess retinal status when screening images are of poor quality.
      When indicated: For people referred from the English National Screening Programme because their retinal images are of poor quality.
    - Test: Optical coherence tomography (OCT)
      Purpose: Diagnose and monitor treatment for retinal disorders.
      When indicated: Where available; its cost limits availability in many low- and middle-income countries.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Retinal screening is described as annual or biennial, depending on the setting; longer-term care is needed for this chronic eye condition.
    Recommended tests:
      - Retinal examination through ophthalmoscopy or retinal imaging
    Long term effects:
      - Vision impairment or blindness may develop without early detection and timely management.

  Heading: Natural History Staging of Angle-closure Disease5
  Content: Primary angle closure suspect denotes ITC with normal IOP and no glaucomatous optic neuropathy. In primary angle closure, IOP is elevated without glaucomatous optic neuropathy; lens opacity or retinal vascular pathology may coexist. Acute angle closure (AAC) crisis warrants rapid care distinct from routine management. Its post-crisis physical signs do not invariably determine long-term vision, although often-reversible current impairment may arise from lens opacity or an unresponsive dilated pupil following iris ischemia. Glaucomatous optic neuropathy at an acute presentation probably predates, rather than results from, a pressure elevation lasting hours or days. Primary angle closure glaucoma is the stage with glaucomatous optic neuropathy in an occluded-angle eye, defined by pre-laminar optic nerve head structural changes together with reproducible visual field loss.

  Description: Separation involving the retina can cause acute visual loss. Prompt treatment may be needed to avoid permanent impairment. Diagnosis usually relies on clinical and ophthalmologic examination rather than initial cross-sectional imaging.

  Subtypes:

      Purpose: Provide high-resolution cross-sectional retinal imaging.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Visual Pathways
  Content: Visual dysfunction is often the main or only manifestation of a tumour infiltrating visual pathways. Optic pathway gliomas (OPG) are mostly histologically low-grade glioma (LGG), but may remain indolent or progress repeatedly and cause severe visual sequelae. A substantial proportion of affected children experience impairment, and 5 - 10% meet legal-blindness criteria. Uni- or bilateral VA and VF defects vary with lesion position; homonymous and bitemporal hemianopia are frequent. Children below 1 year of age and those with post-chiasmatic OPG appear more likely to experience VA deterioration. Approximately 15% of children with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) have OPG. Its course is indolent in up to 70 - 85%, while about 15% - 30% develop more aggressive behaviour and visual deficits. Isolated optic nerve gliomas (IONG), whether or not associated with NF1, may cause proptosis and optic pallor or atrophy as well as acuity or field loss. Optic nerve sheaths meningioma, commonly associated with Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), can present similarly. Large hypothalamic-chiasmatic OPG can obstruct CSF flow, raise intracranial pressure and produce papilledema.

  Heading: Variant 3: Adult. Chronic or progressive unilateral vision loss. Intraorbital mass-like lesion suspected or vascular lesion suspected. Initial imaging.
  Content: Many tumors, tumor-like conditions, systemic diseases, metastases, and high- or low-flow vascular malformations can involve the orbit. Distinguishing vascular from other lesions guides subsequent workup and care. Because the orbital space is restricted, either a soft-tissue or vascular mass may cause proptosis. Orbital-apex masses or inflammation characteristically produce vision loss with ophthalmoplegia. Orbital masses can be classified by location in the globe, optic nerve sheath complex, intraconal or extraconal space, bone, or multiple compartments. Benign lesions predominate, but malignant orbital tumors become more prevalent in adults older than 60 years of age. Among cysts, dermoid cysts are most common; excluding cysts, cavernous venous malformation is the commonest benign adult orbital mass, while non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the commonest malignant one. Imaging seeks to detect and characterize the causative orbital mass or vascular lesion, direct care, and sometimes establish a specific diagnosis.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: Mian et al. 2024 Corneal Edema and Opacification Preferred Practice Pattern®
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: History
  Content: Ask about blurred or fluctuating vision, including morning worsening and later improvement; photophobia, redness, tearing, foreign-body sensation, pain, recent ocular procedures and complications, age and speed of onset, persistence, laterality, and modifying conditions. Edema usually develops over weeks, months, or longer, but elevated IOP, substantial inflammation, hydrops, and trauma can produce more abrupt symptoms. Most noninfectious opacities develop gradually, apart from acute medication-related band keratopathy; infectious opacities often appear acutely. Edema caused by inflammation or pressure can resolve when its cause resolves. Edema after neonatal forceps injury may resolve after Descemet’s membrane heals but recur years later if endothelial injury was substantial. Endothelial dysfunction may produce transient blur after waking, humidity, or showering that improves later through evaporation. Most noninflammatory opacities persist; inflammatory infiltrates often resolve with their cause, and some metabolic deposits may respond to treatment. Laterality may distinguish usually unilateral herpes simplex virus keratitis from typically bilateral dystrophies. Low humidity and modest airflow may improve vision in endothelial dysfunction. Visual acuity can understate disability: a patient with mild Fuchs dystrophy edema or granular corneal dystrophy opacity may measure 20/40 or better yet be unable to drive because of glare; lighting, reflections, screens, and higher order aberrations can impair function. Contact lenses, particularly RGP lenses, may improve vision by regularizing the refracting surface. Review ocular disease, surgery, infection, inflammation, trauma, glaucoma, and keratoconus; systemic inflammatory, developmental, metabolic, hereditary, and immune-mediated disease; malabsorption-associated vitamin A deficiency; topical and systemic exposures; contact lens practices; family history; sun exposure, travel, animal exposure, diet, and chemical exposure. Short exposure to Amantadine may cause reversible endothelial dysfunction, whereas long exposure may cause permanent dysfunction. Accidental corneal exposure to chlorhexidine during facial surgical preparation may predispose to endothelial failure. Other exposures noted include carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, Bupropion, Amiodarone, calcium supplements, periocular radiation, chemotherapeutic agents, and Rho kinase inhibitor-related verticillate changes.

  Content: Neoplastic, inflammatory, ischemic, demyelinating, and traumatic processes can affect the optic nerve or its sheath and produce acute, subacute, or chronic visual loss. Neoplasms tend to develop more slowly than other optic neuropathies. Optic nerve gliomas are the most common primary optic nerve neoplasm; they can be incidental, including in younger patients with neurofibromatosis type 1, or present with visual symptoms or proptosis, and are more likely to be malignant when presenting in adults. Orbital meningiomas can arise from the optic nerve sheath or extend from an intracranial mass; symptomatic sheath lesions classically cause gradual, painless visual decline. Inflammatory and demyelinating ON can resemble one another clinically and radiologically; enhancement reflects edema, inflammation, or demyelination. Possible causes of demyelinating ON include MS, NMO, and MOGAD. ON can also reflect chronic relapsing-remitting inflammatory disease, steroid-dependent recurrence, systemic inflammation, or infection. Enhancement patterns overlap but may help: bilateral simultaneous and longer optic nerve involvement occur more often with MOGAD or NMO than MS, which characteristically affects a shorter unilateral segment. Sheath or perioptic enhancement is more distinctive of MOGAD. Anterior involvement is more typical of MS or MOGAD; NMO tends toward posterior nerves, chiasm, or tracts. Brain and spine MRI may identify associated abnormalities; asymptomatic optic nerve lesions may help distinguish relapsing-remitting MS or clinically isolated syndrome from NMO or MOGAD. Optic perineuritis can arise from idiopathic orbital inflammation, autoimmunity, infection, or other inflammation and may mimic acute demyelinating ON, including visual loss and pain worsened by eye movement. Patients with perineuritis tend to be older and more likely to retain central vision. Ischemic optic neuropathy is anterior, AION, when involving the nerve head, or posterior, PION, when involving the retrobulbar nerve. AION classically causes disc edema and altitudinal field loss. Either form may be nonarteritic, in patients with vascular risk factors such as hypertension or diabetes, or arteritic, most commonly from giant cell arteritis. Imaging aims to identify optic nerve disease, narrow overlapping diagnoses, and inform management.

  Description: Separation involving the retina can cause acute visual loss. Prompt treatment may be needed to avoid permanent impairment. Diagnosis usually relies on clinical and ophthalmologic examination rather than initial cross-sectional imaging.

  Clinical presentation: Acute vision loss may occur. Vitreous hemorrhage can prevent visualization of the posterior eye during funduscopic examination.

      Distinguishing features: A defect in the neurosensory retina allows vitreous fluid to collect between the sensory and pigmented retinal layers.

Document sections:
  Heading: OCULAR SURFACE DYE STAINING
  Content: Fluorescein, rose bengal, and lissamine green help assess ocular-surface abnormalities. Fluorescein penetrates epithelium where intercellular junctions are sufficiently disrupted; use a saline-moistened strip or 1% to 2% sodium fluorescein and examine with slit lamp and cobalt blue illumination. Staining may become clearer after about 2 minutes and with a yellow filter. Mild staining can occur in normal eyes, particularly in the morning; dry eye often produces exposure-zone punctate or blotchy staining, more readily seen on cornea than conjunctiva. Rose bengal may be applied with a moistened strip or 1% solution; advise patients that it can irritate, so topical anesthetic is typically used first. Leave saline against the strip for at least a minute before application. Rose bengal stains conjunctiva more intensely than cornea, highlighting cells lacking mucus coating and tear debris; a red-free filter can aid viewing. Lissamine green has a staining pattern resembling rose bengal with less irritation, but waiting 1 to 2 minutes reduces visibility; unlike fluorescein, it is not recommended to assess corneal epithelial disease. Diffuse corneal and conjunctival staining commonly accompanies viral keratoconjunctivitis or medicamentosa. Inferior corneal and bulbar conjunctival staining is typical of staphylococcal blepharitis, meibomian gland disease, lagophthalmos, or exposure; superior bulbar conjunctival staining is typical of superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis. Interpalpebral corneal and bulbar conjunctival staining commonly accompanies aqueous deficiency.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 1. Introduction
  Content: Retinoblastoma is the most frequent childhood ocular malignancy and affects approximately 1 in 15,000–20,000 live births. Without timely treatment, it can be fatal. In high-income countries, diagnosis generally precedes invasion of the optic nerve, choroid, sclera, or orbit, and disease-free survival approaches 100%. In low-and-middle-income countries, particularly in Africa, invasive presentation is more common, increasing local and distant metastatic risk and substantially lowering survival. Treatment aims to preserve life, prevent metastasis, retain the eye, and maximize vision, although protocols differ between centers. Before the 1990 s, enucleation and external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) predominated but could cause vision loss and serious adverse effects. Subsequent approaches improved disease-free survival, globe salvage, and, in selected cases, vision preservation. Plaque radiotherapy, cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, and transpupillary thermotherapy contributed to this change, while chemotherapy delivered by different routes had a particularly important role. The authors searched PubMed for English-language articles dating back to January 1, 1960, targeting publications from January 1, 1990, to January 31, 2024. Search terms covered retinoblastoma, chemotherapy, intravenous chemotherapy, chemoreduction, intra-arterial chemotherapy, ophthalmic artery chemosurgery, intravitreal chemotherapy, intracameral chemotherapy, and periocular chemotherapy. Their aim was to summarize current knowledge and emerging chemotherapy trends in retinoblastoma.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: Lee et al. 2022 5 Fluorouracil in primary, impending recurrent and recurrent pterygium Systematic review of the eff
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 1. Introduction
  Content: Pterygium is a conspicuous ultraviolet-associated ocular disorder involving centripetal expansion of altered limbal epithelial cells. Squamous metaplasia with goblet-cell hyperplasia develops alongside proliferating stromal fibroblasts, new vessels, inflammation and extracellular-matrix remodeling. Reactivation of this wound-healing process by surgery may explain recurrence better than the older degenerative account involving Bowman’s layer degradation and elastosis. Epidemiological evidence and associations with cataract, climatic droplet keratopathy, photo-aged skin, squamous cell and basal cell carcinoma, melanoma and inherited DNA-repair disease support a role for chronic ultraviolet exposure. Prior studies also implicate peripheral-light focusing, fixation, ocular dominance and eye closure in sunlight, corneal curvature, anterior-chamber depth and handedness in pterygium location or laterality. Management seeks to restore ocular-surface anatomy, function and appearance while relieving symptoms; the authors have advocated excision with a limbal-conjunctival autograft as a reconstructive standard. Recurrence is most likely during the first 12 months after surgery and involves fibrovascular invasion and inflammation. Conjunctival recurrence and corneal recurrence after limbal breach have been described, but no consensus definition exists. Once recurrence is apparent, medical treatment is initially used to lessen or stop progression. Options mentioned include corticosteroids, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, cyclosporine, anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) and antimetabolites. 5-Fluourouracil (5-FU) has been applied topically or by injection as a surgical adjunct; intralesional subconjunctival injections have also attracted interest for primary, impending recurrent and recurrent disease. Its cytotoxicity raises concern about immediate and delayed harms. The authors knew of no prior review devoted exclusively to its application, effectiveness and safety in pterygium. They therefore set out to synthesize clinical recurrence outcomes, complications and possible present and future roles.

  Content: Optic-pathway gliomas can cause anything from no visual symptoms to severe loss. Condition or topic: Global management practices for open globe injuries (OGI)

Clinical background: Ocular trauma is a leading cause of blindness in one eye in the United States of America (USA). Worldwide, nearly 55 million eye injuries occur per year, with reduced visual acuity in 19 million people and blindness in 1.6 million people. The estimated global incidence of OGI is 3.5 per 100,000 people, although limited data from low- and middle-income countries suggest that its true prevalence may be underestimated. Management differs across regions and, more often, institutions. The Birmingham Eye Trauma Terminology System (BETTS), developed in 1996, standardizes injury classification but does not address management. The American Academy of Ophthalmology Preferred Practice Patterns (PPP) do not cover OGI, and disagreements about treatment and standards of care persist. Variation in practice is not necessarily harmful, but unevaluated differences could affect access to care, patient outcomes and resource use.

Objectives:
  - Describe current institutional approaches to managing OGI worldwide.
  - Identify areas of variation in OGI management and seek broadly accepted principles for its care.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_09
  Name: Diabetic macular edema
  Synonyms:
    - DME
  Description: Macular fluid accumulation caused by leakage from retinal vessels. It can accompany any severity level of DR.
  Epidemiology: A global review estimated clinically significant macular edema prevalence at 4.1%, corresponding to 18.83 million adults in 2020; it projected 28.61 million affected adults by 2045. In ETDRS, an estimated 40% of eyes with DME had visual acuity of 20/20 or better.
  Clinical presentation: Retinal thickening and sometimes hard exudates may impair central visual acuity, although good visual acuity can persist despite center-involved edema.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: CI-DME
      Distinguishing features: Edema involves the center of the macula.
    - Name: NCI-DME
      Distinguishing features: Edema does not involve the center of the macula.
    - Name: CSME
      Distinguishing features: The ETDRS definition uses specified proximity and extent criteria for retinal thickening or associated hard exudates.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Dilated stereoscopic macular examination
      Purpose: Assess retinal thickening, hard exudates and center involvement.
      When indicated: When DME is suspected and during follow-up.
      Interpretation: Macular edema should be categorized as center-involved or non-center-involved.
    - Test: OCT
      Purpose: Detect and quantify edema, measure central macular thickness and monitor anatomical response.
      When indicated: For evaluation and follow-up of DME.
      Interpretation: The guide describes OCT as the best method for detecting and quantifying CI-DME; retinal thickness alone does not always correlate with visual acuity.
    - Test: FA
      Purpose: Differentiate DME from another macular disorder, assess otherwise unexplained visual loss or identify leaking microaneurysms and capillary dropout for selected treatment planning.
      When indicated: When the diagnosis or examination is uncertain or focal laser surgery is being planned; not routinely for every patient with diabetes.
    - Test: OCTA
      Purpose: Evaluate macular nonperfusion and foveal avascular zone enlargement.
      When indicated: When vascular or ischemic assessment would be useful.
      Interpretation: It depicts nonperfusion but not vascular leakage.
    - Test: Visual acuity
      Purpose: Assess functional impairment and response alongside retinal imaging.
      When indicated: At initial and follow-up examinations.
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: OCT central subfield thickness (CST)
      Expected result: An increase can reflect central retinal thickening.
      Clinical significance: Changes are used with visual acuity to assess response; a DRCR.net study proposed a CI-DME clinical threshold two standard deviations above the normative study population of diabetics without macular edema.
  Staging:
    System: ETDRS definition of CSME; center-involved and non-center-involved DME classification
    Definitions:
      - Stage: CI-DME
        Description: Macular edema affects the center of the macula.
      - Stage: NCI-DME
        Description: Macular edema does not affect the center of the macula.
      - Stage: CSME
        Description: Retinal thickening lies at or within 500 µm of the macular center; or hard exudates lie at or within 500 µm of the center with adjacent thickening; or a thickened zone measures at least 1 disc area and extends to within 1 disc diameter of the center.
    Additional rules: Residual hard exudates after successfully treated thickening do not, by themselves, satisfy the hard-exudate criterion.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Frequency depends on center involvement, visual acuity and concurrent DR severity. OCT thickness and visual acuity are assessed together during treatment follow-up.
    Recommended tests:
      - Visual acuity
      - Dilated macular examination
      - OCT
    Long term effects:
      - Central vision loss
      - Persistent or recurrent edema

Document sections:
  Heading: Stage 4: Partial Retinal Detachment
  Content: Stage 4A is partial detachment with an attached fovea; stage 4B includes foveal detachment. Findings suggesting detachment include diminished fine detail in choroidal vessels or granular retinal pigment epithelium, a ground-glass appearance compared with adjacent attached retina, or both. Macular displacement and straightening of arcade vessels suggest peripheral traction. OCT can be particularly useful for detecting subtle foveal involvement; photographs may not clearly reveal the detachment's extent. Stage 4 can be exudative or tractional, can occur in treated or untreated eyes, and can differ according to traction direction and associated exudation. Exudative stage 4 detachment occurs most often within days after laser treatment and is usually convex, sometimes localized, and self-limited. Tractional detachment accompanies progressive fibrovascular organization and vitreous haze and may coexist with lipid, subretinal hemorrhage, or both. Clinical examination may not readily distinguish retinoschisis from detachment. A-ROP can produce a posterior volcano-shaped tractional detachment, generally involving the fovea while peripheral retina stays attached. Despite resemblance to a funnel-shaped stage 5 detachment, it is stage 4B because detachment is not total. Warnings and precautions: Administrar únicamente por vía oftálmica.
Este medicamento puede incrementar la presión intraocular, especialmente en pacientes con antecedentes familiares de glaucoma, por lo que únicamente debe emplearse bajo control facultativo.
El uso prolongado de corticosteroides oftálmicos puede ocasionar hipertensión ocular y/o glaucoma, con deterioro del nervio óptico, disminuyendo la agudeza visual y causando defectos en el campo visual. También puede producir catarata subcapsular posterior. Debe controlarse la presión intraocular de forma rutinaria y frecuente. Esto es especialmente importante en pacientes pediátricos ya que el riesgo de hipertensión ocular inducido por corticosteroides, puede ser mayor en niños y puede ocurrir antes que en adultos. El riesgo de presión intraocular elevada y/o formación de cataratas inducido por corticosteroides es mayor en pacientes propensos (p.ej. diabetes).
Se puede producir síndrome de Cushing y/o supresión adrenal asociado a la absorción sistémica de dexametasona administrada por vía oftálmica, después de un tratamiento intensivo o continuado a largo plazo en pacientes predispuestos, incluidos niños y pacientes tratados con inhibidores del CYP3A4 (incluyendo ritonavir y cobicistat). En estos casos, el tratamiento se debe interrumpir de forma progresiva.
Los corticosteroides pueden aumentar la sensibilidad a infecciones: reducen la resistencia a infecciones y dificultan la localización de las mismas pudiendo enmascarar los signos clínicos.
El uso prolongado de tratamientos con corticosteroides por vía oftálmica en afecciónes agudas purulentas del ojo podría enmascarar la infección o intensificar la misma.
Con el uso prolongado de tratamientos con corticosteroides por vía oftálmica podrían producirse infecciones fúngicas persistentes de la córnea, las cuales deberian sospecharse en pacientes con ulceración corneal persistente. Si aparece una infección fúngica debería suprimirse el tratamiento.
El uso oftálmico de corticosteroides puede retrasar la cicatrización de heridas corneales.
También se sabe que los AINES oftálmicos enlentecen o retrasan la cicatrización. El uso concomitante de AINES y esteroides oftálmicos puede aumentar el potencial de problemas de cicatrización (ver sección 4.5).
Se sabe que en pacientes con enfermedades que causan adelgazamiento de la córnea o la esclerótica, el uso oftálmico de corticosteroides provoca perforación corneal.
Alteraciones visuales
Se pueden producir alteraciones visuales con el uso sistémico y tópico de corticosteroides. Si un paciente presenta síntomas como visión borrosa u otras alteraciones visuales, se debe consultar con un oftalmólogo para que evalúe las posibles causas, que pueden ser cataratas, glaucoma o enfermedades raras como coriorretinopatía serosa central (CRSC), que se ha notificado tras el uso de corticosteroides sistémicos y tópicos.
Lentes de contacto
No se recomienda el uso de lentes de contacto durante el tratamiento de una inflamación ocular.
Advertencias sobre excipientes
Este medicamento contiene 0,5 mg de cloruro de benzalconio en cada frasco de 5 ml, equivalente a 0,1 mg/ml.
El cloruro de benzalconio puede producir irritación ocular y alterar el color de las lentes de contacto blandas. En caso de que sea necesario utilizar lentes de contacto durante el tratamiento, debe aconsejarse a los pacientes que se retiren las lentes de contacto antes de la aplicación y que esperen 15 minutos antes de volver a colocarlas.
Se han notificado casos de queratopatía puntiforme y/o queratopatía ulcerativa tóxica producidos por el cloruro de benzalconio. Puesto que este medicamento contiene cloruro de benzalconio, se aconseja un seguimiento cuidadoso de aquellos pacientes que padezcan ojo seco y que utilicen el producto con frecuencia o durante periodos prolongados; o en aquellas condiciones en las que la córnea esté comprometida.
Se debe vigilar a los pacientes en caso de uso prolongado.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_04
  Name: Diabetic retinopathy
  Description: A diabetes-related eye condition that can be prevented or delayed by controlling hyperglycemia, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. Early disease may be asymptomatic.
  Epidemiology: It is the most common microvascular complication of diabetes and a leading global cause of preventable vision impairment and blindness. If current trends persist, the estimated number of affected people rises 1.2-fold, from 146 million in 2014 to 180.6 million in 2030.
  Clinical presentation: Early stages can have no symptoms; vision-threatening disease can result in vision impairment or blindness.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy
      Distinguishing features: Stages targeted for detection through systematic retinal screening and timely treatment.
    - Name: advanced proliferative diabetic retinopathy
      Distinguishing features: An advanced form listed among the indications for vitreoretinal surgery.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Systematic retinal screening
      Purpose: Detect diabetic retinopathy early, including its vision-threatening stages.
      When indicated: For people with diabetes, annually or biennially depending on the setting.
      Interpretation: Refer for assessment and treatment when indicated.
    - Test: Ophthalmoscopy
      Purpose: Examine the retina during diabetic retinopathy screening.
      When indicated: When screening is carried out by trained eye care personnel.
    - Test: Retinal imaging
      Purpose: Screen for diabetic retinopathy using local interpretation or centralized grading through telemedicine.
      When indicated: For people with diabetes undergoing retinal screening.
    - Test: Slit lamp examination
      Purpose: Assess retinal status when screening images are of poor quality.
      When indicated: For people referred from the English National Screening Programme because their retinal images are of poor quality.
    - Test: Optical coherence tomography (OCT)
      Purpose: Diagnose and monitor treatment for retinal disorders.
      When indicated: Where available; its cost limits availability in many low- and middle-income countries.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Retinal screening is described as annual or biennial, depending on the setting; longer-term care is needed for this chronic eye condition.
    Recommended tests:
      - Retinal examination through ophthalmoscopy or retinal imaging
    Long term effects:
      - Vision impairment or blindness may develop without early detection and timely management.

  Content: Bacterial colonisation of the eye becomes more common over time in ICU. Among ventilated medical patients, as many as 77% carry at least one abnormal bacterial species after 7-42 days; 40% of patients receiving prolonged ventilation and sedation carry multiple bacterial species. The organisms most often isolated are Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter spp. and Staphylococcus epidermidis. Respiratory secretions are thought to be the main source of ocular surface infection; aerosols during tracheal suction and direct contact with suction catheters are implicated. Assess best-corrected VA (BCVA) in each eye, at far and near distances if possible, and report the threshold optotype detail in logMAR, from 0.0 for normal vision to 2.0. Document sections:
  Heading: 1. Introduction
  Content: Retinoblastoma is the most frequent childhood ocular malignancy and affects approximately 1 in 15,000–20,000 live births. Without timely treatment, it can be fatal. In high-income countries, diagnosis generally precedes invasion of the optic nerve, choroid, sclera, or orbit, and disease-free survival approaches 100%. Diplopia can accompany depressed orbital-floor fractures, especially anterior- or middle-third injuries and small- to medium-sized defects with soft-tissue herniation. Blowout injury can involve the lamina papyracea, but extraocular-muscle herniation and serious immediate complications are less common than with orbital-floor blowout fractures. Lateral- and superior-wall fractures carry increased traumatic optic neuropathy risk because blunt force can reach the optic canal and shear the nerve. With associated brain injury or obtundation, an afferent pupillary defect may be its sole clinical sign. Urgent diagnosis permits timely intervention when needed. Although optic-canal fractures increase nerve-injury risk, emergency surgery for traumatic optic neuropathy is generally reserved for a bone fragment impinging on the nerve, hematoma in the canal, or enlarging retrobulbar hematoma with proptosis.   Content: Infants in the neonatal intensive care unit underwent ROP screening if birth weight was less than 1,500 g or GA was less than 30 weeks. Findings were classified by retinal zone and stage under the Screening Examination of Premature Infants for Retinopathy of Prematurity. All three zones are centered on the optic disc: Zone I covers the posterior pole within a circle whose radius is twice the disc-to-macula-center distance; Zone II extends to a concentric circle touching the nasal ora serrata, with its temporal boundary approximately at the anatomic equator; Zone III is the remaining anterior temporal retinal crescent. Peripheral abnormalities comprise Stage 1, a demarcation line; Stage 2, a ridge; Stage 3, a ridge accompanied by extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation; Stage 4, partial retinal detachment; and Stage 5, total retinal detachment. These abnormalities may progress to retinal detachment. Markedly increased posterior venous dilation and arteriolar tortuosity define plus disease, which indicates a worse prognosis. Aggressive posterior ROP (AP-ROP) denotes severe, rapidly progressing posterior disease with findings in Zone I or posterior Zone II, prominent plus disease in all four quadrants, and poorly demarcated retinopathy such as neovascularization. Retinal examinations occurred every 1–2 weeks until regression and complete vascularization. Patients meeting treatment criteria received laser photocoagulation and/or an intravitreal anti-VEGF injection. Following the 2006 and 2013 American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines, laser was used first-line in the early period before 2013. From 2013, after studies including BEAT-ROP suggested benefits from intravitreal anti-VEGF monotherapy, the clinic began combining intravitreal bevacizumab with laser. The authors describe anti-VEGF injection as less expensive, easier to administer and less stressful for infants than laser. More recently, following the RAINBOW study comparing ranibizumab with laser in very low birthweight infants with ROP, intravitreal ranibizumab monotherapy has been used first-line. Laser is considered if ROP does not regress after anti-VEGF treatment.

Following intracameral placement with a prefilled, single-use, 28-gauge applicator, it releases bimatoprost continuously for approximately 3 to 4 months while its polymers hydrolyze and are metabolized to carbon dioxide and water. They noted US Food and Drug Administration approval of one intracameral 10 mg implant administration per eye to lower IOP in OAG and OHT. Document sections:
  Heading: INTRODUCTION
  Content: Orbital fractures represent up to 40% of midface traumatic injuries. They may be confined to orbital walls or extend to the orbital rim, and may occur alone or within more extensive injuries, including zygomaticomaxillary complex fractures, Le Fort II fractures (orbital floor fractures), and naso-orbital ethmoid fractures. Under the hydraulic theory, force applied to the globe travels backward to fracture the orbital wall. This mechanism is more likely to produce an isolated orbital floor fracture than a medial wall fracture because ethmoid air cells support the medial wall; cadaver experiments indicate that high-energy force can fracture both walls. Under the buckling theory, force applied to the orbital rim and adjacent structures travels through the wall until it reaches a weak area. The medial orbital wall is the most common fracture site (54.9%), particularly its thin lamina papyracea. Other reported patterns are combined medial wall and nasal fractures (46%), combined naso-orbito-ethmoid fractures (26.8%), isolated inferior wall fractures (18.3%), zygomaticomaxillary complex fractures (3%), and inferior orbital rim fractures (1%). Initial care should follow Advance Trauma Life Support guidance for maxillofacial injuries. History and examination should address blurred or double vision and visual loss; impaired extraocular movement, altered sensation, or orbital instability should heighten suspicion of fracture. A positive oculo-cardiac reflex requires immediate attention and treatment: its triad comprises bradycardia, nausea, and syncope, and prompt care is needed to avert fatal cardiac arrhythmia (1:3500). Orbital computed tomography is the diagnostic gold standard. In floor fractures, coronal views of the inferior and medial rectus muscles are essential for assessing possible entrapment and diplopia. Medial wall fractures are strongly associated with enophthalmos caused by collapse of the lamina papyracea or medial rectus entrapment. Computed tomography findings indicating immediate surgical correction include an orbital apex fracture with deteriorating vision, globe or optic nerve injury, periorbital emphysema, retrobulbar hematoma, and a bone fragment causing impingement. In children, the orbital floor may return to position while trapping tissue, also creating a surgical emergency. Once surgery is recommended, an approach must be selected. The described options are subciliary, subtarsal, transcaruncular/transconjunctival, and endoscopic surgery. Most publications emphasize technique rather than comparative outcomes, and only one randomized control trial compared open approaches without assessing endoscopy. The review aims to clarify each approach’s risks and benefits and identify the lowest-complication option.
