Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_12
  Name: Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma
  Description: These visual field abnormalities can result from compression of, or pathology within, the optic chiasm or the junction between the optic nerve and chiasm. The variant addresses suspected sellar or parasellar disease.
  Clinical presentation: Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma may accompany a sellar or suprasellar mass. Most neoplastic causes develop with gradually progressive visual symptoms; pituitary apoplexy may instead produce headache and rapid visual change.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Pituitary macroadenomas
      Distinguishing features: May extend above the sella and compress the optic chiasm or neighboring optic nerves or tracts.
    - Name: Sellar/suprasellar region meningiomas
      Distinguishing features: May involve sellar, suprasellar or parasellar structures and exert mass effect on the optic nerves or chiasm.
    - Name: Craniopharyngiomas
      Distinguishing features: Suprasellar masses that commonly compress the optic chiasm; the papillary type described in adults is usually solid and enhancing and rarely calcifies.
    - Name: Pituitary apoplexy
      Distinguishing features: Often follows hemorrhagic infarction of an existing adenoma and may cause rapid enlargement, headache and visual changes.
    - Name: Aneurysms
      Distinguishing features: Large lesions of the internal carotid artery or Circle of Willis vessels can compress the optic nerves or chiasm.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: MRI sella without and with IV contrast
      Purpose: Characterize suspected sellar or parasellar pathology, its extent and its relationship to the optic chiasm and neighboring structures.
      When indicated: Usually Appropriate and the preferred initial imaging examination.
      Interpretation: The small-field-of-view, thin-section protocol provides greater anatomical detail than routine head MRI.
    - Test: MRI head without and with IV contrast
      Purpose: Assess disease extending beyond the sella, including granulomatous, metastatic or lymphomatous processes.
      When indicated: May Be Appropriate.
      Interpretation: Routine head MRI can identify a large pituitary macroadenoma but generally provides less sellar detail than a dedicated protocol.
    - Test: CTA head with IV contrast; MRA head with IV contrast; MRA head without IV contrast

      When indicated: These vascular studies are not recommended by the variant table as routine initial imaging; CTA or MRA may follow MRI if aneurysm is suspected.
    - Test: CT sella without IV contrast; CT sella with IV contrast
      Purpose: Provide complementary information on calcification, bone invasion or a mass of osseous origin; noncontrast CT may reveal acute hemorrhage in pituitary apoplexy.
      When indicated: Usually Not Appropriate as routine initial imaging for this variant.
      Interpretation: MRI is more sensitive for diagnosing pituitary apoplexy and can assess an underlying pituitary mass.

  Content: Primary angle closure suspect denotes ITC with normal IOP and no glaucomatous optic neuropathy. In primary angle closure, IOP is elevated without glaucomatous optic neuropathy; lens opacity or retinal vascular pathology may coexist. Acute angle closure (AAC) crisis warrants rapid care distinct from routine management. Its post-crisis physical signs do not invariably determine long-term vision, although often-reversible current impairment may arise from lens opacity or an unresponsive dilated pupil following iris ischemia. Glaucomatous optic neuropathy at an acute presentation probably predates, rather than results from, a pressure elevation lasting hours or days. Document sections:
  Heading: Relevant embryology
  Content: The eye field is specified in the medial anterior neural plate shortly after gastrulation in the 3rd week of gestation. Optic vesicles bud from the forebrain, while adjacent surface ectoderm forms the lens placode and subsequently the lens vesicle. The distal optic vesicle gives rise to neural retina, and its proximal portion gives rise to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Invagination creates the double-layered optic cup: its inner layer forms neural retina and its outer layer forms RPE. A ventral embryonal/choroidal/foetal fissure along the cup and stalk permits mesenchymal entry and normally closes by 5–7 weeks of gestation, around the 17-mm stage. Eye development requires different combinations of transcription factors, including PAX6, SIX3, LHX2, and RAX, at successive stages. Intrinsic transcription factors interact with external signalling. Optic-vesicle stem cells can form neuro-sensory retina, RPE, or optic stalk according to those signals. Prospective neural retina expresses VSX2, prospective RPE expresses MITF, and prospective optic stalk expresses PAX2. Antagonism between MITF and VSX2 establishes the RPE–neural retina boundary; antagonism between PAX2 and PAX6 defines the optic stalk–neural retina boundary. Extrinsic influences include transforming growth factor (TGFβ), fibroblast growth factor, sonic hedgehog (SHH), and WNT signalling.

Document sections:
  Heading: 1. Introduction
  Content: Pterygium is a conspicuous ultraviolet-associated ocular disorder involving centripetal expansion of altered limbal epithelial cells. Squamous metaplasia with goblet-cell hyperplasia develops alongside proliferating stromal fibroblasts, new vessels, inflammation and extracellular-matrix remodeling. Reactivation of this wound-healing process by surgery may explain recurrence better than the older degenerative account involving Bowman’s layer degradation and elastosis. Epidemiological evidence and associations with cataract, climatic droplet keratopathy, photo-aged skin, squamous cell and basal cell carcinoma, melanoma and inherited DNA-repair disease support a role for chronic ultraviolet exposure. Prior studies also implicate peripheral-light focusing, fixation, ocular dominance and eye closure in sunlight, corneal curvature, anterior-chamber depth and handedness in pterygium location or laterality. Management seeks to restore ocular-surface anatomy, function and appearance while relieving symptoms; the authors have advocated excision with a limbal-conjunctival autograft as a reconstructive standard. Recurrence is most likely during the first 12 months after surgery and involves fibrovascular invasion and inflammation. Conjunctival recurrence and corneal recurrence after limbal breach have been described, but no consensus definition exists. Once recurrence is apparent, medical treatment is initially used to lessen or stop progression. Options mentioned include corticosteroids, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, cyclosporine, anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) and antimetabolites. 5-Fluourouracil (5-FU) has been applied topically or by injection as a surgical adjunct; intralesional subconjunctival injections have also attracted interest for primary, impending recurrent and recurrent disease. Its cytotoxicity raises concern about immediate and delayed harms. The authors knew of no prior review devoted exclusively to its application, effectiveness and safety in pterygium. They therefore set out to synthesize clinical recurrence outcomes, complications and possible present and future roles.

Document sections:
  Heading: 4.3 Diagnosis
  Content: Gonioscopy is the principal diagnostic and monitoring examination for primary angle-closure; dynamic assessment reveals drainage-angle anatomy unavailable through other techniques. It may be uncomfortable, requires training and practice, and can take considerable time in established disease. Limbal anterior chamber depth (LACD), or the van Herick test, is a quick non-contact adjunct to gonioscopy that staff can learn and perform in primary and secondary care. High frequency ultrasound biomicroscopy and anterior segment OCT (AS OCT) add anatomical imaging and may yield measurements useful for future risk assessment. AS OCT can rapidly document the angle without contact, support remote review and audit, and, under lower-light conditions, disclose previously unrecognized angle-closure. Identifying the scleral spur or Schwalbe’s line can limit its ability to establish ITC. AS OCT generally detects more ITC than gonioscopy; some studies find LACD and AS OCT more consistent than gonioscopy for identifying at-risk people, but the significance is unproven. AS OCT can document angle-width changes before and after PI and assist discussion with patients. No anterior-segment imaging or biometry method has been proven to identify who will later develop glaucoma. A Cochrane review judged evidence on LACD and AS-OCT diagnostic performance sub-optimal; pooled LACD data indicated high sensitivity and sufficient specificity for case-finding, with performance comparable to more complex imaging, while highlighting the need for better studies. Gonioscopy remains definitive for diagnosis and surveillance; AS OCT supplements rather than replaces it, particularly because it cannot detect PAS in place of gonioscopy. PAS-related visual prognosis remains unclear. Longitudinal research is needed to validate AS OCT measurements for diagnosis, prognosis, progression prediction and intervention assessment. In secondary care, AS-OCT may help triage referrals and avoid some gonioscopy examinations. There is no evidence supporting provocative tests for PAC/PACG diagnosis or monitoring (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong).

A Cochrane review judged evidence on LACD and AS-OCT diagnostic performance sub-optimal; pooled LACD data indicated high sensitivity and sufficient specificity for case-finding, with performance comparable to more complex imaging, while highlighting the need for better studies. Gonioscopy remains definitive for diagnosis and surveillance; AS OCT supplements rather than replaces it, particularly because it cannot detect PAS in place of gonioscopy. PAS-related visual prognosis remains unclear. Longitudinal research is needed to validate AS OCT measurements for diagnosis, prognosis, progression prediction and intervention assessment. In secondary care, AS-OCT may help triage referrals and avoid some gonioscopy examinations. There is no evidence supporting provocative tests for PAC/PACG diagnosis or monitoring (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong).

  Name: Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma
  Description: These visual field abnormalities can result from compression of, or pathology within, the optic chiasm or the junction between the optic nerve and chiasm. The variant addresses suspected sellar or parasellar disease.
  Clinical presentation: Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma may accompany a sellar or suprasellar mass. Most neoplastic causes develop with gradually progressive visual symptoms; pituitary apoplexy may instead produce headache and rapid visual change.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Pituitary macroadenomas
      Distinguishing features: May extend above the sella and compress the optic chiasm or neighboring optic nerves or tracts.
    - Name: Sellar/suprasellar region meningiomas
      Distinguishing features: May involve sellar, suprasellar or parasellar structures and exert mass effect on the optic nerves or chiasm.
    - Name: Craniopharyngiomas
      Distinguishing features: Suprasellar masses that commonly compress the optic chiasm; the papillary type described in adults is usually solid and enhancing and rarely calcifies.
    - Name: Pituitary apoplexy
      Distinguishing features: Often follows hemorrhagic infarction of an existing adenoma and may cause rapid enlargement, headache and visual changes.
    - Name: Aneurysms
      Distinguishing features: Large lesions of the internal carotid artery or Circle of Willis vessels can compress the optic nerves or chiasm.
  Diagnostic workup:

      Purpose: Characterize suspected sellar or parasellar pathology, its extent and its relationship to the optic chiasm and neighboring structures.

Document sections:
  Heading: 1. Introduction
  Content: Pterygium is a conspicuous ultraviolet-associated ocular disorder involving centripetal expansion of altered limbal epithelial cells. Squamous metaplasia with goblet-cell hyperplasia develops alongside proliferating stromal fibroblasts, new vessels, inflammation and extracellular-matrix remodeling. Reactivation of this wound-healing process by surgery may explain recurrence better than the older degenerative account involving Bowman’s layer degradation and elastosis. Epidemiological evidence and associations with cataract, climatic droplet keratopathy, photo-aged skin, squamous cell and basal cell carcinoma, melanoma and inherited DNA-repair disease support a role for chronic ultraviolet exposure. Prior studies also implicate peripheral-light focusing, fixation, ocular dominance and eye closure in sunlight, corneal curvature, anterior-chamber depth and handedness in pterygium location or laterality. Management seeks to restore ocular-surface anatomy, function and appearance while relieving symptoms; the authors have advocated excision with a limbal-conjunctival autograft as a reconstructive standard. Recurrence is most likely during the first 12 months after surgery and involves fibrovascular invasion and inflammation. Conjunctival recurrence and corneal recurrence after limbal breach have been described, but no consensus definition exists. Once recurrence is apparent, medical treatment is initially used to lessen or stop progression. Options mentioned include corticosteroids, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, cyclosporine, anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) and antimetabolites. 5-Fluourouracil (5-FU) has been applied topically or by injection as a surgical adjunct; intralesional subconjunctival injections have also attracted interest for primary, impending recurrent and recurrent disease. Its cytotoxicity raises concern about immediate and delayed harms. The authors knew of no prior review devoted exclusively to its application, effectiveness and safety in pterygium. They therefore set out to synthesize clinical recurrence outcomes, complications and possible present and future roles.

Main conclusion: The authors consider pneumatic retinopexy an effective surgical option for selected cases of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, with a reasonable rate of anatomical success and limited discomfort or complications.

Narrative summary: This retrospective study evaluated anatomical and functional outcomes after pneumatic retinopexy for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. The analysis included 21 eyes of 21 patients treated with C3F8; cases with follow-up shorter than 2 months were excluded. Eligibility focused on primary detachments involving the upper 2/3 of the retina, with a single break no wider than 1 clock hour or closely situated multiple breaks. Patients were examined after treatment, and retinal attachment at 2 months without additional surgery defined primary success.

Pneumatic retinopexy failed in 8 cases (38.1%), which underwent pars plana vitrectomy; additional breaks were identified in 4 of these cases. After a median follow-up of 10 months (4-38), 13 (61.9%) eyes remained attached and pneumatic retinopexy was considered successful. One initially successful case developed a new detachment 9 months after treatment because of a fresh break adjacent to earlier laser treatment. The authors observed no adverse events attributable to pneumatic retinopexy, including increased intraocular pressure or endophthalmitis. In their comparisons, 360-degree laser retinopexy was the sole factor significantly associated with anatomical success (p = 0.042). They identify the retrospective design, small sample, potential treatment-selection bias at their tertiary referral center, and lack of consideration of detachment duration as limitations.

Document sections:
  Heading: A B S T R A C T
  Content: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) is a persistent, progressive ocular inflammatory disease that can threaten vision and mainly affects children and young adults. Its prevalence ranges from <2 per 10,000 in the United States to as high as 1,100 per 10,000 in parts of Africa. Where VKC is uncommon, distinguishing it from other conditions can be difficult; treatment may begin only after disease progression and substantial impairment of quality of life. Although VKC was formerly regarded chiefly as an immunoglobulin E-mediated disorder, approximately 50% of affected patients lack allergic sensitization. Multiple inflammatory pathways contribute to its manifestations and characteristic conjunctival eosinophilic and fibroproliferative lesions. This review examines changes in understanding of VKC immunopathology, available and emerging treatments, their clinical implications, and priorities for research and practice.

Posterior vessel dilation and tortuosity range continuously from normal through preplus disease to plus disease. After spontaneous regression or treatment, abnormalities may resolve incompletely, persist, or reactivate.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: preplus disease
      Distinguishing features: Retinal vascular dilation, tortuosity, or both are abnormal but do not reach the severity of plus disease.
    - Name: plus disease
      Distinguishing features: Posterior retinal vessels show dilation and tortuosity. Iris vascular engorgement, poor pupillary dilation, and peripheral vascular engorgement with vitreous haze can indicate advanced disease but are not required for this designation.
    - Name: persistent avascular retina (PAR)
      Distinguishing features: Vascularization remains incomplete after spontaneous or treatment-associated regression; the avascular area may be peripheral or posterior and is described by location and extent.
    - Name: reactivation
      Distinguishing features: Acute-phase vascular changes or lesions recur after regression. Findings can range from a new, self-limiting demarcation line to stage 3 disease with plus disease and need not follow the usual acute-stage sequence.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: ophthalmoscopy
      Purpose: Assess vascularization, vascular abnormalities, lesions, retinal detachment, and visibility of the optic disc.
      When indicated: During examination and classification of an eye at risk for or affected by ROP.
      Interpretation: Record zone, plus disease, stage, and extent for each eye; also note A-ROP if present. A visible optic disc distinguishes stage 5A from stage 5B and stage 5C.
    - Test: 28-diopter (D) lens
      Purpose: Estimate the temporal limit of zone I during ophthalmoscopy.
      When indicated: When assessing the retinal zone.
      Interpretation: With the nasal edge of the optic disc at one edge of the view, the temporal edge approximately marks the zone I limit.
    - Test: retinal photography
      Purpose: Document vascular and retinal findings.
      When indicated: When retinal imaging is used for assessment.
      Interpretation: Before 39 weeks’ postmenstrual age, the fovea may be difficult to identify; its position may instead be estimated from the macular center. Plus-disease assessment should not rely solely on vessels visible in narrow-angle photographs.
    - Test: OCT
      Purpose: Show features at the vascular–avascular junction and determine whether a partial detachment involves the fovea.
      When indicated: Particularly when foveal involvement is subtle or difficult to judge clinically.
      Interpretation: An attached fovea corresponds to stage 4A; foveal detachment corresponds to stage 4B.
    - Test: B-scan ultrasonography
      Purpose: Determine the extent of retinal detachment.
      When indicated: When fibrosis prevents visualization of the posterior pole.
      Interpretation: Can reveal total detachment and its funnel configuration despite an obstructed fundus view.
    - Test: fluorescein angiography
      Purpose: Characterize vascular abnormalities, avascular retina, leakage, or subtle neovascularization.
      When indicated: When additional vascular assessment is useful, including assessment of late abnormalities or possible reactivation.
      Interpretation: The illustrated findings include persistent avascular retina, leakage in incompletely regressed disease, and leakage at sites of reactivation.
    - Test: OCT angiography
      Purpose: Illustrate macular vascular abnormalities.
      Interpretation: The document illustrates an incompletely developed foveal contour and a poorly defined foveal avascular zone after ROP.
  Staging:
    System: ICROP3
    Definitions:
      - Stage: stage 1
        Description: A relatively flat, thin, white demarcation line lies within the retina at the vascular–avascular junction. Peripheral vessel dilation or tortuosity alone does not establish this stage.
      - Stage: stage 2
        Description: A ridge develops from the demarcation line, acquiring width and height. Isolated neovascular tufts called popcorn may lie behind it without constituting stage 3.
      - Stage: stage 3
        Description: Extraretinal neovascular tissue extends toward the vitreous from the ridge. Apparent flat neovascularization in zone I or posterior zone II also qualifies, even without an obvious ridge or demarcation line.
      - Stage: stage 4
        Description: Partial retinal detachment, which may be tractional or exudative.
      - Stage: stage 4A
        Description: Partial retinal detachment with the fovea remaining attached.
      - Stage: stage 4B
        Description: Partial retinal detachment involving the fovea. A posterior volcano-shaped tractional detachment remains stage 4B if the peripheral retina is attached.
      - Stage: stage 5
        Description: Total retinal detachment.
      - Stage: stage 5A
        Description: Total retinal detachment with an optic disc visible on ophthalmoscopy, suggesting an open funnel.
      - Stage: stage 5B
        Description: Total retinal detachment in which retrolental fibrovascular tissue or a closed funnel obscures the optic disc.
      - Stage: stage 5C
        Description: Findings of stage 5B accompanied by anterior segment abnormalities, such as marked anterior chamber shallowing, adhesions, or corneal opacification, suggesting a closed funnel.
    Additional rules: The most posterior vascularization or lesion determines the eye’s zone. Zone I extends from the optic disc center to a radius twice the estimated disc-center–to–foveal-center distance. Zone II extends from zone I to the nasal ora serrata, with comparable reach in other directions; posterior zone II extends 2 disc diameters beyond the zone I border. Zone III is the remaining peripheral crescent; its designation requires nasal vessels to reach the ora serrata and no ROP in the 2 nasal-most clock hours. A lesion entering a more posterior zone for 1 to 2 clock hours is classified by that zone with the qualifier “secondary to notch.” When stages coexist, use the most severe stage. Assess the preplus-to-plus spectrum using vessels within zone I rather than a quadrant count or only the narrow-angle photographic field. The document describes extent as 12 clock-hour sectors in Table 1 but as 30 sectors in the Extent section; these statements conflict. Document reactivated lesions with their zone and stage and the modifier “reactivated.”
  Follow up:
    Long term effects:
      - Late tractional, rhegmatogenous, or, rarely, exudative retinal detachment.
      - Retinoschisis that can extend into the macula and threaten visual field or acuity.
      - Persistent avascular retina, which is prone to thinning, holes, latticelike changes, and later retinal detachment.
      - Macular abnormalities, including a smaller foveal avascular zone and a blunted or absent foveal depression.
      - Persistent vessel tortuosity, straightened vascular arcades with macular dragging, a falciform retinal fold, abnormal branching, circumferential vascular connections, and telangiectatic vessels.
      - Vitreous hemorrhage.
      - Secondary angle-closure glaucoma later in life.
    Survivorship notes: Describe persistent avascular retina by location and extent. A late detachment without signs of active ROP is a sequela rather than reactivation. Reactivation is reported more often after anti-VEGF treatment than after spontaneous regression and rarely, if ever, after complete laser photocoagulation; current evidence places its most common occurrence after anti-VEGF injection between 37 and 60 weeks’ postmenstrual age, although later reactivation may occur.

Document sections:
  Heading: Additional information
  Content: A further cohort study without a comparator evaluated intravenous liposomal prostaglandin E1 for acute CRAO. Studies of reperfusion, particularly rtPA (alteplase) within 4.5h, consistently reported visual-acuity improvement; significant gains of 0.7–1.0 logMAR were reported after rtPA/alteplase within 4.5h, whereas treatment after that window produced less improvement. Benefit may vary with event and patient characteristics. Although rtPA/alteplase for CRAO has been reported as feasible, safe and associated with better visual function than no treatment, RCT data for intravenous thrombolysis within 4.5h are lacking. Trials of alteplase or tenecteplase—THEIA, TenCRAOS and REVISION—are ongoing. Reported daily-activity differences between intervention and control groups suggest potential functional benefit and support considering thrombolysis for eligible patients, while weighing risks and individual preferences. Most survivors may accept treatment because of concern about sight loss; a small subset, particularly people relying on one unaffected eye, may decline it. Reported adverse events include intracerebral hemorrhage (1%), orolingual angioedema and systemic bleeding (up to 11%); these risks matter during consent discussions. CRAO is followed by increased short-term cerebral-stroke risk, warranting referral for cerebrovascular investigation as with transient ischemic attack or minor stroke. Care requires collaboration among family/general practitioners, primary eye care, ophthalmology and stroke physicians or neurologists.

Document sections:
  Heading: Stage 4: Partial Retinal Detachment
  Content: Stage 4A is partial detachment with an attached fovea; stage 4B includes foveal detachment. Findings suggesting detachment include diminished fine detail in choroidal vessels or granular retinal pigment epithelium, a ground-glass appearance compared with adjacent attached retina, or both. Macular displacement and straightening of arcade vessels suggest peripheral traction. OCT can be particularly useful for detecting subtle foveal involvement; photographs may not clearly reveal the detachment's extent. Stage 4 can be exudative or tractional, can occur in treated or untreated eyes, and can differ according to traction direction and associated exudation. Exudative stage 4 detachment occurs most often within days after laser treatment and is usually convex, sometimes localized, and self-limited. Tractional detachment accompanies progressive fibrovascular organization and vitreous haze and may coexist with lipid, subretinal hemorrhage, or both. Clinical examination may not readily distinguish retinoschisis from detachment. A-ROP can produce a posterior volcano-shaped tractional detachment, generally involving the fovea while peripheral retina stays attached. Despite resemblance to a funnel-shaped stage 5 detachment, it is stage 4B because detachment is not total. Figures 8 and 9 illustrate stage 4A and stage 4B appearances, including the value of OCT for identifying foveal detachment. Figure 8 includes an example of stage 4A detachment with 360 traction along the peripheral ridge.

Document sections:
  Heading: 2.6.2 Strategy for data synthesis
  Content: Data from included articles will be described, and effect sizes will be calculated in line with the Cochrane Collaboration handbook using Cochrane Review Manager v5.3. A preliminary search indicates that mean diameter and total area are common descriptors of optic disc size. The authors will report only mean diameter because its calculation is more straightforward. Where necessary, they plan to derive it from reported maximum and minimum diameters, horizontal diameter, or total area, assuming the optic disc can be approximated by a disc. The printed diameter expressions are partly unclear; the horizontal-diameter rule states that mean diameter equals horizontal diameter, while the total-area expression begins with 2. Data will be pooled as Hedge’s standardized mean difference. A fixed-effects model will be used for low-to-moderate heterogeneity (I2< 50%); otherwise, a random-effects model will be applied. A 95% confidence interval excluding the null value will indicate significance. Between-study variance, t2, will be estimated with the Restricted Maximum-Likelihood formula. Statistical analyses and plots will use R v4.0.3 and the ‘Metafor’ package.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Clinical Features
  Content: Assessment of suspected disease should establish onset and course, which are usually insidious and gradual, and inquire about trauma, contact lenses, systemic illness, and medication use. Symptoms include blurred vision, irritation, redness, photophobia, tearing, and discharge. Pain is usually less pronounced than in bacterial or Acanthamoeba keratitis and does not track the clinical findings. Findings include circumcorneal ciliary hyperemia, corneal infiltration and edema, diminished corneal luster, and typically feathery ulcer margins. Grey or yellow stromal infiltration commonly extends past the ulcer edge. A grey infiltrative ring can appear as raised, fluffy lesions with dirty yellow or brown pigmentation; dense endothelial-level infiltration may form plaques. Multifocal satellite microabscesses occur in more than 10% of cases, and thick hypopyon occurs in more than half. Appearance varies with the causative species. Serrated or feathery margins, raised borders, satellites, and infiltrate color can assist clinical distinction from bacterial keratitis. Candida and other yeast-associated ulcers may have a collar-button configuration: typically a small ulcer with expanding stromal infiltration. Although they resemble bacterial ulcers, they progress more slowly, have more discrete stromal infiltration, and do not respond to topical antibiotics. The illustrated examples include early and advanced ulcers, satellite lesions, hypopyon, and subsequent corneal opacity and vascularization.

question: In the incidence of primary angle closure glaucoma, male to female ratio is:

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__The Management of Angle Closure Glaucoma Clinical Guidelines__JC__000172
retrieved_chunks.document_id: The Management of Angle Closure Glaucoma Clinical Guidelines
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 1.3 Current practice, and why there is scope for change
  Content: Angle-closure glaucoma chiefly affects older people. PACG is uncommon in adults under 40; when present at that age, plateau iris is thought to predominate. Cases in children are documented but very rare. Angle-closure occurs at approximately a 3:1 female-to-male ratio. Asian heritage carries a greater burden; acute angle-closure incidence in Chinese patients is three-fold that in Caucasians, while angle-closure glaucoma is uncommon among Africans. The ICD10 table identifies codes for PACS, PAC, PACG and its acute, chronic, intermittent and residual forms, as well as drug-related glaucoma, aqueous misdirection, plateau iris syndrome and adverse effects of ophthalmological preparations. Surgical iridectomy entered glaucoma treatment in September 1857 and remained central until laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) superseded it in the mid 1970’s. LPI has also become a preventive intervention; prevention in the fellow eye after an acute crisis has an unquestioned role. EAGLE, reported in 2016, compared LPI with clear lens phacoemulsification in PAC with IOP above 30 mmHg or PACG. For patients meeting its entry criteria, lens extraction was generally safe, effective and cost-effective, and improved quality of life relative to LPI, prompting a shift away from LPI in PAC and PACG. Preventive LPI for asymptomatic people without documented pressure elevation remains common despite lacking a firm evidence base. Around 75% of UK ophthalmology consultants offer it for narrow or occluded angles. England's NHS recorded 13,844 patient episodes whose primary procedure was LPI in 2018-19; most likely involved prophylaxis, creating a substantial capacity burden. Pressures on the NHS during the first six months of 2020 further motivated reassessment of established practice.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_12
  Name: Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma
  Description: These visual field abnormalities can result from compression of, or pathology within, the optic chiasm or the junction between the optic nerve and chiasm. The variant addresses suspected sellar or parasellar disease.
  Clinical presentation: Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma may accompany a sellar or suprasellar mass. Most neoplastic causes develop with gradually progressive visual symptoms; pituitary apoplexy may instead produce headache and rapid visual change.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Pituitary macroadenomas
      Distinguishing features: May extend above the sella and compress the optic chiasm or neighboring optic nerves or tracts.
    - Name: Sellar/suprasellar region meningiomas
      Distinguishing features: May involve sellar, suprasellar or parasellar structures and exert mass effect on the optic nerves or chiasm.
    - Name: Craniopharyngiomas
      Distinguishing features: Suprasellar masses that commonly compress the optic chiasm; the papillary type described in adults is usually solid and enhancing and rarely calcifies.
    - Name: Pituitary apoplexy
      Distinguishing features: Often follows hemorrhagic infarction of an existing adenoma and may cause rapid enlargement, headache and visual changes.
    - Name: Aneurysms
      Distinguishing features: Large lesions of the internal carotid artery or Circle of Willis vessels can compress the optic nerves or chiasm.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: MRI sella without and with IV contrast
      Purpose: Characterize suspected sellar or parasellar pathology, its extent and its relationship to the optic chiasm and neighboring structures.
      When indicated: Usually Appropriate and the preferred initial imaging examination.
      Interpretation: The small-field-of-view, thin-section protocol provides greater anatomical detail than routine head MRI.
    - Test: MRI head without and with IV contrast
      Purpose: Assess disease extending beyond the sella, including granulomatous, metastatic or lymphomatous processes.
      When indicated: May Be Appropriate.
      Interpretation: Routine head MRI can identify a large pituitary macroadenoma but generally provides less sellar detail than a dedicated protocol.
    - Test: CTA head with IV contrast; MRA head with IV contrast; MRA head without IV contrast
      Purpose: Establish whether a lesion suggested by initial MRI is an aneurysm.
      When indicated: These vascular studies are not recommended by the variant table as routine initial imaging; CTA or MRA may follow MRI if aneurysm is suspected.
    - Test: CT sella without IV contrast; CT sella with IV contrast
      Purpose: Provide complementary information on calcification, bone invasion or a mass of osseous origin; noncontrast CT may reveal acute hemorrhage in pituitary apoplexy.
      When indicated: Usually Not Appropriate as routine initial imaging for this variant.
      Interpretation: MRI is more sensitive for diagnosing pituitary apoplexy and can assess an underlying pituitary mass.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Initial Physical Exam (Key elements)
  Content: Assess refractive status and pupils. On slit-lamp examination, look for conjunctival redness in acute cases; narrowing of central and peripheral anterior chamber depth; inflammation suggesting a present or recent attack; and corneal swelling, including microcystic or stromal edema, which is common acutely. A small corneal diameter suggests a smaller eye at greater PACD risk. Assess diffuse or localized iris atrophy, posterior synechiae, altered pupil function or shape, and a mid-dilated pupil, which can suggest a current or recent attack. Examine for cataract, glaukomflecken, and corneal endothelial cell loss. Measure IOP and perform gonioscopy. Evaluate the fundus and optic nerve head with a direct ophthalmoscope, slit-lamp biomicroscope and indirect lens, the central part of a gonioscopy lens, or nonmydriatic photography through an undilated pupil.

Document sections:
  Heading: 4.1.3. Vision
  Content: Optic-pathway gliomas can cause anything from no visual symptoms to severe loss. Reduced acuity is the most common manifestation; possible field abnormalities include central scotoma, bitemporal hemianopsia and peripheral constriction. Optic-nerve glioma can cause monocular loss. Optic-tract tumors, described more often with NF1, can cause unilateral loss, strabismus and/or proptosis, whereas optic-radiation tumors can cause homonymous hemianopia. Chiasmatic disease can cause bilateral deterioration, field loss, nystagmus and ultimately reduced acuity. Acuity and field testing, fundoscopy and increasingly optical coherence tomography (OCT) are important but challenging in young or uncooperative children. Younger age at presentation, pre-existing optic-nerve atrophy and postchiasmatic involvement are considered risk factors for visual deficit.

Document sections:
  Heading: Contraindications
  Content: Docking may be infeasible with a deep-set globe, narrow palpebral fissure, prominent nose or brow, or inability to lie supine; these are contraindications for FLACS. Conditions that impede anterior-segment OCT or equivalent imaging are also major contraindications, including prior corneal additive surgery with a ring or inlay implant, severe corneal opacity, and edema. Relative contraindications or added challenges include poor dilation (<6 mm diameter), prior keratoplasty or other corneal surgery, glaucoma surgery, white cataracts, mild corneal scarring, and edema. Approaches to inadequate preoperative dilation include topical phenylephrine, cyclopentolate, atropine, and/or NSAIDs given under different preoperative schedules; intracameral epinephrine or phenylephrine; viscomydriasis using viscoelastic; and iris expansion devices. The additional difficulty depends on pulse energy: high-energy FLACS can further constrict an already small pupil, whereas low-energy FLACS reportedly does not require dilation measures beyond those used with CP. Lens fragmentation is not advised for white cataracts because opaque tissue cannot be imaged adequately; variation in water content in white or brunescent cataracts also alters laser-energy absorption. In systems that fragment after capsulotomy, decompression of an intumescent cataract can change posterior capsule depth and increase rupture risk. This sequence-related issue does not apply to systems that fragment before capsulotomy. Corneal scars or edema may prevent complete capsulotomy or fragmentation, although isolated successful FLACS cases have been reported; opacity severity matters. Pterygium, pinguecula, filtration blebs, and glaucoma drainage tubes complicate treatment but should not automatically be absolute contraindications: successful cases have been reported with additional care. Docking can raise intraocular pressure, more so with applanation than with a liquid interface. Nevertheless, evidence has not shown progression of well-controlled glaucoma or other optic neuropathies from this effect.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_12
  Name: Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma
  Description: These visual field abnormalities can result from compression of, or pathology within, the optic chiasm or the junction between the optic nerve and chiasm. The variant addresses suspected sellar or parasellar disease.
  Clinical presentation: Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma may accompany a sellar or suprasellar mass. Most neoplastic causes develop with gradually progressive visual symptoms; pituitary apoplexy may instead produce headache and rapid visual change.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Pituitary macroadenomas
      Distinguishing features: May extend above the sella and compress the optic chiasm or neighboring optic nerves or tracts.
    - Name: Sellar/suprasellar region meningiomas
      Distinguishing features: May involve sellar, suprasellar or parasellar structures and exert mass effect on the optic nerves or chiasm.
    - Name: Craniopharyngiomas
      Distinguishing features: Suprasellar masses that commonly compress the optic chiasm; the papillary type described in adults is usually solid and enhancing and rarely calcifies.
    - Name: Pituitary apoplexy
      Distinguishing features: Often follows hemorrhagic infarction of an existing adenoma and may cause rapid enlargement, headache and visual changes.
    - Name: Aneurysms
      Distinguishing features: Large lesions of the internal carotid artery or Circle of Willis vessels can compress the optic nerves or chiasm.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: MRI sella without and with IV contrast
      Purpose: Characterize suspected sellar or parasellar pathology, its extent and its relationship to the optic chiasm and neighboring structures.
      When indicated: Usually Appropriate and the preferred initial imaging examination.
      Interpretation: The small-field-of-view, thin-section protocol provides greater anatomical detail than routine head MRI.
    - Test: MRI head without and with IV contrast
      Purpose: Assess disease extending beyond the sella, including granulomatous, metastatic or lymphomatous processes.
      When indicated: May Be Appropriate.
      Interpretation: Routine head MRI can identify a large pituitary macroadenoma but generally provides less sellar detail than a dedicated protocol.
    - Test: CTA head with IV contrast; MRA head with IV contrast; MRA head without IV contrast
      Purpose: Establish whether a lesion suggested by initial MRI is an aneurysm.
      When indicated: These vascular studies are not recommended by the variant table as routine initial imaging; CTA or MRA may follow MRI if aneurysm is suspected.
    - Test: CT sella without IV contrast; CT sella with IV contrast
      Purpose: Provide complementary information on calcification, bone invasion or a mass of osseous origin; noncontrast CT may reveal acute hemorrhage in pituitary apoplexy.
      When indicated: Usually Not Appropriate as routine initial imaging for this variant.
      Interpretation: MRI is more sensitive for diagnosing pituitary apoplexy and can assess an underlying pituitary mass.

Document sections:
  Heading: 2.3. Children
  Content: Prepubertal cysts are uncommon without an associated condition because gonadotropin stimulation falls after the neonatal period and usually remains low until puberty. Associated conditions include idiopathic central precocious puberty, McCune Albright syndrome, thyroid disorders, and hormonally active ovarian tumors. Nevertheless, most simple childhood cysts result from an ovarian follicle failing to regress. A prepubertal cyst may be an incidental imaging finding or an asymptomatic mass with abdominal distension. Larger symptomatic cysts can produce persistent periumbilical or lower-quadrant pain, bloating, urinary frequency or retention, constipation, or fullness. Sudden severe pain generally suggests torsion, perforation, hemorrhage, or infarction. Ultrasound should distinguish ovarian cysts from paraovarian, mesothelial, and broad ligament cysts. Management depends on sonographic features and clinical findings. Observation is preferred for asymptomatic patients, alongside counseling children and parents about torsion symptoms so emergency care can be sought promptly. Prepubertal observational studies report that cysts up to 9 cm usually resolve spontaneously. Surgical exploration is indicated for diameter ≥ 9 cm because malignancy risk increases, tumor-suggestive ultrasound findings such as septations, increased solid tissue or calcification, torsion, or acute rupture with bleeding and hemodynamic instability.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: Corneal edema
  Description: Excess fluid accumulates in one or more corneal layers. Causes include endothelial dysfunction, elevated intraocular pressure, inflammation, trauma, dystrophies, infection, hypoxia, surgery, and toxicity.
  Clinical presentation: Vision may be blurred or fluctuate, often worsening on waking and improving later in the day. Photophobia, redness, tearing, foreign-body sensation, and pain may occur. Onset is usually gradual, although pressure elevation, substantial inflammation, and hydrops can produce a more acute presentation. Peripheral disease may cause few symptoms, while central involvement generally affects vision; functional disability can exceed that suggested by standard visual acuity.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Idiopathic corneal edema
    - Name: Secondary corneal edema
    - Name: Corneal edema due to wearing contact lenses
      Distinguishing features: Contact lens use is the identified cause.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: History and functional-vision assessment
      Purpose: Establish onset, fluctuation, laterality, symptoms, effects on daily activities, and potential causes.
      When indicated: Initial evaluation.
      Interpretation: Morning blur that clears later may accompany endothelial dysfunction; visual acuity alone may understate glare-related disability.
    - Test: Visual acuity, pinhole testing, manifest refraction, and glare testing
      Purpose: Measure visual loss, best-corrected potential, and functional impairment.
      When indicated: Initial evaluation; assessment of visual potential is particularly important before surgery.
      Interpretation: Functional status and measured acuity need not agree.
    - Test: External examination and slit-lamp biomicroscopy
      Purpose: Examine the lids and ocular surface; distinguish epithelial from stromal edema; identify guttae, epithelial breakdown, inflammation, scarring, Descemet’s membrane abnormalities, deposits, and other potential causes.
      When indicated: Initial evaluation and subsequent assessment as clinically indicated.
      Interpretation: Sectoral edema with keratic precipitates or an anterior chamber reaction can point toward endotheliitis. Inferior edema can accompany retained material or a foreign body in the inferior angle.
    - Test: Intraocular pressure measurement
      Purpose: Identify pressure elevation or hypotony contributing to edema.
      When indicated: Evaluation and monitoring, particularly when pressure-related disease or corticosteroid treatment is relevant.
      Interpretation: Goldmann applanation tonometry may be unreliable in an abnormal cornea. Alternative methods include a pneumotonometer, handheld electronic applanation tonometer, dynamic contour tonometer, ocular response analyzer, rebound tonometer, and digital palpation; consistent use of the same valid method supports serial comparison.
    - Test: Fundus examination and B-scan ultrasonography
      Purpose: Assess posterior-segment conditions associated with hypotony and secondary edema when examination warrants it.
      When indicated: When posterior-segment assessment is needed.
      Interpretation: Chronic serous choroidal detachment or retinal detachment may contribute through hypotony.
    - Test: Gonioscopy
      Purpose: Look for retained lens fragments, foreign bodies, or iridocorneal adhesions.
      When indicated: When angle pathology or retained material is suspected.
      Interpretation: Findings can help establish the cause of localized edema.
    - Test: Potential acuity meter or illuminated near-card pinhole testing
      Purpose: Estimate visual potential despite anterior-segment pathology.
      When indicated: Particularly before a surgical treatment decision.
      Interpretation: Better performance than on conventional acuity testing supports the possibility of improvement after treatment; a poor result does not necessarily establish poor visual potential.
    - Test: RGP contact lens over-refraction
      Purpose: Determine whether surface irregularity substantially contributes to visual loss.
      When indicated: When edema or scarring disturbs the central or paracentral surface.
      Interpretation: Improvement with the lens, but not with spectacles, favors surface irregularity as a major contributor.
    - Test: Pachymetry
      Purpose: Measure corneal thickness and assess serial change.
      When indicated: When endothelial function or progression requires assessment.
      Interpretation: Serial thickness measurements can help assess endothelial function. Measurements from different device types are not directly interchangeable.
    - Test: Corneal topography and tomography
      Purpose: Assess irregular astigmatism, corneal thickness, posterior-surface findings, and the depth of associated opacification.
      When indicated: When evaluating visual impairment, prognosis, or surgical planning.
      Interpretation: Peripheral pathology may create visually important central irregularity.
    - Test: Specular microscopy
      Purpose: Assess endothelial cell density, shape, and uniformity.
      When indicated: When endothelial assessment can contribute to evaluation or serial monitoring.
      Interpretation: Cell imaging does not directly measure endothelial function or reserve; diffuse confluent guttae can prevent useful imaging.
    - Test: Confocal microscopy
      Purpose: Image corneal layers and investigate endothelial, stromal, or infectious causes.
      When indicated: Particularly helpful in unilateral edema or when specular imaging is limited by moderate edema.
      Interpretation: Characteristic appearances may help identify iridocorneal endothelial syndrome, epithelial or fibrous ingrowth, PPCD, fungal hyphae, or Acanthamoeba cysts.
    - Test: Anterior segment optical coherence tomography
      Purpose: Image corneal and retrocorneal structures, measure thickness, and assess surgical anatomy.
      When indicated: When deeper structural pathology is suspected or after endothelial keratoplasty.
      Interpretation: Can reveal a detached Descemet’s membrane, retrocorneal membrane, stromal cleft, or an area where donor tissue has not adhered.
    - Test: Ultrasound biomicroscopy
      Purpose: Examine anterior-segment structures despite opacity and locate small foreign bodies.
      When indicated: Especially useful in congenital or traumatic cases and for surgical planning.
      Interpretation: Can show displaced or ruptured Descemet’s membrane, adhesions, and retrocorneal membranes.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Visit intervals depend on clinical judgment, improvement or stability, and the intervention performed. A bandage contact lens used for an extended period requires regular review and periodic replacement; in most cases, the same lens should not remain for longer than one month.
    Recommended tests:
      - Serial pachymetry when monitoring endothelial function
      - Intraocular pressure assessment when pressure elevation or corticosteroid response is a concern
      - Reassessment of the ocular surface, symptoms, and contact lens fit when a bandage contact lens is used
    Long term effects:
      - Persistent endothelial damage may cause edema to recur years after an initially resolving injury.
    Survivorship notes: New or worsening pain, redness, photophobia, or vision changes warrant prompt medical attention.

Document sections:
  Heading: 2.3. Children
  Content: Prepubertal cysts are uncommon without an associated condition because gonadotropin stimulation falls after the neonatal period and usually remains low until puberty. Associated conditions include idiopathic central precocious puberty, McCune Albright syndrome, thyroid disorders, and hormonally active ovarian tumors. Nevertheless, most simple childhood cysts result from an ovarian follicle failing to regress. A prepubertal cyst may be an incidental imaging finding or an asymptomatic mass with abdominal distension. Larger symptomatic cysts can produce persistent periumbilical or lower-quadrant pain, bloating, urinary frequency or retention, constipation, or fullness. Sudden severe pain generally suggests torsion, perforation, hemorrhage, or infarction. Ultrasound should distinguish ovarian cysts from paraovarian, mesothelial, and broad ligament cysts. Management depends on sonographic features and clinical findings. Observation is preferred for asymptomatic patients, alongside counseling children and parents about torsion symptoms so emergency care can be sought promptly. Prepubertal observational studies report that cysts up to 9 cm usually resolve spontaneously. Surgical exploration is indicated for diameter ≥ 9 cm because malignancy risk increases, tumor-suggestive ultrasound findings such as septations, increased solid tissue or calcification, torsion, or acute rupture with bleeding and hemodynamic instability.

  Content: Alcohol can affect the ocular surface through direct contact or oral consumption. Direct exposure, accidental or procedural, loosens corneal epithelium from Bowman’s membrane. Document sections:
  Heading: Visual Pathways
  Content: Visual dysfunction is often the main or only manifestation of a tumour infiltrating visual pathways. Optic pathway gliomas (OPG) are mostly histologically low-grade glioma (LGG), but may remain indolent or progress repeatedly and cause severe visual sequelae. A substantial proportion of affected children experience impairment, and 5 - 10% meet legal-blindness criteria. Uni- or bilateral VA and VF defects vary with lesion position; homonymous and bitemporal hemianopia are frequent. Children below 1 year of age and those with post-chiasmatic OPG appear more likely to experience VA deterioration. Approximately 15% of children with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) have OPG. Its course is indolent in up to 70 - 85%, while about 15% - 30% develop more aggressive behaviour and visual deficits. Isolated optic nerve gliomas (IONG), whether or not associated with NF1, may cause proptosis and optic pallor or atrophy as well as acuity or field loss. Optic nerve sheaths meningioma, commonly associated with Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), can present similarly. Large hypothalamic-chiasmatic OPG can obstruct CSF flow, raise intracranial pressure and produce papilledema.

Document sections:
  Heading: 6.2 Visual acuity
  Content: Because IOP-lowering surgery should preserve acuity, visual acuity is a safety endpoint. A fall in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of >2 Snellen lines, equivalent to doubling of logMAR values, is generally clinically relevant and warrants an explanation. BCVA is unsuitable as the primary endpoint because macular or retinal disease unrelated to surgery is common in older participants. Standardised preoperative and postoperative tests, such as ETDRS charts, should be used, with starting and final acuity displayed in a table or scatterplot. Very poor vision may be categorised as hand movements (HM), light perception (LP) or no light perception (NLP); for analysis these correspond to 1/800 (logMAR 2.3), 1/1600 (logMAR 2.8) and 1/3200 (logMAR >3), respectively. Loss of ≥ 3 ETDRS lines, equivalent to doubling of the visual angle, such as 10/10 to 5/10, is moderate; loss of ≥ 6 lines, equivalent to quadrupling, such as 8/10 to 2/10, is severe. Studies should report the percentages and causes of these losses to assess and compare safety.

retrieved_chunks.text: Interpretation: Ocular coloboma ranges from minor defects with little functional effect to severe abnormalities. Vision may be impaired by involvement of the optic disc or fovea, or by complications including retinal detachment (RD) and choroidal neovascularisation. Genetic causes appear complex, and sporadic cases are more common; the authors consider environmental and maternal factors probable contributors to some sporadic cases, while noting that evidence for environmental causes is largely circumstantial. Identifying inter-calary membrane (ICM) detachment is central to determining whether a coloboma contributes to RD. For coloboma-related RD, pars plana vitrectomy with silicone oil tamponade and laser treatment along the coloboma margin is associated with good anatomical outcomes, although visual recovery can remain limited by disc or macular involvement. Cataract surgery carries an elevated complication risk in these eyes. Complete prophylactic laser treatment may substantially reduce RD risk where it can be performed safely, but the benefit of partial treatment remains unresolved.

Document sections:
  Heading: Examination Schedule
  Content: For type 1 diabetes, sight-threatening DR is rare before puberty, although substantial disease can emerge 6 to 7 years after onset. Begin ophthalmic examinations 5 years after diagnosis and repeat annually; education on early glycemic control should begin at disease onset. Type 2 diabetes may precede its diagnosis by years: up to 3% diagnosed at age 30 or later have CSME or high-risk findings at diagnosis, and about 30% have some DR. Refer for comprehensive examination at diagnosis and continue at least annually. People planning pregnancy with pre-existing diabetes should have an eye examination beforehand and counseling about possible DR development or progression. Examine during the first trimester and arrange repeat visits according to severity; systemic management during pregnancy should address glucose and blood pressure. Gestational diabetes arising during pregnancy does not require a pregnancy eye examination and does not appear to increase pregnancy-related DR risk. During puberty, DR progresses faster; reported relative risk is 4.8 versus prepubescent patients despite comparable diabetes duration.

Document sections:
  Heading: Complicaciones
  Content: Son embarazos de alto riesgo por el aumento de morbilidad materna y fetal. Se incrementan el aborto, especialmente en monocigotos; la preeclampsia, que puede comenzar antes de la 20 semana; la hiperemesis gravídica y la hipertensión inducida por el embarazo. La amenaza de parto pretérmino aumenta por sobredistensión uterina y por polihidramnios, presente en el 15 % de los embarazos gemelares; la prematuridad es la principal causa de morbimortalidad neonatal. Son más frecuentes la rotura prematura de membranas, las malformaciones congénitas —cuya frecuencia se multiplica por 3, sobre todo defectos del tubo neural y cardiopatías—, el prolapso de cordón en monoamnióticos o con polihidramnios y el abruptio placentae tras la descompresión que sigue al nacimiento del primer gemelo. En gestaciones monocoriales, las anastomosis placentarias arteriovenosas pueden causar síndrome de transfusión feto-fetal: el receptor recibe sangre del donante, pesa más y presenta un hematocrito superior al nacimiento (>15 % ó 5 g de Hb); puede desarrollar hipervolemia, HTA, policitemia, polihidramnios e insuficiencia cardiaca de alto gasto. El donante puede presentar hipovolemia, hipotensión, anemia y CIR. Su expresión máxima se denomina secuencia TRAP (twinreversed arterial perfusion sequence): el gemelo bomba mantiene su circulación y la del feto acardio.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Park et al. 2023 Long term visual outcomes in children with regressed retinopathy of prematurity__JC__000069
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Park et al. 2023 Long term visual outcomes in children with regressed retinopathy of prematurity
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: ROP screening and management.
  Content: Infants in the neonatal intensive care unit underwent ROP screening if birth weight was less than 1,500 g or GA was less than 30 weeks. Findings were classified by retinal zone and stage under the Screening Examination of Premature Infants for Retinopathy of Prematurity. All three zones are centered on the optic disc: Zone I covers the posterior pole within a circle whose radius is twice the disc-to-macula-center distance; Zone II extends to a concentric circle touching the nasal ora serrata, with its temporal boundary approximately at the anatomic equator; Zone III is the remaining anterior temporal retinal crescent. Peripheral abnormalities comprise Stage 1, a demarcation line; Stage 2, a ridge; Stage 3, a ridge accompanied by extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation; Stage 4, partial retinal detachment; and Stage 5, total retinal detachment. These abnormalities may progress to retinal detachment. Markedly increased posterior venous dilation and arteriolar tortuosity define plus disease, which indicates a worse prognosis. Aggressive posterior ROP (AP-ROP) denotes severe, rapidly progressing posterior disease with findings in Zone I or posterior Zone II, prominent plus disease in all four quadrants, and poorly demarcated retinopathy such as neovascularization. Retinal examinations occurred every 1–2 weeks until regression and complete vascularization. Patients meeting treatment criteria received laser photocoagulation and/or an intravitreal anti-VEGF injection. Following the 2006 and 2013 American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines, laser was used first-line in the early period before 2013. From 2013, after studies including BEAT-ROP suggested benefits from intravitreal anti-VEGF monotherapy, the clinic began combining intravitreal bevacizumab with laser. The authors describe anti-VEGF injection as less expensive, easier to administer and less stressful for infants than laser. More recently, following the RAINBOW study comparing ranibizumab with laser in very low birthweight infants with ROP, intravitreal ranibizumab monotherapy has been used first-line. Laser is considered if ROP does not regress after anti-VEGF treatment.

  Content: Many tumors, tumor-like conditions, systemic diseases, metastases, and high- or low-flow vascular malformations can involve the orbit. Distinguishing vascular from other lesions guides subsequent workup and care. Because the orbital space is restricted, either a soft-tissue or vascular mass may cause proptosis. Orbital-apex masses or inflammation characteristically produce vision loss with ophthalmoplegia. Orbital masses can be classified by location in the globe, optic nerve sheath complex, intraconal or extraconal space, bone, or multiple compartments. Benign lesions predominate, but malignant orbital tumors become more prevalent in adults older than 60 years of age. Among cysts, dermoid cysts are most common; excluding cysts, cavernous venous malformation is the commonest benign adult orbital mass, while non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the commonest malignant one. Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 6: Adult. Bitemporal hemianopia or junctional scotoma. Sellar or parasellar mass suspected. Initial imaging.
  Content: Bitemporal hemianopia and junctional scotoma can arise from external compression or intrinsic disease of the optic chiasm and the optic nerve–chiasm junction, respectively. A pituitary macroadenoma may extend above the sella and compress the chiasm, adjacent nerves, or tracts. Meningiomas account for a small fraction of sellar-region masses but can involve sellar, suprasellar, or parasellar structures and compress the nerves or chiasm. Sellar or suprasellar meningiomas most often enhance homogeneously; a dural tail is common but not universal. Imaging cannot always distinguish them from a pituitary adenoma when their origin relative to the gland is uncertain. Craniopharyngiomas commonly compress the chiasm. The adamantinomatous type, more frequent in children, is often mixed cystic and solid, calcified, and heterogeneously enhancing; the adult papillary type is generally solid and enhancing and rarely calcifies. Hypophysitis, large Rathke cleft cysts, and other suprasellar masses may compress the chiasm or posterior optic nerves. Neoplastic causes usually produce gradual symptoms, whereas pituitary apoplexy, most often hemorrhagic infarction of an existing adenoma, can rapidly enlarge a lesion and cause headache and visual change. Large internal carotid artery or Circle of Willis aneurysms may also compress the visual pathway. Optic pathway glioma, inflammatory or demyelinating disease, granulomatous disease, and lymphoma may affect the chiasm, optic nerves, or pituitary infundibulum. Imaging aims to identify a sellar or suprasellar mass causing the field defect, demonstrate chiasmal compression, and guide care.

Document sections:
  Heading: 1. Introduction
  Content: VKC is a persistent and progressive inflammatory eye disorder with potential to impair vision. It mainly occurs in children and adolescents (<20 years), and onset precedes 10 years of age in most cases. Although it commonly subsides at puberty, prospective and retrospective analyses indicate that up to 12% of patients with VKC are adults and that up to 82% of adult cases begin after puberty. The review addresses the changing treatment landscape, implications of emerging approaches, and future research and practice.

Document sections:
  Heading: BQ1 What is the pathophysiology of MGD?
  Content: Meibum supplies the superficial tear-film lipid layer. The reported composition includes wax esters 30–48%, cholesterol esters 30–40%, (O-acyl) -ω-hydroxy fatty acid 1–5%, cholesterol 0.5% and free fatty acids 0.1–1%. Its contribution to tear stability is accepted, but the model that MGD causes dry eye primarily by increasing aqueous evaporation is disputed. MGD is better considered a group of meibomian-gland-related pathological states than a single disease. Clinical signs can include eyelid-margin vascularity, plugging and meibum that becomes yellow or white, turbid, granular, viscous or toothpaste-like. The 2011 MGD International Workshop described ductal hyperkeratinization and viscous meibum causing orifice obstruction and reduced drainage, with subsequent acinar atrophy and reduced secretion. The guideline also recognizes primary abnormalities of meibocytes as a possible core mechanism.

question: "Blow out" Fracture of orbit involve-

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Vision Loss__JC__000110
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Vision Loss
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 1: Adult. Acute posttraumatic visual defect. Suspect orbital injury. Initial imaging.
  Content: Orbital fractures most often follow assault or a direct blow, motor-vehicle collisions, falls, or sports injuries. They can occur alone or alongside zygomaticomaxillary complex, Le Fort II and III, or nasoethmoidal complex fractures. Diplopia can accompany depressed orbital-floor fractures, especially anterior- or middle-third injuries and small- to medium-sized defects with soft-tissue herniation. Fractures >2 cm are more likely to produce enophthalmos. Blowout injury can involve the lamina papyracea, but extraocular-muscle herniation and serious immediate complications are less common than with orbital-floor blowout fractures. Most orbital fractures can undergo delayed repair after swelling improves; CT can reveal injuries needing more urgent action, including trapdoor fractures and orbital compartment syndrome. Lateral- and superior-wall fractures carry increased traumatic optic neuropathy risk because blunt force can reach the optic canal and shear the nerve. With associated brain injury or obtundation, an afferent pupillary defect may be its sole clinical sign. Urgent diagnosis permits timely intervention when needed. Although optic-canal fractures increase nerve-injury risk, emergency surgery for traumatic optic neuropathy is generally reserved for a bone fragment impinging on the nerve, hematoma in the canal, or enlarging retrobulbar hematoma with proptosis. Severe proptosis with posterior globe tenting requires emergency orbital decompression to preserve vision. An orbital-apex fracture involving the superior orbital fissure can affect multiple traversing cranial nerves. Retrobulbar hematoma, emphysema, or a blow-in fracture can increase orbital mass effect and cause compartment syndrome and vision loss. Imaging evidence of retrobulbar bleeding does not sensitively predict subsequent compartment syndrome: diagnose it from clinical evidence of optic nerve compression. Extraocular-muscle entrapment after an orbital-floor fracture is likewise a clinical diagnosis; muscle herniation and altered contour have low positive predictive values for entrapment. Imaging aims to identify orbital injuries and complications early enough to guide timely care and prevent permanent visual loss.

Document sections:
  Heading: Evidence considered when developing the guideline
  Content: Recommendations 1.3.5 to 1.3.8 arose from a review of formulas for IOL biometry. It included 18 observational comparisons in previously unoperated eyes of varying axial lengths undergoing phacoemulsification and Six observational studies in eyes with previous corneal refractive surgery; it found no RCTs or economic evidence. The committee noted substantial statistical imprecision across formulas and outcomes. In eyes without previous corneal refractive surgery, SRK/T performed poorly at axial lengths less than 22.00 mm, unlike at lengths greater than 26.00 mm; Hoffer Q performed poorly above 26.00 mm. Haigis ranked among the best choices for 3 of the 4 axial-length subgroups. At short lengths, Hoffer Q and Haigis had similar predictive accuracy; Barrett Universal II and SRK/T performed best at average or medium long lengths. Among eyes with prior corneal refractive surgery, uncertainty and heterogeneity prevented identification of a consistently superior formula.

  Heading: Variant 3: Adult. Chronic or progressive unilateral vision loss. Intraorbital mass-like lesion suspected or vascular lesion suspected. Initial imaging.
  Content: Many tumors, tumor-like conditions, systemic diseases, metastases, and high- or low-flow vascular malformations can involve the orbit. Distinguishing vascular from other lesions guides subsequent workup and care. Because the orbital space is restricted, either a soft-tissue or vascular mass may cause proptosis. Orbital-apex masses or inflammation characteristically produce vision loss with ophthalmoplegia. Orbital masses can be classified by location in the globe, optic nerve sheath complex, intraconal or extraconal space, bone, or multiple compartments. Benign lesions predominate, but malignant orbital tumors become more prevalent in adults older than 60 years of age. Among cysts, dermoid cysts are most common; excluding cysts, cavernous venous malformation is the commonest benign adult orbital mass, while non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the commonest malignant one. Imaging seeks to detect and characterize the causative orbital mass or vascular lesion, direct care, and sometimes establish a specific diagnosis.

Condition or topic: 24-hour intraocular pressure control with a single bimatoprost implant administration in adults with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension.

Clinical background: Lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) is intended to reduce glaucomatous visual field loss, but IOP varies with body position and circadian timing. Peaks can occur outside office hours and are likely to contribute to glaucoma progression, making daytime and nighttime control relevant. Some topical IOP-lowering drug classes have diminished nighttime efficacy, whereas topical prostaglandin analogs/prostamides, including bimatoprost, have lowered IOP over 24 hours. Earlier phase 3 studies found that a single 10- or 15-mg bimatoprost implant was noninferior to twice-daily topical timolol maleate 0.5% for IOP lowering through 12 weeks, but its effects outside usual office hours had not been reported.

Objectives:
  - Primarily, assess hour-matched change from baseline in study-eye IOP in the habitual position across 24 hours at week 8 after a single 10-mg bimatoprost implant administration, using pneumatonometry.
  - Assess change from baseline in the range of habitual-position IOP over 24 hours at week 8.
  - Assess hour-matched IOP change from baseline in the supine position at week 8.
  - Assess change from baseline in hour 0 IOP by Goldmann applanation tonometry and time to first use of additional IOP-lowering treatment through month 12.
  - Assess safety through 12 months, including treatment-emergent adverse events and central corneal endothelial cell density.

Clinical question: In adults with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension requiring IOP-lowering treatment, how does a single intracameral 10-mg bimatoprost implant change habitual-position IOP across 24 hours at week 8 compared with baseline, and what are its IOP-lowering and safety outcomes through 12 months?

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: residual amblyopia
  Synonyms:
    - persisting amblyopia
  Description: Visual acuity loss attributable to amblyopia that remains uncured by the end of the critical period, roughly the child’s first decade of life. An anatomical or physiological cause must not adequately explain the impairment; the document gives optic nerve hypoplasia, media opacity, and cerebral visual impairment as examples of alternative causes.
  Epidemiology: In a comparison at age 8 years during 1988-1990, the screened Haifa cohort had significantly less amblyopia worse than 20/32 than the unscreened Hadera cohort (1% vs 2.6%). For residual amblyopia measured as logMAR lines of visual acuity worse than 20/40 per 1,000 children, the reported values were 6 in Haifa and 61 in Hadera. The document also cites a population-based study in which children born in Israel with good access to screening had less amblyopia and vision loss than children who immigrated from Russia, where widespread screening was less available.
  Clinical presentation: Persistent impairment may affect one or both eyes. Without adequate treatment, amblyopia can cause lifelong monocular and/or binocular visual impairment.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Residual unilateral amblyopia
      Distinguishing features: Reduced best-corrected acuity in the worse eye, an interocular acuity difference, and a corresponding unilateral amblyopia risk factor.
    - Name: Residual bilateral amblyopia
      Distinguishing features: Reduced best-corrected acuity in both eyes with a corresponding bilateral amblyopia risk factor.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Monocular visual acuity screening
      Purpose: Identify children who need a confirmatory examination; an abnormal result alone does not establish that amblyopia caused the vision loss.
      When indicated: For population-level outcome assessment, the committees recommend assessment at 8 years of age.
      Interpretation: Visual acuity poorer than logMAR 0.2 (20/32) in one or both eyes warrants referral for a comprehensive confirmatory outcome examination.
    - Test: Comprehensive confirmatory eye examination
      Purpose: Establish best-corrected visual acuity, identify amblyopia risk factors, and determine whether ocular disease adequately accounts for reduced acuity.

      Purpose: Measure acuity separately in each eye and assess the interocular difference.

      Interpretation: Test with the current glasses prescription; use pinhole testing if it is unavailable. Use an occlusive eye patch and a testing distance of 3 meters or greater. A refined refraction may contribute to determining BCVA.

      Purpose: Assess ocular and neurological findings, including constant or intermittent strabismus, ocular suppression, and stereopsis.

      Purpose: Look for ocular findings that could account for reduced visual acuity.
      When indicated: As part of the complete confirmatory eye examination.
    - Test: Clinical history
      Purpose: Document previous vision screening and eye care, family history of eye disease, and ocular or neurological trauma and/or surgery.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: Park et al. 2023 Long term visual outcomes in children with regressed retinopathy of prematurity
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: ROP screening and management.
  Content: Infants in the neonatal intensive care unit underwent ROP screening if birth weight was less than 1,500 g or GA was less than 30 weeks. Findings were classified by retinal zone and stage under the Screening Examination of Premature Infants for Retinopathy of Prematurity. All three zones are centered on the optic disc: Zone I covers the posterior pole within a circle whose radius is twice the disc-to-macula-center distance; Zone II extends to a concentric circle touching the nasal ora serrata, with its temporal boundary approximately at the anatomic equator; Zone III is the remaining anterior temporal retinal crescent. Peripheral abnormalities comprise Stage 1, a demarcation line; Stage 2, a ridge; Stage 3, a ridge accompanied by extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation; Stage 4, partial retinal detachment; and Stage 5, total retinal detachment. These abnormalities may progress to retinal detachment. Markedly increased posterior venous dilation and arteriolar tortuosity define plus disease, which indicates a worse prognosis. Aggressive posterior ROP (AP-ROP) denotes severe, rapidly progressing posterior disease with findings in Zone I or posterior Zone II, prominent plus disease in all four quadrants, and poorly demarcated retinopathy such as neovascularization. Retinal examinations occurred every 1–2 weeks until regression and complete vascularization. Patients meeting treatment criteria received laser photocoagulation and/or an intravitreal anti-VEGF injection. Following the 2006 and 2013 American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines, laser was used first-line in the early period before 2013. From 2013, after studies including BEAT-ROP suggested benefits from intravitreal anti-VEGF monotherapy, the clinic began combining intravitreal bevacizumab with laser. The authors describe anti-VEGF injection as less expensive, easier to administer and less stressful for infants than laser. More recently, following the RAINBOW study comparing ranibizumab with laser in very low birthweight infants with ROP, intravitreal ranibizumab monotherapy has been used first-line. Laser is considered if ROP does not regress after anti-VEGF treatment.

  Heading: People with diabetes
  Content: The number of people with diabetes has increased across countries during the past 30 years alongside lifestyle changes. Diabetic retinopathy is the most common diabetic microvascular complication and a leading preventable cause of vision impairment and blindness. If existing trends persist, a cited estimate projects a 1.2-fold rise in affected people, from 146 million in 2014 to 180.6 million in 2030. Most associated vision impairment can be avoided through risk-factor control, early identification and timely treatment. Many national and international professional societies have long endorsed systematic retinal screening of people with diabetes to detect vision-threatening disease, annually or biennially according to setting, followed by treatment when needed. Approaches include ophthalmoscopy by trained eye-care staff and retinal imaging interpreted locally or centrally through telemedicine. Lower-cost retinal cameras and artificial-intelligence approaches may improve access and quality closer to home.
