Main conclusion: The authors conclude that management of intraocular foreign bodies (IOFBs) requires careful examination, orbital CT without contrast for localization, and globe closure before extraction. Removal may be immediate or delayed according to the patient’s condition, visibility, and clinical setting; pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) remains the principal approach for posterior-segment IOFBs, while further research is needed to clarify complications, visual prognostic factors, and optimal surgery.

Narrative summary: This mini review synthesizes published evidence on the frequency, assessment, treatment, and outcomes of intraocular foreign bodies (IOFBs). IOFBs are estimated to occur in 18-41% of open globe injuries, and occupational exposure accounts for many cases. The authors emphasize a thorough but gentle examination, including slit-lamp biomicroscopy and assessment of the posterior segment. Orbital CT without contrast is the preferred initial imaging study when an IOFB is suspected; it can identify an IOFB in up to 95% of patients. Magnetic resonance imaging is contraindicated if a metallic foreign body is suspected.

Initial management prioritizes globe closure. The timing of extraction depends on the patient’s stability, the foreign body’s composition, the injury, visualization, and surgical resources. Toxic metals and organic material call for immediate removal; signs of endophthalmitis also indicate immediate surgery unless a simultaneous life-threatening injury precludes it. Delayed extraction may be appropriate in other circumstances. For posterior-segment IOFBs, PPV is the main surgical approach. The review also discusses antimicrobial prophylaxis and techniques for removing difficult-to-grasp objects.

Visual prognosis varies: published reports indicate that at least 21% of affected eyes have final visual acuity worse than 20/200. The authors recommend counseling on eye protection and, when outcomes are poor, monocular precautions and low-vision support. They also stress assessment for trauma-related mental health conditions.

Document sections:
  Heading: 2.6.2 Strategy for data synthesis
  Content: Data from included articles will be described, and effect sizes will be calculated in line with the Cochrane Collaboration handbook using Cochrane Review Manager v5.3. A preliminary search indicates that mean diameter and total area are common descriptors of optic disc size. The authors will report only mean diameter because its calculation is more straightforward. Where necessary, they plan to derive it from reported maximum and minimum diameters, horizontal diameter, or total area, assuming the optic disc can be approximated by a disc. The printed diameter expressions are partly unclear; the horizontal-diameter rule states that mean diameter equals horizontal diameter, while the total-area expression begins with 2. Data will be pooled as Hedge’s standardized mean difference. A fixed-effects model will be used for low-to-moderate heterogeneity (I2< 50%); otherwise, a random-effects model will be applied. A 95% confidence interval excluding the null value will indicate significance. Between-study variance, t2, will be estimated with the Restricted Maximum-Likelihood formula. Statistical analyses and plots will use R v4.0.3 and the ‘Metafor’ package.

  Content: Many tumors, tumor-like conditions, systemic diseases, metastases, and high- or low-flow vascular malformations can involve the orbit. Distinguishing vascular from other lesions guides subsequent workup and care. Because the orbital space is restricted, either a soft-tissue or vascular mass may cause proptosis. Orbital-apex masses or inflammation characteristically produce vision loss with ophthalmoplegia. Orbital masses can be classified by location in the globe, optic nerve sheath complex, intraconal or extraconal space, bone, or multiple compartments. Benign lesions predominate, but malignant orbital tumors become more prevalent in adults older than 60 years of age. Among cysts, dermoid cysts are most common; excluding cysts, cavernous venous malformation is the commonest benign adult orbital mass, while non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the commonest malignant one. Document sections:
  Heading: Abstract
  Content: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the most frequent chronic complication of herpes zoster. It is a form of neuropathic pain that can substantially impair quality of life, particularly in older or immunocompromised people, despite the availability of vaccination. This review examines the effectiveness and safety of oral and topical medicines for PHN-related neuropathic pain. It draws on 49 scientific publications identified through PubMed, PubMedCentral, NCBI and Via Medica Journals and published between 2008–2024. Pharmacological treatment includes several oral and topical drug groups. Gabapentinoids and tricyclic anti-depressants are regarded as first-line options; lidocaine 5% patches have that position in some circumstances. Capsaicin 8% and opioids are considered second-line options. Because monotherapy relatively often fails to control pain, multimodal treatment is increasingly used. PHN remains difficult to manage, and the review emphasizes combining medicines with different mechanisms of action and selecting treatment according to the individual clinical situation.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Posterior Fossa (PF)
  Content: PF tumours are the most common CNS neoplasms of childhood and affect sight through several mechanisms. Raised intracranial pressure commonly causes acute papilledema in the vast majority of children with PF masses. Papilledema usually resolves when the pressure is adequately treated, but severe or prolonged pressure can lead to optic atrophy, axonal death and visual loss. In very young children, papilledema can be absent because unfused sutures allow head enlargement. Early papilledema may cause few symptoms apart from an enlarged blind spot; nasal, arcuate or central VF defects can follow. CN-VI palsy from dorsal pontine compression or brainstem displacement may cause esotropia, horizontal diplopia and compensatory head turning. Reported findings in children with PF tumours include gaze palsy and strabismus (42%), upbeat nystagmus (23%) and abnormal acuity (15%), defined as VA below 20/40 (or > 0.3 logMAR) in one or both eyes. Frequent tumour types are WHO grade IV Medulloblastoma (MBL), cerebellar WHO grade I pilocytic astrocytoma (PA), and ependymoma (EP); MBL and EP carry greater abnormal-vision risk than cerebellar PA. Survivors of MB or cerebellar PA frequently have persistent strabismus (25-29%) or nystagmus (12.5- 18%). ATRT and rare embryonal tumours can occur here with similar features.

Document sections:
  Heading: History
  Content: Ask about blurred or fluctuating vision, including morning worsening and later improvement; photophobia, redness, tearing, foreign-body sensation, pain, recent ocular procedures and complications, age and speed of onset, persistence, laterality, and modifying conditions. Edema usually develops over weeks, months, or longer, but elevated IOP, substantial inflammation, hydrops, and trauma can produce more abrupt symptoms. Most noninfectious opacities develop gradually, apart from acute medication-related band keratopathy; infectious opacities often appear acutely. Edema caused by inflammation or pressure can resolve when its cause resolves. Edema after neonatal forceps injury may resolve after Descemet’s membrane heals but recur years later if endothelial injury was substantial. Endothelial dysfunction may produce transient blur after waking, humidity, or showering that improves later through evaporation. Most noninflammatory opacities persist; inflammatory infiltrates often resolve with their cause, and some metabolic deposits may respond to treatment. Laterality may distinguish usually unilateral herpes simplex virus keratitis from typically bilateral dystrophies. Low humidity and modest airflow may improve vision in endothelial dysfunction. Visual acuity can understate disability: a patient with mild Fuchs dystrophy edema or granular corneal dystrophy opacity may measure 20/40 or better yet be unable to drive because of glare; lighting, reflections, screens, and higher order aberrations can impair function. Contact lenses, particularly RGP lenses, may improve vision by regularizing the refracting surface. Review ocular disease, surgery, infection, inflammation, trauma, glaucoma, and keratoconus; systemic inflammatory, developmental, metabolic, hereditary, and immune-mediated disease; malabsorption-associated vitamin A deficiency; topical and systemic exposures; contact lens practices; family history; sun exposure, travel, animal exposure, diet, and chemical exposure. Short exposure to Amantadine may cause reversible endothelial dysfunction, whereas long exposure may cause permanent dysfunction. Accidental corneal exposure to chlorhexidine during facial surgical preparation may predispose to endothelial failure. Other exposures noted include carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, Bupropion, Amiodarone, calcium supplements, periocular radiation, chemotherapeutic agents, and Rho kinase inhibitor-related verticillate changes.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 5: Adult. Acute or chronic vision loss, optic nerve abnormality suspected. Initial imaging.
  Content: Neoplastic, inflammatory, ischemic, demyelinating, and traumatic processes can affect the optic nerve or its sheath and produce acute, subacute, or chronic visual loss. Neoplasms tend to develop more slowly than other optic neuropathies. Optic nerve gliomas are the most common primary optic nerve neoplasm; they can be incidental, including in younger patients with neurofibromatosis type 1, or present with visual symptoms or proptosis, and are more likely to be malignant when presenting in adults. Orbital meningiomas can arise from the optic nerve sheath or extend from an intracranial mass; symptomatic sheath lesions classically cause gradual, painless visual decline. Inflammatory and demyelinating ON can resemble one another clinically and radiologically; enhancement reflects edema, inflammation, or demyelination. Possible causes of demyelinating ON include MS, NMO, and MOGAD. ON can also reflect chronic relapsing-remitting inflammatory disease, steroid-dependent recurrence, systemic inflammation, or infection. Enhancement patterns overlap but may help: bilateral simultaneous and longer optic nerve involvement occur more often with MOGAD or NMO than MS, which characteristically affects a shorter unilateral segment. Sheath or perioptic enhancement is more distinctive of MOGAD. Anterior involvement is more typical of MS or MOGAD; NMO tends toward posterior nerves, chiasm, or tracts. Brain and spine MRI may identify associated abnormalities; asymptomatic optic nerve lesions may help distinguish relapsing-remitting MS or clinically isolated syndrome from NMO or MOGAD. Optic perineuritis can arise from idiopathic orbital inflammation, autoimmunity, infection, or other inflammation and may mimic acute demyelinating ON, including visual loss and pain worsened by eye movement. Patients with perineuritis tend to be older and more likely to retain central vision. Ischemic optic neuropathy is anterior, AION, when involving the nerve head, or posterior, PION, when involving the retrobulbar nerve. AION classically causes disc edema and altitudinal field loss. Either form may be nonarteritic, in patients with vascular risk factors such as hypertension or diabetes, or arteritic, most commonly from giant cell arteritis. Imaging aims to identify optic nerve disease, narrow overlapping diagnoses, and inform management.

Document sections:
  Heading: 4.3.1. Sturge-Weber-syndrome
  Content: Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS) is an uncommon sporadic neurocutaneous disorder, formerly categorized as a phakomatosis. Among its three variants, types 1 and 2 are suggested by a characteristic facial port-wine angioma, whereas type 3 has leptomeningeal angiomatosis without that readily visible feature. Seizures occur in 75 %–90 % of cases. Extensive pial angiomatosis causes seizures and can affect one lobe or much of a hemisphere; the epileptogenic cortex is presumed to extend beyond visible angiomatous plaques. Native bone-setting computed tomography (CT), contrast-enhanced T1W MRI and especially contrast-enhanced fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) help define the extent of calcified pial angiomatosis. Approximately 60 % of patients develop drug resistance. Patients whose plaques remain strictly unilateral are suitable candidates for disconnection, with reported long-term seizure freedom of 80 %.

  Name: Retinal detachment
  Description: Separation involving the retina can cause acute visual loss. Prompt treatment may be needed to avoid permanent impairment. Diagnosis usually relies on clinical and ophthalmologic examination rather than initial cross-sectional imaging.
  Epidemiology: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is the most common form.
  Clinical presentation: Acute vision loss may occur. Vitreous hemorrhage can prevent visualization of the posterior eye during funduscopic examination.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
      Distinguishing features: A defect in the neurosensory retina allows vitreous fluid to collect between the sensory and pigmented retinal layers.
    - Name: Exudative (serous) retinal detachment
      Distinguishing features: Subretinal fluid accumulates without a break in the neurosensory epithelium. An underlying inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic, vascular or degenerative process may be responsible.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Dilated funduscopic examination
      Purpose: Establish the diagnosis of retinal detachment.
      When indicated: Used in the initial clinical assessment.
    - Test: Ocular US
      Purpose: Establish the diagnosis when funduscopic visualization of the posterior eye is obscured.
      When indicated: May be used, for example, in the presence of vitreous hemorrhage; avoid if globe rupture is known or suspected.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Gousse et al. 2021 The AUASUFU Guideline on Adult Neurogenic Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction__JC__000248
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Gousse et al. 2021 The AUASUFU Guideline on Adult Neurogenic Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Surgical Treatment
  Content: Selected men may be offered sphincterotomy for emptying, with mandatory counseling about its high failure risk and possible further intervention. Urethral bulking agents may be offered for stress incontinence, with counseling that benefit is modest and cure uncommon (both Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Selected patients with stress incontinence and acceptable storage parameters should be offered slings (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C) and may be offered artificial urinary sphincter (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). After discussing risks, benefits, and alternatives, bladder neck closure with another drainage method may be offered for selected refractory stress incontinence (Expert Opinion). Posterior tibial nerve stimulation may be offered to selected spontaneous voiders with urgency, frequency, or urgency incontinence; sacral neuromodulation may be offered to selected patients with these symptoms, but should not be offered to patients with spinal cord injury or spina bifida (each Conditional Recommendation or, for the restriction, Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Selected patients refractory to or intolerant of less invasive treatments for detrusor overactivity or poor compliance may be offered augmentation cystoplasty. Continent catheterizable channels may facilitate catheterization, with or without augmentation. Selected patients may be offered ileovesicostomy after counseling about risks, alternatives, and the high likelihood of additional treatment or surgery (each Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Urinary diversion should be offered if other options fail or are unsuitable to improve long-term quality of life (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Other potential therapies should be treated as investigational, with corresponding patient counseling (Expert Opinion).

Document sections:
  Heading: b.- Embolización de las arterias uterinas
  Content: La embolización de las arterias uterinas (EAU) es mínimamente invasiva y se plantea como alternativa a operaciones más invasivas. Se ha comunicado eficacia y alta satisfacción en mujeres con leiomiomas. Frente a las técnicas quirúrgicas citadas, se describe como menos costosa y asociada a recuperación más breve y menos dolor. Sus efectos secundarios habituales son dolor pélvico, náuseas y fiebre por necrosis isquémica; aproximadamente el 5 % presenta complicaciones importantes, entre ellas hemorragia, reintervención e infección. También se ha comunicado deterioro de función ovárica después de EAU. En adenomiosis sintomática, varios estudios observaron mejoría clínica sostenida. Entre sus limitaciones figuran posible recrecimiento temprano de la adenomiosis y disponibilidad restringida. El dolor puede prolongarse un máximo de 1 a 2 meses, similar al posterior a la escisión laparoscópica. La intervención requiere radiólogos calificados.

question: Which of the following is/are a complication of urethral stricture?

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__EAUN Guideline Urethral intermittent catheterisation in adults 2024__JC__000354
retrieved_chunks.document_id: EAUN Guideline Urethral intermittent catheterisation in adults 2024
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 15.2 Contraindications
  Content: Suspected or confirmed urethral rupture, UTI or false passage are listed contraindications. Injury to urethral epithelium can heal with scarring and stricture formation. Male strictures commonly cause obstructive voiding symptoms and may follow IC, infection, trauma, lichen sclerosus, prostate-cancer treatment such as radiotherapy, or an unidentified cause. UK Hospital Episode Statistics and similar US data suggest male incidence rises from about 10 in every 100,000 up to 25 years to 40 in every 100,000 by the age of 65 years and > 100 in every 100,000 over 65 years. Female urethral strictures affect 0.1–1% of women with voiding complaints and can cause irritative as well as obstructive symptoms. In a review by Chakraborty et al., 53.48% of surgically treated female strictures were presumed idiopathic and 91.29% had a prior intervention. Smith et al. attributed 8% of female strictures to inflammation and infection and 6.6% to trauma. Male strictures may occur anywhere, particularly in the bulbar urethra (50 %) and at the meatus. In selected patients, intermittent dilatation is established as palliative management of refractory strictures and can reduce recurrence up to 68%. Diversion, such as a continent stoma or ileal conduit, is required if reconstruction is impossible or repair attempts fail. A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to determine which of dilatation, endoscopic urethrotomy or urethroplasty best balances effectiveness, adverse effects and costs. A small RCT (n=49) comparing CISC with repeated sounds dilatation reported a statistically significant improvement in flow rate and QoL among patients performing CISC.

  Content: Urinary leakage is the characteristic finding; it is generally painless and constant, although position-dependent leakage can be intermittent. Intraoperative recognition of genitourinary or gastrointestinal injury occurs in only about half of cases. VVF assessment generally combines history and direct-visualisation examination with selected imaging or laboratory investigations. Cystoscopy and retrograde coloured-fluid bladder filling with a vaginal tampon can identify staining; a double-dye test may distinguish UVF from VVF. Creatinine in leaked or collected fluid confirms that the fluid is urine. Late-excretory-phase contrast CT can identify fistulae, ureteric integrity and possible urinoma; MRI, particularly T2-weighted imaging, can also provide diagnostic detail. The evidence table rates the roles of examination, coloured-fluid cystoscopy, CT and MRI at 3. Strong: Obtain a full history and focused examination with direct inspection when fistula is suspected. question: Diversion of urinary bladder is best done at

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__EAU Guidelines on Urethral Strictures 2023__JC__000483
retrieved_chunks.document_id: EAU Guidelines on Urethral Strictures 2023
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 6.3.5.1.4 Extirpative surgery and urinary diversion for non-traumatic posterior urethral stenosis
  Content: In complex or recurrent disease, severe necrosis, calcification or morbidity—particularly severe pain—may make LUT reconstruction inappropriate or impossible. Intractable haematuria and fistulation are other reasons to abandon the urethral outlet. Such patients commonly have previous pelvic irradiation or high-energy prostate cancer treatment and multiple prior treatment attempts. Preserving the bladder requires adequate capacity, compliance and function, as well as healthy distal ureters. The last-resort option is continent or incontinent urinary diversion, with or without cystectomy; selection depends largely on bladder capacity, local symptoms, performance status and patient expectations. Cystectomy at diversion can relieve otherwise unmanageable bladder pain, spasms and haematuria, especially after pelvic radiotherapy. In Sack et al.’s study of fifteen patients, satisfaction was 100%, and the overwhelming majority would have undergone surgery an average of thirteen months earlier. Faris et al. reported that 27% also needed bowel diversion because of intractable gastrointestinal morbidity. Improved QoL and high satisfaction after diversion, and palliation of pain, spasms and haematuria by cystectomy, each have LE 3. Perform diversion for recurrent or complex disease with reduced bladder capacity and/or incapacitating local symptoms (Weak); perform cystectomy during diversion for intractable bladder pain, spasms and/or haematuria (Weak).

Document sections:
  Heading: Clinical Practice
  Content: Offer surgery as one option for endometriosis-associated pain. Before surgery, discuss the procedure, expected effect on symptoms, risks, benefits and possible need for another operation. Use laparoscopy rather than laparotomy unless contraindicated, and consider excision instead of ablation for pain. For endometrioma, consider ovarian cystectomy or CO2 laser vaporisation rather than drainage with coagulation to reduce recurrence and pain. Minimise ovarian injury, particularly with recurrent endometrioma or concern about ovarian reserve.

For women who no longer intend to conceive and have not benefited from conservative treatment, hysterectomy with or without ovarian removal may be considered. If hysterectomy is chosen, the guideline favours total over sub-total hysterectomy because endometriosis may persist in or near a retained cervix. All visible lesions should be excised during hysterectomy. Women should understand that hysterectomy does not necessarily eliminate symptoms. If a woman with previous endometriosis needs menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), a continuous oestrogen-progestogen regimen is advised.

question: Hematuria with dysmorphic RBC are seen in

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Lee et al. 2025 Comparison of Urinary Red Blood Cell Distribution ( URDspan__JC__000113
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Lee et al. 2025 Comparison of Urinary Red Blood Cell Distribution ( URDspan
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 1 | Introduction
  Content: Hematuria means RBCs are present in urine and may be visible or detectable only microscopically. It is a fundamental manifestation of glomerulonephritis (GN); microscopic assessment of urinary sediment is presented as its most effective detection method. Birch et al. proposed in 1979 that urinary RBC morphology could distinguish glomerular from non-glomerular origins. Passage through glomeruli can damage RBC membranes and produce dysmorphic RBCs (dRBCs). Shichiri et al. reported in 1988 that erythrocytes were smaller in glomerular than in non-glomerular disease, and Hyodo et al. later proposed an RBC size range of 4–6 μm for discriminating the origins. Compared with blood, urine has much less albumin and more urea; this environment increases membrane vulnerability and changes RBC shape. High urea concentrations particularly favor burr-cell formation. Passage across the glomerular basement membrane may produce acanthocytes through membrane injury. RBCs in renal disease are also more susceptible to factors including iron deficiency, osmotic lysis, shape distortion, and vesicle formation. Reliable recognition of urinary dRBCs requires an experienced observer, and observer-dependent interpretation may explain differences between laboratories. The authors consider continuing education in RBC morphology essential and mention deep learning for microscopy as another possible approach. Instrument-measured small-RBC fractions are easier to obtain and less dependent on interpretation, making them potentially more objective and standardized. The fully automated UF-5000 uses fluorescence flow cytometry to classify urine particles and reports morphological RBC information, including non-lysed RBCs, lysed RBCs, large RBCs, small RBCs, and RBC-Info. Its classification uses forward scatter light (FSC), side scatter light (SSC), side fluorescence light (SFL), and depolarized side scattered light (DSS). A small RBC has FSC intensity < 70; a non-lysed RBC has a strong FSC signal and morphological stability indicated by SSC. URD is the small-RBC count divided by the non-lysed-RBC count. Earlier studies investigated possible clinical uses, but most were single-center studies. Reported cutoffs for distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular hematuria varied from 30.1% to 40.5% for small RBCs and from 0% to 30.0% for dRBCs. The authors therefore considered a multicenter assessment using the same equipment necessary for clinical application. Across four hospitals, they collected urine microscopy findings, urine measures, serum markers, and kidney-function information to compare institutional dRBC and URD measurements and cutoffs and assess their clinical significance.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: NCCN Prostate Cancer Early Detection Version 2.2024 — March 6, 2024
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: PSA Testing
  Content: PSA is secreted by prostate epithelial cells; its protease activity liquefies coagulated ejaculate and promotes sperm motility. How it enters the circulation is unknown. Commercial serum assays perform similarly when appropriately used apart from small calibration differences, but results from differently calibrated assays cannot be directly exchanged. Repeat an unusually high result, especially near an evaluation threshold; in one study, approximately 25% initially measuring 4 to 10 ng/mL had a normal repeat result. PSA is not specific to cancer: most people with elevated values do not have prostate cancer, and no low value eliminates risk. Total PSA >10 ng/mL corresponds to greater than 67% likelihood of biopsy-detectable cancer; about 18% with PSA 4 to 10 ng/mL have a subsequent positive biopsy. In PCPT data from 18,882 participants, end-of-study biopsy identified cancer in 15% with PSA of 4.0 ng/mL or less and normal DRE. At 3.1 ng/mL, sensitivity for any prostate cancer was about 32% and specificity about 87%. Appropriate PSA testing alone can advance diagnosis by 5 to 10 years, with variation across studies, populations, and protocols. After PSA testing was introduced, detection shifted toward early organ-confined disease and away from metastasis at diagnosis. Population-screening studies have demonstrated survival benefits using PSA, sometimes alongside DRE or other tests.

      Distinguishing features: A residual lumen remains after partial injury or unsuccessful early realignment.
    - Name: obliterative stenosis
      Distinguishing features: A complete injury leaves separated urethral ends with intervening fibrotic tissue.
    - Name: pelvic fracture urethral injury (PFUI)
      Distinguishing features: Pelvic-fracture-associated posterior urethral injury that can result in a distraction defect.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Retrograde urethrography (RUG) and voiding cystourethrography (VCUG)
      Purpose: Delineate the distal and proximal urethra and estimate the injury gap.
      When indicated: Evaluation of PFUI and posterior stenosis before reconstruction.
    - Test: Retrograde urethroscopy and antegrade cystoscopy
      Purpose: Assess gap length, bladder-neck competence, scarring and associated fistulae, false passages, calculi or bony abnormalities.
      When indicated: When additional information is required beyond imaging.
    - Test: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
      Purpose: Assess anatomy and features relevant to operative planning.
      When indicated: Ancillary assessment of PFUI.
      Interpretation: In a cited study, the MRI-measured pubo-urethral stump angle predicted the need for a more elaborate approach.
    - Test: Sexual-function assessment
      Purpose: Document function after injury and during recovery.
      When indicated: Assessment before and after reconstructive surgery.
      Interpretation: Normal erectile function may return during the first two years after trauma.
  Staging:
    Additional rules: The distinction between non-obliterative and obliterative disease determines whether an endoluminal approach can be considered.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Following urethroplasty, offer at least one year of follow-up; the proposed schedule for low-risk bulbar or (bulbo)membranous anastomotic repair is 3 months, 12 months and 24 months when the specified additional risk features are absent.
    Recommended tests:
      - Uroflowmetry and PROM, including sexual function, at proposed visits.
      - Anatomic assessment at 3 months, with later anatomic testing when indicated.
    Long term effects:
      - Recurrent posterior narrowing is possible.
      - Erectile and ejaculatory changes and urinary incontinence may occur after the injury or reconstruction.
    Survivorship notes: Interpret post-operative sexual-function changes in the context of the initial trauma.

Document sections:
  Heading: 3.1 Epidemiology
  Content: UC is the second most frequent urological malignancy in developed countries and can arise in the lower urinary tract or the pyelocaliceal cavities and ureter. Bladder cancer (BC) constitutes 90–95% of UC, whereas UTUC constitutes 5–10%; estimated annual incidence in Western countries is almost two cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Incidence has increased over recent decades, possibly because detection improved and populations aged. Incidence peaks at 70–90 years, and UTUC occurs twice as often in men. In an international retrospective registry of 2,380 people diagnosed between 2014 and 2019 at 101 centres in 29 countries, 70.5% were men, 53.3% were current or former smokers, and 53% received a diagnosis after symptoms, chiefly visible haematuria. A meta-analysis of 44 studies estimated UTUC incidence among people with visible and non-visible haematuria at 0.75% and 0.17%, respectively. Approximately two-thirds of patients presenting with UTUC have muscle-invasive disease at diagnosis, versus 15–25% with newly diagnosed BC; population studies from Germany and England suggest muscle-invasive UTUC accounts for approximately half of recent incident cases. Approximately 9% present with metastases. Pyelocaliceal tumours occur approximately twice as frequently as ureteral tumours; multifocality occurs in approximately 10–20%, and concomitant upper-tract carcinoma in situ in between 11% and 36%. Concurrent BC occurs in 17%; previous BC was recorded in 41% of American men and 4% of Chinese men. These differences, alongside genetic and epigenetic factors, may help explain more advanced, higher-grade presentations in Asian patients. After treatment, bladder recurrence occurs in 29%, varying with patient, tumour and treatment characteristics, versus 2–5% recurrence in the contralateral upper tract. UTUC and BC differ substantially in frequencies of common genomic changes, although tumours in a person with both cancers are often clonally related. UTUC genomic profiling can inform bladder-recurrence risk and identify Lynch syndrome-associated tumours. Among 82 patients given intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) for high-risk BC and imaged regularly between years 1 and 3, 13% developed asymptomatic UTUC; another series of 307 patients without routine upper-tract imaging reported 25% UTUC after BC. A multicentre cohort of n = 402 followed for 50 month reported 7.5% UTUC among NMIBC recipients of BCG; intravesical recurrence and a non-papillary tumour at transurethral resection of the bladder (TURB) predicted UTUC. Following radical cystectomy for MIBC, 3–5% develop metachronous UTUC.

Document sections:
  Heading: 4.8.4.3 Management of ureteric fistulae
  Content: Higher-risk operations require surgeons able to protect ureteric blood supply and promptly recognise injury. An intraoperative injury should be repaired immediately using debridement, adequate vascularity, a tension-free anastomosis and internal stenting. After relevant abdominal or pelvic surgery, unexpectedly slow recovery, fluid leakage or pelvicalyceal dilatation should raise suspicion of delayed upper-tract injury. No operative approach has proved superior; consensus favours established tissue-repair principles and experienced teams. Options include internal or external drainage, nephrostomy and stenting, and repair early (< 2 weeks) or later (> 3 months) when needed. Functional and anatomical imaging after repair should detect ureteric stricture or declining renal function. Early postoperative UVF, chiefly following hysterectomy, is the most frequent upper-tract fistula presentation in urological practice. In an RCT of 3,141 women undergoing open or laparoscopic gynaecological surgery, prophylactic ureteric stents did not alter the low injury risk (1%). Selected endoscopic approaches include retrograde or antegrade stenting with nephrostomy, or ureteroscopic realignment, but long-term success is unknown. Distal antegrade ureteric occlusion plus nephrostomy often palliates terminal malignant-fistula leakage. Failure or secondary stricture after endoluminal treatment usually calls for abdominal repair, potentially including end-to-end anastomosis, reimplantation with psoas hitch or Boari flap, or bowel replacement. Nephrectomy is a last resort, particularly with poor function on the affected side and a normal opposite kidney.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 5.5 Urinary cytology
  Content: Cytology of voided urine or bladder washings detects exfoliated malignant cells with sensitivity 84% for HG/G3 tumours and 16% for LG/G1 tumours; CIS sensitivity ranges from 28–100%. A report using the Paris system found sensitivity 46% for HG disease. Cytology complements cystoscopy for HG/G3 disease but is not intended to detect LG tumours. Positive voided cytology can indicate UC anywhere in the tract, while a negative result cannot exclude it. Interpretation varies by reader and can be impaired by sparse cells, infection, stones or intravesical treatment, although experienced practitioners achieve specificity exceeding 90%. Digital image processing with artificial intelligence in the VisioCyt test raised HG sensitivity up to 92%. The Paris System 2022 (2nd Edn.) uses the full diagnostic categories No adequate diagnosis possible (No diagnosis), Negative for UC (Negative), Atypical urothelial cells (Atypia), Suspicious for HG UC (Suspicious), and High-grade/G3 UC (Malignant). Its terminology emphasizes HG/G3 detection, and retrospective studies have validated it. A prospective study suggested pre-TURB risk stratification: cytology negative for HG had 93% specificity for LG disease; an HG-positive result predicted HG disease with 92% specificity and 91% PPV. One cytospin slide is usually sufficient. Suspicious cytology warrants repeat investigation because the underlying risk of an HG lesion is 24-53%. Adjunctive voided cytology for HG detection and reporting with the Paris System 2nd Edn. each have a Strong recommendation. Obtain at least 25 mL of fresh or adequately fixed urine; first-morning urine is unsuitable because cytolysis is frequent (Strong).

  Content: For asymptomatic patients, the EAU favours initial US because it avoids radiation, costs less and can identify hydronephrosis and stones in the calyces, renal pelvis and pelvic-ureteric or vesico-ureteric junctions. For symptomatic patients, NCCT is preferred: it characterises density, diameter, volume, skin-to-stone distance and surrounding anatomy to inform treatment, and is more accurate than US or IVU (EAU: strong recommendation). Contrast-enhanced imaging is advised when collecting-system anatomy must be assessed before removal (EAU: strong recommendation). The AUA recommends NCCT before PCNL (AUA: strong recommendation) and when choosing between SWL and URS (AUA: conditional recommendation); US alone is discouraged for the latter decision. Suspected substantial renal injury may warrant a DTPA or MAG-3 renogram to guide care (AUA: conditional recommendation). The EAU advises testing serum creatinine, uric acid, ionised calcium, sodium, potassium, blood cell counts and C-reactive protein, plus coagulation when intervention is intended (EAU: strong recommendation). Both organisations strongly recommend urine culture and microscopy before intervention.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 6.8. High Risk for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
  Content: An adolescent symptom constellation can indicate high risk for future PCOS. In adults, Rotterdam criteria confirm PCOS when two of three features are present: oligo-/amenorrhea, hyperandrogenemia or signs of androgenization, and sonomorphological evidence of polycystic ovaries. These criteria should not be applied in adolescence, and PCOS should not be diagnosed until 8 years after menarche. Blood androgen concentrations reach adult female levels only at ages 12–15, and clear cut-offs are lacking. Androgens originate in the adrenal cortex, periphery, and adipose tissue. Polycystic ovarian appearance is unsuitable as an adolescent diagnostic criterion because around 33% of girls of this age have it on sonography; its presence alone does not establish PCOS. Oligomenorrhoea together with hyperandrogenemia appears to signal increased later PCOS risk. Adolescents should therefore be classified as high risk and followed closely without premature diagnostic labeling or distress. Individualized monitoring is important because associated risks include metabolic syndrome, impaired glucose tolerance, type II diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, arterial hypertension, sterility, endometrial cancer, and depression. The Ferriman–Gallwey score permits patient assessment of body hair in hirsutism; Figure 6 illustrates pronounced hirsutism and obesity permagna in a 16-year-old girl at high risk for PCOS. Possible laboratory findings include LH/FSH quotient >>2, Homa index >2.5, abnormal oral glucose tolerance or HbA1c, elevated AMH, and, with obesity, low SHBG or dyslipidemia. Normal 17-OH progesterone helps distinguish this constellation from congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). None of these additional laboratory abnormalities is a diagnostic criterion. Diagnosis requires exclusion of other hyperandrogenemia causes. Etiology remains largely uncertain, although genetic and environmental contributions appear possible. Several mechanisms may lead to anovulation; the proposed “two-hit” theory combines predisposition with a trigger such as insulin resistance. PCOS treatment should be multidisciplinary. An anti-androgen contraceptive pill is the primary treatment for cycle disturbance; oral contraception is also preferred for acne, hirsutism, and regular endometrial transformation during amenorrhea. Cyproterone acetate, dienogest, chlormadinone acetate, and drospirenone are described as potent antiandrogenic progestins. Lowering androgens improves acne and hirsutism, although visible improvement in hair growth can take a good 6–9 months. With obesity, exercise and nutritional counseling are important aspects of lifestyle change; collaboration with dieticians or an obesity center can help, and multidisciplinary care improves treatment success. Metformin is an insulin sensitizer that can support weight reduction, particularly with insulin resistance and BMI over 25 kg/m2. Its dose is increased gradually to a maximum of 2000 mg daily to limit gastrointestinal effects such as diarrhea, and it works only in combination with exercise. Dermatological support may help acne; laser treatment can be tried for distressing hirsutism, and eflornithine cream can slow facial hair growth and reduce shaving frequency. Marked obesity, thrombophilia-related coagulation disorder, arterial hypertension, or nicotine use may contraindicate oral contraception; progestogen-only preparations such as cyproterone acetate or drospirenone can then be tried. Individual contraceptive needs must be considered. Without endometrial transformation during amenorrhea, hyperplasia may arise. Given metabolic risk, close OGTT monitoring, weight and blood-pressure checks even in slim girls, and lipid assessment are sensible to enable timely referral for treatment.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Peris et al. 2023 European consensus based interdisciplinary guideline for diagnosis and treatment of basal cell carci__JC__000190
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Peris et al. 2023 European consensus based interdisciplinary guideline for diagnosis and treatment of basal cell carci
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Abstract
  Content: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most frequent malignancy in white populations. European multidisciplinary experts updated guidance on its diagnosis and treatment and distinguish ‘easy-to-treat’ from ‘difficult-to-treat’ BCC using the EADO clinical classification. Clinical and dermatoscopic findings generally establish the diagnosis, but uncertain lesions require histopathological confirmation. Complete surgical removal is first-line treatment. Micrographically controlled surgery shall be offered for high-risk or recurrent tumours and those at critical anatomical sites. Topical or destructive treatments can be considered for low-risk superficial BCC; photodynamic therapy is effective for superficial and low-risk nodular BCC. A multidisciplinary tumour board should discuss difficult-to-treat cases. Patients with locally advanced or metastatic BCC should be offered the Hedgehog inhibitors vismodegib or sonidegib. Anti-PD1 treatment with cemiplimab is a second-line option after progression, contraindication or intolerance to Hedgehog inhibitors. Radiotherapy is an alternative when surgery is unsuitable or declined, particularly in older patients; electrochemotherapy may be offered if surgery or radiotherapy is contraindicated. Gorlin syndrome requires regular skin examinations for early detection and treatment. Long-term follow-up is recommended for high-risk BCC, multiple BCCs and Gorlin syndrome.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__EAU Guidelines on Sexual and Reproductive Health 2025.cap08__JC__000021
retrieved_chunks.document_id: EAU Guidelines on Sexual and Reproductive Health 2025.cap08
retrieved_chunks.text:
Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_19
  Name: Varicocele
  Description: A common congenital venous abnormality that can be associated with impaired testicular growth, sub-fertility, discomfort or hypogonadism.
  Epidemiology: Present in almost 15% of the general male population, 25% of men with abnormal semen analysis and 35-40% of men presenting with infertility. Reported incidence is 35–44% in primary infertility and 45–81% in secondary infertility.
  Clinical presentation: It may be palpable or visible, cause pain or discomfort, and accompany abnormal semen parameters. Worsening semen parameters are associated with greater grade and age.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Subclinical
      Distinguishing features: Neither palpable nor visible at rest or with Valsalva manoeuvre, but detectable with a special test such as Doppler US.
    - Name: Grade 1
      Distinguishing features: Palpable during Valsalva manoeuvre.
    - Name: Grade 2
      Distinguishing features: Palpable at rest.
    - Name: Grade 3
      Distinguishing features: Visible and palpable at rest.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Physical examination
      Purpose: Establish the clinical diagnosis and grade.
      When indicated: Suspected varicocele.
      Interpretation: Palpability and visibility at rest or during Valsalva manoeuvre distinguish the stated grades.
    - Test: Scrotal Doppler US
      Purpose: Assess reflux, vein diameter and persistent or recurrent varicocele.
      When indicated: Inconclusive examination or persistently unsatisfactory semen analysis after repair.
      Interpretation: A maximum diameter > 3 mm while upright and during Valsalva manoeuvre, together with reflux lasting > 2 seconds, correlates with clinically significant varicocele.
    - Test: Semen analysis
      Purpose: Assess fertility-related semen abnormalities.
      When indicated: Infertility evaluation or assessment after repair.
    - Test: Testicular volume assessment using Lambert’s formula
      Purpose: Estimate volume in patients with infertility and/or varicocele.
      When indicated: Assessment of testicular size.
      Interpretation: The stated formula is V=L x W x H x 0.71.
    - Test: Further abdominal and retroperitoneal assessment
      Purpose: Investigate underlying pathology or congenital anomalies.
      When indicated: Isolated clinical right varicocele.
    - Test: Sperm DNA fragmentation (SDF) testing
      Purpose: Assess DNA damage when relevant to infertility or ART failure.
      When indicated: Evaluation of selected men with infertility, particularly after ART failure or recurrent pregnancy loss.
  Staging:
    System: Varicocele classification
    Definitions:
      - Stage: Subclinical
        Description: Detected by a special examination but not palpable or visible at rest or during Valsalva manoeuvre.
      - Stage: Grade 1
        Description: Palpable only during Valsalva manoeuvre.
      - Stage: Grade 2
        Description: Palpable at rest.
      - Stage: Grade 3
        Description: Both visible and palpable at rest.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: After adolescent treatment decisions, persistent testicular size differences are confirmed at two subsequent visits six months apart; after repair, semen improvement generally takes up to two spermatogenic cycles.
    Recommended tests:
      - Serial clinical or Doppler US assessment of adolescent testicular growth when indicated.
      - Semen analysis after repair when results remain unsatisfactory.
      - Scrotal Doppler US when persistence or recurrence is suspected.
    Long term effects:
      - Potential progressive testicular damage and reduced fertility.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: Male infertility
  Description: Infertility is the failure of a sexually active couple to achieve spontaneous pregnancy within 12 mo without contraception. A male-associated factor is identified in 50% of couples who are involuntarily childless.
  Epidemiology: Approximately 15% of couples do not achieve pregnancy within 12 consecutive months and seek medical care. One in eight couples have difficulty conceiving a first child, and one in six have difficulty conceiving a subsequent child.
  Clinical presentation: Abnormal semen parameters commonly accompany a male-associated factor, but semen analysis alone cannot distinguish fertile from infertile men.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: primary infertility
      Distinguishing features: Difficulty conceiving a first child.
    - Name: secondary infertility
      Distinguishing features: Difficulty conceiving a subsequent child.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Medical, reproductive and family history
      Purpose: Identify possible causes and relevant health, lifestyle and behavioural factors.
      When indicated: During assessment of men seeking help for fertility problems.
    - Test: Physical examination
      Purpose: Assess male reproductive health, including testicular volume.
      When indicated: During assessment of men seeking help for fertility problems.
    - Test: Semen analysis
      Purpose: Assess semen and sperm characteristics using WHO reference values.
      When indicated: During the initial evaluation; obtain at least two consecutive analyses when the baseline result is abnormal.
      Interpretation: One analysis is sufficient if results meet WHO criteria. Abnormal results on at least two analyses warrant further andrological investigation. The 2021 lower reference limits (5th centile, with 95% CI) are semen volume 1.4 (1.3–1.5) ml; total sperm number 39 (35–40) 106/ejaculate; sperm concentration 16 (15–18) 106/ml; total motility 42 (40–43)%; progressive motility 30 (29–31)%; vitality 54 (50–56)%; and normal morphology 4 (3.9–4.0)%.
    - Test: Serum total testosterone, FSH and LH
      Purpose: Assess hormonal status and detect hypogonadism.
      When indicated: At least in all cases of oligozoospermia and azoospermia.
    - Test: Prader orchidometer or testicular US
      Purpose: Estimate testicular volume.
      When indicated: During assessment of infertile men.
    - Test: Scrotal US
      Purpose: Examine testicular structure, identify tumours and assess possible signs of obstruction.
      When indicated: In men with infertility; particularly useful when clinical assessment of testicular volume is difficult.
      Interpretation: Possible signs of obstruction include a dilated rete testis, an enlarged epididymis with cystic lesions, or an absent vas deferens.
    - Test: Female partner fertility assessment, including ovarian reserve
      Purpose: Inform the timing and choice of treatment for the couple.
      When indicated: In parallel with diagnosis and management of the infertile male.
    - Test: ROS measurement
      Purpose: Assess oxidative stress.
      When indicated: Routine testing is not recommended.
      Interpretation: Testing methods are not standardised and require further validation.
  Follow up:
    Long term effects:
      - Infertile men have increased risks of cardiometabolic disorders, cardiovascular mortality and overall mortality compared with fertile controls.
      - Infertile men have increased risks of testicular cancer and other cancers.
    Survivorship notes: The guideline advises counselling infertile men and men with abnormal semen parameters about associated health risks and screening infertile men for modifiable cardiovascular risk factors.

Document sections:
  Heading: Assessing pre-eclampsia
  Content: A professional trained in pregnancy-related hypertensive disorders should assess pre-eclampsia. Perform a complete clinical assessment at every antenatal visit and offer admission for observation or intervention if maternal or fetal wellbeing raises concern. Examples include sustained systolic pressure of 160 mmHg or higher; a new, persistent rise in creatinine to 90 micromol/litre or more, 1 mg/100 ml or more; alanine transaminase over 70 IU/litre or twice the upper limit of normal; platelets under 150,000/microlitre; impending eclampsia or pulmonary oedema; other severe features; suspected fetal compromise; or other concerning clinical findings. Consider fullPIERS or PREP-S alongside assessment to inform care location, possible in utero transfer and intervention thresholds. fullPIERS may be used at any pregnancy stage, whereas PREP-S is intended only up to 34 weeks; neither predicts infant outcomes. question: Most common tumor of urinary bladder is?

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__EAU Guidelines on Upper Urinary Tract Urothelial Carcinoma 2024__JC__000173
retrieved_chunks.document_id: EAU Guidelines on Upper Urinary Tract Urothelial Carcinoma 2024
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 3.1 Epidemiology
  Content: UC is the second most frequent urological malignancy in developed countries and can arise in the lower urinary tract or the pyelocaliceal cavities and ureter. Bladder cancer (BC) constitutes 90–95% of UC, whereas UTUC constitutes 5–10%; estimated annual incidence in Western countries is almost two cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Incidence has increased over recent decades, possibly because detection improved and populations aged. Incidence peaks at 70–90 years, and UTUC occurs twice as often in men. In an international retrospective registry of 2,380 people diagnosed between 2014 and 2019 at 101 centres in 29 countries, 70.5% were men, 53.3% were current or former smokers, and 53% received a diagnosis after symptoms, chiefly visible haematuria. A meta-analysis of 44 studies estimated UTUC incidence among people with visible and non-visible haematuria at 0.75% and 0.17%, respectively. Approximately two-thirds of patients presenting with UTUC have muscle-invasive disease at diagnosis, versus 15–25% with newly diagnosed BC; population studies from Germany and England suggest muscle-invasive UTUC accounts for approximately half of recent incident cases. Approximately 9% present with metastases. Pyelocaliceal tumours occur approximately twice as frequently as ureteral tumours; multifocality occurs in approximately 10–20%, and concomitant upper-tract carcinoma in situ in between 11% and 36%. Concurrent BC occurs in 17%; previous BC was recorded in 41% of American men and 4% of Chinese men. These differences, alongside genetic and epigenetic factors, may help explain more advanced, higher-grade presentations in Asian patients. After treatment, bladder recurrence occurs in 29%, varying with patient, tumour and treatment characteristics, versus 2–5% recurrence in the contralateral upper tract. UTUC and BC differ substantially in frequencies of common genomic changes, although tumours in a person with both cancers are often clonally related. UTUC genomic profiling can inform bladder-recurrence risk and identify Lynch syndrome-associated tumours. Among 82 patients given intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) for high-risk BC and imaged regularly between years 1 and 3, 13% developed asymptomatic UTUC; another series of 307 patients without routine upper-tract imaging reported 25% UTUC after BC. A multicentre cohort of n = 402 followed for 50 month reported 7.5% UTUC among NMIBC recipients of BCG; intravesical recurrence and a non-papillary tumour at transurethral resection of the bladder (TURB) predicted UTUC. Following radical cystectomy for MIBC, 3–5% develop metachronous UTUC.

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_09
  Condition: Erectile dysfunction
  Setting: second_line
  Patient population: Men requiring injection treatment after inadequate response to another option, or well-informed men who choose injections as an alternative first-line treatment.
  Decision rules:
    - Offer intracavernous injections either as an alternative first-line treatment or as second-line treatment.
    - Provide supervised instruction in injection technique and close follow-up to address early discontinuation.
    - Avoid intracavernous alprostadil in men with hypersensitivity to alprostadil, risk of priapism or bleeding disorders.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Alprostadil
      Evidence level: 1a
      Recommendation grade: Strong
      Summary: Approved intracavernous monotherapy at 5-40 μg; 40 μg may be offered off label in some European countries. Teach the injection technique in an office-training programme.
      Key outcomes: Efficacy rates of > 70% are reported in general ED and in subgroups including men with diabetes or CVD. Reported satisfaction is 87-93.5% among patients and 86-90.3% among partners. Intracavernous pharmacotherapy has reported drop-out rates of 41-68%.
      Duration cycles: Erection begins after 5-15 minutes; duration depends on the injected dose and varies substantially between patients.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: Bimix
      Summary: A combination of papaverine 7.5-45 mg and phentolamine 0.25-1.5 mg. It has been used for ED but has never been licensed for this indication.
      Conditions for use: Consider an intracavernous combination where available, with its unlicensed status made clear.
    - Name: Trimix
      Summary: A combination of papaverine 8-16 mg, phentolamine 0.2-0.4 mg and alprostadil 10-20 μg. The guideline reports efficacy reaching 92% and less penile pain than alprostadil monotherapy, but it has never been licensed for ED.
      Conditions for use: Consider a combination injection where available, with its unlicensed status and fibrosis risk made clear.
    - Name: InvicorpTM
      Summary: Combines vasoactive intestinal peptide (25 μg) with phentolamine mesylate (1-2 mg Invicorp). Clinical studies report effectiveness in > 80% of men with ED, including previous non-responders, with little penile pain and a virtually negligible risk of priapism.
      Conditions for use: Consider a combination injection where available, including after inadequate response to other therapies.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: Papaverine monotherapy
      Reason: Its high incidence of adverse effects has led to its abandonment as monotherapy; papaverine is not licensed for ED.
    - Name: Phentolamine monotherapy
      Reason: It produces a poor erectile response as monotherapy and is not licensed for ED.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: After initiation and during close follow-up
      Method: Assess erection quality, pain, prolonged erections, priapism, fibrosis, satisfaction and continued participation in the injection programme.
      Interpretation: Most reported discontinuations of intracavernous pharmacotherapy occur within the first two to three months.
  Supportive care:
    - Provide office-based injection training, careful counselling and close follow-up.
    - For alprostadil-related pain, the guideline describes sodium bicarbonate or local anaesthesia as possible measures.
  Special considerations: The guideline reports that 5-10% of patients do not respond even to combination intracavernous injections. Cavernosal fibrosis usually resolves after a temporary treatment interruption; tunical fibrosis may indicate early Peyronie’s disease and a need to stop injections indefinitely.
  Condition ref: cond_01

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_04
  Name: neurogenic stress incontinence
  Description: Stress urinary incontinence occurring in the setting of neurological disease.
  Clinical presentation: Involuntary urine leakage occurs with increased abdominal pressure; urodynamic stress incontinence is distinguished by the absence of a detrusor contraction.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Urodynamic investigations
      Purpose: Establish a diagnosis of urodynamic stress incontinence and assess function before surgery.
      When indicated: Required to diagnose urodynamic stress incontinence; offer before surgery for neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.
      Interpretation: Urine leakage during increased abdominal pressure without a detrusor contraction meets the document's definition of urodynamic stress incontinence.
    - Test: Specialist pelvic floor assessment
      Purpose: Select people for pelvic floor muscle training.
      When indicated: Before selecting this training.
    - Test: Assessment of low-pressure bladder storage capacity
      Purpose: Determine whether bladder storage is adequate.
      When indicated: When considering insertion of an artificial urinary sphincter.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: After artificial urinary sphincter surgery, monitor the upper urinary tract; annual ultrasound scans are given as an example.
    Recommended tests:

    Long term effects:

Document sections:
  Heading: 3. Ovarian Masses
  Content: Most childhood ovarian masses are functional cysts or benign tumors, but timely diagnosis affects outcomes in malignancy. A mass can be discovered incidentally or cause abdominal pain or enlargement, a palpable abdominal or pelvic mass, nausea, vomiting, fullness, constipation, lower abdominal pressure, urinary frequency or retention, precocious puberty with virilization, menstrual irregularities, or a paraneoplastic or autoimmune syndrome. Presentation depends on age, size, and pathology. Benign and malignant ovarian tumors together represent 1–2% of childhood and adolescent tumors, occurring at roughly 2.6 per 100,000 girls annually. retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__EAU Guidelines on Upper Urinary Tract Urothelial Carcinoma 2024__JC__000173
retrieved_chunks.document_id: EAU Guidelines on Upper Urinary Tract Urothelial Carcinoma 2024
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 3.1 Epidemiology
  Content: UC is the second most frequent urological malignancy in developed countries and can arise in the lower urinary tract or the pyelocaliceal cavities and ureter. Bladder cancer (BC) constitutes 90–95% of UC, whereas UTUC constitutes 5–10%; estimated annual incidence in Western countries is almost two cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Incidence has increased over recent decades, possibly because detection improved and populations aged. Incidence peaks at 70–90 years, and UTUC occurs twice as often in men. In an international retrospective registry of 2,380 people diagnosed between 2014 and 2019 at 101 centres in 29 countries, 70.5% were men, 53.3% were current or former smokers, and 53% received a diagnosis after symptoms, chiefly visible haematuria. A meta-analysis of 44 studies estimated UTUC incidence among people with visible and non-visible haematuria at 0.75% and 0.17%, respectively. Approximately two-thirds of patients presenting with UTUC have muscle-invasive disease at diagnosis, versus 15–25% with newly diagnosed BC; population studies from Germany and England suggest muscle-invasive UTUC accounts for approximately half of recent incident cases. Approximately 9% present with metastases. Pyelocaliceal tumours occur approximately twice as frequently as ureteral tumours; multifocality occurs in approximately 10–20%, and concomitant upper-tract carcinoma in situ in between 11% and 36%. Concurrent BC occurs in 17%; previous BC was recorded in 41% of American men and 4% of Chinese men. These differences, alongside genetic and epigenetic factors, may help explain more advanced, higher-grade presentations in Asian patients. After treatment, bladder recurrence occurs in 29%, varying with patient, tumour and treatment characteristics, versus 2–5% recurrence in the contralateral upper tract. UTUC and BC differ substantially in frequencies of common genomic changes, although tumours in a person with both cancers are often clonally related. UTUC genomic profiling can inform bladder-recurrence risk and identify Lynch syndrome-associated tumours. Among 82 patients given intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) for high-risk BC and imaged regularly between years 1 and 3, 13% developed asymptomatic UTUC; another series of 307 patients without routine upper-tract imaging reported 25% UTUC after BC. A multicentre cohort of n = 402 followed for 50 month reported 7.5% UTUC among NMIBC recipients of BCG; intravesical recurrence and a non-papillary tumour at transurethral resection of the bladder (TURB) predicted UTUC. Following radical cystectomy for MIBC, 3–5% develop metachronous UTUC.

Document sections:
  Heading: Hyperandrogenism Diagnostic Evaluation
  Content: In adult women, hirsutism, alopecia, and acne indicate clinical hyperandrogenism and can signal biochemical hyperandrogenism. Assessment should measure total and free testosterone; the calculated free androgen index can estimate free testosterone. If neither measure is elevated, androstenedione and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) may be considered, recognizing their lower specificity and the tendency of DHEA to decline with age. Laboratories should favor LC-MS/MS assays rather than direct immunoassays, including radiometric or enzyme-linked methods, for total or free testosterone because direct assays have limited accuracy, sensitivity, and precision in this setting. Androgen concentrations substantially above laboratory reference ranges should prompt consideration of ovarian or adrenal neoplasms, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing's syndrome, ovarian hyperthecosis—particularly after menopause—iatrogenic effects, and severe-insulin-resistance syndromes. Some androgen-secreting neoplasms cause only mild or moderate elevations, so the timing of onset and speed of progression are important clinical-history details.

  Event: Prostate-specific antigen changes and prostate cancer safety concerns
  Associated therapies:
    - testosterone therapy
  Recognition:
    - TRAVERSE found a significantly greater rise from baseline in total PSA with testosterone therapy than with placebo, without a difference in PCa incidence or high-grade PCa rate between groups at a mean follow-up of 33.0 ± (SD) 12.1 months.
    - Available evidence does not establish an increased PCa risk from testosterone therapy, but long-term prospective safety data are insufficient, particularly for PCa survivors.
    - A digital rectal examination can detect prostate abnormalities despite a normal PSA value.
  Management:
    - Severity: Advanced or active PCa
      Actions: Avoid testosterone administration.
    - Severity: Previous surgically treated localised PCa without evidence of active disease
      Actions: Discuss the insufficient long-term safety evidence fully with the patient. Restrict consideration of testosterone therapy to men at low risk of recurrence, after at least one year follow-up with PSA < 0.01 ng/mL.
    - Severity: Increase in PSA or detection of a prostate abnormality during treatment
      Actions: Use local PCa guidelines to decide whether to stop testosterone therapy or perform a prostate biopsy.
  Prevention:
    - Assess PSA and perform a digital rectal examination before testosterone therapy; monitor for prostate abnormalities during treatment.
    - In PCa survivors receiving testosterone therapy, measure total PSA at three, six and twelve months in the first year and annually thereafter.

  Dose modifications: Whether to discontinue testosterone therapy because of a PSA increase or prostate abnormality should be determined according to local PCa guidelines.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Context
  Content: The lower urinary tract comprises bladder and urethra and coordinates urine storage and expulsion under central and peripheral nervous-system control. Neurological disease affecting the brain, suprasacral or sacral spinal cord, or peripheral nerves can produce characteristic patterns of bladder and sphincter dysfunction; the nature of the injury also matters. Childhood neurological damage often stems from congenital conditions such as spina bifida or sacral agenesis. Stroke, spinal cord injury and cauda equina compression can cause relatively stable injury, whereas dementia, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis and peripheral neuropathy can cause progressive damage. Table 1 groups example neurological conditions by lesion site and likelihood of progression. Because the neural centres governing urinary, bowel and sexual function are close, dysfunctions often coexist and warrant a holistic rather than isolated urinary approach. Neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction can impair storage, emptying or both; storage symptoms include increased frequency and incontinence. Urinary symptoms can cause embarrassment, social isolation and difficulty with daily activities. Incontinence can result from overactive bladder, urethral sphincter dysfunction or both. Risks include markedly more urinary tract infections and loss of renal function from elevated bladder pressures, infection or kidney stones. Medical treatment often does not restore normal urinary function, and medicines, intermittent self-catheterisation, indwelling catheters, pads and appliances can affect quality of life. Families and carers may face physical, psychological, relationship and social pressures. Costs arise from supplies, medicines, operations, care and professional support, as well as effects on employment, follow-up and long-term surveillance. The full guideline contains 3 algorithms outlining the clinical approach. For recommended uses outside UK marketing authorisation at publication, prescribers should follow relevant professional guidance, take responsibility for the decision, and obtain and document informed consent.

  Content: Testicular germ cell tumour (TGCT) is the most common cancer in Caucasian men aged 15-40 years and affects approximately 1% of sub-fertile men. Annual incidence in Caucasians ranges from 10/100,000 in Denmark and Norway to 2/100,000 in Finland and the Baltic countries. Cancer incidence has increased in countries with reliable registries, alongside deteriorating male reproductive health in western countries.   Heading: 2.2.1. Renal and Ureteric Stones
  Content: For asymptomatic patients, the EAU favours initial US because it avoids radiation, costs less and can identify hydronephrosis and stones in the calyces, renal pelvis and pelvic-ureteric or vesico-ureteric junctions. For symptomatic patients, NCCT is preferred: it characterises density, diameter, volume, skin-to-stone distance and surrounding anatomy to inform treatment, and is more accurate than US or IVU (EAU: strong recommendation). Contrast-enhanced imaging is advised when collecting-system anatomy must be assessed before removal (EAU: strong recommendation). KUB X-ray can establish radiopacity but need not be obtained when NCCT is planned. The AUA recommends NCCT before PCNL (AUA: strong recommendation) and when choosing between SWL and URS (AUA: conditional recommendation); US alone is discouraged for the latter decision. Suspected substantial renal injury may warrant a DTPA or MAG-3 renogram to guide care (AUA: conditional recommendation). The EAU advises testing serum creatinine, uric acid, ionised calcium, sodium, potassium, blood cell counts and C-reactive protein, plus coagulation when intervention is intended (EAU: strong recommendation). Both organisations strongly recommend urine culture and microscopy before intervention.

  Content: Most abdominal masses in girls originate in the ovaries and range from functional cysts to malignancies. Their frequency, presentation, and histology vary with age.   Heading: 1. Introduction
  Content: Ovarian lesions account for most abdominal masses in pediatric girls and span functional cysts through malignant tumors. Cysts constitute 60% of pediatric ovarian lesions. True neoplasms occur at 2.6 cases per 100,000 girls per year; 3–8% of adnexal masses are malignant, representing 1–2% of pediatric cancers. Neoplasms are grouped by origin into germ cell, sex cordstromal, and epithelial tumors. Incidence, causes, and presentation vary by age: germ cell tumors predominate among childhood and adolescent ovarian neoplasms, whereas epithelial tumors predominate in adults. Mature cystic teratomas are the most frequent tumor type, and dysgerminomas are described as the most frequent malignant ovarian neoplasm in the pediatric population. Functional cysts peak in the fetal/neonatal and perimenarchal periods, reflecting maternal gonadotropins or activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis. Ultrasound is the initial imaging choice; MRI offers additional soft-tissue detail without ionizing radiation. Imaging and serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), beta subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), and inhibin A and B contribute to malignancy-risk assessment. Pediatric surgery should favor fertility preservation, minimally invasive laparoscopy, and ovarian conservation when feasible. The review addresses evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment across pediatric age groups.

Document sections:
  Heading: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO)
  Content: Prenatal screening ultrasonography (US) and postnatal imaging have increased detection of hydronephrosis and lowered the age at pyeloplasty. Prenatal hydronephrosis is identified in up to 4.5% of screening ultrasounds; UPJO occurs in 1 per 1000–2000 newborns. UPJO is more common in males, involves the left kidney in up to 67% of cases, and is bilateral in up to 10%. Urinary tract US assesses hydronephrosis severity, pelvocalyceal dilation, and renal cortical thinning at birth. In 1993, the Society for Fetal Urology (SFU) proposed a standardized US grade based on urinary tract dilation and parenchymal thickness. The urinary tract dilation (UTD) classification introduced in 2014 assesses six parameters: anterior–posterior renal pelvic diameter, urinary tract dilatation, parenchymal thickness, parenchymal appearance, ureteral status, and bladder status. The first postnatal US should occur more than 48 h after birth to avoid underestimating dilation. In addition to US, 99mTc-MAG3 is recommended for neonatal renography and visualization of kidneys when renal function is impaired. Functional immaturity of neonatal kidneys can produce increased residual cortical activity when the radiopharmaceutical and furosemide are administered together in an F0 study; activity may remain at up to 50% or more of its peak. This phenomenon resolves after the age of 3 months.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: Lee et al. 2025 Comparison of Urinary Red Blood Cell Distribution ( URDspan
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 1 | Introduction
  Content: Hematuria means RBCs are present in urine and may be visible or detectable only microscopically. It is a fundamental manifestation of glomerulonephritis (GN); microscopic assessment of urinary sediment is presented as its most effective detection method. Birch et al. proposed in 1979 that urinary RBC morphology could distinguish glomerular from non-glomerular origins. Passage through glomeruli can damage RBC membranes and produce dysmorphic RBCs (dRBCs). Shichiri et al. reported in 1988 that erythrocytes were smaller in glomerular than in non-glomerular disease, and Hyodo et al. later proposed an RBC size range of 4–6 μm for discriminating the origins. Compared with blood, urine has much less albumin and more urea; this environment increases membrane vulnerability and changes RBC shape. High urea concentrations particularly favor burr-cell formation. Passage across the glomerular basement membrane may produce acanthocytes through membrane injury. RBCs in renal disease are also more susceptible to factors including iron deficiency, osmotic lysis, shape distortion, and vesicle formation. Reliable recognition of urinary dRBCs requires an experienced observer, and observer-dependent interpretation may explain differences between laboratories. The authors consider continuing education in RBC morphology essential and mention deep learning for microscopy as another possible approach. Instrument-measured small-RBC fractions are easier to obtain and less dependent on interpretation, making them potentially more objective and standardized. The fully automated UF-5000 uses fluorescence flow cytometry to classify urine particles and reports morphological RBC information, including non-lysed RBCs, lysed RBCs, large RBCs, small RBCs, and RBC-Info. Its classification uses forward scatter light (FSC), side scatter light (SSC), side fluorescence light (SFL), and depolarized side scattered light (DSS). A small RBC has FSC intensity < 70; a non-lysed RBC has a strong FSC signal and morphological stability indicated by SSC. URD is the small-RBC count divided by the non-lysed-RBC count. Earlier studies investigated possible clinical uses, but most were single-center studies. Reported cutoffs for distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular hematuria varied from 30.1% to 40.5% for small RBCs and from 0% to 30.0% for dRBCs. The authors therefore considered a multicenter assessment using the same equipment necessary for clinical application. Across four hospitals, they collected urine microscopy findings, urine measures, serum markers, and kidney-function information to compare institutional dRBC and URD measurements and cutoffs and assess their clinical significance.

Document sections:
  Heading: 15.2 Contraindications
  Content: Suspected or confirmed urethral rupture, UTI or false passage are listed contraindications. Injury to urethral epithelium can heal with scarring and stricture formation. Male strictures commonly cause obstructive voiding symptoms and may follow IC, infection, trauma, lichen sclerosus, prostate-cancer treatment such as radiotherapy, or an unidentified cause. UK Hospital Episode Statistics and similar US data suggest male incidence rises from about 10 in every 100,000 up to 25 years to 40 in every 100,000 by the age of 65 years and > 100 in every 100,000 over 65 years. Female urethral strictures affect 0.1–1% of women with voiding complaints and can cause irritative as well as obstructive symptoms. In a review by Chakraborty et al., 53.48% of surgically treated female strictures were presumed idiopathic and 91.29% had a prior intervention. Smith et al. attributed 8% of female strictures to inflammation and infection and 6.6% to trauma. Male strictures may occur anywhere, particularly in the bulbar urethra (50 %) and at the meatus. In selected patients, intermittent dilatation is established as palliative management of refractory strictures and can reduce recurrence up to 68%. Diversion, such as a continent stoma or ileal conduit, is required if reconstruction is impossible or repair attempts fail. A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to determine which of dilatation, endoscopic urethrotomy or urethroplasty best balances effectiveness, adverse effects and costs. A small RCT (n=49) comparing CISC with repeated sounds dilatation reported a statistically significant improvement in flow rate and QoL among patients performing CISC.

  Heading: 3.2 Epidemiology
  Content: Among males, incidence rises sharply after 55 years of age; mean age is 45.1, and estimated overall incidence is 229-627 per 100,000 males. The anterior urethra accounts for 92.2% of affected sites, particularly the bulbar urethra (46.9%). Among females with refractory lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), 2-29% have bladder outflow obstruction (BOO), of whom 4-20% have a urethral stricture; true FUS therefore affects 0.08-5.4% of women with refractory LUTS. Incidence increases markedly after 64 years of age. Following hypospadias repair, meatal stenosis or stricture is reported in 1.3-20% of cases, varying with severity and technique; incidence is significantly higher in well-resourced countries, where repair is more frequent. Up to 18% of all strictures involve the meatus or fossa navicularis, commonly following failed hypospadias repair (FHR), lichen sclerosus (LS), trauma or instrumentation, or without identified cause. Meatal stenosis after neonatal circumcision is reported in less than 0.2% of children. Strictures affect 2-56% of female-to-male (FtM) transgender patients (‘transmen’) and 4-40% of male-to-female (MtF) transgender patients (‘transwomen’); in transwomen, they arise almost exclusively at the neomeatus.
