Pure non-urothelial histology is uncommon, while histological subtypes occur in approximately 25% of UTUCs.
  Epidemiology: UTUC accounts for 5–10% of urothelial carcinomas, with an estimated annual incidence in Western countries of almost two cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Incidence peaks at 70–90 years, and the disease is twice as common in men. Approximately two-thirds of patients present with muscle-invasive disease, although population-based studies suggest that muscle-invasive UTUC has represented approximately half of incident cases in recent years; approximately 9% present with metastasis. Pyelocaliceal tumours occur approximately twice as often as ureteral tumours. Multifocal tumours occur in approximately 10–20% of cases, concomitant upper-tract carcinoma in situ in 11% to 36%, and concurrent bladder cancer in 17%. After treatment, bladder recurrence occurs in 29% of patients, compared with contralateral upper-tract recurrence in 2–5%. Tobacco exposure increases relative risk by 2.5 to 7.0 fold; aristolochic acid exposure is another established risk factor. An association with alcohol was reported in a case-control study of 1,569 cases and 506,797 controls: ever-drinkers had higher risk than never-drinkers (OR: 1.23; 95% CI: 1.08–1.40, p = 0.001), with a reported risk threshold of > 15 g of alcohol/day.
  Clinical presentation: Detection may be incidental. Most patients in an international registry presented with symptoms, principally visible haematuria; flank pain caused by obstruction from a clot or tumour tissue occurs in 20–32% of cases. Anorexia, weight loss, malaise, fatigue, fever, night sweats or cough should prompt assessment for metastases. Symptoms at diagnosis are associated with poorer prognosis.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Low-risk UTUC
      Distinguishing features: Requires unifocal disease, tumour size < 2 cm, negative high-grade cytology, low-grade URS biopsy and no invasive appearance on CT; all listed factors must be present.
    - Name: High-risk UTUC
      Distinguishing features: High-grade cytology, high-grade URS biopsy, local invasion on CT or a histological subtype each constitute a strong high-risk criterion. Multifocal disease, tumour size ≥ 2 cm and hydronephrosis are weaker criteria and, in a low-grade tumour, are not strong predictors of invasion when considered alone.
    - Name: Lynch-related UTUC
      Distinguishing features: UTUC associated with Lynch syndrome and a pathogenic germline mismatch-repair gene mutation.
    - Name: upper tract CIS
      Distinguishing features: Flat carcinoma in situ of the upper urinary tract; its lack of a mass effect or urothelial thickening can make it invisible on CT.
    - Name: metastatic UTUC
      Distinguishing features: Disease with regional nodal involvement or distant metastases, for which the guideline describes separate management pathways.
    - Name: squamous subtype
      Distinguishing features: Urothelial carcinoma with divergent squamous differentiation, present in approximately 15% of cases.
    - Name: sarcomatoid
      Distinguishing features: A rare histological subtype associated with locally advanced disease and poorer outcomes.
    - Name: micropapillary
      Distinguishing features: A histological subtype associated with locally advanced disease and poorer outcomes.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: CT urography
      Purpose: Diagnose and stage UTUC, assess local invasion and examine regional lymph nodes.
      When indicated: In the diagnostic and staging evaluation.
      Interpretation: A meta-analysis of 13 studies involving 1,233 patients reported pooled sensitivity of 92% (CI: 0.85–0.96) and specificity of 95% (CI: 0.88–0.98). Enlarged lymph nodes strongly predict metastases. Flat epithelial lesions without a mass effect or urothelial thickening are generally not visible.
    - Test: chest CT
      Purpose: Assess for thoracic metastatic disease.
      When indicated: During staging and the specified follow-up of high-risk disease.
    - Test: MR urography
      Purpose: Provide upper-tract imaging when CT urography cannot be performed.
      When indicated: Usually when radiation or iodinated contrast is contraindicated.
      Interpretation: Sensitivity after contrast administration is 75% for tumours < 2 cm; CT urography is more sensitive and specific for diagnosis and staging.
    - Test: FDG-PET/CT
      Purpose: Assess nodal or distant metastases.
      When indicated: May be used when iodinated contrast cannot be given because of renal impairment or allergy.
      Interpretation: A retrospective multicentre study of 117 surgically treated patients reported sensitivity of 82% and specificity of 84% for nodal metastases. Suspicious nodes were associated with worse recurrence-free survival; further validation and comparison with MR and CT are needed.
    - Test: urethrocystoscopy
      Purpose: Exclude a concurrent bladder tumour.
      When indicated: As part of the UTUC diagnostic evaluation.
    - Test: voided urine cytology
      Purpose: Help detect high-grade disease.
      When indicated: During diagnostic evaluation and, where specified, surveillance.
      Interpretation: Abnormal cytology can suggest high-grade UTUC if cystoscopy is normal and bladder or prostatic-urethral CIS is absent. It is less sensitive for UTUC than selectively collected upper-tract cytology.
    - Test: selective upper-tract cytology
      Purpose: Assess the affected upper tract, particularly for high-grade tumours and CIS.
      When indicated: When upper-tract sampling is undertaken, including during URS.
      Interpretation: Selective cytology has high sensitivity in high-grade disease, including CIS.
    - Test: barbotage cytology
      Purpose: Obtain cytological material from the renal cavities and ureteral lumen.
      When indicated: Preferably before contrast administration for retrograde ureteropyelography.
      Interpretation: One study detected up to 91% of cancers; contrast can impair cytological specimens.
    - Test: retrograde ureteropyelography
      Purpose: Provide an additional means of detecting UTUC.
      When indicated: As a diagnostic option.
    - Test: diagnostic ureteroscopy (URS) with biopsy
      Purpose: Visualise suspicious lesions, confirm diagnosis, map tumour presence, appearance, multifocality and size, and establish biopsy grade.
      When indicated: When imaging and voided cytology do not adequately establish the diagnosis or risk category, or before considering kidney-sparing management.
      Interpretation: Biopsy establishes grade in more than 90% of cases, but can undergrade disease relative to nephroureterectomy specimens, and biopsy-based stage assessment can be inaccurate. URS with biopsy significantly increased subsequent intravesical recurrence in a systematic review of 16 studies, without an observed effect on overall survival or non-urothelial recurrence.
    - Test: FISH
      Purpose: Detect molecular abnormalities characteristic of UTUC.
      When indicated: As a possible ancillary urinary test.
      Interpretation: Reported sensitivity for characteristic molecular abnormalities is approximately 72–84%. A systematic review reported sensitivity of 35-86% and specificity of 80-100%; the review concluded that available cytology and FISH performance was suboptimal for ruling out UTUC.
    - Test: Xpert Bladder
      Purpose: Evaluate suspected UTUC using upper-tract urine.
      When indicated: Assessed in a prospective study of 79 patients immediately before URS; not established as a routine test in the guideline.
      Interpretation: The study reported sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 4%.
    - Test: Bladder Epicheck
      Purpose: Provide a possible ancillary urinary test for UTUC detection.
      When indicated: Further prospective comparative validation is needed.
      Interpretation: In a prospective study of 79 patients, sensitivity was 64% and specificity was 79%.
    - Test: narrow-band imaging
      Purpose: Improve endoscopic visualisation of lesions.
      When indicated: Investigational use during ureteroscopy.
      Interpretation: Findings are promising but preliminary.
    - Test: optical coherence tomography
      Purpose: Evaluate tumour grade or stage in vivo.
      When indicated: Investigational endoscopic assessment.
      Interpretation: Correlation with definitive histology in high-grade UTUC has been promising.
    - Test: confocal laser endomicroscopy (Cellvizio®)
      Purpose: Evaluate tumour grade or stage in vivo.
      When indicated: Investigational endoscopic assessment.
      Interpretation: Correlation with definitive histology in high-grade UTUC has been promising.
    - Test: pathological examination of resection specimens
      Purpose: Establish stage, grade, histological subtype, lymphovascular invasion, margins and other prognostic findings.
      When indicated: After surgical resection.
      Interpretation: The report should specifically state lymphovascular invasion status and identify positive margins at ureteral transection, the bladder cuff and around the tumour.
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: histological grade
      Clinical significance: Closely associated with pathological stage and a principal factor in risk stratification; the guideline uses both the 1973 and 2004/2016 WHO classifications.
    - Marker: lymphovascular invasion
      Expected result: Present in approximately 20% of invasive UTUCs.
      Clinical significance: An independent predictor of survival that should be explicitly recorded in pathology reports.
    - Marker: tumour necrosis
      Clinical significance: Extensive necrosis involving > 10% of the tumour area independently predicts prognosis after RNU.
    - Marker: sessile growth pattern
      Clinical significance: Associated with poorer outcome in examinations of RNU specimens.
    - Marker: surgical margins
      Clinical significance: A positive soft-tissue margin is associated with greater recurrence risk after RNU.
  Genetic molecular:
    - Marker: FGFR3
      Clinical significance: Activating mutations occur in > 90% of low-grade tumours; FGFR3 signalling is activated in UTUC. Molecular markers have not been validated for routine clinical decision-making in non-metastatic disease.
    - Marker: TP53/MDM2
      Clinical significance: Mutations are depleted in low-grade tumours, whereas high-grade tumours often have alterations in TP53 signalling.
    - Marker: KMT2D
      Clinical significance: Cited among commonly altered chromatin-remodelling genes in UTUC.
    - Marker: KDM6A
      Clinical significance: Cited among commonly altered chromatin-remodelling genes in UTUC.
    - Marker: CDKN2A
      Clinical significance: Cited among genomic alterations observed in UTUC.
    - Marker: RAS
      Clinical significance: Cited among genomic alterations observed in UTUC.
  Staging:
    System: TNM classification 2017
    Definitions:
      - Stage: TX
        Description: The primary tumour cannot be evaluated.
      - Stage: T0
        Description: No primary tumour is evident.
      - Stage: Ta
        Description: Papillary carcinoma without invasion.
      - Stage: Tis
        Description: Carcinoma in situ.
      - Stage: T1
        Description: Tumour infiltrates the subepithelial connective tissue.
      - Stage: T2
        Description: Tumour infiltrates the muscularis.
      - Stage: T3
        Description: In the renal pelvis, tumour extends beyond the muscularis into peripelvic fat or renal parenchyma; in the ureter, it extends beyond the muscularis into periureteric fat.
      - Stage: T4
        Description: Tumour extends into neighbouring organs or passes through the kidney into perinephric fat.
      - Stage: NX
        Description: Regional lymph nodes cannot be evaluated.
      - Stage: N0
        Description: No regional lymph-node metastasis.
      - Stage: N1
        Description: Metastasis in one lymph node measuring 2 cm or less in its greatest dimension.
      - Stage: N2
        Description: Metastasis in one lymph node measuring more than 2 cm, or in multiple lymph nodes.
      - Stage: M0
        Description: No distant metastasis.
      - Stage: M1
        Description: Distant metastasis.
    Additional rules: Regional nodes comprise hilar and retroperitoneal nodes and, for mid- and distal-ureteral tumours, pelvic nodes. Laterality does not change the N classification.
  Prognostic tools:
    - Name: Risk stratification of non-metastatic UTUC according to the risk of progression to a> pT2 /nonorgan-confined disease
      Components:
      - Tumour focality
      - Tumour size
      - High-grade cytology
      - URS biopsy grade
      - Invasive appearance on CT
      - Histological subtype
      - Hydronephrosis
      Risk groups:
      - Group: Low-risk UTUC
      Criteria: All of the following: unifocal disease, tumour size < 2 cm, negative high-grade cytology, low-grade URS biopsy and no invasive appearance on CT.
      Expected outcome: Identifies patients more likely to be suitable for kidney-sparing treatment.
      - Group: High-risk UTUC
      Criteria: Any strong criterion—high-grade cytology, high-grade URS biopsy, local invasion on CT or a histological subtype—supports high-risk classification. Multifocal disease, tumour size ≥ 2 cm and hydronephrosis are weak criteria that should be considered alongside other factors.
      Expected outcome: Identifies patients at greater risk of progression to > pT2 or non-organ-confined disease.
      Interpretation: Multifocality, size or hydronephrosis alone is insufficient to determine risk, particularly with low-grade disease. Their value as individual surrogates of high-risk progression has a low level of evidence.
    - Name: American Society of Anesthesiologists [ASA]
      Interpretation: A higher score is associated with worse cancer-specific survival after RNU; the guideline does not provide scoring thresholds.
    - Name: Charlson Comorbidity Index
      Interpretation: Higher comorbidity indices are associated with poorer survival across disease stages; the guideline does not provide scoring thresholds.
    - Name: modified Glasgow score
      Interpretation: Mentioned among blood-based measures associated with locally advanced disease and cancer-specific mortality; no components or cut-offs are specified.
    - Name: De Ritis ratio
      Components:
      - aspartate transaminase
      - alanine transaminase
      Interpretation: A high ratio has been associated with locally advanced disease and cancer-specific mortality; no cut-off is specified.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Follow-up is determined by risk category and prior treatment; schedules are specified in the corresponding low-risk and high-risk entries.
    Recommended tests:
      - cystoscopy
      - urinary cytology
      - CT urography
      - chest CT
      - URS
    Survivorship notes: Surveillance aims to address rehabilitation needs and detect new or recurrent urothelial tumours and regional or distant metastases. The evidence underlying follow-up recommendations is limited by substantial heterogeneity. Bladder recurrence is not classified as distant recurrence.

  Epidemiology: The bulbar urethra is affected in 46.9% of male strictures in a cited series. Idiopathic disease accounts for 63% of bulbar strictures in another cited series.
  Clinical presentation: In a retrospective study of 214 anterior urethroplasty patients, weak stream was reported by 49%, incomplete emptying by 27% and urinary frequency by 20%.       Distinguishing features: Generally short enough for excision followed by a tension-free anastomosis; the usual limit is around 2 cm.
    - Name: “Longer” bulbar strictures
      Distinguishing features: May not be amenable to tension-free excision and primary anastomosis.
    - Name: short post-traumatic bulbar strictures
      Distinguishing features: May be nearly or completely obliterated with full-thickness spongiofibrosis after straddle injury.

      Interpretation: Can underestimate length.
    - Test: Cystourethroscopy
      Purpose: Confirm narrowing and assess its calibre.
      When indicated: When additional information beyond imaging is required.
    - Test: Sonourethrography (SUG)

      - Late recurrence after bulbar urethroplasty is possible.
      - Post-void dribbling, changes in ejaculation and erectile function can follow reconstruction.

Document sections:
  Heading: 11.3.6.1.1 Testicular neoplasms
  Content: Compared with fertile controls, infertile men had higher testicular cancer risk (pooled OR = 1.91, 95% CI: 1.52-2.42); a study of oligozoospermia reported HR 11.9. A review found ~18fold higher testicular cancer prevalence in infertile men with testicular microcalcification (TM). Routine US screening remains debated because imaging cannot reliably determine whether many lesions are benign. No definitive lesion-size threshold separates benign from malignant masses. A systematic review identified 32 studies and 1692 masses: 28 studies and 1550 masses described scrotal US, and 4 studies and 142 masses described MRI. In post-pubertal men, masses ≤0.5 cm had significantly lower malignancy odds than masses > 0.5 cm (p < 0.001); masses 0.6-1.0 cm also had lower odds than masses > 1.5 cm (p = 0.04). The comparison of 0.6-1.0 with 1.1-1.5 cm was not significant. Lower malignancy odds were reported for heterogeneous versus homogeneous masses (p = 0.04), hyperechogenic versus hypoechogenic masses (p < 0.01), normal versus increased enhancement (p < 0.01), and peripheral versus central vascularity (p < 0.01). Data were limited for pre-pubertal US and MRI and post-pubertal MRI. Small echogenic areas can reflect benign abnormalities; periodic US assessment is warranted, particularly with malignancy risk factors. Lesion growth or added risks may prompt consideration of biopsy or surgery, although evidence is limited. In a series of 145 men with azoospermia, 49 (34%) had focal US findings, including 20 (14%) hypoechoic lesions, 10 (7%) hyperechoic lesions and 19 (13%) heterogeneous testes. Among 18 evaluable patients, 11 lesions measured < 5 mm and all were benign; other sampled hyperechoic or heterogeneous findings were also benign. Those authors suggested surveillance for severe infertility with negative tumour markers and lesions < 5 mm, with biopsy considered for larger or growing findings. Other studies suggested surveillance might replace radical surgery for avascular hyperechoic lesions with negative markers; hypoechoic vascular lesions are more likely malignant. Because most lesions remain indeterminate on US, histology and multidisciplinary discussion, including invasive diagnostic options, should be considered. US-guided biopsy with intra-operative frozen section can be offered as an alternative to radical orchidectomy after counselling and multidisciplinary review; concurrent TESE and sperm banking are possible in azoospermia.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_08
  Name: Non-ischaemic priapism
  Synonyms:
    - high-flow or arterial priapism
  Description: A persistent erection caused by unregulated arterial inflow into the corpora. Blunt trauma can produce a fistula between a cavernosal artery or its branches and the sinusoidal spaces.
  Epidemiology: It comprises 5% of priapism cases. Epidemiological information comes almost entirely from small case series, and blunt perineal or penile trauma is the most frequent cause.
  Clinical presentation: The corpora are tumescent but usually not fully rigid. Penile pain is generally absent, although discomfort is possible, and rigidity may fluctuate. After trauma, onset may be delayed by several hours to weeks; the guide also describes delays of up to two to three weeks. Sexual stimulation can produce full rigidity, so intercourse is usually possible. Erectile dysfunction or distal penile flaccidity may develop over time.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: traumatic
      Distinguishing features: Associated with injury, especially blunt perineal or penile trauma.
    - Name: neurogenic
      Distinguishing features: May follow acute spinal cord injury.
    - Name: iatrogenic
      Distinguishing features: Reported after certain procedures, including shunting for ischaemic priapism.
    - Name: idiopathic
      Distinguishing features: No cause is identified.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Comprehensive medical and sexual history
      Purpose: Establish the diagnosis and distinguish the priapism subtype.
      When indicated: At presentation.
      Interpretation: A history of pelvic, perineal or genital trauma, little or no penile pain, and a persistent erection without full rigidity support arterial priapism.
    - Test: Abdominal, penile and perineal examination
      Purpose: Assess tumescence and identify evidence of trauma.
      When indicated: During diagnostic evaluation.
      Interpretation: The corpora are generally tumescent without being fully rigid.
    - Test: Neurological examination
      Purpose: Investigate a possible neurogenic cause.
      When indicated: If neurogenic non-ischaemic priapism is suspected.
    - Test: Complete blood count with white blood cell differential and coagulation profile
      Purpose: Assess anaemia and other haematological abnormalities.
      When indicated: During laboratory evaluation.
    - Test: Corporal blood aspiration and blood gas analysis
      Purpose: Differentiate non-ischaemic from ischaemic priapism.
      When indicated: During diagnostic evaluation.
      Interpretation: The aspirate is bright red and has normal arterial blood gas values; the listed arterial values are pO2 > 90 mmHg, pCO2 < 40 mmHg and pH 7.40.
    - Test: Colour duplex ultrasound of the penis and perineum
      Purpose: Distinguish priapism subtypes and locate an arterial fistula.
      When indicated: During diagnostic evaluation, without intracavernosal vasoactive drug injection.
      Interpretation: A fistula may appear as a focal colour blush with turbulent, high-velocity flow. Cavernosal arterial velocities are normal to high.
    - Test: Selective pudendal arteriography
      Purpose: Identify the site of arterial injury for planned embolisation.
      When indicated: When embolisation is being considered.
      Interpretation: A characteristic blush may appear at the injury site.
    - Test: MRI
      Purpose: Evaluate selected cases or assess distal penile fibrosis during follow-up.
      When indicated: Its diagnostic role in non-ischaemic priapism is limited; it may be used during close follow-up.
      Interpretation: Small penile vessels and fistulae are difficult to demonstrate with MRI.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Close follow-up is described during conservative management and after selective arterial embolisation; no fixed interval is specified.
    Recommended tests:
      - Physical examination during conservative management
      - Colour duplex ultrasound during conservative management
      - Colour duplex ultrasound and MRI to detect distal penile fibrosis
      - Clinical examination, colour duplex ultrasound and erectile function assessment after embolisation
      - Repeat arteriography if findings remain uncertain
    Long term effects:
      - Erectile dysfunction
      - Distal penile flaccidity
      - Distal penile fibrosis
      - Recurrence after treatment
    Survivorship notes: Follow-up assesses treatment success, recurrence, and anatomical and functional consequences.

Document sections:
  Heading: Context
  Content: The lower urinary tract comprises bladder and urethra and coordinates urine storage and expulsion under central and peripheral nervous-system control. Neurological disease affecting the brain, suprasacral or sacral spinal cord, or peripheral nerves can produce characteristic patterns of bladder and sphincter dysfunction; the nature of the injury also matters. Childhood neurological damage often stems from congenital conditions such as spina bifida or sacral agenesis. Stroke, spinal cord injury and cauda equina compression can cause relatively stable injury, whereas dementia, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis and peripheral neuropathy can cause progressive damage. Table 1 groups example neurological conditions by lesion site and likelihood of progression. Because the neural centres governing urinary, bowel and sexual function are close, dysfunctions often coexist and warrant a holistic rather than isolated urinary approach. Neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction can impair storage, emptying or both; storage symptoms include increased frequency and incontinence. Urinary symptoms can cause embarrassment, social isolation and difficulty with daily activities. Incontinence can result from overactive bladder, urethral sphincter dysfunction or both. Risks include markedly more urinary tract infections and loss of renal function from elevated bladder pressures, infection or kidney stones. Medical treatment often does not restore normal urinary function, and medicines, intermittent self-catheterisation, indwelling catheters, pads and appliances can affect quality of life. Families and carers may face physical, psychological, relationship and social pressures. Costs arise from supplies, medicines, operations, care and professional support, as well as effects on employment, follow-up and long-term surveillance. The full guideline contains 3 algorithms outlining the clinical approach. For recommended uses outside UK marketing authorisation at publication, prescribers should follow relevant professional guidance, take responsibility for the decision, and obtain and document informed consent.

Document sections:
  Heading: KEY POINTS FOR CLINICAL PRACTICE
  Content: Consider CVT with substantial clinical suspicion when common symptoms coexist with pregnancy, the puerperium, oral contraceptive use, thrombophilia, or demographic factors such as being a young woman. Obesity, COVID-19, and vaccine-induced thrombocytopenia are predisposing conditions highlighted since the prior report. MRI/MRV is recommended as the noninvasive confirmatory examination of cerebral veins; CT/CTV is a reasonable alternative where resources are limited or pretest probability is low. For cortical vein thrombosis, contrast-enhanced MRV, gradient-recalled echo, or susceptibility-weighted imaging is recommended. Standard initial treatment comprises parenteral heparin followed by an oral VKA for 3 to 12 months according to cause, or indefinitely when thrombophilia or recurrent VTE is present. Open-label retrospective and prospective randomized studies suggest DOACs are a safe and effective alternative to VKAs. Whether follow-up CTV or MRV evidence of recanalization should determine anticoagulation duration is uncertain. Given the lack of controlled evidence and poorer outcomes in meta-analyses, endovascular treatment is reserved for thrombus extension, neurological deterioration despite medical treatment, or contraindications to anticoagulation. Despite limited evidence, decompressive surgery may save life and improve function when clinical signs of herniation are advanced. For CVT during pregnancy, full-dose LMWH should continue throughout pregnancy; LMWH or a VKA targeting an international normalized ratio of 2.0 to 3.0 should then continue for at least 6 weeks postpartum, with total treatment lasting at least 3 months. It is reasonable to tell women with previous CVT that another pregnancy is not contraindicated; LMWH prophylaxis during future pregnancy and the postpartum period is usually recommended. Pediatric CVT is more common in neonates than in older children and often occurs with infection, dehydration, iron deficiency, anemia, or head trauma. First-line treatment is parenteral anticoagulation, followed by LMWH, a VKA, or rivaroxaban for at least 6 weeks. Rare VITT-associated CVT can arise days or weeks after adenovirus-based SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, generally with a new headache and thrombocytopenia, and requires specialist hematology and multidisciplinary management.

Document sections:
  Heading: Risk factors
  Content: Reduced host immunity and physiological reserve are principal underlying risks. Diabetes mellitus is the most frequently reported comorbidity, affecting 30–40% of FG patients, and is associated with higher mortality. Sustained hyperglycaemia impairs phagocyte activity, chemotaxis, and cellular adherence; microvascular damage also restricts blood supply and wound healing. FG outcomes vary with the degree of hyperglycaemia, supporting strict glycaemic control during illness. Other reported immune-related risks include immunosuppressive medications, malnutrition, and HIV infection. Huayllani et al. reported hypertension (26%), anaemia (10%), heart failure (6%), and obesity (12%) among FG patients, although their effects on outcomes remain disputed. Multivariate analyses in large studies identified age, renal failure, coagulopathy, and congestive heart failure as significant mortality risk factors.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_02
  Name: Benign prostatic obstruction
  Synonyms:
    - BPO
  Description: A form of bladder outlet obstruction in which benign prostatic enlargement is known to cause the outflow obstruction. It is distinct from BPH, which denotes a histological pattern.
  Clinical presentation: Can contribute to male LUTS and may occur alongside bladder dysfunction. Signs or symptoms of BPO are associated with more frequent hydronephrosis, renal insufficiency or urinary retention, although the mechanism linking BPO to these complications is not conclusively established.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Pressure-flow studies
      Purpose: Establish whether outflow obstruction is present and distinguish it from DU.
      When indicated: Selected patients when clarification of the underlying mechanism is needed.
      Interpretation: Obstruction features increased detrusor pressure with reduced urinary flow during voiding.
    - Test: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
      Purpose: Help estimate prostate volume and risk of progression when relevant to management.
      When indicated: When its result assists treatment decisions or a prostate cancer diagnosis would alter management.
      Interpretation: In a community-based study, 1.5 ng/mL best predicted prostate volume > 30 mL, with PPV 78%. Baseline PSA predicted AUR and BPO-related surgery in cited studies; the reported PPV for detecting BPO was 68%.
    - Test: Prostate imaging
      Purpose: Measure volume and assess a middle lobe before selecting an intervention.
      When indicated: When considering surgery, and when size would affect medical treatment selection.
      Interpretation: TRUS is more accurate for volume assessment than transabdominal ultrasound.
    - Test: Post-void residual (PVR) urine measurement
      Purpose: Evaluate emptying and monitor change.
      When indicated: Assessment and follow-up of LUTS.
      Interpretation: PVR alone does not establish BPO. At a threshold of 50 mL, its PPV for BOO was 63% and NPV was 52%.
    - Test: Uroflowmetry
      Purpose: Evaluate urinary flow and monitor treatment response.

Document sections:
  Heading: Urinary tract infection
  Content: Infection morbidity substantially influences bladder-management choices. Pooled proportions across intermittent, urethral indwelling and suprapubic catheterization favor CIC, particularly with longer follow-up, but inconsistent UTI definitions and widely varying early rates limit inference. A database study of n = 1104 with mean symptom duration of 20.3 years found bladder management, botulinum toxin injections and prophylaxis significantly predicted UTI. Annual symptomatic UTI and recurrent UTI were 83.3% and 50.0% with transurethral indwelling catheters, versus 29.6% and 9.9% with voluntary voiding; the associated odds were 10-fold and 4fold greater. retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: General Considerations
  Content: Early detection decisions require consideration of age, life expectancy, family history, African ancestry, inherited mutations, previous tests, general health, comorbidity, and patient preferences, alongside discussion of benefits and harms. Guidance does not replace a clinician's full history and examination. Early prostate cancer has no identifiable symptoms; advanced disease can cause urinary obstruction, prostatic bleeding, hematospermia, or bone pain. Symptoms from benign prostatic enlargement should be distinguished during counseling. Prior DRE, PSA, PSA derivatives, and biopsy results should be reviewed. Patients should understand that detection seeks aggressive cancers but also finds low-risk disease that may be managed with active surveillance rather than immediate treatment. The panel recommends offering baseline PSA to healthy, informed people at average risk aged 45 to 75 years and to those with African ancestry, risk-associated germline mutations, and/or suspicious family history at ages 40 to 75 years. Baseline DRE may complement PSA; elevated PSA should be confirmed. For average-risk people <75 years with PSA below 1 ng/mL, recommended repeat testing is every 2 to 4 years; at PSA 1 to 3 ng/mL, every 1 to 2 years. With elevated risk and PSA ≤3 ng/mL, the interval is 1 to 2 years. The panel strongly recommends multiparametric MRI before biopsy when available. For PSA >3 ng/mL when greater specificity is desired, %fPSA, 4Kscore, SelectMDx, ExoDx Prostate, PHI, MPS, and IsoPSA may be considered before biopsy. After a negative biopsy with persistent higher risk, options include PHI, %fPSA, 4Kscore, ConfirmMDx, PCA3, MPS, and IsoPSA. Biopsy decisions should not rely on PSA threshold alone; age, family history, PSA kinetics, ancestry, health, preferences, MRI, and biomarkers also matter. High suspicion of clinically significant cancer warrants image-guided transrectal or transperineal biopsy; routine MRI targeting is recommended where available. PSA testing after age >75 years warrants cautious consideration only in very healthy patients (category 2B), with careful biopsy assessment. Panel members uniformly discourage testing those unlikely to benefit because of age or comorbidity. The panel considers these early detection recommendations linked to the NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer.

Document sections:
  Heading: 5.5 Urinary cytology
  Content: Cytology of voided urine or bladder washings detects exfoliated malignant cells with sensitivity 84% for HG/G3 tumours and 16% for LG/G1 tumours; CIS sensitivity ranges from 28–100%. A report using the Paris system found sensitivity 46% for HG disease. Cytology complements cystoscopy for HG/G3 disease but is not intended to detect LG tumours. Positive voided cytology can indicate UC anywhere in the tract, while a negative result cannot exclude it. Interpretation varies by reader and can be impaired by sparse cells, infection, stones or intravesical treatment, although experienced practitioners achieve specificity exceeding 90%. Digital image processing with artificial intelligence in the VisioCyt test raised HG sensitivity up to 92%. The Paris System 2022 (2nd Edn.) uses the full diagnostic categories No adequate diagnosis possible (No diagnosis), Negative for UC (Negative), Atypical urothelial cells (Atypia), Suspicious for HG UC (Suspicious), and High-grade/G3 UC (Malignant). Its terminology emphasizes HG/G3 detection, and retrospective studies have validated it. A prospective study suggested pre-TURB risk stratification: cytology negative for HG had 93% specificity for LG disease; an HG-positive result predicted HG disease with 92% specificity and 91% PPV. One cytospin slide is usually sufficient. Suspicious cytology warrants repeat investigation because the underlying risk of an HG lesion is 24-53%. Adjunctive voided cytology for HG detection and reporting with the Paris System 2nd Edn. each have a Strong recommendation. Obtain at least 25 mL of fresh or adequately fixed urine; first-morning urine is unsuitable because cytolysis is frequent (Strong).

  Heading: 8.2.3.2 Surgical treatment
  Content: Conservative care may resolve painful erections in most men but produces substantial straightening in only a small proportion. Surgery seeks to correct curvature so penetrative intercourse is possible and is indicated for substantial deformity with intercourse difficulty and sexual bother. Disease should be stable for 3-6 months, or surgery should occur more than 9-12 months after PD onset. Once stable, failed conservative or medical treatment, extensive plaques or patient preference may also prompt surgery. Before reconstruction, document plaque size and position, curvature, hinge or hourglass deformity, penile length and ED status. Discuss intended benefits and risks to enable informed choice: shortening, ED, numbness, delayed orgasm, recurrent or residual curvature, palpable knots or stitches, possible circumcision and further penile wasting after shortening surgery. Procedure selection considers length, curvature and erectile function, including response to ED drugs, as well as expectations. Patients should understand that the primary aim is a functionally straight penis. Options comprise tunical shortening, tunical lengthening and penile prosthesis implantation, potentially with additional straightening for concurrent ED and residual curvature. Degloving with circumcision to prevent postoperative phimosis is described as the standard approach, although modifications exist; one study suggested circumcision may be unnecessary with a normal preoperative foreskin. Non-degloving approaches have been described to avoid ischaemic and lymphatic complications after subcoronal circumcision. No standardised questionnaire evaluates surgical outcomes. Prospective evidence is sparse and low-level; most outcomes come from retrospective, usually non-comparative and non-randomised single-centre studies or expert opinion, so they require caution.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: Urinary tract infection in under 16s diagnosis and management
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Symptoms and signs
  Content: In its rationale for recommendations 1.1.1 to 1.1.9, the committee says timely, accurate UTI diagnosis matters for preventing avoidable illness and serious complications such as renal scarring. Table 1 provides greater clarity about features that raise or lower UTI likelihood, including dysuria, urinary frequency, loin tenderness and bedwetting retained from the 2007 guideline. Evidence for many features was low- or very-low quality because studies often were not designed to assess diagnostic accuracy and defined features poorly; the table therefore supplements clinical judgement. Its incomplete list must not prevent testing an unwell person when UTI remains suspected. Studies of algorithms combining features found none particularly accurate, so the committee did not recommend them; multiple features nevertheless probably increase UTI likelihood. Most evidence concerned children under 5 years, and trials seldom separated outcomes by age. The committee considered the features broadly applicable across ages but emphasised that age and communication ability affect their assessment. Dysuria, for example, raised UTI likelihood when present and lowered it when absent across ages, yet can be difficult to assess in a person who cannot communicate or is not toilet trained. Confirmed previous UTI was included despite not itself being a symptom or sign because it raises likelihood. Evidence reviewed did not establish sleepiness or lethargy, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, failure to thrive or jaundice as clinically useful indicators of UTI. Haematuria, cloudy urine and dark urine may be reported by the child or carers before a clinician has a sample; dark urine is not specific and may accompany illness and dehydration, while reported visible blood is, in the committee's view, uncommon in UTI and always needs further investigation. Less specific features may still help when combined. Features that lower UTI likelihood can indicate another infection site but do not rule UTI out. Routine urine testing is unnecessary when another infection is suggested in those aged 3 months and over, although persistent illness with diagnostic uncertainty can warrant testing. The specified fever guideline may assist when an under-5 has otherwise unexplained fever but UTI is no longer suspected. Urine collection and testing should not be delayed; culture can miss some UTIs, for which recommendation 1.1.23 addresses clinical decision-making. Concern about sepsis supports specialist referral and urgent microscopy and culture for suspected UTI under 3 months. Evidence gaps prompted the research questions about ages 5 years and above but under 16 years, recurrent UTI and long-term (chronic) UTI.

Document sections:
  Heading: 2.2.1. Renal and Ureteric Stones
  Content: For asymptomatic patients, the EAU favours initial US because it avoids radiation, costs less and can identify hydronephrosis and stones in the calyces, renal pelvis and pelvic-ureteric or vesico-ureteric junctions. For symptomatic patients, NCCT is preferred: it characterises density, diameter, volume, skin-to-stone distance and surrounding anatomy to inform treatment, and is more accurate than US or IVU (EAU: strong recommendation). Contrast-enhanced imaging is advised when collecting-system anatomy must be assessed before removal (EAU: strong recommendation). KUB X-ray can establish radiopacity but need not be obtained when NCCT is planned. The AUA recommends NCCT before PCNL (AUA: strong recommendation) and when choosing between SWL and URS (AUA: conditional recommendation); US alone is discouraged for the latter decision. Suspected substantial renal injury may warrant a DTPA or MAG-3 renogram to guide care (AUA: conditional recommendation). The EAU advises testing serum creatinine, uric acid, ionised calcium, sodium, potassium, blood cell counts and C-reactive protein, plus coagulation when intervention is intended (EAU: strong recommendation). Both organisations strongly recommend urine culture and microscopy before intervention.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: Bašković et al. 2025 The Evaluation, Diagnosis, and Management of Ovarian Cysts, Masses, and Their Complications in Fetus
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Abstract
  Content: Most abdominal masses in girls originate in the ovaries and range from functional cysts to malignancies. Their frequency, presentation, and histology vary with age. Assessment focuses on malignancy risk because benign and malignant lesions require substantially different management. Ultrasound is the principal examination for size, location, and morphology; MRI or CT can provide further assessment when ultrasound is inconclusive or malignancy is suspected, particularly in older adolescents. Serum markers may help assess malignancy risk in older adolescents but are less useful in younger patients because normal values change during development. Many functional cysts, especially fetal and infant cysts, resolve without treatment. Large symptomatic cysts or suspected malignancy may warrant surgery, preferably an ovary-preserving laparoscopy or laparotomy. Torsion, rupture, and hemorrhage may require urgent surgery. Specialized centers can help prevent unnecessary oophorectomies. This review examines age-specific evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment of pediatric ovarian masses.

Document sections:
  Heading: 3.3.1 Histological types
  Content: Upper-tract tumours are nearly always UC; exclusively non-urothelial histology is unusual, although histological subtypes occur in approximately 25% of UTUC. Pure urinary-tract squamous cell carcinoma is often thought to relate to chronic inflammation or infection arising from urolithiasis. Divergent squamous differentiation within UC occurs in approximately 15%. Keratinising squamous metaplasia raises squamous-cancer risk and therefore requires surveillance. UTUC with histological subtypes is high-grade and has a poorer prognosis than pure UC. Other rare subtypes include sarcomatoid; inverted growth is also described as frequent in the upper urinary tract. Collecting duct carcinomas can resemble UC but have a distinctive renal-cancer-like transcriptomic signature and a proposed origin in distal convoluted tubules; they are classified as renal tumours.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: Peris et al. 2023 European consensus based interdisciplinary guideline for diagnosis and treatment of basal cell carci
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 2. Definition
  Content: BCC is a carcinoma of epidermal origin and the most frequent human malignancy. Its name reflects the resemblance of cells at the edge of tumour nests to epidermal basal cells; it is now thought to arise from hair-follicle stem cells. It usually develops on sun-exposed skin in fair-skinned individuals, most often on the head or neck. With chronic sun exposure as the principal carcinogen, incidence rises in older people and peaks at around 80 years of age. The usual lesion is a slowly enlarging, skin-coloured, shiny pearly nodule with surface arborising vessels; larger lesions can ulcerate centrally. Superficial BCC (sBCC) commonly affects the trunk and is associated mainly with intermittent sun exposure. Other presentations include pigmented or sclerosing tumours. Fewer than 1% of patients develop metastases, but delayed detection, inadequate management or neglect can allow extensive, locally advanced and deeply infiltrative disease.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__EAU Guidelines on Urethral Strictures 2023__JC__000002
retrieved_chunks.document_id: EAU Guidelines on Urethral Strictures 2023
retrieved_chunks.text:
Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: urethral stricture disease
  Description: The guideline covers urethral narrowing in male, female and transgender patients. In males, an anterior urethral stricture involves fibrosis of the mucosa and surrounding corpus spongiosum; narrowing in the posterior urethra is preferably called stenosis. Narrowing of a reconstructed urethra is also termed a stricture despite the absence of surrounding spongiosal tissue.
  Epidemiology: In males, estimated incidence is 229-627 per 100,000, mean age is 45.1, and incidence rises sharply after 55 years. The anterior urethra is involved in 92.2% of cases, particularly the bulbar urethra (46.9%). Aetiology varies significantly between regions.
  Clinical presentation: In a retrospective series of 611 patients with endoscopically confirmed strictures, presentations included LUTS (54.3%), acute urinary retention (22.3%), UTI (6.1%) and difficult catheterisation (4.8%). Genitourinary pain affected 22.9-71% across cited studies. Other reported complaints included spraying (9%), visible haematuria (3.1-5%), urethral abscess or necrotising fasciitis (2.3%), urgency (14%) and incontinence (1-4%). Sexual-function problems may coexist.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: anterior urethral strictures in males
      Distinguishing features: Involve the spongiosum-surrounded urethra between the meatus and urogenital diaphragm.
    - Name: posterior urethral stenosis
      Distinguishing features: Involves the membranous urethra, prostatic urethra or bladder neck, where there is no corpus spongiosum.
    - Name: female urethral stricture (FUS)
      Distinguishing features: Most authors describe a persistent anatomical reduction in urethral calibre.
    - Name: strictures in trans men
      Distinguishing features: Can occur in distinct segments of the reconstructed urethra.
    - Name: strictures in trans women
      Distinguishing features: Usually occur at the neomeatus.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Patient history
      Purpose: Establish symptom severity and duration, possible cause, previous treatment, associated problems, sexual function and factors affecting surgery.
      When indicated: Suspected urethral stricture disease.
      Interpretation: Ask specifically about pelvic, genital or perineal injury, instrumentation, surgery, irradiation, focal therapy and urethritis; record the most recent intervention.
    - Test: Physical examination
      Purpose: Assess the bladder, genitalia, urethra, prostate, potential graft donor site and suitability for operative positioning.
      When indicated: Suspected urethral stricture disease.
      Interpretation: Assess the meatus, scars suggestive of LS, fistulae, urethral induration and any mass; examine the oral cavity, measure BMI and assess hip mobility.
    - Test: Urinalysis and urine culture
      Purpose: Identify infection and, when indicated, its organism and antibiotic sensitivity.
      When indicated: Urinalysis during assessment of LUTS; culture if infection is suspected.
      Interpretation: Treat bacteriuria before surgical intervention.
    - Test: Uroflowmetry and post-void residual (PVR) assessment
      Purpose: Assess flow obstruction and identify retention; measurements can also monitor treatment response.
      When indicated: Suspected urethral stricture disease.
      Interpretation: A reduced maximum flow with a prolonged plateau is characteristic, but visual interpretation of the curve alone is not a reliable screening method.
    - Test: Urodynamic studies
      Purpose: Assess bladder function or whether impaired flow and raised PVR reflect detrusor underactivity.
      When indicated: Selected patients with suspected bladder dysfunction; not indicated for the vast majority.
      Interpretation: May help estimate the likelihood of needing post-operative ISC.
    - Test: Retrograde urethrography (RUG)
      Purpose: Determine the presence, site and length of a stricture and assess associated abnormalities.
      When indicated: Particularly in men being considered for reconstructive surgery.
      Interpretation: Reported diagnostic sensitivity and specificity are 91% and 72%; RUG may underestimate stricture length.
    - Test: Voiding cystourethrography (VCUG)
      Purpose: Show urethra proximal to narrowing and improve assessment of length or an injury gap.
      When indicated: Combine with RUG for nearly or completely obliterative strictures, stenoses and PFUI.
    - Test: Cystourethroscopy
      Purpose: Confirm or rule out a narrowing and assess other urethral or bladder pathology.
      When indicated: An adjunct to imaging when additional information is required.
      Interpretation: Usually cannot establish stricture length when the instrument cannot traverse the narrowing.
    - Test: Retrograde urethroscopy and antegrade cystoscopy
      Purpose: Assess injury-gap length, bladder-neck competence, scarring and associated fistulae, false passages, stones or bony abnormalities.
      When indicated: Additional assessment of PFUI when imaging does not provide sufficient information.
    - Test: Sonourethrography (SUG)
      Purpose: Assess anterior stricture location, length and spongiofibrosis.
      When indicated: Additional assessment of anterior urethral strictures.
      Interpretation: In a cited comparison, correlation of measured length with operative findings was 94% for SUG versus 59% for RUG (p < 0.001); the pre-operative clinical significance of measuring spongiofibrosis remains uncertain.
    - Test: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) urethrography
      Purpose: Provide anatomical detail and identify associated pathology.
      When indicated: Consider as an ancillary investigation for posterior urethral stenosis.
      Interpretation: May estimate posterior stenosis length more accurately than RUG and VCUG.
    - Test: Validated patient reported outcome measure (PROM)
      Purpose: Measure symptom burden, quality-of-life effects and patient-perceived outcomes.
      When indicated: Men undergoing surgery and subsequent follow-up.
      Interpretation: A patent urethra does not necessarily mean that the patient regards treatment as successful.
    - Test: Validated sexual-function assessment
      Purpose: Document erectile and ejaculatory function and subsequent change.
      When indicated: Before and after urethral stricture surgery.
  Staging:
    System: EAU classification according to the degree of urethral narrowing
    Definitions:
      - Stage: 0
        Description: Imaging shows a normal urethra; lumen and degree are recorded as -.
      - Stage: 1
        Description: Subclinical narrowing with a lumen > 16 Fr; degree Low.
      - Stage: 2
        Description: Low-grade narrowing with a lumen of 11-15 Fr.
      - Stage: 3
        Description: High-grade or flow-significant narrowing with a lumen of 4-10 Fr; degree High.
      - Stage: 4
        Description: Almost obliterative narrowing with a lumen of 1-3 Fr.
      - Stage: 5
        Description: Complete obliteration with no lumen (0 Fr).
    Additional rules: The Panel proposed this consensus classification for male patients with normally functioning bladders. A urethral plate < 3 mm is considered tight or high-grade; with normal bladder function, flow generally does not fall until luminal diameter is below 10 Fr.
  Prognostic tools:
    - Name: Risk-stratified proposals during follow-up after urethral surgery
      Components:
      - Urethroplasty type
      - History of radiotherapy
      - History of hypospadias
      - LS features
      - Stricture location
      Risk groups:
      - Group: low risk of recurrence
      Criteria: Anastomotic repair in the bulbar or (bulbo)membranous segment without prior radiotherapy, hypospadias or BXO/LS features.
      - Group: standard risk of recurrence
      Criteria: Bulbar anastomotic repair with prior radiotherapy, hypospadias or BXO/LS features; penile or non-traumatic posterior urethroplasty; or graft or flap substitution urethroplasty.
      Interpretation: The groups determine the proposed intensity and duration of post-urethroplasty surveillance.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Offer follow-up after urethroplasty for at least one year. For low-risk repairs, the proposed assessments are at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months; follow-up may end after two years with advice to return if symptoms worsen. For standard-risk repairs, assess at 3 months, 12 months, 24 months and 5 years; follow-up may end after five years, although longer surveillance should be considered after penile or substitution urethroplasty.
    Recommended tests:
      - Uroflowmetry and PROM, including sexual function, at each scheduled low- or standard-risk visit.
      - For low-risk repairs, anatomic assessment by urethrocystoscopy or RUG-VCUG at 3 months as suggested by the Panel, and subsequently when indicated.
      - For standard-risk repairs, anatomic assessment at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months, and at 5 years when indicated.
      - Investigate deterioration suggesting recurrence with anatomic testing.
    Long term effects:
      - Recurrent narrowing can occur after initially patent reconstruction.
      - Late recurrence later than five years was reported in up to 15% of cases.
      - Persistent voiding symptoms, pain, sexual dysfunction, penile shortening and curvature may adversely affect patient satisfaction despite anatomical patency.
    Survivorship notes: Follow-up should capture both anatomical findings and patient-reported function. Patients should seek urological assessment if symptoms recur after scheduled surveillance ends.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS)
  Description: Symptoms affecting urine storage, voiding or the period after micturition. Possible sources include the prostate, urethra, bladder and sphincters; other potential causes include detrusor dysfunction, prostatitis, urinary tract infection, prostate cancer and neurological disease.
  Epidemiology: Age is an important risk factor, and prevalence rises as men get older. Bothersome symptoms affect up to 30% of men older than 65 years.
  Clinical presentation: Symptoms can substantially impair quality of life and may indicate serious urogenital disease, although they do not usually cause severe illness.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: voiding symptoms
      Distinguishing features: May involve a weak or intermittent stream, straining, hesitancy, terminal dribbling or incomplete emptying.
    - Name: storage symptoms
      Distinguishing features: May involve urgency, frequency, urgency incontinence or nocturia.
    - Name: post-micturition symptoms
      Distinguishing features: Post-micturition dribbling is the principal symptom described.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Medical history and medication review
      Purpose: Identify possible causes, associated conditions and medicines that might contribute to symptoms, including herbal and over-the-counter products.
      When indicated: Initial and specialist assessment.
    - Test: Physical examination, including abdomen, external genitalia and digital rectal examination
      Purpose: Assess findings relevant to urological symptoms and other medical conditions.
      When indicated: Initial and specialist assessment.
      Interpretation: An abnormal-feeling prostate is one reason to discuss PSA testing.
    - Test: Urinary frequency volume chart
      Purpose: Record the pattern and volume of urination.
      When indicated: At initial assessment for bothersome LUTS; at specialist assessment for LUTS.
    - Test: Urine dipstick test
      Purpose: Detect blood, glucose, protein, leucocytes and nitrites.
      When indicated: Initial assessment.
    - Test: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing
      When indicated: Discuss the test and allow time for a decision if symptoms suggest bladder outlet obstruction secondary to BPE, the prostate feels abnormal on digital rectal examination, or the man is concerned about prostate cancer.
    - Test: Serum creatinine test and estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] calculation
      Purpose: Assess suspected renal impairment.
      When indicated: At initial assessment only when renal impairment is suspected, for example with a palpable bladder, nocturnal enuresis, recurrent urinary tract infections or a history of renal stones.
    - Test: Flow-rate measurement and post-void residual volume measurement
      When indicated: Specialist assessment; not routinely at initial assessment.
    - Test: Cystoscopy
      Purpose: Investigate when clinically indicated.
      When indicated: At specialist assessment, for example with a history of recurrent infection, sterile pyuria, haematuria, profound symptoms or pain; not routinely at initial assessment for uncomplicated LUTS.
    - Test: Imaging of the upper urinary tract
      Purpose: Investigate when clinically indicated.
      When indicated: At specialist assessment, for example with a history of chronic retention, haematuria, recurrent infection, sterile pyuria, profound symptoms or pain; not routinely at initial assessment for uncomplicated LUTS.
    - Test: Multichannel cystometry
      When indicated: May be considered during specialist assessment if surgery is being contemplated.
    - Test: Pad tests
      Purpose: Measure the extent of urinary incontinence.
      When indicated: At specialist assessment only when quantification of incontinence is needed.
    - Test: Validated symptom score, for example the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)
      Purpose: Establish symptom severity before treatment so subsequent changes can be assessed.
      When indicated: When considering any treatment for LUTS.
      Interpretation: The guideline defines mild as 0 to 7, moderate as 8 to 19 and severe as 20 to 35.
  Prognostic tools:
    - Name: International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)
      Risk groups:
      - Group: mild
      Criteria: 0 to 7
      - Group: moderate
      Criteria: 8 to 19
      - Group: severe
      Criteria: 20 to 35
      Interpretation: The score categorises symptom severity and provides a baseline against which change after treatment can be assessed.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Offer review if previously non-bothersome or uncomplicated symptoms change. Discuss regular follow-up when choosing active surveillance. For men taking alpha blockers, review at 4 to 6 weeks and then every 6 to 12 months; for 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, at 3 to 6 months and then every 6 to 12 months; for anticholinergics, every 4 to 6 weeks until symptoms stabilise and then every 6 to 12 months.

  Content: Recurrent infections cause substantial morbidity: they may worsen incontinence, cause malaise or involve the upper urinary tract with possible renal-function loss. retrieved_chunks.document_id: Bęben et al. 2024 Post herpetic neuralgia currently available oral and topical medications in the management of pain
retrieved_chunks.text:
Clinical implications:
  - Because post-herpetic neuralgia commonly affects older people with other illnesses and concomitant medicines, adverse effects and altered drug handling can complicate pain treatment.
  - Using medicines with different mechanisms may improve analgesia when one medicine is inadequate, potentially allowing lower doses, provided the combination is safe for the patient.
  - The low systemic absorption of topical lidocaine and capsaicin limits systemic exposure, although local reactions remain relevant; the authors also describe a low risk of interactions when gabapentinoids are combined with topical medicines.
  - Renal failure, particularly in patients receiving dialysis, increases concern about gabapentinoid toxicity. Respiratory depression has been described with combined gabapentinoid and opioid use.

Practice implications:
  - Individualize medicine selection according to the clinical case, including comorbidities, concomitant medicines and susceptibility to adverse effects.
  - Consider gabapentinoids or tricyclic antidepressants as oral first-line treatment, either alone or, when appropriate, alongside topical lidocaine 5% or capsaicin 8%.
  - Consider multimodal treatment with medicines acting through different mechanisms when monotherapy does not provide adequate analgesia or adverse effects prevent an effective dose, as long as the regimen is safe for the patient.
  - Use caution with tricyclic antidepressants in patients with cardiac disease and in older patients; the authors suggest considering desipramine or nortriptyline in older patients because of their more linear pharmacokinetics and lower cholinolytic activity than amitriptyline.
  - Exercise particular care with gabapentinoids in renal failure and when they are combined with opioids, especially in older patients.
  - Reserve opioids for second- or, in some circumstances, third-line treatment or for multimodal therapy. The authors state that they should not be used in patients with respiratory failure.
  - Include psychological and social support in a multidisciplinary approach to this chronic condition.

Document sections:
  Heading: Symptoms and signs
  Content: In its rationale for recommendations 1.1.1 to 1.1.9, the committee says timely, accurate UTI diagnosis matters for preventing avoidable illness and serious complications such as renal scarring. Table 1 provides greater clarity about features that raise or lower UTI likelihood, including dysuria, urinary frequency, loin tenderness and bedwetting retained from the 2007 guideline. Evidence for many features was low- or very-low quality because studies often were not designed to assess diagnostic accuracy and defined features poorly; the table therefore supplements clinical judgement. Its incomplete list must not prevent testing an unwell person when UTI remains suspected. Studies of algorithms combining features found none particularly accurate, so the committee did not recommend them; multiple features nevertheless probably increase UTI likelihood. Most evidence concerned children under 5 years, and trials seldom separated outcomes by age. The committee considered the features broadly applicable across ages but emphasised that age and communication ability affect their assessment. Dysuria, for example, raised UTI likelihood when present and lowered it when absent across ages, yet can be difficult to assess in a person who cannot communicate or is not toilet trained. Confirmed previous UTI was included despite not itself being a symptom or sign because it raises likelihood. Evidence reviewed did not establish sleepiness or lethargy, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, failure to thrive or jaundice as clinically useful indicators of UTI. Haematuria, cloudy urine and dark urine may be reported by the child or carers before a clinician has a sample; dark urine is not specific and may accompany illness and dehydration, while reported visible blood is, in the committee's view, uncommon in UTI and always needs further investigation. Less specific features may still help when combined. Features that lower UTI likelihood can indicate another infection site but do not rule UTI out. Routine urine testing is unnecessary when another infection is suggested in those aged 3 months and over, although persistent illness with diagnostic uncertainty can warrant testing. The specified fever guideline may assist when an under-5 has otherwise unexplained fever but UTI is no longer suspected. Urine collection and testing should not be delayed; culture can miss some UTIs, for which recommendation 1.1.23 addresses clinical decision-making. Concern about sepsis supports specialist referral and urgent microscopy and culture for suspected UTI under 3 months. Evidence gaps prompted the research questions about ages 5 years and above but under 16 years, recurrent UTI and long-term (chronic) UTI.

Document sections:
  Heading: 10.3.1 Epidemiology/aetiology/pathophysiology
  Content: Epidemiological estimates largely come from small case series. Non-ischaemic priapism is significantly less common than ischaemic priapism and represents only 5% of cases. Blunt perineal or penile injury is the commonest cause. Laceration of a cavernous artery or branch creates an artery-to-lacunar-space fistula, increasing flow and causing a prolonged erection. Onset after trauma may be delayed up to two to three weeks, possibly because arterial spasm or ischaemic necrosis precedes fistula formation. Priapism typically emerges after nocturnal or sexually related erection raises cavernous arterial flow and pressure. Erections are usually incompletely rigid and painless because venous drainage persists and tissue does not become ischaemic. Acute spinal cord injury may also cause this form, presumably through loss of sympathetic input and predominance of parasympathetic-driven arterial flow. Other reported antecedents are internal urethrotomy, Nesbit procedure, circumcision, transrectal prostate biopsy, prostate-cancer brachytherapy, and shunting for ischaemic priapism that lacerates a cavernous artery and converts low to high flow. Occasional high-flow cases occur with SCD, but their mechanism is unclear. Penile metastatic malignancy is another rare cause.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_04
  Name: ED after RP
  Synonyms:
    - post-RP ED
  Description: Erectile difficulty following radical prostatectomy. Damage to neurovascular structures during pelvic surgery may contribute, even though nerve-sparing approaches are used.
  Epidemiology: Studies cited by the guide report post-RP ED in 25-75% of men, while unassisted recovery of post-operative erectile function ranges between 20 and 25% in most studies. In the ProtecT trial, erections firm enough for intercourse were reported by 67% at baseline and, at six-year follow-up, by 30% in the active monitoring group, 27%% in the RT group and 17% in the RP group. Patient age, erectile function before surgery, surgical volume and preservation of neurovascular bundles influence post-operative erectile outcomes; evidence comparing surgical approaches is conflicting.
  Clinical presentation: Reduced erectile function after RP may occur alongside other changes in sexual health. The guide reports that penile rehabilitation following nerve-sparing RP has not been shown to increase spontaneous erectile-function recovery.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Baseline and post-operative erectile-function assessment
      Purpose: Establish pre-operative function and evaluate erectile outcomes following surgery.
      When indicated: Assessment of patients undergoing or recovering from RP.
      Interpretation: Age, baseline EF and the quality of nerve-sparing technique are identified as potential predictors of outcome.
    - Test: EPIC-26
      Purpose: Measure sexual function, including erectile function.
      When indicated: Used for sexual-function assessment in the cited ProtecT trial and a cited comparison of surgery with RT.
  Follow up:
    Recommended tests:
      - Assess erectile function
      - Assess treatment efficacy and safety
      - Assess patient satisfaction
    Long term effects:
      - Persistent post-operative erectile difficulty
      - Possible changes in sexual desire, orgasm, ejaculation, penile shape or penile size after active treatment for prostate cancer
    Survivorship notes: The guide states that evidence is insufficient to identify a particular penile-rehabilitation regimen that reliably produces spontaneous, unassisted erections.

Document sections:
  Heading: 5.4 Patient selection for LUTS/BPO treatment
  Content: Treatment choice depends on assessment findings, achievable changes, personal preferences and expectations concerning onset, efficacy, adverse effects, QoL and progression. Behavioural measures, with or without medicines, are usually initial options. Surgery is usually required for recurrent or refractory retention, overflow incontinence, recurrent UTI, bladder stones or diverticula, treatment-resistant visible haematuria due to BPH/BPE, or upper-tract dilatation from BPO with or without renal insufficiency; these are absolute indications. Surgery is also usually needed if conservative or drug therapy does not adequately relieve LUTS or PVR, a relative indication. Choice of operation reflects gland size, comorbidity, anaesthetic fitness, patient preference and acceptance of adverse effects, equipment and surgeon experience. Figure 3 sets out conservative and medical choices by symptom bother, predominant nocturnal polyuria or storage symptoms, gland volume > 40 mL, persistent storage symptoms and whether long-term treatment is intended. Figure 4 organises surgical choices by operative indications or treatment preference, high-risk status, anaesthetic fitness, ability to interrupt anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy and gland sizes < 30 mL, 30 – 80 mL or > 80 mL; it identifies current standard/first-choice procedures and alternatives. Patient preferences may change the route selected.

Document sections:
  Heading: 3.1 Epidemiology
  Content: UC is the second most frequent urological malignancy in developed countries and can arise in the lower urinary tract or the pyelocaliceal cavities and ureter. Bladder cancer (BC) constitutes 90–95% of UC, whereas UTUC constitutes 5–10%; estimated annual incidence in Western countries is almost two cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Incidence has increased over recent decades, possibly because detection improved and populations aged. Incidence peaks at 70–90 years, and UTUC occurs twice as often in men. In an international retrospective registry of 2,380 people diagnosed between 2014 and 2019 at 101 centres in 29 countries, 70.5% were men, 53.3% were current or former smokers, and 53% received a diagnosis after symptoms, chiefly visible haematuria. A meta-analysis of 44 studies estimated UTUC incidence among people with visible and non-visible haematuria at 0.75% and 0.17%, respectively. Approximately two-thirds of patients presenting with UTUC have muscle-invasive disease at diagnosis, versus 15–25% with newly diagnosed BC; population studies from Germany and England suggest muscle-invasive UTUC accounts for approximately half of recent incident cases. Approximately 9% present with metastases. Pyelocaliceal tumours occur approximately twice as frequently as ureteral tumours; multifocality occurs in approximately 10–20%, and concomitant upper-tract carcinoma in situ in between 11% and 36%. Concurrent BC occurs in 17%; previous BC was recorded in 41% of American men and 4% of Chinese men. These differences, alongside genetic and epigenetic factors, may help explain more advanced, higher-grade presentations in Asian patients. After treatment, bladder recurrence occurs in 29%, varying with patient, tumour and treatment characteristics, versus 2–5% recurrence in the contralateral upper tract. UTUC and BC differ substantially in frequencies of common genomic changes, although tumours in a person with both cancers are often clonally related. UTUC genomic profiling can inform bladder-recurrence risk and identify Lynch syndrome-associated tumours. Among 82 patients given intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) for high-risk BC and imaged regularly between years 1 and 3, 13% developed asymptomatic UTUC; another series of 307 patients without routine upper-tract imaging reported 25% UTUC after BC. A multicentre cohort of n = 402 followed for 50 month reported 7.5% UTUC among NMIBC recipients of BCG; intravesical recurrence and a non-papillary tumour at transurethral resection of the bladder (TURB) predicted UTUC. Following radical cystectomy for MIBC, 3–5% develop metachronous UTUC.

Document sections:
  Heading: Epidemiology
  Content: Fungal infection is described as the second most common cause of infectious keratitis after bacterial infection and as more severe and destructive. Its prolonged course carries substantial risks of complications and perforation, so therapeutic keratoplasty is frequently necessary. Incidence depends strongly on geography, humidity, and other local risk factors, even within one country. Most reports place fungal disease at 17% to 36% of corneal infections; reported proportions are 5–20% in the United States and more than 50% in developing countries. A recent Egyptian delta study reported fungal infection in as many as two-thirds of microbial keratitis cases, with culture-confirmed mixed infection in 20% of those fungal cases. Any age can be affected, but disease is more frequent in middle-aged people and in males. It is reported to be more endemic in winter because of humidity. Filamentous fungi predominate over yeast and yeast-like fungi; Aspergillus and Fusarium are the filamentous organisms most often observed, and Candida is the commonest yeast.

Document sections:
  Heading: 1. Introduction
  Content: Ovarian lesions account for most abdominal masses in pediatric girls and span functional cysts through malignant tumors. Cysts constitute 60% of pediatric ovarian lesions. True neoplasms occur at 2.6 cases per 100,000 girls per year; 3–8% of adnexal masses are malignant, representing 1–2% of pediatric cancers. Neoplasms are grouped by origin into germ cell, sex cordstromal, and epithelial tumors. Incidence, causes, and presentation vary by age: germ cell tumors predominate among childhood and adolescent ovarian neoplasms, whereas epithelial tumors predominate in adults. Mature cystic teratomas are the most frequent tumor type, and dysgerminomas are described as the most frequent malignant ovarian neoplasm in the pediatric population. Functional cysts peak in the fetal/neonatal and perimenarchal periods, reflecting maternal gonadotropins or activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis. Ultrasound is the initial imaging choice; MRI offers additional soft-tissue detail without ionizing radiation. Imaging and serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), beta subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), and inhibin A and B contribute to malignancy-risk assessment. Pediatric surgery should favor fertility preservation, minimally invasive laparoscopy, and ovarian conservation when feasible. The review addresses evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment across pediatric age groups.

  Content: Son embarazos de alto riesgo por el aumento de morbilidad materna y fetal. Se incrementan el aborto, especialmente en monocigotos; la preeclampsia, que puede comenzar antes de la 20 semana; la hiperemesis gravídica y la hipertensión inducida por el embarazo. La amenaza de parto pretérmino aumenta por sobredistensión uterina y por polihidramnios, presente en el 15 % de los embarazos gemelares; la prematuridad es la principal causa de morbimortalidad neonatal. Son más frecuentes la rotura prematura de membranas, las malformaciones congénitas —cuya frecuencia se multiplica por 3, sobre todo defectos del tubo neural y cardiopatías—, el prolapso de cordón en monoamnióticos o con polihidramnios y el abruptio placentae tras la descompresión que sigue al nacimiento del primer gemelo. El donante puede presentar hipovolemia, hipotensión, anemia y CIR.   Content: Most abdominal masses in girls originate in the ovaries and range from functional cysts to malignancies. Their frequency, presentation, and histology vary with age. Assessment focuses on malignancy risk because benign and malignant lesions require substantially different management. Ultrasound is the principal examination for size, location, and morphology; MRI or CT can provide further assessment when ultrasound is inconclusive or malignancy is suspected, particularly in older adolescents. Document sections:
  Heading: 4.4. Ruptured Hemorrhagic Ovarian Cyst
  Content: A ruptured hemorrhagic cyst generally causes sudden focal, one-sided lower abdominal pain, often midway through the menstrual cycle, sometimes with intraperitoneal hemorrhage. Massive bleeding may produce shoulder or upper abdominal pain from blood beneath the diaphragm. Bleeding may stop spontaneously or cause hemodynamic instability. Self-limited cases warrant serial hemoglobin and hematocrit measurements. Unstable patients should be stabilized before surgery, often laparoscopic. Laparotomy is recommended only if the surgeon lacks pediatric laparoscopic experience or an unstable patient cannot be stabilized. An illustrated 14-year-old had acute pain and vomiting; ultrasound showed a left ovarian cystic-solid mass measuring 11 × 8 cm with disruption and free abdominal fluid. Exploratory laparotomy and left adnexectomy identified a ruptured, twisted tumor, confirmed histologically as a ruptured ovarian cystic mature teratoma.
