Document sections:
  Heading: 3 Guideline policies for orchidopexy
  Content: Physical examination is the primary means of assessment. For a non-palpable testis, ultrasound can help when its findings would determine the operative approach or whether diagnostic laparoscopy is needed. Imaging should otherwise be selective and must not postpone referral after diagnosis. EAU, AUA and Nordic Consensus guidelines all recommend intervention between 6 to 18 months of age. For palpable undescended testes, the AUA favors a standard inguinal approach; EAU and Nordic Consensus guidance also accepts a scrotal approach in selected cases. For nonpalpable testes, EAU and Nordic guidance favors laparoscopy, whereas the AUA accepts open or laparoscopic surgery. The AUA leaves the one-stage versus twostage decision to the surgeon, informed by testicular position, vascular supply and adjacent anatomy. The EAU suggests a two-stage approach might reduce atrophy and improve mobility. EAU and AUA guidance does not recommend hormonal therapy as primary treatment. Nordic guidance likewise notes limited effectiveness and possible adverse effects in childhood, although it allows consideration in exceptional cases; convincing evidence for benefit before or after surgery remains lacking. All three sets of guidance stress long-term follow-up.

Document sections:
  Heading: 11.4.2.2 Testicular microcalcification (TM)
  Content: TM occurs in 0.6-9% of men referred for testicular US; its general-population incidence is unknown and probably low. It has been observed with malignancy and several benign reproductive conditions, and reported TGCT-associated incidence is 6-46%. Its association with infertility is uncertain. A case-control meta-analysis associated TM in infertile men with testicular cancer (pooled OR: 18.11, 95% CI: 8.09, 40.55; p < 0.0001). Although TM merits counselling in this setting and biopsies show more GCNIS, especially with bilateral findings, calcification itself is not malignant and its association with TGCT remains controversial. Possible GCNIS risk factors include infertility, atrophy, undescended testis, prior TGCT and contralateral TM; biopsy has been suggested for selected patients after discussion of its risks. Most asymptomatic patients do not develop cancer. Decastro et al. suggested no testicular cancer developed in most men with TM (98.4%) during 5-year follow-up; extensive screening would therefore principally benefit high-risk men. Advise regular self-examination with incidental TM, particularly with other cancer risks. Annual urological examination and US have been suggested for higher-risk men, but follow-up may be difficult; evidence is lacking for higher cancer prevalence specifically with both TM and atrophy.

Document sections:
  Heading: Clinical assessment History and examination
  Content: Because FG can progress rapidly and become fatal, early recognition and vigorous resuscitation are essential. An A–E assessment and indicated resuscitation may need to precede a full history, depending on haemodynamic stability. Symptoms are often nonspecific and can resemble scrotal cellulitis, scrotal abscess, or severe epididymo-orchitis. Local manifestations include scrotal swelling, scrotal or perineal pain, erythema, and skin necrosis; advanced infection may cause fever, vomiting, and altered consciousness. Progression varies but can occur over 3–5days, beginning with increasing discomfort or pain and pruritus. Swelling and skin changes indicate more advanced soft-tissue gangrene. Diabetes mellitus, HIV infection, or immunosuppressive medication should lower the threshold for suspecting FG. Genital and perineal examination is performed with a chaperone. Swelling, erythema, warmth, and tenderness indicate inflammation; the edge of erythema should be marked for comparison at later examinations. Palpable crepitus indicates subcutaneous gas from gas-producing anaerobic infection. Any wound discharge should be sampled for culture. Extension from the genital or perineal area to the thighs or abdominal wall is concerning. Foul-smelling, purple-black skin necrosis is characteristic. PR examination should assess perianal involvement and may reveal a perianal or perirectal abscess as the infectious source.

Document sections:
  Heading: Context
  Content: The lower urinary tract comprises bladder and urethra and coordinates urine storage and expulsion under central and peripheral nervous-system control. Neurological disease affecting the brain, suprasacral or sacral spinal cord, or peripheral nerves can produce characteristic patterns of bladder and sphincter dysfunction; the nature of the injury also matters. Childhood neurological damage often stems from congenital conditions such as spina bifida or sacral agenesis. Stroke, spinal cord injury and cauda equina compression can cause relatively stable injury, whereas dementia, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis and peripheral neuropathy can cause progressive damage. Table 1 groups example neurological conditions by lesion site and likelihood of progression. Because the neural centres governing urinary, bowel and sexual function are close, dysfunctions often coexist and warrant a holistic rather than isolated urinary approach. Neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction can impair storage, emptying or both; storage symptoms include increased frequency and incontinence. Urinary symptoms can cause embarrassment, social isolation and difficulty with daily activities. Incontinence can result from overactive bladder, urethral sphincter dysfunction or both. Risks include markedly more urinary tract infections and loss of renal function from elevated bladder pressures, infection or kidney stones. Medical treatment often does not restore normal urinary function, and medicines, intermittent self-catheterisation, indwelling catheters, pads and appliances can affect quality of life. Families and carers may face physical, psychological, relationship and social pressures. Costs arise from supplies, medicines, operations, care and professional support, as well as effects on employment, follow-up and long-term surveillance. The full guideline contains 3 algorithms outlining the clinical approach. For recommended uses outside UK marketing authorisation at publication, prescribers should follow relevant professional guidance, take responsibility for the decision, and obtain and document informed consent.

  Content: LUTS encompass storage, voiding and post-micturition symptoms. Possible causes involve abnormal structure or function of the prostate, urethra, bladder or sphincters. In men, the most common cause is benign prostate enlargement (BPE), which obstructs the bladder outlet; BPE arises from an increase in prostate cell numbers called benign prostatic hyperplasia. Other possible causes include detrusor weakness or overactivity, prostate inflammation (prostatitis), urinary tract infection, prostate cancer and neurological disease. Categorising symptoms as voiding, storage or post-micturition helps identify their source. Voiding symptoms comprise a weak or intermittent stream, straining, hesitancy, terminal dribbling and incomplete emptying. Storage symptoms comprise urgency, frequency, urgency incontinence and nocturia. Post-micturition dribbling is the main post-micturition symptom and is common and bothersome. LUTS usually do not cause severe illness but can substantially impair quality of life or indicate serious urogenital disease. They impose a major burden on ageing men: age is an important risk factor, prevalence rises with age, and bothersome LUTS occur in up to 30% of men older than 65 years.   Content: In males, the anterior urethra extends from the meatus to the urogenital diaphragm and remains surrounded by corpus spongiosum. Meatal strictures occur at the external opening and may extend into the fossa navicularis. Penile strictures occupy the region between fossa navicularis and bulbar urethra; externally it runs approximately from the balanopreputial sulcus to the penoscrotal junction, ventral to the corpora cavernosa within a thin spongiosal layer. The bulbar urethra runs from the penoscrotal junction to the membranous urethra at the urogenital diaphragm and is surrounded by bulbospongiosus muscle. Its proximal segment lies within 5 cm of the membranous urethra, with eccentric urethral position and abundant ventral spongiosum; its distal segment extends towards the penoscrotal junction. Extension into the membranous region is termed bulbomembranous strictures (BMS). Penobulbar strictures span penile and bulbar segments. retrieved_chunks.document_id: Bowen et al. 2024 Fournier’s gangrene a review of predictive scoring systems and practical guide for patient manageme
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Use of scoring systems
  Content: Scores in clinical practice can support diagnosis, treatment decisions, and predictions of morbidity or mortality. Wong et al. created Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) in 2004 from biochemical markers using multivariate logistic regression. At a cut-off of six points, they reported positive and negative predictive values of 92.0% and 96.0%, respectively. LRINEC uses six routinely obtained biochemical markers. Some evidence supports distinguishing necrotising fasciitis from other soft-tissue infections, and some studies suggest seven as a better cut-off. In contrast, a meta-analysis of 23 studies reported poor sensitivity: 68.2% for LRINEC ⩾6 and 40.8% for LRINEC ⩾8. Clinical assessment, with imaging when appropriate, therefore remains necessary. No published study has assessed LRINEC specifically as a diagnostic test for FG; some case studies suggest it may predict FG mortality and mechanical ventilation. In 1995, Laor et al. examined demographic, clinical, laboratory, disease-extent, and debridement data from 30 FG patients and developed Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index (FGSI) through regression analysis to predict mortality. Unlike LRINEC, FGSI includes temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate. Affected body-surface percentage and number of debridements were excluded because they did not significantly predict mortality. Other studies have repeatedly validated FGSI for mortality prediction and reported associations with further surgery, longer hospitalization, sepsis, and FG-specific complications, suggesting possible value for morbidity prediction. In 2010, Yilmazlar et al., concerned that FGSI underestimated mortality, analysed a series of 80 patients. Their logistic regression identified disease spread and age as additional significant mortality predictors, leading to Uludag Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index (UFGSI). At a cut-off of nine points, their reported probability of death was 94% for UFGSI >9 and probability of survival was 81% for UFGSI ⩽9; corresponding published FGSI figures were 75% and 78%. External studies validated UFGSI, and one comparison suggested greater sensitivity (75.0% compared with 58.3%) but lower specificity (84.0% compared with 97.3%) than FGSI. Although FGSI and UFGSI have broad validation, calculating them during rapid deterioration can take time. In Roghmann et al.’s prospective cohort, Charlson Comorbidity Index and Surgical Apgar Score predicted outcomes as well as FG-specific indices while being simpler, more broadly applicable, and better validated. Surgical Apgar Score relies on intraoperative anaesthetic measurements, limiting preoperative use. Lin et al. proposed Simplified Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index in 2013 using serum creatinine, haematocrit, and serum potassium; it is the quickest and simplest of these FG indices and was reported non-inferior to FGSI and UFGSI. An outcome score should be quick and straightforward, robust to differences between operators, sensitive and specific, and supported by evidence that it affects management. There is no consensus on whether FG scoring systems are useful or which to prefer, nor is it clear whether a high predicted mortality should alter decisions about aggressive resuscitation and debridement. Emerging work examines neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), previously correlated with mortality in sepsis, pneumonia, COVID-19, and cancer. NLR has been reported to predict intensive care admission, mechanical ventilation, and mortality in FG, but routine prognostic use requires more research. Table 1 summarizes the scoring systems’ proposed cut-offs, original authors’ death and survival probabilities, advantages, and disadvantages.

  Content: TM occurs in 0.6-9% of men referred for testicular US; its general-population incidence is unknown and probably low. It has been observed with malignancy and several benign reproductive conditions, and reported TGCT-associated incidence is 6-46%. Its association with infertility is uncertain. A case-control meta-analysis associated TM in infertile men with testicular cancer (pooled OR: 18.11, 95% CI: 8.09, 40.55; p < 0.0001). Although TM merits counselling in this setting and biopsies show more GCNIS, especially with bilateral findings, calcification itself is not malignant and its association with TGCT remains controversial. Possible GCNIS risk factors include infertility, atrophy, undescended testis, prior TGCT and contralateral TM; biopsy has been suggested for selected patients after discussion of its risks. Most asymptomatic patients do not develop cancer. Decastro et al. suggested no testicular cancer developed in most men with TM (98.4%) during 5-year follow-up; extensive screening would therefore principally benefit high-risk men. Advise regular self-examination with incidental TM, particularly with other cancer risks. Annual urological examination and US have been suggested for higher-risk men, but follow-up may be difficult; evidence is lacking for higher cancer prevalence specifically with both TM and atrophy.

  Content: Complex anatomy requires experienced dissection of the UPJ to avoid vascular injury. Examples include a completely intrarenal pelvis, high ureteral insertion, a long ureteral stricture, horseshoe kidney (HSK), renal malrotation, ectopic kidney, and a duplex kidney with lower-moiety UPJO. In the largest multicenter series of complex cases described in the review, Esposito et al. recommended Anderson–Hynes pyeloplasty using da Vinci Xi. They described its adaptability to UPJ vascular anatomy in HSK or ectopic kidney, crossing vessels, lower-pole UPJO requiring preservation of upper-moiety ureteral blood supply to prevent stenosis, and fibrosis after unsuccessful open pyeloplasty. A cited multicenter HSK study by the same group reported that RALP was safe and feasible with good medium-term results: average operative time including docking was 143.5 min (range 100–205), with no conversions to laparoscopic or open surgery, no intraoperative complications, and an overall success rate of 92.8%.   Content: Adolescent ovaries contain follicles at different stages. Most adolescent cysts are follicular, arising when a developing follicle neither ovulates nor involutes. The differential diagnosis includes obstructive genital anomalies, ovarian tumors, tubal disease, uterine masses, and urinary or gastrointestinal conditions. Ultrasound is the first imaging examination. Follicular cysts generally resolve within eight weeks. Monophasic combined estrogen/progestin oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) with ≥ 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol are commonly recommended to inhibit the ovarian-hypothalamic axis, suppress ovulation, and prevent new functional cysts. Persistence for ≥3 months, size ≥ 6 cm, pelvic pain, or urinary frequency are indications for laparoscopic cystectomy or aspiration, although some simple cysts measuring 6 to 12 cm resolve and can be monitored safely in selected patients. Cystectomy is usually preferred over aspiration because aspiration has a high recurrence rate. For asymptomatic corpus luteum cysts, observation for three months is recommended; monophasic combined estrogen/progestin OCPs containing ≥ 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol are also prescribed, and cystectomy alone is seldom justified. Persistent or non-involuting cysts should undergo cystectomy with preservation of ovarian tissue. Document sections:
  Heading: Introduction
  Content: UPJO can result from intrinsic fibrosis or stenosis of the proximal ureter, or from extrinsic compression by aberrant lower-pole vessels. Prenatal hydronephrosis has been detected in up to 4.5% of screening ultrasounds, with UPJO accounting for up to 41% of cases. A large proportion of presentations resembling UPJO, consisting of isolated hydronephrosis with or without calyceal dilation, are benign and resolve spontaneously; approximately 25% of prenatally diagnosed UPJO cases require surgery. Earlier diagnosis has significantly lowered the age at pyeloplasty. Since Anderson and Hynes first described their operation in 1949, surgeons have sought to simplify it and reduce complications. Anderson–Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty, traditionally performed through an open flank incision, remains the gold standard for UPJ obstruction and has an overall success rate of 90 to 100%. Pediatric laparoscopic pyeloplasty (LP) was first reported in 1995 and was subsequently established as a safe and effective minimally invasive alternative. Robotic surgery for children has advanced throughout the last 10 years; RALP has become the most commonly performed pediatric robotic urology operation, with reported success rates of 95%–100%.   Heading: 5.1. Paediatric Population
  Content: Children may have vague, age-dependent symptoms: older children can have haematuria, flank pain or recurrent UTIs, whereas infants may vomit, become irritable or cry. To limit radiation under ALARA, the EAU recommends initial US; inadequate findings may prompt KUB X-ray or NCCT (strong recommendation). The AUA recommends NCCT before paediatric PCNL (strong recommendation). The EAU notes little evidence for observation but allows it initially for asymptomatic lower-pole stones <7 mm without struvite or cystine composition or anatomical abnormalities. It states that MET may improve passage and pain but causes more side effects in children. The AUA recommends observation with or without MET first for ureteral stones ≤10 mm; patients or parents should be informed if MET is used off-label (AUA: moderate recommendation). Routine stenting before paediatric URS is discouraged (AUA: expert opinion). SWL, URS and PCNL generally have indications similar to those in adults. For a single ureteral stone <10 mm, the EAU favours SWL first and URS if SWL fails or cannot be used (strong recommendation). URS with lasertripsy can have good, safe outcomes when performed by surgeons experienced in paediatric complications. After failed observation or MET, the AUA recommends choosing SWL or URS according to anatomy and habitus (strong recommendation). It cautions that ultrasound-based lithotriptors may poorly visualise the ureter, particularly its middle portion, while SWL can be useful in small children for whom URS access is difficult. For renal stones <20 mm, the EAU favours SWL first (strong recommendation) and FURS may follow failed SWL, especially for lower-calyceal stones; the AUA supports SWL or URS (moderate recommendation). For renal stones >20 mm, the EAU recommends PCNL (strong recommendation). In children, PCNL's higher SFR comes with more side effects, although mini and ultra-mini PCNL have reduced complications related to tract size, including renal extravasation and haematuria. The AUA instead accepts either PCNL or SWL with stent or nephrostomy for >20 mm stones (moderate recommendation). It also favours observation with routine US surveillance for asymptomatic, non-obstructing renal stones (expert opinion). All children's stones should undergo material analysis, with subsequent metabolic assessment guided by the result (EAU: strong recommendation).

Document sections:
  Heading: PSA Testing
  Content: PSA is secreted by prostate epithelial cells; its protease activity liquefies coagulated ejaculate and promotes sperm motility. How it enters the circulation is unknown. Commercial serum assays perform similarly when appropriately used apart from small calibration differences, but results from differently calibrated assays cannot be directly exchanged. Repeat an unusually high result, especially near an evaluation threshold; in one study, approximately 25% initially measuring 4 to 10 ng/mL had a normal repeat result. PSA is not specific to cancer: most people with elevated values do not have prostate cancer, and no low value eliminates risk. Total PSA >10 ng/mL corresponds to greater than 67% likelihood of biopsy-detectable cancer; about 18% with PSA 4 to 10 ng/mL have a subsequent positive biopsy. In PCPT data from 18,882 participants, end-of-study biopsy identified cancer in 15% with PSA of 4.0 ng/mL or less and normal DRE. At 3.1 ng/mL, sensitivity for any prostate cancer was about 32% and specificity about 87%. Appropriate PSA testing alone can advance diagnosis by 5 to 10 years, with variation across studies, populations, and protocols. After PSA testing was introduced, detection shifted toward early organ-confined disease and away from metastasis at diagnosis. Population-screening studies have demonstrated survival benefits using PSA, sometimes alongside DRE or other tests.

Document sections:
  Heading: 5.3.1.1 Monopolar and bipolar transurethral resection of the prostate
  Content: TURP removes varying amounts of transition-zone tissue, reducing prostate volume and PSA by 25 -58%. Unlike M-TURP, B-TURP confines current locally and uses saline irrigation, eliminating TUR-syndrome. A meta-analysis of twenty RCTs found mean M-TURP changes of Qmax +162%, IPSS -70%, QoL -69% and PVR -77% through five years; studies extending eight to 22 years support durability. A study with mean thirteen-year follow-up associated failure with DUA rather than BPH regrowth. Repeat prostatic operations occur at approximately 1-2% annually; a review of 29 RCTs reported 2.6% retreatment after mean sixteen-month follow-up. In Austrian cohorts totalling 41,059 men, overall retreatment at three months, one year, five years and eight years was 0.9%, 3.7%, 9.5% and 12.7%, respectively; re-TURP at those times was 0.8%, 2.4%, 6.1% and 8.3%. Pooled evidence from 59 RCTs generally finds comparable B-TURP and M-TURP symptom, QoL and Qmax outcomes at twelve months and through 60 months, including 36-month IPSS and Qmax; trial quality was often poor. Ten TURis RCTs involving 1,870 patients found efficacy equivalent to M-TURP. Reported M-TURP peri-operative mortality and morbidity were 0.1% and 11.1%; Austrian data showed a 20% mortality reduction over time, to 0.1% at 30 days and 0.5% at 90 days. TUR-syndrome risk fell to < 1.1%; among 10,654 M-TURPs, transfusion-requiring bleeding occurred in 2.9%. Comparator RCTs reported transfusion-requiring bleeding 2% (0-9%), TUR-syndrome 0.8% (0-5%), AUR 4.5% (0-13.3%), clot retention 4.9% (0-39%) and UTI 4.1% (0-22%). Later problems include UI, retention, UTIs, BNC, urethral stricture, retrograde ejaculation and ED. B-TURP offers better peri-operative safety without a consistent efficacy difference; the largest meta-analysis estimated twenty fewer TUR-syndrome events and 28 fewer transfusions per 1,000 participants versus M-TURP, with potentially similar UI and short-term re-TURP rates (four fewer UI events and one more re-TURP per 1000 participants). TURis studies likewise reported improved bleeding and TUR-syndrome outcomes. Limited follow-up can miss late strictures or BNC. Most longer RCTs found similar stricture/BNC rates, but one reported more strictures with quasi-bipolar TURis for glands > 70 mL at 36-months and another more BNC with a true bipolar system among 137 patients at twelve months. Erectile and ejaculatory outcomes generally did not differ. In a comparative study continuing antithrombotic treatment during B-TURP, acetylsalicylic acid outcomes resembled untreated controls; oral anticoagulation increased median catheterisation (41-hours vs. 24-hours), median hospitalisation (four days vs. three days) and AUR (18% vs. 6%) without a transfusion difference; anti-platelet treatment increased transfusion (19% vs. 1%) and re-hospitalisation (19% vs. 3%). M-TURP is suitable for glands of 30-80 mL. The suggested 80 mL upper limit is Panel consensus, varies with surgical factors, and complication risk increases with size; surgery is safest under 90 minutes. Selection of B-TURP also depends on equipment, experience and patient preference. The evidence summary identifies either TURP as standard for bothersome moderate-to-severe LUTS/BPO with 30-80 mL glands and B-TURP as comparably effective with better peri-operative safety (both LE 1a). Offer bipolar- or monopolar-TURP for moderate-to-severe LUTS with prostate size 30-80 mL (Strong).

  Content: Higher-risk operations require surgeons able to protect ureteric blood supply and promptly recognise injury. An intraoperative injury should be repaired immediately using debridement, adequate vascularity, a tension-free anastomosis and internal stenting. After relevant abdominal or pelvic surgery, unexpectedly slow recovery, fluid leakage or pelvicalyceal dilatation should raise suspicion of delayed upper-tract injury. No operative approach has proved superior; consensus favours established tissue-repair principles and experienced teams. Options include internal or external drainage, nephrostomy and stenting, and repair early (< 2 weeks) or later (> 3 months) when needed. Functional and anatomical imaging after repair should detect ureteric stricture or declining renal function. Early postoperative UVF, chiefly following hysterectomy, is the most frequent upper-tract fistula presentation in urological practice. In an RCT of 3,141 women undergoing open or laparoscopic gynaecological surgery, prophylactic ureteric stents did not alter the low injury risk (1%). Selected endoscopic approaches include retrograde or antegrade stenting with nephrostomy, or ureteroscopic realignment, but long-term success is unknown. Distal antegrade ureteric occlusion plus nephrostomy often palliates terminal malignant-fistula leakage. Failure or secondary stricture after endoluminal treatment usually calls for abdominal repair, potentially including end-to-end anastomosis, reimplantation with psoas hitch or Boari flap, or bowel replacement. Nephrectomy is a last resort, particularly with poor function on the affected side and a normal opposite kidney.

  Content: Reported postoperative problems include rejection; graft-interface separation or graft displacement; irregular astigmatism; primary or late graft failure; leaking or misaligned wounds; persistent epithelial defects; filamentary keratitis; immune infiltrates, infection, or abscess related to sutures; cataract; endophthalmitis; increased intraocular pressure; blepharoptosis; anterior synechiae; hyphema; choroidal or retinal detachment; IOL dislocation; and lamellar-interface infection. Primary graft failure means that donor tissue has not cleared within the first 8 weeks after surgery without another explanation for stromal edema, such as persistent epithelial defect, raised pressure, rejection, or inflammation. Inadequate endothelial function from cell damage or too few cells is suspected; donor selection, preparation, storage, or excessive operative handling may contribute. Regrafting is generally required. Endophthalmitis after PK is uncommon but severe. Organisms may come from periocular inoculation, postoperative surface or interface defects, donor tissue, or storage medium. Routine donor-rim cultures poorly predict bacterial endophthalmitis, and fungal cultures have low positive predictive value for infection; fungal cultures may nevertheless be considered, while clinical findings direct management. Late graft failure develops years after transplantation and is thought to reflect progressive endothelial loss, possibly accelerated by rejection, infection, traumatic iritis, or elevated pressure. Donor manipulation during surgery, anterior-chamber shallowing after wound separation, and graft repositioning or rubbing after EK may also contribute to early loss of function. Rejection reactions are the most frequent cause of graft failure. Prompt intensive topical, periocular, and systemic corticosteroids may reverse endothelial rejection. Patients at high risk or with recurrent inflammation, including herpes simplex virus keratitis, herpes zoster ophthalmicus, or uveitis, may need greater daily corticosteroid doses or oral antivirals than standard post-PK protocols. Two studies comparing PK with DSAEK in Fuchs dystrophy and PBK found no statistically significant rejection-rate difference. More recent studies suggest that implanting less allogenic tissue, as with EK, lowers long-term rejection risk. Long-term topical corticosteroids may reduce rejection but call for surveillance for pressure elevation and infectious keratitis, including infection crystalline keratitis. EK became more common than PK in the United States in 2012. Reports documented fungal infection increasing from 0.014% in a 2013 report to 0.023% in a 2016 report. Studies found that three quarters of companion grafts had positive rim cultures when a fungal donor-rim culture was positive, and two thirds of recipients of culturepositive companion tissue developed infection.   Heading: 9 Conclusion
  Content: Orchidopexy remains central to pediatric urologic surgery while techniques continue to develop. For palpable cryptorchidism, open single-stage surgery is established and safe. Available evidence cautiously favors a single incision for lower testes, but superiority over two incisions is not definitive. Non-palpable disease remains difficult to treat, and maintaining perfusion is important for preventing atrophy. Gubernaculum-sparing secondstage FS and the Shehata variant appear promising but require further research. Across the studies discussed, single-stage laparoscopic orchidopexy that sacrifices the gubernaculum and its associated vessels was linked to greater atrophy risk. Hormonal treatment remains controversial: it may have therapeutic value, but possible infertility and delays to surgery require further investigation. Hormonal assessment may eventually complement orchidopexy and support more individualized treatment. Emerging laparoscopic methods need stronger evidence before guideline inclusion. Document sections:
  Heading: 7.3.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the treatment of metastatic UTUC
  Content: The evidence summary reports first-line OS benefit for Enfortmab vedotin + Pembrolizumab over gemcitabinecisplatin (LE 1b); improved median survival with cisplatin combinations (LE 2); cisplatin combinations as standard when cisplatin is tolerated but Enfortumab + Pembrolizumab is unsuitable (LE 1b); additional first-line survival benefit from nivolumab with cisplatin chemotherapy (LE 1b); and benefit from carboplatin combinations if cisplatin is unsuitable (LE 1b). Non-platinum combinations have not been compared against standard chemotherapy in either cisplatin-fit or cisplatin-unfit groups (LE 4). Maintenance avelumab improves OS versus supportive care after no progression on 4 to 6 cycles of gemcitabine plus cisplatin or carboplatin (LE 1b). The summary records approvals of post-platinum pembrolizumab (LE 1b) and nivolumab (LE 2a) when prior immunotherapy was not given, and first-line pembrolizumab or atezolizumab restricted to PD-L1-positive patients unsuitable for platinum (each LE 2a). It associates erdafitinib with improved OS in platinum-refractory FGFR-altered UC (LE 1b), and enfortumab vedotin with OS benefit after platinum and subsequent progression during or after PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibition (LE 1b). Palliative nephroureterectomy may improve quality of life through symptom control (LE 3); selected metastatic patients may gain survival from RNU, for example after platinum response with limited metastatic burden (LE 4). The recommendations are first-line Enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab in advanced/metastatic disease (Strong); if that combination is unsuitable, a platinum combination for platinum-eligible patients (Strong), gemcitabine-cisplatin + nivolumab for cisplatin-eligible patients (Weak), gemcitabine/cisplatin or HD-MVAC for cisplatin-eligible patients (Strong), and gemcitabine/carboplatin if cisplatin-ineligible (Strong). Offer maintenance avelumab after no progression on 4 to 6 first-line platinum-combination cycles (Strong). For PD-L1-positive patients unable to receive any combination, offer pembrolizumab or atezolizumab (Weak). In later lines, offer a platinum combination second-line if not given first-line (Strong); offer pembrolizumab after progression during or after platinum combinations if maintenance avelumab was not received (Strong); and offer enfortumab vedotin after platinum and progression during or after a PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitor (Strong). Test for FGFR alterations, specified as FGFR2/3 mutations or FGFR3 fusions, before erdafitinib (Strong); offer erdafitinib as a subsequent-line alternative if platinum was previously given, disease progressed during or after PD-1 or PD-L1 treatment, and the specified FGFR alteration is present (Strong). Offer vinflunine second-line only if immunotherapy or combination chemotherapy is infeasible, or use it third-line or later (Strong). Offer nephroureterectomy for palliation of symptomatic, resectable locally advanced tumours (Weak). Figure 7.3 sets out eligibility-based first-line and later-line options; its gemcitabine-cisplatin plus nivolumab branch carries a caution about unavailable UTUC subgroup-analysis data.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_08
  Name: Non-ischaemic priapism
  Synonyms:
    - high-flow or arterial priapism
  Description: A persistent erection caused by unregulated arterial inflow into the corpora. Blunt trauma can produce a fistula between a cavernosal artery or its branches and the sinusoidal spaces.
  Epidemiology: It comprises 5% of priapism cases. Epidemiological information comes almost entirely from small case series, and blunt perineal or penile trauma is the most frequent cause.
  Clinical presentation: The corpora are tumescent but usually not fully rigid. Penile pain is generally absent, although discomfort is possible, and rigidity may fluctuate. After trauma, onset may be delayed by several hours to weeks; the guide also describes delays of up to two to three weeks. Sexual stimulation can produce full rigidity, so intercourse is usually possible. Erectile dysfunction or distal penile flaccidity may develop over time.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: traumatic
      Distinguishing features: Associated with injury, especially blunt perineal or penile trauma.
    - Name: neurogenic
      Distinguishing features: May follow acute spinal cord injury.
    - Name: iatrogenic
      Distinguishing features: Reported after certain procedures, including shunting for ischaemic priapism.
    - Name: idiopathic
      Distinguishing features: No cause is identified.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Comprehensive medical and sexual history
      Purpose: Establish the diagnosis and distinguish the priapism subtype.
      When indicated: At presentation.
      Interpretation: A history of pelvic, perineal or genital trauma, little or no penile pain, and a persistent erection without full rigidity support arterial priapism.
    - Test: Abdominal, penile and perineal examination
      Purpose: Assess tumescence and identify evidence of trauma.
      When indicated: During diagnostic evaluation.
      Interpretation: The corpora are generally tumescent without being fully rigid.
    - Test: Neurological examination
      Purpose: Investigate a possible neurogenic cause.
      When indicated: If neurogenic non-ischaemic priapism is suspected.
    - Test: Complete blood count with white blood cell differential and coagulation profile
      Purpose: Assess anaemia and other haematological abnormalities.
      When indicated: During laboratory evaluation.
    - Test: Corporal blood aspiration and blood gas analysis
      Purpose: Differentiate non-ischaemic from ischaemic priapism.
      When indicated: During diagnostic evaluation.
      Interpretation: The aspirate is bright red and has normal arterial blood gas values; the listed arterial values are pO2 > 90 mmHg, pCO2 < 40 mmHg and pH 7.40.
    - Test: Colour duplex ultrasound of the penis and perineum
      Purpose: Distinguish priapism subtypes and locate an arterial fistula.
      When indicated: During diagnostic evaluation, without intracavernosal vasoactive drug injection.
      Interpretation: A fistula may appear as a focal colour blush with turbulent, high-velocity flow. Cavernosal arterial velocities are normal to high.
    - Test: Selective pudendal arteriography
      Purpose: Identify the site of arterial injury for planned embolisation.
      When indicated: When embolisation is being considered.
      Interpretation: A characteristic blush may appear at the injury site.
    - Test: MRI
      Purpose: Evaluate selected cases or assess distal penile fibrosis during follow-up.
      When indicated: Its diagnostic role in non-ischaemic priapism is limited; it may be used during close follow-up.
      Interpretation: Small penile vessels and fistulae are difficult to demonstrate with MRI.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Close follow-up is described during conservative management and after selective arterial embolisation; no fixed interval is specified.
    Recommended tests:
      - Physical examination during conservative management
      - Colour duplex ultrasound during conservative management
      - Colour duplex ultrasound and MRI to detect distal penile fibrosis
      - Clinical examination, colour duplex ultrasound and erectile function assessment after embolisation
      - Repeat arteriography if findings remain uncertain
    Long term effects:
      - Erectile dysfunction
      - Distal penile flaccidity
      - Distal penile fibrosis
      - Recurrence after treatment
    Survivorship notes: Follow-up assesses treatment success, recurrence, and anatomical and functional consequences.

  Content: History should establish symptom severity and duration, possible cause, prior interventions, complications, associated conditions and factors influencing surgical outcomes. In a retrospective series of 611 endoscopically confirmed cases, initial presentations were LUTS in 54.3%, acute retention in 22.3%, urinary tract infection (UTI) in 6.1% and difficult catheterisation in 4.8%. Among 214 anterior-urethroplasty patients, weak stream occurred in 49%, incomplete emptying in 27% and frequency in 20%; another series of 614 found post-void dribble in 73%. Other reported complaints include spraying (9%), visible haematuria (3.1-5%), urethral abscess or necrotising fasciitis (2.3%), urgency (14%) and incontinence (1-4%). Establish trauma, instrumentation, surgery, irradiation or focal therapy, and urethritis history. Record prior approaches and the latest intervention date because they may affect imaging or operative timing. Document baseline erectile and ejaculatory function with validated tools: sexual problems are common and surgery may affect function. The recommendations are to assess personal and family history using modified Amsterdam II criteria for Lynch syndrome screening (Strong), perform germline DNA sequencing if hereditary UTUC is clinically suspected (Weak), and offer MMR-protein or microsatellite-instability testing when hereditary UTUC is not clinically suspected (Weak).

  Heading: 3.3. Uncomplicated cystitis
  Content: Uncomplicated cystitis comprises acute, sporadic, or recurrent cystitis in nonpregnant women without relevant known urinary-tract anatomical or functional abnormalities or comorbidities. Risk factors include intercourse, spermicide use, a new sexual partner, maternal UTI history, and childhood UTI. Escherichia coli causes most cases. A focused history of dysuria, frequency, and urgency, together with absence of vaginal discharge, permits a high-probability diagnosis. Genitourinary symptoms in older women do not necessarily indicate cystitis. For typical symptoms, urine culture or dipstick testing adds little diagnostic accuracy, although a dipstick can help when the diagnosis is uncertain. Urine culture is recommended for suspected acute pyelonephritis, atypical symptoms, pregnancy, or symptoms that persist or return within 4 wk after treatment completion. Women with mild to moderate symptoms may consider symptomatic treatment, such as ibuprofen, instead of an antimicrobial after individual consultation. Antimicrobial selection should account for pathogen coverage and susceptibility, clinical efficacy for the indication, tolerability and adverse effects, ecological consequences, and cost or availability. Table 2 presents suggested antimicrobial regimens. Routine urinalysis or culture after treatment is not indicated in an asymptomatic patient. If symptoms persist to treatment completion or disappear and recur within 2 wk, obtain urine culture and susceptibility results. In that situation, assume the organism is not susceptible to the original agent and consider a different agent for a 7-d course.

En un análisis post‑hoc de los 80 pacientes de la cohorte B del ensayo CA209205, se encontró que 37 no habían tenido respuesta al tratamiento previo con brentuximab vedotina. Entre estos 37 pacientes, el tratamiento con nivolumab obtuvo una TRO de 62,2% (23/37). Cáncer de células escamosas de cabeza y cuello
La seguridad y eficacia de nivolumab 3 mg/kg en monoterapia para el tratamiento del CCECC metastásico o recurrente se evaluó en un ensayo abierto de fase 3 y aleatorizado (CA209141). El ensayo incluyó pacientes (18 años de edad o mayores), con CCECC recurrente o metastásico histológicamente confirmado (cavidad oral, faringe, laringe), de estadio III/IV y que no eran candidatos a tratamiento local con intención curativa (cirugía o radioterapia con o sin quimioterapia) y que habían experimentado progresión de la enfermedad durante o dentro de los 6 meses tras recibir una pauta de tratamiento basada en platino y tuvieron un estado funcional, ECOG, de 0 o 1. La pauta de tratamiento previo basada en platino, se pudo administrar en adyuvancia, neoadyuvancia, en el tumor primario, recurrente o metastásico. Los pacientes se reclutaron de forma independiente de la expresión de PD‑L1 en el tumor o de la expresión del virus del papiloma humano (VPH). Se excluyeron del ensayo, los pacientes con enfermedad autoinmune activa, condiciones médicas que requieran inmunosupresión, carcinoma recurrente o metastásico de nasofaringe, carcinoma de células escamosas con tumor primario de origen desconocido, de glándulas salivares o de histologías no escamosas (p.ej, melanoma de mucosas), o con metástasis cerebrales activas o leptomeníngeas. Los pacientes con metástasis cerebrales tratadas fueron elegibles si neurológicamente habían vuelto al nivel basal, como mínimo 2 semanas antes del reclutamiento y o habían abandonado el tratamiento con corticosteroides, o habían estabilizado o disminuido su dosis a < 10 mg diarios de prednisona o equivalente.
Un total de 361 pacientes fueron aleatorizados para recibir o nivolumab 3 mg/kg (n = 240) administrados por vía intravenosa durante 60 minutos cada 2 semanas o el tratamiento de elección del investigador cetuximab (n = 15), 400 mg/m2 dosis de carga seguido por 250 mg/m2 semanales o metotrexato (n = 52) 40 a 60 mg/m2 semanales, o docetaxel (n = 54) 30 a 40 mg/m2 semanales. Los pacientes se estratificaron en función de si habían recibido o no cetuximab. El tratamiento continuó mientras se observó beneficio clínico o hasta que no se toleró el tratamiento. Las evaluaciones del tumor se realizaron de acuerdo a los criterios RECIST, versión 1,1, 9 semanas después de la aleatorización y continuaron cada 6 semanas. Se permitió el tratamiento después de la evaluación inicial del investigador de acuerdo a los criterios RECIST, versión 1,1 como progresión en pacientes que recibían nivolumab, si el paciente tenía beneficio clínico y se toleraba el medicamento del ensayo de acuerdo a la decisión del investigador. La variable primaria de eficacia fue SG. Las variables secundarias de eficacia, fueron SLP y TRO evaluados por el investigador. Se realizaron análisis de subgrupos pre‑especificados para evaluar la eficacia por expresión de PD‑L1 en el tumor a niveles predefinidos de 1%, 5% y 10%.
Se recogieron de forma sistemática muestras de tejido tumoral, antes del tratamiento para realizar los análisis de eficacia previamente planificados de acuerdo a la expresión de PD‑L1 en el tumor. Los niveles de expresión de PD‑L1 en el tumor se evaluaron utilizando el test PD‑L1 IHC 28‑8 pharmDx.
Las características basales estaban en general equilibradas entre los dos grupos. La mediana de edad fue 60 años (rango: 28‑83) con un 31% ≥ 65 años de edad y un 5% ≥ 75 años de edad, el 83% fueron varones y un 83% fueron blancos. El estado funcional ECOG en el nivel basal fue 0 (20%) o 1 (78%), un 77% eran fumadores y exfumadores, un 90% tenía enfermedad en el estadio IV, un 66% tenía dos o más lesiones, el 45%, 34% y 20% recibieron 1, 2, o 3 o más líneas de tratamiento sistémico previas, respectivamente, y un 25% eran VPH‑16 positivos.
Con un seguimiento mínimo de 11,4 meses, el ensayo demostró una mejora estadísticamente significativa en la SG para los pacientes aleatorizados al grupo de nivolumab comparado con el grupo de tratamiento de elección del investigador. El nivel de expresión de PD‑L1+ TAIC en el microambiente tumoral se evaluó cualitativamente y se caracterizó como “numeroso”, “intermedio” y “raro” en base a las evaluaciones de los patólogos. Los grupos “numeroso” e “intermedio” se combinaron para definir grupo “abundante”.
Los pacientes evaluados por el investigador como cáncer orofaríngeo primario se analizaron para el VPH (determinación de p16 por immunohistoquímica [IHC]). El beneficio de SG se observó con independencia del estado del VPH (VPH‑positivo: HR = 0,63; IC del 95%: 0,38; 1,04, VPH‑negativo: HR = 0.64; IC del 95%: 0,40; 1,03, y VPH‑desconocido HR = 0,78; IC del 95%: 0,55; 1,10).
Los resultados notificados por el paciente (PROs, por sus siglas en inglés) fueron evaluados utilizando la escala EORTC QLQ‑C30, EORTC QLQ‑H&N35 y el nivel‑3 EQ‑5D. Durante 15 semanas de seguimiento, los pacientes tratados con nivolumab mostraron PROs, estables mientras que aquellos asignados al grupo tratamiento de elección del investigador mostraron descensos significativos en su funcionalidad (p.ej., escala física, escala social) y estado de salud, así como un incremento de la sintomatología (p.ej., fatiga, disnea, pérdida del apetito, dolor, problemas sensoriales, problemas de contacto social). Los datos de PRO se deben interpretar en el contexto de un ensayo con diseño abierto y por lo tanto tomarse con cautela.
Carcinoma urotelial avanzado
Tratamiento adyuvante del carcinoma urotelial
Ensayo de fase 3 aleatorizado de nivolumab adyuvante frente a placebo (CA209274)
La seguridad y eficacia de nivolumab en monoterapia para el tratamiento adyuvante del carcinoma urotelial se evaluó en un ensayo de fase 3 multicéntrico, aleatorizado, controlado con placebo, doble ciego (CA209274). El ensayo incluyó pacientes (18 años o más) que se habían sometido a una resección radical del carcinoma urotelial músculo invasivo (CUMI) originado en la vejiga o el tracto urinario superior (pelvis renal o uréter) y con un alto riesgo de recurrencia. El criterio de estadificación patológica del CUMI que define a los pacientes de alto riesgo fue ypT2‑ypT4a o ypN+ para pacientes adultos que recibieron quimioterapia neoadyuvante con cisplatino y pT3‑pT4a o pN+ para pacientes adultos que no recibieron quimioterapia neoadyuvante con cisplatino y no fueron elegibles o rechazaron la quimioterapia adyuvante con cisplatino. El ensayo incluyó a pacientes independientemente de su estado de PD‑L1, con una puntuación del estado funcional ECOG de 0 o 1 (se permitió un ECOG de 2 para los pacientes no elegibles para quimioterapia neoadyuvante con cisplatino). Los niveles de expresión de PD‑L1 en células tumorales se evaluaron utilizando el test PD‑L1 IHC 28‑8 pharmDx. El ensayo excluyó a pacientes con enfermedad autoinmune activa, conocida o sospechada, pacientes que habían recibido tratamiento con cualquier quimioterapia, radioterapia, medicamentos biológicos para el cáncer, terapia intravesical o terapia en investigación dentro de los 28 días posteriores a la primera administración del tratamiento del ensayo.
Se aleatorizaron un total de 709 pacientes para recibir nivolumab 240 mg (n = 353) cada 2 semanas o placebo (n = 356) cada 2 semanas hasta recurrencia o toxicidad inaceptable durante una duración máxima de tratamiento de 1 año. De estos, 282 pacientes tenían una expresión de PD‑L1 en células tumorales ≥ 1 %; 140 en el grupo de nivolumab y 142 en el grupo de placebo. La aleatorización se estratificó por estado ganglionar patológico (N+ frente a N0/x con < 10 ganglios extraídos frente a N0 con ≥ 10 ganglios extraídos), expresión de PD‑L1 en células tumorales (≥ 1% frente a < 1%/indeterminado) y uso de quimioterapia neoadyuvante con cisplatino. Las evaluaciones de imágenes del tumor se debían realizar cada 12 semanas desde la fecha de la primera dosis hasta la semana 96, luego cada 16 semanas desde la semana 96 hasta la semana 160, luego cada 24 semanas hasta recurrencia del tracto no urotelial o suspensión del tratamiento (lo que ocurra más tarde) hasta un máximo de 5 años. Las variables de eficacia primarias fueron la supervivencia libre de enfermedad (SLE) en todos los pacientes aleatorizados y la SLE en pacientes aleatorizados con expresión de PD‑L1 en células tumorales ≥ 1%. La SLE se definió como el tiempo entre la fecha de la aleatorización y la fecha de la primera recurrencia documentada evaluada por el investigador (tracto urotelial local, tracto local no urotelial o distante), o muerte (por cualquier causa), lo que ocurra primero. Las variables de eficacia secundarias incluyeron la supervivencia global (SG).
Las características basales estaban generalmente equilibradas entre los grupos de tratamiento. En pacientes con expresión de PD‑L1 en células tumorales ≥ 1%, la mediana de edad era de 66 años (rango: 34‑92 años), el 76% eran hombres y el 76% eran de raza blanca. El 82% tenía cáncer de vejiga músculo invasivo , el 18% tenía carcinoma urotelial del tracto superior (pelvis renal y uréter), el 42% de los pacientes recibieron previamente cisplatino en el entorno neoadyuvante, el 45% de los pacientes eran N+ en resección radical, los pacientes tenían un estado funcional ECOG de 0 (61%), 1 (37%) o 2 (2%) y el 7% de los pacientes tenía una hemoglobina < 10 g/dl.
En el análisis intermedio preespecificado primario en pacientes con expresión de PD‑L1 en células tumorales ≥ 1% (seguimiento mínimo de 6,3 meses y mediana de seguimiento de 22,1 meses para el grupo de nivolumab), el ensayo demostró una mejora estadísticamente significativa en la SLE para los pacientes aleatorizados a nivolumab en comparación con placebo. No se alcanzó la mediana de la SLE determinada por el investigador (IC del 95%: 21,19; NA) para nivolumab versus 8,41 meses (IC del 95%: 5,59; 21,19) para placebo, HR 0,55 (IC del 98,72%: 0,35; 0,85), valor‑p = 0,0005. El análisis primario de la SLE incluyó la censura de nuevos tratamientos contra el cáncer. Los resultados de la SLE con y sin censura para un nuevo tratamiento contra el cáncer fueron consistentes.
En un análisis de la SLE descriptivo actualizado en pacientes con expresión de PD‑L1 en células tumorales ≥ 1% (seguimiento mínimo de 11,4 meses y mediana de seguimiento de 25,5 meses para el grupo de nivolumab), se confirmó la mejora de la SLE.

Ensayo de fase 3 aleatorizado y abierto de nivolumab en combinación con quimioterapia frente a quimioterapia (CA209901)
Se evaluaron la seguridad y la eficacia de nivolumab en combinación con cisplatino y gemcitabina seguido de nivolumab en monoterapia en un ensayo aleatorizado y abierto, el ensayo CA209901, llevado a cabo con pacientes con carcinoma urotelial irresecable o metastásico elegibles para el tratamiento con cisplatino. El ensayo incluyó pacientes (18 años o mayores) con evidencia citológica o histológica de carcinoma de células transicionales (CCT) del urotelio de la pelvis renal, uréter, vejiga o uretra con enfermedad metastásica o quirúrgicamente irresecable, que fueron elegibles para el tratamiento con cisplatino y gemcitabina. Se aceptaron variantes histológicas menores (< 50% del total) (el CCT debía ser la histología dominante). Se requirió que todos los pacientes presentaran enfermedad medible mediante tomografía computarizada (TC) o resonancia magnética (RM), de acuerdo con los criterios RECIST, versión 1.1. No se permitió ningún tratamiento anti-cancerígeno sistémico previo para el carcinoma urotelial metastásico o quirúrgicamente irresecable. Se permitieron la quimioterapia neoadyuvante previa o la quimioterapia adyuvante previa basada en platino posteriores a una cistectomía radical, siempre y cuando la recurrencia de la enfermedad se produjera ≥ 12 meses después de la finalización del tratamiento. Se permitió el tratamiento intravesical previo si se completó al menos 4 semanas antes del inicio del tratamiento del ensayo. Se permitió la radioterapia (con o sin quimioterapia) con intención curativa si el tratamiento se completó al menos ≥ 12 meses antes del reclutamiento. Se permitió la radioterapia paliativa siempre y cuando se completara al menos 2 semanas antes del tratamiento.
Un total de 608 pacientes fueron aleatorizados para recibir nivolumab en combinación con cisplatino y gemcitabina (n = 304) o cisplatino y gemcitabina (n = 304). La aleatorización se estratificó por estado de PD‑L1 del tumor (≥ 1% frente a < 1% o indeterminado) y metástasis hepáticas (sí frente a no). La mediana de edad fue de 65 años de edad (rango: 32 a 86), con un 51% de pacientes ≥ 65 años de edad y un 12% de pacientes ≥ 75 años de edad; el 23% eran asiáticos, el 72% eran de raza blanca y el 0,3% eran de raza negra; y el 77% eran hombres y el 23% eran mujeres. El estado funcional basal ECOG fue 0 (53%) o 1 (46%). Los pacientes del grupo de nivolumab en combinación con cisplatino y gemcitabina recibieron tratamiento con 360 mg de nivolumab cada tres semanas en combinación con cisplatino y gemcitabina durante un máximo de 6 ciclos, tras lo cual recibieron 480 mg de nivolumab en monoterapia cada 4 semanas durante un total de hasta 24 meses. Los pacientes recibieron 1000 mg/m2 de gemcitabina por vía intravenosa durante 30 minutos los días 1 y 8 del ciclo de tratamiento de 3 semanas, y 70 mg/m2 de cisplatino por vía intravenosa durante 30‑120 minutos el día 1 del ciclo de tratamiento de 3 semanas. Un total de 92 pacientes (49 en el grupo de nivolumab en combinación con cisplatino y gemcitabina y 43 en el grupo de cisplatino y gemcitabina) cambiaron de cisplatino a carboplatino después de al menos un ciclo de cisplatino.
El ensayo demostró un beneficio estadísticamente significativo en la SG y la SLP para los pacientes aleatorizados a nivolumab en combinación con cisplatino y gemcitabina en comparación con cisplatino y gemcitabina solos. Los resultados de eficacia se presentan en la Tabla 52 y las Figuras 26 y 27.

Document sections:
  Heading: Other Blocks and Infusion Techniques
  Content: Case reports support brachial plexus blockade (level 4). Described indications for continuous infusion include peri-operative, post-trauma, and post-operative pain; vascular compromise; intractable CRPS I and II pain; and phantom-limb pain. Catheters have remained in place as long as three weeks and can deliver anesthetic, opioid, clonidine, or other adjuncts (level 4). Sympatholysis may last up to 2–3 weeks with 0.1 to 0.2% ropivacaine (level 4). In one severe CRPS II case 30days after carpal tunnel release, axillary bupivacaine at 0.1% and 2.5 mL/hour provided analgesia but dense motor and sensory blockade. Reduction within one day to 0.05%, cessation of basal infusion, and patient-controlled 1 mL every 15minutes maintained analgesia while allowing active PT; the catheter stayed for 1 week (level 4). Potential complications include bleeding, infection, intravascular or intrathecal injection, pneumothorax, and phrenic nerve paralysis. Epidural infusion permits titration of analgesia to preserve participation in PT; commonly described treatment combines clonidine and bupivacaine, with opioids added if necessary (level 4). Patient-controlled boluses may address fluctuations around exercise. In a blinded RCT of 26 patients, daily epidural clonidine 300 or 600mcg or placebo was administered for 3 consecutive days (level 2). The account also describes open-label treatment at a mean dose of 32mcg/hour for a mean of 32days and, separately, substantial relief with 300 and 700 microgram doses. It reports that 19 of 26 patients chose continued infusion averaging 43days at 3266 micrograms per hour; 17 of 19 improved significantly. These dose and duration accounts are inconsistent within the document. Adverse effects included dizziness, dry mouth, oral sores, and nausea; six of 19patients developed catheter infections and one developed meningitis. In a 14-patient open-label study, epidural bupivacaine-opioid infusion for an average of 4 days improved pain and movement in 13 of fourteen, with 11 of the 14 described as having CRPS resolution at trial end (level 3). Another 26-patient study combined 0.25% cervical epidural bupivacaine for seven days with PT: 83% reported pain improvement, 63% considered their condition acceptable, and only 8% became completely pain-free (level 3). Epidural-catheter infection rates in CRPS have been reported as high as 31%. For prolonged use, surgical sterility, subcutaneous tunneling away from the spinal entry site, and weekly dressing changes are recommended (level 4). Back pain, sensorimotor loss, and bowel or bladder dysfunction suggest epidural abscess; fever, neck pain, or photophobia may precede them. In a separate catheter study, 19 out of 350 patients developed infection; all received antibiotics and catheter removal, with none requiring surgery. Intrathecal bupivacaine initially relieved pain in a series of three refractory patients, but CRPS progressed in all (level 4). Intrathecal baclofen produced analgesia and functional improvement in n =7 patients with severe dystonia (level 3 evidence); its original investigators later stopped using the infusion because of adverse effects. Evidence for intrathecal infusion without dystonia is limited. Epidural infusion is sometimes adopted after intermittent blocks, but infection risk requires further prospective study.

  Content: Intraparenchymal/intraventricular hemorrhage (IH/IVH) can obstruct CSF flow and cause acute obstructive hydrocephalus. retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Painful Diabetic Neuropathy Background
  Content: PDN is a painful diabetes mellitus (DM) complication involving persistent pain and altered sensation in the extremities. It is reported in as many as 16%–26% of people with diabetes, yet often remains undiscussed and untreated, impairing physical and psychological quality of life. Metabolic and vascular processes contribute to PDN: sustained hyperglycemia, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation promote length-dependent nerve injury and pain. Manifestations range from mild discomfort to disabling pain and may include disturbed sleep, anxiety, or depression. Diagnosis draws on symptoms, medical and family history, examination, and additional testing. The history explores symptoms, comorbid conditions, and alternative causes of neuropathic pain; examination assesses sensation, reflexes, and strength. Clinicians may apply Toronto Diabetic Neuropathy Expert Group criteria. Nerve conduction studies evaluate injury and help exclude other neuropathy causes; quantitative sensory testing assesses responses to sensory stimuli and small-fiber function. Laboratory assessment evaluates glycemic control and kidney function and investigates alternatives such as vitamin deficiency or autoimmune disease. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or nerve ultrasound may identify structural abnormalities or compression. Management is multimodal: tricyclic antidepressants, anticonvulsants, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, opioids, topical 8% capsaicin, lidocaine, or amitriptyline, physical therapy, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, and acupuncture are discussed. Nerve blocks and spinal cord stimulation are emerging options for refractory disease. Despite positions taken by organizations including the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and American Academy of Neurology (AAN), opioids remain the most commonly prescribed PDN medication, followed by gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine, amitriptyline, and venlafaxine. Treatment should reflect comorbidities and patient preferences and involve relevant primary care, endocrine, interventional pain, podiatric, and other professionals.

Document sections:
  Heading: Context
  Content: LUTS encompass storage, voiding and post-micturition symptoms. Possible causes involve abnormal structure or function of the prostate, urethra, bladder or sphincters. In men, the most common cause is benign prostate enlargement (BPE), which obstructs the bladder outlet; BPE arises from an increase in prostate cell numbers called benign prostatic hyperplasia. Other possible causes include detrusor weakness or overactivity, prostate inflammation (prostatitis), urinary tract infection, prostate cancer and neurological disease. Categorising symptoms as voiding, storage or post-micturition helps identify their source. Voiding symptoms comprise a weak or intermittent stream, straining, hesitancy, terminal dribbling and incomplete emptying. Storage symptoms comprise urgency, frequency, urgency incontinence and nocturia. Post-micturition dribbling is the main post-micturition symptom and is common and bothersome. LUTS usually do not cause severe illness but can substantially impair quality of life or indicate serious urogenital disease. They impose a major burden on ageing men: age is an important risk factor, prevalence rises with age, and bothersome LUTS occur in up to 30% of men older than 65 years. This represents a large population that might need treatment.

  Content: The tubal ampulla is the most frequent attachment site. Reportedly, 95% of ectopic pregnancies arise in the ampullary, infundibular, or isthmic portions of the tubes. Histologic identification of villus-like structures, trophoblasts, or an embryo in a tube or another ectopic site establishes the diagnosis. Spiegelberg's criteria are often used to distinguish ovarian implantation from other sites and require 4 findings: a fallopian tube intact and separate from the affected ovary; a gestational sac occupying the ovary's position; attachment of that ovary to the uterus through the ovarian ligament; and ovarian tissue both attached to and present within the gestational-sac wall. In cesarean-scar pregnancy, residual scar defects permit blastocyst migration into the myometrium. Histology shows villous invasion of myometrial or scar tissue with little decidua. Implantation depth defines type 1, nearer the uterine wall, and type 2, nearer the urinary bladder.

question: Red urine without RBCs is seen in:

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Lee et al. 2025 Comparison of Urinary Red Blood Cell Distribution ( URDspan__JC__000113
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Lee et al. 2025 Comparison of Urinary Red Blood Cell Distribution ( URDspan
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 1 | Introduction
  Content: Hematuria means RBCs are present in urine and may be visible or detectable only microscopically. It is a fundamental manifestation of glomerulonephritis (GN); microscopic assessment of urinary sediment is presented as its most effective detection method. Birch et al. proposed in 1979 that urinary RBC morphology could distinguish glomerular from non-glomerular origins. Passage through glomeruli can damage RBC membranes and produce dysmorphic RBCs (dRBCs). Shichiri et al. reported in 1988 that erythrocytes were smaller in glomerular than in non-glomerular disease, and Hyodo et al. later proposed an RBC size range of 4–6 μm for discriminating the origins. Compared with blood, urine has much less albumin and more urea; this environment increases membrane vulnerability and changes RBC shape. High urea concentrations particularly favor burr-cell formation. Passage across the glomerular basement membrane may produce acanthocytes through membrane injury. RBCs in renal disease are also more susceptible to factors including iron deficiency, osmotic lysis, shape distortion, and vesicle formation. Reliable recognition of urinary dRBCs requires an experienced observer, and observer-dependent interpretation may explain differences between laboratories. The authors consider continuing education in RBC morphology essential and mention deep learning for microscopy as another possible approach. Instrument-measured small-RBC fractions are easier to obtain and less dependent on interpretation, making them potentially more objective and standardized. The fully automated UF-5000 uses fluorescence flow cytometry to classify urine particles and reports morphological RBC information, including non-lysed RBCs, lysed RBCs, large RBCs, small RBCs, and RBC-Info. Its classification uses forward scatter light (FSC), side scatter light (SSC), side fluorescence light (SFL), and depolarized side scattered light (DSS). A small RBC has FSC intensity < 70; a non-lysed RBC has a strong FSC signal and morphological stability indicated by SSC. URD is the small-RBC count divided by the non-lysed-RBC count. Earlier studies investigated possible clinical uses, but most were single-center studies. Reported cutoffs for distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular hematuria varied from 30.1% to 40.5% for small RBCs and from 0% to 30.0% for dRBCs. The authors therefore considered a multicenter assessment using the same equipment necessary for clinical application. Across four hospitals, they collected urine microscopy findings, urine measures, serum markers, and kidney-function information to compare institutional dRBC and URD measurements and cutoffs and assess their clinical significance.

  Heading: 2.2.1. Renal and Ureteric Stones
  Content: For asymptomatic patients, the EAU favours initial US because it avoids radiation, costs less and can identify hydronephrosis and stones in the calyces, renal pelvis and pelvic-ureteric or vesico-ureteric junctions. For symptomatic patients, NCCT is preferred: it characterises density, diameter, volume, skin-to-stone distance and surrounding anatomy to inform treatment, and is more accurate than US or IVU (EAU: strong recommendation). Contrast-enhanced imaging is advised when collecting-system anatomy must be assessed before removal (EAU: strong recommendation). KUB X-ray can establish radiopacity but need not be obtained when NCCT is planned. The AUA recommends NCCT before PCNL (AUA: strong recommendation) and when choosing between SWL and URS (AUA: conditional recommendation); US alone is discouraged for the latter decision. Suspected substantial renal injury may warrant a DTPA or MAG-3 renogram to guide care (AUA: conditional recommendation). The EAU advises testing serum creatinine, uric acid, ionised calcium, sodium, potassium, blood cell counts and C-reactive protein, plus coagulation when intervention is intended (EAU: strong recommendation). Both organisations strongly recommend urine culture and microscopy before intervention.

  Content: Larger ureteral and renal-pelvis tumours are more likely to be muscle-invasive or extend beyond the organ. For renal-pelvis UTUC, median tumour size is 3.5 to 4.0 cm, and each 1 cm increase corresponds to a 1.25-fold increase in risk of muscle-invasive disease at RNU. Size alone must not dictate treatment or high-risk assignment: a tumour exceeding 2 cm needs accompanying high-risk factors for that classification.

  Content: Epididymitis is common and may be acute, chronic, or recurrent. Acute disease presents with epididymal pain, swelling, and increased temperature, sometimes extending to the testis and scrotal skin. In up to 90% of cases, pathogens migrate from the urethra or bladder and can be identified through appropriate testing. Enterobacterales, C. trachomatis, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are the principal isolated organisms. Fig. 2 supplies the diagnostic and treatment decision pathway for adult men with acute scrotal pain and swelling: suspected torsion prompts urgent surgical exploration; suspected epididymitis prompts microbiological investigation and treatment according to the likelihood of gonorrhoea, with assessment for abscess or treatment failure and follow-up for proven sexually transmitted infection. It specifies ceftriaxone 1000 mg i.m. or i.v. plus an antibiotic active against Chlamydia trchomatics when gonorrhoea is likely; otherwise, it specifies treatment active against Chlamydia trachomatis and Enterobacterales, with parenteral treatment considered for severe infection. Document sections:
  Heading: History
  Content: Common presentations include activity-limiting dysmenorrhoea, chronic pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia during or after intercourse, cyclical gastrointestinal symptoms—particularly dyschezia—cyclical urinary symptoms and infertility accompanied by one or more other symptoms. A retrospective UK general-practice analysis reported associations with abdominopelvic pain (odds ratio (OR) = 5.2), dysmenorrhea (OR = 8.1), infertility (OR = 8.2) and dyspareunia (OR = 6.8). In a prospective multicentre study (n=1396), a symptoms-only model for Stage 3 and Stage 4 disease at first laparoscopy had sensitivity 82.3% and specificity 75.8%; combining symptoms with ultrasound improved prediction. A table adapted from Chapron et al. presents symptom-specific odds ratios and illustrates the predictive importance of cyclical symptoms. Other possible manifestations include fatigue (50-87% of women with endometriosis), cyclical cough, haemoptysis, chest pain, pneumothorax, shoulder-tip pain and scar swelling. Multiple symptoms, especially combined with clinical signs, increase diagnostic likelihood. Patient-reported information collected through technological tools may help predict disease and facilitate earlier diagnosis and referral.

Document sections:
  Heading: Diagnosis of Testosterone Deficiency
  Content: 1. Clinicians should regard total testosterone below 300 ng/dL as a reasonable threshold supporting low testosterone (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B). 2. Diagnosis requires two early-morning total testosterone measurements obtained on separate occasions (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade A). 3. Clinical testosterone deficiency requires both low total testosterone and symptoms and/or signs (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B). The panel describes low testosterone as consistently <300 ng/dL on at least two early-morning serum measurements, preferably performed by the same laboratory with the same measurement method and instrumentation. 4. Clinicians should consider total testosterone testing, even without associated symptoms or signs, in patients with unexplained anemia, bone density loss, diabetes, chemotherapy exposure, testicular radiation exposure, HIV/AIDS, chronic narcotic use, male infertility, pituitary dysfunction, or chronic corticosteroid use (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B). A literature meta-analysis identifies histories of these conditions, including direct or scatter radiation to the testes and HIV, as risk factors; the panel recommends testosterone measurement for all patients with such histories. Symptoms to record include reduced energy or endurance, poorer work or physical performance, fatigue, visual field changes such as bitemporal hemianopsia, anosmia, depression, diminished motivation or concentration, impaired memory, irritability, infertility, reduced sexual desire, and altered erectile function. A focused examination should assess body habitus; virilization through hair distribution and quantity in androgen-dependent areas; body mass index or waist circumference; gynecomastia; testicular presence, size, consistency, and masses; varicocele; and prostate size and morphology. 5. Validated questionnaires are not currently recommended to select candidates for testosterone therapy or to monitor symptomatic response during treatment (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Screening questionnaires cannot replace clinical evaluation and laboratory testing: their sensitivity and specificity vary substantially, making them unsuitable as screening tools or substitutes for measured testosterone.

Document sections:
  Heading: 5.5 Diagnostic ureteroscopy
  Content: Flexible ureteroscopy (URS) can visualise the ureter, renal pelvis and collecting system, obtain suspicious-lesion biopsies and, when needed, confirm UTUC. It is also essential for detailed tumour mapping before kidney preservation, assessing presence, appearance, number and size of lesions. Ureteroscopic biopsy identifies grade in more than 90% of cases with a low false-negative rate regardless of sample size, although grade can be underestimated relative to nephroureterectomy; second-look URS is therefore necessary in follow-up after kidney-sparing treatment. URS permits selective ureteral cytology. Biopsy staging can be inaccurate, so biopsy grade, imaging and cytology may jointly inform the choice between radical nephroureterectomy (RNU) and kidney-sparing therapy. In a meta-analysis comparing pre-RNU URS with no URS, 8 out of 12 studies reported more intravesical recurrences after URS; URS biopsy was also identified as a risk factor. Another review of 16 studies found no significant association for URS alone, but significantly increased intravesical recurrence after URS plus biopsy, without an effect on overall survival or non-urothelial recurrence. A study is needed to determine whether immediate intravesical chemotherapy after URS with biopsy or laser treatment reduces post-RNU bladder recurrence. Improved flexible instruments and newer imaging may aid detection of flat lesions. Narrow-band imaging is promising but preliminary; optical coherence tomography and confocal laser endomicroscopy (Cellvizio®) have shown promising correspondence with definitive histology for high-grade UTUC grading and/or staging.

Document sections:
  Heading: 5.3.3.1 Bipolar transurethral vaporisation of the prostate
  Content: B-TUVP forms a plasma field with a bipolar electrode to vaporise tissue. Its coagulation zone is < 2 mm, versus up to 10 mm with monopolar TUVP, potentially reducing irritation and SUI. Thirteen RCTs included 1,244 men with glands < 80 mL; most followed patients for twelve months, with maximum follow-up of 36 months in a small RCT (n = 40) and eighteen months in a later RCT (n = 340). Reviews generally found similar short-term IPSS, QoL, Qmax and PVR versus TURP. Possible inferior mid-term IPSS and Qmax with PK B-TUVP and methodological limitations prevent firm longer-term conclusions. Early pooled results found fewer peri-operative complications with B-TUVP, but did not directly report pooled comparisons for individual complications. A seven-RCT review reported shorter catheterisation (42.5 vs. 77.5 hours) and admission (3.1 vs. 4.4 days); another cautioned that heterogeneous, limited trials preclude firm conclusions. A meta-analysis found less clot retention and transfusion versus M-TURP but not B-TURP, with other complications generally similar. A six-RCT analysis of plasma B-TUVP found similar overall complications and transfusions versus TURP but fewer major Clavien 3, 4 complications and shorter catheterisation. Better standardised, multicentre and longer RCTs are needed. Evidence summaries describe similar short-term efficacy (LE 1a), favourable peri-operative but inferior mid-term efficacy of plasmakinetic B-TUVP (LE 1a), and lower short-term major morbidity with plasma B-TUVP (LE 1a). Offer B-TUVP as a TURP alternative for moderate-to-severe LUTS with prostate volume 30-80 mL (Weak).
