retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__EAU Guidelines on Upper Urinary Tract Urothelial Carcinoma 2024__JC__000002
retrieved_chunks.document_id: EAU Guidelines on Upper Urinary Tract Urothelial Carcinoma 2024
retrieved_chunks.text:
Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: upper urinary tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC)
  Synonyms:
    - upper tract urothelial carcinoma
    - UTUC
  Description: Urothelial carcinoma arising in the pyelocaliceal cavities or ureter. Histological grade often guides clinical decisions because biopsy samples may not reliably distinguish non-invasive papillary lesions, carcinoma in situ and invasive carcinoma. Pure non-urothelial histology is uncommon, while histological subtypes occur in approximately 25% of UTUCs.
  Epidemiology: UTUC accounts for 5–10% of urothelial carcinomas, with an estimated annual incidence in Western countries of almost two cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Incidence peaks at 70–90 years, and the disease is twice as common in men. Approximately two-thirds of patients present with muscle-invasive disease, although population-based studies suggest that muscle-invasive UTUC has represented approximately half of incident cases in recent years; approximately 9% present with metastasis. Pyelocaliceal tumours occur approximately twice as often as ureteral tumours. Multifocal tumours occur in approximately 10–20% of cases, concomitant upper-tract carcinoma in situ in 11% to 36%, and concurrent bladder cancer in 17%. After treatment, bladder recurrence occurs in 29% of patients, compared with contralateral upper-tract recurrence in 2–5%. Tobacco exposure increases relative risk by 2.5 to 7.0 fold; aristolochic acid exposure is another established risk factor. An association with alcohol was reported in a case-control study of 1,569 cases and 506,797 controls: ever-drinkers had higher risk than never-drinkers (OR: 1.23; 95% CI: 1.08–1.40, p = 0.001), with a reported risk threshold of > 15 g of alcohol/day.
  Clinical presentation: Detection may be incidental. Most patients in an international registry presented with symptoms, principally visible haematuria; flank pain caused by obstruction from a clot or tumour tissue occurs in 20–32% of cases. Anorexia, weight loss, malaise, fatigue, fever, night sweats or cough should prompt assessment for metastases. Symptoms at diagnosis are associated with poorer prognosis.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Low-risk UTUC
      Distinguishing features: Requires unifocal disease, tumour size < 2 cm, negative high-grade cytology, low-grade URS biopsy and no invasive appearance on CT; all listed factors must be present.
    - Name: High-risk UTUC
      Distinguishing features: High-grade cytology, high-grade URS biopsy, local invasion on CT or a histological subtype each constitute a strong high-risk criterion. Multifocal disease, tumour size ≥ 2 cm and hydronephrosis are weaker criteria and, in a low-grade tumour, are not strong predictors of invasion when considered alone.
    - Name: Lynch-related UTUC
      Distinguishing features: UTUC associated with Lynch syndrome and a pathogenic germline mismatch-repair gene mutation.
    - Name: upper tract CIS
      Distinguishing features: Flat carcinoma in situ of the upper urinary tract; its lack of a mass effect or urothelial thickening can make it invisible on CT.
    - Name: metastatic UTUC
      Distinguishing features: Disease with regional nodal involvement or distant metastases, for which the guideline describes separate management pathways.
    - Name: squamous subtype
      Distinguishing features: Urothelial carcinoma with divergent squamous differentiation, present in approximately 15% of cases.
    - Name: sarcomatoid
      Distinguishing features: A rare histological subtype associated with locally advanced disease and poorer outcomes.
    - Name: micropapillary
      Distinguishing features: A histological subtype associated with locally advanced disease and poorer outcomes.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: CT urography
      Purpose: Diagnose and stage UTUC, assess local invasion and examine regional lymph nodes.
      When indicated: In the diagnostic and staging evaluation.
      Interpretation: A meta-analysis of 13 studies involving 1,233 patients reported pooled sensitivity of 92% (CI: 0.85–0.96) and specificity of 95% (CI: 0.88–0.98). Enlarged lymph nodes strongly predict metastases. Flat epithelial lesions without a mass effect or urothelial thickening are generally not visible.
    - Test: chest CT
      Purpose: Assess for thoracic metastatic disease.
      When indicated: During staging and the specified follow-up of high-risk disease.
    - Test: MR urography
      Purpose: Provide upper-tract imaging when CT urography cannot be performed.
      When indicated: Usually when radiation or iodinated contrast is contraindicated.
      Interpretation: Sensitivity after contrast administration is 75% for tumours < 2 cm; CT urography is more sensitive and specific for diagnosis and staging.
    - Test: FDG-PET/CT
      Purpose: Assess nodal or distant metastases.
      When indicated: May be used when iodinated contrast cannot be given because of renal impairment or allergy.
      Interpretation: A retrospective multicentre study of 117 surgically treated patients reported sensitivity of 82% and specificity of 84% for nodal metastases. Suspicious nodes were associated with worse recurrence-free survival; further validation and comparison with MR and CT are needed.
    - Test: urethrocystoscopy
      Purpose: Exclude a concurrent bladder tumour.
      When indicated: As part of the UTUC diagnostic evaluation.
    - Test: voided urine cytology
      Purpose: Help detect high-grade disease.
      When indicated: During diagnostic evaluation and, where specified, surveillance.
      Interpretation: Abnormal cytology can suggest high-grade UTUC if cystoscopy is normal and bladder or prostatic-urethral CIS is absent. It is less sensitive for UTUC than selectively collected upper-tract cytology.
    - Test: selective upper-tract cytology
      Purpose: Assess the affected upper tract, particularly for high-grade tumours and CIS.
      When indicated: When upper-tract sampling is undertaken, including during URS.
      Interpretation: Selective cytology has high sensitivity in high-grade disease, including CIS.
    - Test: barbotage cytology
      Purpose: Obtain cytological material from the renal cavities and ureteral lumen.
      When indicated: Preferably before contrast administration for retrograde ureteropyelography.
      Interpretation: One study detected up to 91% of cancers; contrast can impair cytological specimens.
    - Test: retrograde ureteropyelography
      Purpose: Provide an additional means of detecting UTUC.
      When indicated: As a diagnostic option.
    - Test: diagnostic ureteroscopy (URS) with biopsy
      Purpose: Visualise suspicious lesions, confirm diagnosis, map tumour presence, appearance, multifocality and size, and establish biopsy grade.
      When indicated: When imaging and voided cytology do not adequately establish the diagnosis or risk category, or before considering kidney-sparing management.
      Interpretation: Biopsy establishes grade in more than 90% of cases, but can undergrade disease relative to nephroureterectomy specimens, and biopsy-based stage assessment can be inaccurate. URS with biopsy significantly increased subsequent intravesical recurrence in a systematic review of 16 studies, without an observed effect on overall survival or non-urothelial recurrence.
    - Test: FISH
      Purpose: Detect molecular abnormalities characteristic of UTUC.
      When indicated: As a possible ancillary urinary test.
      Interpretation: Reported sensitivity for characteristic molecular abnormalities is approximately 72–84%. A systematic review reported sensitivity of 35-86% and specificity of 80-100%; the review concluded that available cytology and FISH performance was suboptimal for ruling out UTUC.
    - Test: Xpert Bladder
      Purpose: Evaluate suspected UTUC using upper-tract urine.
      When indicated: Assessed in a prospective study of 79 patients immediately before URS; not established as a routine test in the guideline.
      Interpretation: The study reported sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 4%.
    - Test: Bladder Epicheck
      Purpose: Provide a possible ancillary urinary test for UTUC detection.
      When indicated: Further prospective comparative validation is needed.
      Interpretation: In a prospective study of 79 patients, sensitivity was 64% and specificity was 79%.
    - Test: narrow-band imaging
      Purpose: Improve endoscopic visualisation of lesions.
      When indicated: Investigational use during ureteroscopy.
      Interpretation: Findings are promising but preliminary.
    - Test: optical coherence tomography
      Purpose: Evaluate tumour grade or stage in vivo.
      When indicated: Investigational endoscopic assessment.
      Interpretation: Correlation with definitive histology in high-grade UTUC has been promising.
    - Test: confocal laser endomicroscopy (Cellvizio®)
      Purpose: Evaluate tumour grade or stage in vivo.
      When indicated: Investigational endoscopic assessment.
      Interpretation: Correlation with definitive histology in high-grade UTUC has been promising.
    - Test: pathological examination of resection specimens
      Purpose: Establish stage, grade, histological subtype, lymphovascular invasion, margins and other prognostic findings.
      When indicated: After surgical resection.
      Interpretation: The report should specifically state lymphovascular invasion status and identify positive margins at ureteral transection, the bladder cuff and around the tumour.
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: histological grade
      Clinical significance: Closely associated with pathological stage and a principal factor in risk stratification; the guideline uses both the 1973 and 2004/2016 WHO classifications.
    - Marker: lymphovascular invasion
      Expected result: Present in approximately 20% of invasive UTUCs.
      Clinical significance: An independent predictor of survival that should be explicitly recorded in pathology reports.
    - Marker: tumour necrosis
      Clinical significance: Extensive necrosis involving > 10% of the tumour area independently predicts prognosis after RNU.
    - Marker: sessile growth pattern
      Clinical significance: Associated with poorer outcome in examinations of RNU specimens.
    - Marker: surgical margins
      Clinical significance: A positive soft-tissue margin is associated with greater recurrence risk after RNU.
  Genetic molecular:
    - Marker: FGFR3
      Clinical significance: Activating mutations occur in > 90% of low-grade tumours; FGFR3 signalling is activated in UTUC. Molecular markers have not been validated for routine clinical decision-making in non-metastatic disease.
    - Marker: TP53/MDM2
      Clinical significance: Mutations are depleted in low-grade tumours, whereas high-grade tumours often have alterations in TP53 signalling.
    - Marker: KMT2D
      Clinical significance: Cited among commonly altered chromatin-remodelling genes in UTUC.
    - Marker: KDM6A
      Clinical significance: Cited among commonly altered chromatin-remodelling genes in UTUC.
    - Marker: CDKN2A
      Clinical significance: Cited among genomic alterations observed in UTUC.
    - Marker: RAS
      Clinical significance: Cited among genomic alterations observed in UTUC.
  Staging:
    System: TNM classification 2017
    Definitions:
      - Stage: TX
        Description: The primary tumour cannot be evaluated.
      - Stage: T0
        Description: No primary tumour is evident.
      - Stage: Ta
        Description: Papillary carcinoma without invasion.
      - Stage: Tis
        Description: Carcinoma in situ.
      - Stage: T1
        Description: Tumour infiltrates the subepithelial connective tissue.
      - Stage: T2
        Description: Tumour infiltrates the muscularis.
      - Stage: T3
        Description: In the renal pelvis, tumour extends beyond the muscularis into peripelvic fat or renal parenchyma; in the ureter, it extends beyond the muscularis into periureteric fat.
      - Stage: T4
        Description: Tumour extends into neighbouring organs or passes through the kidney into perinephric fat.
      - Stage: NX
        Description: Regional lymph nodes cannot be evaluated.
      - Stage: N0
        Description: No regional lymph-node metastasis.
      - Stage: N1
        Description: Metastasis in one lymph node measuring 2 cm or less in its greatest dimension.
      - Stage: N2
        Description: Metastasis in one lymph node measuring more than 2 cm, or in multiple lymph nodes.
      - Stage: M0
        Description: No distant metastasis.
      - Stage: M1
        Description: Distant metastasis.
    Additional rules: Regional nodes comprise hilar and retroperitoneal nodes and, for mid- and distal-ureteral tumours, pelvic nodes. Laterality does not change the N classification.
  Prognostic tools:
    - Name: Risk stratification of non-metastatic UTUC according to the risk of progression to a> pT2 /nonorgan-confined disease
      Components:
      - Tumour focality
      - Tumour size
      - High-grade cytology
      - URS biopsy grade
      - Invasive appearance on CT
      - Histological subtype
      - Hydronephrosis
      Risk groups:
      - Group: Low-risk UTUC
      Criteria: All of the following: unifocal disease, tumour size < 2 cm, negative high-grade cytology, low-grade URS biopsy and no invasive appearance on CT.
      Expected outcome: Identifies patients more likely to be suitable for kidney-sparing treatment.
      - Group: High-risk UTUC
      Criteria: Any strong criterion—high-grade cytology, high-grade URS biopsy, local invasion on CT or a histological subtype—supports high-risk classification. Multifocal disease, tumour size ≥ 2 cm and hydronephrosis are weak criteria that should be considered alongside other factors.
      Expected outcome: Identifies patients at greater risk of progression to > pT2 or non-organ-confined disease.
      Interpretation: Multifocality, size or hydronephrosis alone is insufficient to determine risk, particularly with low-grade disease. Their value as individual surrogates of high-risk progression has a low level of evidence.
    - Name: American Society of Anesthesiologists [ASA]
      Interpretation: A higher score is associated with worse cancer-specific survival after RNU; the guideline does not provide scoring thresholds.
    - Name: Charlson Comorbidity Index
      Interpretation: Higher comorbidity indices are associated with poorer survival across disease stages; the guideline does not provide scoring thresholds.
    - Name: modified Glasgow score
      Interpretation: Mentioned among blood-based measures associated with locally advanced disease and cancer-specific mortality; no components or cut-offs are specified.
    - Name: De Ritis ratio
      Components:
      - aspartate transaminase
      - alanine transaminase
      Interpretation: A high ratio has been associated with locally advanced disease and cancer-specific mortality; no cut-off is specified.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Follow-up is determined by risk category and prior treatment; schedules are specified in the corresponding low-risk and high-risk entries.
    Recommended tests:
      - cystoscopy
      - urinary cytology
      - CT urography
      - chest CT
      - URS
    Survivorship notes: Surveillance aims to address rehabilitation needs and detect new or recurrent urothelial tumours and regional or distant metastases. The evidence underlying follow-up recommendations is limited by substantial heterogeneity. Bladder recurrence is not classified as distant recurrence.

Document sections:
  Heading: 6.8.3 Investigations
  Content: History and assessment should seek the cause; despite an extensive differential diagnosis, most cases reflect infection or inflammation. Initial history should address the symptom and systemic health and establish whether blood truly originates in semen. Apparent haemospermia can instead reflect haematuria or a partner's blood entering the urethra during intercourse. Sexual history should assess STI risk; travel to areas affected by schistosomiasis or tuberculosis and possible hypertension, liver disease, coagulopathy, weight loss, appetite loss or bone pain should also be considered. Examination should include blood pressure because case reports suggest an association with uncontrolled hypertension. Authors broadly agree on initial investigations but have not reached consensus. Urinalysis, urine microscopy, culture and sensitivity testing are advised. If tuberculosis or schistosomiasis is suspected, semen or prostatic secretions should be analysed. A full STI screen using first-void urine, serum and genitourinary samples should test for Chlamydia, Ureaplasma and Herpes Simplex virus; this may identify infection in cases otherwise called idiopathic. Appropriately counselled men aged > 40 years should have serum PSA measured. Full blood count, liver function and clotting tests can help identify systemic disease. Decisions about further tests depend on clinical judgement, age and risk factors. Digital rectal examination is advised, with re-examination of the meatus afterwards for bloody discharge. A palpable prostatic nodule matters because an association of haemospermia with PCa has been proposed but not fully established. MRI is increasingly used to investigate haemospermia and can show structural changes in the prostate, seminal vesicles, vas-deferens ampulla and ejaculatory ducts, particularly the origin of midline or paramedian prostatic cysts and information needed for surgical planning. An endorectal coil can improve accuracy in locating and explaining bleeding. Cystoscopy is included in many proposed protocols for higher-risk patients with persistent haemospermia unresponsive to conservative treatment; direct inspection can reveal polyps, urethritis, prostatic cysts, foreign bodies, calcifications or vascular abnormalities. Small-diameter ureteroscopes permit examination of ejaculatory ducts and seminal vesicles. In a prospective study of 106 patients with prolonged haemospermia, transrectal US plus seminal vesiculoscopy established a diagnosis in 87.7%; diagnostic yields were 45.3% for TRUS and 74.5% for seminal vesiculoscopy (P < 0.001). Melanospermia due to genitourinary malignant melanoma is rare and has been reported in two case reports; semen chromatography can detect melanin when distinction is needed.

Document sections:
  Heading: 2. Definition
  Content: BCC is a carcinoma of epidermal origin and the most frequent human malignancy. Its name reflects the resemblance of cells at the edge of tumour nests to epidermal basal cells; it is now thought to arise from hair-follicle stem cells. It usually develops on sun-exposed skin in fair-skinned individuals, most often on the head or neck. With chronic sun exposure as the principal carcinogen, incidence rises in older people and peaks at around 80 years of age. The usual lesion is a slowly enlarging, skin-coloured, shiny pearly nodule with surface arborising vessels; larger lesions can ulcerate centrally. Superficial BCC (sBCC) commonly affects the trunk and is associated mainly with intermittent sun exposure. Other presentations include pigmented or sclerosing tumours. Fewer than 1% of patients develop metastases, but delayed detection, inadequate management or neglect can allow extensive, locally advanced and deeply infiltrative disease.

Conditions:

  Name: Urethral diverticulum
  Synonyms:
    - female urethral diverticulum
  Description: A sac-like protrusion of the entire urethral wall or its mucosa into the space between peri-urethral tissues and the anterior vaginal wall.
  Epidemiology: Estimated prevalence is 1–6%; up to 10% was reported in women with LUTS attending a tertiary referral centre. The true incidence remains uncertain because cases may be asymptomatic or misdiagnosed.
  Clinical presentation: Possible symptoms include pain, urgency, frequency, recurrent UTI, vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, voiding difficulty and UI, but none is diagnostic. A palpable urethral mass may be present, sometimes with expressed purulent material or a stone in the diverticulum.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Mid-urethral
      Distinguishing features: Diverticulum situated at the mid-urethra.
    - Name: Distal
      Distinguishing features: Diverticulum situated distally.
    - Name: Proximal
      Distinguishing features: Diverticulum situated proximally; more proximal lesions may pose greater postoperative SUI risk.
    - Name: Full length
      Distinguishing features: Diverticulum extending across the urethral length.
    - Name: Single
      Distinguishing features: Single-cavity configuration.
    - Name: Multi-loculated
      Distinguishing features: Configuration with multiple compartments.
    - Name: Saddle shaped
      Distinguishing features: Saddle-shaped configuration.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Clinical examination
      Purpose: Identify a urethral mass, expressed material and associated symptoms.
      When indicated: Suspected diverticulum.
      Interpretation: No symptom cluster is pathognomonic.
    - Test: MRI
      Purpose: Confirm and characterise the diverticulum, guide repair and assess possible inflammation or tumour.
      When indicated: Diagnosis and operative planning.
      Interpretation: The guideline identifies MRI as the diagnostic gold standard, while noting that a case series found a 25% discrepancy between MRI and surgical findings.
    - Test: Urethrocystoscopy
      Purpose: Locate and count diverticular ostia for surgical planning.
      When indicated: Further characterisation as needed.
      Interpretation: Ostia were seen in 42% of cases in the cited series.
    - Test: VCUG
      Purpose: Characterise diverticular configuration.
      When indicated: When additional imaging is needed.
      Interpretation: Antero-posterior and lateral views are needed; false negatives can occur. Reported sensitivity is 73.5%.
    - Test: US
      Purpose: Identify the number, size, location and contents of a diverticulum.
      When indicated: Selected diagnostic evaluation.
      Interpretation: A meta-analysis reported sensitivity of 82.0% for US of any type; a trans-labial US publication reported 95%.
    - Test: Double balloon urethrography
      Purpose: Provide an alternative means of demonstrating the diverticulum.
      When indicated: When MRI cannot be performed and ostia cannot be identified on cystoscopy.
      Interpretation: Reported sensitivity is 94.7%, but the procedure is technically demanding and can cause pain or UTI.
    - Test: Pressure–flow studies or video-urodynamics
      Purpose: Assess coexisting voiding dysfunction, obstruction or SUI and distinguish genuine from diverticulum-related apparent leakage.
      When indicated: Selected preoperative cases with concomitant symptoms.
    - Test: Urethral pressure profilometry
      Purpose: Assess urethral pressure changes at the lesion.
      When indicated: Selected investigations.
      Interpretation: A biphasic pattern or pressure reduction at the diverticulum has been described.
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: nephrogenic metaplasia
      Expected result: Reported in 8% of cases in a meta-analysis.
      Clinical significance: A reported pathological finding in urethral diverticula.
  Staging:
    System: LNS C3
    Additional rules: The limited classification records localisation, configuration, communication and continence status rather than numerical stages.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Follow after surgery for recurrent diverticulum, persistent or new LUTS and UI; no fixed schedule is specified.
    Recommended tests:
      - Evaluate recurrent symptoms and new or persistent UI after diverticulectomy.
    Long term effects:
      - Recurrence, de novo SUI, urgency or UUI, urethral stricture and urethro-vaginal fistula are reported after surgery.
      - For patients managed conservatively, the reported risk of cancer within the diverticulum is 1–6%.

  Heading: 7.2.1.1.2 Minimal invasive radical nephroureterectomy
  Content: Manipulating large tumours under pneumoperitoneum can lead to retroperitoneal or trocar-tract metastatic spread. Precautions include avoiding entry into the urinary tract except for bladder-cuff excision after clipping the ureter and draining the bladder, preventing instrument contact with tumour, operating in a closed system without morcellation, using an extraction bag and removing kidney, ureter and bladder cuff together. An open approach is favoured for invasive or large T3/T4 and/or N+/M+ tumours because oncological outcomes may be better. Laparoscopic RNU is safe with experienced operators applying strict oncological principles, and several studies suggest outcomes resembling open RNU. A small randomised study of n = 80 instead found laparoscopy inferior in non-organ-confined disease. Despite advances in staging and surgery, post-RNU oncological outcomes have not significantly changed over the past three decades. A population dataset associated centres treating > 6 RNU patients yearly with improved 30- and 90-day mortality and long-term overall survival. Robot-assisted laparoscopy can be considered: peri-operative benefits resemble standard laparoscopy, and data suggest oncological equivalence across approaches. Both laparoscopic and robotic RNU may, however, carry higher intravesical recurrence risk than open surgery.

Document sections:
  Heading: 1. Introduction
  Content: Ovarian lesions account for most abdominal masses in pediatric girls and span functional cysts through malignant tumors. Cysts constitute 60% of pediatric ovarian lesions. True neoplasms occur at 2.6 cases per 100,000 girls per year; 3–8% of adnexal masses are malignant, representing 1–2% of pediatric cancers. Neoplasms are grouped by origin into germ cell, sex cordstromal, and epithelial tumors. Incidence, causes, and presentation vary by age: germ cell tumors predominate among childhood and adolescent ovarian neoplasms, whereas epithelial tumors predominate in adults. Mature cystic teratomas are the most frequent tumor type, and dysgerminomas are described as the most frequent malignant ovarian neoplasm in the pediatric population. Functional cysts peak in the fetal/neonatal and perimenarchal periods, reflecting maternal gonadotropins or activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis. Ultrasound is the initial imaging choice; MRI offers additional soft-tissue detail without ionizing radiation. Imaging and serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), beta subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), and inhibin A and B contribute to malignancy-risk assessment. Pediatric surgery should favor fertility preservation, minimally invasive laparoscopy, and ovarian conservation when feasible. The review addresses evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment across pediatric age groups.

Document sections:
  Heading: 1.1 Initial assessment
  Content: Initial assessment may take place in any setting and is performed by a healthcare professional without specific training in managing LUTS in men. Offer a review of medical history, possible causes and comorbidities; examine current medicines, including herbal and over-the-counter products, for possible contributors. Offer an examination informed by urological symptoms and other conditions, including the abdomen, external genitalia and a digital rectal examination. Ask men with bothersome LUTS to complete a urinary frequency volume chart. Offer urine dipstick testing for blood, glucose, protein, leucocytes and nitrites. Provide information, advice and time to decide about prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing if symptoms suggest bladder outlet obstruction due to benign prostate enlargement (BPE), the prostate feels abnormal on digital rectal examination, or the man is concerned about prostate cancer. Manage suspected prostate cancer according to the NICE guidelines on prostate cancer and suspected cancer. Offer serum creatinine testing with estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] calculation only when renal impairment is suspected; examples include a palpable bladder, nocturnal enuresis, recurrent urinary tract infections or previous renal stones. Do not routinely offer cystoscopy or upper urinary tract imaging for uncomplicated LUTS at this stage, or routinely measure flow rate or post-void residual volume. For symptoms that are neither bothersome nor complicated, provide reassurance, information and lifestyle advice, such as advice about fluid intake, and offer review if symptoms change. Offer specialist referral when bothersome LUTS have not responded to conservative or drug treatment. Refer for specialist assessment when LUTS are complicated by recurrent or persistent urinary tract infection, retention, renal impairment suspected to arise from lower urinary tract dysfunction, or suspected urological cancer. Before any LUTS treatment, offer assessment of baseline symptoms with a validated score, such as IPSS, so subsequent changes can be assessed. These recommendations are marked [2010].

  Content: For asymptomatic patients, the EAU favours initial US because it avoids radiation, costs less and can identify hydronephrosis and stones in the calyces, renal pelvis and pelvic-ureteric or vesico-ureteric junctions. For symptomatic patients, NCCT is preferred: it characterises density, diameter, volume, skin-to-stone distance and surrounding anatomy to inform treatment, and is more accurate than US or IVU (EAU: strong recommendation). Contrast-enhanced imaging is advised when collecting-system anatomy must be assessed before removal (EAU: strong recommendation). KUB X-ray can establish radiopacity but need not be obtained when NCCT is planned. The AUA recommends NCCT before PCNL (AUA: strong recommendation) and when choosing between SWL and URS (AUA: conditional recommendation); US alone is discouraged for the latter decision. Suspected substantial renal injury may warrant a DTPA or MAG-3 renogram to guide care (AUA: conditional recommendation). The EAU advises testing serum creatinine, uric acid, ionised calcium, sodium, potassium, blood cell counts and C-reactive protein, plus coagulation when intervention is intended (EAU: strong recommendation). Both organisations strongly recommend urine culture and microscopy before intervention.

  Description: The guideline distinguishes resectable disease, disease after resection, and unresectable and/or metastatic disease for systemic treatment.

  Clinical presentation: Regional lymphadenopathy can be detected clinically in patients with known or suspected regional nodal metastasis. Disease may also present with cutaneous, subcutaneous, or nodal injectable lesions, or with brain metastases.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: resectable stage IIIB-IV cutaneous melanoma
      Distinguishing features: Clinical disease eligible for resection is addressed in the neoadjuvant recommendations.
    - Name: resected stage IIA melanoma
      Distinguishing features: Adjuvant therapy is addressed separately from that for resected stage IIB or IIC disease.
    - Name: resected stage IIB or IIC melanoma
      Distinguishing features: Adjuvant treatment is considered after resection.
    - Name: resected stage IIIA-D disease
      Distinguishing features: Adjuvant options differ by BRAF status.
    - Name: resected stage IV melanoma
      Distinguishing features: The guideline addresses adjuvant treatment after resection.
    - Name: unresectable and/or metastatic cutaneous melanoma
      Distinguishing features: Systemic options differ by BRAF status and prior treatment.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: core needle biopsy
      Purpose: Establish pathology and permit molecular characterization of suspected regional nodal melanoma.
      When indicated: Clinically detected lymphadenopathy in a patient with known or suspected regional nodal metastasis.
      Interpretation: The guideline favors this approach over excisional biopsy, which has greater morbidity and is not routinely needed for these purposes.
    - Test: BRAF mutation testing
      Purpose: Inform treatment selection because recommended options differ by BRAF mutation status.
      When indicated: When selecting systemic treatment for melanoma.
      Interpretation: A BRAF wild-type result may rarely be falsely negative; repeat testing at progression could be considered, although the Panel identifies no high-quality supporting data.
  Genetic molecular:
    - Marker: BRAF
      Clinical significance: Mutation status affects selection of recommended systemic treatment.
    - Marker: NTRK fusion
      Clinical significance: The guideline cites an estimated prevalence of 0.2% in cutaneous melanoma and notes a higher prevalence in spitzoid melanoma. Testing may be reasonable when recommended therapies have been exhausted or no viable alternative remains.

  - Renal transplant recipients: the EAU recommends prompt treatment of stone-related obstruction and allows SWL, URS or PCNL according to graft anatomy and function and the patient's clotting status. Document sections:
  Heading: 3. Epidemiology
  Content: cSCC is the second most common skin cancer and accounts for 20% of keratinocyte carcinomas; basal cell carcinoma-to-cSCC ratios range from 2 to 4:1. Most primary lesions, 80–90%, occur on the head and neck. Incidence estimates are limited partly because some datasets include AK or in situ disease, but available data indicate rising rates in most white populations, with further increases predicted. Table 2 compares international age-standardized incidence. Incidence rises with age, male sex (standardized incidence ratio, 2.1; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.06–2.14) and lower latitude; multiple tumours correlate strongly with age. In the United Kingdom during 2013–2015, 62.7% of cases occurred in men, whose median age was 80 years, and the mean annual percentage increase was 5%. Norwegian age-adjusted incidence rose nine-fold in females and six-fold in males from 1963 to 2011, particularly at ages 70–79 years. Swedish registry data linked higher incidence at the same latitude to sunnier coastal residence. The Rochester Epidemiology Project reported a 263% incidence increase between 1976 and 1984 and 2000–2010, disproportionately affecting women and people under 40 years. Inconsistent registration, sometimes recording only a first tumour, substantially understates the public-health burden. Higher rates occur after solid organ transplantation and with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Danish and US haematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients had 9–18-fold greater risk than the general population. In a US cohort, patients with HIV and CD4 count < 200 cells/mL had a 2.2 times higher risk of another cSCC after their first than uninfected people.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: EAU Guidelines on Sexual and Reproductive Health 2025.cap08
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 11.4.1.2.2 Surgical treatment
  Content: Removal of an intra-abdominal testis in adolescence can be recommended when the other testis is normal because of malignancy risk. Adults with a palpable undescended testis and a normally functioning contralateral testis may be offered orchidectomy because of GCNIS and future germ-cell-tumour risk and the inability to self-examine that testis. With unilateral undescended testis and contralateral biochemical hypogonadism or impaired sperm production, orchidopexy may preserve hormones and fertility; panel consensus recommends multiple biopsies during orchidopexy to assess GCNIS. Bilateral correction even in adulthood may permit sperm production in previously azoospermic men and can be considered when fertility preservation is valued. Vascular injury is the most severe orchidopexy complication; atrophy occurs in 1-2% of cases, was 12% in non-palpable testes with long vascular pedicles permitting scrotal positioning, and has been reported in up to 40% after staged orchidopexy. During orchidectomy for germ-cell tumour, offer contralateral biopsy to patients at high GCNIS risk, including cryptorchidism history, testicular volume < 12 mL or poor spermatogenesis.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_02
  Name: Primary Hypogonadism
  Synonyms:
    - hypergonadotropic hypogonadism
  Description: Hypogonadism arising from impaired testicular function. Listed causes include congenital or developmental disorders, acquired testicular injury or disease, drug exposures and systemic conditions; some systemic conditions can affect both central and peripheral function.
  Clinical presentation: Symptoms and signs need not differ from those of secondary hypogonadism. A milder peripheral defect presenting before or around puberty may produce delayed puberty and a eunuchoid phenotype.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Klinefelter syndrome
      Distinguishing features: A genetic cause associated with a 47,XXY karyotype.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: serum total testosterone
      Purpose: Document testosterone deficiency.
      When indicated: When compatible symptoms or signs are present; obtain fasting morning measurements and confirm a pathological result.
      Interpretation: Interpret together with symptoms, signs and gonadotropin levels.
    - Test: luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
      Purpose: Distinguish testicular from central causes.
      When indicated: When testosterone deficiency is identified.
      Interpretation: Elevated LH supports primary rather than secondary hypogonadism.
    - Test: Clinical history and physical examination
      Purpose: Identify possible congenital, acquired, treatment-related or systemic causes and assess fertility wishes.
      When indicated: During diagnostic evaluation.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: When testosterone therapy is used, review at three months and subsequently according to clinical and biochemical findings; monitor testosterone and haematocrit at three, six and twelve months, then annually.
    Recommended tests:
      - Testosterone
      - Haematocrit
      - PSA
      - Digital rectal examination
    Long term effects:
      - Exogenous testosterone suppresses gonadotropin secretion and spermatogenesis.
      - Monitor for elevated haematocrit and prostate abnormalities during testosterone therapy.

  Content: Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is described as the most common endocrine disorder among females of reproductive age worldwide.   Content: cSCC is the second most common skin cancer and accounts for 20% of keratinocyte carcinomas; basal cell carcinoma-to-cSCC ratios range from 2 to 4:1. Most primary lesions, 80–90%, occur on the head and neck. Incidence estimates are limited partly because some datasets include AK or in situ disease, but available data indicate rising rates in most white populations, with further increases predicted. Table 2 compares international age-standardized incidence. Incidence rises with age, male sex (standardized incidence ratio, 2.1; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.06–2.14) and lower latitude; multiple tumours correlate strongly with age. In the United Kingdom during 2013–2015, 62.7% of cases occurred in men, whose median age was 80 years, and the mean annual percentage increase was 5%. Norwegian age-adjusted incidence rose nine-fold in females and six-fold in males from 1963 to 2011, particularly at ages 70–79 years. Swedish registry data linked higher incidence at the same latitude to sunnier coastal residence. The Rochester Epidemiology Project reported a 263% incidence increase between 1976 and 1984 and 2000–2010, disproportionately affecting women and people under 40 years. Inconsistent registration, sometimes recording only a first tumour, substantially understates the public-health burden. Higher rates occur after solid organ transplantation and with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Danish and US haematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients had 9–18-fold greater risk than the general population. Document sections:
  Heading: 3.1 Epidemiology
  Content: UC is the second most frequent urological malignancy in developed countries and can arise in the lower urinary tract or the pyelocaliceal cavities and ureter. Bladder cancer (BC) constitutes 90–95% of UC, whereas UTUC constitutes 5–10%; estimated annual incidence in Western countries is almost two cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Incidence has increased over recent decades, possibly because detection improved and populations aged. Incidence peaks at 70–90 years, and UTUC occurs twice as often in men. In an international retrospective registry of 2,380 people diagnosed between 2014 and 2019 at 101 centres in 29 countries, 70.5% were men, 53.3% were current or former smokers, and 53% received a diagnosis after symptoms, chiefly visible haematuria. A meta-analysis of 44 studies estimated UTUC incidence among people with visible and non-visible haematuria at 0.75% and 0.17%, respectively. Approximately two-thirds of patients presenting with UTUC have muscle-invasive disease at diagnosis, versus 15–25% with newly diagnosed BC; population studies from Germany and England suggest muscle-invasive UTUC accounts for approximately half of recent incident cases. Approximately 9% present with metastases. Pyelocaliceal tumours occur approximately twice as frequently as ureteral tumours; multifocality occurs in approximately 10–20%, and concomitant upper-tract carcinoma in situ in between 11% and 36%. Concurrent BC occurs in 17%; previous BC was recorded in 41% of American men and 4% of Chinese men. These differences, alongside genetic and epigenetic factors, may help explain more advanced, higher-grade presentations in Asian patients. After treatment, bladder recurrence occurs in 29%, varying with patient, tumour and treatment characteristics, versus 2–5% recurrence in the contralateral upper tract. UTUC and BC differ substantially in frequencies of common genomic changes, although tumours in a person with both cancers are often clonally related. UTUC genomic profiling can inform bladder-recurrence risk and identify Lynch syndrome-associated tumours. Among 82 patients given intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) for high-risk BC and imaged regularly between years 1 and 3, 13% developed asymptomatic UTUC; another series of 307 patients without routine upper-tract imaging reported 25% UTUC after BC. A multicentre cohort of n = 402 followed for 50 month reported 7.5% UTUC among NMIBC recipients of BCG; intravesical recurrence and a non-papillary tumour at transurethral resection of the bladder (TURB) predicted UTUC. Following radical cystectomy for MIBC, 3–5% develop metachronous UTUC.

  Heading: 15.2 Contraindications
  Content: Suspected or confirmed urethral rupture, UTI or false passage are listed contraindications. Injury to urethral epithelium can heal with scarring and stricture formation. Male strictures commonly cause obstructive voiding symptoms and may follow IC, infection, trauma, lichen sclerosus, prostate-cancer treatment such as radiotherapy, or an unidentified cause. UK Hospital Episode Statistics and similar US data suggest male incidence rises from about 10 in every 100,000 up to 25 years to 40 in every 100,000 by the age of 65 years and > 100 in every 100,000 over 65 years. Female urethral strictures affect 0.1–1% of women with voiding complaints and can cause irritative as well as obstructive symptoms. In a review by Chakraborty et al., 53.48% of surgically treated female strictures were presumed idiopathic and 91.29% had a prior intervention. Smith et al. attributed 8% of female strictures to inflammation and infection and 6.6% to trauma. Male strictures may occur anywhere, particularly in the bulbar urethra (50 %) and at the meatus. In selected patients, intermittent dilatation is established as palliative management of refractory strictures and can reduce recurrence up to 68%. Diversion, such as a continent stoma or ileal conduit, is required if reconstruction is impossible or repair attempts fail. A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to determine which of dilatation, endoscopic urethrotomy or urethroplasty best balances effectiveness, adverse effects and costs. Document sections:
  Heading: 5.1. Paediatric Population
  Content: Children may have vague, age-dependent symptoms: older children can have haematuria, flank pain or recurrent UTIs, whereas infants may vomit, become irritable or cry. To limit radiation under ALARA, the EAU recommends initial US; inadequate findings may prompt KUB X-ray or NCCT (strong recommendation). The AUA recommends NCCT before paediatric PCNL (strong recommendation). The EAU notes little evidence for observation but allows it initially for asymptomatic lower-pole stones <7 mm without struvite or cystine composition or anatomical abnormalities. It states that MET may improve passage and pain but causes more side effects in children. The AUA recommends observation with or without MET first for ureteral stones ≤10 mm; patients or parents should be informed if MET is used off-label (AUA: moderate recommendation). Routine stenting before paediatric URS is discouraged (AUA: expert opinion). SWL, URS and PCNL generally have indications similar to those in adults. For a single ureteral stone <10 mm, the EAU favours SWL first and URS if SWL fails or cannot be used (strong recommendation). URS with lasertripsy can have good, safe outcomes when performed by surgeons experienced in paediatric complications. After failed observation or MET, the AUA recommends choosing SWL or URS according to anatomy and habitus (strong recommendation). It cautions that ultrasound-based lithotriptors may poorly visualise the ureter, particularly its middle portion, while SWL can be useful in small children for whom URS access is difficult. For renal stones <20 mm, the EAU favours SWL first (strong recommendation) and FURS may follow failed SWL, especially for lower-calyceal stones; the AUA supports SWL or URS (moderate recommendation). For renal stones >20 mm, the EAU recommends PCNL (strong recommendation). In children, PCNL's higher SFR comes with more side effects, although mini and ultra-mini PCNL have reduced complications related to tract size, including renal extravasation and haematuria. The AUA instead accepts either PCNL or SWL with stent or nephrostomy for >20 mm stones (moderate recommendation). It also favours observation with routine US surveillance for asymptomatic, non-obstructing renal stones (expert opinion). All children's stones should undergo material analysis, with subsequent metabolic assessment guided by the result (EAU: strong recommendation).

Document sections:
  Heading: General Considerations
  Content: Early detection decisions require consideration of age, life expectancy, family history, African ancestry, inherited mutations, previous tests, general health, comorbidity, and patient preferences, alongside discussion of benefits and harms. Guidance does not replace a clinician's full history and examination. Early prostate cancer has no identifiable symptoms; advanced disease can cause urinary obstruction, prostatic bleeding, hematospermia, or bone pain. Symptoms from benign prostatic enlargement should be distinguished during counseling. Prior DRE, PSA, PSA derivatives, and biopsy results should be reviewed. Patients should understand that detection seeks aggressive cancers but also finds low-risk disease that may be managed with active surveillance rather than immediate treatment. The panel recommends offering baseline PSA to healthy, informed people at average risk aged 45 to 75 years and to those with African ancestry, risk-associated germline mutations, and/or suspicious family history at ages 40 to 75 years. Baseline DRE may complement PSA; elevated PSA should be confirmed. For average-risk people <75 years with PSA below 1 ng/mL, recommended repeat testing is every 2 to 4 years; at PSA 1 to 3 ng/mL, every 1 to 2 years. With elevated risk and PSA ≤3 ng/mL, the interval is 1 to 2 years. The panel strongly recommends multiparametric MRI before biopsy when available. For PSA >3 ng/mL when greater specificity is desired, %fPSA, 4Kscore, SelectMDx, ExoDx Prostate, PHI, MPS, and IsoPSA may be considered before biopsy. After a negative biopsy with persistent higher risk, options include PHI, %fPSA, 4Kscore, ConfirmMDx, PCA3, MPS, and IsoPSA. Biopsy decisions should not rely on PSA threshold alone; age, family history, PSA kinetics, ancestry, health, preferences, MRI, and biomarkers also matter. High suspicion of clinically significant cancer warrants image-guided transrectal or transperineal biopsy; routine MRI targeting is recommended where available. PSA testing after age >75 years warrants cautious consideration only in very healthy patients (category 2B), with careful biopsy assessment. Panel members uniformly discourage testing those unlikely to benefit because of age or comorbidity. The panel considers these early detection recommendations linked to the NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer.

Document sections:
  Heading: ERSPC Trial
  Content: ERSPC randomized about 182,000 participants aged 50 to 74 years in seven European countries to offered PSA screening, on average once every 4 years, or no such offer; the screened group could also receive DRE or ancillary tests. Its predefined core comprised 162,388 aged 55 to 69 years, and prostate cancer death was the primary outcome. At median follow-up of 11 years, cumulative incidence was 7.4% with screening versus 5.1% in control; prostate cancer deaths numbered 299 versus 462. The screening-to-control prostate cancer death rate ratio was 0.79 (95% CI, 0.68–0.91; P = .001). Investigators concluded that PSA screening lowered disease-specific mortality by 21% and estimated that 1055 needed screening and 37 additional people needed treatment over 11 years to avert one death. Modeling by Heijnsdijk and colleagues instead estimated 98 needed screening and 5 needed treatment. At 13-year follow-up, 7408 screening-arm participants and 6107 controls had prostate cancer; the unadjusted mortality rate ratio was 0.79 (95% CI, 0.69–0.91), and the ratio adjusted for nonparticipation was 0.73 (95% CI, 0.61–0.88). Investigators estimated that inviting 781 people or diagnosing 27 additional cancers would avert one prostate cancer death. Another analysis of those 13-year data reported fewer metastatic diagnoses with screening (incidence rate ratio, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.52–0.70). By 16 years, the corresponding numbers invited and additionally diagnosed per death averted were 570 and 18. Rotterdam ERSPC analysis reported a 32% reduction in prostate cancer-specific mortality; after accounting for contamination and nonattendance, its investigators estimated a possible reduction of up to 51%. The Finnish component reported a small, non-statistically significant disease-specific mortality reduction after 12 years.

Document sections:
  Heading: Pharmacotherapy.
  Content: Most drug treatments require physiological-range haematological, liver and kidney results and exclusion of major pulmonary or cardiac disease or infection before and during treatment. Most patients receive an alkylating agent during their disease course. Temozolomide is the most commonly used glioma drug; it is an oral DNA alkylator that crosses the blood–brain barrier. Its main dose-limiting toxicity is myelosuppression, particularly thrombocytopenia, and liver function needs regular monitoring. Nitrosoureas such as lomustine, carmustine, nimustine and fotemustine cause later leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, at 4–6 weeks rather than 2–3 weeks, often with cumulative effects that may require interruption, dose reduction, discontinuation or another treatment. Pulmonary fibrosis is reported mainly with carmustine and rarely with lomustine. PCV combines lomustine, procarbazine and vincristine. Implanted carmustine wafers produced a modest OS benefit in newly diagnosed WHO grade 3 or 4 glioma or recurrent glioblastoma, but the pivotal trial found no statistically significant outcome difference after excluding WHO grade 3 cases from survival analysis. Benefits demonstrated for alkylating therapy in RCTs need weighing against late toxicity and a treatment-induced hypermutator phenotype linked to greater malignancy, particularly in longer-surviving patients with IDH-mutant disease. Bevacizumab, an anti-VEGF antibody, is approved for recurrent glioblastoma in the USA, Canada, Switzerland and other countries outside the European Union, without demonstrated OS benefit. Patients on systemic therapy should carry treatment records with laboratory results, complications and contraindications. Treating centres should maintain standardized procedures for chemotherapy delivery and complication management.

Document sections:
  Heading: Pediatric Population
  Content: CVT is more frequent in neonates (6.4/100000) than in older children and adolescents. Prompt consideration of the diagnosis is important when a child acutely develops headache, seizures, focal deficits, or coma, or has circumstances such as sepsis—including mastoiditis, Lemierre syndrome, COVID-19, or meningitis—head trauma, including abuse, hypoxia, or dehydration. Particular vigilance is warranted with congenital heart disease or its surgical treatment, cancer or its treatment, iron-deficiency anemia or hemoglobinopathies, and inflammatory diseases such as nephrotic syndrome or inflammatory bowel disease. Emergency imaging to establish or exclude dural or cortical venous thrombosis, with or without parenchymal damage or hemorrhage, typically requires anesthesia. Initial blood testing may identify low platelets associated with platelet factor 4 mutations; elevated platelets and hemoglobin associated with JAK2 mutations; or signs of iron deficiency, whether or not anemia is present. Acute management generally uses LMWH or unfractionated heparin. As in adults, worsening consciousness may justify considering more invasive, potentially lifesaving procedures. Acute anticoagulation in premature and term neonates is more controversial but is reasonable: evidence of posttreatment hemorrhage is lacking, whereas withholding anticoagulation may permit thrombus extension. Pediatric CVT mortality is 3%; recurrent venous thrombosis occurs in ≈6% and is usually associated with absent anticoagulation and lack of venous recanalization. Trials published since the earlier statement have examined treatment duration and DOACs. Kids-DOTT studied individuals 4 months to 20.9 years of age with provoked VTE, including 59/417; 25% patients with CVT, and compared 6 weeks with 3 months of anticoagulation. The 6-week course was noninferior for recurrent VTE and bleeding. In EINSTEIN-Jr, after initial heparinization, 114 children with confirmed CVT were randomized 2:1 to 3 months of rivaroxaban or standard anticoagulation with continued heparin or a switch to an oral VKA. Its main efficacy measure was symptomatic recurrent VTE; its principal safety measure was major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding. Follow-up was 100%. Symptomatic recurrent VTE occurred in none of the 73 rivaroxaban-treated children and 1 of the 41 standard-treatment children (absolute difference, 2.4% [95% CI, −2.6% to 13.5%]). Five rivaroxaban recipients experienced nonmajor, noncerebral bleeding, while 1 standard-treatment recipient had a major subdural bleed. Complete and partial recanalization occurred, respectively, in 18 (25%) and 39 (53%) rivaroxaban recipients and 6 (15%) and 24 (59%) standard-treatment recipients. No child died during the 3-month treatment period. At study end, focal deficits affected 5 (6.8%) children receiving rivaroxaban and 3 (7.3%) receiving standard anticoagulation. Other long-term studies suggest that, despite treatment, 1 in 4 children may develop late epilepsy; infantile spasms after neonatal CVT, cognitive impairment, and intracranial hypertension are also reported.

Document sections:
  Heading: 3.1.3 Classification
  Content: Aetiological classification distinguishes primary from secondary hypogonadism. A compensated or subclinical form has normal serum testosterone with elevated LH, but its clinical importance remains uncertain. Classical/ Organic hypogonadism involves congenital or acquired structural and/or irreversible pituitary or testicular disease. Functional hypogonadism lacks a recognised organic HPG-axis lesion, usually arises with comorbidity, and calls first for improvement or resolution of the underlying condition. Labelling all functional cases LOH is incorrect. LOH encompasses adult-onset organic or functional disease of either primary or secondary origin; its definition requires persistent specific symptoms plus biochemical testosterone deficiency. Testosterone deficiency can also arise through reduced sensitivity to testosterone or its metabolites. Classification helps select therapy: appropriate treatment of secondary hypogonadism can theoretically restore both testosterone and fertility, whereas primary hypogonadism permits consideration of testosterone therapy, which may impair fertility through HPT-axis suppression. Symptoms can be similar regardless of disease origin, but onset influences phenotype. Foetal-onset disease may produce an almost complete female phenotype or varying virilisation defects; pre- or peripubertal disease may cause delayed puberty and a eunuchoid phenotype; post-pubertal disease, particularly with ageing, may produce mild symptoms mistaken for ageing.

  Content: Lynch syndrome arises from pathogenic germline variants in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, or EPCAM. Age at onset and aggressiveness generally appear similar to sporadic prostate cancer. IMPACT enrolled carriers aged 40 to 69 years of MLH1, MSH2, or MSH6 mutations (n = 644), related age-matched noncarriers (n= 184), and an additional 134 randomly selected noncarriers from its BRCA1/2 cohort. Participants were assigned annual PSA testing for at least 5 years. After the first round, prostate cancer incidence was 4.3% among MSH2 carriers (13 of 305; 95% CI, 2.3–7.2), 3.0% among MSH6 carriers (4 of 135; 95% CI, 0.8–7.4), and 0.5% among MSH2 noncarrier controls (1 of 210; 95% CI, 0–2.6); no MLH1 carrier or other noncarrier control received a diagnosis.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 1 Introduction
  Content: Cryptorchidism affects approximately 1-5% of full-term boys at birth in Western Countries and means that one or both testes have not reached the scrotum. Its incidence falls by approximately 50% during the first six months through spontaneous descent; persistent cases require clinical intervention. Untreated cryptorchidism increases the risks of impaired fertility and testicular cancer. Early treatment can substantially reduce, and potentially eliminate, those risks. Although the scrotum's cooler environment is thought necessary for spermatogenesis, the precise contribution of temperature remains disputed. Stem-cell niches require tightly controlled conditions for cell propagation and differentiation. Despite uncertainty about the biological mechanisms, orchidopexy remains the principal intervention. After orchidopexy, the germ cells per tubular cross-section ration (G/T) can indicate fertility potential: a lower ratio signals greater infertility risk, including in unilateral disease. Sertoli cells produce Inhibin-B, an indicator of seminiferous-tubule function; serum levels correlate with prepubertal Sertoli-cell counts and strongly with G/T. Recent research suggests that low serum inhibin-B reliably predicts impaired G/T in bilateral cryptorchidism. Histology indicates that unilateral disease can affect both testes: 70% of scrotal testes in patients with unilateral cryptorchidism showed impaired transformation of Ad spermatogonia into Ap spermatogonia. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism can cause cryptorchidism but is relatively uncommon compared with cryptorchidism overall. Gonadotropins vary substantially during minipuberty, making precise age-matched measurements important; available studies suggest hypergonadotropism rather than hypogonadotropism. Current guidelines therefore reserve gonadotropin/Gonadotropin hormone releasing hormone (GNRH) treatment mainly for clinical hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, not routine cryptorchidism treatment. Congenital disease raises infertility risk and calls for early intervention. Retractile testes and acquired cryptorchidism may also affect fertility, to differing degrees. Mobility informs treatment decisions, while emerging evidence suggests that acquired disease may have greater fertility implications than previously thought; reported histological changes resemble those in congenital disease. Careful management of all forms is consequently relevant to reducing fertility risk. Among Dutch schoolboys, acquired undescended testis prevalence was 1.2% at age 6 years, 2.2% at age 9 years and 1.1% at age of 13 years. In 66% of boys with acquired cryptorchidism, earlier records placed the testes normally, supporting continued examination throughout childhood. Fetal testicular descent is biphasic and involves complex physiological changes. The gubernaculum is important in both phases but can occasionally elongate the epididymis. Over 50% of patients with cryptorchidism have epididymal or ductus deferens abnormalities; testisepididymis dissociation, reported in 45-80%, is thought to reflect a persistently abnormal genital mesentery. Surgeons need to recognize these anatomical variations. Early detection and repair before 1 year of age remain the most important measures for limiting harm in unilateral and bilateral disease. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, Allin et al. found no difference in atrophy between orchidopexy before and after one year, but earlier surgery was associated with greater testicular volume and more spermatogonia per tubule across fifteen eligible studies, suggesting better fertility potential. A retrospective cohort study by Boehme et al. attributed more than half of orchidopexies after the first year to acquired undescended testes. Hack et al. proposed in a Netherlands study from 2003 that acquired cryptorchidism occurs three times as often as primary disease. A German retrospective study of over 3500 patients found that 42% of orchidopexies during 2003-2012 involved patients aged 4 to 17 years; the acquired proportion was unclear. One-stage orchidopexy preserving spermatic vessels is standard for palpable inguinal testes. Short spermatic vessels often restrict mobilization of intra-abdominal testes, leaving the optimal one-stage or two-stage strategy debated. In one-stage surgery, the testis is moved directly into the scrotum during one operation, with possible spermatic-vessel division. In two-stage surgery, vessels are divided first and scrotal placement follows at a second operation. The staged Fowler and Stephens (FS) approach, introduced in 1959, is commonly used for high intra-abdominal testes when vessel tension prevents mobilization. Vessel ligation may, however, cause atrophy; reported success is between 80-86%. The Shehata technique uses traction-induced elongation to improve mobilization while preserving vascular supply. Ellis et al. reported that the gubernaculum contributes to blood supply alongside the spermatic vessels and vas deferens. Gubernaculum-sparing FS orchidopexy consequently aims to support testicular survival while preserving cremasteric collateral vessels. The review evaluates surgical methods in relation to the Nordic consensus statement and current EAU and AUA guidelines.

  Content: TM occurs in 0.6-9% of men referred for testicular US; its general-population incidence is unknown and probably low. It has been observed with malignancy and several benign reproductive conditions, and reported TGCT-associated incidence is 6-46%. Its association with infertility is uncertain. A case-control meta-analysis associated TM in infertile men with testicular cancer (pooled OR: 18.11, 95% CI: 8.09, 40.55; p < 0.0001). Although TM merits counselling in this setting and biopsies show more GCNIS, especially with bilateral findings, calcification itself is not malignant and its association with TGCT remains controversial. Possible GCNIS risk factors include infertility, atrophy, undescended testis, prior TGCT and contralateral TM; biopsy has been suggested for selected patients after discussion of its risks. Most asymptomatic patients do not develop cancer. Decastro et al. suggested no testicular cancer developed in most men with TM (98.4%) during 5-year follow-up; extensive screening would therefore principally benefit high-risk men. Advise regular self-examination with incidental TM, particularly with other cancer risks. Annual urological examination and US have been suggested for higher-risk men, but follow-up may be difficult; evidence is lacking for higher cancer prevalence specifically with both TM and atrophy.

  Content: Ovarian lesions account for most abdominal masses in pediatric girls and span functional cysts through malignant tumors. Cysts constitute 60% of pediatric ovarian lesions. retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: DISCUSSION
  Content: The authors relate ED to endothelial dysfunction and impaired NO signaling and propose that addressing oxidative stress may help when endothelial dysfunction contributes to ED. Across 23 double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials, oral antioxidants produced statistically significant, clinically important short-term improvements relative to placebo, with greater benefit among men with more severe ED. Side effects were infrequent, non-serious, and not significantly more frequent than with placebo. Supplementation was generally brief (median 12 weeks), so the authors characterize it as an apparently low-risk, non-pharmacologic option with demonstrated short-term efficacy, not established long-term efficacy. On the 6 to 30-point IIEF-EF scale, cited MCIDs were 2.4 points for mild ED, 6.0 points for moderate ED, and 8.4 points for severe ED. The review’s improvement was 5.5 points. As contextual comparisons drawn from cited literature, the authors give 2 points for testosterone replacement, 4 points for shockwave therapy, and 4 to 8 points for PDE5 inhibitors. Minor side effects occurred in 3.8% of antioxidant recipients, a frequency comparable with placebo. In cited evidence on PDE5 inhibitors, effects such as headache and flushing occurred in over 25% of patients, at a rate 2 to 3 times that with placebo. The authors suggest antioxidants may be a low-risk option across ED severities. They state that patients could consider them instead of PDE5 inhibitors, potentially delaying or avoiding drug therapy, and that a benefit comparable to PDE5 inhibitors warrants consideration of antioxidants in ED treatment algorithms. The authors caution that benefit might vary by ED cause. In a cited study, Aldemir et al found lower total antioxidant capacity and higher oxidative-stress markers in men with ED than in men without ED; those differences were more pronounced in arteriogenic ED. This raises, but does not establish, the possibility of greater benefit in arteriogenic ED. Further research is needed to test variation by etiology. Included products encompassed amino acids, vitamins, enzymes, and plant extracts. Despite structural differences, their shared proposed actions against oxidative stress provide the rationale for pooling them. The authors propose that reduced oxidative stress may improve vasodilation and smooth-muscle relaxation and that individual or combined antioxidants may affect endothelial NO synthase uncoupling by scavenging free radicals and limiting pathways that generate them. Different doses and durations, together with combination products whose individual contributions cannot be measured, complicate estimates for particular antioxidants. Although the subgroup analysis suggested possible benefit from pycnogenol and L-arginine, additional studies are needed to isolate and assess specific products.

Document sections:
  Heading: 10.3.1 Epidemiology/aetiology/pathophysiology
  Content: Epidemiological estimates largely come from small case series. Non-ischaemic priapism is significantly less common than ischaemic priapism and represents only 5% of cases. Blunt perineal or penile injury is the commonest cause. Laceration of a cavernous artery or branch creates an artery-to-lacunar-space fistula, increasing flow and causing a prolonged erection. Onset after trauma may be delayed up to two to three weeks, possibly because arterial spasm or ischaemic necrosis precedes fistula formation. Priapism typically emerges after nocturnal or sexually related erection raises cavernous arterial flow and pressure. Erections are usually incompletely rigid and painless because venous drainage persists and tissue does not become ischaemic. Acute spinal cord injury may also cause this form, presumably through loss of sympathetic input and predominance of parasympathetic-driven arterial flow. Other reported antecedents are internal urethrotomy, Nesbit procedure, circumcision, transrectal prostate biopsy, prostate-cancer brachytherapy, and shunting for ischaemic priapism that lacerates a cavernous artery and converts low to high flow. Occasional high-flow cases occur with SCD, but their mechanism is unclear. Penile metastatic malignancy is another rare cause.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 5.3.4. Radiotherapy
  Content: Chemotherapy is used to defer or avoid radiotherapy and thereby reduce potential cognitive, endocrine and vascular injury, dependent on site, and radiation-induced malignancy. Patients with panhypopituitarism already have impaired HPA-axis function. Children younger than 5 years appear at greatest risk of conformal-radiotherapy sequelae, including moya-moya, increasing deficits over time for supratentorial midline tumors and the greatest cognitive decline. Neurocognitive decline has also been observed in children with LGG younger than 7 years when tumor location increases dose or exposed volume in the left temporal lobe or hippocampus, even with proton therapy and regardless of NF1. Younger age therefore limits first-line radiotherapy choice; age <10 years has also been identified as a vasculopathy risk factor. Radiotherapy is consequently deferred particularly in young patients. Once the main treatment for incompletely resected pLGG, radiotherapy remains standard salvage therapy or a primary option in selected cases where nearby normal tissue can be optimally spared. High-precision methods, including proton therapy, may reduce long-term toxicity, but prospective comparisons with systemic therapy are needed. A radiotherapy dose between 50.4 and 54 Gy is recommended; a dose under 54 Gy could reduce vasculopathy risk. With multidisciplinary-board agreement, upfront radiotherapy may be considered if even minimal growth threatens substantial morbidity or radiotherapy-related neurocognitive risk is low. Craniospinal irradiation may be an option for disseminated disease after chemotherapy failure. Radiotherapy should be avoided as far as possible in children with NF1 because their risks of second malignancy and late vascular effects are higher. Older patients with unresectable diffuse astrocytoma or midbrain/thalamic tumors may have suboptimal long-term survival and might benefit from early radiotherapy.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 1.1 Initial assessment
  Content: Initial assessment may take place in any setting and is performed by a healthcare professional without specific training in managing LUTS in men. Offer a review of medical history, possible causes and comorbidities; examine current medicines, including herbal and over-the-counter products, for possible contributors. Offer an examination informed by urological symptoms and other conditions, including the abdomen, external genitalia and a digital rectal examination. Ask men with bothersome LUTS to complete a urinary frequency volume chart. Offer urine dipstick testing for blood, glucose, protein, leucocytes and nitrites. Provide information, advice and time to decide about prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing if symptoms suggest bladder outlet obstruction due to benign prostate enlargement (BPE), the prostate feels abnormal on digital rectal examination, or the man is concerned about prostate cancer. Manage suspected prostate cancer according to the NICE guidelines on prostate cancer and suspected cancer. Offer serum creatinine testing with estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] calculation only when renal impairment is suspected; examples include a palpable bladder, nocturnal enuresis, recurrent urinary tract infections or previous renal stones. Do not routinely offer cystoscopy or upper urinary tract imaging for uncomplicated LUTS at this stage, or routinely measure flow rate or post-void residual volume. For symptoms that are neither bothersome nor complicated, provide reassurance, information and lifestyle advice, such as advice about fluid intake, and offer review if symptoms change. Offer specialist referral when bothersome LUTS have not responded to conservative or drug treatment. Refer for specialist assessment when LUTS are complicated by recurrent or persistent urinary tract infection, retention, renal impairment suspected to arise from lower urinary tract dysfunction, or suspected urological cancer. Before any LUTS treatment, offer assessment of baseline symptoms with a validated score, such as IPSS, so subsequent changes can be assessed. These recommendations are marked [2010].

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_03
  Name: Carcinoma in situ
  Synonyms:
    - CIS
    - Tis
  Description: An intra-epithelial, HG, non-invasive UC that can occur in the bladder, UUT, prostatic ducts or prostatic urethra. It cannot be cured by endoscopic treatment alone.
  Epidemiology: Without treatment, approximately 54% of patients with CIS progress to muscle-invasive disease. Approximately 10 to 20% of complete responders to intravesical treatment eventually progress, compared with 66% of nonresponders.
  Clinical presentation: Irritative voiding symptoms can prompt suspicion. At cystoscopy, CIS can resemble a reddish, velvet-like inflammatory area or be invisible.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Primary
      Distinguishing features: Isolated CIS without earlier CIS and without previous or simultaneous papillary tumours.
    - Name: Secondary
      Distinguishing features: CIS found during surveillance after a previous non-CIS tumour.
    - Name: Concurrent
      Distinguishing features: CIS occurring together with another bladder urothelial tumour.
    - Name: CIS in the epithelial lining of the prostatic urethra
      Distinguishing features: Epithelial involvement must be distinguished from prostatic duct involvement and invasion of prostatic stroma.
    - Name: CIS in the prostatic ducts
      Distinguishing features: The document describes limited treatment evidence from small BCG-treated series.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Cystoscopy and urinary cytology
      Purpose: Raise suspicion of CIS.
      When indicated: Initial assessment or surveillance, including evaluation of positive urine cytology.
      Interpretation: Cystoscopy can miss CIS or mistake it for inflammation; cytology alone does not establish the diagnosis.
    - Test: Multiple bladder biopsies
      Purpose: Confirm CIS histologically.
      When indicated: Suspicious mucosa or positive cytology with normal-looking mucosa.
      Interpretation: Mapping samples include the trigone, dome, and right, left, anterior and posterior bladder walls.
    - Test: PDD-guided biopsies
      Purpose: Target suspicious mucosa for histological assessment.
      When indicated: Where equipment is available, particularly with positive cytology and no visible lesion.
      Interpretation: PDD improves detection, particularly of CIS, but cannot rule out prostatic involvement.
    - Test: Prostatic urethral biopsy
      Purpose: Identify prostatic urethral or duct involvement.
      When indicated: Positive cytology without a visible bladder tumour, suspected bladder CIS or other specified clinical indications.
    - Test: CT urography
      Purpose: Investigate UUT involvement.
      When indicated: Positive cytology without a visible bladder tumour or indicated surveillance for extravesical recurrence.
      Interpretation: CT urography, IVU, US and MRI cannot establish CIS without histology.
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: HG
      Expected result: HG
      Clinical significance: CIS is defined as a high-grade intra-epithelial tumour.
  Staging:
    System: 2017 Tumour, Node, Metastasis Classification (TNM)
    Definitions:
      - Stage: Tis
        Description: Flat carcinoma in situ.
      - Stage: T4a
        Description: In bladder tumours, invasion of the prostatic stroma is classified separately from epithelial or ductal CIS.
    Additional rules: CIS of the epithelial lining or ducts of the prostatic urethra must be distinguished from invasion of prostatic stroma.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Cystoscopy is required three months after TURB. Subsequent surveillance reflects the patient's risk group; conservatively treated high- and very high-risk patients undergo cystoscopy and cytology every 3 months for 2 years, every 6 months until 5 years, then annually for life.
    Recommended tests:
      - Cystoscopy
      - Urinary cytology
      - Upper tract imaging when indicated
      - Prostatic urethral assessment when indicated
    Long term effects:
      - Muscle-invasive progression
      - Bladder recurrence
      - UUT or prostatic urethral involvement
    Survivorship notes: Response to intravesical BCG or chemotherapy is an important prognostic factor for subsequent progression and bladder cancer death.
